question: Will Manitoba’s 2025/26 Second Quarter fiscal update forecast a summary deficit of at least $850 million?
background:
Status quo (as of Sept 30, 2025): Manitoba’s 2025/26 First Quarter Report (September 2025) forecasts a net loss (summary deficit) of $890 million for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026, and notes wildfire-related emergency expenditures with $179 million expended to date. The report also states the province expects to report a recovery from the Government of Canada under the Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements (DFAA) in the second or third quarter, which would offset some wildfire costs. DFAA is a federal program administered by Public Safety Canada that cost-shares eligible provincial/territorial disaster expenses; provinces may request assistance within six months of the end of an eligible disaster, and the program supports response, relief, recovery, and risk-reduction activities. Manitoba publishes quarterly fiscal updates on its official Fiscal Updates page; past naming conventions include “2024/25 Second Quarter Report (December 2024),” implying the 2025/26 Second Quarter Report is expected to be posted to the same page in December 2025. In Manitoba’s budgeting and reporting, the “Summary Budget” consolidates the government reporting entity (including core government, government business enterprises such as Manitoba Hydro and Manitoba Public Insurance, and other entities like health authorities and school divisions) in accordance with Public Sector Accounting Board (PSAB) standards; fiscal-year presentations are for the “Fiscal Year Ending March 31” (i.e., April 1–March 31). The key bottom-line label used in summary statements is Operating Surplus (Deficit), which corresponds to net income (loss) at the summary level.

Why this threshold and why this resolves in 2025: Q1’s forecast is a net loss of $890 million; setting the threshold at $850 million makes the outcome plausibly move either direction in Q2, given potential additional emergency expenditures versus anticipated DFAA recoveries, while relying on a clear, timely source-of-truth (the officially published Q2 report) before year-end.
resolution_criteria:
What resolves: This question resolves to Yes if, in Manitoba’s official 2025/26 Second Quarter Report (the “Second Quarter fiscal update”) published on the Province of Manitoba Fiscal Updates page, the forecast Operating Surplus (Deficit) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026 (i.e., 2025/26) indicates a summary deficit of at least CAD 850,000,000; otherwise No.

Definitions (with sources):
- “Second Quarter fiscal update” means the Province of Manitoba’s “2025/26 Second Quarter Report (December 2025)” PDF as posted to the official Fiscal Updates page (https://www.manitoba.ca/government/finances/fiscalupdates.html). If the naming differs slightly, it is the Second Quarter Report for fiscal year 2025/26 posted on that page.
- “Summary deficit” means the forecasted Operating Surplus (Deficit) for the consolidated Manitoba government reporting entity (Summary Budget), prepared under PSAB standards, for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026. In Manitoba reports, this figure is presented as Operating Surplus (Deficit) and corresponds to net income (loss) at the summary level.
- “At least $850 million” means the forecasted Operating Surplus (Deficit) is less than or equal to -850,000,000 (i.e., a net loss of ≥ 850,000,000). All amounts are nominal Canadian dollars as reported in the document.

How to read the number: Use the single authoritative 2025/26 forecast Operating Surplus (Deficit) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026 reported in the Q2 PDF (typically found in the fiscal summary/introductory table and/or narrative). If both a table and a narrative state the figure and they conflict, the value in the main fiscal summary table (often labeled “Operating Surplus (Deficit)”) takes precedence. If the Q2 PDF provides figures only in millions, use the stated integer; if it provides more precision, compare the exact number. Parentheses indicate a deficit (negative value).

Primary resolution source: The Province of Manitoba Fiscal Updates page (https://www.manitoba.ca/government/finances/fiscalupdates.html) and the linked 2025/26 Second Quarter Report PDF posted there.

Fallbacks and edge cases:
- If the 2025/26 Second Quarter Report is not published by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, resolve using the latest official Manitoba fiscal update for 2025/26 published on or before that time (e.g., the 2025/26 First Quarter Report), applying the same definition of the forecast Operating Surplus (Deficit). For context, the 2025/26 First Quarter Report forecasted a net loss of $890 million and noted wildfire costs and expected DFAA recoveries, but those figures are background only; the resolution will use the most recent official fiscal update available by the deadline.
- If multiple Q2 versions/revisions are posted before the deadline, use the latest version available on the Fiscal Updates page as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
- If the Fiscal Updates page is temporarily inaccessible but the Q2 PDF is accessible at its direct government URL, the PDF itself suffices. If neither is accessible at the deadline, postpone resolution until the site resumes within a reasonable period and then apply the criteria as of the deadline snapshot; do not use third-party summaries unless explicitly posted by the Manitoba government.

Temporal scope: The eligible document for primary resolution must be published between 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. The question resolves no later than 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Background sources used to set context and definitions: Manitoba 2025/26 First Quarter Report (deficit forecast $890M; wildfire costs $179M; expected DFAA recoveries in Q2 or Q3) ; Public Safety Canada description of DFAA (program definition and timing) ; Manitoba Fiscal Updates page (official hosting and naming conventions) ; Manitoba Budget 2025 (Summary Budget scope, PSAB basis, fiscal year end, and labeling of Operating Surplus/Deficit).

question: At its November 24–25, 2025 MPC meeting, will the Central Bank of Nigeria announce a Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) strictly below 27.00%?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:

- Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN): Nigeria’s monetary authority responsible for formulating and implementing monetary policy. See https://www.cbn.gov.ng and general overview https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Nigeria.
- Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): The CBN’s committee that meets to set policy rates and other monetary parameters. See general description https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy_committee and CBN communiqués (official records of decisions).
- Monetary Policy Rate (MPR): Defined by the CBN as “the anchor rate that the CBN uses to implement or signal the stance of monetary policy,” and “the policy rate that provides an indication of the Bank’s stance regarding current monetary conditions as well as its preferred path of action”.

Status quo and recent decisions:
- At the 302nd MPC meeting held on September 22–23, 2025, the MPC reduced the MPR by 50 basis points to 27.00%. Earlier in 2025, the MPC retained the MPR at 27.50% at meetings held on May 19–20 (No. 300) and July 21–22 (No. 301).
- The September 2025 MPC communiqué cites “sustained disinflation” and notes “increased momentum of disinflation in August 2025, being the highest in the past five months,” as part of the reasoning for the rate cut.
- The next MPC meeting is scheduled for November 24–25, 2025 (Meeting No. 303), per the CBN MPC calendar and reiterated in the September communiqué.

Definitions for clarity:
- “Announce”/“announced MPR” means the MPR figure stated in the official post-meeting records: (a) the CBN’s Monetary Policy Decisions page for the relevant meeting, and/or (b) the official MPC communiqué PDF for the meeting. These are recurring, authoritative publications by the CBN.
- “Strictly below 27.00%” means any value less than 27.00, e.g., 26.75% or 26.50%, and excludes 27.00% itself. “Percent (%)” is the unit indicating parts per hundred; “basis point (bps)” is one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%), see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point.
- Time zone: All resolution timing references use Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

Why this is forecastable with non-trivial uncertainty:
- As of late September 2025, the MPR stands at 27.00% following a modest cut. The MPC’s rationale highlights disinflation momentum, yet future inflation, growth, FX conditions, and policy priorities could argue for holding or further easing—making another sub-27% MPR plausible but not assured.

Primary sources for resolution and context:
- CBN Monetary Policy Decisions page (meeting-by-meeting summaries).
- September 2025 MPC Communiqué (No. 159).
- MPC calendar confirming November 24–25, 2025 meeting (No. 303).
resolution_criteria:
Question: At its November 24–25, 2025 MPC meeting, will the Central Bank of Nigeria announce a Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) strictly below 27.00%?

Event window and time zone:
- Eligible events and publications for resolution must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What counts:
- Resolve based on the MPR stated in official CBN post-meeting publications for the November 24–25, 2025 MPC meeting: (a) the CBN Monetary Policy Decisions page entry for that meeting, and/or (b) the official MPC communiqué PDF for that meeting.
- Answer Yes if the announced MPR is strictly less than 27.00%; otherwise answer No.

Source hierarchy and edge cases:
- Primary resolution sources: the CBN Monetary Policy Decisions page and the official MPC communiqué for the November 24–25, 2025 meeting. Use either if both clearly report the same figure.
- If both sources exist but conflict, use the figure reported in the official MPC communiqué PDF for the November 24–25, 2025 meeting (as it is the formal record of the Committee’s decisions).
- If the November MPC meeting is postponed but an official MPC decision on the MPR is published by the CBN in November or December 2025 (via the Decisions page and/or an MPC communiqué), resolve using that published MPR for the rescheduled meeting.
- If no official MPR decision related to the November meeting is published by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC on either the Monetary Policy Decisions page or via an MPC communiqué, resolve No.

Clarifications:
- Only the MPR outcome is relevant; changes to other parameters (e.g., CRR, liquidity ratio, standing facilities corridor) do not affect resolution.
- “Announced MPR” refers to the rate set at the conclusion of the relevant MPC meeting and communicated in the official CBN publications cited above—these are recurrent, authoritative sources for MPC outcomes.
- Meeting scheduling context: The CBN MPC calendar lists the November 24–25, 2025 meeting as Meeting No. 303; this establishes the intended meeting and timing.

Verification steps (for resolver):
1) Navigate to the CBN Monetary Policy Decisions page and find the entry for the November 24–25, 2025 meeting; record the MPR.
2) Open the official MPC communiqué for that meeting and confirm the MPR stated therein.
3) Apply the threshold: if MPR < 27.00%, resolve Yes; else No.

Notes and references:
- Definition of MPR (anchor rate used to signal stance of monetary policy) is per CBN educational material.
- September 2025 decision and reasoning (including sustained disinflation and noted momentum in August 2025) are per the MPC communiqué.
- 2025 meeting chronology and prior decisions (May/July hold at 27.50%; September cut to 27.00%) and the Decisions page structure are per the CBN Monetary Policy Decisions page.
- November 2025 meeting scheduling is per the CBN MPC calendar and reiterated in the September communiqué.

question: EU: At least two additional Iran-related sanctions acts adding listings between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (OJ L)
background: Status quo as of 2025-09-30: On 29 September 2025, following the UN “snapback” of Iran sanctions, the Council of the EU reimposed EU nuclear-related restrictive measures that had been lifted under the JCPOA. The Council publicized a package of legal acts on that date, including amendments and implementing measures tied to the Iran sanctions frameworks. For example: (a) Council Decision (CFSP) 2025/1978 amended Decision 2010/413/CFSP concerning restrictive measures against Iran, in the context of reimposing nuclear-related measures after UN sanctions returned ; (b) Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1975 amended Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 concerning restrictive measures against Iran ; (c) Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1980 implemented Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 ; and (d) Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1982 implemented Iran-related listings by adding persons/entities to the relevant annex(es). Beyond the nuclear-related framework (Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Regulation 267/2012), the EU maintains other Iran-related regimes where listings are regularly updated via Council acts, including: the human-rights regime under Regulation (EU) No 359/2011 (e.g., Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/689 of 4 April 2025 implements that regime) , and the regime addressing Iran’s military support to Russia’s war and to armed groups in the Middle East and the Red Sea region under Regulation (EU) 2023/1529 (e.g., Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1548). The Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU) is the EU’s official gazette that publishes binding EU legislation in its L (Legislation) series, which is the primary public record used to verify publication of Council Decisions and Regulations. Under EU law, a Regulation is a binding legal act of general application directly applicable in Member States, and a Decision is binding in its entirety (which may be of general application or have specific addressees). This question focuses on whether, after 15 October 2025, the Council will publish at least two additional Iran-related sanctions legal acts that add at least one new listed person or entity to the relevant annexes of the specified frameworks, over and above the 29 September 2025 package.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will there be at least two distinct Council legal acts (Council Decisions (CFSP), Council Regulations, Council Implementing Decisions (CFSP), or Council Implementing Regulations) published in the Official Journal L series that add at least one named person or entity to an EU Iran-related sanctions list between 00:00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025 (inclusive)?

Definitions (authoritative sources in brackets):
- Official Journal L series: The Legislation series of the Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU), the EU’s official gazette of binding acts.
- Council Regulation and Council Decision: EU legal acts as defined by Article 288 TFEU; a Regulation has general application and is binding in its entirety and directly applicable; a Decision is binding in its entirety and may be of general application or addressed to specific persons.
- Iran-related sanctions frameworks that count for this question: Only Council acts that implement or amend the annexed lists of listed persons/entities under any of the following instruments count: (1) Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (nuclear-related restrictive measures) ; (2) Regulation (EU) No 359/2011 (restrictive measures directed against certain persons, entities and bodies in view of the situation in Iran) ; (3) Regulation (EU) 2023/1529 (restrictive measures in view of Iran’s military support to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and to armed groups and entities in the Middle East and the Red Sea region). CFSP Decisions and Implementing Decisions accompanying these frameworks also count if they add listings.
- Add (a “new listing”): An act “adds” if, in its operative provisions and annex(es), it introduces at least one new named natural or legal person, entity or body to a relevant annex listing persons/entities subject to restrictive measures under one of the frameworks above, where that entry was not present immediately prior to the act’s publication. Acts that solely correct clerical errors, update identifying details, extend designation periods without adding new entries, or only delete/delist do not count.
- Distinct acts: Separate legal acts with unique OJ citations/numbers (e.g., 2025/xxxx). A Decision and an Implementing Regulation published on the same day are counted separately if both add at least one new listing. Corrigenda, consolidated versions, and non-L-series publications do not count.
- Publication date for eligibility: The publication date shown on the act’s OJEU L-series entry must fall within 2025-10-15 to 2025-12-31 (inclusive), measured in UTC. Adoption dates are irrelevant; only OJ L publication dates determine eligibility.

Inclusions and exclusions:
- Count each qualifying act once, even if it adds multiple names or adds entries across multiple annexes.
- If an act both delists and adds, it counts as long as it adds at least one new entry.
- Acts published on 29 September 2025 or earlier do not count (they are baseline context).

Resolution procedure (source of truth):
- Primary: Verify on EUR-Lex that at least two qualifying acts were published in the OJEU L series during the eligibility window. Use the OJ L daily/browse views or the individual act pages to confirm publication dates and whether the annexes add at least one person/entity.
- Secondary (if needed): Council press releases can be used for supplementary confirmation that an act adds listings (but OJEU entries control in case of conflict).

Outcome:
- YES if two or more qualifying acts are found.
- NO otherwise.

This question resolves as soon as it is logically determined (e.g., upon the second qualifying act’s publication in the window, or at latest on 2025-12-31).

question: Will Russia enact, extend, or broaden any nationwide legal ban on exports of motor gasoline or diesel fuel between 00:00 UTC Oct 15 and 23:59 UTC Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: Russia has extended a nationwide ban on motor gasoline exports until Dec 31, 2025, and imposed a partial ban on diesel exports (applying to resellers/traders, not direct producers), according to government statements reported by Reuters and TASS. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed on Oct 1 that the government had extended gasoline export restrictions until year-end and introduced a diesel export ban for traders, while stating the domestic supply situation was being addressed and export markets could reopen if supply exceeds demand. These measures followed sustained Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian energy infrastructure which reduced refining by almost a fifth on certain days and cut exports from key ports , including incidents at the Afipsky refinery in late August and again on Sept 26, 2025.

Definitions and scope:
- Motor gasoline (petrol): a petroleum-derived fuel used in spark-ignition engines, formulated as a motor fuel.
- Diesel fuel (also termed diesel oil or gas oil): a liquid fuel for compression-ignition (diesel) engines; the common type is a petroleum distillate; “gas oil” is sometimes used interchangeably with diesel fuel.
- Nationwide legal ban on exports: a prohibition enacted via a federal government legal act (e.g., decree/resolution) that suspends or forbids the export of the specified fuel types outside the Russian Federation, applicable across the country. TASS reporting on the Sept 30, 2025 Cabinet decree explicitly described a ban on motor gasoline exports “outside the country” until Dec 31, 2025, and a separate decree banning exports of diesel, marine fuel oil, and other gasoils purchased on exchange, with exemptions for direct producers.
- Federal government legal act: an official normative legal act (e.g., “postanovlenie” or “rasporyazhenie”) published on Russia’s Official Internet Portal of Legal Information (pravo.gov.ru), which is the official source for the text of legal acts.
- Producers vs resellers/traders: consistent with Russian government and state media descriptions, “producers” are entities that manufacture the fuel; “resellers/traders” are entities that export fuel they did not produce themselves (e.g., purchased via exchanges). Sept 30 reporting distinguishes bans by exporter category.

Why this question is plausible and uncertain: While current bans run through end-2025, authorities have signaled that further restrictions are possible if needed, and the fuel market remains sensitive to refinery outages and security incidents, creating genuine uncertainty about whether Moscow will enact new measures or extend/broaden existing ones during Oct–Dec 2025.

Primary resolution sources: Official publications on the Russian government’s legal portal (http://pravo.gov.ru). If needed for verification, contemporaneous reporting by credible outlets such as Reuters and TASS will be used.
resolution_criteria:
This resolves to Yes if, between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025, at least one new nationwide legal ban or a formal extension/expansion of an existing ban on exports of motor gasoline or diesel fuel is enacted by the Russian federal government and published on its official legal portal (pravo.gov.ru) , or is clearly confirmed by credible contemporaneous reporting such as Reuters or TASS. Otherwise, the resolution is No.

Operational definitions and tests:
- Eligible action: A federal government legal act (e.g., decree/resolution) that (a) newly imposes an export ban on motor gasoline or diesel fuel (as defined) that was not in force for the affected exporter category or product as of 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025; or (b) formally extends the expiration date of any such export ban beyond its prior end date; or (c) broadens the scope of an existing export ban by adding fuel products within the definitions above or expanding covered exporter categories (e.g., extending a diesel ban from resellers/traders to include producers). TASS and Reuters reporting on Sept 30, 2025 exemplify the types of acts and distinctions by exporter category.
- In-scope fuels: Motor gasoline (petrol)  and diesel fuel/gas oil. If a legal act references “gas oil” or “diesel fuel,” it counts under diesel; if it references “motor gasoline,” it counts under gasoline. Acts exclusively covering other petroleum products (e.g., crude oil) do not count.
- Nationwide: The measure must be federal and applicable across the Russian Federation; regional or local restrictions do not count.
- Evidence required: A URL to the promulgated act on pravo.gov.ru  (or an official government site hosting the text) is sufficient. If the legal text is not immediately available, two credible reports from Reuters and/or TASS confirming the act’s enactment and scope are acceptable.
- Time standard: Eligibility is based on the date-time of promulgation/publication of the act (or the date-time of the government’s official notice) in UTC. Acts promulgated before 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025, or after 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025, do not count.
- Non-qualifying actions: Non-binding statements, policy discussions, price controls, rationing, internal distribution measures, or administrative adjustments that do not constitute a formal export ban on the specified fuels are out of scope.

Resolution notes: The resolver will search pravo.gov.ru for relevant decrees during the specified window , and cross-check with Reuters/TASS coverage if necessary. Context about current bans and the refinery situation is provided for forecasters’ background.

question: Will Colors place in the top 3 of BARC India’s weekly “Top Channels” (All-India) ranking in any eligible week of November–December 2025?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Public source of truth: BARC India’s Data Insights page publishes a weekly “Top Channels” table with a RANK column and the metric “WEEKLY AMA’000 {AVG.}” for television channels, providing a clear, regularly updated leaderboard of channel viewership.
- Metric definition: AMA ’000 (Average Minute Audience) is defined by BARC as the number of individuals in thousands (000s) of a target audience who viewed a TV channel/event, averaged across minutes. BARC’s methodology page further describes AMA as total viewing minutes for the target group divided by the total minutes for the event/daypart (and explains Rating% as the relative equivalent of AMA).
- Universe and “All-India, 2+”: BARC’s standard national universe covers individuals aged 2+ in television households across India (with certain unreachable geographies excluded for panel purposes), commonly referred to as “All India, 2+”. In public “Top Channels” tables, the default presentation is a national ranking; when labeled, it is often “All India, 2+”.
- BARC week definition and release cadence: BARC defines a measurement week as Saturday to Friday, with public weekly data releases occurring on Thursdays.
- Channel identity: “Colors” (Colors TV) is a Hindi general entertainment television channel in India; it may be labeled “Colors” or “Colors TV” in public listings.
- Recent landscape example: A recent snapshot of BARC’s public “Top Channels” listing shows STAR Maa, STAR Utsav, and Sun TV among the leaders by WEEKLY AMA’000 {AVG.}; in that snapshot, “Colors” was not listed among the top 10, underscoring that a top-3 placement is plausible but not guaranteed.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial:
- Colors has historically been competitive among national entertainment channels, but its top-3 placement in any given week varies with programming slates and seasonal effects. The Nov–Dec window coincides with high-profile programming periods for multiple networks, contributing to uncertainty.
- The question resolves on a single public dataset (BARC’s weekly table) and focuses on a single, precisely measurable outcome (a top-3 rank in any eligible week), allowing research-driven forecasts while avoiding trivial lookups at the time of asking.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible weeks are BARC-defined weeks (Saturday–Friday) for which at least one day falls between 2025-11-01 00:00:00 IST and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 IST (India Standard Time; UTC+05:30).
- Only weeks whose “Top Channels” table is publicly available on BARC’s website on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 IST will be considered for resolution.

Question restated precisely:
- Resolve YES if, for any eligible week, BARC India’s publicly available “Top Channels” weekly table (as published on https://www.barcindia.co.in/data-insights) shows the channel “Colors”/“Colors TV” ranked 1, 2, or 3 by “WEEKLY AMA’000 {AVG.}” in the national (“All-India”) listing. Resolve NO otherwise.

Definitions and clarifications:
- “Top Channels” table: The weekly leaderboard on BARC India’s Data Insights page that lists channels with columns including RANK and WEEKLY AMA’000 {AVG.}.
- Metric used for ranking: WEEKLY AMA’000 {AVG.}, where AMA ’000 is defined as the number of individuals in thousands of a target audience who viewed the channel, averaged across minutes.
- “All-India” scope: The national BARC universe sometimes labeled “All India, 2+,” meaning individuals aged 2+ in TV households across India (with specific excluded geographies per BARC’s panel definition). If the public table explicitly offers multiple scopes, use the one labeled “All India, 2+.” If the public table presents a single national list without explicit scope labeling, use that default national list.
- Channel identity to count as “Colors”: The Hindi general entertainment channel “Colors TV” (stylized “Colors”). Entries explicitly labeled as regional variants (e.g., “Colors Kannada,” “Colors Marathi,” “Colors Bangla,” etc.) do not count toward this question. If the listing shows “Colors” or “Colors TV” without a regional qualifier, it is considered the correct channel.
- Rank threshold: “Top 3” means appearing at positions 1, 2, or 3 in the RANK column for the relevant weekly table.

Primary resolution source and procedure:
- Source: BARC India’s official Data Insights page that lists the weekly “Top Channels” table: https://www.barcindia.co.in/data-insights. The resolver will check all eligible weeks with a table publicly available on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 IST and determine whether “Colors”/“Colors TV” appears at ranks 1–3 in any of those weeks.
- If multiple versions of the same week are visible (e.g., due to later corrections), use the version publicly accessible on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 IST.
- Outcome: YES if at least one eligible week meets the criterion; NO if none do.

Start date for events: 2025-11-01 00:00:00 IST.
End of observation and resolution deadline: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 IST.

question: Will global oil inventory builds average more than 2.0 million barrels per day during July 1–December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
This question operationalizes “global oil inventory builds” using the EIA’s standard global balance metric: the implied change in global petroleum and other liquids stocks, labeled “Total stock change” in the EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) World petroleum and other liquids balance. Positive values indicate inventory builds; negative values indicate draws. For definitional clarity:
- Petroleum and other liquids: As used by EIA in STEO/global balances (includes crude oil and lease condensate, natural gas plant liquids, biofuels, refinery/blender net production, and other hydrocarbon liquids). See EIA overview: https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/oil-and-petroleum-products/
- Primary source and access: EIA STEO landing and data pages, which publish/host the “World petroleum and other liquids balance” (PDF and data browser): https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/
- Timeframe: Second half of 2025 (2H25) is precisely 2025-07-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
Context from the user-supplied artifact: Major agencies in 2025 have highlighted potential oversupply and implied global inventory builds averaging above ~2 mb/d in 2H25; this question asks whether that outcome is borne out in the official EIA balance once July–December 2025 values are published by year-end 2025. No external documents beyond the EIA pages linked above are required to resolve the question.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and units:
- Window: 2025-07-01 00:00:00 UTC to 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Series: EIA STEO “World petroleum and other liquids balance” → “Total stock change” (million barrels per day, mb/d). Positive values are treated as builds; negative values as draws.
Primary source and versioning:
- Use the EIA STEO December 2025 issue/data as published on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Acceptable locations: (a) the STEO PDF (steo_full.pdf) table titled “World petroleum and other liquids balance,” or (b) the STEO data browser (https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/data.php) for the same series. Ignore any revisions released after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
Computation method:
- Prefer monthly values for July–December 2025. Compute the day-weighted average build across the six months as:
  Average = [Σ over m∈{Jul–Dec 2025} (StockChange_m × Days_m)] / 184
  with Days per month: Jul 31; Aug 31; Sep 30; Oct 31; Nov 30; Dec 31 (total 184 days).
- If one or more monthly values for Jul–Dec 2025 are not published in the December 2025 STEO materials, use quarterly values instead: 3Q25 and 4Q25 “Total stock change,” day-weighted equally (92 days each). If both monthly and quarterly are present, monthly prevails.
- Rounding: Do not round intermediate values. Round the final computed average to three decimals solely for comparison to the threshold.
Resolution rule:
- YES if the computed average > 2.000 mb/d; NO otherwise (i.e., if ≤ 2.000 mb/d).
Exclusions and clarifications:
- Only the EIA STEO “Total stock change” series is used; IEA or other agencies are not used for resolution.
- “Global oil inventory builds” in this question is precisely the EIA STEO “Total stock change” series. No adjustments are made for SPR/emergency stock policies beyond what is embedded in the EIA balance.
- If, exceptionally, the December 2025 STEO PDF lacks the table but the data browser provides the series, the data browser governs. If both are absent in December 2025, use the latest STEO issue/data published on or before 2025-12-31 UTC that contains the necessary values.

question: Will total affordable housing completions in England be higher in 2024–25 than in 2023–24?
background: Context as of 2025-09-30: The Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities (DLUHC) publishes an annual “Affordable housing supply in England” statistical bulletin and accompanying live tables. These statistics report the gross annual supply of affordable homes (new build plus acquisitions for affordable use), and do not subtract losses such as demolitions or sales; the publication is recurring and typically released in November–December, with revisions reflected in the live tables. In the most recent bulletin, DLUHC reported that 62,289 affordable homes were delivered (completions) in England in the 2023–24 financial year; figures are presented by financial year running from 1 April to 31 March. DLUHC uses “delivered” and “completions” interchangeably for the final provision of affordable homes and includes both new builds and acquisitions; coverage aggregates delivery reported by Homes England (England outside London) and the Greater London Authority (London), along with other routes such as Section 106 (nil grant). As a pipeline indicator, Homes England reported 28,370 affordable housing completions through programmes it manages in 2024–25 (mostly outside London, with specific programme exceptions). Definitions and scope: Affordable housing in these statistics comprises housing (units or bed spaces) for rent or sale to specified eligible households whose needs are not met by the market, across tenures such as social rent, affordable rent, and shared ownership; the figures capture gross additions in England. Publication cadence: The 2023–24 bulletin was published on 21 November 2024, and the next 2024–25 bulletin is pre-announced on GOV.UK; the collection page hosts the series, and the live tables always reflect the latest data and revisions.
resolution_criteria: This binary question resolves at or before 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC. Resolution will use DLUHC’s national headline total of affordable housing completions (“affordable homes delivered”) in England for 2024–25, compared to the published 2023–24 total of 62,289. Definitions and measurement follow DLUHC’s Affordable housing supply statistics: gross additional affordable homes in England (including both new builds and acquisitions for affordable use), with figures presented by financial year (1 April to 31 March). Primary source: the statistical bulletin “Affordable housing supply in England: 2024 to 2025” and/or its accompanying data tables on GOV.UK. If the 2024–25 bulletin is not yet published by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, use the latest value available in the “Live tables on affordable housing supply,” specifically the headline total for 2024–25 in Table 1000 (or its successor), which “always reflect the latest data and revisions”. Outcome determination: YES if the 2024–25 total is strictly greater than 62,289; NO if it is less than or equal to 62,289. Use the integer totals as published by DLUHC at the time of resolution. Notes: Coverage is England (including London via GLA data incorporated into the national totals); Homes England statistics are not used for resolution but are noted as background indicators. If DLUHC publishes a correction or revision before the resolution timestamp, use the latest figure available on the GOV.UK bulletin page or live tables as of the resolution deadline.

question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will OFAC issue, amend, or revoke at least one Venezuela-related general license?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers Venezuela-related sanctions and routinely uses general licenses (GLs) to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations (VSR), 31 CFR part 591. OFAC’s Venezuela program page lists and hosts Venezuela-related GLs and related guidance. A general license authorizes a particular type of transaction for a class of persons without the need to apply; a specific license is a written document issued to a particular person or entity in response to an application.

Recent 2025 activity (examples):
- GL 41B (Chevron JV wind-down) was issued on March 24, 2025 and, per the Federal Register notice, "Effective March 24, 2025, General License No. 41A, dated March 4, 2025, is replaced and superseded in its entirety by this General License No. 41B". OFAC’s Recent Actions page also records the March 24 issuance of GL 41B.
- GL 5S (PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond) was issued on June 20, 2025, authorizing certain transactions on or after December 20, 2025, and "replaced and superseded" GL 5R.
- GL 40D (offloading of liquefied petroleum gas in Venezuela) was issued on July 7, 2025; it authorized specified transactions through September 5, 2025, provided the LPG was loaded on a vessel on or before July 7, 2025, and it "replaced and superseded" GL 40C (dated July 8, 2024).

OFAC posts such actions (including issuances and amendments of GLs) to its official Recent Actions page with associated dates, and the page was last updated September 16, 2025. OFAC’s web general licenses are also formally published in the Federal Register, which records issuance dates and replacement/supersession relationships (e.g., GL 41B, GL 5S, GL 40D). These official sources together provide a clear, timely basis to verify whether any qualifying action occurs during the forecast window.

Why this question: OFAC has actively modified Venezuela sanctions instruments in 2025 (multiple GL issuances and amendments). Additional changes between mid-October and year-end are plausible but not guaranteed, creating non-trivial uncertainty suitable for forecasting.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome definitions and time window:
- Forecast window: From 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Resolve Yes if, during the forecast window, OFAC either issues, amends, or revokes at least one Venezuela-related general license (GL) as evidenced by at least one of the following official sources: (a) an entry on OFAC’s Recent Actions page, or (b) a publication in the Federal Register of a web general license pertaining to the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR part 591). Resolve No otherwise.

Term definitions and qualifying evidence:
- "Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) Recent Actions page": The official U.S. Treasury OFAC listing of recent actions, which posts GL issuances and amendments with dates.
- "Federal Register publication of a web general license": A notice in the Federal Register that publishes a GL previously made available on OFAC’s website, and which specifies the GL’s issuance date and any replacement/supersession relationships (e.g., GL 41B, GL 5S, GL 40D).
- "Venezuela-related general license": A general license that explicitly pertains to the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations (VSR), 31 CFR part 591, as indicated on the license itself or by its inclusion on OFAC’s Venezuela-Related Sanctions program page (e.g., GL 41B, GL 5S, GL 40D).
- "Issue": OFAC makes available a new Venezuela GL (by number/letter) and records the action with an issuance date on its Recent Actions page or the issuance date is recorded in a Federal Register notice publishing that web GL.
- "Amend": OFAC issues a Venezuela GL that explicitly states it "replaces and supersedes" a prior GL (e.g., GL 41B replacing GL 41A; GL 5S replacing GL 5R; GL 40D replacing GL 40C).
- "Revoke": OFAC explicitly states in an official posting (Recent Actions or Federal Register) that a Venezuela GL is "revoked". For resolution, the word "revoked" must appear in the official source describing the GL action during the forecast window; expirations without explicit revocation do not count.
- "General license" and "specific license": A general license authorizes a particular type of transaction for a class of persons without the need to apply; a specific license is a written document issued to a particular person or entity in response to a license application. This question concerns general licenses only; actions related solely to specific licenses do not count.

Resolution process:
1) At close of the forecast window, check OFAC’s Recent Actions page and the Federal Register for any qualifying Venezuela GL action dated within the window.
2) If at least one action meeting the above definitions is found, resolve Yes. If none are found, resolve No.

Notes and edge cases:
- If multiple qualifying actions occur, any single one suffices for Yes.
- The operative date for eligibility is the issuance date shown in OFAC’s Recent Actions entry or the issuance date specified in the Federal Register notice; Federal Register publication dates outside the window do not disqualify the action if the notice states an issuance date within the window.
- Actions limited to FAQs, guidance, executive orders, specific licenses, or designations that do not meet the GL criteria above do not count.

question: Will the IMF Executive Board complete the fifth review of Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF program between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (inclusive)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- Bangladesh is under IMF-supported arrangements approved by the IMF Executive Board on January 30, 2023: Extended Credit Facility (ECF) and Extended Fund Facility (EFF), alongside a Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) arrangement. The Board approval specified SDR amounts and a multi-year duration.
- The IMF Executive Board concluded Bangladesh’s second review under the ECF/EFF and RSF on June 24, 2024, using the standard phrasing “The IMF Executive Board concluded the second review …”.
- Most recently, the IMF Executive Board completed the combined third and fourth reviews of Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF/RSF on June 23, 2025. In that decision, the Board also approved an augmentation of access and a six-month extension to the ECF/EFF arrangements. The press release uses the canonical resolution language (“The IMF Executive Board concluded the combined third and fourth reviews …”) and provides the decision date. It also notes the augmentation and extension details.
- Before that June 23 Board decision, IMF staff and the Bangladesh authorities reached a staff-level agreement on May 14, 2025, explicitly noting that Board completion would be subject to Executive Board approval and certain prior actions (e.g., tax revenue measures and exchange-rate reform implementation). Staff-level agreements typically precede Board reviews but do not themselves complete a review.

Why this is forecastable now:
- The June 23, 2025 Board release did not specify the timing of the fifth review, leaving uncertainty about whether the fifth review will be completed by year-end 2025.
- The IMF’s standard language in press releases clearly indicates when a review has been “completed” or “concluded,” which is the operative event for resolution (see phrasing examples in 2024 and 2025 Bangladesh releases).

Definitions and references for forecasters:
- International Monetary Fund (IMF): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund
- IMF Executive Board: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund#Governance
- Extended Credit Facility (ECF): IMF factsheet (reference link): https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2023/Extended-Credit-Facility-ECF
- Extended Fund Facility (EFF): IMF factsheet (reference link): https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2023/Extended-Fund-Facility-EFF
- Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF): IMF factsheet (reference link): https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2023/Resilience-Sustainability-Facility-RSF
- “Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF program” in this question refers to the ECF and EFF arrangements approved by the IMF Executive Board on January 30, 2023. For background, see the 2023 Board approval press release.

Practical pointers for tracking:
- IMF Bangladesh newsroom entries and press releases will typically post the Board’s decision and the date (e.g., the June 23, 2025 and June 24, 2024 examples).
- IMF Country Reports/eLibrary entries released immediately after Board decisions also generally state the Board date and review completion. The June 2025 materials for the combined third and fourth reviews illustrate this pattern.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether the IMF Executive Board completes the fifth review of Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF arrangements during the period from 2025-10-15 00:00:00 through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 (inclusive), measured as calendar dates. Details below.

Eligible event window and time convention:
- Eligible completion dates are those that fall between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31, inclusive. Because the IMF typically reports a calendar date (without a timestamp) for Board decisions, dates are interpreted as the calendar date stated by the IMF in the relevant official document; no time-zone conversion is applied.

What counts as “completed the fifth review”:
- “Completed” or “concluded” means the IMF Executive Board has formally completed (i.e., concluded) the fifth review under Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF arrangements, as evidenced by IMF communications that use standard language such as “The IMF Executive Board concluded the fifth review under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) and Extended Fund Facility (EFF) arrangements for Bangladesh.” The June 24, 2024 and June 23, 2025 releases provide clear examples of the operative phrasing for completed reviews.
- The review numbering follows the ECF/EFF arrangement approved on January 30, 2023: after completion of the first, second, and combined third and fourth reviews, the next review is the fifth. The 2023 approval press release establishes the relevant program; subsequent press releases confirm completed reviews and their numbering.
- If the Executive Board completes the fifth review together with another review (e.g., a combined “fifth and sixth review”), this still counts as the fifth review having been completed, provided the Board communication indicates completion of a “fifth review” on an eligible date.
- The presence or absence of a simultaneous RSF review does not affect resolution; only completion of the ECF/EFF fifth review matters for this question.

Primary resolution sources (any one is sufficient):
1) An IMF press release on imf.org stating that the Executive Board completed (or concluded) the fifth review of Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF arrangements, including the Board decision date. The phrasing in Bangladesh’s 2024 and 2025 releases illustrates the exact language to look for.
2) An IMF Country Report/Executive Board document (e.g., Staff Report or Press Release annex) on imf.org or the IMF eLibrary that states the Board completed the fifth review and provides the Board decision date.

Fallback sources (only if no IMF primary source is available by the resolution date):
- Credible wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) reporting that the IMF Executive Board completed the fifth review on a specific date. The reporting must clearly attribute the event and date to the IMF decision; if later an IMF primary source becomes available and contradicts the report, the IMF primary source prevails.

Resolution logic:
- YES: If an eligible source shows the IMF Executive Board completed the fifth review on a date between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 inclusive.
- NO: Otherwise (including if the fifth review is completed before 2025-10-15, after 2025-12-31, or not completed at all by 2025-12-31).

Edge cases and clarifications:
- If the review is completed by “lapse-of-time” procedure, it still counts provided the IMF source states the review was completed on an eligible date.
- If only a press release publication date is visible but it clearly states the Board completed the fifth review “today” or “on [date]”, use the explicit Board date in the text; if no explicit Board date is in the text, use the press release date as the Board date for resolution.
- If no IMF primary document exists by 2025-12-31 but a credible wire report asserts completion on an eligible date, resolve based on that report; if an IMF primary source is published within 14 days thereafter and contradicts the report, update the resolution to follow the IMF primary source.

Key references for context and phrasing:
- 2025-06-23 Board decision completing combined third and fourth reviews; also notes augmentation and a six-month extension to the ECF/EFF arrangements.
- 2024-06-24 Board decision concluding the second review.
- 2023-01-30 Board approval of Bangladesh’s ECF/EFF and RSF arrangements.
- 2025-05-14 staff-level agreement (preceding Board action) clarifying that Board completion is subject to Executive Board approval and prior actions.

question: EU‑27 underground gas storage ≥93% full on 1 December 2025 (per AGSI)
background:
Context and policy: The European Union has extended and adjusted its gas storage rules. The binding 90% filling target is maintained, but member states are allowed to reach it at any point between 1 October and 1 December (replacing a hard 1 November deadline). In difficult market conditions, deviations of up to 10 percentage points are allowed, and the European Commission may, via delegated act, permit an additional 5 percentage points of flexibility for one filling season if unfavourable market conditions persist.

Definitions and data source: 
- EU‑27 refers to the 27 European Union member states after the UK left the EU. 
- Underground gas storage (UGS) facilities store natural gas in depleted gas reservoirs, aquifers, or salt caverns. Working gas is the portion of gas in storage that can be withdrawn for use; working gas capacity equals total capacity minus base (cushion) gas. A storage “filling level” or “fullness percentage” is commonly measured as working gas in stock divided by working gas capacity, expressed as a percent. 
- AGSI (Aggregated Gas Storage Inventory), provided by Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE), publishes daily inventory reporting for underground gas storages. AGSI covers 100% of the EU‑27 underground gas storage market and is widely used as a benchmark to monitor pan‑European filling levels.

Status quo (as of early Q4 2025): EU storage levels built from a low spring base. The European Commission notes that EU storage stood at 34% on 1 April 2025 at the end of the gas winter season. By 25 June 2025, EU storage reached about 56.6% (approximately 642 TWh). In late September 2025 (Week 38), Bruegel’s weekly tracker reported EU storage “currently at 82% of capacity”. These figures frame the run‑up to the early‑winter target window under the new flexibility rules.

Why this threshold/date: December 1, 2025 is the end of the new two‑month window for meeting the 90% target. Setting the bar at 93% tests whether inventories not only meet the target but remain substantially above it, which is uncertain given lower starting levels in spring 2025 and the added flexibility that could reduce pressure to over‑fill.

Primary resolution source: AGSI’s EU aggregate daily data, which reports EU‑level filling (fullness) as a percent on a calendar‑date basis.
resolution_criteria:
Yes-resolution: Resolve Yes if the AGSI platform’s EU (EU‑27) aggregate filling level (fullness percentage) for the calendar date 2025‑12‑01 is greater than or equal to 93.00%. Otherwise resolve No. 

Operationalization details:
- Metric: “Filling level (fullness percentage)” means the percentage of working gas in stock relative to total working gas capacity (i.e., stock ÷ working gas capacity × 100) as reported by AGSI for the EU aggregate.
- Geography: Use the EU aggregate as presented on AGSI, which corresponds to the EU‑27 (the 27 EU member states). Non‑EU countries (e.g., the UK, Ukraine) are not included.
- Date and time standard: Use the value associated with the calendar date 2025‑12‑01 as displayed on AGSI. To allow for routine data updates, the resolver should check the value no earlier than 2025‑12‑02 12:00 UTC. If AGSI revises the value for 2025‑12‑01 after that time, use the value displayed at 2025‑12‑03 12:00 UTC.
- Source of truth: AGSI (Aggregated Gas Storage Inventory) Transparency Platform’s EU‑level daily data. 
- Ties and rounding: Compare the published percentage to 93.00% to two decimal places; values of 93.00% or higher count as meeting the threshold.
- Contingency: If AGSI is temporarily inaccessible, delay resolution until it becomes accessible; do not substitute other sources unless AGSI is unavailable for at least 7 consecutive days after 2025‑12‑02 12:00 UTC. If that occurs, resolution may use an archived AGSI snapshot (e.g., web archive) captured after 2025‑12‑02 12:00 UTC showing the EU aggregate value for 2025‑12‑01. No other secondary datasets will be used.

question: EU BEV share: Will battery‑electric cars reach ≥17.5% market share in the EU in November 2025 (single month, not YTD)?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) publishes monthly “New passenger car registrations” statistics for the European Union (EU). According to ACEA’s press-release calendar, the release covering November 2025 is scheduled for Tuesday 23 December 2025, ensuring data availability within 2025. ACEA’s latest context indicates that by August 2025 year-to-date (YTD), battery‑electric vehicles (BEVs) accounted for 15.8% of EU new passenger car registrations, underscoring ongoing growth but leaving significant month-to-month uncertainty.

What forecasters should know:
- Source and timing: ACEA’s statistical press release for November 2025 will be the primary resolution source and is scheduled for 23 December 2025. December 2025 data is scheduled for 27 January 2026, which is why November is chosen to ensure resolution within 2025.
- Measurement: ACEA typically reports monthly registration counts by fuel type and may report shares YTD; the single-month BEV share for November may need to be computed from counts if not directly reported.
- Current status: As of August 2025 YTD, BEV market share is 15.8% in the EU. This provides a baseline but does not determine the single-month outcome for November.
- Why this threshold/month: November avoids the common issue that December data is published in late January, and a 17.5% single-month threshold is plausibly uncertain given the YTD context and typical intra-year volatility.

Useful references for definitions:
- Battery electric vehicle (BEV): Vehicles propelled exclusively by electric motors using energy stored in rechargeable batteries; excludes hybrids and plug‑in hybrids. See Battery electric vehicle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicle
- Market share (in this question): Percentage of new passenger car registrations that are BEVs in the defined geography and month.
- European Union (EU): Political and economic union of member states; for this question, use the EU aggregate as defined and reported by ACEA in the relevant press release. See European Union: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union
resolution_criteria:
This question concerns the single-month BEV market share for November 2025 in the European Union, as published by ACEA. The evaluation and resolution will be based on ACEA publications available as of 23:59 UTC on 31 December 2025.

Primary resolution rule:
- Resolve Yes if ACEA’s “New passenger car registrations” press release covering November 2025 reports the EU BEV market share for November 2025 (the single month, not year‑to‑date) as ≥17.5%.
- Resolve No otherwise.

If ACEA does not explicitly report the single‑month BEV market share for November 2025 but provides raw monthly counts by fuel type:
- Compute BEV share as: BEV registrations ÷ total EU new passenger car registrations for November 2025 (sum of all passenger‑car fuel‑type categories used by ACEA in that release) × 100.
- Then round the resulting percentage to one decimal place using standard round‑half‑up before comparing to the 17.5% threshold.

Definitions and scope:
- “Battery‑electric vehicle (BEV)” means vehicles propelled exclusively by one or more electric motors using energy stored in rechargeable battery packs; excludes hybrid‑electric and plug‑in‑hybrid electric vehicles. Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicle.
- “Market share” means the percentage of new EU passenger car registrations in November 2025 that are BEVs, equal to 100 × (BEV registrations ÷ total passenger car registrations) for the month.
- “European Union (EU)” means the EU aggregate as reported by ACEA in the relevant press release (e.g., “EU” or “EU27”); use ACEA’s EU‑only figure and do not substitute EU+EFTA+UK or other aggregates.
- “New passenger car registrations” is as defined and reported by ACEA in its monthly statistics; use the EU totals and BEV counts as published in the November 2025 release.
- Month covered: November 2025 refers to registrations counted by ACEA for the calendar month of November 2025.

Sources for resolution:
- ACEA Statistics press release calendar confirming publication date for the November 2025 release: https://www.acea.auto/press-release-calendar/.
- The November 2025 “New passenger car registrations” press release on ACEA’s website (pc‑registrations section). If multiple ACEA pages conflict, use the press release landing page or its downloadable PDF for November 2025.

Revision handling and edge cases:
- If ACEA revises the November 2025 figures prior to 23:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, use the latest ACEA version available by that time.
- If ACEA publishes both EU‑only and broader aggregates (EU+EFTA+UK), select the EU‑only figures.
- If the November 2025 ACEA press release is not published by 31 December 2025, this question will resolve based on the latest ACEA data products or press materials available on acea.auto by that time (e.g., the November 2025 registrations tables or release PDF in the pc‑registrations area). Calendar indicates publication on 23 December 2025.

Status‑quo references:
- BEV share context: “By August 2025 year‑to‑date (YTD)… The battery‑electric car market share for August 2025 YTD held at 15.8%…”.
- November 2025 publication timing: “New passenger car registrations in Europe… November 2025 — Tuesday 23 December 2025; December 2025 — Tuesday 27 January 2026”.

question: Will the EU adopt any legally binding restriction on exports of ferrous waste and scrap (CN heading 7204) to destinations other than the United States between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of Oct 1, 2025:
- On July 23, 2025, the European Commission announced it had activated the customs surveillance system to monitor imports and exports of metal waste and scrap, covering ferrous waste and scrap (including steel), aluminium, and copper. The stated rationale was to ensure sufficient access to scrap for EU metals industries amid declining availability and “scrap leakage” to third countries, and to assess whether further action is necessary by the end of Q3 2025.
- Reporting on July 24, 2025 noted the Commission “has started monitoring imports and exports of scrap metal,” including steel, aluminium and copper, citing shortages, smelter shutdown risks, and export flows to Asia and Turkey; the article indicated the Commission would decide on any action by the end of September based on the data.
- Under the EU’s common rules for exports, exports are generally free and not subject to quantitative restrictions, except where restrictions are introduced in conformity with Regulation (EU) 2015/479. That regulation provides legal bases for protective measures, including making exports subject to authorisation and introducing quantitative restrictions, to prevent or remedy critical shortages of essential products, with measures adopted via implementing acts following the comitology procedures.
- Separately, on July 24, 2025, the Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1564 on commercial rebalancing measures in response to U.S. actions. Among other measures, it prohibits, from Sept 7, 2025, the direct or indirect export to the United States of certain products originating in the Union listed in an annex that includes CN code 7204 (ferrous waste and scrap) and CN code 7602 (aluminium waste and scrap). Because this is a U.S.-specific rebalancing measure, the forecasting question below explicitly excludes the United States as a destination to maintain non-trivial uncertainty.

Why this could be high-entropy:
- Policymakers signaled the potential for “further action” after Q3 2025, yet any move to EU-level curbs on scrap exports beyond the U.S.-specific rebalancing measure remains uncertain. Forecasters must weigh industrial supply pressures, decarbonisation goals, trade policy constraints under EU law and WTO commitments, and political economy factors.

Definitions and references forecasters may need:
- Ferrous waste and scrap refers to goods classified under CN heading 7204 in the EU’s Combined Nomenclature (per Council Regulation (EEC) No 2658/87, Annex I). Reference link: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/1987/2658/2025-01-01/eng
- EU legal acts are published in the Official Journal (OJ). Regulations, implementing regulations, delegated acts, and certain decisions are binding. Reference overview: https://eur-lex.europa.eu
- Regulation (EU) 2015/479 (common rules for exports) is the core legal framework for EU export restrictions (authorisations/quantitative limits).
- Commission surveillance announcement and timeline (end-Q3 2025 assessment) ; contextual reporting on shortages and the assessment timeline.
- U.S.-specific export prohibition under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1564 (rebalancing).
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window: Eligible legal acts must be adopted and published, and enter into force, between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025.

YES criteria:
- A legally binding EU-level measure is adopted, published in the Official Journal, and in force within the resolution window, that imposes any restriction on exports from the EU customs territory of ferrous waste and scrap (CN heading 7204) to destinations other than the United States. Qualifying restrictions include:
  - An export duty (a levy specifically applied to exports of CN 7204 goods).
  - A quantitative restriction/limit (e.g., quotas or caps) on exports of CN 7204 goods.
  - An export authorisation/licensing requirement that functions as a quantitative restriction under Regulation (EU) 2015/479, Article 5 or Article 6 (i.e., making exports subject to authorisation with limits or conditions that restrict quantities).
  - An outright prohibition/ban on exporting CN 7204 goods to one or more specified non-U.S. destinations.
- The act may be an EU Regulation, Implementing Regulation, Delegated Act, or Decision adopted by the Commission, Council, or co-legislators, provided it is binding and specifically restricts exports of CN 7204 goods as described above.

NO criteria:
- No such binding EU-level measure meeting the YES criteria is adopted, published, and in force within the resolution window.

Explicit exclusions and clarifications:
- Measures limited solely to exports to the United States adopted as commercial rebalancing measures (e.g., Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1564) do NOT count for this question.
- Non-binding communications, guidance, or surveillance/monitoring actions (including the July 23, 2025 customs surveillance activation) do NOT count.
- Member State-level measures (national laws/regulations) do NOT count; the measure must be EU-level and published in the OJ.
- Anti-dumping, countervailing duties, safeguard measures on imports, or CBAM-related reporting do NOT count unless they impose a restriction specifically on exports of CN 7204 goods as defined above.
- Acts adopted within the window but entering into force after Dec 31, 2025 do NOT count.

Primary resolution source and how to verify:
- Official Journal of the European Union (EUR-Lex). The resolver will search the OJ L series for 2025 acts published between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 that (a) are binding EU legal acts, and (b) explicitly impose any of the qualifying restrictions on exports of CN heading 7204 goods to destinations other than the United States. Key legal bases likely include Regulation (EU) 2015/479 for export authorisations/quantitative restrictions.
- Supporting context sources confirming surveillance and assessment timeline: European Commission news announcement of July 23, 2025 ; Reuters reporting on shortages and timeline.

Operational details for resolvers:
- Search terms: “7204 Official Journal export authorisation,” “Regulation (EU) 2015/479 export authorisation 7204,” “quantitative restriction export CN 7204 Official Journal,” “export duty 7204 EU Regulation,” and exclude U.S.-specific rebalancing acts.
- Confirm the act’s scope includes CN heading 7204 and explicitly applies to destinations other than the U.S.
- Confirm the act’s in-force date falls within the resolution window.

Notes:
