question: China wind + solar installed capacity ≥ 1.75 TW as of end-November 2025
background:
Summary of status quo (as of 2025-10-01): The National Energy Administration (NEA) of the People’s Republic of China publishes monthly “National Electricity Industry Statistics” with end-of-month cumulative installed generation capacity figures by technology. As of end-August 2025, NEA reported solar power installed capacity at 1,120 GW and wind power installed capacity at 580 GW, implying a combined wind+solar capacity of approximately 1,700 GW. Year-over-year growth rates cited by NEA for August were +48.5% for solar and +22.1% for wind. Earlier in the year, as of end-May 2025, NEA reported solar capacity at 1,080 GW and wind at 570 GW. From May to August, the combined figures rose by about 50 GW, with observed monthly additions slowing compared to the early-year pace. Given the proximity to 1,750 GW and variability in monthly additions, whether China reaches ≥1.75 TW by end-November 2025 is plausibly uncertain.

Key definitions and units:
- China refers to the People’s Republic of China: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China
- National Energy Administration (NEA) is China’s energy regulator that publishes monthly electricity statistics: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Energy_Administration
- Installed capacity means the cumulative nameplate capacity of power generation installations as reported by NEA at month-end under 发电装机容量 (installed generation capacity). Nameplate capacity definition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nameplate_capacity
- Wind power installed capacity is the NEA category 风电装机容量, which includes both onshore and offshore wind power generation capacity: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_power
- Solar power installed capacity is the NEA category 太阳能发电装机容量, which includes solar photovoltaic (PV) and any solar thermal generation capacity the NEA counts under 太阳能发电: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_power
- Units and conversion: 1 terawatt (TW) = 1,000 gigawatts (GW) = 1,000,000 megawatts (MW). NEA often reports capacity in 亿千瓦 (hundred million kilowatts), where 1 亿千瓦 = 100 GW.

Data context and sources:
- End-August 2025 cumulative installed capacity: solar 1,120 GW; wind 580 GW; total installed generation capacity 3,690 GW.
- End-May 2025 cumulative installed capacity: solar 1,080 GW; wind 570 GW; total installed generation capacity 3,610 GW.
- NEA monthly statistical releases typically include an overview table titled “全国电力工业统计数据一览表（截至 YYYY年MM月）”. The relevant November 2025 release is expected to provide the authoritative end-November figures used to resolve this question, similar in format to prior months.

Forecast period and time zones:
- Forecast period: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC to 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- The as-of date for measurement is end-November 2025, interpreted as 2025-11-30 23:59:59 China Standard Time (UTC+8), i.e., 2025-11-30 15:59:59 UTC.

Why this is non-trivial: As of August 2025, wind+solar stood near 1.70 TW , and recent month-to-month additions suggest a borderline case for reaching 1.75 TW by end-November. Outcome uncertainty arises from potential seasonal and policy-driven fluctuations in commissioning and grid connection rates, and differing dynamics between solar and wind additions.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution: Yes if, according to the NEA’s official monthly electricity statistics published by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the sum of China’s end-November 2025 solar power installed capacity (太阳能发电装机容量) and wind power installed capacity (风电装机容量) is at least 1.75 terawatts (1,750 GW). Otherwise, No.

Scope and measurement:
- Use the end-of-month cumulative installed capacities reported by the NEA for November 2025 (截至2025年11月末) in the “全国电力工业统计数据一览表（截至2025年11月）” or the November 2025 statistical communique/bulletin.
- Sum the figures for 太阳能发电装机容量 and 风电装机容量 exactly as reported by NEA. If figures are reported in 亿千瓦, convert using 1 亿千瓦 = 100 GW. If both rounded (e.g., one decimal place) and more precise table values are presented, use the more precise table values.
- Include all sub-categories encompassed by NEA’s definitions (e.g., onshore+offshore wind; PV+any solar thermal counted under 太阳能发电).

Cutoffs and tie-breakers:
- Publication cutoff: Only NEA releases published on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC may be used for resolution.
- If NEA publishes multiple November statistical releases or issues corrections within the cutoff, use the latest official NEA release available by the cutoff.
- If NEA’s November 2025 monthly statistics are not published by the cutoff, but NEA publishes a “1–11 months” (1-11月) national electricity industry statistics document with end-November figures by the cutoff, resolve based on that document.

Primary source of truth:
- NEA’s official November 2025 electricity industry statistics page (e.g., in the same format and location as the 1–8 months bulletin published on 2025-09-26 , and the 1–5 months bulletin published on 2025-06-23 ). If needed for navigation, the NEA news release index is typically where these are posted: https://www.nea.gov.cn/xwfb/index.htm.

Resolution steps (for the resolver):
1) Locate the NEA November 2025 electricity statistics release by the cutoff date on the NEA website.
2) In the overview table “全国电力工业统计数据一览表（截至2025年11月）”, record the values for 太阳能发电装机容量 and 风电装机容量.
3) Convert units to GW if necessary and sum. If the sum ≥ 1,750 GW, resolve Yes; otherwise No.

Examples of prior-month documents (for format reference): NEA 2025 1–8 months statistics release showing solar 1,120 GW and wind 580 GW ; NEA 2025 1–5 months statistics release showing solar 1,080 GW and wind 570 GW.

question: By December 31, 2025 (UTC), will at least 6 of the 12 regular FY2026 appropriations bills have been enacted?
background:
Summary and definitions a forecaster needs now (as of 2025-09-30):

- What are “regular appropriations bills”? In the U.S. federal budget process, appropriations bills provide discretionary funding to departments and agencies for one fiscal year. There are twelve “regular” annual appropriations bills aligned to the House and Senate Appropriations subcommittees (e.g., Defense; Labor–HHS–Education; Transportation–HUD). See general definition of a U.S. appropriations bill (Wikipedia) and the list of Senate/House appropriations subcommittees, which map to the 12 bills.
- FY2026 runs from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026 (U.S. federal fiscal year timing).
- “Enacted” in this question means signed into law by the President. The authoritative tracking source for the status of each of the 12 FY2026 regular appropriations bills is the CRS-maintained Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov. That table includes a “Presidential Approval” column; when signed, it shows the date (and typically the public law number) indicating enactment. We will use those “Presidential Approval” dates to count enactments.
- Continuing resolutions (CRs) are temporary appropriations measures used to continue funding when regular appropriations have not been enacted; they are not “regular appropriations bills” for the purposes of this count.

Status quo as of late September 2025:
- As of September 29, 2025, no FY2026 regular appropriations bills had been enacted into law.
- On September 19, 2025, the House passed a CR to extend funding through November 21 by a vote of 217–212; that measure failed in the Senate (44–48). The Senate’s alternative also failed (47–45). This underscores ongoing uncertainty about near-term funding outcomes.
- Legislative activity on individual FY2026 bills has advanced in at least one chamber for several bills (e.g., the House passed the Defense bill on July 18, 2025; House also advanced Energy & Water and MilCon–VA; the Senate passed its Legislative Branch and MilCon–VA bills on August 1, 2025), but these actions do not constitute enactment absent presidential approval.
- The FY2026 CRS Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov is active and updated during the cycle; it lists the 12 regular bills and includes a “Presidential Approval” column we will use for resolution.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial:
- Historically, Congress often turns to CRs and sometimes passes consolidated or “minibus/omnibus” packages late in the year; whether at least six FY2026 regular bills receive presidential approval between mid-October and year-end is uncertain and sensitive to evolving negotiations.

Useful links for forecasters (for definitions; resolution will rely on the source named below):
- Appropriations bill (United States): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appropriations_bill_(United_States) 
- Senate Appropriations Subcommittees: https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/subcommittees 
- House Appropriations Subcommittees: http://appropriations.house.gov/subcommittees 
- U.S. federal fiscal year timing: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_budget_process 
- Continuing resolution (CR): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuing_resolution 
- CRS Appropriations Status Table (FY2026): https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the CRS Appropriations Status Table for FY2026 on Congress.gov as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. It asks whether at least six of the twelve regular FY2026 appropriations bills were enacted between the start and end timestamps below.

- Event window: Count only enactments (Presidential signatures) dated between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. The date to use for each bill is the date shown in the “Presidential Approval” column in the FY2026 Appropriations Status Table. We do not infer times; we use the date as displayed by the table.
- Universe of bills: The “twelve regular FY2026 appropriations bills” are the twelve rows shown under the Appropriations Bills section of the FY2026 CRS Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov (e.g., Agriculture; Commerce–Justice–Science; Defense; Energy–Water; Financial Services; Homeland Security; Interior–Environment; Labor–HHS–Education; Legislative Branch; Military Construction–Veterans Affairs; State–Foreign Operations/House’s National Security–Department of State equivalent; Transportation–HUD). If Congress enacts funding via a consolidated/omnibus act, count any regular bill rows that the CRS table shows as having a Presidential Approval date within the event window; the packaging does not affect counting as long as the table credits the relevant row with a Presidential Approval date.
- What counts as “enacted”: A bill counts as enacted if and only if the FY2026 Appropriations Status Table displays a non-empty date in the “Presidential Approval” column for that bill, and that date falls within the event window. Vetoes without subsequent enactment do not count. Continuing resolutions and supplemental appropriations do not count toward the twelve regular bills.
- Resolution rule: On or immediately after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, check the FY2026 Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov. Count how many of the 12 regular appropriations bill rows have a “Presidential Approval” date within the event window. Resolve “Yes” if the count is 6 or more; resolve “No” otherwise.

Notes and tie-breakers:
- If the Congress.gov FY2026 Appropriations Status Table is temporarily unavailable at the resolution time, the resolution should be based on the earliest subsequently available snapshot of the same page after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. If an individual row’s status on the table appears inconsistent with its Congress.gov bill page (e.g., shows a different public law date), prefer the Appropriations Status Table for consistency; only if the Table is clearly not updated for a bill that was signed within the window (e.g., publicly signed and listed as public law in Congress.gov bill details) should the resolver consult the individual bill’s Congress.gov page to confirm the Presidential Approval date and apply the same counting rule.

Definitions and sources:
- Appropriations bill (United States): legislation to appropriate funds to agencies and programs.
- U.S. federal fiscal year dates (FY2026 = 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30).
- Continuing resolution (CR): a type of appropriations legislation used to provide temporary funding when regular appropriations have not been enacted.
- CRS Appropriations Status Table (FY2026): the Congress.gov tracking table for the 12 regular bills, including a “Presidential Approval” column used here for determining enactment.

Context snapshots for forecasters:
- As of 2025-09-29, no FY2026 regular appropriations bills had been enacted.

question: Will China’s CPCA-reported passenger NEV exports be ≥ 210,000 units in November 2025?
background: Context as of 2025-09-30: The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) publishes monthly data on China’s passenger vehicle market that is widely summarized by trade media. Recent reporting shows that “passenger NEVs exported from China reached 204,000 units in August 2025, surging 102.7 percent year-on-year but declining 6.5 percent month-on-month”. In China, “new energy vehicles (NEVs)” is a regulatory category that includes battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and fuel cell vehicles (FCVs). Policy-wise, China announced that an export license management system for pure electric passenger vehicles will take effect on January 1, 2026, indicating evolving oversight of EV exports. These dynamics, together with shipping capacity and foreign trade policies, create genuine uncertainty around November 2025 export volumes. Definitions to guide forecasters: • China refers to the People’s Republic of China. • CPCA refers to the China Passenger Car Association (official site: cpca.org.cn). • NEV refers to the PRC regulatory category encompassing BEVs, PHEVs, and FCVs. • Passenger NEV exports refers to the CPCA-reported monthly count of new energy passenger vehicles exported from China; trade media describe this metric as “passenger NEVs exported from China”.
resolution_criteria: Observation window and timezone: The relevant month is November 2025, defined as November 1, 2025 00:00:00 China Standard Time (CST; UTC+8) through November 30, 2025 23:59:59 CST. What is being measured: The single CPCA-reported metric for November 2025 labeled as passenger NEV exports (i.e., the monthly count of new energy passenger vehicles exported from China). NEV categories are as defined in PRC regulation: BEVs, PHEVs, and FCVs. Units are whole vehicles. Threshold and logic: Resolve Yes if the official CPCA passenger NEV export figure for November 2025 is greater than or equal to 210,000 units; otherwise resolve No. Inclusion/exclusion specifics: • Only the CPCA’s export count for passenger NEVs for November 2025 is considered. Other export metrics (e.g., total passenger car exports, total vehicle exports) do not apply unless explicitly labeled by CPCA as passenger NEV exports. • If CPCA issues multiple figures (e.g., preliminary and revised), use the latest figure available as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC for resolution. Ignore any revisions published after that cutoff. Source of truth and acceptable citations: • Primary: CPCA’s official channels (e.g., cpca.org.cn monthly market analysis posts or official CPCA press releases). • Secondary (if primary is unavailable): Credible trade media that explicitly attribute the November 2025 passenger NEV export figure to CPCA, such as CnEVPost’s CPCA summaries. Resolution deadline and fallback: • The question will be resolved no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. • If no CPCA figure for November 2025 passenger NEV exports is publicly available by the deadline and no credible trade media have published a CPCA-attributed figure, resolve No by default to ensure a definite outcome. Notes for resolvers: • The NEV category in China includes BEV, PHEV, and FCV under the PRC’s NEV credits regulation. • Trade media phrasing of the target metric is “passenger NEVs exported from China” and refers to CPCA’s monthly export count. • Policy context about export license management effective January 1, 2026 is noted for background only and does not affect November 2025 measurement.

question: Will U.S. headline CPI-U (12-month change) for October 2025 be ≥ 3.0%?
background:
Context and current status (as of 2025-09-30):
- What is being measured: The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U) measures the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of goods and services; the “all items” index refers to the overall CPI for all urban consumers. The “12‑month percent change” compares the index level for a given month to the same month one year earlier and, in the CPI news release, is reported “before seasonal adjustment” (i.e., not seasonally adjusted).
- Latest published reading: In the most recent national CPI news release available as of this writing (covering August 2025), “Over the last 12 months, the all items index increased 2.9 percent before seasonal adjustment.” The release also notes: “The Consumer Price Index for September 2025 is scheduled to be released on Wednesday, October 15, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).” 
- How BLS presents the number: The CPI news release tabulates the 12‑month change for “All items” in Table 1, shown to one decimal place under the “Unadjusted percent change” columns.
- Relevant upcoming methodology note: With the release of October 2025 data on November 13, 2025, BLS will remove long-term care (LTC) insurance from the health insurance index used within the CPI medical care category, due to market changes rendering LTC out of scope for the CPI market basket.
- Release timing for the target month: The BLS schedule lists “Consumer Price Index for October 2025” for Thursday, November 13, 2025 at 08:30 AM (Eastern Time).

Why this is forecastable: As of August 2025, headline YoY CPI‑U was 2.9%. Whether October’s YoY prints at or above 3.0% depends on movements in components such as energy and shelter, base effects from October 2024, and any small measurement changes, leaving reasonable uncertainty through the November 13, 2025 release.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if the 12‑month percent change in the U.S. CPI‑U “All items” index for October 2025 is greater than or equal to 3.0% as published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in its CPI news release for October 2025 on November 13, 2025; otherwise resolve “No”.

Authoritative source and where to read the number:
- Primary source: BLS “Consumer Price Index Summary” news release web page for the October 2025 data published on November 13, 2025, 08:30 AM Eastern Time (ET). Use the value appearing in Table 1 (“Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U): U.S. city average, by expenditure category”), in the “Unadjusted percent change” 12‑month column for “All items,” which is reported to one decimal place. The scheduled publication date/time is listed on the BLS release calendar as Thursday, November 13, 2025 at 08:30 AM (ET).

Definitions and clarifications:
- CPI‑U “All items” refers to the overall Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (U.S. city average) produced by BLS.
- “12‑month percent change” is the percent change from October 2024 to October 2025 in the not seasonally adjusted CPI‑U all‑items index; BLS describes the headline 12‑month change in the news release as “before seasonal adjustment”.
- Rounding/tie rule: Use the value as published to one decimal place in the CPI news release Table 1. A published value of 3.0% counts as meeting the ≥ 3.0% threshold (i.e., “Yes”). If the value in the news release narrative text and Table 1 differ (rare), Table 1 governs.
- Scope note: BLS indicates that with the release of October 2025 data, long‑term care (LTC) insurance is removed from the CPI health insurance index; this is informational background only and does not change the resolution approach.

Timing and contingencies:
- Resolution will occur after the October 2025 CPI news release is published on November 13, 2025 at 08:30 AM ET, which falls within the overall October 15–December 31, 2025 resolution window.
- If BLS issues an official correction (erratum) to the October 2025 CPI news release by December 31, 2025 that changes the Table 1 12‑month value for “All items,” the corrected value will be used; otherwise, the initially published value on November 13, 2025 will govern.
- If, contrary to schedule, BLS does not publish the October 2025 CPI news release by December 31, 2025, resolve as N/A.

question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025, will a U.S. federal continuing resolution (CR) be enacted with a statutory expiration date after November 21, 2025?
background:
Context as of October 1, 2025: The U.S. federal government entered a shutdown after the Senate rejected both (a) a House-passed stopgap funding bill that would have extended funding through November 21, 2025, and (b) a Senate Democratic alternative; the shutdown began at 12:01 a.m. on October 1, 2025. A continuing resolution (CR) is appropriations legislation that temporarily funds federal programs—typically at prior-year levels—until a specified date or until full-year appropriations are enacted, often to avert or end shutdowns.

Key definitions and sources forecasters may find useful:
- Continuing resolution (CR): A type of U.S. federal appropriations law that provides temporary funding for existing federal programs, usually at prior-year levels, for a fixed period or until regular appropriations are enacted. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuing_resolution.
- Enacted (for purposes of this question): A measure becomes law (Public Law) after being signed by the President or enacted over a veto, and it appears in the Public Laws list on Congress.gov with a Public Law number and slip law text published by the Government Publishing Office (GPO). See: https://www.congress.gov/public-laws.
- Status quo details: The House approved a CR to extend funding to November 21, 2025; the Senate rejected it, and a separate Democratic proposal also failed, leading to a shutdown starting October 1, 2025.

Why this is forecastable now: As of early October 2025, negotiations on the length and structure of any eventual stopgap are ongoing and uncertain. CRs can be freestanding or included as a division within larger omnibus/minibus legislation (e.g., titled “Further Continuing Appropriations Act”), and the date they set for the end of continuing appropriations can vary widely.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if, between October 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC, a U.S. federal continuing resolution (CR) is enacted into law (becomes a Public Law) and that CR’s statutory expiration date (the fixed “through/until” date for continuing appropriations stated in the law) is strictly later than November 21, 2025. Resolve “No” otherwise.

Operational definitions:
- Continuing Resolution (CR): Any enacted public law (including a division within a broader omnibus/minibus) that provides continuing appropriations at a rate for operations for ongoing federal programs for a defined period, as commonly termed “Continuing Appropriations Act” or equivalent in the law’s short title or division title.
- Enacted: The law must be listed on Congress.gov’s Public Laws page with a Public Law number (i.e., signed by the President or enacted over a veto).
- Statutory expiration date: The fixed calendar date stated in the CR that ends the general period of continuing appropriations (e.g., “through [Month Day, Year]”). If the CR states funding lasts “until enactment of appropriations or [date], whichever occurs first,” use the fixed date. “After November 21, 2025” means any fixed date of November 22, 2025, or later.
- Multiple CRs: If multiple CRs are enacted within the eligibility window, evaluate the latest statutory expiration date among them.
- Program-specific anomalies: If a CR contains program- or account-specific provisions with different dates, use the general CR date that applies to continuing appropriations broadly; program-specific dates do not change the CR’s overall statutory expiration date for this question.
- Time window: Only CRs enacted between October 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC are eligible.

Resolution procedure:
1) Navigate to Congress.gov Public Laws (https://www.congress.gov/public-laws) and identify any laws enacted in the eligibility window that constitute a CR as defined above.
2) Open the slip law text (linked from Congress.gov) and locate the section that specifies the period of continuing appropriations (e.g., “through [Month Day, Year]”).
3) If at least one eligible CR’s statutory expiration date is strictly later than November 21, 2025 (i.e., November 22, 2025 or later), resolve “Yes”; otherwise resolve “No.”

Notes:
- Background confirmation of status quo as of Oct. 1, 2025 (shutdown; failed Senate votes) is drawn from contemporaneous reporting and official communications.
- Congress.gov’s Public Laws page and its linked slip law texts are the source of truth for resolution.

question: Will CME Group’s cryptocurrency derivatives notional ADV be at least $15.0B in any month of October–November 2025?
background: Context as of 2025-09-22 (UTC): According to the user’s provided artifact, CME Group’s cryptocurrency derivatives have grown rapidly. In Q2 2025, average daily notional volume reached about $10.5 billion, a 140% year-over-year increase versus Q2 2024. The crypto product suite comprises Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), Solana (SOL), and XRP futures and options, with Ether products showing particularly strong growth versus a year earlier and XRP futures launching in May 2025 (per the artifact). This question aims to test whether notional ADV can reach at least $15.0B for any single calendar month in October or November 2025. CME routinely publishes monthly market statistics via press releases that include a “Cryptocurrency ADV” figure stated in both contracts and USD notional; these releases are typically posted in the first few business days of the following month on the CME Media Room press releases page. Definitions for clarity: “CME Group” refers to the derivatives exchange operator (see Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CME_Group). “Cryptocurrency derivatives” refers to CME-listed futures and options in the CME “Cryptocurrencies” market segment (see: https://www.cmegroup.com/markets/cryptocurrencies.html), currently including BTC, ETH, SOL, and XRP contracts (including standard and micro-sized futures and their options, where listed). “Average daily volume (ADV)” means the average number of contracts traded per trading day over a defined period; when CME reports “Cryptocurrency ADV ($X billion notional),” the $X figure is CME’s own USD notional calculation for that month. “Notional value” is the monetary value of a derivatives position based on the underlying (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notional_amount).
resolution_criteria: Start and end of eligible window: 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC. The question resolves YES if, for either October 2025 or November 2025 (treated as separate calendar months), CME Group’s official monthly market statistics press release states a Cryptocurrency average daily volume (ADV) in USD notional of at least $15.0 billion for that month; otherwise NO. “Cryptocurrency ADV (… $Y billion notional)” refers to the figure CME explicitly publishes for the monthly Cryptocurrency category in the press release. Resolution is based on the first CME-published figure available for October and/or November 2025, as posted on the CME Media Room press releases page: https://www.cmegroup.com/media-room/press-releases.html. Precedence and tie-breakers: (1) If both months are published before Dec 31, 2025 and at least one meets or exceeds $15.0B, resolve YES immediately upon publication of the qualifying month. (2) If CME publishes multiple official figures for a given month that conflict, the later official correction supersedes. (3) If a given month’s press release omits the USD notional but an accompanying CME official page/document linked from that release provides the month’s Cryptocurrency notional ADV before Dec 31, 2025, that figure may be used. (4) Comparison uses CME’s reported USD notional figure as published; if CME rounds to one decimal place, the comparison is made using the rounded value. Thus, a reported $15.0B counts as “at least $15.0B,” while $14.9B does not. Included products: All CME-listed cryptocurrency futures and options contracts that CME includes in its monthly “Cryptocurrency” category for the relevant month (e.g., BTC, Micro BTC, ETH, Micro ETH, SOL, XRP futures and their options, where applicable). Currency: USD. Time zone: UTC for defining the calendar months. Outcome must be determined no later than 2025-12-31 based on the October and/or November 2025 publications; December 2025 data is not considered for this market.

question: Will the European Commission open formal antitrust proceedings into interchange fees charged by Visa and/or Mastercard between 2025-09-22 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context for forecasters (status quo as of 2025-09-22):
- What this is about: Interchange fees are transaction fees paid between banks for the acceptance of card-based transactions (see definition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interchange_fee). Visa (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_Inc.) and Mastercard (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastercard) operate the largest card schemes in Europe.
- EU regulatory backdrop: The Interchange Fee Regulation (IFR), Regulation (EU) 2015/751, caps interchange fees for consumer debit and credit card transactions within the EU, while commercial cards are not subject to the same caps. Primary text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32015R0751 (definitions and scope). The European Commission (EC) is the EU’s competition enforcer under Articles 101–102 TFEU (overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directorate-General_for_Competition and EC competition portal: https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/).
- Why this matters now: In 2024–2025, trade groups and large retailers publicly urged the EC to scrutinize card fees, and media have reported information-gathering steps by the EC regarding fees charged by Visa and Mastercard. Forecasters should consider regulatory incentives, prior EC actions concerning card fees (e.g., commitments decisions in the past), market power concerns, political economy, and timing processes at DG Competition.
- Where to check developments: Official EC Press corner (https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/home/en) and the Competition case register (https://competition-cases.ec.europa.eu/) list antitrust actions; if the EC opens proceedings, it typically issues a press release titled along the lines of “Antitrust: Commission opens investigation …”. Third-party reporting (e.g., Reuters, AP) can provide early indicators, but resolution for this question relies on EC official publications (see criteria below).
- Note on baseline: If any formal proceedings into interchange fees against Visa and/or Mastercard were opened before the start date, they do not count for this question; only actions announced within the time window below are eligible. Forecasters should verify status on the EC sites above at the start date and over the forecasting horizon.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive), the European Commission publicly announces that it has opened formal antitrust proceedings into possible infringement of Articles 101 and/or 102 TFEU by at least one of Visa or Mastercard, where the scope explicitly includes “interchange fees” (also acceptable: “multilateral interchange fees” or “MIFs”).

Definitions and requirements:
- European Commission (EC): The EU’s executive that enforces competition law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission). For this market, action is by the Directorate‑General for Competition (DG COMP).
- Open formal antitrust proceedings / opens investigation: An EC action signaled by an official publication on an EC channel that the Commission has “opened proceedings” or “opens investigation” under EU antitrust rules (Articles 101/102 TFEU). Acceptable sources: (a) an EC Press corner press release categorized under Antitrust/Cartels stating that the Commission “opens investigation” (or materially equivalent phrasing) into Visa and/or Mastercard and expressly mentioning interchange fees; or (b) an entry on the EC Competition case register showing “Opening of proceedings” that names Visa and/or Mastercard and identifies interchange fees in the case description.
- Interchange fees: Fees as commonly defined in card payment systems (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interchange_fee). For this question, the EC communication must explicitly refer to interchange fees or multilateral interchange fees (MIFs). Investigations focused exclusively on other fee types (e.g., scheme fees, processing fees) do not count unless interchange fees are expressly included in the scope.
- Visa / Mastercard: Any of Visa entities (e.g., Visa Europe, Visa Inc.) or Mastercard entities (e.g., Mastercard Europe SA) named as subjects of the EC proceeding. Either network suffices; proceedings against both also count. Proceedings that exclusively target acquirers/issuers or other third parties without naming Visa or Mastercard as investigated undertakings do not count.
- Time window and timezone: The announcement must be published between 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). If publication time is ambiguous, use the timestamp on the EC page in UTC; if only local time is shown, convert Brussels time (CET/CEST) to UTC and document the conversion.

Inclusions:
- EC Press corner press release stating “Antitrust: Commission opens investigation …” (or equivalent) that names Visa and/or Mastercard and mentions interchange fees/MIFs.
- EC case register entry indicating “Opening of proceedings” and describing an antitrust case against Visa and/or Mastercard with interchange fees in scope.

Exclusions:
- Preliminary steps: information requests, market questionnaires, consultations, sector inquiries, or other pre‑investigation activities without formal opening of proceedings.
- Non-antitrust actions: investigations or enforcement under regulatory instruments (e.g., the Interchange Fee Regulation) without an antitrust opening; merger control cases; or actions under the Digital Markets Act.
- National cases: actions by Member State authorities (e.g., CNMC, Bundeskartellamt) or by UK authorities (CMA/CAT) do not count.
- Cases focused solely on non‑interchange fee types unless the EC’s communication explicitly includes interchange fees.

Resolution sources and tiebreakers:
- Primary: EC Press corner (https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/home/en) and Competition case register (https://competition-cases.ec.europa.eu/).
- If EC sites are temporarily inaccessible on the resolution date, resolution may rely on credible wire services mirroring the EC announcement (e.g., Reuters, AP, AFP, Bloomberg) provided the EC publication later confirms the same content; if later confirmation contradicts initial reports, the EC publication prevails.
- If multiple announcements occur, the earliest within the window controls. If nothing qualifying is announced within the window, resolves No.

question: Will OFAC add at least one sitting Colombian cabinet minister to any OFAC sanctions list between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30: In late January 2025, the U.S. and Colombia had a public dispute over deportation flights. The White House stated on January 26, 2025 that Colombia agreed to accept deportation flights, and that fully drafted tariffs and sanctions would be held in reserve unless Colombia failed to honor the agreement; it also noted State Department visa sanctions remaining in effect until the first return flight was completed. Major wire reporting the same day described U.S. threats of tariffs, visa restrictions, and financial sanctions against Colombia and confirmed that these measures were put on hold contingent on the agreement.

About OFAC sanctions lists and how updates are published: The U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) maintains the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List and several non-SDN “other” sanctions lists; OFAC provides authoritative access to both the SDN List and the Consolidated (non‑SDN) lists via its Sanctions List Service (SLS) and publishes updates and archives of list changes. OFAC’s “Other OFAC Sanctions Lists” page defines the Non‑SDN Menu‑Based Sanctions (NS‑MBS) List and other non‑SDN lists (e.g., Sectoral Sanctions Identifications List, Foreign Sanctions Evaders List, CAPTA List, NS‑PLC, NS‑CMIC) and clarifies that these non‑SDN lists are part of the Consolidated Sanctions List. OFAC also maintains an archive of changes to the SDN List with date‑stamped records of additions, modifications, and removals, enabling quick verification of new designations by date.

Defining “cabinet minister” in Colombia for resolution: Colombia’s national executive cabinet (Council of Ministers) is composed of the most senior appointed politicians who head the country’s ministries (e.g., Ministers of Defense, Finance, Foreign Relations, Interior, Justice, etc.). For quick verification of who is “sitting” (i.e., in office) at any given time, the CIA World Leaders page lists the current ministers for Colombia and is regularly updated (e.g., as of September 11, 2025).

Why this question is non‑trivial: Sanctions on high‑level Colombian officials would be a notable escalation beyond visa restrictions and tariff threats previously floated, yet still plausible in the event of renewed disputes or other triggering developments; the outcome is uncertain and hinges on evolving U.S.–Colombia relations and OFAC’s enforcement posture.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether OFAC publishes a new sanctions action adding at least one individual who is a sitting Colombian cabinet minister to any OFAC‑administered sanctions list during the specified window.

Time window: Eligible actions must be published by OFAC between October 15, 2025 at 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 at 23:59:59 UTC.

Definitions and what counts:
- “OFAC publishes a new sanctions action” means an action that results in a name being newly added to an OFAC sanctions list, evidenced by either: (a) an OFAC press release, (b) a dated change in OFAC’s list‑change archives showing the name was added on a date within the window, or (c) a Federal Register notice documenting the addition on a date within the window.
- “OFAC sanctions list” includes the SDN List and any OFAC non‑SDN lists that impose sanctions or prohibitions, specifically those contained in OFAC’s Consolidated Sanctions List (e.g., NS‑MBS, SSI, FSE, CAPTA, NS‑PLC, NS‑CMIC).
- “Sitting Colombian cabinet minister” means the incumbent head (Minister) of any national executive ministry of the Republic of Colombia (e.g., Defense, Finance, Foreign Relations, Interior, Justice, etc.) at the time OFAC publishes the action (UTC). Verification of incumbency will be made using the CIA World Leaders page entry for Colombia as of the date of the OFAC action (Internet Archive snapshot nearest to the action date may be used), or, if needed, official Government of Colombia announcements or credible wire reporting; if sources conflict, preference is given in order: Government of Colombia official communiqué/decree, CIA World Leaders page, then major wire services (Reuters/AP/AFP).

What does not count:
- Visa restrictions (State Department) or other non‑OFAC measures (e.g., CBP inspections, BIS Entity List changes) do not count unless the individual is added to an OFAC sanctions list.
- Updates that only modify or correct an existing entry (without first adding the person in the window) do not count; removals do not negate a “Yes” outcome if the initial addition occurred within the window.

Resolution:
- YES if OFAC adds at least one individual who, at the moment of publication, is a sitting Colombian cabinet minister to the SDN List or any OFAC non‑SDN sanctions list, within the time window.
- NO if no such addition occurs within the time window.

Primary sources of truth (for the resolver to check within ~10 minutes):
- OFAC Press Releases index: https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases 
- OFAC Archive of SDN List Changes (and links to other list change archives): https://ofac.treasury.gov/specially-designated-nationals-list-sdn-list/archive-of-changes-to-the-sdn-list 
- OFAC “Other OFAC Sanctions Lists” (definitions and links to non‑SDN lists and Consolidated List): https://ofac.treasury.gov/other-ofac-sanctions-lists 
- Federal Register notices by the Foreign Assets Control Office: https://www.federalregister.gov/agencies/foreign-assets-control-office (search by date) 
- CIA World Leaders – Colombia (to confirm incumbency): https://www.cia.gov/resources/world-leaders/foreign-governments/colombia 

Notes and edge cases:
- If an OFAC addition occurs within the window and is later removed, the question still resolves YES because the qualifying addition occurred during the window.
- If multiple sources give different dates for publication, the date in OFAC’s own list‑change archive or press release governs.
- Timezone for all publication date checks is UTC.

Background sources cited: White House statement (Jan. 26, 2025) and wire reporting on the U.S.–Colombia deportation flight dispute and threats of tariffs/visa restrictions/financial sanctions. OFAC list definitions and publication/archiving practices. Definition of Colombia’s cabinet (Council of Ministers). Verification source for current ministers.

question: Will any adopted COP30 decision include the exact phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels” in its operative paragraphs (English text) by December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30: The 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30) is scheduled to be held in Belém, Brazil, from 10 to 21 November 2025. At COP28 (Dubai, 2023), Parties adopted outcomes under the “UAE Consensus” that, for the first time in a UN climate conference outcome, called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” while stopping short of a negotiated call for a “phaseout” of oil, coal, and gas. This has focused attention ahead of COP30 on whether Parties will agree to stronger language, including an explicit “phase-out of fossil fuels.”

Key definitions and context for forecasters:
- Conference bodies: The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the formal meeting of UNFCCC Parties that assesses progress and adopts decisions. The conferences have also served as the CMP (for the Kyoto Protocol) and, following the Paris Agreement’s entry into force, include meetings of the Parties to the Paris Agreement (CMA). Decisions can be adopted by the COP and/or the CMA during a given conference.
- Operative paragraphs (operative text) vs preambular paragraphs: In UN-style decisions, preambular paragraphs explain background/basis (e.g., “Recalling…”) and are typically unnumbered; operative paragraphs contain the actions/decisions adopted (e.g., “Decides…,” “Requests…”) and are typically numbered. Operative paragraphs begin with a capitalized verb in the present tense and generally end with semicolons (final paragraph with a period). In this question, “operative paragraphs” and “operative text” refer to this action-oriented, numbered section of an adopted decision—not its preambular part.
- Fossil fuels: Fossil fuels are hydrocarbon-containing energy sources formed from ancient organic matter in the Earth’s crust; the main types are coal, petroleum (oil), and natural gas.

Why this matters for forecasting: COP28’s “transitioning away” formulation set a precedent without explicitly committing to a “phase-out of fossil fuels.” Whether COP30 moves to include the exact phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels” in the operative text of any adopted decision remains contested and uncertain as of today, making for a high-entropy policy question.

Where results will be visible: Adopted decisions for COP30 (for the COP and/or CMA) are published on UNFCCC’s official website in its documents database and/or on the session’s Outcomes/Decisions pages. A resolver can navigate from the UNFCCC COP30 page (https://unfccc.int/cop30) to the Documents/Decisions listings, or use the documents portal (https://unfccc.int/documents) to filter for official decisions for the COP30 session. (Links provided for navigation; see Resolution Criteria below for the exact source-of-truth specification.)
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if, between 00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59 UTC on 2025-12-31, at least one decision adopted at COP30 by the COP (Conference of the Parties) and/or the CMA (Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement) includes the exact phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels” in the English-language operative paragraphs (operative text). Otherwise resolve “No.”

Authoritative source of truth:
- Primary: Official UNFCCC English-language decision texts adopted at COP30 (COP and/or CMA) as posted on the UNFCCC website by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC at either the session’s “Outcomes/Decisions” page (navigable from https://unfccc.int/cop30) or the UNFCCC documents portal (https://unfccc.int/documents) when filtered to COP30 decisions.
- If both the final edited decisions and “advance unedited versions” are posted, use the latest posted version as of the resolution deadline.

What counts as “includes the exact phrase”:
- The exact contiguous word sequence “phase-out of fossil fuels” must appear in the English text, with a hyphen between “phase” and “out,” and single spaces as shown. Matching is case-insensitive. Variants such as “phase out of fossil fuels” (no hyphen), “phaseout of fossil fuels” (one word), or “transition(ing) away from fossil fuels” do not count.

What counts as “operative paragraphs” (operative text):
- For this market, “operative paragraphs” are the numbered action/decision paragraphs of an adopted decision (e.g., clauses beginning with verbs like “Decides,” “Requests,” “Urges”), as distinguished from preambular paragraphs, per UN resolutions conventions. The phrase must appear within these operative paragraphs of the decision proper (not solely in preambular text).

Scope clarifications:
- Eligible bodies: COP and/or CMA decisions adopted during COP30. Decisions solely of subsidiary bodies (e.g., SBI, SBSTA) do not count unless they are explicitly adopted as decisions by the COP or CMA.
- Language: Only the official English version counts for phrase matching.
- Location within document: The phrase must appear within the operative paragraphs of the decision text. Occurrences only in titles, headings, footnotes, preambular paragraphs, or annexes do not count.
- Multiple decisions: A single qualifying occurrence in any one adopted COP or CMA decision suffices for a “Yes.”
- Timing: The adoption must occur at COP30 (Belém, 10–21 Nov 2025) , and the qualifying text must be visible in an official English decision posted on the UNFCCC site by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC.

How to resolve (step-by-step):
1) Go to unfccc.int/cop30 and/or unfccc.int/documents. Locate the list of decisions adopted at COP30 by the COP and the CMA. Download the English versions.
2) For each adopted decision, identify the operative paragraphs (the numbered action clauses) per UN drafting conventions.
3) Search within the operative paragraphs for the exact case-insensitive string “phase-out of fossil fuels.”
4) If found in any COP or CMA decision, resolve “Yes.” If not found in all such decisions posted by the deadline, resolve “No.”

Definitions cited:
- COP, CMA roles and conference context.
- Operative vs preambular paragraphs.
- Fossil fuels (coal, oil/petroleum, and natural gas).

Background cited:
- COP30 dates/location.
- COP28 outcome language (“transitioning away from fossil fuels” and absence of an agreed “phaseout” call).

question: Will DfT’s provisional estimates for the year ending June 2025 report fewer e‑scooter‑related casualties than the provisional estimates for the year ending June 2024?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- The UK Department for Transport (DfT) publishes “Reported road casualties in Great Britain, provisional estimates” for rolling 12‑month periods, including a mid‑year release covering the year ending June. Provisional mid‑year statistics are typically published in November each year. The year ending June refers to the 12 months up to and including the end of June (for example, YE Jun 2025 covers 12 months to June 2025).
- The YE Jun 2024 provisional release exists and is the relevant benchmark. In that release, DfT states that it has “implemented the proposed changes,” including no longer publishing separate provisional e‑scooter factsheets, and instead summarising e‑scooter figures within the main publication. The same release reports overall road casualty totals such as 1,607 fatalities, 29,540 killed or seriously injured (KSI), and 128,920 casualties of all severities for YE Jun 2024, giving an indication of the scale of reported road harm.
- DfT also publishes a dedicated e‑scooter factsheet for final annual statistics. The latest factsheet covers data “to the end of 2024” and is considered final; it summarises “e‑scooter casualties in reported road collisions” and includes breakdowns by who is injured (age/sex), other casualties involved in accidents with e‑scooters, and geography. Although e‑scooters have historically not been a designated vehicle type in STATS19, DfT has issued guidance to identify them in reported collisions, and the official e‑scooter outputs collate casualties from collisions involving e‑scooters [6daa4a; f4b3fe].
- Data source and definitions: DfT road casualty statistics are based on police‑reported personal‑injury collisions on public roads in Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales), collected via STATS19; damage‑only collisions and collisions on private roads or car parks are excluded. A “casualty” is “a person killed or injured in a collision,” sub‑divided into killed, seriously injured, and slightly injured; definitions of severity are standardised and, in most forces, injury‑based through systems such as CRASH/COPA. DfT applies a severity‑adjustment methodology (developed with ONS) to ensure consistency across police forces and over time as injury‑based reporting rolled out [093e6d; b7187e].
Why this is forecastable now: The YE Jun 2025 provisional release is expected on GOV.UK in roughly November 2025 based on DfT’s standard publication pattern for mid‑year estimates , enabling unambiguous resolution by December 31, 2025. The benchmark YE Jun 2024 figure for “casualties in collisions involving e‑scooters” is in the existing main publication.
Key term summaries and links:
- Reported road casualties in Great Britain (GOV.UK collection): https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/road-accidents-and-safety-statistics 
- Provisional estimates YE Jun 2024: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/reported-road-casualties-in-great-britain-provisional-estimates-year-ending-june-2024 
- e‑scooter factsheet (final, to end‑2024): https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/reported-road-casualties-great-britain-e-scooter-factsheet-2024 
- Definitions of casualty and severity: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/road-accidents-and-safety-statistics-notes-and-definitions/reported-road-casualties-in-great-britain-notes-definitions-symbols-and-conventions 
- Severity adjustment methodology: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guide-to-severity-adjustments-for-reported-road-casualty-statistics/guide-to-severity-adjustments-for-reported-road-casualties-great-britain 
- Coverage and methodology (STATS19, GB scope, publication timing): https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/road-accidents-and-safety-statistics-notes-and-definitions/road-casualty-statistics-overview-and-coverage 
Notes for forecasters:
- Geographic scope is Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales). Northern Ireland publishes separately and is out of scope.
- “Casualties in collisions involving e‑scooters” include e‑scooter users and other road users injured in such collisions, and are reported as “casualties of all severities” unless explicitly stated otherwise in the DfT release [f4b3fe; 093e6d].
- The YE Jun 2024 e‑scooter figure is summarised within the main YE Jun 2024 provisional publication (not a separate provisional factsheet).
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve YES if the total number of casualties in collisions involving e‑scooters (all severities, Great Britain) reported in DfT’s provisional estimates for the year ending June 2025 is strictly less than the corresponding total reported in DfT’s provisional estimates for the year ending June 2024. Resolve NO otherwise.

Operationalisation and definitions:
- Eligible measure: Use the DfT headline/statistical figure labeled (or equivalently described as) “casualties in collisions involving e‑scooters” for the 12 months to June 2025, as reported in the “Reported road casualties in Great Britain, provisional estimates: year ending June 2025” publication on GOV.UK. Compare it to the same measure for the 12 months to June 2024 reported in the “Reported road casualties in Great Britain, provisional estimates: year ending June 2024” publication on GOV.UK.
- Scope: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales). Data are derived from police‑reported personal‑injury collisions on public roads (STATS19). Damage‑only collisions and private road/parking incidents are excluded.
- Casualty definition: “A person killed or injured in a collision,” subdivided into killed, seriously injured, and slightly injured. Unless DfT explicitly states otherwise, interpret the “e‑scooter casualties” figure as casualties of all severities combined.
- E‑scooter identification: DfT recognises e‑scooters in reported road collisions even though e‑scooters have historically not been a designated STATS19 vehicle type; guidance has been issued to identify them, and official outputs collate casualties in collisions involving e‑scooters [6daa4a; f4b3fe].
- Time period: “Year ending June 2025” refers to the 12 months ending June 30, 2025 (inclusive); “year ending June 2024” refers to the 12 months ending June 30, 2024 (inclusive). Times are treated in local GB time; exact time‑of‑day is immaterial because DfT reports by collision date.

Source of truth and documentation:
- Primary sources: GOV.UK pages for the provisional estimates for YE Jun 2025 and YE Jun 2024. Example for YE Jun 2024: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/reported-road-casualties-in-great-britain-provisional-estimates-year-ending-june-2024. The YE Jun 2025 page is expected to be published in November 2025 per DfT’s stated publication pattern for mid‑year estimates. If multiple figures appear (e.g., in text and in an accompanying table), use the figure in the main publication text; if absent there, use the corresponding figure in the main accompanying data table linked from the publication page.
- Versioning cutoff: If the YE Jun 2025 page is updated after initial publication, use the latest version as it appears on GOV.UK as of 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31 to determine the figure. If the YE Jun 2024 page is updated, likewise use the version as of the same cutoff for the comparator.

Edge cases:
- If DfT does not publish the YE Jun 2025 provisional estimates by 2025-12-31, the question is unresolved under these criteria. This is unlikely given DfT’s typical November schedule for YE‑June provisional statistics.
- If DfT changes terminology but clearly provides an equivalent aggregate (e.g., “casualties in collisions involving e‑scooters (all severities)”), use that equivalent. If DfT publishes a range/interval for the figure, resolve using the central/point estimate it designates [40eb70; 6daa4a].

question: Will the Reserve Bank of India change the policy repo rate at its December 3–5, 2025 Monetary Policy Committee meeting?
background:
Summary of what forecasters need to know as of 2025-09-30 (IST)

- What is being decided and by whom: The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is the body responsible for setting India’s benchmark policy interest rate. The MPC meets at least once per quarter and publishes its decision after each meeting.

- What is the “policy repo rate”: In India’s Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), the policy repo rate is the interest rate at which the RBI lends to banks via repurchase agreements; it is the key policy rate used by the MPC to signal the monetary stance.

- When the relevant meeting is scheduled: According to widely reported coverage of the RBI’s FY 2025–26 MPC calendar, the December 2025 MPC meeting is scheduled for December 3, 4, and 5, 2025 (IST).

- Where the decision will be published: The RBI publishes its Monetary Policy Statements and “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)” as official press releases on its Press Releases portal. Past MPC resolutions appear there on the last day of the meeting, indicating this is the canonical source to check for the repo rate decision.

- Status quo (current level): As of late September 2025, the policy repo rate stands at 5.50%, and a Reuters poll at that time expected the RBI to hold at 5.50% at the Sep 29–Oct 1 meeting as well.

Key terms and references
- Monetary Policy Committee (India): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_Policy_Committee_(India) 
- Liquidity Adjustment Facility (definition underpinning the repo rate): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquidity_adjustment_facility 
- RBI Press Releases portal (source of the MPC resolution and policy statement): https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/English/scripts/pressreleases.aspx 
- December 2025 MPC meeting dates reported: https://www.moneycontrol.com/banking/rbi-releases-mpc-meeting-schedule-for-fy26-here-are-the-dates-article-12976619.html 
- Current repo rate (late Sep 2025) and expectations: https://www.reuters.com/world/india/reuters-poll-reserve-bank-india-hold-repo-rate-550-october-1-said-45-61-2025-09-24/ 

All dates/times are India Standard Time (IST; UTC+05:30) unless noted otherwise.
resolution_criteria:
Operationalization and scope
- Time window: This market resolves based on the RBI’s December 2025 MPC decision announced between 00:00 IST on December 1, 2025 and 23:59 IST on December 31, 2025. All dates/times are IST (UTC+05:30).
- Focal event: The first RBI press release for the MPC meeting scheduled on December 3–5, 2025 (IST) that contains the “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)” and/or the “Monetary Policy Statement” will be used to determine the outcome.

Definitions (to remove ambiguity)
- “Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)”: The RBI committee responsible for fixing the benchmark policy interest rate in India.
- “Policy repo rate”: The interest rate at which the RBI lends to banks under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility; it is the key policy rate in India.
- “Change” in the policy repo rate: Any increase or decrease in the policy repo rate level relative to the level in effect immediately prior to the December 2025 MPC announcement, as determined by comparing the rate stated in the December 2025 MPC resolution/statement with the rate level stated in the most recent prior MPC resolution/statement.

Resolution rule (Yes/No)
- Resolve Yes if the RBI’s official press release for the December 2025 MPC meeting explicitly states that the policy repo rate has been increased or decreased, or if it states a policy repo rate level that differs from the level in effect immediately prior (as per the last MPC resolution/statement).
- Resolve No if the press release explicitly states that the policy repo rate is unchanged, or if the level stated matches the level in effect immediately prior (as per the last MPC resolution/statement).

Source of truth and document precedence
- Primary source: RBI Press Releases portal page hosting the relevant press release(s) (the “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)” and/or “Monetary Policy Statement”) for the December 2025 meeting. If both an HTML page and a linked PDF are available for the same press release, either may be used so long as it is RBI-hosted.
- Document precedence: If multiple documents are released for the same meeting, precedence is: (1) “Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)”, then (2) “Monetary Policy Statement”, then (3) any errata/corrigendum specific to that meeting released by RBI within 48 hours of the initial release. If RBI issues a correction within 48 hours, the corrected version governs.

Scheduling contingencies (to ensure resolvability)
- Rescheduling within December 2025: If the December 3–5, 2025 MPC meeting is officially rescheduled but still occurs within December 2025 (IST), the first RBI press release carrying the MPC resolution/statement for that rescheduled December meeting will be used for resolution.
- Postponement beyond December 31, 2025 or cancellation: If no MPC resolution/statement corresponding to the December 2025 meeting is published by 23:59 IST on December 31, 2025 (because the meeting is postponed beyond that date or cancelled), resolve No.

Practical notes
- Typical publication timing: Historically, MPC resolutions are posted on the RBI Press Releases portal on the last day of the meeting, which for a Dec 3–5, 2025 schedule would typically be Dec 5, 2025 (IST). Forecasters should check the portal on and after that date.

Context as of today for forecasters
- Meeting dates: December 3–5, 2025 (IST) per reporting on the RBI FY 2025–26 MPC calendar.
- Current policy repo rate: 5.50% as of late September 2025, with a contemporaneous poll expecting a hold at that level at the Sep 29–Oct 1 meeting.

Verification time budget
- A resolver should be able to verify the outcome within 10 minutes by locating the December 2025 MPC resolution/statement on the RBI Press Releases portal and reading whether the policy repo rate was changed or left unchanged.

question: Will Spain’s day-ahead wholesale electricity market monthly average price in November 2025 exceed €100/MWh?
background:
Context and definitions
- Market and operator: The Iberian Electricity Market (MIBEL) integrates the electricity markets of Spain and Portugal; OMIE (Operador del Mercado Ibérico de Energía – Spanish pole) manages the spot market (day-ahead and intraday) for both countries. OMIE publishes day-ahead prices separately for the Spanish and Portuguese electricity systems.
- Day-ahead price series granularity and timezone: OMIE’s day-ahead results page shows the market is cleared in 15-minute settlement/scheduling periods (e.g., “period 1 H1Q1, from 00:00 to 00:15 CET”) and explicitly notes CET in the period description. In November, mainland Spain observes Central European Time (CET), which is UTC+01:00.
- Units: OMIE and system reports express day-ahead prices in euros per megawatt-hour (€/MWh) and report arithmetic average prices for the Spanish and Portuguese zones. A megawatt-hour (MWh) equals 1,000 kilowatt-hours (kWh). The euro (symbol €, code EUR) is the official currency of the euro area.
- Arithmetic mean: The arithmetic mean is the sum of values divided by the count of values. OMIE also publishes an arithmetic daily average price for each day.

Status quo and why this is forecastable
- Recent levels: REE’s official system reports indicate the day-ahead market’s annual average price in 2023 was €87.1/MWh. Monthly averages in 2024 ranged widely; notably, November 2024 (104.43 €/MWh) and December 2024 (111.24 €/MWh) exceeded €100/MWh, while spring months were far lower (e.g., April 13.67 €/MWh, March 20.31 €/MWh), illustrating substantial variability and making a €100/MWh threshold for November a non-trivial, high-entropy target. OMIE’s reporting confirms the Spanish zone is treated distinctly from Portugal and that arithmetic averages are standard for summarizing day-ahead prices.

Primary data sources for resolution and verification
- OMIE day-ahead price series (Spanish bidding zone): OMIE’s “Day-ahead price” results page presents per-period marginal prices for the Spanish system and a daily arithmetic average, with period labels and CET timestamps (https://www.omie.es/en/market-results/daily/daily-market/day-ahead-price).
- REE (Red Eléctrica) system reports: REE’s official “Day-ahead market” section provides authoritative statistics on average prices, and their reporting demonstrates the availability of monthly price figures used in official summaries (https://www.sistemaelectrico-ree.es/en/spanish-electricity-system/markets/day-ahead-market) , including explicit monthly values for 2024 that show examples above €100/MWh (https://www.sistemaelectrico-ree.es/es/informe-del-sistema-electrico/mercados/mercado-diario).

Notes on reproducibility and timing
- All necessary raw period-by-period data to compute a November 2025 monthly arithmetic mean will be available from OMIE immediately after November concludes; resolution can therefore occur in December 2025 and no later than December 31, 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if the arithmetic mean of OMIE’s Spanish day-ahead marginal prices for all settlement periods scheduled for delivery in calendar November 2025 is strictly greater than 100.00 €/MWh; resolve “No” otherwise.

Scope and window
- Market/scope: Spanish bidding zone of the MIBEL day-ahead (OMIE) spot market. The “day-ahead market price” is the marginal price determined for each scheduling period in the relevant bidding area as defined in OMIE’s market rules (prices quoted in euros per MWh).
- Time window: Include every OMIE day-ahead settlement/scheduling period with delivery timestamps in calendar November 2025 in CET (UTC+01:00). November 2025 is from 2025-11-01 00:00 CET through 2025-11-30 23:45 CET, inclusive.

Computation
- Data to include: Use the complete set of OMIE-published Spanish zone day-ahead marginal prices (€/MWh) for each 15-minute settlement/scheduling period in the window above. Include any negative or zero prices if published, with no exclusions.
- Statistic: Compute the arithmetic mean (unweighted average) across all included settlement/scheduling periods. Definition: arithmetic mean = sum of all values divided by the number of values. Do not round the computed mean prior to comparison; compare the full-precision mean against the 100.00 €/MWh threshold.
- Threshold comparison: Resolve “Yes” if the computed mean > 100.00 €/MWh; resolve “No” if the computed mean ≤ 100.00 €/MWh.

Primary resolution source and procedure
- Primary source: OMIE “Day-ahead price” results for the Spanish system (https://www.omie.es/en/market-results/daily/daily-market/day-ahead-price). Aggregate the 15-minute marginal prices for each delivery day from 2025-11-01 to 2025-11-30 (CET) to form the full November 2025 set, then compute the arithmetic mean as specified.

Fallback and tiebreakers
- If OMIE’s site is temporarily unavailable or materially incomplete for any November 2025 delivery period by 2025-12-15 12:00 UTC, use REE’s official “Day-ahead market” reporting for the Spanish system’s November 2025 monthly average price, if published on their system reports site (https://www.sistemaelectrico-ree.es/en/spanish-electricity-system/markets/day-ahead-market or its Spanish counterpart). If both are available but differ due to methodological notes, prefer the directly computed OMIE arithmetic mean of per-period marginal prices as defined above.

Term definitions and references
- Day-ahead market (OMIE): OMIE manages the spot (day-ahead and intraday) markets for the Iberian Peninsula (MIBEL); prices are reported separately for Spain and Portugal. The day-ahead marginal price per scheduling period in the bidding zone is the settlement price referred to in OMIE’s rules (Euros per MWh).
- Settlement/scheduling period: The discrete trading interval used by OMIE in the day-ahead market; OMIE’s public results page illustrates 15-minute periods with labels such as H1Q1 (00:00–00:15 CET).
- CET: Central European Time, UTC+01:00. Spain in November observes CET (except the Canary Islands, which are not a separate OMIE day-ahead bidding zone for this purpose).
- Currency and units: Euro (EUR, €) ; megawatt-hour (MWh) equals 1,000 kWh. Prices are expressed in €/MWh, and arithmetic averages are standard in OMIE/REE reporting.

Resolution timing
- Earliest resolution: After all November 2025 delivery periods have occurred and are published by OMIE; not before 2025-12-01 00:00 UTC.
- Latest resolution: No later than 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, using the primary procedure or the fallback as specified.

question: EU implementation of the US–EU trade Framework: Will the EU adopt and publish in the Official Journal the Regulation arising from COM(2025)471 between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- On 2025-08-21, the United States and the European Union released the “Joint Statement on a United States–European Union Framework on an Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade,” which outlines tariff commitments and states that the parties will “promptly document the Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade to implement this Framework Agreement”. The statement describes, among other points, a U.S. baseline combined tariff rate of 15% for EU-origin goods in specified contexts and details on autos and auto parts treatment tied to EU legislative steps.
- The U.S. subsequently published a Federal Register notice titled “Implementing Certain Tariff-Related Elements of the U.S.-EU Framework on an Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade,” which amended the HTSUS to implement parts of the Framework. This included setting the combined rate on covered autos and auto parts at 15% and making the adjustment effective for entries on or after 2025-08-01 (retroactive effect).
- On 2025-08-28, the European Commission proposed COM(2025)471: a Regulation to implement EU commitments associated with the 2025 joint statement/Framework, including eliminating customs duties (0%) on all U.S. industrial goods and providing preferential market access for certain U.S. seafood and agricultural products via tariff adjustments and quotas. This is a Commission proposal that would require adoption and publication in the Official Journal to take legal effect.

Why this matters for the forecast:
- The joint statement explicitly signals that the parties intend to “promptly document” the Agreement, but as of 2025-10-01, the legally binding EU-side measures remained at the proposal stage (COM(2025)471) pending adoption. Whether the EU will adopt and publish the resulting Regulation in the Official Journal by year-end is uncertain and consequential for the practical implementation of the Framework.

Helpful references/definitions (for clarity; not resolution sources):
- Official Journal of the European Union (OJ): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/oj/direct-access.html
- Regulation (European Union): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_(European_Union)
- Coordinated Universal Time (UTC): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible publication window: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). All dates/times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

What counts for “Yes”:
- Resolve Yes if, within the above window, a Regulation (EU) of the European Parliament and of the Council that constitutes the adoption of the Commission’s proposal COM(2025)471 is published in the Official Journal of the European Union (OJ), L series. Verification must show that the adopted act’s legislative procedure traces to COM(2025)471 (e.g., via the “Procedure”/“Legislative history” on EUR-Lex) and that it is published in the OJ L series with an official publication date within the window.

What does NOT count (exclusions):
- Press releases, joint statements, Q&As, draft texts, public inspection previews, or Commission proposals alone (including COM(2025)471) do not count.
- U.S.-side implementing notices (e.g., Federal Register notices) do not count for this question, which is solely about EU adoption and publication in the OJ.
- Publications in the OJ C series (non-binding) do not count; the act must appear in the OJ L series.

Primary resolution source:
- EUR-Lex (Official Journal) entry for the adopted act in the OJ L series (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/oj/direct-access.html). The resolver should confirm the OJ citation (e.g., “OJ L …, [date]”) and that the act’s legislative history on EUR-Lex shows it is the adoption of COM(2025)471.

Fallback if EUR-Lex is inaccessible at resolution time:
- Use an official EU legal database mirror (e.g., CELEX via EUR-Lex once restored) or an official EU press notice that directly links to the OJ L entry. If none is accessible at resolution time, the question should be held open until the OJ page is accessible. No non-official or secondary media sources should be used for final resolution.

Edge cases:
- If more than one act is adopted from COM(2025)471, any one qualifying Regulation (EU) published in OJ L within the window is sufficient for Yes.
- If adoption occurs but OJ L publication is dated outside the window, resolve No (publication date on EUR-Lex governs).

question: Will CDER approve at least 25 orphan‑designated novel drugs between 2025‑01‑01 and 2025‑12‑31 (UTC)?
background: Status quo and context (as of 2025-09-22): In 2024, the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) approved 50 novel drugs, of which 26 (52%) were approved for rare (“orphan”) diseases. This recent base rate motivates setting the threshold at 25 for 2025. Definitions used here: • FDA CDER is the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (overview: https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder). • A novel drug, for FDA annual lists, refers to new drugs never before approved/marketed in the U.S., typically including new molecular entities (NMEs) under NDAs and new therapeutic biologics under BLAs reviewed by CDER (see FDA’s overview: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/development-approval-process-drugs/novel-drug-approvals-fda; the 2025 list lives at: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/novel-drug-approvals-fda/novel-drug-approvals-2025). • Orphan Drug designation is a status FDA grants to drugs/biologics intended to diagnose, prevent, or treat a rare disease or condition under the Orphan Drug Act (program overview: https://www.fda.gov/industry/medical-products-rare-diseases-and-conditions/designating-orphan-product-drugs-and-biological-products). • Rare disease or condition is defined in regulation at 21 CFR 316.3 as one affecting fewer than 200,000 persons in the United States (definition: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-316/section-316.3). Resolution data source: FDA’s “Novel Drug Approvals for 2025” page (CDER) and the individual drug approval summary pages (Drugs@FDA), which indicate whether a drug carries “Orphan Drug” designation on approval. Rationale for uncertainty: orphan share of novel approvals has often been around ~50%, but total novel approvals per year vary; thus whether the orphan count reaches 25 is non-trivial. Start date/time: 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. End date/time: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
resolution_criteria: This question resolves YES if, between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC inclusive, CDER approves at least 25 “novel” drugs that have Orphan Drug designation at the time of approval. It resolves NO otherwise. Counting and definitions: • Inclusion universe: items listed on FDA’s “Novel Drug Approvals for 2025” page (CDER). Each item corresponds to a CDER novel approval. • Orphan status test: open the FDA approval summary page (linked from the list) or the Drugs@FDA record for the approval; count the drug if the page displays the “Orphan Drug” designation label at/for the 2025 approval. • Approval date rule: use the FDA-recorded “Approval Date” shown on the drug’s FDA page; treat dates as calendar days (no time-of-day needed). • Exclusions: do not count supplemental approvals, line extensions, or non-novel approvals; exclude CBER-only approvals not listed on the CDER novel page. • Multiple orphan indications do not increase the count; each novel approval counts at most once. • Tie-breaker: if the CDER list and Drugs@FDA disagree on inclusion or orphan status, use the Drugs@FDA approval record as authoritative. Resolution sources: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/novel-drug-approvals-fda/novel-drug-approvals-2025 and the linked Drugs@FDA approval pages. Timing: resolution occurs based on the count as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Notes: 2024 base-rate context (26 of 50) is from FDA’s annual report ; it is not used in resolution but informs threshold selection.

question: Between 2025-09-22 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the FOMC’s federal funds rate target range upper bound be at least 50 basis points lower on 2025-12-31 than on 2025-09-22?
background:
Definitions and context a forecaster needs:
- Federal funds rate: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances to each other overnight; since 2008 the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range with a lower and upper bound. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate
- FOMC: The body within the Federal Reserve System that sets monetary policy, including the target range for the federal funds rate. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Open_Market_Committee
- Target range (upper bound): The upper limit of the FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate. Example: a range stated as “4 to 4-1/4 percent” has an upper bound of 4.25%.
- Basis point (bp): One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%), i.e., 0.0001 in decimal. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point
Status quo as of today (2025-09-22): On 2025-09-17, the FOMC lowered the target range by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00%–4.25%, effective 2025-09-18. The Federal Reserve’s implementation note explicitly states “maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 4 to 4-1/4 percent” effective 2025-09-18. The St. Louis Fed FRED “Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit (DFEDTARU)” series shows the upper bound moved from 4.50% on 2025-09-17 to 4.25% on 2025-09-18, remaining 4.25% through 2025-09-19–21.
Why this matters: Measuring net change in the upper bound provides an unambiguous proxy for cumulative rate cuts, avoids ambiguity around intra-range changes or midpoint conventions, and has high-quality public data available for resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end window:
- Eligible period: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
Primary measure and source:
- Measure the upper bound of the FOMC’s federal funds rate target range on the start date and on the end date, using the St. Louis Fed FRED series “Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit (DFEDTARU)”: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU.
