- If FRED is unavailable or shows a gap for the specific dates needed, use the Federal Reserve Board’s post-meeting press releases and Implementation Notes to identify the target range in effect on those dates: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases.htm (specifically, the 2025-09-17 statement and implementation note establish the current range).
Resolution rule:
- YES if: Upper bound on 2025-12-31 (as represented by DFEDTARU for that date in UTC) is at least 50 basis points (0.50 percentage points) lower than the upper bound on 2025-09-22.
- NO otherwise.
Clarifications:
- “Upper bound” means the upper limit of the target range. If, at any point, the FOMC sets a single-point target instead of a range, treat that single point as the upper bound for this question.
- Ignore the effective federal funds rate (EFFR); only the target range as set by the FOMC is relevant.
- If multiple changes occur on 2025-12-31, the range in effect at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC governs.
- If the start date’s range changes on 2025-09-22, use the value in effect at 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC (as represented by DFEDTARU’s value for 2025-09-22).

question: Will Great Britain’s “Time to 3” passenger rail punctuality for Jul–Sep 2025 be at least 87.0%?
background:
Summary of the metric and current status (as of 2025-09-30):
- What is “Time to 3”? The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) defines Time to 3 as the percentage of recorded station stops arrived at early or less than three minutes after the scheduled time. It is cumulative with the On Time measure (≤1 minute late).
- What is a “recorded station stop”? A recorded station stop is a location with both a planned timetable time and an actual recorded time where a train has stopped; ORR notes that up to around 96% of all station stops are currently recorded, with no estimates made for the c.4% not recorded.
- Coverage and publication: ORR’s Passenger rail performance statistics cover passenger trains operating on the mainline network in Great Britain and are published quarterly as Accredited Official Statistics. ORR lists the next publication (covering Jul–Sep 2025) for 11 December 2025. ORR’s quarterly labelling uses financial-year quarters, with Q1 defined as 1 April to 30 June and Q2 as 1 July to 30 September.
- Latest available figure: For Apr–Jun 2025 (Q1 2025–26), Time to 3 at the Great Britain level was reported as 86.3% (18.6 million of 21.6 million recorded station stops arrived within three minutes).

Additional context for forecasters:
- The ORR Passenger rail performance landing page provides the current headline figures and links to the detailed quarterly PDF release and methodology.
- The methodology/quality report explains the relationship between On Time and Time to 3, the handling of cancellations, and inclusion rules (e.g., early arrivals included; request stops included when activated), which can inform expectations about seasonal performance movements and data completeness.
- This question targets the single GB-level Time to 3 percentage that ORR will report for Jul–Sep 2025, aiming for a threshold near the recent quarter’s value to promote uncertainty and informative forecasting.

Useful links (for orientation; primary resolution sources are specified below):
- ORR Passenger rail performance landing page: https://dataportal.orr.gov.uk/statistics/performance/passenger-rail-performance/ 
- ORR publication schedule (shows 11 December 2025 for Jul–Sep 2025): https://dataportal.orr.gov.uk/publication-dates-for-statistics/ 
- Methodology/quality report: https://dataportal.orr.gov.uk/media/lvqlsyh3/passenger-performance-quality-report.pdf 
- Background example release (Apr–Jun 2025): https://dataportal.orr.gov.uk/media/w0bg30gk/performance-stats-release-2025-26-apr-jun.pdf 

Terminology note:
- Great Britain refers to the island comprising England, Scotland, and Wales (distinct from the United Kingdom, which also includes Northern Ireland). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain. ORR’s publications cited here use GB-level coverage.
resolution_criteria:
How this resolves (all times UTC):
1) Primary source: The ORR “Passenger rail performance” quarterly release covering Jul–Sep 2025 (Q2 2025–26), scheduled for publication on 2025-12-11, as listed on ORR’s publication-dates page and the Passenger rail performance landing page. Use the GB-level Time to 3 percentage for Jul–Sep 2025 reported by ORR. Do not use any moving annual average; use the quarter’s headline GB figure.
2) Measurement definition to use: Time to 3 is defined by ORR as the percentage of recorded station stops that were arrived at early or less than three minutes after the scheduled time; use the figure as presented by ORR for the Jul–Sep 2025 quarter. A recorded station stop has both a planned and an actual recorded time where a train has stopped.
3) Precedence if multiple sources differ: If the landing page and the PDF release present different numbers for the GB-level Jul–Sep 2025 Time to 3, the PDF release value takes precedence. If the PDF is not yet available but the landing page shows the GB-level value, the landing-page value may be used provisionally for resolution; if a later same-day PDF appears and differs, the PDF value prevails.
4) Rounding/precision: Use the percentage value exactly as presented by ORR (typically to one decimal place). Do not recompute or re-round from underlying counts.
5) Resolution rule: Resolve Yes if the reported GB-level Time to 3 for Jul–Sep 2025 is greater than or equal to 87.0%; otherwise resolve No.
6) Timing: The question resolves once the relevant ORR quarterly release (covering Jul–Sep 2025) is available, and in any case no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Notes and references for verification:
- Example of the metric’s presentation and definition (from the prior quarter): “Time to 3 is the percentage of recorded station stops that were arrived at early or less than three minutes after the scheduled time. In the latest quarter, 86.3% of recorded station stops in Great Britain … were arrived at within three minutes.” (Apr–Jun 2025 release).
- Coverage and publication cadence (landing page) and schedule for Jul–Sep 2025 (11 Dec 2025).

question: Will China file a WTO DSU Article 4 request for consultations against Mexico concerning Mexico’s April 2024 temporary import tariffs between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Mexico’s April 2024 tariff decree: On April 22, 2024, Mexico published a decree establishing temporary import tariffs ranging from 5% to 50% across 544 Harmonized System (HS) codes, effective April 23, 2024 through April 23, 2026. The measure targets imports from countries without a free trade agreement (FTA) with Mexico and spans categories including steel, aluminum, textiles/apparel, footwear, plastics, chemicals, electrical materials, vehicles/transport equipment, and furniture. The decree is available in the Official Gazette (Diario Oficial de la Federación, DOF) referenced by the U.S. International Trade Administration’s market intelligence note.
- China’s response: On September 26, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) launched a trade and investment barrier investigation into Mexico’s tariff measures on Asian imports (including duties up to 50% on various products) and other recent restrictive measures pertaining to China. This investigation signals the potential for escalation, including initiating WTO dispute settlement consultations.
- WTO process basics: Under the WTO Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) Article 4, a "request for consultations" is a written document by a WTO Member that states the reasons for the request, identifies the measures at issue, and indicates the legal basis for the complaint; it must be notified to the Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) and relevant Councils/Committees. In the WTO system, consultation requests are the first official document of a dispute, carrying the symbol WT/DS[case number]/1, and are circulated/posted publicly on wto.org to inform Members and the public of the dispute’s initiation. The WTO maintains an official chronological list of dispute cases on its disputes portal, prepared by the Secretariat and presented in reverse chronological order.

Definitions and scope for this question:
- China: The People’s Republic of China, a WTO Member.
- Mexico: The United Mexican States, a WTO Member.
- Tariff: A tax on imports levied at the border. See Tariff on Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff.
- "Mexico’s April 2024 temporary import tariffs": The specific tariff measure introduced by Mexico via the April 22–23, 2024 decree establishing temporary MFN tariffs of 5%–50% on 544 HS lines for imports from non-FTA countries, effective through April 23, 2026.
- "Request for consultations" (for resolution purposes): A WTO DSU Article 4 written request circulated by the WTO Secretariat as an official WTO dispute settlement (WT/DS) document (typically symbolized as WT/DS[case number]/1), which identifies measures at issue and the legal basis, and is notified to the DSB and relevant bodies.

Why this question may have non-trivial uncertainty:
- China has publicly initiated a barrier investigation but has not committed to WTO litigation; whether it escalates to consultations in Q4 2025 depends on evolving trade/diplomatic dynamics, the content of Mexico’s measures, and bilateral or plurilateral negotiations.
- The timeframe (Oct–Dec 2025) is short but plausibly sufficient for China to decide and file if it chooses to leverage WTO processes.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve Yes if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC inclusive, the WTO publishes a DSU Article 4 "request for consultations" document by China against Mexico that concerns Mexico’s April 2024 temporary import tariffs, as evidenced by at least one of the following:
- An official WTO dispute settlement document with symbol WT/DS[case number]/1 posted on wto.org (WTO Documents Online), where China is the complainant, Mexico is the respondent, and the measures at issue explicitly include Mexico’s April 2024 temporary import tariffs described in the decree (e.g., identifying the tariff increases across HS codes for non-FTA countries). The qualifying date is the publication/circulation date shown on the WTO document record, which must fall within the defined timeframe.
- The official WTO "dispute settlement – chronological list of disputes cases" page shows an entry for a China v. Mexico dispute with a "Consultations requested" date within the defined timeframe, and the short description or accompanying WT/DS[case number]/1 document indicates that the measures at issue include Mexico’s April 2024 temporary import tariffs.

Resolve No if no such qualifying WTO publication (as defined above) appears within the timeframe.

Additional notes:
- To "concern Mexico’s April 2024 temporary import tariffs," the request must identify as measures at issue the import tariff increases established by the April 2024 decree (temporary MFN 5%–50% across 544 HS codes for non-FTA countries). If China files consultations against Mexico on different measures (e.g., non-tariff restrictions or unrelated policies) without identifying the April 2024 tariff decree or its resulting import tariff increases as measures at issue, do not count it.
- Acceptable resolution sources are limited to official WTO publications: WT/DS documents (e.g., WT/DS####/1) and/or the WTO disputes portal page maintained by the Secretariat. Media reports alone are not sufficient. At resolution, cite the specific WT/DS document and/or the WTO disputes portal entry.
- Background sources supporting the definition of the relevant Mexican tariff measures and the DSU consultation process: US ITA market intelligence on Mexico’s 2024 tariff decree ; MOFCOM’s announced investigation into Mexico’s tariff measures (for current context) ; DSU Article 4 legal text and WTO procedural guidance about consultation requests and document symbols ; WTO disputes portal overview of chronological listings.

question: Between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, will the IMF Executive Board complete the second review of Argentina’s 48‑month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) arrangement approved on April 11, 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Program approval: The IMF Executive Board approved a 48‑month Extended Arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) for Argentina on April 11, 2025, amounting to SDR 15.267 billion (about US$20 billion).
- First review: The IMF Executive Board completed the first review of this arrangement on July 31, 2025, enabling a disbursement of SDR 1.529 billion (about US$2 billion).
- Targets adjusted and timing for next review: Reporting based on IMF documents indicates the Fund lowered the net international reserves (NIR) accumulation target for end‑December 2025 and that the next review is due after Argentina’s October local elections.
- Political and implementation risks: As of September 26, 2025, analysis highlights that Argentina faces a demanding reform agenda under the IMF program (rebuilding FX reserves, moving to a more flexible exchange rate, labor reforms, privatizations), with heightened political sensitivity around the October vote and market‑reaction risks if policy implementation slips.
- Where updates are published: The IMF maintains an Argentina country page that aggregates press releases and updates (see the "What’s New" section), and IMF press releases/news items document Executive Board actions.

Key definitions and clarifications:
- IMF Executive Board: The IMF’s Executive Board is the body that conducts the day‑to‑day business of the IMF and formally completes program reviews. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Board_of_the_International_Monetary_Fund.
- Extended Fund Facility (EFF): An IMF lending instrument providing medium‑term support for structural reforms; Argentina’s program is an “extended arrangement under the EFF.” See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Fund_Facility.
- “Argentina’s 48‑month EFF arrangement approved on April 11, 2025”: The specific arrangement referenced by IMF press release PR25101 (approval on April 11, 2025).
- “Second review” and “completion”: In IMF practice, a review is considered completed when the Executive Board formally decides to complete it; IMF press releases typically state “IMF Executive Board Completes [Nth] Review of the Extended Arrangement Under the Extended Fund Facility for [Country]” (see the wording used for the first review on July 31, 2025).
- Time window: Events counted for resolution must occur between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Why this is non‑trivial: The second review’s timing depends on policy implementation, reserve accumulation, political calendar, and Board scheduling. The IMF already eased the NIR target for end‑2025, suggesting both flexibility and remaining risk, and reporting indicates the review is slated after October elections—making completion by year‑end uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, based on official IMF communications, the IMF Executive Board completes the second review of Argentina’s current 48‑month EFF arrangement (approved April 11, 2025) on or before 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, and the completion date falls within the window starting 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025.

Operationalization:
- Acceptable resolution sources: An official IMF press release or IMF “News” article on imf.org stating that the “IMF Executive Board completed the second review” of Argentina’s extended arrangement under the EFF (the arrangement approved April 11, 2025). The Argentina country page’s "What’s New" feed on imf.org may also host/aggregate such press releases.
- Determining the event date: Use the date stated in the IMF communication for when the Board completed the review (e.g., “July 31, 2025: The Executive Board … completed today…” in prior releases). If the communication clearly states the Board completion occurred on a specific date, that date governs. If the communication only indicates completion “today,” use the publication date on imf.org.
- Identifying the correct review: The communication must explicitly refer to the “second review” under the extended arrangement approved on April 11, 2025 (to avoid confusion with older arrangements). Mentions of staff‑level agreements, staff reports, or Board meetings that do not state “Executive Board completes the second review” do not count.
- Exclusions: Announcements of staff‑level agreements, waivers, or modifications that are not accompanied by a clear statement that the Executive Board has completed the second review do not count. If the arrangement is canceled, expires, or is replaced before a second review is completed, resolve No.

Adjudication steps:
1) Check imf.org press releases/news and the Argentina country page for a statement that the IMF Executive Board completed the second review of Argentina’s EFF arrangement approved April 11, 2025.
2) Confirm the stated completion date is between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. If yes, resolve Yes; otherwise, resolve No.

Notes:
- Examples of the exact wording and format the IMF uses for a completed review can be seen in the first review press release on July 31, 2025.
- Background on the approval and program size is in the April 11, 2025 press release.
- Background on lowered NIR targets and timing expectations for the next review is reported by Reuters with reference to IMF documents , and broader program context and risks are summarized in Reuters analysis as of September 26, 2025.

question: Will Colombia’s CPI (IPC) year-over-year inflation for November 2025 be at or below 5.00%?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: Colombia’s official Consumer Price Index (Índice de Precios al Consumidor, IPC) is produced by DANE and is published on the fifth business day of each month. The release includes the monthly change, the year-to-date change, and the 12‑month (year-over-year) change. In March 2023, DANE announced that IPC releases would henceforth occur on the fifth business day at 6:00 p.m. local time (COT), aligning with international dissemination standards.

Recent inflation dynamics: The latest DANE technical material publicly highlighting August 2025 stated: “En agosto de 2025 la variación mensual del IPC fue 0,19%, la variación año corrido fue 4,22% y la anual 5,10%,” i.e., August’s 12‑month (YoY) IPC was 5.10%. A Reuters analyst poll just before the September 2025 release expected a 0.23% monthly increase for September and implied 12‑month inflation around 5.10%; the same poll’s median saw end‑2025 inflation at 5.03% and noted that inflation remained above the central bank’s 3% target.

Why this threshold and timing: Given the August YoY reading (5.10%) and consensus pointing to inflation hovering near 5% into late 2025, a 5.00% threshold for November 2025 is intended to maximize uncertainty while remaining realistic. The November 2025 IPC “variación anual (12 meses)” will be published in early December under DANE’s schedule (fifth business day, 6:00 p.m. COT), ensuring the question can resolve before year‑end.

Key references/definitions for forecasters:
- IPC definition and regular publication cadence (fifth business day) — Banco de la República glossary entry for IPC.
- Publication time change to 6:00 p.m. on the fifth business day — DANE announcement coverage.
- Latest cited DANE figures (August 2025 YoY = 5.10%) and DANE’s terminology for variación anual (12 meses) — DANE IPC technical information page excerpt showing headline phrasing.
- Market expectations around September and year‑end 2025 — Reuters poll.
resolution_criteria:
Question and timeframe
- This question asks whether the year‑over‑year (12‑month) inflation rate for Colombia’s IPC in November 2025 will be at or below 5.00%.
- “November 2025” refers to the calendar month of November 1–30, 2025 in Colombia (COT).
- The question will resolve upon DANE’s publication of the November 2025 IPC bulletin, expected on the fifth business day of December 2025 at 18:00 (6:00 p.m.) COT , and in any case no later than December 31, 2025.

Definitions (with authoritative sources)
- IPC (Índice de Precios al Consumidor): Colombia’s official consumer price index measuring the evolution of prices of the most representative goods and services consumed by households. DANE publishes IPC monthly and reports the monthly change, year‑to‑date change, and 12‑month (last twelve months) change.
- Year‑over‑year inflation rate (YoY) for the IPC: DANE’s “variación anual (12 meses),” i.e., the percentage change in the IPC index compared to the same month of the prior year, as reported in the monthly release (e.g., DANE’s August 2025 headline: “la anual 5,10%”).
- Time zone: All publication times referenced are in Colombia Time (COT).

What is checked to resolve
- Source of truth: DANE’s official monthly IPC “Boletín técnico” for November 2025, published on dane.gov.co on the fifth business day of December 2025 (18:00 COT). DANE’s standard schedule (fifth business day) and the 18:00 COT release time are documented by authoritative sources.
- Specific data point: the “variación anual (12 meses)” for “Total nacional” (all items), as shown in the November 2025 IPC release’s headline/summary tables or charts. If multiple summaries exist (e.g., press release vs. technical bulletin), the technical bulletin value prevails.

How the comparison is made
- Resolve Yes if the reported “variación anual (12 meses)” for November 2025 (Total nacional, all items) is less than or equal to 5.00%. Resolve No if it is greater than 5.00%.
- Use the percentage value as printed in the DANE bulletin (typically to two decimal places). No transformations or alternative rounding will be applied beyond what DANE reports.

Contingencies and edge cases
- If DANE publishes an official erratum/correction to the November 2025 IPC on or before December 31, 2025, that corrected figure supersedes the initial number. Corrections after December 31, 2025 will not be considered.
- If there is any discrepancy between different DANE pages for the same release date, the “Boletín técnico” PDF or official technical bulletin page for November 2025 is the source of record.
- If, contrary to expectations, DANE fails to publish the November 2025 IPC by December 31, 2025, the question will resolve N/A. (This is not expected given the regular publication cadence on the fifth business day at 18:00 COT).

question: Will at least 19 APEC economy leaders attend the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Gyeongju (Oct 31–Nov 1, 2025, KST)?
background:
Status quo and key facts as of 2025-10-01:
• Event and timing: The APEC Economic Leaders’ Week (AELW) 2025 will be held in Gyeongju, Republic of Korea, from 27 October to 1 November 2025. Within AELW, the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting (AELM) will take place from Friday, October 31 to Saturday, November 1, 2025, in Gyeongju. Korea Standard Time (KST) is UTC+9.
• APEC membership and terminology: APEC has 21 member economies (APEC uses the term “economies” rather than “countries”). The 21 member economies are: Australia; Brunei Darussalam; Canada; Chile; People’s Republic of China; Hong Kong, China; Indonesia; Japan; Republic of Korea; Malaysia; Mexico; New Zealand; Papua New Guinea; Peru; The Philippines; The Russian Federation; Singapore; Chinese Taipei; Thailand; United States of America; Viet Nam.
• How APEC records who attends: APEC typically publishes an “Economy Representatives” page associated with the Leaders’ Declaration that lists who attended the AELM for each economy and their titles (e.g., President, Prime Minister, Chief Executive, Sultan, or other roles). In 2024, for example, some economies were represented by non-leader officials such as a Deputy Prime Minister, Special Envoy, Chargé d’affaires, or a “Representative” (e.g., Chinese Taipei), illustrating that not all economies are represented by their head of state or head of government every year.
• Definitions relevant to counting leaders: In political systems, the head of government is the highest or second-highest official within the executive branch (e.g., Prime Minister, Chancellor, Premier), while the head of state is the public persona of a sovereign state (e.g., President, Monarch). In presidential systems, these roles are often combined in one person; in parliamentary and semi‑presidential systems, they are often distinct.

Rationale for this question: Leader attendance at AELM varies year-to-year and can be influenced by domestic politics, international relations, and scheduling. The threshold of 19 aims to balance difficulty and plausibility so forecasters must assess travel intentions, domestic constraints, and bilateral issues leading into the summit. The event occurs Oct 31–Nov 1, 2025, and official attendance information is typically published promptly, allowing resolution well before Dec 31, 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: Resolve Yes if 19 or more of the 21 APEC member economies are represented in person at the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting (AELM) in Gyeongju by their head of state or head of government (including any officially designated acting head of state or acting head of government) during the period from 00:00 KST on 31 October 2025 to 23:59 KST on 1 November 2025 (KST = UTC+9). Resolve No otherwise.

What counts as a “leader” for this question:
• A “head of state” or “head of government” as defined in standard political usage (e.g., President, Prime Minister, Sultan, Monarch, Chief Executive of Hong Kong).
• An “officially designated acting” head of state or head of government (e.g., Acting President, Acting Prime Minister) at the time of AELM.

What does not count:
• Any attendee whose title indicates they are not the head of state/government and not an official acting head (e.g., Deputy Prime Minister, Minister, Special Envoy, Chargé d’affaires, “Representative” for Chinese Taipei, or similar), even if they attend AELM sessions.

Attendance modality:
• Only in-person attendance in Gyeongju counts. Remote/virtual participation, statements, or messages do not count.

Counting method and source-of-truth:
• Primary source: the official APEC “Economy Representatives” page associated with the 2025 Leaders’ Declaration (the page APEC typically publishes listing the attendee and their title for each economy). For each economy, count “leader” if the title on that page clearly indicates head of state or head of government (e.g., President, Prime Minister, Sultan, Monarch, Chief Executive) or explicitly “Acting President/Acting Prime Minister.”
• Secondary/backup sources (if the primary page is not available or is incomplete by 31 December 2025): official APEC news releases or host economy (Republic of Korea) official attendance lists/readouts published during/after AELM indicating in-person attendance of leaders ; corroboration by major international wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP) if needed.
• If sources conflict, prefer the official APEC “Economy Representatives” page; if unavailable, prefer host government official readouts, cross-checked with credible wire services.

Scope of economies to be counted (fixed set of 21): Australia; Brunei Darussalam; Canada; Chile; People’s Republic of China; Hong Kong, China; Indonesia; Japan; Republic of Korea; Malaysia; Mexico; New Zealand; Papua New Guinea; Peru; The Philippines; The Russian Federation; Singapore; Chinese Taipei; Thailand; United States of America; Viet Nam.

Event boundaries:
• The AELM is scheduled in Gyeongju on Oct 31–Nov 1, 2025, within AELW (Oct 27–Nov 1, 2025). Only attendance at AELM sessions on Oct 31–Nov 1, 2025 (KST) counts towards this question.

Resolution timing:
• The question will be resolved as soon as the official attendee information is available, and in any case no later than 31 December 2025.

question: By 23:59 Eastern Time on December 31, 2025, will the State of North Carolina have cumulatively drawn at least $200,000,000 from its HUD CDBG‑DR grant(s) for Hurricane Helene recovery?
background:
Context as of 2025‑09‑30:
- Allocation and program set‑up. HUD published its Allocation Announcement Notice (AAN) for 2023/2024 disasters on January 16, 2025 (FR‑6512‑N‑01). The notice lists the State of North Carolina and the City of Asheville as grantees under the 2025 disaster appropriations for unmet needs and mitigation. The North Carolina Department of Commerce’s Division of Community Revitalization (DCR) states that North Carolina was awarded roughly $1.4 billion for Hurricane Helene recovery (with Asheville separately awarded $225 million), received the grant agreement on July 8, 2025, and fully executed it on July 29, 2025. DRGR training occurred August 13–14, 2025, after which DCR received DRGR access. 
- Early implementation progress. North Carolina launched the Renew NC Single‑Family Housing Program and completed its first HUD CDBG‑DR‑enabled home repair on August 27, 2025. As of September 26, 2025, the state reported more than 3,400 homeowner applications and highlighted multiple recovery milestones one year after Helene.
- DRGR and draws. HUD’s Disaster Recovery Grant Reporting (DRGR) system is the official system of record grantees use to access grant funds (“draw down” funds) and report quarterly performance to HUD. question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will SCO member states sign and publicly release a founding treaty establishing an “SCO Development Bank”?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) is a Eurasian political, economic, and security organization founded in 2001; its 10 member states (as of 2025) are Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
- In the Astana Declaration (July 9, 2024), SCO member states stressed the need for financial support of projects and continued consultations on establishing an SCO Development Bank and an SCO Development Fund (Special Account).
- At the Tianjin SCO Summit (Sept 1, 2025), China’s foreign minister Wang Yi stated that “a political decision was made to set up an SCO Development Bank,” and that the SCO would launch this process. News coverage contemporaneous with the summit reported that President Xi announced plans to accelerate creation of an SCO development bank.
- The SCO Interbank Consortium (SCO IBC), established in 2005, is an existing platform for joint financing by member banks and is distinct from a proposed, treaty-based multilateral “SCO Development Bank”.

Why this question is interesting and non-trivial: There appears to be political momentum but significant institutional and legal work remains to move from a political decision to a signed intergovernmental founding instrument. Differences among member states’ preferences, legal frameworks, and timelines could affect whether a formal treaty is signed and publicly released before year-end 2025. Forecasters can analyze signals such as draft texts, domestic ratification processes, and official agendas.

Key definitions and clarifications used in this question (with links for clarity):
- "Treaty" / founding intergovernmental instrument: An international agreement concluded between states in written form and governed by international law (see Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties; link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Convention_on_the_Law_of_Treaties). For resolution purposes, acceptable instruments include a founding charter, agreement, convention, or similar treaty text that establishes a new multilateral financial institution.
- "SCO Development Bank": A new multilateral financial institution explicitly named “SCO Development Bank,” “Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Development Bank,” or a clear translation thereof (e.g., in Chinese, Russian, or other SCO official languages). This must be distinct from the SCO Interbank Consortium and not merely an expansion, memorandum of understanding, or financing framework of the SCO IBC.
- "SCO member states": The 10 states listed above; membership status as of Oct 1, 2025 is used for counting signatories.
- "Sign": The act of signature by duly authorized representatives of states on the treaty text (e.g., heads of state/government, foreign ministers, or plenipotentiaries) within the defined time window.
- "Publicly release": Publication of the signed treaty text or an official announcement confirming the signing, by the SCO Secretariat (e.g., on https://eng.sectsco.org/) or by at least two founding signatory governments on their official websites or gazettes. Credible reporting by major international news agencies (e.g., Reuters, AP) may be used as corroboration if official postings are temporarily unavailable (examples: https://www.reuters.com, https://apnews.com).
- Time window and timezone: Events counted must occur between October 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC.

Notes on what does NOT count:
- Statements of intent, political decisions, declarations, communiqués, or resolutions that do not include the signing of a founding treaty text do not count.
- Announcements about establishing only a “Development Fund (Special Account)” without a treaty establishing a “Development Bank” do not count.
- Internal banking consortium agreements among existing banks (SCO IBC) do not count.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves YES if all of the following are true:
1) Between October 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC, at least five SCO member states (as defined above) sign an intergovernmental founding treaty that establishes a new multilateral financial institution explicitly named “SCO Development Bank” or “Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Development Bank” (or a clear equivalent translation).
2) The signing is publicly released, meaning the treaty text or an official announcement confirming the signing is published by the SCO Secretariat or by at least two of the founding signatory governments on their official websites or gazettes, within the time window or no later than January 15, 2026 (publication lag allowance). Major international news agencies (e.g., Reuters, AP) can serve as corroborating sources if official postings are temporarily unavailable (examples: https://www.reuters.com, https://apnews.com).

This question resolves NO if the above conditions are not met.

Primary resolution sources:
- SCO Secretariat official website pages and communiqués: https://eng.sectsco.org/ (e.g., summit declarations and official news; Astana Declaration precedent references consultations toward bank/fund).
- Official announcements or legal publications by founding signatory governments (e.g., foreign ministry releases, treaty registries, official gazettes).
- If needed for corroboration only: Major international news agencies (e.g., Reuters, AP) contemporaneous reports.

Edge cases and tie-breakers:
- If the treaty uses a different word order or official language naming but clearly translates to “SCO Development Bank” (e.g., “Development Bank of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation”), it counts.
- If signatures occur in stages with accessions later, only signatures within the time window count toward the “at least five signatories” threshold.
- If a political decision/declaration to establish the bank is issued without a signed founding treaty text, the resolution is NO.
- If the instrument establishes only a fund (e.g., “SCO Development Fund”) without establishing a “Development Bank,” the resolution is NO.
- If the instrument expands or formalizes the SCO Interbank Consortium without establishing a separate treaty-based “Development Bank,” the resolution is NO.

question: Between Nov 1 and Dec 31, 2025, will the ICE Brent front‑month futures daily settlement price be below $60.00 per barrel on at least 18 trading days?
background:
Status quo and context as of September 30, 2025:
- On September 29, 2025, Brent crude futures fell 3.1% to close at $67.97 per barrel amid expectations that OPEC+ would confirm a production increase for November and as Kurdistan crude exports to Turkey resumed at roughly 150,000–160,000 bpd, potentially rising to ~230,000 bpd. These developments point to looser supply conditions into Q4 2025.
- The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) published in September 2025 projects Brent crude prices to decline substantially in the coming months, averaging about $59 per barrel in Q4 2025, driven by large inventory builds as OPEC+ increases production. This suggests a plausible scenario where the front-month settlement spends a significant share of trading days under $60.

Key instrument and definitions:
- ICE Brent Crude Futures: The benchmark Brent Crude Futures contract is listed on ICE Futures Europe (product page ID 219). Prices are quoted in U.S. dollars and cents per barrel, and ICE publishes daily settlement prices for listed futures contracts. ICE’s Report Center includes “Daily Settlement Prices” under Deliveries & Settlements, enabling verification of each trading day’s official settlements [0a9d4].
- Daily settlement price: ICE determines daily settlement prices during a designated settlement/marker period using trade-weighted methodologies subject to volume thresholds (for Brent Crude Futures, a designated settlement window is around 19:28–19:30; ICE documents describe designated settlement periods and thresholds used to compute settlements). For resolution, we rely on the official daily settlement price as published by ICE.
- Front-month futures contract: In futures markets, the “front month” (also called the near or spot month) is the contract with the nearest expiration date at any given time. Applied here, on each ICE trading day within the question’s window, the front-month ICE Brent Crude Futures contract is the Brent futures delivery month with the nearest remaining time to expiration on that day.

Why this question has forecasting entropy:
- EIA’s Q4 forecast near $59, alongside ongoing supply changes (OPEC+ output hikes, Kurdistan exports), implies meaningful uncertainty around how often daily settlements print below $60 in Nov–Dec 2025. The threshold of 18 days aims to balance plausibility and uncertainty.

Data availability and verification:
- ICE publishes daily settlement prices in its Report Center, which allows counting of sub-$60 daily settlements for the identified front-month contract across November and December 2025 [0a9d4].
- ICE’s Brent product specifications page documents the contract and pricing conventions for Brent Crude Futures , while ICE’s settlement period documentation explains how daily settlements are computed.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: Yes if there are at least 18 distinct ICE trading days between 2025-11-01 and 2025-12-31 (inclusive) on which the official ICE daily settlement price for the ICE Brent Crude Futures front-month contract is strictly below $60.00 per barrel; No otherwise.

Precise definitions and counting rules:
- Date window and timezone: The eligible period is from 2025-11-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. We count ICE trading days whose settlement dates fall within November and December 2025, as stamped on ICE’s official daily settlement reports [0a9d4].
- Trading day: An ICE trading day is any ICE Futures Europe business day on which the ICE Brent Crude Futures contract has an official daily settlement published by ICE. Use the dates shown in the ICE Report Center’s “Daily Settlement Prices” for Brent Crude Futures to identify trading days [0a9d4].
- Instrument: ICE Brent Crude Futures (ICE Futures Europe; product page ID 219).
- Front-month definition: For each trading day in the window, identify the Brent Crude Futures delivery month with the nearest time to expiration on that day (i.e., the “front month,” also known as the near or spot month). This is the specific contract month whose daily settlement is evaluated for the threshold.
- Daily settlement price: Use the official “daily settlement price” for the front-month Brent Crude Futures contract, as published by ICE. ICE determines these settlements during designated settlement periods using trade-weighted methodologies subject to volume thresholds; the official value published by ICE is the one to be used for comparison.
- Price comparison: “Below $60.00 per barrel” means the published ICE daily settlement price is strictly less than $60.00 (USD per barrel) for that trading day. A settlement of exactly $60.00 does not count.
- Distinct trading days: Count each eligible trading date at most once. Corrections: If ICE publishes corrections to a day’s daily settlement, use the latest official value available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Primary resolution source:
- ICE Report Center → Deliveries & Settlements → Daily Settlement Prices for ICE Brent Crude Futures. The adjudicator will tally the number of days in Nov–Dec 2025 on which the front-month’s official ICE daily settlement is < $60.00 [0a9d4].

Secondary/backup sources (if ICE’s Report Center is temporarily inaccessible):
- ICE Brent Crude Futures product page confirms the instrument and pricing conventions; it does not list daily settlements but supports the contract definition.
- The Brent 1st Line Future contract page documents that ICE publishes daily settlement prices for Brent Futures and references those settlements in its floating price/final settlement methodology, corroborating the existence and nature of daily settlements.

Background citations for context (not used for the mechanical resolution):
- Recent market conditions and price level on Sept 29, 2025: Reuters reported Brent at $67.97 and described OPEC+ output hike plans and resumption of Kurdistan exports.
- EIA STEO (September 2025) forecast for Q4 2025 average Brent price near $59/b, driven by inventory builds.

question: Will Archer’s “Midnight” (Model M001) receive an FAA Type Certificate by December 31, 2025?
background:
Summary of what forecasters need to know as of 2025-09-30:
- Aircraft and program: “Midnight” is Archer Aviation Inc.’s electric powered‑lift air taxi. In FAA documents it is designated the Archer Aviation, Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift, a special‑class aircraft intended for Parts 91 and 135 operations; the FAA finalized special‑class airworthiness criteria for this model on 2024‑05‑24. The criteria describe its configuration (12 electric motors/props; tilt on six forward props; pilot + four passengers) and the special‑class certification path under 14 CFR 21.17(b).
- What a Type Certificate (TC) is: Under 14 CFR §21.41, a TC includes the type design, operating limitations, the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), applicable regulations with which the FAA records compliance, and any other prescribed conditions/limitations. For resolution, the TC is evidenced by publication of a TCDS in the FAA’s Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) or an official FAA issuance notice.
- Powered‑lift definition: The FAA defines powered‑lift aircraft as capable of vertical takeoff, vertical landing, and low‑speed flight; many are electric VTOL “air taxis”. Midnight falls in this powered‑lift category per the FAA’s criteria.
- How/where TCs are listed: The FAA states that TCDS documents can be located via the FAA website/DRS; this is the canonical place to find an aircraft’s TCDS and confirm issuance.
- Program status and milestones in 2024–2025: Archer secured key operational/maintenance certificates on the path to commercialization: Part 145 repair station certification (2024‑02‑08) ; Part 135 air carrier & operator certificate (2024‑06‑05) ; and Part 141 flight school certification for its pilot training academy (2025‑02‑18). On 2025‑09‑22, Archer reported a Midnight flight‑test milestone reaching 7,000 ft, with a 45‑mile flight at >120 mph as part of envelope expansion; a prior flight covered ~55 miles in 31 minutes at >126 mph. These releases underscore progress but (as of their dates) do not announce TC issuance.

Why this question is plausibly uncertain: The FAA has finalized airworthiness criteria for the model and Archer has progressed on Part 135/141/145 and flight testing, but initial eVTOL type certifications are novel and complex; timing by year‑end 2025 remains genuinely uncertain yet objectively verifiable via FAA records.
resolution_criteria:
This market resolves based on whether the FAA has issued a Type Certificate (TC) for Archer Aviation Inc.’s Model M001 powered‑lift (commonly branded “Midnight”) between 2025‑01‑01 00:00:00 UTC and 2026‑01‑01 04:59:59 UTC (which corresponds to 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 Eastern Time, UTC‑5).

Definitions and sources:
- Type Certificate (TC): As defined in 14 CFR §21.41, a TC includes the type design, operating limitations, the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), the applicable regulations with which the FAA records compliance, and any other prescribed conditions or limitations.
- Relevant product: Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift (the FAA’s designation for Archer’s “Midnight”), certified as a special‑class powered‑lift per the FAA’s published criteria. Powered‑lift aircraft are defined by the FAA as capable of vertical takeoff/landing and low‑speed flight.
- Primary resolution source: FAA Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) listing of a TCDS for Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift (e.g., the presence of a TCDS entry for Model M001 in DRS). The FAA’s guidance indicates TCDS are available via the FAA website/DRS.

Resolution rules:
- Resolve Yes if, by the deadline above, any of the following are true:
  1) The FAA DRS contains a Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) for Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift, indicating the TC has been issued; or
  2) The FAA publishes an official announcement or database entry clearly stating that a Type Certificate has been issued for Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift (e.g., an FAA press/news release or official FAA database record of a TC issuance for Model M001).
- Resolve No if neither condition is met by the deadline.
- Evidence and tie‑breakers: The resolver should first search the FAA DRS for a TCDS for “Archer Aviation Inc.” and “Model M001” (or equivalent TC numbering). If DRS is unavailable at the time of resolution, the resolver may use an official FAA announcement as specified above. Company press releases or third‑party media may be considered corroborating but are insufficient on their own unless they link to or are explicitly mirrored by official FAA publications.
- Time zone: All times are interpreted as stated above; the cutoff is 2026‑01‑01 04:59:59 UTC (2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 Eastern Time, UTC‑5).

Notes for resolvers:
- The FAA finalized special‑class airworthiness criteria for the Archer Aviation Inc. Model M001 powered‑lift on 2024‑05‑24. This is background only; issuance of airworthiness criteria is not itself a Type Certificate issuance under §21.41.
- As of the latest cited Archer and FAA materials in 2024–2025, Archer has received Part 145 (2024‑02‑08), Part 135 (2024‑06‑05), and Part 141 (2025‑02‑18), and has continued flight‑test expansion through September 2025. These do not constitute a TC. The question resolves solely on TC issuance as defined above.

question: Will StandardAero’s net debt be at or below $2.200 billion as of September 30, 2025?
background:
Context as of today (2025-09-30): StandardAero, Inc. (CIK 2025410) is an SEC registrant that files quarterly reports on Form 10‑Q. Its Q2 2025 Form 10‑Q (for the quarter ended June 30, 2025) was filed on August 14, 2025 under the legal name “StandardAero, Inc.”. In the company’s Q2 2025 earnings press release, StandardAero stated: “Net debt, calculated as total funded debt, net of cash and cash equivalents on our balance sheet as of June 30, 2025, was $2,262.5 million compared to $3,266.0 million as of June 30, 2024.” The same release reports Net Debt to Adjusted EBITDA of 3.0x and defines net debt in narrative terms, as quoted above. The Q2 2025 Form 10‑Q provides balance sheet components relevant to net debt: cash of $91,513 thousand and total debt (including current portion) of $2,318,592 thousand as of June 30, 2025.

Why this threshold may be high-entropy: Movements in net debt between June 30 and September 30, 2025 can reflect free cash flow generation, working capital seasonality, acquisition/disposition activity, and financing transactions. The company’s net debt has declined year over year, but quarter-to-quarter variability creates uncertainty around whether the September 30 figure will cross below a $2.200 billion threshold.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- Form 10‑Q: the SEC quarterly report for U.S. public companies. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Form_10-Q
- Net debt: commonly defined as total debt minus cash and cash equivalents. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_debt. StandardAero’s press release describes net debt as “total funded debt, net of cash and cash equivalents,” which is consistent with common usage.
- Cash and cash equivalents: highly liquid assets with maturities of three months or less; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_and_cash_equivalents
- United States dollar (USD): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar

Primary sources likely to contain the resolving figure:
- StandardAero’s Form 10‑Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2025 on EDGAR under CIK 2025410 (company: StandardAero, Inc.).
- If needed as a fallback, the company’s Q3 2025 earnings press release on its investor relations site, which in prior quarters has disclosed an explicit “net debt” figure and its calculation description.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve Yes if StandardAero’s net debt as of September 30, 2025 is less than or equal to $2,200,000,000 USD; resolve No if it is greater than $2,200,000,000 USD.

Eligible time window for sources: The resolving source must be first published between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Company and scope:

- Currency: U.S. dollars. Where figures are presented in thousands or millions, convert exactly (e.g., $2,200,000,000 ≡ $2,200.0 million ≡ 2,200,000 thousand USD).

Source hierarchy and how to read it:
1) Primary: StandardAero’s Form 10‑Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2025 (Q3 2025). If the filing explicitly states a “net debt” amount as of September 30, 2025, use that figure without adjustment. If multiple “net debt” figures appear, use the one clearly labeled “as of September 30, 2025.” Ignore ratios (e.g., “Net debt to Adjusted EBITDA”); only the net debt amount counts. The Form 10‑Q should be accessed via EDGAR under CIK 2025410.
2) Fallback (if the Q3 2025 Form 10‑Q does not state a “net debt” figure, or is not filed by the UTC cutoff): Use StandardAero’s Q3 2025 earnings press release posted on its investor relations site, provided it explicitly states “net debt” for September 30, 2025. This is acceptable because prior quarters’ releases included an explicit net debt figure and described its calculation (“total funded debt, net of cash and cash equivalents”).
3) Computation fallback (only if neither of the above explicitly states net debt): Compute net debt as “total debt (including current portion)” minus “cash and cash equivalents,” both taken from the Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheet as of September 30, 2025 in the Q3 2025 Form 10‑Q. Use the exact numbers as presented (typically in thousands) and perform a simple subtraction to arrive at net debt. Compare the resulting USD amount to $2,200,000,000. This fallback mirrors common net debt practice and aligns with how the company presents components relevant to net debt in its financial statements.

Rounding and comparison:
- Compare the numeric amounts as reported. If a net debt figure is presented to one decimal place in millions (e.g., $2,262.5 million), compare that number directly to $2,200.0 million. If computing from the balance sheet, perform the subtraction in the native units (e.g., thousands) and convert precisely to USD before comparing. Do not round in a way that changes the side of the threshold.

Restatements and multiple sources:
- If a restated Q3 2025 Form 10‑Q or corrected press release is published before the UTC cutoff, use the latest version available before the cutoff. If multiple eligible sources exist and provide different net debt amounts, prefer the explicit “net debt” figure from the Q3 2025 Form 10‑Q (if present); otherwise, prefer the explicit “net debt” figure from the Q3 press release; otherwise, use the computed fallback as specified above.

Exclusions:
- Do not use covenant definitions of debt, pro forma metrics, or forward-looking statements. Only use amounts as of September 30, 2025. Do not use leverage ratios or non‑GAAP reconciliations except insofar as they show an explicit net debt amount as of September 30, 2025.

Resolution timing and verifiability:
- The question resolves upon identification of the applicable figure from the first eligible source in the hierarchy published within the time window. A human should be able to verify the outcome within 10 minutes by checking the Q3 2025 Form 10‑Q on EDGAR (CIK 2025410) or the Q3 2025 earnings press release on StandardAero’s IR site.

question: Between 00:00 UTC Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC Dec 31, 2025, will an official U.S. government website publish an announcement of at least $100 million USD in new humanitarian assistance for Palestinian civilians in Gaza?
background:
Context and recent precedent
- The U.S. government has periodically announced large, discrete packages of humanitarian assistance for Palestinians, often via official press releases or statements. For example, on October 18, 2023, the White House announced $100 million in humanitarian assistance for Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. In June 2024, the United States announced an additional $404 million in life‑saving humanitarian aid to support Palestinian civilians in Gaza, the West Bank, and the region.
- In early 2025, U.S. foreign assistance underwent a significant procedural change: on January 24, 2025, the Secretary of State ordered a pause in all new obligations of foreign assistance pending an 85‑day review; a narrow waiver for “emergency food assistance” was initially granted and subsequently expanded on January 28, 2025 to include disbursements under existing “lifesaving humanitarian assistance” programs. USAID OIG reported that these actions affected the ability to disburse and oversee humanitarian programming, including in high‑risk environments like Gaza.
- Humanitarian assistance (also termed humanitarian aid) refers to immediate, short‑term material and logistical support to save lives, alleviate suffering, and maintain human dignity, distinct from longer‑term development aid.

What forecasters should watch
- Official U.S. government communications channels that have historically carried such announcements, including: White House Briefing Room (https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/), U.S. Department of State Press Releases/Media Notes (https://www.state.gov/press-releases/; https://www.state.gov/media-notes/), and USAID Press Releases (https://www.usaid.gov/news-information/press-releases). Past announcements cited above illustrate the format and language typically used (“announces additional humanitarian assistance,” “new aid”).
- Policy and operational constraints in 2025 (e.g., the January 2025 pause and limited waivers) that could affect the likelihood, timing, or scale of any new announcements.

Definitions and geographic scope (for context)
- Gaza/Gaza Strip: the Palestinian territory on the Mediterranean bordered by Israel and Egypt; references to “Gaza” in U.S. announcements typically denote this territory as the beneficiary area.
- Palestinian people: an Arab ethnonational group native to Palestine; U.S. announcements often refer to “Palestinian civilians” when designating beneficiaries.

Status as of 2025‑10‑01
- As of the question’s publication date, forecasters should use the 2023–2024 precedents for scale and phrasing of announcements and the 2025 policy context to inform their estimates.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and time zone
- The eligible window runs from 00:00 UTC on 2025‑10‑15 through 23:59 UTC on 2025‑12‑31, inclusive. If an official page displays only a calendar date (no time), that date must fall within this window to qualify.

What resolves “Yes”
- A “Yes” resolution requires at least one qualifying announcement, posted within the window, on an official U.S. government executive branch website (a.gov domain controlled by the White House or an executive department/agency such as whitehouse.gov, state.gov, or usaid.gov), that:
  1) Publicly announces a single package of humanitarian assistance (aka humanitarian aid) ; and
  2) Explicitly identifies Palestinian civilians in Gaza as beneficiaries (Gaza alone or Gaza together with the West Bank and/or the region); and
  3) States a total amount for that package of at least $100,000,000 (one hundred million U.S. dollars). The amount must be unambiguous and represent a firm commitment (e.g., “announces $X,” “will provide $X,” “additional $X”). Language such as “up to $X” does not qualify unless a minimum equal to or greater than $100,000,000 is also explicitly stated; and
  4) Characterizes the funding as new or additional relative to prior U.S. commitments (e.g., uses words like “new,” “additional,” or equivalent), indicating that this is not merely a restatement of cumulative totals.

Definitions and counting rules
- Humanitarian assistance/humanitarian aid: immediate, short‑term material/logistics aid to save lives and alleviate suffering; excludes military/security assistance and development/reconstruction funding unless the announcement itself characterizes it as humanitarian assistance/aid.
- Gaza/Gaza Strip: the territory commonly referred to as Gaza; references to “Gaza” in the announcement satisfy the geographic condition. “Palestinian civilians” refers to members of the Palestinian people as commonly understood in humanitarian contexts.
- Package: a discrete funding commitment announced in a single official communication. If a qualifying announcement lists multiple line items for Palestinians (e.g., food, medical, shelter) within the same communication, those amounts may be summed to determine whether the $100,000,000 threshold is met. If an announcement covers multiple countries/beneficiaries, only the amounts explicitly designated for Palestinians (with Gaza included) may be counted toward the threshold.
- Currency: The qualifying announcement must state the package amount in U.S. dollars (USD). If multiple currencies are shown, a USD figure must be present in the same announcement.

Exclusions (do not count)
- Media reporting or third‑party summaries without a corresponding official U.S. government executive branch web page meeting the criteria.
- Announcements that solely restate cumulative totals provided “since [year]” without a distinct new/additional package meeting the threshold.
- Announcements that use only “up to $X” without stating a committed minimum ≥ $100,000,000.
- Military/security assistance or non‑humanitarian development/reconstruction funding unless the announcement explicitly frames it as humanitarian assistance/aid.

Resolution sources and verification
- Primary sources for verification include: White House Briefing Room (https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/), U.S. Department of State Press Releases/Media Notes (https://www.state.gov/press-releases/; https://www.state.gov/media-notes/), and USAID Press Releases (https://www.usaid.gov/news-information/press-releases). Past examples of qualifying announcement formats include the White House’s Oct 18, 2023 $100 million announcement  and references to the June 2024 $404 million U.S. announcement. If multiple qualifying announcements occur, a single instance is sufficient for “Yes”; otherwise resolve “No.”

question: Will global passenger plug-in vehicle registrations (BEV+PHEV) reach at least 18.5 million between 2025-01-01 and 2025-10-31 (UTC)?
background:
Why this matters: Plug-in electric vehicle adoption is a key driver of electronic content growth in the auto sector (e.g., connectors, sensors, harnesses), benefiting suppliers to EV platforms. Measuring cumulative global plug-in registrations through October provides a timely signal of 2025 momentum while allowing resolution before year-end.

Scope and definitions forecasters should use:
- Sales means new vehicle registrations (i.e., first-time registrations of new vehicles), not shipments or production, and excludes used-vehicle imports and re-registrations. See general concept: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_vehicle_registration
- Plug-in vehicles include only Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) and Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs). BEV definition: a vehicle powered exclusively by electricity from onboard batteries and electric motors: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicle. PHEV definition: a hybrid with a rechargeable battery that can be charged via an external power source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plug-in_hybrid
- Passenger plug-in vehicles are light-duty passenger vehicles (cars, SUVs, crossovers, MPVs, and light pickup trucks) as classified by the reporting source, and exclude buses, coaches, medium/heavy trucks, and two/three-wheelers. When sources label data as “passenger (light-duty) BEV+PHEV,” use that scope; if a dataset mixes commercial/heavy vehicles, it is not eligible unless it provides a clearly labeled passenger-only figure.
- Global means all countries/territories combined.

Status quo (approximate, for context only):
- 2023 global electric car sales were on the order of the mid-teens of millions (widely reported around ~14 million), with China, Europe, and the United States the top markets.
- 2024 global electric car sales were widely reported in the high-teens of millions, with EV share exceeding one-fifth of new car sales. Monthly plug-in registrations in mid-2025 were often reported around the mid-to-high 1.x million range per month globally. Forecasters should consult current monthly sources for precise, up-to-date figures.

Forecasting considerations:
- Policy changes (e.g., incentives, tariffs, emissions standards), pricing and discounting, battery costs, China market dynamics, and supply chain constraints can materially influence monthly run-rates.
- Seasonality and end-of-quarter pushes (notably in China and Europe) affect Oct totals.
- Data coverage and lag vary; using sources with consistent global passenger BEV+PHEV definitions is critical for accurate comparisons.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if the cumulative number of global passenger plug-in vehicle registrations (BEV+PHEV) from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-10-31 23:59:59 UTC is at least 18,500,000 units, and No otherwise.

Counting rules and definitions:
- Count only first-time registrations of new passenger light-duty BEVs and PHEVs within the period defined above. Exclude HEVs (non-plug-in hybrids), FCEVs, two/three-wheelers, buses, medium/heavy trucks, used imports, and re-registrations.
- If a source includes range-extended EVs (EREVs) within PHEVs, count them as PHEVs.
- “Units” means one vehicle.

Eligible data and source priority (must be published on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC):
1) EV-Volumes (ev-volumes.com) cumulative global plug-in passenger vehicle registrations for Jan–Oct 2025. Use the latest public figure posted on or before the resolution deadline (e.g., a year-to-date chart, a world summary post, or a 2025 monthly wrap-up explicitly stating Jan–Oct global cumulative passenger BEV+PHEV registrations).
2) If (1) is not publicly available by the deadline: a reputable outlet that directly cites EV-Volumes’ Jan–Oct 2025 global cumulative passenger BEV+PHEV total (examples include CleanTechnica, InsideEVs, Autovista24), provided the article clearly attributes the number to EV-Volumes and gives a single global Jan–Oct passenger BEV+PHEV cumulative total.
3) If neither (1) nor (2) is available: Rho Motion or BloombergNEF publications explicitly stating the Jan–Oct 2025 global passenger BEV+PHEV cumulative total; the publication must clearly indicate passenger (light-duty) scope. If both are available and disagree, prioritize the source that explicitly states passenger-only BEV+PHEV scope without commercial/heavy vehicles mixed in. If both have clear passenger scope and disagree, take the lower of the two to avoid overcounting across scope differences.

Ties, discrepancies, and revisions:
- If multiple eligible sources provide different Jan–Oct global cumulative passenger BEV+PHEV totals by the deadline, apply the priority order above. If two sources at the same priority level disagree, resolve using the lower figure to ensure conservative counting.
- Only publications with a visible date on or before the deadline are eligible. Revisions or publications dated after the deadline do not affect resolution.
- If no eligible source publishes a global Jan–Oct 2025 cumulative figure by the deadline, the market will be resolved N/A (void). However, based on historical publication cadence, at least one eligible source is expected to have published such a figure before year-end.

Documentation for resolution:
- The resolver will archive the relevant page(s) (web capture) showing the global Jan–Oct 2025 passenger BEV+PHEV cumulative figure and publication date. Definitions in this question supersede ambiguous source labeling; if a posted figure is clearly not passenger-only or includes non-plug-in vehicles, it is ineligible.

Clarifications:
- Timezone: All dates/times in this question are in UTC.
- Geographic scope: All countries and territories worldwide.
- Vehicle scope: Passenger light-duty vehicles only; if a source’s “passenger EV” category explicitly includes light pickup trucks/SUVs under ~8,500 lb GVWR, those count; commercial vans/trucks do not.
- Technology scope: Only BEVs and PHEVs count; HEVs and FCEVs do not.

question: Will the UK CPI 12‑month rate (All items) for November 2025 be at least 3.6%?
background:
Overview and definitions:
- Consumer Prices Index (CPI): The UK CPI is a measure of consumer price inflation produced to international standards and aligned with the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP). It measures the average change from month to month in the prices of consumer goods and services purchased in the UK. The CPI excludes owner occupiers’ housing costs and Council Tax, whereas CPIH includes them. CPI is the inflation measure used in the UK government’s inflation target. See also general background on the UK CPI’s compilation and methodology.
- 12‑month rate (year‑on‑year, YoY): The most common approach to measuring inflation is the 12‑month rate, which compares the price index for the latest month with the same month a year earlier. In ONS bulletins, this is reported for “CPI All items” and presented to one decimal place.

Current status (as of 2025‑10‑01):
- Latest published headline CPI YoY: The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 3.8% in the 12 months to August 2025, unchanged from July 2025. ONS reports the “CPI All items” 12‑month rate in the bulletin summary and tables.
- Near‑term projection context: The Bank of England’s August 2025 Monetary Policy Report projects CPI inflation to average around 3¾% in H2 2025, peaking near 4.0% in September, then easing, with a baseline forecast of 3.8% in 2025 Q3 and 3.6% in 2025 Q4. This makes a 3.6% threshold for November plausibly balanced between higher and lower outcomes.

Release timing and source:
- The Office for National Statistics (ONS) “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025” release is scheduled for 07:00 UK time (UTC) on 17 December 2025, and is the authoritative source for the November 2025 CPI figures.

Why this threshold and question design:
- The 3.6% threshold is chosen to target a non‑trivial forecast given recent outcomes (3.8% in August) and official projections (Q4 2025 around 3.6%), aiming for uncertainty where skilled research can improve forecasts.

Clarifications:
- “CPI (YoY)” in this question refers specifically to the ONS‑published “CPI All items” 12‑month rate for November 2025, reported to one decimal place in the statistical bulletin.
- CPI vs CPIH: CPI is used here (not CPIH). CPIH is ONS’s lead index for measuring consumer price inflation including owner occupiers’ housing costs, but CPI remains the measure used for the government’s inflation target and is the one specified in this question.
- Timezone and window: The event and resolution are based on the ONS bulletin released at 07:00 UK time (UTC) on 2025‑12‑17. The question concerns the period between 2025‑10‑15 00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59 UTC.

Key links for forecasters:
- ONS release page (will host the bulletin): “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025”.
- ONS methodology overview for CPI/CPIH: “Consumer price inflation (includes CPIH, CPI and RPI): QMI”.
- General CPI overview (reference): “Consumer price index in the United Kingdom”.
resolution_criteria:
- Resolution rule: Resolve “Yes” if the ONS “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025” bulletin reports the headline “CPI All items” 12‑month rate for November 2025 as greater than or equal to 3.6% (using the one‑decimal figure ONS publishes). Resolve “No” if it is less than 3.6%.
- Source of truth: The ONS release page and its bulletin for “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025” are the primary source. The resolver will verify the one‑decimal CPI 12‑month rate shown in the bulletin text and tables (e.g., the table of CPI annual and monthly inflation rates by division that includes “CPI All items”).
- Timing: Use the figure as published at 07:00 UK time (UTC) on 2025‑12‑17. If the bulletin is temporarily inaccessible, use the downloadable PDF bulletin or ONS‑hosted datasets linked from the release page. Later revisions or corrections, if any, will not be considered for resolution unless ONS issues an explicit same‑day correction to the headline CPI 12‑month rate; in the absence of such a same‑day correction, the initial published value is final for resolution.
- Definitions binding this question:
  • “CPI (YoY)” means the ONS‑reported “CPI All items” 12‑month rate: the percentage change comparing the CPI index level for November 2025 to November 2024, as defined by ONS methodology.
  • “At least 3.6%” means ≥ 3.6% using ONS’s published one‑decimal figure; no independent rounding or re‑calculation will be applied.
- Date window: Eligible event for resolution is the ONS bulletin publication occurring between 2025‑10‑15 00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59 UTC; the scheduled release is 2025‑12‑17 07:00 UK time (UTC).

question: Will Canada’s seasonally adjusted employment in NAICS 54 be higher in November 2025 than in August 2025?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
- What is being compared: Canada’s seasonally adjusted employment level in the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) sector 54, “Professional, scientific and technical services,” for the reference months August 2025 and November 2025, as measured by Statistics Canada’s Labour Force Survey (LFS) and published in data table 14-10-0355-01 (“Employment by industry, monthly, seasonally adjusted and unadjusted, and trend-cycle, last 5 months”). This table presents monthly LFS employment by detailed industry and includes a seasonally adjusted series suitable for month-to-month comparisons.
- NAICS 54 definition: Statistics Canada defines NAICS 2022 sector 54 as establishments “primarily engaged in activities in which human capital is the major input,” selling expertise such as legal, accounting, architectural and engineering, specialized design, computer systems design, management/scientific/technical consulting, R&D, and advertising/public relations. Most industries in this sector depend on worker skills rather than equipment/materials.
- LFS “employment” definition (who counts as employed): In the LFS, employed persons are those who, during the reference week, (a) did any work at a job or business (paid work or self-employment, including unpaid family work contributing to a family enterprise), or (b) had a job but were not at work due to temporary reasons such as illness/disability, personal/family responsibilities, vacation, or labour dispute (excluding those on layoff, between casual jobs, or without a current job).
- “Seasonally adjusted” definition: In the LFS, seasonally adjusted series remove seasonal and calendar effects (e.g., trading days, moving holidays) to facilitate meaningful month-to-month comparisons; they are constructed by decomposing the original series into components and removing seasonal/calendar effects. LFS seasonally adjusted national estimates are published monthly in The Daily and in Statistics Canada data tables.
- Recent industry context: In August 2025, employment in professional, scientific and technical services decreased by 26,000 (-1.3%) month over month, though it was up 36,000 (+1.8%) compared with 12 months earlier.
- Availability for resolution: The LFS release for the November 2025 reference month is scheduled for December 5, 2025, ensuring that the November 2025 value will be publicly available before December 31, 2025.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial: NAICS 54 employment is sensitive to macroeconomic conditions (e.g., demand for professional services, tech/business investment, government spending) and can show meaningful month-to-month variation. The direction-of-change framing (November versus August) avoids the need to pick a fixed numeric threshold while keeping the outcome uncertain and researchable via sectoral news, hiring surveys, and macro indicators.

Primary data source for resolution: Statistics Canada Table 14-10-0355-01, “Employment by industry, monthly, seasonally adjusted and unadjusted, and trend-cycle, last 5 months” (product ID 1410035501).
resolution_criteria:
Operational question: Resolve YES if the seasonally adjusted national employment level for NAICS 54 (“Professional, scientific and technical services”) published for November 2025 is strictly greater than the value published for August 2025 in Statistics Canada data table 14-10-0355-01; otherwise resolve NO.

Series selection and labels to use in the table:
- Geography: Canada (national total)
- Industry: Professional, scientific and technical services (NAICS 54) as defined by Statistics Canada’s NAICS 2022 sector 54 
- Data type: Employment (persons), seasonally adjusted, as defined by the LFS 
- Reference months to compare: August 2025 and November 2025.

Comparison rule:
- “Higher” means strictly greater than (i.e., November 2025 value > August 2025 value). If the two values are equal, resolve NO.
- Use the exact numeric values as published in Statistics Canada Table 14-10-0355-01 at or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Timing and source availability:
- The November 2025 LFS release is scheduled for December 5, 2025, which ensures the November 2025 value will be available for resolution before December 31, 2025. If Statistics Canada publishes the data earlier than expected, the earlier publication is valid. If publication is delayed but occurs on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, use the published values available by that time.

Definitions (for avoidance of doubt):
- “Employment”: as defined in the LFS Guide (see Background), i.e., persons who worked during the reference week or had a job but were temporarily absent for specified reasons.
- “Seasonally adjusted”: as defined in the LFS Guide; a series with seasonal and calendar effects removed using standard decomposition techniques to enable meaningful period-to-period comparisons.
- “NAICS 54”: the Statistics Canada NAICS 2022 sector “Professional, scientific and technical services” (see Background for scope).

Primary resolution source:
- Statistics Canada Table 14-10-0355-01 (product 1410035501), which displays the last five months of monthly employment by industry, including a seasonally adjusted series appropriate for this comparison.

Notes:
- This question concerns exactly the two reference months specified (August 2025 and November 2025). No other months will be considered.
- If Statistics Canada issues revisions to either value prior to 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, use the values as displayed in Table 14-10-0355-01 by that timestamp.

question: Will U.S. utility-scale solar PV capacity additions from Jan 1 to Nov 30, 2025 exceed 29 GW (AC, net summer)?
background:
Context: The user-provided background indicates solar is dominating new U.S. capacity additions in 2025 and that forecasts put 2025 solar additions around the low-30s GW range, with utility-scale leading and distributed solar also significant (user artifact). To ensure unambiguous and timely resolution by Dec 31, 2025, this question focuses on utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) additions measured on an AC basis using EIA’s net summer capacity metric.

Key definitions and scope:
- Technology: Solar photovoltaic (PV) only, excluding solar thermal/CSP. See photovoltaic technology overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaics and note EIA distinguishes “Solar Photovoltaic” from “Solar Thermal” in its capacity tables.
- Capacity metric: Net summer capacity (AC), the EIA’s measure of the maximum output during summer peak conditions, in megawatts (MW). See EIA capacity concepts: https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us-generation-capacity-and-sales.php
- Utility-scale scope: Utility-scale plants are those with total generating capacity of at least 1 megawatt (MW). See EIA explanation: https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us-generation-capacity-and-sales.php
- Geography: United States total = 50 states and the District of Columbia.

Why Jan–Nov and AC net summer? EIA’s Electric Power Monthly (EPM) Table 6.1 reports utility-scale capacity additions monthly in net summer MW. Because EIA publications have a short data lag, the December 2025 EPM (and/or the December 2025 EIA-860M release) should provide data through at least November 2025, enabling resolution by Dec 31, 2025 without waiting for December’s final data. This avoids ambiguity around DC vs AC ratings and aligns with a recurring, authoritative data source that will exist by the resolution date.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if the sum of U.S. utility-scale Solar Photovoltaic capacity additions, measured in net summer capacity (AC), from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC exceeds 29,000 MW (i.e., >29.000 GW). Otherwise, it resolves No.

Measurement and data sources:
1) Primary source: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Electric Power Monthly (EPM), Table 6.1 “Electric Generating Summer Capacity Changes (MW) for Utility Scale Units” (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/). Use the latest EPM available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Sum the monthly “Additions” for the technology category “Solar Photovoltaic” for January–November 2025 across the United States (50 states + DC). This table is in net summer MW (AC) and includes only utility-scale units (≥1 MW).
2) If the November 2025 “Additions” are not yet available in EPM by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, use EIA’s Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory (EIA-860M) December 2025 release (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia860m/) to obtain November 2025 utility-scale Solar Photovoltaic “new generator(s) placed in service” and their net summer capacity (AC).
