Add this November value to the January–October 2025 sum from EPM Table 6.1.

Counting rules and definitions:
- Include only Solar Photovoltaic (PV). Exclude Solar Thermal/CSP and hybrid non-PV solar technologies.
- Include only utility-scale units (plants with ≥1 MW total generating capacity as defined by EIA) and only “Additions” (i.e., new units placed in service). Exclude retirements, uprates/derates, re-ratings, or capacity changes not representing new PV additions.
- Use net summer capacity (AC) in MW as reported by EIA. Convert to GW only for the threshold (29,000 MW = 29 GW). Do not use DC nameplate ratings.
- Geography: U.S. total = 50 states + District of Columbia; exclude U.S. territories.
- Timing: EIA’s monthly data are reported by effective month; time-of-day is not applicable beyond month boundaries. The window is inclusive of January and November 2025.

Precedence and revisions:
- If EPM and EIA-860M disagree for overlapping months, prefer EPM Table 6.1 for those months. Use EIA-860M only for November 2025 if EPM’s November is unavailable by the resolution time.
- If EIA publishes revisions before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, use the latest data available at that time. Revisions after this timestamp are ignored.

Outcome mapping:
- Yes: Sum of Jan–Nov 2025 U.S. utility-scale Solar PV additions (net summer MW AC) > 29,000 MW.
- No: Otherwise.

question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, will the Council of the European Union adopt a 19th sanctions package against Russia?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- The Council of the EU adopted the 16th sanctions package against Russia on 24 February 2025.
- The Council adopted the 17th sanctions package on 20 May 2025; while the press release title says “EU agrees 17th package,” the body states “The Council adopted today the 17th package of economic and individual restrictive measures”.
- The Council adopted the 18th sanctions package on 18 July 2025, with a press release titled “EU adopts 18th package of economic and individual measures” stating “The Council adopted today a 18th package of economic and individual restrictive measures…”.
- On 19 August 2025, European Council President António Costa said the EU was “moving forward with the preparation of the 19th package of sanctions” against Russia.
- On 16 September 2025, discussion of a new Russia sanctions package was removed from an EU meeting agenda with “no new date planned” at that time.
- On 19 September 2025, Reuters reported that the European Commission proposed a 19th package to member states, including measures touching energy (e.g., advancing an LNG import ban to 1 January 2027), finance (transaction bans on additional banks and crypto platforms), export controls, and listings; proposals require member-state agreement before adoption.
- On 25 September 2025, Poland’s energy minister said the proposed 19th package would close a loophole on imports of certain LPG fractions (e.g., butane/isobutane) used to circumvent prior bans.

Why this is forecast-relevant now: A 19th package has been publicly trailed and formally proposed, but not adopted as of 2025-10-01; adoption requires Council action and has shown variable timing and internal negotiation in prior rounds, leaving uncertainty for Q4 2025.

Helpful references (for context and verification):
- Council press releases for the 16th, 17th, and 18th packages demonstrate the usual phrasing and publication venue used when adoption occurs.
- The Council’s timeline pages also summarize measures by package and date (useful for cross-checking).
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and timezone:
- Eligible adoption events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). All dates/times referenced are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

What counts as “adopt a 19th sanctions package against Russia”:
- Adopt means that the Council of the European Union has formally adopted a new, numbered package of restrictive measures targeting Russia, and this is explicitly stated in an official Council press release.
- For the purposes of this market, a qualifying press release must:
  1) be published on the official Council of the EU website under Press releases and statements (consilium.europa.eu), and
  2) explicitly reference that the Council “adopted” (or “has adopted”) the “19th package” of “sanctions” and/or “economic and individual restrictive measures” against Russia (wording may include phrases like “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine”), in the body text of the release. Note: Past practice shows that even when a title says “EU agrees [n]th package,” the body text states “The Council adopted today…”; for example, on 20 May 2025 the 17th package press release body stated adoption.

Primary source of truth:
- Council of the European Union press releases: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/ (search within for relevant Russia sanctions entries). The 16th and 18th packages show the typical adoption phrasing used in press releases.

Timing determination:
- If the qualifying Council press release is dated within the resolution window, the question will resolve Yes. If the press release only indicates political agreement without stating that the Council “adopted” the 19th package in the body text during the window, this does not count.
- If no qualifying Council press release dated within the window is found by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the question resolves No.

Clarifications and edge cases:
- The press release must pertain to a package “against Russia” (e.g., “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine: EU adopts 19th package of economic and individual measures”). If paired measures concerning Belarus are included in the same communication, this still counts as long as the Council’s press release itself characterizes the adoption as the 19th package against Russia.
- Proposals by the European Commission, draft texts, political announcements, agenda items, or discussions without formal adoption do not count.
- Individual listings or targeted measures published outside a numbered package do not count unless the Council explicitly labels them as adoption of the “19th package.”
- If multiple packages (e.g., 19th and 20th) were adopted within the window, this question only concerns whether the 19th was adopted within the window.

Definitions (for clarity; links provided for general reference):
- Council of the European Union (“the Council”): one of the EU’s institutions where government ministers negotiate and adopt laws and policies. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union
- Sanctions package / restrictive measures: In this context, the numbered set of economic and/or individual restrictive measures targeting Russia, as described in Council press releases (e.g., the 16th, 17th, and 18th packages).
- Press release: An official news item published by the Council on consilium.europa.eu under “Press releases and statements,” which includes a date and explanatory body text.

Resolution procedure:
- The resolver will search the Council’s press releases page for an item that meets the criteria. If found with a date within the specified window, resolve Yes; otherwise resolve No. Examples of the required wording appear in prior adoption press releases for the 16th and 18th packages.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the Council of the European Union adopt and publish in the Official Journal restrictive measures listing either Itamar Ben‑Gvir or Bezalel Smotrich under any EU sanctions regime?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- What the Council of the European Union is and how EU sanctions are adopted: The Council of the European Union (Council) is the EU institution where ministers from member state governments adopt legislation and coordinate policies; in Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) matters (which include autonomous EU sanctions), the Council generally decides by unanimity. The EU sanctions adoption process typically involves: (1) a CFSP Council Decision (unanimity) laying down restrictive measures; and, where asset freezes or other economic/financial measures are included, (2) a Council Regulation under Article 215 TFEU (adopted by the Council, usually after a joint proposal by the High Representative and the Commission) to implement those measures. Both acts are published in the Official Journal (OJ) and usually enter into force upon publication. Listed persons are notified, including via a notice in the OJ’s C‑series. Under the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime, listings entail a travel ban (via the CFSP Decision) and an asset freeze (via the Regulation); the Regulation defines what an asset freeze and freezing of funds/economic resources mean and maintains a consolidated Annex of listed persons/entities.
- Commission proposal naming the ministers and current political environment: On 2025-09-17, the European Commission unveiled a package proposing (i) a partial suspension of EU–Israel trade concessions and (ii) sanctions listings targeting “extremist ministers” and violent settlers; adoption of the sanctions requires unanimous approval by EU member states in the Council. Reporting the same day specified the proposed sanctions include Israeli ministers Itamar Ben‑Gvir (National Security Minister) and Bezalel Smotrich (Finance Minister), certain violent settlers, and 10 Hamas members, and noted diplomats’ assessment that such sanctions were unlikely to pass because they require unanimity.
- International pressure (non‑EU): On 2025-06-10, the United Kingdom, together with Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and Norway, announced coordinated measures sanctioning Itamar Ben‑Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, including travel bans and asset freezes, citing repeated incitement of violence against Palestinian civilians. These moves underscore international scrutiny but have no legal bearing on EU decision‑making.

Why this is forecast‑worthy now: The Commission has tabled draft listings, but Council unanimity is required for CFSP listings and diplomats signal political obstacles; nevertheless, significant allied pressure exists. This creates genuine uncertainty about whether either minister will be listed by the EU within the question’s timeframe.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- Council of the European Union: Intergovernmental EU institution representing member state governments; CFSP decisions generally require unanimity.
- Restrictive measures (sanctions): Measures imposed by the Council to change a target’s behavior, adopted by unanimity under Article 29 TEU for CFSP decisions, and implemented via Council regulations under Article 215 TFEU for economic/financial aspects.
- Listing (for this question): Inclusion of a natural person’s name in an annex to a CFSP Council Decision and/or a Council Implementing Decision/Regulation that establishes or amends an EU sanctions regime (for example, under Council Regulation (EU) 2020/1998 and its corresponding CFSP Decision), as published in the OJ. Listings under the Global Human Rights regime carry a travel ban and an asset freeze; the Regulation defines and applies the asset freeze to those listed in Annex I.
- Official Journal (OJ) / EUR‑Lex: The OJ is the EU’s official gazette where CFSP Decisions and Council Regulations are published; publication triggers entry into force and is accessible via EUR‑Lex. Listed persons are also notified via an OJ C‑series notice.

Current baseline: A Commission proposal to list both ministers exists; adoption would require Council unanimity. Diplomats assess passage as uncertain/unlikely as of 2025-09-17; no adoption has been reported at the EU level as of that date.
resolution_criteria:
Question scope and timing
- Eligible window: From 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC (inclusive) through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive).
- Geographic/jurisdictional scope: European Union (EU) restrictive measures adopted by the Council of the European Union.

What counts as a Yes
- Resolve YES if, during the eligible window, the Official Journal of the European Union (OJ) publishes at least one act adopted by the Council of the European Union that lists either of the following individuals (as identified by the OJ entry’s identifying details) under any EU sanctions regime:
  - Itamar Ben‑Gvir
  - Bezalel Smotrich
- For the purpose of this market, “lists” means that the person is added as a designated individual in an annex to a CFSP Council Decision and/or to a Council Implementing Regulation/Decision under an EU restrictive measures regime (for example, the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime, which imposes travel bans via the CFSP Decision and asset freezes via the Regulation). The OJ publication must clearly identify the individual such that it unambiguously corresponds to the named minister (e.g., by name and, where provided, other identifying details like date of birth, function).
- Either a CFSP Decision listing that imposes a travel ban, or a Council Implementing Regulation/Decision adding the person to the asset-freeze annex (or both), suffices, provided the act is published in the OJ within the eligible window.

What does NOT count
- Drafts, leaks, Commission proposals, European Parliament resolutions, member state national measures, or third‑country measures do not count. Only Council‑adopted acts published in the OJ count.
- Acts published before 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC or after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC do not count, even if the legal effect date is back‑dated or forward‑dated.

Resolution sources and procedure
- Primary source of truth: The Official Journal of the European Union (as accessible via EUR‑Lex) entries publishing the relevant CFSP Decision and/or Council Implementing Regulation/Decision. The OJ is where these acts are published and enter into force.
- Secondary corroboration (optional): Council press releases summarizing adopted listings; however, only OJ publication determines resolution.

Resolution
- The market resolves to YES upon verification that the OJ, during the eligible window, publishes an EU act listing either Itamar Ben‑Gvir or Bezalel Smotrich under any EU restrictive measures regime as described above. Otherwise, the market resolves to NO.

Notes for verifiers
- Use EUR‑Lex to search the OJ for the individuals’ names during the eligible window; listings under the EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime will appear as amendments to annexes to Council Decision (CFSP) 2020/1999 and Council Regulation (EU) 2020/1998 (or their subsequent amendments), but listings under other regimes also qualify.
- If both individuals are listed, this still resolves YES. If neither is listed, resolves NO.
- Spelling variants and diacritics: The OJ’s listing (in English) controls for identity; minor spelling variations that clearly correspond to the same person are acceptable when corroborated by the OJ entry’s identifying details.

question: Will Mexico’s Official Journal (DOF) publish a change to the April 22, 2024 temporary MFN tariff decree (544 TIGIE lines) between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context and definitions (with sources)
- Diario Oficial de la Federación (DOF): Mexico’s official government gazette that publishes laws, decrees, and other binding legal acts; publication in the DOF is the step that makes such acts effective nationally. See: https://www.dof.gob.mx/ and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Journal_of_the_Federation_(Mexico)
- LIGIE/TIGIE: The Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación (LIGIE) is Mexico’s law establishing the Tarifa (customs tariff schedule). The tariff schedule is commonly referred to as the TIGIE (Tarifa de la LIGIE). The LIGIE text uses “Tarifa de la Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación (TIGIE)” and sets the structure and tariff items (“fracciones arancelarias”) by which duties are assessed. See official LIGIE PDF: https://www.diputados.gob.mx/LeyesBiblio/pdf/LIGIE_2022.pdf
- April 22, 2024 decree (the “2024 temporary tariff decree”): On April 22, 2024, Mexico published in the DOF the “Decreto por el que se modifica la Tarifa de la Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación,” establishing temporary Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) import duties ranging from 5% to 50% on 544 TIGIE tariff lines, largely in strategic sectors (e.g., steel, aluminum, textiles, clothing, footwear, wood, plastics, chemicals, paper/cardboard, ceramics, glass, electrical equipment, transport equipment, musical instruments, furniture). The decree applies the temporary MFN duties to imports from countries without a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with Mexico, preserving preferential rates for FTA-origin goods. The decree entered into force on April 23, 2024, and its temporary duties are valid for two years (through April 23, 2026) unless modified earlier.

Status quo as of 2025-10-01
- The 2024 temporary MFN duties on the 544 TIGIE lines remain scheduled to be in force until April 23, 2026, absent further modification or repeal. This question targets whether an official modification is published in the DOF during the Oct 15–Dec 31, 2025 window.

Why this may change
- Mexico periodically adjusts tariff measures via DOF-published decrees and agreements. The April 22, 2024 measure was broad and time-limited, creates sectoral incentives, and was explicitly framed as temporary, making mid-course adjustments plausible before expiry.

Key references (for forecasters)
- DOF home/search: https://www.dof.gob.mx/
- 2024 decree identifier and title (as referenced by legal summaries): “Decreto por el que se modifica la Tarifa de la Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación,” DOF, April 22, 2024.
- SNICE FAQ (MFN temporary duties; two-year validity; FTA caveat): https://www.snice.gob.mx/~oracle/SNICE_DOCS/PREGUNTASFRECUENTES-LIGIE22abr-PREGUNTAS_20240429-20240429.pdf.
- Sectoral scope summary (544 lines, strategic sectors): https://www.snice.gob.mx/cs/avi/snice/ligie.info22.mod24.html.

Note on terminology
- “Tariff line”/“fracción arancelaria” refers to the specific TIGIE code-level entries in the Tarifa used to assess duties; the LIGIE’s Tarifa structure governs classification and duty rates, and the law explicitly references “Tarifa de la Ley … (TIGIE)”.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and time zone
- Eligible publication window: On or after 2025-10-15 and on or before 2025-12-31, inclusive, based on the publication date shown on the DOF entry (Mexico City local date; Central Time, UTC−06:00 standard/UTC−05:00 daylight). If both a matutina/vespertina edition exist on a given date, any edition on an eligible date counts.

What resolves “Yes”
- Resolve Yes if the DOF publishes a legally binding instrument within the window that explicitly alters the April 22, 2024 decree establishing the temporary MFN duties on 544 TIGIE lines. Qualifying instruments include a Decreto (Decree) or Acuerdo (Agreement) that, in its text, does at least one of the following with respect to that April 22, 2024 decree:
  1) Changes any applicable MFN ad valorem duty rate for any of the 544 TIGIE fracciones covered by the April 22, 2024 decree; or
  2) Adds to or removes TIGIE fracciones from the set covered by the April 22, 2024 decree; or
  3) Changes the temporal validity (start/end dates) of the April 22, 2024 temporary MFN duties; or
  4) Expands, limits, suspends, or repeals (wholly or partly) the April 22, 2024 decree’s application (e.g., modifies country-of-origin scope), provided that the instrument expressly cites and modifies that decree by title/date or modifies the specific transitory or annex provisions introduced by it.

Identification requirements for a qualifying instrument
- The instrument must explicitly reference and modify the April 22, 2024 DOF decree titled “Decreto por el que se modifica la Tarifa de la Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación” (published April 22, 2024). Acceptable language includes verbs such as “modifica,” “reforma,” “adiciona,” “deroga,” or “suspende,” coupled with a citation to that decree’s title/date or to the specific provisions/annexes it introduced.

What does NOT count
- Instruments that do not modify the April 22, 2024 decree or its directly affected TIGIE fracciones (e.g., unrelated TIGIE updates that leave all 544 lines and the decree’s temporal validity unchanged) do not count.
- Antidumping/countervailing duty resolutions (cuotas compensatorias) adopted under separate legal authorities that impose or review trade remedies without changing the MFN duty rates, coverage, or validity established by the April 22, 2024 decree do not count unless they explicitly amend that decree.
- Programmatic/administrative measures (e.g., PROSEC list updates, operational rules) that do not alter the MFN duties, covered lines, or validity of the April 22, 2024 decree do not count.
- Media reports, press releases, or unofficial compilations are not acceptable for resolution; only DOF publications count.

Source of truth and how to verify
- Primary and sufficient source: The DOF publication itself (web entry or official PDF) at https://www.dof.gob.mx/.
- The resolver will search the DOF for instruments published in the window that match the identification and content criteria above. If multiple instruments are published, any single qualifying instrument is sufficient for Yes.

Edge cases
- If an instrument is published in the DOF within the window but states a future effective date outside the window, it still counts (publication date governs eligibility).
- If an instrument consolidates prior changes published before 2025-10-15 without introducing a new modification, it does not count. If it introduces any new modification per the criteria above, it counts.
- If the DOF website is temporarily unavailable, resolution is deferred until access is restored; only the official DOF publication determines the outcome.

Resolve No otherwise (i.e., if no qualifying DOF instrument is published within the defined window).

References supporting background and definitions
- DOF definition and role: Wikipedia entries for DOF/Official Journal.
- LIGIE/TIGIE definition/usage in law: LIGIE official text (references “Tarifa … (TIGIE)”).
- April 22, 2024 decree details: scope (544 lines), rate range (5–50%), sectors, non-FTA limitation, two-year validity from April 23, 2024: legal/official summaries and SNICE FAQ.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025, will the European Commission announce a DMA non‑compliance fine against any designated gatekeeper other than Apple or Meta?
background:
Status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- Designated gatekeepers: The European Commission has designated the following undertakings as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act (DMA): Alphabet, Amazon, Apple (including iPadOS, designated 2024-04-29), ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft, and Booking (for Booking.com, designated 2024-05-13).
- First DMA non‑compliance fines (April 23, 2025): The Commission announced non‑compliance decisions imposing fines on Apple (€500 million) for breaching the DMA’s anti‑steering obligation, and on Meta (€200 million) for failing to offer users a less data‑intensive but equivalent service in its “consent or pay” model. These were the first-ever DMA fines.
- Ongoing enforcement activity: On March 19, 2025, the Commission sent preliminary findings to Alphabet indicating an initial view of DMA non‑compliance relating to Google Search and Google Play; this does not prejudge the final outcome. EU analysis around this period notes a 12‑month aim to issue non‑compliance decisions after opening proceedings (proceedings opened on March 25, 2024), implying additional decisions could plausibly occur in 2025.

Key legal definitions and what “counts” for this question:
- Gatekeeper: An undertaking designated by the Commission as a gatekeeper for at least one core platform service under the DMA (designation framework in Article 3; core concepts and definitions in Article 2).
- Fine under the DMA: A financial penalty imposed by the Commission for infringing obligations laid down in the DMA, pursuant to Article 30 (up to 10% of worldwide turnover for certain infringements; up to 1% for providing incorrect/incomplete/misleading information or refusing inspections).
- Periodic penalty payments: Coercive daily payments (up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover) to compel compliance; these are not “fines” for the purpose of this question and do not count.

Why this is forecastable now: Only Apple and Meta have been fined under the DMA so far. Other designated gatekeepers (Alphabet/Google, Amazon, ByteDance, Microsoft, Booking) remain under varying degrees of scrutiny, including Alphabet’s preliminary findings. Additional non‑compliance decisions with fines could plausibly be announced before year‑end, but are far from certain, leading to non‑trivial uncertainty.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve YES if, between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 inclusive (Europe/Brussels local time), the European Commission publishes an official announcement stating that it has adopted a decision imposing a fine pursuant to Article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (Digital Markets Act) against any gatekeeper other than Apple or Meta. Otherwise resolve NO.

Eligible entities: Any undertaking that is designated as a DMA gatekeeper at the time of the decision (e.g., Alphabet, Amazon, ByteDance, Microsoft, Booking, and Apple/Meta). However, outcomes involving Apple or Meta do not qualify for a YES. Designations as gatekeepers are as listed on the Commission’s official DMA gatekeeper page.

What counts as a qualifying “fine”: A fine imposed under the DMA (Article 30), announced in connection with a non‑compliance decision under the DMA. Periodic penalty payments (Article 31), commitments/undertakings without fines, or fines under other legal bases (e.g., EU antitrust rules under TFEU Articles 101/102) do not count.

Primary resolution source: The European Commission’s Press corner publication announcing the decision and fine (an official press release). For context on how DMA non‑compliance fines are announced, see the Commission’s April 23, 2025 announcements regarding Apple and Meta.

Time window and timezone: The announcement must be published between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 and 2025-12-31 23:59:59, Europe/Brussels local time (CEST/CET as applicable). If the press release shows only a date (no time), the local Brussels date will govern eligibility.

Start date: Only announcements first published on or after 2025-10-15 (Europe/Brussels local date) are eligible. Announcements published before that date do not count.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- If multiple fines are announced in the window, a single qualifying fine is sufficient for YES.
- If a qualifying announcement is published within the window but the decision is later annulled, modified, or appealed, resolution remains based on the original announcement within the window.
- Updates or corrections to previously published press releases do not create a new “fine” unless the Commission publishes a distinct press release announcing a separate DMA Article 30 fine within the window.

Definitions (for reference):
- Gatekeeper and core platform services are defined in the DMA (Articles 2 and 3).
- Fines and periodic penalty payments are defined in DMA Articles 30 and 31, respectively.

Evidence/examples for past practice (non‑binding but illustrative): The Commission’s April 23, 2025 DMA non‑compliance fines against Apple (€500m) and Meta (€200m) were publicly announced via official EU channels. This demonstrates the type of publication that will be used to resolve this question.

Sources to consult at resolution time:
- European Commission Press corner (official press releases). If needed to verify gatekeeper status or context, consult the Commission’s DMA gatekeeper list. For legal grounding of what constitutes a DMA fine and periodic penalty payment, consult DMA Articles 30 and 31 summaries.

question: Will a new section 26 U.S.C. § 899 be enacted into law in 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:

• Legislative status in mid-2025: A “Section 899” provision targeting "unfair foreign taxes" (including the OECD Pillar Two Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR) and certain digital services taxes) was included in the House-passed One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), but it was removed prior to enactment; the final law did not include Section 899. On June 26, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asked congressional leaders to remove Section 899 from the bill, and Senate/House tax Chairs publicly confirmed its removal, citing an understanding reached with G7 partners.

• G7 “side-by-side” understanding: On June 28, 2025, the G7 released a statement describing a shared understanding for a "side-by-side" approach that would fully exclude U.S.-parented groups from the UTPR and IIR, recognizing existing U.S. minimum tax rules. The statement explicitly characterizes this as a high-level understanding to be developed within the OECD Inclusive Framework and notes the removal of Section 899 as crucial to enabling discussion; it is not a finalized agreement.

• Possibility of revival: Reporting and analysis in late September 2025 indicate that if OECD work to finalize Pillar Two exemptions stalls, Treasury officials and House leadership may support reviving Section 899 in fall legislation (e.g., a supplemental bill), making enactment by year-end plausible but uncertain.

• What proposed Section 899 would have done (for forecaster context): The provision would have increased U.S. taxes on "applicable persons" from "offending foreign countries" deemed to impose unfair foreign taxes, raising rates on categories such as FDAP income and ECI and expanding BEAT; House and Senate drafts varied on scope and maximum surcharges (e.g., up to 20 percentage points in the House; up to 15 in the Senate). The CRS notes it was projected to raise significant revenue, and as of July 9, 2025 it was not enacted.

Key definitions and links for clarity:
• Internal Revenue Code (IRC): Title 26 of the United States Code (U.S.C.). See general reference: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26
• UTPR and IIR: Elements of OECD/G20 BEPS Pillar Two minimum tax rules. Overview of UTPR: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_minimum_tax (overview page; forecasters may consult OECD sources directly).
• Public Law: A statute enacted by Congress and signed by the President or enacted via veto override; see Congress.gov for official legislative history: https://www.congress.gov
• Official law text repository: govinfo.gov for Public Law PDFs and XML: https://www.govinfo.gov/app/collection/plaw
• U.S. Code updates: Office of the Law Revision Counsel (OLRC): https://uscode.house.gov (updates may lag; the primary evidence will be the enacted Public Law text and OLRC classification tables).

Why this question has non-trivial uncertainty now: The G7 “side-by-side” remains a shared understanding pending OECD work, while U.S. policymakers have signaled potential legislative reintroduction if multilateral progress falters. Enactment by year-end is plausible via omnibus or supplemental legislation but far from guaranteed.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome determination
• Eligible event window: Between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
• Yes: If, within the eligible window, a Public Law is enacted that amends Title 26 of the United States Code (the Internal Revenue Code) to create or designate a section numbered 899 (i.e., a new 26 U.S.C. § 899 exists as a result of the enacted law). This can occur by adding a new section designated “899” or by redesignating an existing section to “899.”
• No: If no such Public Law is enacted within the eligible window.

Resolution procedure (as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC):
1) Verify whether any Public Law enacted in 2025 includes text that amends Title 26 to add, insert, or redesignate a section to be numbered “899.” Use the official Public Law text on govinfo.gov (primary source) and confirm the law number/date (e.g., via Congress.gov legislative history).
2) If needed, consult OLRC classification tables (uscode.house.gov) to confirm that the enacted law is classified to Title 26 and results in a section number 899 in the U.S. Code (acknowledging OLRC updates may lag; the Public Law text itself is controlling for whether Congress enacted a new section 899).

Disambiguation and definitions
• "Public Law enacted": A bill that becomes law upon the President’s signature or via Congressional veto override and is assigned a Public Law number; resolvable via Congress.gov/govinfo.gov official records.
• "Amends Title 26 to create/designate section 899": The enacted law must explicitly amend Title 26 (the Internal Revenue Code) and create a section numbered 899 in Title 26; references to "Sec. 899" as a section of the Act itself (internal section numbering of the bill) do not count unless they expressly amend Title 26 to add or redesignate 26 U.S.C. § 899. The content of the section is immaterial to resolution; only the creation/designation of the section number in Title 26 matters.
• Time zone: All dates/times are UTC.

Primary resolution sources
• govinfo.gov: Public Law text repository (authoritative law text).
• Congress.gov: Legislative history confirming enactment dates and law numbers.
• OLRC (uscode.house.gov): Classification tables and/or updated U.S. Code showing 26 U.S.C. § 899 when available.

Background sources supporting current status and context:
• CRS overview and status (proposed, not enacted; differences in House/Senate drafts; final law omission).
• Tax Foundation analysis noting Section 899 did not end up in the final law and its impact on expediting G7 side-by-side.
• Treasury/press reporting on June 26 removal request and congressional confirmation of removal.
• G7 Treasury statement characterizing the “side-by-side” as a shared understanding to be developed, and noting removal of Section 899 as crucial.
• Reporting that revival could be pursued in fall 2025 if OECD progress stalls.

question: By 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, will OPEC’s officially published “required production levels” for December 2025, summed across Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman, be strictly greater than the sum for October 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- OPEC+ has been conducting monthly adjustments in 2025 among a subset of eight “voluntary cut” participants: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman. OPEC press releases describe changes relative to each country’s “required production level,” and note the eight will meet monthly to review market conditions, conformity, and compensation.
- In mid-2025 OPEC press releases documented successive monthly production adjustments measured in thousand barrels per day (kb/d): e.g., a 411 kb/d adjustment from May to June 2025, and later a 548 kb/d adjustment from July to August 2025, with language such as “equivalent to monthly increments” and referencing “required production level” tables (these tables are the source for the per-country targets). On August 3, 2025, OPEC stated the eight would implement a 547 kb/d production adjustment for September 2025 from the August 2025 required production level.
- Reporting indicates that the eight began unwinding an additional layer of voluntary cuts starting in October 2025, with plans for at least a 137 kb/d increase in November 2025 to be decided at an October 5 online meeting. Market commentary around September 30 highlighted bearish sentiment on expectations of a supply surplus and noted the resumption of Kurdistan crude exports via Turkey; contemporaneous pricing cited Brent in the high-$60s and WTI near $63.

Why this question: Comparing the official OPEC-required production levels for these eight participants in October versus December 2025 captures the policy trajectory (continued unwinding vs. pauses/reversals) in a way that is (a) concretely defined by OPEC documentation and (b) sensitive to evolving market conditions, yielding a non-trivial forecasting target.

Key definitions and links:
- OPEC: Intergovernmental organization of oil-exporting countries. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC.
- OPEC+: Informal term for the wider group including non-OPEC producers cooperating with OPEC (notably Russia). See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC#OPEC+.
- Required production level: The per-country target figure OPEC uses in 2025 press releases for the eight participating countries, stated in barrels per day (b/d) and often presented in a table; OPEC press releases explicitly use the term “required production level” for these monthly targets.
- Barrel (bbl): Unit of volume commonly used in oil markets; 1 barrel = 42 US gallons. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrel_(unit)#Oil_barrel.
- kb/d and mb/d: Thousand barrels per day and million barrels per day, respectively.

As of the date of this question, OPEC’s press releases identify the eight countries explicitly and use “required production level” as the official term for country targets in 2025. The December 2025 and October 2025 per-country levels are expected to be published by OPEC in press releases (with tables) and can be summed to form group totals. Additionally, news reporting anticipates further increases being discussed at the October 5 meeting, reflecting evolving policy and market sentiment.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: Resolve YES if the sum of the officially published “required production levels” for December 2025 for the following eight countries — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman — is strictly greater than the sum of the officially published “required production levels” for October 2025 for the same eight countries. Resolve NO otherwise.

- Countries included: Exactly these eight, as identified in OPEC press releases in 2025 regarding the monthly adjustments by the “eight participating countries”: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, UAE, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, Oman. The set of countries is fixed for this question.
- Measurement unit: Use the per-country “required production level” figures as printed by OPEC (typically in million barrels per day, mb/d). Convert to barrels per day (b/d) only if necessary; sum the raw figures to derive the group totals for October 2025 and December 2025.
- Source of truth: OPEC official Media Centre press releases (opec.org), specifically the 2025 press releases that provide the “required production level” tables for these eight countries for October 2025 and for December 2025. Start at https://www.opec.org/ and navigate to Media Centre → Press Releases. The wording and the tables referenced in OPEC press releases (e.g., mentions of “required production level” and “monthly increments”) confirm this is the correct data source.
- Multiple publications/revisions: If OPEC publishes more than one press release affecting a month’s required production levels, use the latest official OPEC press release for that month published no later than 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
- Data availability contingency: If OPEC does not publish a press release with the December 2025 required production level table by the resolution cutoff, resolve NO by default (because the condition “strictly greater” cannot be verified). If OPEC publishes the December table but not the October table, use the last official OPEC press release applicable to October 2025 (e.g., the document that sets October’s “required production levels” via “monthly increments”) published no later than 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
- Timeframe: The resolution decision will be made using OPEC materials available up to and including 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
- Tie and rounding: “Strictly greater” means the December 2025 sum must exceed the October 2025 sum by any positive amount (after summing the officially printed figures). If the sums are equal or if December is less than October, resolve NO.

Notes for resolvers:
- OPEC press releases in 2025 explicitly use “required production level” for the eight participating countries and reference monthly increments and adjustments, which are reflected in per-country tables; these tables should be used to compute the totals.
- Market reporting around late September 2025 anticipates at least a 137 kb/d increase in November following an October hike, with an online meeting scheduled for October 5; this context explains why December vs October totals are meaningfully uncertain.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 (ART), will the BCRA “Tipo de Cambio Mayorista ($ por USD) Comunicación A 3500 – Referencia” be at least 8% higher on Dec 31 than on Oct 15?
background:
Context and definitions a forecaster needs:

- Who publishes the rate: The Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) is Argentina’s central bank (acronym: BCRA). Official exchange-rate reference data are published on the BCRA website.
- The specific series: The daily wholesale exchange-rate reference series labelled “Tipo de Cambio Mayorista ($ por USD) Comunicación A 3500 – Referencia” is available on the BCRA Principales Variables site; it is presented as a daily economic/financial variable. The series page includes the series identifier 272 in the URL parameters and provides date-filtered historical values. The same label appears on the BCRA Principales variables summary page, which displays the latest value/date for this series. A download link for “Tipo de Cambio de Referencia Comunicación A 3500 (Mayorista)” in.xls format is also provided on the BCRA “Tipos de cambios” page.
- What the rate measures: It is quoted as Argentine pesos (ARS) per United States dollar (USD), as indicated by “($ por USD)” in the series label. The United States dollar (USD) is the official currency of the United States. The Argentine peso (ARS) is the currency of Argentina; ISO 4217 code ARS. An exchange rate is the rate at which one currency will be exchanged for another, i.e., the value of one currency in relation to another.
- Depreciation vs. the numeric test used here: Currency depreciation is a loss of value of a currency relative to another; for a rate quoted as ARS per USD, depreciation of ARS vs. USD corresponds to an increase in the ARS-per-USD figure. This question operationalizes “depreciation by at least 8%” as “the ARS-per-USD reference rate on Dec 31, 2025 being at least 8% higher than on Oct 15, 2025”.
- Time zone and date conventions: The question’s date boundaries are defined in Argentina Time (ART, UTC−03:00). The BCRA series is presented as a daily series; if an endpoint falls on a non-business day, the next published daily value will be used per the resolution criteria below.
- Status quo (as of late September 2025): The BCRA Principales variables page displays “Tipo de Cambio Mayorista ($ por USD) Comunicación A 3500 – Referencia” with a latest visible value of 1,341.00 for date 29/09/2025. Forecasters should check the series page for Oct 15 and Dec 31 values when resolving.

Primary resolution source URLs (for forecasters’ reference):
- Principales Variables – series 272: https://www.bcra.gob.ar/PublicacionesEstadisticas/Principales_variables_datos.asp?serie=272&detalle=Tipo%20de%20Cambio%20Mayorista%20($%20por%20US$)%20Comunicaci%C3%B3n%20A%203500%20-%20Referencia 
- Principales variables summary (shows latest daily value/date): https://www.bcra.gob.ar/PublicacionesEstadisticas/Principales_variables.asp 
- Tipos de cambios (download page,.xls): https://www.bcra.gob.ar/PublicacionesEstadisticas/Tipos_de_cambios.asp
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution (Yes/No). Window: Events between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 in Argentina Time (ART; UTC−03:00) are eligible. This is a single-measure comparison at the endpoints.

Definitions for this question:
- “BCRA ‘Tipo de Cambio Mayorista ($ por USD) Comunicación A 3500 – Referencia’” means the daily wholesale reference exchange-rate series published on the BCRA Principales Variables site under that exact label; the series appears with identifier 272 in the series URL parameters and provides date-filtered historical values.
- “ARS per USD” denotes Argentine pesos per United States dollar, consistent with the “($ por USD)” label on the series. USD definition ; ARS definition.
- “Percentage change” is computed as: (Value on Dec 31, 2025 − Value on Oct 15, 2025) / (Value on Oct 15, 2025). Because the series is ARS-per-USD, a positive percentage change corresponds to ARS depreciation vs. USD.
- “Business day handling”: If either endpoint date (Oct 15, 2025 or Dec 31, 2025) is a non-business day with no published value for that date, use the next calendar date on which the BCRA publishes a value for this series (i.e., the next available daily value).

Procedure:
1) Navigate to the BCRA Principales Variables series page for “Tipo de Cambio Mayorista ($ por USD) Comunicación A 3500 – Referencia” (series identifier visible in URL as 272) and retrieve the daily value for Oct 15, 2025 and for Dec 31, 2025. If a value is not published for either date, use the next available published daily value after that date.
2) Compute Percentage change = (Dec 31 value − Oct 15 value) / (Oct 15 value).
3) Resolve “Yes” if the percentage change is greater than or equal to 0.08 (≥ 8%); resolve “No” otherwise.

Primary resolution source: The BCRA Principales Variables series page described above. As a secondary check or if the primary page is temporarily unavailable, use the BCRA “Tipos de cambios” download page for “Tipo de Cambio de Referencia Comunicación A 3500 (Mayorista)” (.xls) to obtain the relevant dates’ values.

Notes:
- Use the values as displayed by BCRA at the time of resolution; no adjustments or alternative averaging should be applied.
- All dates/times referenced are in ART (UTC−03:00).
- The Principales variables summary page can be used to verify the latest displayed value/date for situational awareness, but the series page (or the download) is the authoritative source for the endpoint values.

question: Will Brazil’s central bank publish a binding regulation capping credit card interchange fees between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of Sept 30, 2025: On May 29, 2025, Reuters reported that the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) would soon launch a public consultation to discuss limits on credit card interchange fees, with the consultation focusing solely on interchange fees and remarks made at an Abipag payments-sector event. Previously, in September 2022, BCB announced a 0.7% cap for prepaid card interchange fees and simplified debit card interchange to a 0.5% per-transaction cap, with these changes scheduled to take effect from April 2023. These prior actions establish precedent for interchange fee regulation in Brazil and provide context for the potential extension of caps to credit card interchange.

Key definitions and links a forecaster may need:
- Interchange fee: A fee paid between banks for the acceptance of card-based transactions—specifically, paid by the merchant’s acquiring bank to the cardholder’s issuing bank—typically set by card networks and commonly a flat fee plus a percentage of the transaction value (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interchange_fee).
- Credit card: A payment card, typically issued by a bank, allowing consumers to purchase goods or services or withdraw cash on credit with a revolving balance subject to interest (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_card).
- Brasília Time (BRT): UTC−03:00 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_Brazil).
- Diário Oficial da União (Official Gazette) portal (Imprensa Nacional): https://www.in.gov.br/ (official federal portal where normative acts are published).

Status quo and why this is non-trivial: The BCB’s stated intention to consult on credit card interchange caps indicates policy movement but does not commit to timing or the issuance of a final, binding regulation by year-end. While Brazil has already capped prepaid and debit interchange , whether BCB will finalize and publish caps for credit cards within the specified window is uncertain and depends on the consultation outcome, stakeholder input, and regulatory priorities. This uncertainty creates a meaningful forecasting question.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves to Yes or No based on the following criteria:

Event window and time zone:
- Eligible publication events must occur between 00:00:00 on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 on Dec 31, 2025, Brasília Time (BRT, UTC−03:00).

What counts as a Yes:
- Yes if, within the event window, the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) publishes a binding normative act (i.e., a regulation, resolution, circular, instruction or similar instrument with legal effect) that establishes explicit numerical caps on interchange fees for credit card transactions in Brazil. “Caps” here means maximum limits, which may be specified as a percentage of transaction value, a weighted-average ceiling, and/or a per-transaction value ceiling (forms analogous to prior BCB actions on prepaid and debit interchange are acceptable examples ).
- The act must be final (not a draft or consultation), and the publication must be publicly accessible via official channels: either on BCB’s official website or in the Diário Oficial da União (Imprensa Nacional) portal (https://www.in.gov.br/). The act may specify an effective date in the future; publication within the window suffices for Yes.

Definitions to avoid ambiguity:
- “Interchange fee” is as defined by Wikipedia: a fee paid by the acquiring bank to the issuing bank for card-based transactions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interchange_fee).
- “Credit card” is as defined by Wikipedia: a payment card that enables purchases on credit with a revolving balance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_card).
- “Publish” means the act is officially released and viewable by the public via BCB’s site or the Diário Oficial da União portal.

What counts as a No:
- No if, by 23:59:59 BRT on Dec 31, 2025, no BCB-issued binding normative act meeting the above criteria is published within the event window.
- No if, during the window, BCB issues only draft texts, consultation documents, press releases, speeches, or non-binding guidance, without publishing a final binding normative act establishing explicit caps.

Primary resolution sources:
- Official publication of the normative act on BCB’s website (resolver may use BCB’s normative act listings) and/or its publication in the Diário Oficial da União (https://www.in.gov.br/).

Secondary corroborative sources (if needed for context, not for final determination):
- Credible media such as Reuters reporting on BCB announcements (e.g., the May 29, 2025 consultation announcement).

Notes:
- The scope is credit card interchange fees only; prepaid and debit interchange are out of scope except as examples of acceptable cap forms.
- The issuer of the act must be BCB; acts issued solely by other bodies (e.g., CMN) without a corresponding BCB binding act do not satisfy Yes within this question’s scope.
- All times are in BRT (UTC−03:00).

question: Will AAA’s “Today’s AAA National Average” for regular gasoline be below $3.000 on December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo and source: AAA’s Fuel Prices homepage displays a prominently labeled, date-stamped figure, “Today’s AAA National Average,” with the format “Price as of MM/DD/YY.” On September 30, 2025, this value was shown as $3.150 with the date stamp “Price as of 9/30/25”. The homepage also provides a breakdown table for fuel grades (Regular, Mid-Grade, Premium, Diesel, E85) with rows such as Current Avg., Yesterday Avg., Week Ago Avg., Month Ago Avg., and Year Ago Avg., and the “Regular” Current Avg. corresponds to the “Today’s AAA National Average” figure. AAA states that its Gas Prices website is updated daily by Oil Price Information Service (OPIS) and that up to 120,000 stations are surveyed for statistical reliability, making this the most comprehensive retail gasoline survey available; it publishes average national, state, and local prices.

Definitions and clarifications:
- “Today’s AAA National Average” refers to the numeric value displayed on AAA’s Fuel Prices homepage adjacent to the label “Today’s AAA National Average,” accompanied by a date stamp of the form “Price as of MM/DD/YY”.
- Fuel grade: The “Today’s AAA National Average” corresponds to Regular gasoline (the “Regular” Current Avg. in the grade table) as presented on AAA’s site. For general context on regular gasoline as a fuel grade, see Gasoline on Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasoline.
- Units and precision: Prices are displayed in U.S. dollars (USD) with three decimal places (e.g., $3.150). A U.S. gallon is the customary unit for retail gasoline in the United States; see U.S. gallon: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallon#US_gallon.
- Comparison operator: “Below $3.000” means strictly less than 3.000 when comparing the three-decimal figure displayed by AAA on the resolution date.

Timing window: This question evaluates the AAA figure dated 12/31/25; values shown for other dates are not used. The overall forecasting window is from October 1, 2025, 00:00 UTC to December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC, but only the value date-stamped “12/31/25” is relevant for resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Primary source of truth: On December 31, 2025 (UTC), visit AAA’s Fuel Prices homepage at https://gasprices.aaa.com/ and observe the value displayed next to the label “Today’s AAA National Average” with the exact date stamp “Price as of 12/31/25.” If that three-decimal figure is < $3.000 per U.S. gallon, resolve Yes; otherwise resolve No.

Operational details and edge cases:
- Grade and precision: Use the figure directly associated with “Today’s AAA National Average,” which corresponds to the Regular grade “Current Avg.” and is displayed in USD to three decimal places. No rounding should be applied beyond how AAA displays the figure (e.g., $3.000 resolves No; $2.999 resolves Yes).
- Display variance: If multiple instances of the national average appear, use the one directly adjacent to the “Today’s AAA National Average” banner element (with the date stamp).
- Fallback source: If the homepage is unavailable or the banner is not rendering but AAA’s State Gas Price Averages page is accessible, use the “Today’s AAA National Average” value and date stamp displayed there (it also shows “Today’s AAA National Average $X.XXX Price as of MM/DD/YY”). If both pages are inaccessible on the resolution date, use the most recent archived snapshot from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine of either page showing a date stamp of 12/31/25. In all cases, the date stamp must read “12/31/25,” and the figure used must be the three-decimal USD value displayed by AAA for the national average on that date.
- Contested data: If AAA publishes an explicit methodological note that changes the interpretation of the “Today’s AAA National Average” prior to resolution, rely on the numeric value displayed under that exact label on the date-stamped banner (regardless of methodological changes), consistent with the intent of measuring the publicly presented national average for Regular gasoline.

Resolution date: The question resolves on the basis of the AAA value date-stamped “12/31/25,” observed between 00:00 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

question: According to OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR), will Nigeria’s crude oil production (secondary sources) for November 2025 be at least 1.60 million barrels per day?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is published monthly and covers short-term oil market developments, including tables and analysis of OPEC crude production. The MOMR provides a consistent, timely source for monthly crude output by member country, enabling resolution by year-end.
- The MOMR includes the table titled “OPEC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” (commonly Table 5–7), reporting monthly average crude production for each OPEC member in thousand barrels per day (tb/d). Recent issues show Nigeria’s production in mid-2025 around the mid‑1.5 mb/d range (1 mb/d = 1,000 tb/d). For example:
  - December 2024: 1,507 tb/d for Nigeria (with Oct–Nov 2024 at 1,403 and 1,477 tb/d, respectively).
  - May 2025: 1,528 tb/d; June 2025: 1,547 tb/d.
  - July 2025: 1,559 tb/d.
- “Crude oil” in OPEC statistical usage covers liquid hydrocarbons produced from oil wells and, for statistical purposes, includes natural condensates, distinct from natural gas liquids (NGLs) and other non-conventional liquids. MOMR materials and glossary language indicate that crude oil figures include condensates while excluding NGLs/non-conventional liquids.
- “Secondary Sources” refers to the external entities and methodologies OPEC uses to derive monthly average crude oil production volumes for member and DoC countries; OPEC emphasizes coordination and data-quality meetings with these Secondary Sources to improve accuracy and transparency.

Why this threshold: Nigeria’s recent monthly production has hovered near 1.55–1.56 mb/d, making a 1.60 mb/d cutoff for November 2025 a high-entropy, non-trivial forecast that plausibly could resolve either way based on security, maintenance, OPEC+ policy, and field restart dynamics.

Definitions and terms:
- Nigeria: The sovereign country officially known as the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria (for general identification).
- Crude oil: As per OPEC statistical usage in MOMR/glossary, crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that exists in liquid phase in underground reservoirs and remains liquid at atmospheric pressure after separation; for statistical purposes, crude includes natural condensates, and is distinct from NGLs/non‑conventional liquids.
- Secondary sources: The set of external data providers and methods OPEC uses to derive monthly average crude production; OPEC engages these sources via regular meetings to assess and improve data accuracy and transparency.
- Units: tb/d = thousand barrels per day; mb/d = million barrels per day, where 1 mb/d = 1,000 tb/d. The MOMR table reports in tb/d.
- Month definition for measurement: November 2025 refers to the calendar month from 00:00:00 on 2025‑11‑01 to 23:59:59 on 2025‑11‑30 (UTC). MOMR “secondary sources” figures represent the monthly average daily crude production for that calendar month.

Primary source location:
- OPEC MOMR landing page (where the December 2025 report is expected to be accessible): https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html.
resolution_criteria:
- This question resolves based on the Nigeria figure for November 2025 in the “OPEC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” table (commonly Table 5–7) in the December 2025 issue of OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR).
- Procedure:
  1) Obtain the December 2025 MOMR from OPEC’s official publications portal (e.g., the MOMR page at https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html).
  2) Locate the table titled “OPEC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” (Table 5–7 or its equivalent wording in that issue).
  3) Read the November 2025 value for Nigeria.
- Resolution:
  - Resolve YES if Nigeria’s November 2025 value is greater than or equal to 1,600 tb/d (i.e., ≥1.60 mb/d).
  - Resolve NO if the value is below 1,600 tb/d.
- Fallbacks and edge cases:
  - If the December 2025 MOMR is not available by 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, use the most recent MOMR published on or before that timestamp that reports November 2025 “secondary sources” crude production by country.
  - If the table name/numbering changes, use the clearly corresponding MOMR table that lists OPEC member country monthly crude oil production based on secondary sources, expressed in tb/d.
  - If MOMR issues publish post‑hoc revisions after 2025‑12‑31, ignore revisions; use the first MOMR published on or before 2025‑12‑31 UTC that reports November 2025 values.
- Verification time and source clarity: The MOMR is a single authoritative source, released monthly, allowing a resolver to verify the outcome in under 10 minutes.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025, will a rescission “special message” under the Impoundment Control Act propose ≥$3.0B in rescissions from State/USAID/International Assistance accounts?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01 and why this matters:
- On August 28, 2025, the President transmitted a rescission “special message” to Congress proposing nearly $5 billion in rescissions from foreign assistance appropriations, explicitly framed by the White House as a “pocket rescission” strategy aimed at funds set to expire at the end of FY2025. The Federal Register notice reflecting this special message shows proposals totaling about $4.9 billion and itemizes the affected State/USAID/International Assistance accounts with amounts, demonstrating how such messages are published and structured for verification. Earlier in 2025, a separate special message (dated May 28, 2025; published June 9, 2025) proposed 22 rescissions totaling about $9.4 billion, also documented in the Federal Register with agency/account-level amounts.
- The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has stated that “pocket rescissions” are not authorized by the Impoundment Control Act (ICA) and are illegal—arguing the ICA does not permit withholding through funds’ expiration—and cites prior GAO decisions (e.g., B‑330330 (2018)) to that effect. Congressional Research Service (CRS) legal analysis describes the competing interpretations of ICA Section 1012 and the late‑2025 litigation surrounding the August 28 message, including a D.C. district court preliminary injunction, subsequent D.C. Circuit action, and a Supreme Court administrative stay limited to the Aug. 28 proposals. These developments create uncertainty about whether the administration will transmit further large rescission messages in late 2025.
- What a “rescission special message” is and where it is published: Under 2 U.S.C. § 683(a), when the President proposes rescinding budget authority, he transmits a “special message” to Congress specifying the proposed rescissions. Such messages and their contents are commonly reflected in Federal Register notices titled “Rescissions proposals pursuant to the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974,” which list the date of the message, agencies/accounts, and “Amount proposed for rescission” in U.S. dollars.
- Defining the relevant accounts: The State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS) appropriations measure funds U.S. international activities and foreign assistance via Department of State, U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and International Assistance Programs accounts (e.g., Development Assistance, Economic Support Fund, Global Health Programs, International Disaster Assistance, Migration & Refugee Assistance; security assistance like INCLE, NADR, PKO, IMET, FMF; and multilateral accounts such as CIO, CIPA, and MDB contributions). CRS overviews the SFOPS structure and typical accounts and notes SFOPS closely aligns with the International Affairs budget function (150).

Key references and context for forecasters:
- August 28, 2025 special message scope, strategy, and amounts 
- GAO position that pocket rescissions are illegal 
- CRS legal analysis of ICA pocket rescissions and 2025 litigation timeline 
- Federal Register examples that show how special messages are published and how to read agency/account amounts 
- SFOPS/SFOPS-account taxonomy used to define “international assistance accounts” for this question
resolution_criteria:
Start and end dates; what counts; sources; tie‑breakers:
- Date window: The special message must be dated on or after 2025-10-15 and on or before 2025-12-31 (inclusive). The operative date is the calendar date printed on the message (e.g., “To the Congress of the United States: [Month Day, Year]”) as reflected in the published text; no time‑of‑day is used for resolution.
- What counts as a qualifying special message: A rescission “special message” transmitted pursuant to 2 U.S.C. § 683 that proposes rescission(s) of budget authority and is publicly posted in a manner customary for such messages (see “Resolution sources” below).
- Threshold and how to measure it: The message qualifies if, within that single special message, the sum of the “Amount proposed for rescission” lines for eligible accounts (defined below) is greater than or equal to $3,000,000,000 (three billion U.S. dollars). The sum is computed using the nominal dollar amounts printed in the special message for each proposal; rounding does not apply. Only proposals in that specific special message are included; do not sum across different special messages.
- Eligible accounts (for summing): An account is eligible if, in the Federal Register (or equivalent official publication of the special message), the proposal is categorized under any of the following agency headings: “Department of State,” “U.S. Agency for International Development,” or “International Assistance Programs.” Examples of accounts typically appearing under these headings include, but are not limited to: Development Assistance (DA), Economic Support Fund (ESF), Global Health Programs (GHP), International Disaster Assistance (IDA), Migration and Refugee Assistance (MRA), Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance (ERMA), Democracy Fund (DF), Assistance for Europe, Eurasia, and Central Asia (AEECA), International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement (INCLE), Nonproliferation, Anti‑terrorism, Demining and Related Programs (NADR), Peacekeeping Operations (PKO), International Military Education and Training (IMET), Foreign Military Financing (FMF), Contributions to International Organizations (CIO), Contributions for International Peacekeeping Activities (CIPA), and multilateral development bank and related Treasury international programs accounts. The SFOPS account taxonomy and examples are described by CRS; actual eligibility is determined by the agency heading under which each proposal is listed in the published special message.
- “Additional” means not the August 28, 2025, message: Any special message within the date window qualifies regardless of earlier 2025 messages. The August 28, 2025 special message does not fall within the window and therefore does not itself satisfy the condition.
- Resolution sources (primary): YES resolves if there exists at least one qualifying special message within the date window as evidenced by a Federal Register notice titled “Rescissions proposals pursuant to the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974” that reflects the message, lists the date, and itemizes proposals with “Amount proposed for rescission” by agency/account. The Federal Register’s notice and tables will be used to (a) confirm the message date and (b) sum eligible account amounts.
- Resolution sources (backup): If, unusually, a qualifying special message is posted on an official White House or OMB webpage (e.g., a page hosting the text of the special message) but a Federal Register notice has not yet posted by 2025-12-31, the message can still be used for resolution if it contains the date and itemized “Amount proposed for rescission” entries by agency/account. If multiple sources conflict, the Federal Register controls when available.
- Outcome: Resolve YES if at least one qualifying special message (as above) exists; otherwise resolve NO.

Definitions (for clarity and unambiguous resolution):
- “Special message” (rescission): A presidential communication to Congress proposing the rescission of budget authority under 2 U.S.C. § 683(a) (Impoundment Control Act).
- “Rescission bill” and “calendar days of continuous session”: Terms defined in 2 U.S.C. § 682; included here for background on ICA timing, though not needed to compute the threshold for this question.
- “Eligible accounts”/“State/USAID/International Assistance accounts”: For this question, these are accounts listed under the “Department of State,” “U.S. Agency for International Development,” or “International Assistance Programs” headings in the published special message/notice (typically Federal Register). CRS descriptions of SFOPS illustrate the kinds of accounts that appear under these headings.

Notes to resolver:
- Examples of how these messages and amounts appear can be seen in the June 9, 2025 and September 3, 2025 Federal Register notices, which display the message date and include proposal‑by‑proposal “Amount proposed for rescission” entries by agency and account—sufficient to verify both the dating and the amount summing rules.

question: From 2025-10-15 through 2025-12-31 (UTC), will NOAA SWPC record at least 3 X‑class solar flares?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Solar Cycle 25 timing: The NOAA/NASA/ISES Solar Cycle 25 Prediction Panel forecast a peak around July 2025 with a smoothed sunspot number near 115, with uncertainty windows spanning November 2024 to March 2026. NASA and NOAA announced in October 2024 that the Sun had entered its solar maximum phase and that activity had slightly exceeded expectations, with maximum conditions anticipated to persist for about another year—i.e., into late 2025. This suggests elevated probabilities for significant flares during the period in question.
- Recent X‑class activity in 2025: NOAA SWPC reported a strong (R3) solar flare on 2025‑03‑28 that peaked at X1.1 at 15:20 UTC, illustrating that Solar Cycle 25 is producing X‑class events.

Definitions and data sources forecasters should know:
- Solar flare classification (GOES XRS): SWPC classifies flares by peak soft X‑ray flux in the 0.1–0.8 nm band (GOES XRS‑B channel) measured by GOES satellites. Letter classes (A, B, C, M, X) correspond to powers of ten in W/m^2, with X‑class at ≥1×10^−4 W/m^2. The numerical part of the flare class is defined by truncating (not rounding) the peak irradiance; for example, 1.00×10^−4 W/m^2 is X1.0, while values are truncated to determine the decimal classification.
- Event timing definitions (GOES X‑ray events): For GOES X‑ray events used by SWPC, "Begin Time" is the first minute, in a sequence of 4 minutes, of steep monotonic increase in 0.1–0.8 nm flux; "Maximum Time" is the minute of the peak flux; and "End Time" is when flux decays to halfway between the maximum and pre‑flare background. The detection algorithm may miss gradual rise events, which can be manually entered by forecasters.
- SWPC event/alert products: SWPC maintains Solar and Geophysical Event Reports that are preliminary but edited by duty forecasters and updated frequently (today’s list updated every 30 minutes; yesterday’s list every 3 hours; the past 3 days recreated daily). Documentation for fields is provided via their README, and these reports serve as curated logs of solar events. SWPC also provides an Alerts/Warnings product stream with current alerts in JSON and archived alerts since 2002 via FTP; these include X‑ray alerts and event summaries that can serve as a durable archive of X‑class event notifications. The Notifications Timeline page explains that alerts and summaries for X‑ray events are plotted with UTC issue times and that summaries are issued for X‑ray events at thresholds including X1, X10, and higher, making it a useful visual/log reference and pointing to archived alert timelines.

Why this is non‑trivial: Late‑2025 lies within the solar maximum window, which tends to increase flare rates, but the exact count of X‑class flares in any ~2.5‑month span remains uncertain. Forecasting requires integrating solar cycle progression, active region evolution, and short‑term flare probabilities, rather than simply reading off an existing forecast.

All terms used in the resolution are defined below and tied to SWPC/GOES standards , and resolution relies on SWPC’s maintained logs and archives.
resolution_criteria:
What is being counted:
- Count distinct solar flare events with GOES X‑ray classification of at least X1.0, where the classification is based on the peak 0.1–0.8 nm (GOES XRS‑B) irradiance measured by GOES. X‑class is defined as peak flux ≥1×10^−4 W/m^2, and the numerical index (e.g., X1.0, X2.5) is determined by truncating (not rounding) the actual peak irradiance value.

Eligible time window:
- Include events whose GOES X‑ray Begin Time is between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. Begin Time is defined per SWPC’s GOES X‑ray event rules: the first minute, in a sequence of 4 minutes, of steep monotonic increase in 0.1–0.8 nm flux. All times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

Primary resolution source:
- NOAA SWPC Solar and Geophysical Event Reports page and associated files, which list preliminary but edited solar events and are updated frequently. Use the edited reports to enumerate events and their Begin Times and peak classifications. Where needed, consult the linked README describing fields for confirmation.

Secondary/tie‑breaker sources:
- If an event in the eligible window is not clearly listed or classifications differ, consult SWPC’s Alerts/Warnings archives: current alerts JSON and archived alert files (FTP). Use X‑ray event summaries and alerts to verify that an X‑class event occurred and its timing/classification.
- Use the Notifications Timeline page for corroboration that summaries for X‑ray events (including X1 and higher) were issued with UTC issue times, and refer to the archived alert timelines pointed to there; this helps validate the presence and timing of X‑class summaries for the window.

Counting rules:
- Count each distinct event once. Distinct events are those represented as separate entries in SWPC’s Solar and Geophysical Event Reports (or, if using alerts/summary archives, separate X‑ray event summaries), each with its own Begin Time and peak classification. Do not double‑count observations of the same event from multiple GOES spacecraft; SWPC’s event entries/summaries refer to a single physical flare event.
- Manual entries: If SWPC notes manual entry due to algorithm limitations (e.g., gradual rise), such events still count if classified at X1.0 or higher and have Begin Times in the eligible window.

Resolution:
- On or after 2026‑01‑01 00:00:00 UTC, enumerate eligible events from the sources above. If the total number of distinct X‑class (≥X1.0) events with Begin Times in the window is ≥3, resolve Yes; otherwise resolve No.

Notes on source availability:
- SWPC’s event reports and alerts are active operational products with current and archived availability documented by SWPC (including JSON feeds and FTP archives), ensuring an unambiguous source of truth by year‑end.

question: Will the EU open at least one accession negotiating cluster with Ukraine between 00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59 UTC on 31 December 2025?
background:
Context as of 1 October 2025: Accession negotiations between the European Union (EU) and Ukraine were formally opened at the first Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) at ministerial level on 25 June 2024, following the Council’s approval of the negotiating framework on 21 June 2024. Under the EU’s revised enlargement methodology, negotiating chapters are grouped into six thematic “negotiating clusters,” and the “Fundamentals” cluster is designed to open first and close last, with progress there guiding the overall pace of talks. The six clusters are: (1) Fundamentals; (2) Internal market; (3) Competitiveness & inclusive growth; (4) Green agenda & sustainable connectivity; (5) Resources, agriculture & cohesion; and (6) External relations. In practice, clusters open via formal accession conferences (IGCs) and Council-supervised procedures; the Council (in its General Affairs configuration) supervises enlargement and generally operates by unanimous agreement on enlargement-related decisions. As an example of how a cluster opening is publicly communicated, on 14 April 2025 the EU held an Accession Conference with Albania and announced “EU opens negotiations on the internal market cluster,” explicitly listing the cluster and its chapters in the official press release.

Key definitions and links forecasters may need:
- Negotiating cluster: a thematic grouping of negotiation chapters under the revised enlargement methodology; clusters open as a whole once opening benchmarks are met, and individual chapters within them are provisionally closed separately. Reference/overview: EU accession process clusters (European Commission PDF): https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2022-10/eu_accession_process_clusters%20%28oct%202022%29.pdf 
- Intergovernmental Conference (IGC)/Accession Conference: the formal meeting between EU member states and the candidate country at which accession negotiations are conducted and milestones (such as opening clusters) can be decided and announced; the first IGC with Ukraine took place on 25 June 2024 to open negotiations. Council’s role in enlargement and supervision of negotiations: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/how-enlargement-works/ 
- Example phrasing of a “cluster opening” in an official communication (for pattern matching when verifying resolution): “EU opens negotiations on the internal market cluster” (Accession Conference with Albania, 14 April 2025): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/04/14/accession-conference-with-albania-eu-opens-negotiations-on-the-internal-market-cluster/ 
- Press release announcing the first IGC with Ukraine (illustrates the format/source to monitor): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/06/25/eu-opens-accession-negotiations-with-ukraine/ 

Process cues for forecasters:
- The Fundamentals cluster is expected to open first under the revised methodology, and the Council supervises the process with unanimity generally required on enlargement matters, implying political dynamics among member states can affect the timing.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on official, time-stamped actions occurring between 00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59 UTC on 31 December 2025 (inclusive).

Resolve YES if, during that period, at least one accession negotiating cluster with Ukraine is officially opened, evidenced by any one of the following primary sources:
1) An official press release on consilium.europa.eu (Council of the EU/European Council) for an Intergovernmental/Accession Conference with Ukraine stating that the EU and Ukraine “open negotiations on” a specific cluster (e.g., “EU opens negotiations on the [Cluster name] cluster”), analogous in form to the Albania example. The first IGC press format for Ukraine is here for reference.
2) An official Council document (e.g., EU Common Position or Council press release) published on consilium.europa.eu or its data portal explicitly stating that a specified cluster with Ukraine is opened.

Definitions and inclusions/exclusions for resolution:
- “Accession negotiating cluster” refers to one of the six thematic groupings under the revised enlargement methodology: Fundamentals; Internal market; Competitiveness & inclusive growth; Green agenda & sustainable connectivity; Resources, agriculture & cohesion; External relations. A “cluster” is counted as opened only when negotiations on the cluster as a whole are officially declared open in an eligible source during the period.
