- Recent values: BEA reports the YoY core PCE (“excluding food and energy”) at +2.9% for August 2025 in both the August news release and the BEA data page; June–August 2025 values are 2.8%, 2.9%, and 2.9%, respectively.

Definitions and links for forecasters
- Core PCE price index (PCE excluding food and energy): BEA’s definition and recent YoY values are here: https://www.bea.gov/data/personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index-excluding-food-and-energy.
- Year-over-year (YoY) as used by BEA: the 12‑month percent change, labeled in BEA materials as “Change From Month One Year Ago”.
- Resolution source: BEA’s news post for “Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025” (release code BEA 25-55).

Why this threshold: The latest YoY core readings have hovered near the high‑2% range (2.8%–2.9% in June–August 2025), making 2.8% a plausible and uncertain cutoff for the November figure.
resolution_criteria:
What counts
- Target statistic: The 12‑month percent change in the PCE price index excluding food and energy (core PCE), for November 2025, as reported by BEA in its “Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025” news release (release code BEA 25-55) published on December 19, 2025.
- Acceptable fields/sources within the release: Use the YoY figure appearing in the news release text (e.g., the sentence of the form “Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased X percent from one year ago,” as exemplified in BEA’s August 2025 release). If that explicit sentence is absent, use the accompanying BEA table value for “Change From Month One Year Ago” for “PCE price index excluding food and energy” for November 2025 (same measure shown on BEA’s core PCE data page). Do not recalculate from index levels.

Resolution rule
- YES if the BEA-reported YoY core PCE for November 2025 is less than or equal to 2.8% as stated in the December 19, 2025 news release; NO if it is greater than 2.8%.

Timing, updates, and rounding
- Timing: This market resolves upon publication of the BEA news release dated December 19, 2025 (regardless of the exact posting time that day). All dates and times in this question are interpreted in UTC when relevant; however, only the content of that specific BEA release determines resolution.
- Rounding: Use the value as BEA reports it (typically to one decimal place). Do not attempt to infer additional precision beyond what BEA publishes in the release/tables.
- Revisions: Only the initially published values in the December 19, 2025 BEA release count for resolution. Any later revisions (e.g., in subsequent releases) are ignored.

Direct links for resolution (when available)
- BEA news index entry referencing the scheduled release and code: https://www.bea.gov/node/41776 
- BEA core PCE definition and recent YoY values (for context on the measurement used): https://www.bea.gov/data/personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index-excluding-food-and-energy 
- Example of how BEA states the YoY core PCE in a monthly release (August 2025): https://www.bea.gov/news/2025/personal-income-and-outlays-august-2025

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the European Union announce a single, new EU-level funding commitment of at least €250,000,000 explicitly earmarked for counter‑UAS infrastructure along the EU’s eastern external land borders (Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland), including or tied to the “drone wall”/Eastern Flank initiatives?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: 
- The EU officially launched an initiative to establish a “drone wall” along its eastern flank on 2025-09-26, holding an inaugural meeting with ten participating Member States (Bulgaria, Denmark, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Finland), with Ukraine invited and NATO observing. The initiative prioritizes detection and intervention, with immediate focus on detection. The launch coverage did not specify any new, dedicated EU-level funding commitments for the drone wall itself.
- In the 2025 State of the Union address (delivered 2025-09-10), President von der Leyen stated: “We must heed the call of our Baltic friends and build a drone wall… This is not an abstract ambition. It is the bedrock of credible defence,” situating the drone wall within broader initiatives such as Eastern Flank Watch, a Drone Alliance with Ukraine, and large-scale defence investment programs.
- Reuters reporting (2025-09-22) noted the EU is “looking at how to create a ‘drone wall’ along the EU’s eastern border,” with urgency heightened by Russian drone incursions into Poland’s airspace, underscoring gaps in Europe’s drone defence capabilities.
- As of the above dates, public coverage did not identify a specific EU-level funding commitment dedicated to counter‑UAS infrastructure along the eastern external land borders (“drone wall”) totaling ≥€250m; whether such a commitment will be announced during the resolution window is uncertain.

Definitions (for clarity and forecasting):
- Unmanned aircraft system (UAS), “drone”: An aircraft without a human on board, controlled remotely or autonomously; the term UAS includes the unmanned aircraft plus control and communication components.
- Counter‑UAS (C‑UAS) infrastructure: Systems and capabilities to detect, track, identify, neutralize, or otherwise mitigate threats from drones. This includes detection sensors (e.g., RF, radar, EO/IR), electronic warfare/jamming, directed‑energy systems, kinetic interceptors, integrated command and control (C2), and related fixed infrastructure deployed for border area protection.
- EU’s eastern external land borders (scope for this question): Land border segments of EU Member States that directly border Russia or Belarus (Finland–Russia, Estonia–Russia, Latvia–Russia/Belarus, Lithuania–Russia/Belarus, Poland–Russia/Belarus). Frontex describes EU external borders as the boundaries of the Schengen Area where common border management applies.

Resolution sources and how to find them quickly:
- Official Journal (OJ) L series entries and other authentic publications of EU legal acts (Implementing Decisions, work programmes) via EUR‑Lex direct access. Since 2013, electronic editions are authentic; the OJ L series is the official source for binding acts.
- European Commission Press Corner (press releases, speeches, factsheets) or Council press releases for adopted EU‑level funding decisions. The SOTEU reference and Commission defence initiatives context are public in the Press Corner.

Why this question has meaningful uncertainty:
- The initiative is newly launched at EU level, with political momentum but unclear short‑term budgetary commitments specific to counter‑UAS infrastructure along the defined borders. A ≥€250m single commitment within a ~10‑week window is plausible but not assured, creating high entropy.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone: 
- Eligible announcements must be dated between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What resolves “Yes”: 
- There exists at least one official EU‑level announcement (see acceptable evidence below), published and dated within the above window, that commits an amount ≥€250,000,000 in EU budgetary funding (grants, appropriations, or EU‑funded procurement; excluding loans and purely national budgets) explicitly earmarked for procurement, deployment, integration, or operation of counter‑UAS infrastructure along the EU’s eastern external land borders (Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland). The announcement must either (a) explicitly reference the “drone wall” or “Eastern Flank”/“Eastern Flank Watch”; or (b) explicitly state that the funding is for counter‑UAS systems to protect the specified border areas (i.e., Member State borders with Russia/Belarus).

Key term clarifications for resolution:
- “Single, new EU‑level funding commitment”: One discrete commitment instrument or decision (e.g., a Commission Implementing Decision, work programme adoption, financing decision, or EU procurement/award notice) stating an amount ≥€250m. Aggregating multiple smaller commitments is not permitted; the threshold must be met in a single announced commitment.
- “EU‑level funding”: Financing from the EU budget or EU institutions’ centrally managed programs (e.g., Commission‑managed funds). National Member State budgets or purely intergovernmental pledges without EU budget execution do not count.
- “New”: The commitment instrument must be newly adopted/announced within the window and must not merely re‑state or re‑label funding adopted prior to 2025‑10‑15.
- “Counter‑UAS infrastructure”: As defined in Background (detection, EW/jamming, directed‑energy, kinetic interceptors, integrated C2, fixed installations supporting these).
- “Eastern external land borders”: As defined in Background (Member State land borders with Russia or Belarus).
- “Explicitly earmarked”: The announcement text must clearly limit the purpose to counter‑UAS infrastructure for the specified border areas or tie it to the “drone wall”/Eastern Flank initiatives.
- Currency/amount: The announcement must specify the euro amount (EUR). If an amount is stated in another currency, it must also explicitly state the euro equivalent; otherwise, it does not qualify.

Acceptable evidence (one is sufficient):
- An authentic Official Journal (OJ) L‑series publication of a legal act adopting or committing the funds (e.g., Commission Implementing Decision/work programme) accessible via EUR‑Lex direct access.
- A European Commission Press Corner press release or adopted decision/communication page explicitly stating the qualifying commitment and purpose.
- A Council of the EU press release that records adoption of an EU‑level funding decision with the qualifying commitment and purpose.

What resolves “No”:
- No qualifying single commitment meeting all the above conditions is announced within the time window.
- Announcements that discuss intent, proposals, studies, or general defence envelopes without an explicit ≥€250m commitment for counter‑UAS infrastructure along the specified borders.
- Commitments comprised solely of loans; or national funding announcements; or commitments that lack explicit earmarking for the specified border areas.

Resolution notes:
- The resolver will check the EUR‑Lex OJ L‑series daily view and the Commission Press Corner for the relevant dates. 
- If multiple qualifying commitments exist, any one suffices for “Yes.”
- If the same commitment is described in multiple sources, the OJ L‑series publication is preferred as the primary source of truth.

question: Ukraine: Will the enacted 2026 State Budget appropriate at least 191.6 billion UAH to the Program of Medical Guarantees (PMG)?
background:
Status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
- Draft figures for 2026. Ukraine’s Minister of Health Viktor Liashko stated that the government’s 2026 draft state budget earmarks UAH 258 billion for the healthcare system, including UAH 191.6 billion for the Program of Medical Guarantees (PMG).
- Reference point for 2025. According to reporting on the launch of the PMG for 2025, the allocation for 2025 is “over 175.5 billion UAH,” up roughly 16 billion from 2024. This provides a recent baseline for the size and trend of PMG funding.
- What the PMG is and who implements it. The PMG (Ukrainian: “Програма державних гарантій медичного обслуговування населення”) is the annual program that defines the publicly financed package of health services guaranteed by the state and is implemented/purchased by the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU/NSZU), the central executive body that implements state policy on financial guarantees for medical care under the PMG. For general orientation on NSZU/NHSU: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service_of_Ukraine

Why this question is forecastable with uncertainty: The Cabinet’s draft often changes during parliamentary deliberations before final enactment. The PMG is typically the largest single health allocation, so macro-fiscal conditions, security needs, and donor financing can all push the final figure above or below the draft proposal. With a draft figure of 191.6 billion UAH, the ultimate enacted appropriation could plausibly end up either side of that threshold.

Key terms and links for clarity:
- “Program of Medical Guarantees (PMG)” refers to the budget program titled in Ukrainian as “Програма державних гарантій медичного обслуговування населення,” as it appears in the annexes to the Law of Ukraine “Про Державний бюджет України на 2026 рік.”
- “National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU/NSZU)” is the main purchaser/implementer for the PMG (see above and ).
- “UAH” denotes Ukrainian hryvnia, the national currency of Ukraine. The budget annexes typically present appropriations in thousands of UAH; see Resolution Criteria for how we compare values.

Timing window for this market: Events considered must occur between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. The 2026 State Budget Law is typically enacted in late Q4, well within this window. If enactment occurs earlier, resolution will still occur only within the stated window.

Sources for the status quo figures cited above:
- Government proposes UAH 191.6B for PMG in the 2026 draft (Ukrinform, 2025-09-16).
- PMG 2025 allocation “over 175.5B UAH” (Ukrinform, 2025-01-01).
- NHSU role in implementing PMG (Wikipedia entry summarizing the official role).
resolution_criteria:
Resolution: The question resolves based on the text of the enacted Law of Ukraine “Про Державний бюджет України на 2026 рік” (Law on the State Budget of Ukraine for 2026) as published on the official legal portal: https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/

Question: Will the enacted 2026 State Budget appropriate at least 191.6 billion UAH to the Program of Medical Guarantees (PMG)?

Operationalization and measurement:
1) Identify the specific budget program: In the annexes of the enacted 2026 Budget Law, under the main spending unit “Національна служба здоров’я України” (National Health Service of Ukraine), locate the budget program titled “Програма державних гарантій медичного обслуговування населення.” This is the PMG program.
2) Quantity to compare: Use the sum of planned expenditures (видатки) for 2026 for that program across the General Fund and Special Fund combined, as presented in the enacted law’s annexes. Do not include lending/credits (надання кредитів) or other non-expenditure items.
3) Units and table format: Annex figures are typically expressed in thousands of UAH. For comparison to the threshold, convert the published value to UAH by multiplying by 1,000. The threshold of 191.6 billion UAH is equal to 191,600,000,000 UAH, which corresponds to 191,600,000.0 when expressed in thousands of UAH. The forecast resolves “Yes” if the enacted annex value for the PMG program is greater than or equal to 191,600,000.0 (thousand UAH). It resolves “No” if it is strictly below that value.
4) Version of the law: Use the version of the law that reflects the appropriations at the moment of enactment (i.e., the version that has entered into force and includes the final enacted annexes). Subsequent amendments (if any) after enactment are not considered for this question.
5) Timing and timezone: The observation is made as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, or earlier if the law is enacted and published before that time. All times are UTC.
6) Source of truth: The official text and annexes as published on https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/ for the Law “Про Державний бюджет України на 2026 рік.” If the zakon.rada.gov.ua publication is temporarily unavailable on the resolution date, the resolver may use the identical official text hosted by the Verkhovna Rada’s site (same portal) once accessible. The primary and intended source of truth is the zakon.rada.gov.ua page for the enacted 2026 budget law.
7) Edge cases: If, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the 2026 State Budget Law has not been enacted and published on zakon.rada.gov.ua, the question will resolve “No,” since there would be no enacted appropriation meeting the condition within the resolution window.

Notes and references for context (not used to adjudicate the outcome):
- Draft 2026 PMG figure: UAH 191.6B (within a UAH 258B health total).
- 2025 PMG allocation: “over 175.5B UAH”.
- NHSU implements the PMG.

question: Will the Bank of England change Bank Rate at its 6 November 2025 MPC meeting?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- What is Bank Rate: Bank Rate (also called the Official Bank Rate) is the United Kingdom’s core policy interest rate set by the Bank of England. It is the rate of interest the Bank of England pays on overnight deposits (reserves) placed with it by eligible banks and financial institutions, and is the primary tool used to influence other interest rates in the economy. See the Bank of England explainer: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy/the-interest-rate-bank-rate.
- MPC meeting and publication date: The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has a confirmed announcement and minutes publication date of Thursday 6 November 2025. The specific November 2025 Monetary Policy Summary (MPS) and minutes page exists and is scheduled “to be published at 12pm” (UK time) on that date: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy-summary-and-minutes/2025/november-2025.
- Current Bank Rate and recent decisions: The MPC maintained Bank Rate at 4.00% at its meeting ending on 17 September 2025. The official Bank Rate database shows the most recent change prior to that was a reduction to 4.00% effective 7 August 2025.
- Inflation backdrop: The UK Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose 3.8% in the 12 months to August 2025, unchanged from July 2025. See ONS bulletin: https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/consumerpriceinflation/august2025.
- Market expectations for the 6 November 2025 decision: In the Bank of England’s Market Participants Survey (September 2025), respondents’ mean probabilities for Bank Rate after the 6 November 2025 meeting were 57.8% for 4.00% and 38.7% for 3.75% (with very low probabilities elsewhere), indicating material uncertainty about whether a cut occurs at that meeting. See survey results: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/markets/market-intelligence/survey-results/2025/market-participants-survey-results-september-2025.
Definitions and links:
- Bank Rate/Official Bank Rate: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy/the-interest-rate-bank-rate ; official history: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/boeapps/database/Bank-Rate.asp.
- Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting dates: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/news/2024/september/monetary-policy-committee-dates-for-2025.
- November 2025 MPS and minutes landing page (resolution source): https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy-summary-and-minutes/2025/november-2025.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves on the content of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Summary (MPS) and minutes page for November 2025.

- Event window: This question concerns the MPC decision whose MPS and minutes are published on 6 November 2025 (scheduled for 12:00 UK time). All times referenced are UK local time.
- Key term – “Bank Rate”: The United Kingdom’s Official Bank Rate set by the Bank of England (see BoE explainer and official history).
- Key term – “change Bank Rate”: Any decision by the MPC at that meeting to set Bank Rate at a numeric level different from its immediately previous level (increase or decrease). The immediately previous level is the last published Bank Rate prior to 6 November 2025, as recorded in the Bank of England’s official Bank Rate database  and/or the prior meeting’s MPS.

Resolution steps:
1) Access the November 2025 MPS and minutes page: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy-summary-and-minutes/2025/november-2025.
2) Determine the MPC’s decision text. Resolve “Yes” if the MPS states the MPC decided to change Bank Rate (e.g., “the Committee voted to reduce/increase Bank Rate to X%”). Resolve “No” if the MPS states the MPC voted to maintain Bank Rate at its previous level (e.g., “voted to maintain Bank Rate at 4%”).
3) If the November 2025 MPS page is unavailable or the wording is ambiguous (unlikely), use the official Bank Rate database to verify whether the Bank Rate changed on 6 November 2025 relative to the prior level. If the database shows a new effective date and rate on 6 November 2025 differing from the prior rate, resolve “Yes”; if it shows no change on that date, resolve “No”.

Primary source of truth: The Bank of England’s November 2025 MPS and minutes page. Fallback source: Bank of England Official Bank Rate history database. Confirmation of meeting/publication date: BoE MPC dates for 2025.

question: Will Israel transfer any previously withheld 2025 Palestinian Authority clearance revenues between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Definition and mechanism: “Clearance revenues” are Value Added Tax (VAT) and import duties collected by the Government of Israel under the Paris Protocol and transferred (net of an administrative fee) to the Palestinian Authority (PA); they are a primary source of PA revenue. See also background on the PA (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Authority) and the Paris Protocol within the Oslo framework (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Protocol).
- Withholding in 2025: As of late September 2025, UN officials reported that, according to the PA, Israel had not transferred any clearance revenues since May 2025, and that the cumulative total withheld had reached over USD 2 billion. The World Bank likewise reports that no disbursements were received by the PA for May, June, July, and August 2025. A late-September Reuters report adds that since May 2025 Israel’s finance ministry withheld around 10 billion shekels in taxes and duties collected on behalf of the PA.
- Fiscal impact: Due to the withholding and earlier deductions, PA salary payments have been repeatedly reduced since late 2023, with further declines in mid-2025 following the suspension of transfers [498b0f; c67877].
- Earlier 2025 actions with withheld funds: In January 2025, Israel planned to apply some withheld PA tax/clearance revenues toward electricity-related debts and fuel purchases rather than transferring those funds to the PA, and the PA finance ministry cited billions of shekels as withheld at that time.
- Diplomatic pressure: On September 26, 2025, an Emergency Coalition of states publicly demanded Israel immediately release all Palestinian clearance revenues and cease measures that weaken the PA.

Why this matters: Whether any portion of the clearance revenues collected in 2025 but withheld is actually transferred to the PA by year-end depends on evolving Israeli policy decisions, domestic political dynamics, international pressure, and the PA’s fiscal and banking arrangements—creating meaningful uncertainty suitable for forecasting [7e7bf4; c67877; 498b0f; 1abb04].
resolution_criteria:
Resolve Yes if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, there is credible public reporting that Israel has transferred any positive amount (>0 NIS) of previously withheld 2025 clearance revenues to the Palestinian Authority (PA), as defined below. Otherwise resolve No.

Definitions and scope:
- Palestinian Authority (PA): The governing body established under the Oslo framework (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_Authority). For this market, “transfer to the PA” means funds credited to a bank account controlled by the PA or its Ministry of Finance (MoF).
- Clearance revenues: VAT and import duties collected by Israel under the Paris Protocol for goods destined for Palestinian markets, net of the administrative fee.
- Previously withheld 2025 clearance revenues: Amounts collected by Israel in calendar year 2025 under the clearance revenue mechanism but not transferred to the PA by 2025-10-14 23:59:59 UTC. This includes funds held in escrow or third-country accounts if they were collected in 2025 and are released to PA-controlled accounts during the resolution window. It excludes any amounts collected prior to 2025, and any sums that Israel applies to pay third parties or offsets (e.g., electricity debts) without crediting a PA-controlled account.
- Transfer: An irrevocable credit of funds to a PA- or PA MoF-controlled account. Announcements of intent, conditional approvals, or bookkeeping offsets without cash credited to a PA-controlled account do not count. Payments made directly to non-PA third parties do not count.

Eligible resolution sources:
- Official announcements or releases from: Israel’s Ministry of Finance or relevant authority; the Palestinian Authority Ministry of Finance; or COGAT, confirming a qualifying transfer.
- Major international wire services: Reuters, Associated Press (AP), or Agence France-Presse (AFP), reporting a qualifying transfer. For instance, a report that “Israel transferred withheld PA clearance revenues collected in [month(s)] 2025 to the PA” would qualify if it clearly ties the funds to 2025 collections.

Disambiguation rules:
- The report must clearly indicate that the transfer pertains to clearance revenues collected in 2025 and previously withheld. If a report mentions a transfer of withheld revenues but does not specify the collection period, it will not qualify unless a second eligible source clarifies that the funds were collected in 2025.
- Transfers applied to settle PA or distribution-company debts directly with Israeli entities (e.g., Israel Electric Corporation) do not qualify.
- Transfers of clearance revenues from 2024 or earlier do not qualify. Mixed transfers that contain both 2025 and pre-2025 withheld funds qualify only if the reporting specifies that at least some portion collected in 2025 was credited to a PA-controlled account; in that case, resolve Yes.
- Multiple installments: Any qualifying transfer within the window is sufficient for a Yes resolution; otherwise No.

Time zone: All dates and times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

Primary references for context (not required for resolution but informative): UN/UNSCO note (no transfers since May 2025; >$2B withheld) ; World Bank definition and suspension detail ; Reuters reporting on scale of withholdings ; Reuters report on application of withheld funds to debts (exclusion example) ; coalition call to release funds.

question: Will IATA report that European carriers’ international RPK grew by at least 3.5% year-over-year in October 2025?
background:
Context and definitions as of 2025-09-30:
- Metric: Revenue passenger kilometre (RPK) is a measure of traffic calculated by multiplying the number of revenue-paying passengers by the distance traveled. IATA press releases and monthly market analyses report “demand” as RPK growth versus the same month in the prior year (YoY) and provide regional breakdowns.
- What “Europe” means in IATA regional stats: In IATA’s methodology, airline traffic is allocated according to the region in which the carrier is registered; it should not be interpreted as traffic within that geographic region.
- What will be reported and where: IATA’s monthly air passenger press releases include a “Regional Breakdown – International Passenger Markets” section that lists European carriers’ year-over-year demand (RPK) growth for the month, with accompanying capacity (ASK) and load factor figures. The associated “Air Passenger Market Analysis” PDF provides additional methodological detail and data tables.
- Recent baseline: For July 2025, the IATA press release reported that European carriers had a 4.0% YoY increase in international passenger demand (RPK). In IATA’s July 2025 Air Passenger Market Analysis, it also notes “Passenger traffic of European airlines rose by 2.9% YoY in July” (this refers to total market for European carriers). As a seasonal reference point, Europe’s total-market YoY RPK growth for October 2024 was 7.9% according to IATA’s Air Passenger Market Analysis table for that month.
- Publication timing and choice of month: IATA typically publishes October data in early December (e.g., “Solid Growth in Passenger Demand Continued in October” published on December 4, 2024). In contrast, November data are typically published in January of the following year (e.g., November 2024 data published January 9, 2025). Therefore, targeting October 2025 allows resolution by year-end 2025, whereas targeting November 2025 likely would not.
Rationale for threshold: With European carriers’ international demand up 4.0% YoY in July 2025  and total-market growth at 2.9% YoY that month , alongside stronger October 2024 base effects , a 3.5% threshold for October 2025 plausibly sits near the range of reasonable uncertainty.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will IATA report that European carriers’ international passenger demand (measured in revenue passenger kilometres, RPK) grew by at least 3.5% year-over-year (YoY) in October 2025?

- Time window for the data month: October 1, 2025 00:00:00 to October 31, 2025 23:59:59, calendar month, UTC. The comparison baseline is October 2024.
- Primary resolution source: The IATA press release covering October 2025 global passenger demand, specifically the “Regional Breakdown – International Passenger Markets” section. Use the percentage reported for “European carriers” demand (RPK) growth YoY. IATA routinely publishes this table in monthly press releases (e.g., the July 2025 release includes this section).
- Secondary source (tie-breaker/backup): If needed for clarification, consult the IATA “Air Passenger Market Analysis – October 2025” PDF, which is the monthly analysis report series that includes methodology and detailed tables (e.g., October 2024 report contains regional tables). If the press release and analysis PDF differ (rare), the press release figure prevails for this question.
- Definitions:
  - RPK: Revenue passenger kilometre as defined by Wikipedia (also known as revenue passenger mile in imperial units).
  - YoY: Percentage change relative to the same calendar month one year prior (here, October 2025 vs. October 2024). Use the value as stated by IATA; do not recompute.
  - “European carriers”: IATA allocates airline traffic according to the region in which the carrier is registered; this is not a geographic-traffic definition.
  - “International … markets”: As per IATA press releases, this refers to international scheduled air traffic; IATA statistics cover both international and domestic scheduled traffic for member and non-member airlines.
- Threshold and rounding: “At least 3.5%” means the reported value must be greater than or equal to 3.5%. Use the figure exactly as stated by IATA (typically to one decimal place). If IATA reports a range, take the midpoint; if they report multiple figures for Europe in the relevant section, use the headline YoY “demand (RPK)” percentage.
- Publication cutoff and versioning: The outcome will be determined from the latest version of the IATA October 2025 passenger press release (and, if consulted, its analysis PDF) available as of December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC. If IATA revises the document prior to this cutoff, use the latest revision available by the cutoff.
- Resolution: YES if the IATA October 2025 press release reports European carriers’ international RPK growth YoY ≥ 3.5%; otherwise NO. This is expected to resolve by early December based on historical release timing for October data  and avoids November because those data typically post in January.
- Source locations (for verifier convenience): IATA pressroom (press releases) and the IATA Economics “Air Passenger Market Analysis” repository. Examples of the relevant format and series are evidenced in prior months’ materials.

question: Will the ECB lower its deposit facility rate at its 18 December 2025 monetary policy meeting?
background:
Context as of 1 Oct 2025:
- Meeting and communications cadence: The ECB Governing Council is scheduled to hold a monetary policy meeting in Frankfurt on 18 December 2025, followed by a press conference. ECB monetary policy decisions are communicated via a same-day press release, and the President comments at a press conference; for example, the 11 September 2025 release states the press conference starts at 14:45 CET, and the decisions page notes decisions are published on the day of the meeting.
- What is the “deposit facility rate”? It is the interest rate banks receive when they deposit money with the central bank overnight; it is one of the ECB’s three key interest rates.
- Status quo of key rates: On 11 September 2025, the ECB kept its three key interest rates unchanged at: deposit facility 2.00%, main refinancing operations 2.15%, marginal lending facility 2.40%. Earlier in the year (6 March 2025), the ECB lowered the three key rates by 25 basis points, illustrating standard phrasing used when rates change.
- Market context: As of 11 September 2025, Reuters reported that ECB policymakers viewed the 18 December meeting as the more likely date to debate a reduction in borrowing costs, while emphasizing that the decision would depend on incoming data and projections.
- Where the decision will be published: The authoritative record is the ECB’s “Monetary policy decisions” press release for the meeting date, with details on the three key interest rates. The ECB’s “Key ECB interest rates” page documents definitions and current/past values of the three key rates.
resolution_criteria:
What will be judged
- This question concerns the ECB Governing Council’s monetary policy decision announced on 18 December 2025 (Frankfurt local time, CET).

Primary resolution rule
- Resolve Yes if the ECB’s official “Monetary policy decisions” press release published on 18 December 2025 states that the interest rate on the deposit facility is being lowered relative to its level immediately before the announcement. This can be evidenced by language such as “The Governing Council today decided to lower the three key ECB interest rates …” or “the interest rate on the deposit facility will be decreased to X% …”.
- Resolve No if that press release states the deposit facility rate is unchanged or higher, e.g., “decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged”.

Definitions and sources
- “Deposit facility rate” means the interest rate banks receive when they deposit money with the Eurosystem overnight, one of the ECB’s three key interest rates.
- “Lowered” means the new deposit facility rate set in the 18 December 2025 decision is strictly less than the rate in force immediately before the announcement. If a numerical comparison is needed, the prior rate can be established from the ECB’s “Key ECB interest rates” page as it appeared immediately prior to the 18 December decision or from the most recent prior monetary policy press release.
- The effective date of any change (e.g., “with effect from [date]”) does not affect resolution; if the decision sets a lower value, it counts as lowered regardless of when it takes effect.

Timing window and scope
- Eligible announcements for this question must occur between 00:00 on 15 October 2025 and 23:59 on 31 December 2025, Frankfurt local time (CET). In practice, the relevant announcement is expected on 18 December 2025, when a monetary policy meeting followed by a press conference is scheduled.

Authoritative sources for resolution
- Primary: ECB “Monetary policy decisions” press release for 18 December 2025 (published on ecb.europa.eu).
- Secondary (only if the primary is unavailable on the day): the ECB introductory statement/press conference text for 18 December 2025; if neither ECB source is accessible by end of day, resolve based on concordant reporting by major wire services (e.g., Reuters).

Edge cases
- If the ECB does not hold a monetary policy meeting on 18 December 2025 and no “Monetary policy decisions” press release is published that day, resolve No. This condition ensures the question remains unambiguously resolvable on or before 31 December 2025.

question: Will the UK government launch a public pilot of a digital driving licence via GOV.UK Wallet by December 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- The UK government has publicly stated that GOV.UK Wallet will launch “later this year” and will include “a pilot digital driving licence,” following the summer 2025 trial launch of the GOV.UK App. A separate January 2025 announcement said a digital driving licence is “coming this year,” with an early version to be piloted later in 2025, as part of the GOV.UK Wallet ecosystem.
- Official GOV.UK Wallet guidance describes the Wallet as an app that will let users save government documents (including, in future, their driving licence) to their phone. It notes that Wallet is not ready to use yet for the general public, and that One Login is required to access it.
- Government guidance for departments and the digital identity sector indicates a staged rollout: Wallet will first hold the HM Armed Forces Veteran Card from summer 2025, followed by the full driving licence as one of the first documents to be added.
- DVLA’s 2024–25 Annual Report states discovery is complete and development is about to commence “with the aim to add a digital driving licence to the GOV.UK Wallet by the end of 2025”.
- The Data (Use and Access) Act received Royal Assent on June 19, 2025, formalising Digital Verification Services and supporting the broader digital identity ecosystem within which GOV.UK Wallet operates.

Why this question is non-trivial: Large public IT projects often slip; while multiple official statements signal a 2025 pilot, actual launch could be delayed. The resolution depends on real-world delivery milestones and official announcements, creating meaningful uncertainty.

Key definitions and links:
- Digital driving licence (DDL): A government-issued digital credential representing an individual’s UK driving licence (issued by DVLA) that can be stored and presented via the GOV.UK Wallet app. Government materials describe Wallet as enabling users to save and use government documents like the full driving licence on their phone. See GOV.UK Wallet overview: https://www.gov.uk/wallet.
- GOV.UK Wallet: A UK government app and platform that will allow people (via GOV.UK One Login) to save and use government-issued documents on their phone, starting with selected credentials and expanding over time.
- UK driving licence (general concept): The official authorisation to drive vehicles in Great Britain, issued by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA). Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driving_licence_in_the_United_Kingdom (link provided for general definition; not used for resolution).
- GOV.UK One Login: The government identity and login service required to access Wallet. Overview: https://www.gov.uk/using-your-gov-uk-one-login.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, an official UK government source announces and evidences that a public pilot of a digital driving licence (DDL) via GOV.UK Wallet has launched and is live for some members of the public (outside internal testing), as defined below. Otherwise it resolves No.

Definitions for resolution:
- Public pilot: A government-run limited release intended to test the DDL with members of the public who are not part of internal government testing. The pilot is considered “launched” when eligible members of the public (e.g., drivers in a defined cohort, region, or invite list) can enroll and add a DDL to their GOV.UK Wallet and use it in real-world contexts. Platform limitations (e.g., iOS-only) or cohort restrictions are acceptable; internal closed tests limited to civil servants or contractors do not count.
- Digital driving licence (DDL): A digital version of the UK driving licence issued under DVLA authority, stored and presented via GOV.UK Wallet. It must be the driving licence credential, not other documents (e.g., the HM Armed Forces Veteran Card). Government guidance indicates the full driving licence is planned as one of the first Wallet documents.
- Official UK government source: A page or publication under the gov.uk domain (including GOV.UK News releases, DVLA pages, Cabinet Office/GDS or DSIT publications), or the live GOV.UK Wallet user-facing page/app instructions. Primary resolution sources include:
  • GOV.UK News (“Government news and communications”): https://www.gov.uk/government/news 
  • GOV.UK Wallet overview and guidance pages: https://www.gov.uk/wallet; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-govuk-wallet-in-government; https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-govuk-wallet-in-the-digital-identity-sector 
  • DVLA pages and publications on gov.uk (for example, DVLA press releases and updates) 

What counts as sufficient evidence:
Any one of the following published between the start and end timestamps will resolve the question Yes:
1) A GOV.UK News post or DVLA/GDS/DSIT gov.uk page explicitly stating that a pilot digital driving licence has launched and is now available for eligible members of the public to use (e.g., “pilot digital driving licence launched today…”), or
2) The GOV.UK Wallet user-facing page or app instructions updated to state that users in a defined cohort can now add their driving licence to Wallet (e.g., “You can now save your driving licence to GOV.UK Wallet…”), or
3) An official gov.uk page providing a live sign-up or enrollment pathway clearly open to non-government participants to obtain and use a DDL during the pilot.

Exclusions:
- Announcements that only state intention (e.g., “will launch later this year”) without stating that the pilot is live do not count.
- Pilots or releases involving other documents (e.g., HM Armed Forces Veteran Card) do not count toward this question.
- Reporting by third parties without an official gov.uk source does not count.

If sources conflict:
- Prefer the most recent official gov.uk publication. If ambiguity remains, the GOV.UK Wallet user-facing page and the relevant GOV.UK News post will be decisive.

Notes and context for resolvers:
- Government statements indicate intent to pilot the DDL later in 2025 and to add the full driving licence to Wallet after the Veteran Card, with DVLA aiming for end-of-2025 availability. The legislative foundation for digital verification services was established in June 2025.

question: Will Drewry’s World Container Index (composite) be below $1,500 per 40ft container in the weekly assessment dated 11 December 2025?
background:
Overview and status quo as of today (2025-09-30)
- What is being forecast: This question targets a single, dated weekly reading of Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) composite and asks whether that reading will be strictly below $1,500 per 40-foot container (FEU) on the weekly assessment dated 11 December 2025.
- About the WCI: The WCI is a composite index reporting actual spot container freight rates on eight major East–West trade routes. The composite is volume-weighted across these routes and is reported in US dollars per 40-foot container. Rates are collected from transport intermediaries (e.g., freight forwarders/NVOCCs) and include certain common ocean surcharges such as BAF, CAF, PSS, WRS, and SSC, while excluding inland/intermodal and various ancillary charges; THCs may vary by route. Methodology reference: Drewry’s “World Container Index methodology” page (https://www.drewry.co.uk/logistics-executive-briefing/logistics-executive-briefing-articles/world-container-index-methodology).
- FEU / 40-foot container definition: One FEU is a forty-foot equivalent unit, a standard measure of cargo capacity based on a 40-foot intermodal container; 1 FEU equals 2 TEU. See Wikipedia entry on twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-foot_equivalent_unit).
- Publication cadence and verification location: Drewry publishes a dated weekly post titled “World Container Index – assessed by Drewry”, which presents the composite value prominently as “$X per 40ft container,” along with route-level details. Example: the assessment dated Thursday, 25 Sep 2025 shows the composite at $1,761 per 40ft container and notes the weekly change; this illustrates the format and cadence relevant for the December reading (verification URL pattern: https://www.drewry.co.uk/supply-chain-advisors/supply-chain-expertise/world-container-index-assessed-by-drewry).
- Status today: In the weekly assessment dated 25 September 2025, Drewry reported the WCI composite at $1,761 per 40ft container, marking the 15th consecutive week of declines, underscoring recent downward momentum heading into Q4 2025.

Why this may be uncertain: Container spot rates in 2025 have shown substantial variability due to demand, capacity deployment, and policy/geopolitical factors. With the composite recently at $1,761 and trending down as of late September, a sub-$1,500 print by mid-December is plausible but not assured.
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution (Yes/No). All dates/times refer to UTC for deadlines; the decisive date label is the one printed by Drewry on its weekly web page.

Primary rule
- Resolve Yes if the Drewry World Container Index (WCI) composite value shown on Drewry’s weekly assessment dated 11 December 2025 is strictly less than $1,500.00 (i.e., < $1,500.00). Resolve No otherwise (including if it is exactly $1,500.00).

What to check and where
- Source of truth: Drewry’s “World Container Index – assessed by Drewry” weekly page, specifically the post carrying the date label “11 December 2025.” Canonical location: https://www.drewry.co.uk/supply-chain-advisors/supply-chain-expertise/world-container-index-assessed-by-drewry. Use the composite value presented in the headline/intro text of that dated post, expressed as “$X per 40ft container.”

Definitions and unit handling
- “World Container Index (WCI) composite”: The volume-weighted composite across eight major East–West routes as defined by Drewry’s methodology, reported as US dollars per 40-foot container (FEU), based on spot rates from transport intermediaries; includes BAF/CAF/PSS/WRS/SSC, excludes inland/intermodal and various ancillary charges; THCs may vary by route.
- “Per 40ft container” and “FEU”: One FEU corresponds to one 40-foot intermodal container (1 FEU = 2 TEU).
- Currency and rounding: Use the USD value exactly as displayed by Drewry on the dated page. If Drewry lists whole dollars, that printed whole-dollar figure governs; if decimals are shown, the printed decimal figure governs. “Strictly less than $1,500” means any value below $1,500.00; a value of exactly $1,500.00 resolves No.

Edge cases and contingencies
- If Drewry posts the weekly assessment under a different URL or section but with the same titled series and the date label “11 December 2025,” use that page. The date label on the Drewry page is authoritative for identifying the correct weekly assessment.
- If Drewry is temporarily unreachable, postpone resolution until the page is accessible, but in all cases finalize by 31 December 2025, 23:59 UTC, using the value displayed on the Drewry page carrying the 11 December 2025 date label.
- If, exceptionally, Drewry does not publish any WCI weekly assessment bearing the date label “11 December 2025” by 31 December 2025, this market should be resolved as No Resolution (N/A). This contingency is included solely to guarantee an unambiguous outcome by year-end; it is expected to be unnecessary given Drewry’s weekly cadence.

question: Will Memphis be awarded at least $30 million from Tennessee’s Downtown Public Safety grant program by December 31, 2025?
background:
Summary of the relevant program and current status as of 2025-10-01:
- Tennessee enacted a $100,000,000 Downtown Public Safety grant program (DPSG) in 2025. Statute language specifies that the funds are for direct grants to local governments (including the City of Memphis) and certain Business Improvement District (BID) entities, with grants "awarded no later than December 31, 2025," subject to approval by the Commissioner of Finance and Administration.
- Press coverage on September 26–29, 2025 reported Governor Bill Lee’s announcement of $100 million in state funding tied to Memphis public safety initiatives, but did not include administrative specifics or disbursement timelines in those reports.
- To avoid confusion with other programs: Tennessee’s Violent Crime Intervention Fund (VCIF) is a distinct, statewide $100 million fund appropriated in the 2022–23 budget; it is not Memphis-specific and is separate from the 2025 DPSG described above.

Why this question is non-trivial: The DPSG allows multiple eligible recipients (including Memphis government and certain Memphis BID entities) to be awarded grants before 2025-12-31. How much of the $100,000,000 will be awarded to Memphis-linked recipients versus other eligible cities and BIDs is uncertain, making the $30,000,000 threshold a realistic and non-obvious pivot.

Key definitions and links for forecasters:
- Downtown Public Safety grant program (DPSG): As codified by Public Chapter No. 530 (2025), Item 23(b), allocating $100,000,000 and defining eligible recipients, purposes, and the award deadline.
- City of Memphis: The municipal government of Memphis, Tennessee (for general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee).
- Business Improvement District (BID): A defined district funded by assessments to improve and manage a commercial area. For general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_improvement_district. The DPSG statute requires eligible BID entities to manage or oversee at least one central business improvement district created under Tennessee Code Annotated Title 7, Chapter 84, and operate in a municipal/metropolitan government with population ≥181,000 (2020 census).
- Award vs. other funding: This question is limited to awards under the 2025 DPSG  and explicitly excludes VCIF and other programs.

Resolution sources forecasters should expect:
- Primary: Official Tennessee Department of Finance & Administration publications (including tn.gov press releases or award lists) confirming DPSG awards and amounts, or executed grant contracts posted in the State of Tennessee’s public contracting systems, showing recipient legal name and award amount.
- Secondary: Official City of Memphis media releases confirming receipt of a DPSG award and the award amount; credible reporting by major outlets (e.g., AP News, WREG) that specify DPSG award amounts to Memphis recipients.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the aggregate of DPSG awards to Memphis-linked eligible recipients is at least $30,000,000 USD; otherwise, it resolves No.

Definitions and counting rules:
- Program scope: Only awards under the Downtown Public Safety grant program established in 2025 Public Chapter No. 530, Item 23(b) count toward the total. Awards from other programs (e.g., VCIF) do not count.
- Eligible Memphis-linked recipients that count:
  1) The City of Memphis municipal government; and/or
  2) Business Improvement District (BID) entities that meet the DPSG statutory eligibility and operate within the municipal boundaries of Memphis (i.e., they manage or oversee at least one central business improvement district created under Tennessee Code Annotated Title 7, Chapter 84, and operate in a qualifying city).
- Award definition: An "award" is a formal grant award under the DPSG that identifies the recipient legal entity and a specific dollar amount, evidenced by any of the following:
  a) An official Tennessee Department of Finance & Administration (tn.gov) publication (e.g., press release or award list) that names the DPSG recipient and award amount;
  b) An executed DPSG grant contract posted in the State of Tennessee’s public contracting systems (e.g., Edison) showing recipient name and award amount;
  c) An official City of Memphis media release explicitly stating that the City (or an eligible Memphis BID entity) has been awarded a DPSG grant and providing the award amount;
  d) Credible reporting by major outlets (e.g., AP News, WREG) specifying a DPSG award and amount to a Memphis-linked recipient.
- Aggregation: Sum multiple DPSG awards to eligible Memphis-linked recipients during the defined time window; the resolution threshold is met if the summed total is ≥ $30,000,000 USD.
- Currency and rounding: Use nominal USD amounts stated in award documentation. If amounts are stated with cents, include them in the sum; rounding is not required.
- Time window: Awards must be dated (or contract execution dated) between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Awards announced outside this window do not count.
- Ambiguity handling: If sources conflict, prefer official tn.gov publications or executed contracts over media reports. If an award is announced but later rescinded before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, it does not count.

Automatic invalidation guardrails:
- If no official DPSG awards exist (per the statutory program) by the deadline, resolve No.
- Awards from the VCIF or any non-DPSG program must be excluded.

Citations supporting program details and current status:
- DPSG statutory authorization, eligible recipients, and award deadline language.
- Press reporting of the governor’s $100 million public safety announcement tied to Memphis initiatives, lacking disbursement specifics at the time.
- VCIF is a distinct statewide $100 million fund from 2022–23, not the DPSG.

question: Will the World Bank approve at least one additional Board-approved IDA/IBRD financing operation for Syria between October 1 and December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Status quo as of today (2025-09-30):
- Syria’s arrears to IDA (~US$15.5 million) were cleared effective May 12, 2025 via payments by Saudi Arabia and Qatar, reinstating Syria’s eligibility for new World Bank operations.
- On June 25, 2025, the World Bank Board of Executive Directors approved a US$146 million International Development Association (IDA) grant for the Syria Electricity Emergency Project (SEEP), described as the first World Bank project in Syria in almost four decades. This establishes at least one Board-approved operation for Syria in 2025 already.

Why this question has non-trivial uncertainty: Re-engagement has begun but remains subject to operational, policy, and geopolitical constraints. A second Board-approved financing operation by year-end is plausible but not guaranteed, creating meaningful forecasting uncertainty.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- World Bank Board of Executive Directors: The governance body that approves IBRD/IDA-financed operations. See: https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership/board-of-executive-directors
- International Development Association (IDA): The World Bank’s fund for the poorest countries that provides highly concessional credits and grants. See: https://ida.worldbank.org/en/financing
- International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD): The World Bank entity that lends to middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries. See: https://www.worldbank.org/en/who-we-are/ibrd
- Projects & Operations database (P&O): The World Bank’s official database listing project pages with “Board Approval Date” and financing type. See: https://projects.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/projects-home
- Country definition: “Syria” refers to “Syrian Arab Republic” (ISO 3166-1 alpha-3: SYR). Forecasters can use the P&O country filter for Syrian Arab Republic.

Context sources:
- Arrears clearance and reinstated eligibility for new operations.
- SEEP approval details (amount, instrument, Board approval).
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Count approvals that occur between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

What counts as an “additional Board-approved IDA/IBRD financing operation for Syria”:
- An operation recorded in the World Bank Projects & Operations database with:
  1) Country listed as “Syrian Arab Republic” (Syria), and
  2) Financing type under IBRD/IDA (e.g., IBRD Loan; IDA Credit; IDA Grant), and
  3) A “Board Approval Date” that falls within the time window above.
- Multi-country/regional operations count only if Syria is explicitly listed as a recipient country on the project page (e.g., “Country(s): Syrian Arab Republic”).
- Operations approved prior to 2025-10-01 do not count (including the June 25, 2025 SEEP approval ).
- Advisory Services and Analytics (ASA), trust-funded grants or activities that do not go to the Board (i.e., without a Board Approval Date), restructurings, additional financings without a fresh Board approval within the window, and pipeline announcements without Board approval do not count.

Resolution procedure (to be performed after 2025-12-31):
- Resolve Yes if at least one qualifying operation exists. Verification steps:
  1) Go to the World Bank Projects & Operations database (https://projects.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/projects-home).
  2) Filter by Country: “Syrian Arab Republic” and by Approval Date within the specified window.
  3) Confirm the project page shows “Financing” as IBRD/IDA and displays a “Board Approval Date” within the window.
- Alternatively, an official World Bank press release (https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release) announcing Board approval of an IBRD/IDA-financed Syria operation within the window is acceptable. If there is any discrepancy between press release timing and the project page’s Board Approval Date, the date on the official project page governs.
- Resolve No if no qualifying operation is found.

Primary resolution sources:

question: By December 31, 2025, will the United States reduce or suspend the additional 25% ad valorem duty on products of India imposed under Executive Order 14329?
background:
Status quo as of September 30, 2025:
- On August 6, 2025, the President issued Executive Order 14329 (“Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of the Russian Federation”) imposing an additional ad valorem duty of 25% on imports of articles of India. The order’s duty becomes effective 21 days after the order’s date for goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, with specified transit exceptions.
- U.S. Customs and Border Protection implemented the measure via a Federal Register Notice on August 27, 2025. The notice establishes HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 for “products of India,” sets the additional duty at 25%, provides the effective time (12:01 a.m. EDT on August 27, 2025), and details exceptions (e.g., certain in-transit shipments, specified iron/steel and aluminum articles, passenger vehicles and parts, humanitarian donations, informational materials). It explicitly states this additional duty is in addition to duties under Executive Order 14257 (reciprocal tariffs) unless otherwise specified.
- Separately, under the July 31, 2025 presidential action “Further Modifying the Reciprocal Tariff Rates,” India’s baseline reciprocal tariff rate was set at 25% effective August 7, 2025, which stacks with the EO 14329 duty where applicable. In practice, this means many Indian-origin goods face combined duties of approximately 50% before other exceptions or sector-specific measures, as the EO 14329 duty is “in addition to” applicable reciprocal tariffs.
- As context, U.S. officials have stated that curbing India’s purchases of Russian oil is crucial to reducing India’s tariff rate and advancing a trade deal. Reporting indicates the extra 25% duty was imposed to pressure India to halt discounted Russian crude purchases and that tariff relief has been linked to India’s actions on Russian oil.

Key definitions and references forecasters may use:
- “Ad valorem duty” refers to a duty calculated as a percentage of the value of the goods. See general definition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_valorem_tax.
- “Federal Register” is the official journal of the U.S. federal government where rules, notices, and presidential documents are published: https://www.federalregister.gov.
- “Products of India” means articles for which India is the country of origin under U.S. Customs rules; in the EO 14329 implementation, these are covered by HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 (with enumerated exceptions).

Why this question is non-trivial:
- The policy is explicitly tied to geopolitical and trade negotiations. Actions that reduce or suspend the additional duty could occur via a new executive order or an implementing/terminating notice in the Federal Register. The linkage to India’s Russian oil purchases and ongoing trade talks adds genuine uncertainty.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on official U.S. government publications between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

Operational question:
- Will the United States reduce or suspend the additional 25% ad valorem duty on products of India imposed under Executive Order 14329 and implemented in HTSUS heading 9903.01.84?

Definitions (for resolution purposes):
- “Additional 25% ad valorem duty on products of India” means the duty established by Executive Order 14329 (August 6, 2025) and implemented for HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 in the Federal Register Notice of August 27, 2025.
- “Reduce” means any official action that modifies HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 to set the additional ad valorem rate below 25% (but above 0%) for products of India on a general basis (i.e., a change to the heading’s rate, not merely adding or adjusting product-specific exceptions).
- “Suspend” means any official action that sets the HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 additional ad valorem rate to 0% or removes the heading such that the EO 14329 duty no longer applies to products of India on a general basis (again, not limited to product-specific exceptions).
- “Official action” means one of:
  1) A Presidential Action or Executive Order published on whitehouse.gov that explicitly reduces or suspends the EO 14329 additional duty for products of India (general application), or
  2) A Federal Register notice that modifies or removes HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 to reduce or suspend the duty (general application).
- “General basis” excludes changes that only add or alter exceptions for specific products or subheadings (e.g., carving out a particular sector under HTSUS heading 9903.01.87). Such product-specific exceptions do not count as a reduction or suspension for this question.

Resolution:
- Yes: If, within the resolution window, an official action (as defined above) is published that reduces the rate below 25% or suspends it to 0% for HTSUS heading 9903.01.84 covering products of India. The effective date of the change may be after December 31, 2025; publication within the window is sufficient.
- No: If no such official action is published within the resolution window.

Primary sources of truth:
- Federal Register (e.g., the August 27, 2025 “Notice of Implementation of Additional Duties on Products of India” establishing HTSUS 9903.01.84).
- White House Presidential Actions page for any Executive Orders or Presidential documents that modify or terminate EO 14329’s duty.

Notes for resolvers:
- Use the publication timestamp/date as shown on federalregister.gov or whitehouse.gov. If only a date is shown, treat publication as occurring on that date (UTC). If both sites publish relevant actions, the existence of either suffices for “Yes,” provided it unambiguously reduces or suspends the general duty as defined.

question: Will U.S. headline CPI-U (12‑month percent change, “all items,” U.S. city average) for November 2025 be at least 3.1%?
background:
Context and definitions
- What is being measured: The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U) measures the average change over time in prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of goods and services and covers over 90% of the U.S. population. The “all items” index is the broadest, most widely used CPI‑U aggregate (often called “headline CPI”) and includes all consumer expenditure categories in the U.S. city average; taxes directly associated with purchase/use (e.g., sales and excise taxes) are included in prices.
- The statistic in question: The “12‑month percent change” (year‑over‑year, YoY) compares the index level for a given month to the same month a year earlier. Per BLS, compute it by subtracting the earlier index value from the later index value, dividing by the earlier index value, and multiplying by 100. In BLS CPI news releases, this is the rate typically summarized as “The all items index rose X percent for the 12 months ending [Month]”.
- Status quo: In the most recent published CPI release as of September 11, 2025 (covering August 2025), the all‑items CPI‑U 12‑month change was 2.9%.
- Timing and source: The November 2025 CPI (reference month) is scheduled for release on December 10, 2025 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time (ET) on the BLS site; the BLS schedule explicitly notes that all calendar times are Eastern Time. The corresponding “Consumer Price Index Summary” news release page (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm) will contain the official November 2025 all‑items CPI‑U 12‑month percent change used for resolution.

Why this is forecastable now
- Inflation remained near 3% YoY in late 2025 (2.9% in August), and plausible paths for September–November could move the November YoY either above or below 3.1%, making the 3.1% threshold a non‑trivial target.

Key term clarifications (used in the resolution)
- “CPI‑U”: CPI for All Urban Consumers, the broadest CPI population group.
- “All items, U.S. city average”: The headline CPI‑U aggregate across urban areas; includes all categories, with taxes directly tied to purchases included.
- “12‑month percent change”: The percent change between the index value for November 2025 and November 2024, as defined by BLS.
- Release date/time: December 10, 2025, 08:30 a.m. ET (13:30 UTC); BLS calendar notes all times are Eastern Time.
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution (Yes/No)
- Question: Will the U.S. headline CPI‑U (12‑month percent change, “all items,” U.S. city average) for November 2025 be at least 3.1%?
- Resolve YES if the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index news release (“Consumer Price Index Summary”) published on December 10, 2025 reports the all‑items CPI‑U 12‑month percent change for November 2025 as greater than or equal to 3.1%; resolve NO otherwise.

What exactly to read
- Primary source: BLS “Consumer Price Index Summary” page at https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm for the December 10, 2025 release (reference month: November 2025). Use the all‑items CPI‑U “12‑month percent change” value for the U.S. city average shown in the news release (commonly stated in the opening paragraph as “The all items index rose X percent for the 12 months ending November”) and/or in the accompanying table for the “All items” line.

Precision and tie‑breakers
- Use the 12‑month percent change value as presented by BLS in the news release. If multiple places present the value, prefer the value in the release’s tables for “All items, U.S. city average” CPI‑U if there is any discrepancy; otherwise use the figure stated in the text.
- If BLS issues a correction or erratum to the November 2025 CPI news release on or before December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC, resolve using the corrected value; otherwise, resolve using the initially published news release value.

Scope and timing
- Event window: This question concerns only the single statistic described above for November 2025.
- Resolution timing: Resolve upon publication of the BLS release on December 10, 2025 at 08:30 a.m. ET (13:30 UTC), or upon any BLS correction/erratum issued by December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC.

Definitions and references
- CPI and CPI‑U overview and coverage: BLS CPI FAQ and Handbook of Methods.
- Inclusion of taxes/fees in “all items”: BLS CPI technical notes.
- 12‑month percent change calculation: BLS CPI factsheet on calculating percent changes.
- Latest baseline (August 2025 YoY = 2.9%): BLS Consumer Price Index Summary for August 2025.
- Release schedule confirming December 10, 2025 at 08:30 a.m. ET for the November 2025 CPI: BLS release calendar (note: all times Eastern Time).

question: Will ERCOT declare at least one Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) Level 2 or Level 3 between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- ERCOT’s Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) trigger levels were updated on November 1, 2023, increasing minimum operating reserve thresholds and tightening frequency-based criteria. As of that update: EEA 1 at reserves ≤2,500 MW (not expected to recover within 30 minutes); EEA 2 at reserves ≤2,000 MW (not expected to recover within 30 minutes) or if frequency <59.91 Hz for 15 minutes; EEA 3 at reserves <1,500 MW (not expected to recover within 30 minutes) or if frequency <59.8 Hz at any time. These thresholds shape when ERCOT enters EEA emergency operations.
- ERCOT communicates EEA declarations via official channels such as news releases; for example, ERCOT publicly announced an EEA Level 2 on September 6, 2023 (“ERCOT Has Initiated Energy Emergency Alert Level 2”), illustrating the type of communication that would resolve this question if it occurred within the time window.
- Resource adequacy context: ERCOT publishes recurring reports to indicate risk of tight reserves and potential for EEA events, including the Monthly Outlook for Resource Adequacy (MORA) and the Capacity, Demand and Reserves (CDR) report. The October 2025 MORA quantified a low but non-zero probability of EEA conditions in October, with the highest-risk hour (HE 8 p.m. CDT) carrying a 0.17% chance of ERCOT declaring an EEA and a 0.08% chance of controlled outages; it also noted ongoing capacity additions (e.g., net +2,320 MW since the prior MORA across solar, gas, wind, and batteries). While that report addresses October specifically, it demonstrates ERCOT’s methodology and the types of resource and risk drivers forecasters monitor.

Why this is forecastable now:
- Late fall and early winter conditions in Texas can create tight reserve conditions due to weather, outages, and renewable variability, but ERCOT has also seen capacity additions and procedural changes. Both “Yes” and “No” outcomes are plausible, and the event would be publicly documented if it occurs.
resolution_criteria:
Eligible period and time zone:
- The question resolves to Yes if, at any time between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, ERCOT publicly declares an Energy Emergency Alert Level 2 (EEA 2) or an Energy Emergency Alert Level 3 (EEA 3). Otherwise, it resolves to No.

Definitions (for clarity, not as operative triggers):
- Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) levels are ERCOT’s emergency operating conditions. As of the November 1, 2023 update, EEA 2 occurs if operating reserves are ≤2,000 MW and not expected to recover within 30 minutes, or if frequency is <59.91 Hz for 15 minutes; EEA 3 occurs if reserves are <1,500 MW and not expected to recover within 30 minutes, or if frequency is <59.8 Hz at any time. The resolution depends on ERCOT’s public declaration of “EEA 2” or “EEA 3,” regardless of the underlying thresholds in effect at that time.

What counts as “publicly declares” and acceptable resolution sources:
- A qualifying declaration is an official ERCOT communication that explicitly states ERCOT has initiated or is in “Energy Emergency Alert Level 2” or “Energy Emergency Alert Level 3.” Acceptable sources include:
  - ERCOT News Releases (e.g., “ERCOT Has Initiated Energy Emergency Alert Level 2” on 2023-09-06 demonstrates the format).
  - ERCOT Market Notices and/or other official ERCOT pages on ercot.com that document entering EEA levels. ERCOT’s Resource Adequacy page lists recurring reliability publications and is indicative of ERCOT’s practice of publishing operational information on ercot.com.
- If ERCOT’s site is unavailable, credible contemporaneous reporting that directly attributes an EEA 2 or EEA 3 declaration to ERCOT (e.g., wire services such as AP or Reuters) is acceptable as a fallback.

Inclusions/exclusions and edge cases:
- Multiple EEA declarations within the window still resolve Yes (only one is required).
- Only the initial declaration timestamp is used for eligibility. An EEA 2/3 first declared before the UTC window does not count even if it remains active into the window; an EEA 2/3 first declared within the UTC window counts, even if later escalated, de-escalated, or rescinded within the window.
- Drills, tests, training exercises, or simulations that do not state ERCOT has actually entered EEA 2 or EEA 3 for real-world operating conditions do not count.

How to verify (intended URLs; examples, not exhaustive):
- ERCOT News: https://www.ercot.com/news (see example declaration format )
- ERCOT Resource Adequacy and related reports: https://www.ercot.com/gridinfo/resource (demonstrates ERCOT’s practice of publishing recurring operational information )

Notes:
- The background thresholds are provided for forecasters’ context and reflect ERCOT’s November 1, 2023 update. The operative resolution criterion is the presence of an official ERCOT declaration of “EEA 2” or “EEA 3” during the specified UTC window.

question: Will the Council of the EU adopt decisions on the signature and conclusion of both the EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA) and the interim Trade Agreement (iTA) between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Context and current status as of 2025-10-01:
- On 3 September 2025, the European Commission adopted proposals for Council decisions on the signature and conclusion of two parallel legal instruments with Mercosur: the EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA) and an interim Trade Agreement (iTA), starting the Council approval process. The Council’s own information page notes these two instruments and that the iTA is designed to expire once the EMPA is fully ratified and enters into force.
- The Council of the European Union (Council) is one of the EU’s two legislators, composed of national ministers; it adopts EU laws and international agreements, typically by qualified majority voting (QMV). According to reporting by Reuters, consent for this accord requires a vote in the European Parliament and a qualified majority among EU governments, meaning at least 15 of 27 members representing 65% of the EU population, and the Commission floated safeguard mechanisms on sensitive agricultural imports to address concerns from France. Spain’s economy minister stated on September 29, 2025, that he expects the agreement to be ratified by year-end, indicating momentum but not certainty.
- Legal procedure: Under Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), the Council adopts a decision authorizing the signing of international agreements (Article 218(5)) and a separate decision concluding them (Article 218(6)), often after obtaining the European Parliament’s consent depending on the agreement type [a8dc21; e5b084].
- Publication source: The Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU) is the EU’s gazette of record; its L series (Legislation) publishes binding EU legal acts, including Council decisions and international agreements.

Key definitions for this question:
- Council of the European Union (Council): The institution of EU national ministers that, with the European Parliament, legislates and decides on EU agreements.
- EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA): The comprehensive partnership agreement between the EU and Mercosur (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay) for trade, investment, and sustainable development; proposed to the Council for signature and conclusion on 3 September 2025.
- Interim Trade Agreement (iTA): A parallel legal instrument intended to apply provisionally and be repealed/replaced by the EMPA once the EMPA is fully ratified and enters into force [7093f5; 674a32].
- Decision on the signature: A Council decision under Article 218(5) TFEU that authorizes the EU to sign an international agreement (and, if necessary, to apply it provisionally before entry into force).
- Decision on the conclusion: A Council decision under Article 218(6) TFEU that concludes an international agreement on behalf of the EU, making it binding, typically after European Parliament consent where required.
- Official Journal L series: The Legislation series of the OJEU where EU legal acts, including Council decisions and international agreements, are published.
- Qualified majority voting (QMV) threshold (context): As reported by Reuters for this accord, adoption requires at least 15 of 27 EU member states representing 65% of the EU population.

Why this is a non-trivial forecast: The outcome depends on political negotiations among EU member states, the European Parliament’s stance, and timing/logistical factors for formal adoption. Signals are mixed: safeguards proposed to ease French concerns , Spain’s public optimism , and an expedited pathway via the iTA [7093f5; 674a32]. Forecasters must track Council agendas, member-state positions, EP consent, and publication logistics in OJEU.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone: Eligible events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Resolve Yes if, within the above window, ALL of the following four Council decisions have been formally adopted:
1) A Council decision authorizing the signature of the EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA) under Article 218(5) TFEU.
2) A Council decision concluding the EMPA under Article 218(6) TFEU.
3) A Council decision authorizing the signature of the interim Trade Agreement (iTA) under Article 218(5) TFEU.
4) A Council decision concluding the iTA under Article 218(6) TFEU.

Definitions and evidentiary standards:
- “Formally adopted” means the Council has adopted the relevant decision pursuant to Article 218 TFEU (signature per 218(5), conclusion per 218(6)) [a8dc21; e5b084].
- Evidence of adoption must be verifiable via at least one of the following:
  a) Publication of the decision in the Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU) L series (Legislation) , or
  b) An official Council communication confirming adoption (e.g., a Council press release or official Council document) on the Council/Consilium website (consilium.europa.eu) that clearly identifies the decision and its adoption date.

Resolve No if any of the four decisions above have not been formally adopted within the time window, or if adequate evidence (as defined) is not available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Notes:
- The focus of this question is exclusively on the Council decisions authorizing signature and concluding the agreements; subsequent steps (e.g., national ratifications for the EMPA, entry into force, repeal of iTA) are not required for a Yes resolution [a8dc21; 7093f5; 674a32].
- The Official Journal L series is the preferred single source of truth; Council press releases or official Council documents are allowed as alternative evidence to avoid delays due to OJEU publication timing.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will at least one FY2026 regular appropriations bill be enacted into U.S. law?
background:
Summary and scope
- This question asks whether any one of the twelve “regular” fiscal year 2026 (FY2026) appropriations bills will become law during the inclusive window from 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Key definitions and context a forecaster needs
- Appropriations bill: In the United States, an appropriations bill is legislation that provides funding to federal departments, agencies, and programs for a fiscal year.
