To be enacted, a bill must pass both chambers and become law (e.g., by presidential signature, veto override, or becoming law without signature). The federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30 of the following year. See “Appropriations bill (United States)” on Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appropriations_bill_(United_States)).
- Regular appropriations bills: These are the twelve standard annual bills intended to fund the government for one fiscal year, distinct from continuing resolutions or supplemental appropriations. For FY2026, Congress.gov’s Appropriations Status Table tracks twelve regular bills and lists them by subcommittee/topic; this table is the authoritative tracker we will use (https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table).
- FY2026: The U.S. federal fiscal year that begins on 2025-10-01 and ends on 2026-09-30.

Where to track progress and what counts
- Congress.gov hosts an “Appropriations Status Table: FY2026” that lists the twelve regular appropriations bills and tracks their progress across legislative stages (e.g., House/Senate subcommittee and committee approvals, chamber passage, resolution of differences, and a final “Presidential Approval” stage). The page also displays a last-updated timestamp, indicating active maintenance. Link: https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table.
- For FY2026, the table includes the following twelve rows/bills (names as displayed on the table), any one of which can satisfy this question if enacted:
  1) Agriculture; 2) Commerce-Justice-Science; 3) Defense; 4) Energy-Water; 5) Financial Services; 6) Homeland Security; 7) Interior-Environment; 8) Labor-HHS-Education; 9) Legislative Branch; 10) Military Construction–Veterans Affairs; 11) State–Foreign Operations (House) / National Security–Dept of State (Senate); 12) Transportation–HUD.

Status quo as of today (for calibration)
- As of late September 2025, independent tracking indicates no FY2026 regular appropriations bills had been enacted into law. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget’s Appropriations Watch (FY 2026) reported no indication of any enacted regular FY2026 bills by the end of September; it also noted continuing resolution efforts and broader year-end deadlines (https://www.crfb.org/blogs/appropriations-watch-fy-2026).
- The FY2026 Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov showed a recent update timestamp as of 2025-09-26 and tracks the “Presidential Approval” stage for each of the twelve bills (https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table).

Why this is forecastable
- Year-end enactment of some subset of the regular appropriations often hinges on evolving negotiations; outcomes can range from continued short-term funding to passage of one or more regular bills (sometimes in consolidated packages). As of late September 2025, both outcomes (at least one enacted vs. none) appear plausible, creating meaningful uncertainty.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome to forecast
- Resolve “Yes” if at least one of the twelve FY2026 regular appropriations bills becomes law between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). Otherwise resolve “No.”

Eligible bills (exhaustive list)
- The twelve “regular” FY2026 appropriations bills, as listed on Congress.gov’s Appropriations Status Table: FY2026, are: Agriculture; Commerce-Justice-Science; Defense; Energy-Water; Financial Services; Homeland Security; Interior-Environment; Labor-HHS-Education; Legislative Branch; Military Construction–Veterans Affairs; State–Foreign Operations (House) / National Security–Dept of State (Senate); Transportation–HUD. Only these twelve count for this question. Continuing resolutions or supplemental appropriations do not count as “regular” bills for the purpose of this question.

What “enacted into law” means for this market
- A bill is considered “enacted into law” for this question if it has “Became Law” status on its Congress.gov bill page with an assigned Public Law number, reflecting presidential signature, veto override, or becoming law without signature. For timing, use the “Became Law” date reported by Congress.gov (date-only); if that date falls within the inclusive window above, it counts as “Yes” regardless of time-of-day uncertainty (https://www.congress.gov/).

Primary resolution source and procedure
- Primary check: Congress.gov’s Appropriations Status Table: FY2026 (https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table). Resolve “Yes” if, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, at least one of the twelve rows shows an entry corresponding to the final stage (Presidential Approval/Became Law) with a date within the window. If none do, proceed to the fallback check.
- Fallback check: If the table appears lagging, ambiguous, or temporarily inaccessible at the resolution time, check the Congress.gov bill page(s) for each of the twelve eligible bills. If any show “Became Law (Public Law …)” with a “Became Law” date within the window, resolve “Yes”; if none do, resolve “No”.

Edge cases and clarifications
- Consolidated/omnibus or “minibus” enactments: If a regular FY2026 bill’s funding is enacted as a division of a larger appropriations package, it counts only if Congress.gov credits the corresponding regular bill as “Became Law” (i.e., with a Public Law number) within the window. In practice, the Appropriations Status Table will attribute enactment to the relevant row when applicable.
- Veto/override timing: If a bill is vetoed but subsequently becomes law via override within the window (per Congress.gov’s “Became Law” date), it counts.
- Time zone: All dates/times in this question use UTC. Congress.gov generally reports dates rather than precise times for “Became Law”; use the reported date. If the reported date is 2025-12-31, it counts; if 2026-01-01 or later, it does not.
- Inaccessible sources: If Congress.gov is broadly inaccessible at resolution time, the question should remain pending until it becomes accessible; do not substitute other sources absent Congress.gov confirmation.

question: Will Iran’s free‑market USD/IRR sell rate reach at least 1,250,000 at any point between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025‑09‑30:
- Unofficial/free‑market quotes for the Iranian rial have been at historic lows in late September 2025. The Associated Press reported that on 2025‑09‑24 the rial fell to an all‑time low of 1,074,000 per U.S. dollar. Reuters reported that United Nations “snapback” sanctions on Iran were reinstated at 8:00 p.m. EDT on Saturday 2025‑09‑27 (0000 GMT on Sunday 2025‑09‑28), reimposing an arms embargo and other restrictions, increasing macroeconomic pressure.
- AlanChand, a tracker of Iran’s free‑market exchange rates, shows late‑September prices around 1.12–1.14 million rials per USD. For example, its per‑day USD page labeled “USD to IRR Exchange Rate on Tuesday 30 September 2025” shows a price of 1,135,000 Iranian rials and links to a full price archive. Its “Live Exchange Rates in Iranian Rial (IRR)” table explicitly lists “Sell Price” for “US Dollar” (standard USD, distinct from variants like Istanbul/Herat/Remittance), with sell quotes around 1,135,000 IRR in this period. The AlanChand USD archive notes a highest price of 1,130,000 IRR on Sunday 2025‑09‑28 and shows 1,135,000 IRR on 2025‑09‑30.
- Bonbast, another widely used free‑market tracker, provides a dated archive with “Sell” and “Buy” columns for USD. Prices are shown in Iranian toman and explicitly labeled “All prices are in Iranian Toman (1 Toman = 10 Rials).” For example, on 2025‑09‑29 the USD sell price is shown as 110,850 toman (equivalent to 1,108,500 rials). Bonbast’s FAQ also states that prices are quoted in toman and that 1 toman equals 10 rials.

Definitions and references:
- Iranian rial (IRR): the official currency of Iran. In everyday usage, prices are often quoted in toman, where 1 toman = 10 rials. See Wikipedia on the Iranian rial (and its note on toman usage) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_rial. See also Wikipedia on the Iranian toman https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_toman (background on colloquial usage).
- Toman–rial conversion for quoted sources: Bonbast quotes in toman and states 1 toman = 10 rials; multiply by 10 to obtain rials. We will apply the same conversion when interpreting Bonbast’s USD/IRR prices. AlanChand quotes in rials (IRR) on both its per‑day USD page and live table.
- “Free‑market USD/IRR sell rate” in this question refers specifically to the value labeled “Sell” (Bonbast) or “Sell Price” (AlanChand) for standard USD (not location‑specific or remittance variants) on those trackers.

Why this threshold and window:
- With recent prints roughly between 1.07m and 1.14m IRR per USD and new UN sanctions reinstated, a threshold of 1,250,000 IRR (i.e., 125,000 toman) is plausibly reachable yet uncertain within the Oct 15–Dec 31, 2025 window, supporting a high‑entropy forecast.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution
- Resolve Yes if, at any time between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive), EITHER of the following is observed:
  1) Bonbast’s USD/IRR “Sell” price is greater than or equal to 125,000 toman (i.e., 1,250,000 rials), as shown on the Bonbast Archive for USD on any date within the window; or
  2) AlanChand’s “US Dollar” (standard) “Sell Price” is greater than or equal to 1,250,000 rials (IRR) on the Live Exchange Rates page on any timestamped snapshot within the window.

- Otherwise, resolve No.

Key definitions and inclusions/exclusions
- Unit conversions: Bonbast prices are quoted in toman; convert to rials by multiplying by 10. Bonbast explicitly states “All prices are in Iranian Toman (1 Toman = 10 Rials)”. AlanChand pages and tables quote in rials (IRR). For general background: 1 toman = 10 rials in everyday usage.
- Qualifying rate on AlanChand: Use only the row labeled “US Dollar” (standard USD) on the Live Exchange Rates page, not location‑specific or remittance variants (e.g., USD‑Istanbul, USD‑Herat, USD‑Sulaymaniyah, USD‑Remittance), which are separately listed with distinct labels. If the Live page is inaccessible, a per‑day USD page that clearly displays the “Sell Price” for standard USD would also qualify; if no “Sell Price” is shown on that per‑day page, it does not qualify for AlanChand evidence (Bonbast evidence remains valid).
- Qualifying rate on Bonbast: Use the Bonbast Archive “Sell” price for USD on the selected date. The Bonbast Archive is date‑addressable and displays “Sell” and “Buy” columns in toman.

Evidence and verification
- Primary sources for resolution:
  • Bonbast Archive: https://bonbast.com/archive (shows date‑stamped “Sell” and “Buy” in toman).
  • AlanChand Live Exchange Rates: https://alanchand.com/en/currencies-price (shows a table with “Sell Price” for “US Dollar”).
  • AlanChand per‑day USD page: for context and archival structure, see e.g., https://alanchand.com/en/currencies-price/usd; however, only “Sell Price” values qualify for AlanChand evidence per the rule above.
- Acceptable forms of evidence include: (a) the platforms’ own date‑stamped archive pages within the window, and/or (b) third‑party web archives (e.g., the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine) with capture timestamps in UTC falling within the window, showing the qualifying values on the specified pages. When using third‑party archives, the capture timestamp must be within the window in UTC.
- If sources conflict at a given time, Bonbast Archive (USD “Sell” in toman) takes precedence for resolution. If Bonbast is unavailable for the entire window, AlanChand evidence as defined above suffices.

Additional references and context (non‑resolutive, for forecasters)
- AP’s report of a record low (1,074,000 per USD on 2025‑09‑24) contextualizes the prior trajectory.
- Reuters’ confirmation of UN “snapback” sanctions reinstated at 8:00 p.m. EDT on 2025‑09‑27/0000 GMT on 2025‑09‑28 provides macro backdrop.
- Wikipedia references for currency units: Iranian rial (official currency; everyday toman usage) and Iranian toman (background) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_rial; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_toman.

question: U.S. existing-home sales: Will NAR report November 2025 existing-home sales ≥ 4.1 million (SAAR)?
background:
Context and current status (as of 2025-09-30):
- The National Association of Realtors (NAR) publishes monthly Existing-Home Sales (EHS) for the nation and four regions. EHS covers closed sales of existing single-family homes, condominiums, and co-ops, and is reported as a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR). SAAR is an annualized rate that accounts for typical seasonal patterns in the data.
- Latest available snapshot: August 2025 EHS was reported at 4.0 million (SAAR), with a median sales price of $422,600 and 4.6 months of inventory.
- Release cadence: NAR notes that EHS figures are released monthly and the newsroom provides scheduled dates; the November 2025 EHS (covering sales pace in November) is scheduled to be released on December 19, 2025, before year-end. NAR also indicates EHS updates are issued around the 25th of each month in general communications.
- Methodological notes: NAR constructs EHS from a representative sample of 210 Boards/MLSs, aggregates by region, and converts to SAAR using the Census Bureau’s X-13 method. NAR performs annual revisions to seasonal factors with the February release of revised December data; such revisions can retroactively alter SAAR figures for the prior three years.

Definitions for this question:
- "Existing-Home Sales (EHS)": NAR’s nationwide measure of monthly sales volume of existing single-family homes, condos, and co-ops, with regional breakdowns, reported in SAAR.
- "Seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR)": A rate adjusted for typical seasonal fluctuations and expressed as an annual total.
- "National" scope: United States overall (not regional), as published by NAR in its EHS release.

Why this threshold: Recent readings around 4.0 million SAAR suggest plausible upside or downside through late 2025, making ≥ 4.1 million a non-trivial target that forecasters may reasonably disagree about.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and source-of-truth:
- This market resolves based on NAR’s published November 2025 Existing-Home Sales national SAAR figure. The primary source is the NAR Existing-Home Sales monthly news release page and/or the associated EHS Housing Snapshot infographic that reports the SAAR for November 2025. The November 2025 EHS release is scheduled for December 19, 2025, ensuring availability before 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Exact test:
- Resolve Yes if NAR’s November 2025 national EHS SAAR is reported as at least 4.1 million. Resolve No otherwise.

Measurement and rounding:
- Use the SAAR value as NAR reports it for November 2025 at the national level. If NAR presents the figure rounded to one decimal place (e.g., "4.1 million"), resolve using that published rounded value; do not attempt to infer unrounded internal values. For the avoidance of doubt, "4.1 million" counts as ≥ 4.1 million; "4.0 million" does not.

Multiple publications and corrections:
- If both the press release and the Housing Snapshot present the SAAR, and they differ, use the numeric SAAR in the press release’s data table if available; otherwise, use the figure stated in the press release text; if neither is available, use the Housing Snapshot. If NAR issues a correction or erratum to the November 2025 figure before 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, use the corrected figure.
- Annual seasonal-factor revisions published with the February 2026 release (which can retroactively alter SAAR figures) must be ignored for resolution; only publications and corrections available by the resolution deadline are eligible.

If the scheduled release is delayed beyond the resolution deadline (unlikely per NAR’s newsroom schedule), resolve based on the earliest credible reporting that directly cites NAR’s November 2025 national EHS SAAR (e.g., major wire services), provided such reporting is published by the deadline. If no such reporting exists, the question will remain unresolved until the NAR figure is published.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the U.S. and India jointly announce a framework bilateral trade agreement that explicitly includes at least one quantified tariff reduction on goods?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Strategic intent to reach a 2025 deal: On 2025-02-13, the United States and India issued a Joint Leaders’ Statement that set “Mission 500” (aiming to grow bilateral trade to $500B by 2030) and announced plans to negotiate the first tranche of a mutually beneficial, multi‑sector Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) by fall 2025. The statement said both sides would work toward increasing market access and “reducing tariff and non‑tariff barriers.” 
- Linkage to Russian oil purchases and leverage via U.S. tariffs: As of 2025-09-26, Reuters reported U.S. negotiators told India that curbing purchases of Russian oil was “crucial to reducing [India’s] tariff rate and sealing a trade deal,” and that the U.S. imposed an extra 25% tariff on imports from India, bringing total punitive duties to around 50%, which has complicated talks described as “on a positive track” but needing more work. 
- Recent incremental tariff actions (context/base rates): In September 2023 the United States and India resolved a WTO poultry dispute; India agreed to reduce tariffs on several U.S. products, including frozen turkey/duck and various forms of blueberries and cranberries, alongside other tariff adjustments connected to the termination of multiple WTO disputes (e.g., almonds, walnuts, apples). 
  In April 2024, USTR highlighted that India further reduced its tariffs on frozen turkey, frozen duck, and fresh/frozen/dried/processed blueberries and cranberries. 
- Trade policy forum machinery: The 14th Ministerial-level India–U.S. Trade Policy Forum (TPF) in January 2024 agreed to establish a Joint Facilitative Mechanism to mitigate non-tariff barriers and to pursue a roadmap for enhanced cooperation (e.g., critical minerals, customs/trade facilitation, high-tech trade). This indicates active institutional channels for a framework arrangement. 

Key definitions for forecasters:
- Tariff: A customs duty/tax imposed by a government on imports of goods (occasionally exports). It is paid by the importer (for imports) and is typically expressed as an ad valorem rate (%) or a specific amount per unit. 
- Harmonized System (HS) code: The Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System is a standardized product classification maintained by the World Customs Organization and used by customs authorities as a basis for tariff schedules and trade statistics. HS codes are globally standardized at 6 digits, with countries allowed to add national subdivisions beyond 6 digits. 

Why this question is non-trivial now: The White House set an explicit 2025 timeline to negotiate a first tranche of a BTA with tariff reduction goals, but reporting in late September 2025 indicates U.S. demands linking trade progress and tariff relief to India’s curbing of Russian oil purchases, alongside high U.S. punitive tariffs—factors that could either catalyze concessions or derail any joint announcement before year-end.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and outcome:
- Event window: From 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Resolve Yes if, within the event window, the United States and India issue a joint announcement of a framework bilateral trade agreement that explicitly includes at least one quantified tariff reduction on goods, as defined below. Otherwise resolve No.

What counts as a “joint announcement” and acceptable sources:
- Joint announcement means any of the following issued within a 24-hour span that clearly reference the same agreement: (a) a single co‑branded joint statement/press release; or (b) matching statements on official government websites of both countries, each referencing the other party and the same agreement text/terms.
- Acceptable official U.S. sources include: whitehouse.gov, ustr.gov. Acceptable official Indian sources include: pib.gov.in (Press Information Bureau) and commerce.gov.in (Ministry of Commerce & Industry). If an official site is temporarily unavailable, credible wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) explicitly quoting the joint announcement are acceptable as secondary sources. 

What qualifies as a “framework bilateral trade agreement” for this market:
- A bilateral, government‑to‑government arrangement concerning trade in goods and/or services that is described in the joint announcement as one of the following or equivalent: “framework agreement,” “framework trade agreement,” “first tranche” of a Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA), “agreement in principle” on a bilateral trade deal, or a “framework”/“BTA” that the parties state they have agreed to or concluded (as opposed to merely launching, planning, or continuing negotiations). Announcements that only express an intention to negotiate or to explore an agreement do not qualify. 

Required content on tariff reductions (to qualify as “includes tariff reductions”):
- The joint announcement must contain an explicit, binding commitment by at least one party to reduce a customs duty (tariff) on imports of at least one identified good originating in the other party. It must specify the reduction in a way that is objectively verifiable, such as:
  - stating the current and new ad valorem rate (e.g., from X% to Y%) or the amount of reduction;
  - stating elimination of the tariff on a named product(s);
  - or providing a schedule/table of tariff lines (HS at 6-digit or more detailed national level) with new rates.
- The goods must be identifiable either by HS code(s) or by common product name(s) that unambiguously map to HS lines. Reductions may be unilateral or reciprocal, but they must be framed as commitments under the announced framework agreement (not merely general MFN changes unrelated to the framework). 

What does NOT qualify:
- Announcements that only include aspirations (e.g., “aim to,” “seek to”) without a definite commitment to reduce a tariff rate.
- Announcements limited to non‑tariff measures (e.g., standards cooperation, customs facilitation) with no tariff rate reduction commitment. 
- Announcements outside the event window, or leaked reports without official confirmation as defined above.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- Tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) or temporary duty suspensions count only if the announcement specifies a reduced in-quota rate or a zero rate for identified goods and ties the measure to the framework agreement; general administrative or case-by-case duty remission, export subsidies, or duty drawback do not count. 
- If multiple announcements occur, the earliest qualifying one in the event window determines resolution.
- Time is measured in UTC based on the timestamp of the official publication; if not timestamped, the earliest credible wire report timestamp in UTC citing the official announcement will be used. 

How to verify at resolution:
- Primary source: A joint statement or two matching statements on the specified official websites that include the agreement characterization (framework/BTA/first tranche/agreement in principle) and an explicit, quantified tariff reduction commitment as defined above. 
- Secondary corroboration (if official sites are inaccessible): Credible wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) quoting and linking to the joint announcement. 

Informational notes for forecasters (non‑binding examples):
- Prior, limited tariff reductions (e.g., poultry and berry products) illustrate feasible product‑level cuts but were not part of a broader bilateral framework trade deal. 
- Institutional mechanisms (TPF/JFM) may facilitate non‑tariff progress, but do not by themselves meet this question’s bar without explicit tariff cut commitments in a framework announcement. 
- The February 2025 Joint Leaders’ Statement established both the ambition (BTA by fall 2025) and the intention to reduce tariffs, raising the prospect of a qualifying announcement within the window.

question: US TV usage: Will YouTube’s share in Nielsen’s Media Distributor Gauge be at least 14.0% for November 2025?
background:
Overview and definitions
- Nielsen’s The Gauge is a monthly macroanalysis of TV viewing in the U.S., combining data from panels to report total broadcast, cable, and streaming consumption through a television screen. Data represents a broadcast month and uses Live+7 for linear content.
- The Media Distributor Gauge is an expansion of The Gauge that aggregates total TV viewing by parent media company (distributor) across broadcast, cable, and streaming. “Share of TV watch-time” refers to the percentage of total minutes viewed on a TV screen attributable to a given parent media company, based on mapping national media distributors to their parent and summing TV minutes across their properties. A 1.0% share is the minimum threshold for inclusion.
- In Nielsen’s articles, the term “YouTube” refers to the distributor label used in the Media Distributor Gauge. For purposes of this question, “YouTube’s share” means the percentage printed as “YouTube” in Nielsen’s November 2025 Media Distributor Gauge article or data-center visualization. We do not re-categorize minutes; we use Nielsen’s own labeling and figure.

Status quo (as of Sep 30, 2025) and recent trend
- February–August 2025 showed YouTube rising to record shares and maintaining the No.1 distributor position for multiple consecutive months:
  - April 2025: YouTube 12.4% (largest to date then); Disney 10.7%; Paramount 8.9%; NBCUniversal 8.2%; Warner Bros. Discovery 6.7%.
  - June 2025: YouTube 12.8% (largest to date then); Disney 10.0%; Netflix 8.3%.
  - July 2025: YouTube 13.4% (platform record at the time), widening its lead over Disney at 9.4% by 4.0 points.
  - August 2025: YouTube 13.1%; Disney 9.7% (+0.3 point month over month); Netflix 8.7% (−0.1 point).
- Nielsen publishes these monthly Media Distributor Gauge insights on its News Center and updates The Gauge data center; revisions can occur (e.g., a July 2025 correction to Paramount’s share), and Nielsen notes such corrections in their posts.

Why 14.0% in November?
- YouTube’s shares have trended upward through mid-2025, with a slight seasonal dip in August due to back-to-school dynamics and football returning (which tends to boost traditional TV and Disney/FOX affiliates). November is influenced by holiday viewing, NFL/college football, and major streaming releases, creating plausible uncertainty around whether YouTube’s share reaches or exceeds 14.0%.

Key term links (authoritative references)
- The Gauge (Nielsen data center): https://www.nielsen.com/data-center/the-gauge/ 
- Media Distributor Gauge (Nielsen launch explainer): https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2024/nielsen-launches-the-media-distributor-gauge-first-convergent-tv-comparison-of-its-kind/ 
- YouTube (reference): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube (only for general context; resolution uses Nielsen’s label) 

Timeframe
- The measurement month is “November 2025” as defined and labeled by Nielsen’s broadcast calendar in the Media Distributor Gauge. The question will resolve once Nielsen’s November 2025 Media Distributor Gauge figure for YouTube is available and fixed by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome
- Resolve YES if Nielsen reports YouTube’s share at 14.0% or higher for November 2025 in its Media Distributor Gauge; resolve NO otherwise.

Primary resolution source
- Use the percentage printed for “YouTube” in Nielsen’s official November 2025 Media Distributor Gauge article on the Nielsen News Center (nielsen.com/news-center). If Nielsen publishes the November figure in the The Gauge data center (nielsen.com/data-center/the-gauge/), that figure may also be used. If there are multiple Nielsen sources, use the latest corrected figure as of the resolution deadline.

Scope and definitions (for resolution)
- Geographic scope: U.S. TV viewing, per Nielsen’s The Gauge methodology.
- Viewing scope: TV-set viewing only; The Gauge aggregates viewing through a television screen. Media Distributor Gauge aggregates across broadcast, cable, and streaming to distributors; “share of TV watch-time” is the percent of total TV minutes attributed to a distributor by Nielsen’s mapping.
- “YouTube’s share” is the value labeled “YouTube” within Nielsen’s Media Distributor Gauge for November 2025. No alternative categorizations are permitted; rely on Nielsen’s labeling.

Corrections and timing
- If Nielsen issues a correction to the November 2025 figure before 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, use the corrected value. Nielsen has previously issued such corrections and notes them, e.g., a July 2025 update to Paramount’s share.

Fallback (only if necessary)
- If, by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, Nielsen has not yet published any November 2025 Media Distributor Gauge figure, resolve using at least two independent major outlets that report the Nielsen November 2025 Media Distributor Gauge figure for YouTube (e.g., Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, TheWrap, Adweek), ensuring consistency between them. If such consistent reporting does not exist, resolve as “insufficient data,” and the question should be voided. This fallback is unlikely given Nielsen’s monthly cadence and data center availability.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the IMF Executive Board complete Ghana’s Fifth Review under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) and approve/make available the associated disbursement?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Ghana is in a 36‑month IMF Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangement. The IMF Executive Board completed Ghana’s Fourth Review on 2025-07-07, which “allows for an immediate disbursement of approximately US$367 million (SDR 267.5 million)”. 
- An IMF staff mission arrived in Accra on 2025-09-29 to commence the Fifth Review of Ghana’s IMF‑supported program, per Ghana’s Ministry of Finance communication (naming IMF mission lead Dr. Ruben Atoyan).
- Definitions and where to monitor: The IMF’s ECF is a concessional lending facility for low‑income countries with protracted balance of payments problems; the factsheet provides the official definition and scope (IMF factsheet). The IMF Executive Board conducts the day‑to‑day business of the IMF, including completing program reviews (IMF Executive Board page). IMF press releases and Executive Board decisions for Ghana are published on imf.org, including via the Ghana country page aggregator (IMF Ghana country page). The typical phrasing for a completed review and its disbursement is shown in the Fourth Review press release (e.g., “Executive Board … completed the [Nth] Review … This allows for an immediate disbursement of …”).

Why this is forecast‑relevant now: Ghana’s Fourth Review completion in July 2025 establishes cadence, while the Fifth Review staff mission commencing on 2025-09-29 indicates the process is underway but not guaranteed to conclude at the Board level within the Oct 15 – Dec 31, 2025 window. Continued adherence to macroeconomic policy adjustment and reforms was emphasized as key for future progress.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome to forecast (binary): YES if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the IMF publishes on imf.org an official press release or Executive Board news item that explicitly states both (a) the IMF Executive Board completed Ghana’s Fifth Review under its ECF arrangement, and (b) a disbursement was approved/made available/allowed as a result of that completion. NO otherwise.

Authoritative resolution sources:
- Primary: A press release or Board communication on imf.org (for example, through the Ghana country page at https://www.imf.org/en/Countries/GHA) that includes the explicit phrase(s) indicating Board completion of the Fifth Review and that a disbursement is available/approved/allowed. The phrasing and structure expected are as in the Fourth Review press release: “Executive Board … completed the [Nth] Review … This allows for an immediate disbursement of …”. Definitions of ECF and the Executive Board are per IMF factsheets/pages.

Operational definitions and rules:
- “Completed the Fifth Review under the ECF” means a communication on imf.org states the Executive Board completed Ghana’s “Fifth Review under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangement” (or substantively identical phrasing).
- “Approved/made available the associated disbursement” is satisfied if the same IMF communication states that the completion allows for or makes available a disbursement (e.g., “allows for an immediate disbursement of …” or “approved a disbursement of …”).
- Time window: The publication date/time used for resolution is the timestamp displayed on the relevant imf.org page. If only a date is displayed (no time), it is treated as occurring on that date in UTC. The event must be published on or after 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Exclusions: Staff‑level agreements, staff concluding statements, and mission announcements do not count without an Executive Board completion notice. Ghanaian government or media reports do not count without corroborating publication on imf.org. Partial actions (e.g., extensions or waivers without completion) do not count.
- Conflict/Corrections: If multiple IMF postings differ, use the latest corrected IMF publication as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. If imf.org is temporarily unreachable, resolution is deferred until it is accessible; only imf.org content is used for resolution.

Current status references for forecasters: Fourth Review completion and disbursement (2025-07-07) ; Fifth Review staff mission arrival (2025-09-29) ; ECF definition ; IMF Executive Board role ; IMF Ghana page as publishing hub.

question: Does FEMA’s December 2025 Disaster Relief Fund (DRF) monthly report project the DRF will be exhausted before March 31, 2026?
background:
Overview and purpose: The Disaster Relief Fund (DRF) is the federal government’s primary funding source for disaster response, recovery, and certain mitigation activities under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, administered by FEMA. Since 2012, DRF resources are tracked in two categories: the Major Disasters portion (for costs tied to presidentially declared major disasters) and the DRF Base (for other Stafford Act-related activities such as emergency declarations, Fire Management Assistance Grants, and readiness/support). Base funds cannot be used for major disaster costs.

Monthly DRF reports: FEMA publishes DRF Monthly Reports on its website, as required by statute, by the 5th day of each month. These reports include a funding summary, monthly activity tables, a catastrophic events summary, and an estimate of when the DRF will be exhausted. The reports commonly contain a section titled “Appendix E: Fund Exhaustion Date” with a table/graph labeled “DRF End-of-Month Balance,” which shows monthly projected balances for the Major Disasters portion, the Base, subtotals, and the Total DRF Balance. The first month the Total DRF Balance turns negative indicates exhaustion in the projection.

How the December report is dated and published: For example, FEMA’s December 2024 DRF Monthly Report covered data “as of November 30, 2024” and was published on December 9, 2024. It included Appendix E: Fund Exhaustion Date with projected end‑of‑month balances by month and separate lines for Base vs. Majors and the Total DRF Balance. FEMA’s DRF Monthly Reports page is the canonical index where the December 2025 report is expected to appear (“Disaster Relief Fund: Monthly Reports”).

Status quo as of 2025: DRF solvency has been an active concern in FY2024–FY2025. FEMA’s reports in 2024–2025 featured an Appendix E titled “Fund Exhaustion Date” that projected negative Total DRF Balances (i.e., potential exhaustion) in the projections if sufficient funding was not available—for example, the March 2025 report’s Appendix E projected the Total DRF Balance to become negative by mid‑calendar 2025 in its month‑by‑month table. The Congressional Research Service describes the DRF’s role, the Base and Major Disasters categories, and policy context in FY2025, including that appropriations have struggled to keep pace with costs in recent years.

Where to find the resolution source: FEMA’s DRF Monthly Reports index page (fema.gov/about/reports-and-data/disaster-relief-fund-monthly-reports) hosts links to each month’s PDF; the December 2025 report should be listed there and is the source of truth for this question.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve YES if the DRF Monthly Report that FEMA publishes in December 2025 (covering data as of November 30, 2025) projects an exhaustion date earlier than March 31, 2026. Resolve NO otherwise.

Operationalization of “projects an exhaustion date”: Use the December 2025 DRF Monthly Report PDF as posted on FEMA’s DRF Monthly Reports index page. Within that PDF, locate “Appendix E: Fund Exhaustion Date” (or the section that presents the projected month‑by‑month balances, typically titled “DRF End‑of‑Month Balance”). Identify the first FY2026 month (Oct 2025–Sep 2026) in the table where the “Total DRF Balance” is negative (< $0). If that first negative month is any of October 2025, November 2025, December 2025, January 2026, or February 2026, resolve YES. If the first negative month is March 2026 or later, or if there is no negative Total DRF Balance in FY2026, resolve NO.

Primary source of truth: The December 2025 DRF Monthly Report PDF posted on FEMA’s “Disaster Relief Fund: Monthly Reports” page (https://www.fema.gov/about/reports-and-data/disaster-relief-fund-monthly-reports). FEMA states these reports are published by the 5th day of each month and include an estimate of when funds will be exhausted. As corroborated by the December 2024 report, the December DRF Monthly Report typically covers data as of November 30 and includes Appendix E: Fund Exhaustion Date and a “DRF End-of‑Month Balance” table separating Base, Majors, and Total DRF balances.

Timing and timezone: The qualifying report is the one published by FEMA on fema.gov during the period from 2025‑12‑01 00:00 UTC through 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. The cutoff date for “before March 31, 2026” is operationalized in month‑granularity as described above (i.e., March 2026 does not count as “before March 31, 2026”).

Definitions and links:
- Disaster Relief Fund (DRF): FEMA‑administered account funding Stafford Act disaster response, recovery, and mitigation; structured into Major Disasters and Base categories. General info on FEMA: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Emergency_Management_Agency
- DRF Monthly Report: FEMA’s statutorily required monthly publication that includes a funding summary and an estimate of when DRF funds will be exhausted; canonical index: https://www.fema.gov/about/reports-and-data/disaster-relief-fund-monthly-reports.
- Fund Exhaustion Date / DRF End‑of‑Month Balance: The section/table in the report’s Appendix E that presents monthly projected balances by category and the total; a negative Total DRF Balance for a month indicates exhaustion has occurred by that month’s end.

Edge cases:
- If FEMA posts multiple versions of the December 2025 report in December 2025, use the most recently published version in that month (by the PDF’s listed publication date or file metadata on fema.gov).
- If Appendix E is absent or renamed, use the section that clearly presents projected monthly end‑of‑month balances and/or explicitly labels the fund exhaustion date; precedence is given to the numeric table over narrative text if they conflict.
- Only the FEMA‑hosted December 2025 DRF Monthly Report will be used to resolve. FEMA’s monthly report cadence and content description are documented on the FEMA DRF Monthly Reports page.

question: Will the Bank of Canada change its target for the overnight rate on December 10, 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- The Bank of Canada’s policy interest rate is the target for the overnight rate (sometimes called the “overnight rate target”), which the Bank uses as its primary monetary policy tool. The “Target for the Overnight Rate” is defined by the Bank as the average rate it seeks to see in the market for overnight money market financing.
- The Bank announces the setting for the overnight rate on eight fixed dates per year via an “Interest rate announcement” press release. For 2025, the Bank’s published schedule lists Wednesday, October 29, 2025 and Wednesday, December 10, 2025 as fixed announcement dates, with all interest rate announcements scheduled for 09:45 (ET).
- Most recent status: On September 17, 2025, the Bank of Canada reduced its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% and stated that the next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 29, 2025.
- The Bank’s “Upcoming events” page lists the October 29, 2025 “Interest Rate Announcement and Monetary Policy Report” at 09:45 (ET) and the December 10, 2025 “Interest Rate Announcement” at 09:45 (ET).

These official schedules and definitions ensure the decision window and data sources are clear and public as of today.
resolution_criteria:
This question concerns the Bank of Canada’s fixed-date Interest Rate Announcement on 2025-12-10 (Eastern Time, ET). It will resolve as soon as the corresponding press release is published on bankofcanada.ca, and in any case no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What is being forecast
- Resolve YES if the Bank of Canada’s official “Interest Rate Announcement” press release for the 2025-12-10 fixed date states a target for the overnight rate that is numerically different from the target stated in the official “Interest Rate Announcement” press release for 2025-10-29.
- Resolve NO if the target for the overnight rate stated on 2025-12-10 is the same as on 2025-10-29.

Definitions (authoritative sources cited for terms)
- “Target for the overnight rate” (also “policy interest rate”): The Bank’s policy instrument; the average rate the Bank wants to see in the market for overnight money market financing.
- “Interest Rate Announcement” press release: The official fixed-date communication in which the Bank announces the setting for the overnight rate; these occur on eight fixed dates each year and are listed on the Bank’s schedule and Upcoming events pages.
- “Different/same”: Two targets are considered the same if they are equal when expressed to one basis point (0.01 percentage point). Typographical variants (e.g., 2½% vs 2.50%) are treated as the same numeric value. Any nonzero difference at the one–basis-point level counts as “different.”

Timeframe and timezone
- Relevant period: The event of interest is the fixed-date announcement on 2025-12-10 (ET). For clarity, the overall eligibility window for events considered by this question is from 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Only the 2025-12-10 fixed-date Interest Rate Announcement counts for resolution.
- Timezone: Dates for Bank announcements follow Eastern Time (ET), as specified by the Bank’s schedule; any UTC timestamps mentioned here are for the market’s resolution timeline only and do not alter which press release is in scope.

Source of truth and how to verify (single-source resolution)
- Primary sources: The Bank of Canada’s official “Interest Rate Announcement” press releases on bankofcanada.ca for (a) 2025-10-29 and (b) 2025-12-10. The Bank’s 2025 schedule confirms these fixed dates and the 09:45 (ET) release time.
- Verification steps for the resolver:
  1) Navigate to bankofcanada.ca and locate the “Interest Rate Announcement” press release for 2025-10-29; record the target for the overnight rate stated therein.
  2) Navigate to bankofcanada.ca and locate the “Interest Rate Announcement” press release for 2025-12-10; record the target for the overnight rate stated therein.
  3) Compare the two targets at one-basis-point precision to determine YES/NO.

Edge cases and clarifications
- Only the target for the overnight rate determines the outcome. Changes to the Bank Rate or deposit rate do not affect resolution unless accompanied by a change in the target for the overnight rate.
- If the Bank posts multiple communications on 2025-12-10, the authoritative one is the “Interest Rate Announcement” press release for the fixed date (as labeled on bankofcanada.ca).
- If the 2025-10-29 Interest Rate Announcement press release is not published by 2025-12-10 23:59 (ET), compare the 2025-12-10 target to the most recent prior 2025 fixed-date Interest Rate Announcement press release instead (this preserves resolvability while adhering to the Bank’s fixed-date communications).

Notes on current status (for forecasters)
- As of 2025-09-17, the target for the overnight rate is 2.5%, with the next scheduled announcement on 2025-10-29. This provides a recent reference point ahead of the October and December fixed-date decisions.

question: Will Manitoba Hydro’s consolidated net loss for the first six months of FY2025/26 be at least $120 million?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Manitoba Hydro (the Manitoba Hydro-Electric Board) reported a consolidated net loss of $63 million for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, driven primarily by low water conditions (drought).
- In its First Quarter Report for FY2025/26 (three months ended June 30, 2025), Manitoba Hydro reported a consolidated net loss of $61 million. The report attributes the result largely to below-average precipitation and low water conditions reducing net export revenues, and notes unprecedented wildfire-related operational disruptions (e.g., temporary evacuation/shutdown of generating stations at Pointe du Bois and Slave Falls, additional O&A costs, and infrastructure repairs). Management guidance indicated results for 2025/26 remain highly sensitive to summer/fall precipitation, with it being unlikely to recover from a net loss position even with average precipitation.
- For the prior year’s comparable period, the Second Quarter Report for the six months ended September 30, 2024 showed a consolidated net loss of $123 million, also driven by low water conditions and reduced net export revenues.
- Manitoba Hydro publishes quarterly reports and an annual report on its corporate publications page (including the First Quarterly Report for 2025/26). The “six months ended September 30” second-quarter report is typically posted in November; for example, the report for the six months ended September 30, 2024 was published November 14, 2024.
- Manitoba public finance/statutory materials and Manitoba Hydro reporting indicate fiscal years run April 1 to March 31; the 2024/25 annual communication explicitly refers to the fiscal year ended March 31, 2025, and provincial statute defines the board’s fiscal year as April 1–March 31 for regulatory purposes.

Why this threshold? With a Q1 loss of $61M, the H1 (first six months) outcome will depend on Q2 precipitation, export markets, wildfire impacts, and operational choices (e.g., conserving water for winter). The prior-year H1 loss was $123M, making a threshold of $120M near the range where outcomes plausibly cut either way given uncertainty in Q2 conditions and net export revenues.

Notes:
- Dollar amounts in Manitoba Hydro reports are presented in dollars; this question interprets $ as Canadian dollars (CAD, ISO 4217) unless otherwise specified.
- All dates mentioned use the Gregorian calendar. Where a time-of-day would be relevant, times are UTC; however, financial reporting periods are date-bounded and time-of-day is not expected to affect resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Timeframe: Consider results for the period from 2025-04-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-09-30 23:59:59 UTC (the first six months of FY2025/26), and resolve the question no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Primary resolution source: Manitoba Hydro’s official Second Quarter (Q2) FY2025/26 quarterly report covering the six months ended September 30, 2025, published on the corporate publications page (https://www.hydro.mb.ca/corporate/publications/). Use the figure labeled “Consolidated net income (loss) attributable to Manitoba Hydro” for the six months ended September 30, 2025, exactly as presented in the Q2 report.

- YES if the Q2 report shows a consolidated net loss (i.e., a negative value for “Consolidated net income (loss) attributable to Manitoba Hydro”) whose magnitude is greater than or equal to $120,000,000 (i.e., loss ≥ $120 million CAD).
- NO if the Q2 report shows a consolidated net loss whose magnitude is less than $120,000,000, or if it shows consolidated net income (a positive value).

Measurement details and definitions:
- “FY2025/26” means Manitoba Hydro’s fiscal year beginning April 1, 2025 and ending March 31, 2026. This aligns with Manitoba Hydro reporting (e.g., “fiscal year ended March 31, 2025”) and provincial fiscal definitions applicable to the board.
- “Consolidated net income (loss) attributable to Manitoba Hydro” refers to the bottom-line line item in Manitoba Hydro’s consolidated statement of income used in its quarterly reports. Use the year-to-date (six months) figure reported in the Q2 FY2025/26 report. This is the exact label used in prior Q2 reporting (e.g., six months ended Sep 30, 2024). If the Q2 FY2025/26 report presents the equivalent figure under the same meaning but with slightly different wording, use that directly.
- Currency: Interpret “$” as Canadian dollars (CAD). Use the amount as reported; do not perform currency conversion. If figures are presented “in millions,” interpret values accordingly (e.g., “(123)” represents a $123 million loss). If decimals are shown, use the precise number as printed.

Back-up resolution source (only if the Q2 FY2025/26 report is not available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC): Use any official Manitoba Hydro news release or article posted on hydro.mb.ca that explicitly states the consolidated net income (loss) attributable to Manitoba Hydro for the six months ended September 30, 2025, or otherwise unambiguously provides the first-half consolidated net result. Manitoba Hydro’s news releases have previously summarized key financial results alongside report publications (e.g., the 2024/25 annual results and reference to the 2025/26 first quarter). If multiple official sources exist and conflict, prefer the more detailed financial report (Q2) over summaries.

question: Will combined 2025 New Jersey gubernatorial spending (candidate committees plus independent expenditures) reach or exceed $220,000,000 by 11:59 pm ET on December 31, 2025, according to ELEC?
background:
Overview: This question concerns total spending associated with New Jersey’s 2025 gubernatorial election as tracked by the New Jersey Election Law Enforcement Commission (ELEC). Specifically, it sums (a) spending by gubernatorial candidate committees and (b) independent expenditures related to the 2025 gubernatorial election, as reported by ELEC.

Status quo as of today (2025-09-30): In a September 3, 2025 news release, ELEC reported that through the primary election, gubernatorial candidate committees spent $62,300,974 and independent expenditure committees spent $82,814,049, for a combined primary total of $145,115,023. ELEC characterized these figures as record-breaking versus prior cycles and noted scope caveats about what is included in independent expenditure totals. An earlier June 6, 2025 release reported preliminary combined totals through May 27, 2025 of about $122.5 million (candidate spending $54.8 million; independent committee spending $67.6 million) and provided historical context (e.g., the 2021 general election cost about $72 million in today’s dollars).

Key definitions and scope (as used by ELEC):
- Independent expenditure: An expenditure not coordinated with a candidate or political party that expressly advocates the election/defeat of a clearly identified candidate (or is the functional equivalent of express advocacy), subject to ELEC’s reporting regime. The ELEC glossary also describes an independent expenditure as one made without cooperation, consent, or consultation with a candidate or committee acting on the candidate’s behalf.
- Independent expenditure committee (IEC): A person or group organized under IRC § 527 or § 501(c)(4)/(6) that makes independent expenditures in excess of $7,500, in the aggregate, in an election and that is not another ELEC committee type; IECs must register (Form D-6) and report (Form R-1) when exceeding the $7,500 threshold. The first Form R-1 for an election is cumulative from January 1 of the preceding year; IECs itemize independent expenditures and follow election-specific pre/post-election reporting schedules.
- Candidate spending totals: ELEC reports the expenditures made by gubernatorial candidate committees; candidates are required to report all expenditures.

Important scope notes from ELEC’s releases:
- Independent expenditure totals in ELEC’s press releases include committees registered with ELEC and do not include entities that file only with the Federal Election Commission or IRS; expenditures that may benefit gubernatorial candidates without naming them may also be excluded.

Why this is non-trivial: As of early September, combined primary spending reached $145.1 million, leaving uncertainty about how much additional general-election spending by campaigns and IECs will occur. Historical totals provide context but do not directly determine a final combined number for 2025, making late-cycle advertising rates, fundraising, and outside group mobilization relevant drivers.
resolution_criteria:
Observation window and timezone: The observation window begins at 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and ends at 23:59:59 Eastern Time (ET) on December 31, 2025 (04:59:59 UTC on January 1, 2026).

Proposition: Resolve Yes if, by the end of the observation window, the ELEC-reported combined total for the 2025 New Jersey gubernatorial election—defined as the sum of (1) gubernatorial candidate committee spending and (2) independent expenditures related to the gubernatorial election—equals or exceeds $220,000,000 (USD). Resolve No otherwise.

Measurement and sources:
- Primary source of truth: ELEC official publications (e.g., press releases, official summaries, and aggregate tables on elec.nj.gov) that report totals for the 2025 gubernatorial election’s candidate committee spending and independent expenditures. If ELEC publishes a single combined total, use that figure. If ELEC publishes separate totals, sum the latest available ELEC-reported totals for the two categories as of 23:59:59 ET on December 31, 2025.
- Scope alignment: Use ELEC’s own scope/methodology for each category, including the definition of independent expenditures (express advocacy or its functional equivalent, non-coordinated) and the exclusion of spenders that file only with the FEC/IRS from independent expenditure totals, as noted in ELEC publications.

Operational details:
- Currency and precision: Use whole-dollar totals as posted by ELEC. No inflation adjustments or rebasings. Cents, if present in sources, are disregarded for threshold comparison.
- Tie-breaking: If multiple ELEC publications conflict, use the most recent ELEC official publication dated on or before the resolution timestamp.
- Verification steps (for resolver):
  1) Locate the latest ELEC official publication(s) on elec.nj.gov reporting 2025 gubernatorial spending totals for candidate committees and independent expenditures.
  2) If a combined total is provided, compare that number to $220,000,000.
  3) If only separate totals are provided, sum the two ELEC-reported totals and compare the sum to $220,000,000.

Eligible categories and exclusions (to ensure clarity):
- Include: Spending by 2025 NJ gubernatorial candidate committees and independent expenditures tied to clearly identified gubernatorial candidates, as defined in ELEC guidance and reported by ELEC.
- Exclude: Independent expenditures by entities that report only to the FEC/IRS and any spending that may benefit gubernatorial candidates without naming them, consistent with ELEC’s scope in its publications.

Resolution example references: ELEC’s September 3, 2025 press release provides combined primary totals and scope notes; similar post-election releases or summary pages will provide updated totals that the resolver will use at the end of the observation window.

question: Will a Federal Register document published between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC) implement an ad valorem tariff rate of at least 50% on at least one HTSUS Chapter 30 pharmaceutical subheading?
background:
Status quo as of 2025‑09‑30: On September 25, 2025, President Trump publicly announced that the United States will impose a 100% tariff on imports of “branded or patented” pharmaceutical products starting October 1, 2025, with exemptions for companies building U.S. manufacturing plants; reporting noted that specific implementation details were not yet public and companies anticipated exemptions based on U.S. investments. Earlier in the year, the White House issued an executive order focused on domestic drug pricing measures and PBM transparency that did not address tariffs or customs duties, underscoring that any tariff action would proceed via separate legal pathways. Separately, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) initiated a Section 232 national security investigation into imports of pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients and solicited public comments; the Federal Register notice confirms the scope (finished drug products and inputs), legal authority (19 U.S.C. § 1862), and that remedies under consideration include tariffs or quotas. BIS’s investigations page lists “Pharmaceuticals and Pharmaceutical Ingredients” as an active Section 232 investigation initiated on April 1, 2025, with a Regulations.gov docket reference (BIS‑2025‑0022).

Why this question and threshold: The announced 100% duty implies a plausible pathway to high rates, but formal implementation typically appears as Federal Register documents (e.g., presidential proclamations, agency notices, or rules that amend the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) or direct CBP to collect additional duties). Choosing a 50% threshold balances plausibility and uncertainty: it is high enough to be non‑trivial, yet could be met if any subset of pharmaceutical products (HTSUS Chapter 30) is subjected to elevated ad valorem tariffs via Section 232, Section 301, or other authorities.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- Federal Register: The official daily journal of the U.S. government that publishes rules, proposed rules, and notices of federal agencies and organizations, and executive orders and other presidential documents. Source of truth: https://www.federalregister.gov/ (general reference).
- Tariff (customs duty): A tax imposed on imports; an ad valorem duty is expressed as a percentage of the customs value. See Tariff and Ad valorem tax: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_valorem_tax (definitions).
- HTSUS Chapter 30 (Pharmaceutical products): The U.S. Harmonized Tariff Schedule chapter covering pharmaceutical products (e.g., medicaments), under headings such as 3003 and 3004. Reference: U.S. International Trade Commission HTSUS Chapter 30 at https://hts.usitc.gov/ (authoritative tariff classifications).
- Section 232 investigations: Conducted under the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (19 U.S.C. § 1862) to assess national security impacts of imports; may result in the President adjusting imports, including imposing tariffs or quotas. See DOC/BIS overview: https://www.bis.doc.gov/ (general reference). Specific pharma Section 232 Federal Register notice confirms scope and potential remedies ; BIS investigations page lists the active pharma investigation.

Recent context to monitor:
- The September 25–26, 2025 announcement referenced tariffs on branded/patented drugs with exemptions for companies building U.S. facilities; no implementing Federal Register document was cited in those reports.
- The April 15, 2025 executive order on drug pricing did not include tariff instructions, implying any tariff action would be via other instruments.
- BIS’s April 16, 2025 Federal Register notice on pharmaceuticals and ingredients under Section 232 solicited comments and stated tariffs or quotas could be remedies , and the BIS investigations page lists this investigation and docket.

Scope and practical notes:
- This question focuses on whether any Federal Register document in the specified window implements a duty rate ≥50% on at least one HTSUS Chapter 30 subheading (e.g., 3003.xx.xx, 3004.xx.xx). It is agnostic to which legal authority is used (e.g., Section 232, Section 301, reciprocal tariffs, or other), which agency issues the document (e.g., USTR, DOC/BIS, Treasury, CBP), or whether exemptions carve out particular firms. Forecasters should track daily Federal Register publications, Presidential proclamations, and notices amending HTSUS additional duty chapters (e.g., subchapter III notes, Chapter 99 provisions) for pharmaceutical headings.
- A Federal Register “public inspection” posting that is later published in the daily Federal Register within the window counts only if the actual publication date falls between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC).

Current datapoints (as of 2025‑09‑30):
- Trump’s 100% tariff announcement on brand‑name/patented drugs starting October 1, with exemptions tied to U.S. manufacturing construction, and lack of publicly detailed implementation at the time of reporting.
- April 2025 EO on drug pricing lacks tariff directives.
- Pharma Section 232 investigation exists; the FR notice confirms scope and potential tariff/quota remedies , and BIS investigations page lists it with docket info.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end time window: Events must occur between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

Question resolves “Yes” if all of the following are true:
1) A document is published on federalregister.gov within the window (publication date, not just public inspection) that is one of: Presidential Proclamation, Final Rule, Notice, or other final implementing action by a U.S. federal entity (e.g., USTR, Department of Commerce/BIS, Department of the Treasury, Customs and Border Protection) and
2) That document establishes or implements an ad valorem duty rate of at least 50% (including “additional duties” assessed as a percentage of the customs value) and
3) The applicability explicitly covers at least one HTSUS Chapter 30 subheading (Pharmaceutical products) by reference to HTSUS classification (e.g., headings 3003 or 3004 and their subheadings) and requires CBP assessment of that ≥50% rate for imports of those subheadings.

Clarifications:
- “Ad valorem duty rate” includes any rate expressed as a percentage of value, whether as baseline duty or as an “additional duty” under Chapter 99 (e.g., Section 232/301 measures). Specificity to HTSUS subheading(s) is required; an action that only references “branded” or “patented” products without identifying HTSUS subheadings counts only if the document also defines the scope in a way that maps to Chapter 30 subheadings for enforcement (e.g., by cross‑referencing HTSUS headings).
- Actions limited to quotas, licensing, non‑ad valorem specific duties (e.g., $X per unit), or purely prospective notices (e.g., requests for comments, proposed rules) do not count.
- If the document sets multiple rates, the criterion is met if at least one Chapter 30 subheading is subjected to a rate ≥50%.
- Exemptions or carve‑outs for certain firms or products do not prevent a “Yes” if the ≥50% rate applies to any non‑exempt Chapter 30 subheading.

Primary source of truth for resolution: federalregister.gov. The resolver will search the Federal Register for documents within the window meeting the criteria and verify HTSUS references and duty rates in the text.

Context sources supporting the set‑up of this question and demonstrating plausibility:
- Trump’s announcement and noted lack of immediate implementation details in public reporting.
- April 2025 EO on drug pricing not addressing tariffs.
- Federal Register notice opening the pharma Section 232 investigation and noting tariffs/quotas as potential remedies.
- BIS’s investigations page listing the active pharmaceuticals investigation and docket.

question: Will Banco de la República announce a change to its monetary policy interest rate in November or December 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: Banco de la República’s monetary policy interest rate (Spanish: “tasa de interés de política monetaria,” also called the intervention or reference rate) is 9.25%, and recent Board decisions (e.g., press releases dated July 31, 2025 and September 30, 2025) stated the rate was maintained at 9.25%. The monetary policy interest rate is the central bank’s primary instrument to conduct monetary policy; it is the minimum rate at which Banrep supplies liquidity to financial institutions (typically via overnight repos) and a reference for other rates. Monetary policy minutes are published the third business day after the Board (Junta Directiva) meeting, in Spanish and English. Official Board press releases are published on Banrep’s “Comunicados de prensa emitidos por la Junta” page; an English mirror page also exists.

Why this is forecastable: Late-2025 decisions will depend on incoming inflation and activity data and Board guidance; forecasters can incorporate recent decisions (holding at 9.25% through at least late September) and the communication cadence (same-day press releases; minutes within three business days) to assess the likelihood of a change being announced in November or December.
resolution_criteria:
Yes-resolution: Resolve “Yes” if at least one official Board (Junta Directiva) press release, published on the Banco de la República website’s Board press releases page (“Comunicados de prensa emitidos por la Junta”: https://www.banrep.gov.co/es/comunicados-junta), and dated between 2025-11-01 00:00 and 2025-12-31 23:59 (inclusive), announces a change (increase or decrease) to the monetary policy interest rate (“tasa de interés de política monetaria”). If both the Spanish and English versions exist, the Spanish page governs; the English mirror is at https://www.banrep.gov.co/en/press-releases-board.

No-resolution: Resolve “No” if no such press release dated in that window announces a change to the monetary policy interest rate.

Definitions and scope:
- Monetary policy interest rate: The policy/intervention/reference rate used by Banrep to conduct monetary policy, as defined in Banrep’s glossary. Synonyms: intervention rate (“tasa de intervención”), reference rate (“tasa de referencia”).
- Change: Any announced increase or decrease in the level of the monetary policy interest rate relative to its level immediately before that decision, regardless of the effective date of implementation (i.e., an announcement of a future-dated change still counts if the announcement is within the window).
- Announcement window and timestamps: A decision counts if the press release entry on the Banrep Board press releases page shows a publication date between 2025-11-01 and 2025-12-31 inclusive. If only a date (no time) is displayed, the entire day is treated as within the window; no timezone conversion is required.
- Eligible sources for verification: Primary—Banrep Board press releases page (“Comunicados de prensa emitidos por la Junta”). Secondary (if needed for confirmation)—the corresponding monetary policy minutes (https://www.banrep.gov.co/es/minutas), which are typically published the third business day after the meeting; if there is any discrepancy between minutes and press release, the press release governs for resolution.

Operational notes and edge cases:
- Multiple meetings/decisions: If multiple press releases within the window are published, any one announcing a change suffices for “Yes.”
- Extraordinary meetings: Unscheduled or extraordinary decisions count if announced via an official Board press release dated within the window.
- Other instruments: Changes to tools other than the monetary policy interest rate (e.g., reserve requirements, FX interventions) do not count unless they explicitly announce a change to the monetary policy interest rate.
- Site availability: If the primary page is temporarily inaccessible, use the English mirror and/or the minutes page to verify the decision text; once accessible, the Spanish press release page governs final resolution.

Context sources for forecasters (not required for resolution):
- Current rate at 9.25% and recent decisions to hold at that level in 2025 (e.g., July 31 and September 30 press releases).
- Definition and role of the monetary policy interest rate.
- Publication timing for minutes.

question: Will Auckland Transport report at least 8.25 million total public transport boardings in November 2025?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025-10-01:

- Data source and publication cadence: Auckland Transport (AT) publishes public transport patronage data (bus, train, ferry) on its "How many people are taking buses, trains and ferries" page, with reports updated monthly and downloadable in CSV/XLSX formats.
- Definition (what is counted): AT defines public transport boardings as "the number of times passengers get on a bus, train or ferry". The monthly patronage counts include AT HOP card transactions, contactless payment transactions, train line-to-line transfers, special events, and group travel on trains.
- Recent context: AT reported the highest weekly usage in five years in mid-February 2024 (1.9 million boardings across the week; 345,000 on the busiest day), with usage at roughly 90% of 2019 levels at that time. Monthly totals in 2024–2025 show variability across months: for example, Nov 2024 totaled approximately 7.739 million boardings (bus 5.889M; ferry 0.449M; train 1.400M), and Mar 2025 totaled approximately 9.199 million (bus 7.164M; ferry 0.507M; train 1.529M). These figures are sourced from AT via Figure.NZ.

Why this threshold: November has historically been mid-high relative to the year. Using a threshold of 8.25 million aims to sit near the plausible range for Nov 2025 given recent levels, encouraging non-trivial, researchable disagreement. The question resolves using AT’s own monthly patronage workbook, ensuring a single source of truth available by late December.

Links for definitions and context: 
- AT HOP card: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT_HOP (for general context)
- Auckland Transport page (source of truth): https://at.govt.nz/about-us/reports-publications/how-many-people-are-taking-buses-trains-and-ferries
resolution_criteria:
- Metric and threshold: Resolve YES if AT’s monthly patronage report shows total public transport boardings (the sum of bus, train, and ferry boardings) for the month labelled "November 2025" greater than or equal to 8,250,000; resolve NO otherwise.

- Definitions (authoritative):
  - "Public transport boardings" are defined by AT as "the number of times passengers get on a bus, train or ferry".
  - Monthly patronage counts include AT HOP card transactions, contactless payment transactions, train line-to-line transfers, special events, and group travel on trains.

- Counting method:
  - Use AT’s "Bus, train and ferry passengers by month" workbook (XLSX/CSV) published on the "How many people are taking buses, trains and ferries" page.
  - If the workbook provides a single "Total" for November 2025, use that exact value. If not, compute the total as the exact sum of the November 2025 values for bus boardings, train boardings, and ferry boardings reported in the workbook; do not round.

- Scope and month definition:
  - "November 2025" refers to the calendar month labeled "November 2025" in AT’s monthly patronage workbook; no reinterpretation of time zones is required because resolution relies on AT’s labeled reporting periods.

- Source of truth and precedence:
  - Primary source: AT’s "How many people are taking buses, trains and ferries" page, specifically the monthly patronage workbook covering November 2025.
  - If multiple versions exist, use the most recently published file accessible by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
  - If the monthly patronage workbook including November 2025 has not yet been posted by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve using the November 2025 total boardings figure displayed on the same AT page (if provided on-page).

- Resolution deadline: The question will be resolved based on the data available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Notes for resolvers:
- The AT page also notes that patronage data is available and reported monthly in CSV/XLSX formats.
- Background monthly totals for Nov 2024 (~7.739M) and Mar 2025 (~9.199M) are provided for context and should not be used for resolution.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will at least €5.0 billion of principal cash derived from immobilised Russian central bank assets be transferred out of Euroclear to an EU/G7‑controlled vehicle for a Ukraine loan instrument?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Scale and composition of the immobilised assets at Euroclear: As of June 30, 2025, Euroclear reported about €194 billion of Russian sanctioned assets on its balance sheet [13bcdc; 94adbe]. Reuters reporting and official briefings indicate that a large share of these immobilised assets have matured and become cash, with officials putting the cash share at roughly €170 billion (about 90%) by September 2025 [35c49f; 0fc4e2].
- Windfall profits (interest) vs. principal: The EU has been using windfall profits (interest/extraordinary revenues) generated by the immobilised balances to support Ukraine. In H1 2025, interest arising on cash balances from Russian‑sanctioned assets totaled about €2.7 billion, which Euroclear reports separately from principal. The EU made a first transfer of €1.5 billion of such proceeds on July 26, 2024, channelled via the European Peace Facility and the Ukraine Facility; these proceeds are explicitly described as windfall profits/extraordinary revenues, not principal. Separately, Ukraine received the first €3 billion tranche of the G7’s roughly $50 billion loan in January 2025; that loan is backed by earnings from the frozen assets, not by transfers of principal.
- Policy debate on moving principal: Belgium’s prime minister has publicly warned against moving or seizing principal, while deeming use of income acceptable, citing legal immunity and systemic risk concerns (statement of Aug 26, 2025). Meanwhile, the European Commission has floated an EU “reparations loan” concept that could involve replacing the assets at Euroclear with EU zero‑coupon bonds and placing the cash into a special‑purpose vehicle (SPV) owned by participating governments; officials argue moving the assets away from Euroclear would allow greater investment flexibility and potentially higher returns. The Commission is consulting the IMF on sizing, and press reporting in September 2025 references potential volumes up to roughly €130 billion, after accounting for obligations to the G7 loan [eddda0; 8d6501; 35c49f].

Why this question: The transfer of principal cash out of Euroclear to a designated public vehicle is a concrete event distinct from the already‑ongoing transfers of windfall profits. It is legally and politically contentious but under active discussion as of late September 2025, making both “Yes” and “No” outcomes plausible within the remainder of 2025 [d5a443; eddda0; 8d6501].

References for key facts above: Euroclear holdings and interest figures [13bcdc; 94adbe]; share now in cash [35c49f; 0fc4e2]; EU proceeds transfer July 2024 ; G7 loan first tranche Jan 2025 ; Belgian opposition ; EU/SPV proposal and rationale [eddda0; 8d6501].
resolution_criteria:
Time window and unit:
- Eligible transfers must settle between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Amounts are measured in euros; if any qualifying transfer settles in another currency, convert to EUR at the ECB euro foreign exchange reference rate for the settlement date.

What counts (operational definitions):
- Euroclear: Euroclear Bank SA/NV, the Belgium‑based central securities depository and international central securities depository. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euroclear.
- Immobilised Russian central bank assets: Assets of the Central Bank of Russia (or other Russian sovereign monetary authorities) that were immobilised/frozen under EU sanctions from 2022 onward and are or were held via Euroclear. For the purposes of this question, “principal cash” means the cash balances arising from maturities, redemptions, and principal repayments on those immobilised assets and held on Euroclear’s balance sheet, explicitly excluding any investment income/windfall profits/extraordinary revenues generated by investing those cash balances [13bcdc; 35c49f; 94adbe].
- EU/G7‑controlled vehicle: A legal entity (e.g., an SPV) that is majority‑owned or otherwise controlled (≥50% voting/control) by: (a) an EU institution (e.g., the European Commission) or EU Member State(s), or (b) any G7 government(s) (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States) or their designated public financial entities. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Seven.
- Ukraine loan instrument: A publicly announced lending program to Ukraine in which the vehicle’s mandate explicitly references the use or management of immobilised Russian principal as collateral or source of funds (e.g., an EU “reparations loan” SPV as described by the European Commission in September 2025 press reporting) or other G7/EU‑backed loan structures if they are explicitly funded by immobilised principal (not merely backed by windfall profits) [eddda0; 8d6501].
- Transfer (for this question): A cash movement that (i) reduces Euroclear Bank’s cash balances attributable to immobilised Russian principal, and (ii) credits cash to the account(s) of an EU/G7‑controlled vehicle as defined above. Purely internal reclassifications at Euroclear or book‑entry substitutions (e.g., Euroclear receiving EU bonds while retaining the cash) do not count unless accompanied by an actual cash outflow from Euroclear to the vehicle’s accounts.

Threshold and aggregation:
- Resolve “Yes” if, in aggregate across one or more qualifying transfers within the window, the cumulative principal cash moved from Euroclear to eligible vehicle(s) is at least €5,000,000,000. Otherwise, resolve “No”. Partial transfers are summed.

Exclusions (do not count toward the threshold):
- Transfers of windfall profits, extraordinary revenues, or net profits generated from immobilised assets (e.g., the July 2024 €1.5 billion proceeds transfer) [e38420; 94adbe].
- Payments to private investors or non‑public entities; tax payments; litigation escrows; collateral postings; or any movement that leaves the cash within Euroclear while substituting securities (e.g., issuance of EU zero‑coupon bonds to Euroclear without an accompanying cash outflow).

Evidence required to resolve:
