For example, after the First G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting on 26–27 February 2025 in Cape Town, the official page states: “A consensus for a communique was not reached and this represents the Chair’s summary of the meeting”. While this example is from the Finance Track, it illustrates the practice that the absence of consensus leads to a Chair’s Summary rather than a consensus outcome document.
- Where the Leaders’ Declaration is published: Official G20 Leaders’ Declarations are posted on the G20’s official website (g20.org). For instance, the 2024 Rio de Janeiro Leaders’ Declaration is hosted at g20.org.

Key term definitions (for clarity in forecasting and resolution):
- Group of Twenty (G20): An intergovernmental forum comprising 19 countries and the European Union; overview at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Twenty.
- 2025 G20 Leaders’ Summit (“Leaders’ Summit”): The heads of state/government meeting scheduled for 22–23 November 2025 in Gauteng, South Africa, under South Africa’s G20 Presidency.
- Leaders’ Declaration: The official, final outcome document of a G20 Leaders’ Summit, typically titled “G20 [Host City/Host] Leaders’ Declaration,” and posted on the G20’s official website (g20.org). An example of such a document is the “G20 Rio de Janeiro Leaders’ Declaration” (2024).
- Consensus (operational definition for this question): For the purpose of this market, “by consensus” is satisfied if and only if an official Leaders’ Declaration for the 2025 Leaders’ Summit is published by the G20 on g20.org (i.e., not merely a Chair’s Summary or a non-consensus document). No separate assessment of unanimity will be made.
- Disassociate/disassociation (operational definition): An explicit statement in the Leaders’ Declaration itself, in a footnote/annex to it, or on an accompanying official G20 webpage on g20.org, indicating that a specified member “does not join,” “does not endorse,” “rejects,” or “disassociates from” the Leaders’ Declaration as a whole. Reservations or statements about specific paragraphs do not count as disassociating from the Declaration “as a whole” unless explicitly phrased as not joining or endorsing the Declaration.
- Argentina: The Republic of Argentina; overview at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina.

Why this is forecastable now: The Summit is scheduled for late November 2025, and Leaders’ Declarations (when agreed) are typically released during or immediately after the summit on g20.org. Argentina’s 2024 stance introduces real uncertainty about both the existence of a consensus Leaders’ Declaration and Argentina’s participation in it. The fallback practice of issuing a Chair’s Summary if consensus fails provides a clear alternative outcome.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone: Consider documents and events occurring between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC.

Primary resolution source: The official G20 website (g20.org). Resolution will be determined exclusively from materials posted on g20.org that pertain to the 2025 G20 Leaders’ Summit outcome documents. If multiple versions exist, the latest version timestamped on or before 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC will govern. If necessary, archived snapshots of g20.org (e.g., from the Internet Archive) captured on or before the deadline may be used solely to verify what was publicly available on g20.org by the deadline.

Resolve YES if, by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC:
1) An official Leaders’ Declaration for the 2025 G20 Leaders’ Summit is publicly available at a g20.org URL; and
2) Neither the Declaration itself nor any official accompanying g20.org note/footnote/annex states that Argentina “does not join,” “does not endorse,” “rejects,” or “disassociates from” the Leaders’ Declaration as a whole.

Notes for YES evaluation:
- The Declaration’s title may use standard variants such as “Leaders’ Declaration” or “Leaders’ Communiqué.” It must clearly be the outcome document of the Leaders’ Summit and be posted on g20.org.
- For the purposes of this question, the presence of a Leaders’ Declaration on g20.org is the operational indicator of consensus at the Leaders’ level. A separate Chair’s Summary (with no Leaders’ Declaration) indicates no consensus.

Resolve NO if, by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, any of the following is true:
A) No Leaders’ Declaration for the 2025 Leaders’ Summit is posted on g20.org (e.g., only a Chair’s Summary or similar non-consensus document exists) ; or
B) The Leaders’ Declaration (or an official accompanying g20.org note/footnote/annex) explicitly states that Argentina does not join/endorse the Leaders’ Declaration as a whole.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- Partial reservations: If Argentina expresses reservations or alternative views on specific paragraphs but does not explicitly state non-endorsement of the Declaration as a whole, resolve YES.
- Terminology variations: If the official Leaders’ Summit outcome document is titled “Leaders’ Communiqué” instead of “Leaders’ Declaration,” treat it as a Leaders’ Declaration for the purposes of this question if it is clearly presented on g20.org as the Leaders’ Summit outcome document.
- Multiple postings: If both a Leaders’ Declaration and a Chair’s Summary are posted, assess the Leaders’ Declaration against the criteria above; the existence of a Chair’s Summary does not preclude YES unless condition B is met.
- Publication timing: Leaders’ Declarations are typically released during or shortly after the Summit (scheduled for 22–23 November 2025 in Gauteng under South Africa’s Presidency). If by the deadline no Leaders’ Declaration is on g20.org, resolve NO.

Definitions references for forecasters:
- G20 South Africa Presidency timeline and Leaders’ Summit dates/location.
- Example of Chair’s Summary being issued when no consensus is reached.
- Example of where Leaders’ Declarations are hosted on g20.org.
- Context on Argentina’s 2024 rejection of a G20 gender equality declaration.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (inclusive, by BGBl issue date), will Germany promulgate its NIS 2 implementation act in the Bundesgesetzblatt (Teil I)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- What this is about: The EU’s NIS 2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) is the updated EU-wide cybersecurity framework, expanding the number of covered sectors and entities, strengthening risk-management and incident-reporting obligations, and assigning accountability to top management. Member states were required to transpose it into national law by 2024-10-17.
- German promulgation mechanics: In Germany, promulgation (Verkündung) is the formal publication of a law in the Federal Law Gazette (Bundesgesetzblatt, BGBl) following the Federal President’s signature (Ausfertigung). Promulgation in BGBl completes the legislative process and is a prerequisite for validity. The BGBl is the official promulgation gazette; its Part I (Teil I) publishes federal laws and ordinances. Since 2023 it has been published electronically; each issue bears a publication date and an official electronic seal, and entries are cited as “BGBl. I S. [page]”. The BGBl is accessible at the Federal government’s official legal portal (recht.bund.de), which describes it as the Federation’s official promulgation channel for federal laws and statutory instruments.
- German NIS2 implementation status: On 2025-07-30, the Federal Government announced that the Cabinet adopted the bill to implement NIS 2, using the long title “Gesetz zur Umsetzung der NIS-2-Richtlinie und zur Regelung wesentlicher Grundzüge des Informationssicherheitsmanagements in der Bundesverwaltung.” The communication outlines stricter IT security requirements, comprehensive incident-reporting obligations, stronger penalties, and coverage of critical sectors and the federal administration.
- Institutional context: Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) is the federal cybersecurity authority responsible for prevention, detection, and response in the state, economy, and society.

Why this is forecast-relevant now: With Cabinet adoption in late July 2025, subsequent steps (parliamentary passage, presidential signature, and promulgation in BGBl) could plausibly culminate in publication during Q4 2025, but timing remains uncertain. The question resolves on a single, authoritative source (BGBl Teil I) and focuses on a concrete, checkable event.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and counting rule:
- Start and end: Consider only Bundesgesetzblatt (Teil I) issues whose printed publication date (“Ausgegeben zu Bonn am …” or equivalent) falls between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31, inclusive. Dates are evaluated by the calendar date printed on the BGBl issue (i.e., as used by BGBl itself), not by time of day. 

Definitions:
- Bundesgesetzblatt (BGBl): Germany’s official promulgation gazette. Part I (Teil I) contains federal laws and ordinances. The BGBl is published electronically and each issue bears an official publication date and seal.
- Promulgated (Verkündung): The act of officially publishing a federal law in the BGBl following the Federal President’s signature; this completes the legislative process.
- NIS 2 implementation act (for the purpose of this question): A federal law whose long title explicitly indicates that it implements the EU’s NIS 2 Directive, i.e., the long title includes either the phrase “zur Umsetzung der NIS-2-Richtlinie” or “zur Umsetzung der Richtlinie (EU) 2022/2555”. Variations that add additional elements to the long title (e.g., “… und zur Regelung wesentlicher Grundzüge des Informationssicherheitsmanagements in der Bundesverwaltung”) count as long as one of the two quoted NIS 2 references appears in the long title. This must be a “Gesetz” (act of parliament), not a “Verordnung” (ordinance).

Resolution source and procedure:
- Primary source: The electronic Bundesgesetzblatt (Teil I) for the year 2025 on the official legal portal (recht.bund.de). Navigate to the BGBl section and the 2025 Part I issues. The BGBl is the Federation’s official promulgation channel for laws and statutory instruments ; Part I is where federal laws are published.
- How to resolve YES: Resolve YES if at least one BGBl Teil I issue with a printed publication date between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (inclusive) contains a promulgated federal law whose long title includes either “zur Umsetzung der NIS-2-Richtlinie” or “zur Umsetzung der Richtlinie (EU) 2022/2555”. 
- How to resolve NO: Resolve NO if no such law appears in any BGBl Teil I issue with a printed publication date in the specified window.

Tie-breakers and exclusions:
- If multiple relevant federal laws appear, the existence of any one meeting the definition yields YES.
- Ordinances (Verordnungen), administrative notices, or EU acts do not count; it must be a federal Gesetz published in BGBl Teil I.
- If the law is promulgated before 2025-10-15 or after 2025-12-31, that does not count for this question (and the appropriate resolution is NO), even if it is the NIS 2 implementation act.

Notes for checkers and forecasters:
- Background references on NIS 2 scope and the transposition deadline: European Commission NIS 2 page.
- Cabinet adoption and the official long title used in German government communications: Federal Government announcement dated 2025-07-30.
- Definitions of promulgation and the BGBl’s role and contents: Wikipedia entries summarizing German legislative procedure and the BGBl; and the official legal portal’s description of BGBl.

question: Will Guatemala’s INACIF-reported homicide count for January–November 2025 exceed the count for January–November 2024?
background:
Context and data source: The Instituto Nacional de Ciencias Forenses de Guatemala (INACIF) operates an official Statistics Portal (Portal de Estadísticas INACIF) that provides processed records from the Sistema de Información Nacional Forense (SINAF) across multiple forensic specialties, including Necropsias. The portal supports filtering by variables such as month (Mes) and year (Año), and offers visualizations and downloads of filtered data. Necropsia (autopsy) is defined by INACIF as a procedure performed at the request of a competent authority that involves internal and external evaluation of a cadaver, with objectives including determining the cause of death, the time of death, identification of the cadaver, and preparing the death report. INACIF’s Glosario de variables specifies that for Necropsias, “Año” and “Mes” correspond to the year and month recorded in SINAF at the time the necropsia is performed, and provides definitions for other filters (Departamento, Municipio, Sexo). It also states that the cause of death is determined as a result of the necropsia and laboratory results when applicable. INACIF notes that the portal’s records and tool are dynamic and subject to changes or adjustments, that the date of data acquisition is indicated on viewed or downloaded files, and that static PDFs published on the INACIF website do not reflect adjustments that the dynamic tool may show.

Definitions of key terms and how they map to INACIF data:
- “Homicide” (Homicidio): For this question, homicide refers to deaths classified by INACIF under the cause-of-death category “Homicidio” within the Necropsias specialty. For general clarity, homicide is commonly defined as the killing of one person by another (see: https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homicidio). The operational definition for resolution relies on INACIF’s cause-of-death categorization in its Statistics Portal.
- “Homicide count” for a period: The total number of Necropsias where cause of death is categorized as “Homicidio” in the INACIF Statistics Portal, filtered to the specified months and year(s).
- “January–November” period: Calendar months January (Mes=1) through November (Mes=11) as recorded in SINAF for Necropsias (Año and Mes variables per INACIF definitions).
- Geographic scope: National-level totals (i.e., without restricting filters by Departamento/Municipio) as reported by the INACIF Statistics Portal.

Status quo and practical notes for forecasters (as of 2025-10-01):
- INACIF’s portal is the authoritative and up-to-date source, with month and year filters available for Necropsias. Data are dynamic; figures may be updated as records are adjusted. Always rely on the portal rather than static PDFs for the most current figures.
- Variable meanings: For Necropsias, “Año” and “Mes” reflect when the necropsia was performed/recorded in SINAF, which is the basis for month-by-month aggregation for this question.

Useful portal entry points:
- INACIF Statistics Portal: https://www.inacif.gob.gt/estadisticasweb/ 
- Necropsias section/pages within the portal (for filtering and viewing necropsias counts): https://www.inacif.gob.gt/estadisticasweb/necropsias.php and related necropsias views.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution date/time: Resolve using data available as of 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC.

Primary source of truth: INACIF Statistics Portal (Portal de Estadísticas INACIF).

What to measure:
- For each period (January–November 2024 and January–November 2025), obtain the INACIF-reported national total of Necropsias classified under the cause of death “Homicidio,” filtered by:
  - Specialty: Necropsias.
  - Cause of death: Homicidio (as categorized by INACIF in the portal).
  - Year (Año): 2024 or 2025 (per period).
  - Months (Mes): 1 through 11 (January to November).
  - No restrictions on Departamento/Municipio (i.e., aggregate national total).

Operational steps:
1) Navigate to https://www.inacif.gob.gt/estadisticasweb/. Access the Necropsias section (e.g., https://www.inacif.gob.gt/estadisticasweb/necropsias.php).
2) Use the portal’s filters to obtain the total counts for:
   - Period A: January–November 2024 (Año=2024; Mes=1..11; cause of death=Homicidio).
   - Period B: January–November 2025 (Año=2025; Mes=1..11; cause of death=Homicidio).
   If the portal provides an explicit cumulative figure for January–November for Homicidio, use that. Otherwise, retrieve month-level totals for Homicidio within each year and sum them to obtain the period totals.
3) Record the data acquisition timestamp shown by the portal (the tool indicates the date of data acquisition in viewed/downloaded files) to document the snapshot used for resolution. Do not use static PDF reports in lieu of the dynamic portal; PDFs may not reflect adjustments to records.

Decision rule:
- Resolve “Yes” if the INACIF-reported national Homicidio necropsias count for January–November 2025 is strictly greater than the count for January–November 2024.
- Resolve “No” if it is less than or equal to the 2024 count.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- Ties (equal counts) resolve “No.”
- If the portal is temporarily unavailable at the resolution timestamp, attempt access again within a 48-hour window; use the first successful snapshot as of 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC. If the portal remains inaccessible, resolution is deferred until access is restored; the source of truth remains the INACIF Statistics Portal.
- Use only INACIF’s categorization (cause of death) and variables “Año” and “Mes” as defined in SINAF for Necropsias when aggregating counts.

This question resolves between October 15 and December 31, 2025, and will be resolved on December 31, 2025, using the steps above.

question: Will FY2026 Department of Defense appropriations be enacted (become Public Law) on or before 2025-12-31?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: The U.S. federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30; FY2026 spans 2025-10-01 through 2026-09-30. When regular appropriations are not enacted by the start of the fiscal year, Congress often passes a continuing resolution (CR), a temporary appropriations measure that generally extends prior-year funding levels to a date certain to avert a shutdown. Congress sometimes bundles multiple appropriations into an omnibus spending bill, a single measure that packages several appropriations into one vehicle. A bill becomes law (a Public Law) once it has passed both chambers and is signed by the President, enacted without a signature, or enacted over a veto; enacted laws receive a Public Law number.

Status quo: According to the Congressional Research Service’s Appropriations Status Table for FY2026 on Congress.gov, as of 2025-09-26 10:30 AM (page timestamp), the Defense appropriations row showed no date in the “Presidential Approval” column, i.e., FY2026 Defense appropriations had not been enacted by that time. This Appropriations Status Table is the primary, centralized tracker for the twelve annual appropriations, including Defense, and will be used for resolution.

What counts for this question: FY2026 Defense appropriations may be enacted either as a standalone Department of Defense appropriations act or as part of a larger appropriations vehicle (e.g., an omnibus/minibus) that provides full-year FY2026 appropriations for the Department of Defense. Partial-year funding via CRs does not count toward a Yes outcome for this question.
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Evaluate enactment dates between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. The date used for resolution is the calendar date displayed on the authoritative source (see below); if that displayed date is 2025-12-31 or earlier, it counts as on or before 2025-12-31.

YES resolution:
- Resolve Yes if the FY2026 Defense appropriations are enacted into law (i.e., become a Public Law) on or before 2025-12-31. Primary check: the FY2026 Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov shows a date in the “Presidential Approval” (a.k.a. enacted/public law) column for the Defense row that is on or before 2025-12-31. “Enacted/Public Law” means the measure has become a Public Law under U.S. practice.
- The enactment may occur via a standalone Department of Defense appropriations act or via a broader appropriations vehicle (e.g., omnibus/minibus) so long as it provides full-year FY2026 appropriations for the Department of Defense (i.e., funding through 2026-09-30). Partial-year continuing resolutions do not satisfy this criterion.

NO resolution:
- Resolve No if by 2025-12-31 there is no date in the “Presidential Approval” column for the Defense row in the FY2026 Appropriations Status Table , or if the enacted date displayed is after 2025-12-31.

Primary resolution source:
- FY2026 Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov (maintained by CRS): https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table.

Fallback sources (used only if the primary source is unavailable or clearly out of date as of 2026-01-05 17:00 UTC):
- Congress.gov Public Law entry for the enacted appropriations vehicle indicating inclusion of FY2026 Defense appropriations and displaying an enacted (Public Law) date on or before 2025-12-31. If needed, corroborate by the text/title of the public law on Congress.gov identifying that it provides full-year FY2026 appropriations for the Department of Defense. 

Clarifications and edge cases:
- Authorizations (e.g., the National Defense Authorization Act) do not count; only appropriations becoming Public Law count for this market.
- “Omnibus spending bill” refers to a legislative vehicle that packages multiple appropriations measures together; such a vehicle can satisfy this question if it enacts full-year FY2026 Defense appropriations.
- “Continuing resolution” refers to a temporary appropriations measure; partial-year CRs do not count toward a Yes outcome.

question: October 2025 U.S. CPI (headline YoY) ≥ 3.0%
background:
Definition and scope. For this market, “headline CPI YoY” means the 12‑month percent change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U), U.S. city average, All Items, 1982–84=100, not seasonally adjusted, as reported by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in its national Consumer Price Index Summary news release. Headline inflation refers to the aggregate CPI including volatile components such as food and energy. BLS commonly phrases this figure as “Over the last 12 months, the all items index increased X percent before seasonal adjustment” in the national CPI news release.

Status quo as of 2025‑09‑30. The latest published national CPI news release (August 2025 data, released September 11, 2025) reports: “Over the last 12 months, the all items index increased 2.9 percent before seasonal adjustment”. The same release states that “The Consumer Price Index for September 2025 is scheduled to be released on Wednesday, October 15, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. (ET)”.

Release timing for October 2025 CPI. The BLS “Schedule of Selected Releases” lists the October 2025 CPI news release for Thursday, November 13, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time (13:30 UTC). The calendar notes that all listed times are Eastern Time.

Why this is non‑trivial. The 12‑month headline CPI outcome reflects multiple moving components (e.g., energy, food, shelter, core goods/services), and forecasters may incorporate data such as commodity moves, housing measures, and monthly CPI sub‑index trends. The threshold (3.0%) is close to the latest reading (2.9% for August 2025), creating genuine uncertainty around whether October 2025’s 12‑month change rounds to ≥3.0%.
resolution_criteria:
Yes if the BLS national Consumer Price Index Summary (news release) for October 2025, published on bls.gov, reports the headline CPI 12‑month percent change (U.S. city average CPI‑U, All Items, 1982–84=100, not seasonally adjusted) as at least 3.0%; No otherwise.

Operational details:
- Source of truth: the BLS national CPI news release webpage (“Consumer Price Index Summary”) for October 2025 on bls.gov. The figure will be taken from the sentence of the form “Over the last 12 months, the all items index increased X percent before seasonal adjustment,” consistent with BLS phrasing used in recent releases.
- Release timing: Scheduled for Thursday, November 13, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time (13:30 UTC). Resolution occurs upon publication of the October 2025 CPI news release or any official correction posted by BLS by December 31, 2025.
- Measurement specifics: Use the 12‑month percent change for the U.S. city average CPI‑U, All Items, not seasonally adjusted, as explicitly defined by BLS. The decision threshold is based on the percent figure as reported by BLS; no independent recalculation or alternative data series will be used.
- Revisions and corrections: If BLS issues an erratum or correction to the October 2025 CPI news release by December 31, 2025, the corrected figure will be used. Any revisions or methodological changes posted after December 31, 2025, will not affect resolution.
- Time window: The question concerns the October 2025 CPI YoY figure and resolves no later than December 31, 2025, based on the BLS publication schedule.

question: Will the EIA’s December 2025 Short‑Term Energy Outlook report that U.S. retail electricity sales in 2025 grew by more than 3.0% year over year?
background:
What is being forecast: whether the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) will, in its Short‑Term Energy Outlook (STEO) issue published in December 2025, report that total U.S. retail electricity sales to ultimate customers in calendar year 2025 exceed the 2024 total by more than 3.0%.

Metric definition: “U.S. retail electricity sales to ultimate customers (all sectors)” refers to the sum of retail electricity sales across residential, commercial, industrial, and transportation end‑use sectors in the United States (50 states and DC), measured in kilowatthours (kWh). This is the standard consumption metric used by EIA, distinct from generation, and is the basis of EIA’s sales data products (monthly EIA‑861M, Electric Power Monthly, and annual sales/revenue/price tables). Kilowatthour definition: see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilowatt_hour.

Current context (as of 2025‑09‑22): EIA has highlighted rising electricity demand driven by data centers and industrial customers and has projected continued growth in electric power sector activity, including an indicative projection of about 2.3% growth in 2025 and 3.0% in 2026 for total U.S. electric power sector generation, reflecting elevated load growth. EIA regularly publishes retail sales data and summaries via EIA‑861M and Electric Power Monthly, which provide the underlying measurement of sales/consumption. Because finalized annual 2025 sales data typically publish after year‑end, this question resolves using the December 2025 STEO full‑year figures to ensure decision before 2025‑12‑31.
resolution_criteria:
Timeframe: Events relevant to the outcome occur between 2025‑09‑22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. The measurement period for the statistic is calendar year 2025 (2025‑01‑01 00:00:00 to 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC).

Primary source for resolution: The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Short‑Term Energy Outlook (STEO) issue published in December 2025, available at https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/. Use the table(s)/dataset in that issue reporting “Total U.S. sales of electricity to ultimate customers (all sectors)” for full year 2024 and full year 2025, typically expressed in billion kWh. If both text and tables present figures, the tables take precedence. If multiple tables present the metric, use the total “all sectors” U.S. sales figure.

Definitions and geography:
- “U.S.” includes the 50 states and the District of Columbia; U.S. territories and possessions are excluded unless the STEO table explicitly includes them (if it does, use the figure labeled for the United States consistent with other STEO tables).
- “Retail electricity sales to ultimate customers” means sales directly to end‑use consumers across all sectors and is the standard EIA sales/consumption measure (see EIA electricity data resources for scope).
- Units are kilowatthours (kWh); if the STEO table is in billion kWh, use those values directly.

Computation and threshold:
- Let S2024 be the total retail electricity sales for 2024 and S2025 be the total for 2025 as reported in the December 2025 STEO tables.
- Compute growth g = (S2025 / S2024) − 1. If g > 0.030000..., resolve YES; otherwise, resolve NO.
- Use the most precise published figures available in the STEO tables. If figures are rounded (e.g., to the nearest whole billion kWh), compute using those. If the computed growth equals exactly 3.0% when using the published precision, resolve NO (strictly greater than 3.0% required).

Ties, revisions, and conflicts:
- If conflicting figures appear within the December 2025 STEO, the numerical tables override narrative text. If multiple STEO December files exist (e.g., revisions within December), use the latest version timestamped before or on 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Post‑December 2025 revisions are ignored for resolution purposes.

Fallback (only if the December 2025 STEO is not published by 2025‑12‑31): Use the most recent STEO issue published in 2025 available at https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/ prior to the deadline and apply the same procedure.

question: Between 00:00 UTC on 15 Oct 2025 and 23:59 UTC on 31 Dec 2025, will the European Commission announce that it has imposed periodic penalty payments on Apple under the Digital Markets Act?
background:
Context and current status (as of 2025-10-01)
- What is the DMA: The Digital Markets Act (DMA) is Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, an EU regulation aimed at ensuring contestable and fair digital markets and enforced by the European Commission (EC). The DMA empowers the EC to impose fines for non-compliance and to use strong investigative and enforcement powers. In plain language, the EC can impose (a) fines up to 10% of a company’s total worldwide annual turnover (up to 20% for repeated infringements), and (b) periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of the average daily turnover to compel compliance.
- Apple’s DMA enforcement status: On 23 April 2025, the EC issued its first non‑compliance decisions under the DMA, finding that Apple breached the DMA’s anti‑steering obligation (Article 5(4)) and imposing a €500 million fine on Apple. The Official Journal summary of the Apple decision confirms a fine of €500,000,000 under Article 30(1), includes a cease‑and‑desist order, and indicates that if Apple fails to comply, Apple shall incur periodic penalty payments pursuant to Article 31(1). The summary was published in the OJ C series on 16 June 2025.
- Prior procedural history: The EC opened DMA non‑compliance proceedings against Apple on 25 March 2024, including concerns over App Store steering rules and other areas, and noted its intention to conclude such proceedings within 12 months; where applicable, it would issue preliminary findings and consider measures to ensure compliance.

Why this forecast is interesting
- The EC has already imposed a monetary fine on Apple for DMA non‑compliance in April 2025. The next enforcement step could include imposing periodic penalty payments if the Commission determines ongoing non‑compliance, a tool explicitly provided by the DMA. Whether the EC will escalate to periodic penalty payments within the specified window is uncertain and depends on Apple’s compliance posture and the Commission’s enforcement strategy, creating a non‑trivial and time‑bounded question.

Key definitions (with links)
- European Commission (EC): The EU’s executive institution responsible for enforcing the DMA. EC announcements typically appear on the Commission’s Press corner and/or the Digital Markets Act website. Examples of past DMA decisions and press materials include the Commission’s announcement on 23 April 2025 regarding Apple and Meta. Press corner: https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/home; DMA site: https://digital-markets-act.ec.europa.eu/
- Digital Markets Act (DMA): Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (text on EUR‑Lex: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj). The DMA’s enforcement toolkit includes fines and periodic penalty payments.
- Periodic penalty payments: Recurring financial penalties the EC may impose to compel compliance, up to 5% of the company’s average daily turnover. For Apple’s April 2025 decision, the OJ summary states Apple shall incur such payments if it fails to comply with the cease‑and‑desist order.
- Apple: For this question, “Apple” refers to Apple Inc. and any Apple group entity expressly named as an addressee in an EC DMA enforcement decision (e.g., entities designated in the Commission’s decision text or OJ summary).

Status‑quo sources to monitor for resolution
- EC Press corner announcements for DMA enforcement decisions: https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/home (e.g., IP_25_1085 for 23 April 2025).
- EC Digital Markets Act website news items: https://digital-markets-act.ec.europa.eu/ (e.g., the 23 April 2025 announcement page).
- Official Journal (OJ) publication of decision summaries/texts on EUR‑Lex (C or L series): an example summary for Apple’s 23 April 2025 decision is published in OJ C on 16 June 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Question and timeframe
- Resolve Yes if, between 00:00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, the European Commission announces that it has imposed periodic penalty payments on Apple under Article 31 of the Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925). Resolve No otherwise.

What counts as “announces … imposed periodic penalty payments”
- “Announces” means any of the following official EC publications that clearly state the Commission has imposed periodic penalty payments on Apple under the DMA within the timeframe:
  1) An EC Press corner press release or notice stating that periodic penalty payments have been imposed on Apple under the DMA; or
  2) A news post on the EC’s Digital Markets Act website stating that periodic penalty payments have been imposed on Apple under the DMA; or
  3) Publication in the Official Journal (OJ) of a decision or summary that states the Commission has imposed periodic penalty payments on Apple under Article 31 of the DMA and identifies Apple as an addressee.
- The accepted sources above are exemplified by the Commission’s press and OJ publications for the 23 April 2025 Apple non‑compliance decision (press release IP_25_1085 and OJ C summary), which demonstrate the standard venues where such decisions are announced.

Necessary elements for a qualifying event
- The publication must expressly state that the Commission imposed periodic penalty payments (not merely indicating that Apple “shall incur” such payments if it fails to comply in the future, and not merely warning of potential future periodic penalty payments). The decision must be one under Article 31 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 and must identify Apple (Apple Inc. and/or specified Apple group entities) as addressee(s).
- If both a press release and an OJ publication exist, the earliest publication time (UTC) within the timeframe governs resolution. If only one exists by 31 December 2025 (UTC), resolution is based on that source.

Scope, inclusions, exclusions, and edge cases
- Included: Any EC decision adopting periodic penalty payments under Article 31 of the DMA against Apple (any addressee entity within the Apple group), regardless of whether the payments start accruing immediately or are suspended later pending appeal. Suspension, partial annulment, or later modification does not negate a Yes resolution if the imposition was announced during the timeframe.
- Excluded: (a) Decisions that only warn or indicate that periodic penalty payments may be incurred upon future non‑compliance (e.g., cease‑and‑desist orders referencing potential Article 31 payments but not imposing them) ; (b) Monetary fines under Article 30 without periodic penalty payments ; (c) Actions by national authorities or courts; (d) Announcements outside the timeframe or by non‑official sources.

How to resolve
- A resolver should check the EC Press corner and the EC DMA website for announcements within the timeframe, and/or EUR‑Lex for OJ publications. If any of these sources clearly state that the EC has imposed periodic penalty payments on Apple under Article 31 of the DMA during the specified window, resolve Yes. Otherwise, resolve No at 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025. The DMA’s enforcement tools and definitions used here (fines vs periodic penalty payments) are supported by official EC descriptions and the OJ summary of Apple’s decision.

question: Will total Suez Canal vessel transits in November 2025 be at least 15% higher than in July 2025?
background:
Overview and current status as of 2025-09-30:
- The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) publishes monthly counts of vessels (“NO (Vessel)”) and net tonnage (“Net Ton (1000)”) in its Annual Navigation Reports, with calendar-month totals presented in tables titled “Monthly NO & Net Ton”. In these reports, “NO” denotes the number of vessels that completed a transit, and “Net Ton” is reported in thousands of tons.
- As a recent baseline, 1,055 ships transited the Suez Canal in July 2025 (total “NO”), according to sector reporting that tracks monthly Suez traffic.
- Traffic has been recovering from the Red Sea disruptions: daily Suez Canal traffic in mid-2025 was reported at approximately 36–37 ships per day, up from a low of around 20 per day in August 2024.
- For independent, high-frequency measurements, the “Maritime passageway transits during disruptions” dataset hosted on the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX) provides AIS-derived daily and monthly transit counts for key chokepoints, including the Suez Canal. The dataset documentation describes AIS-based transit detection, includes daily and monthly Suez Canal series, and shows coverage extending into 2025.

Key definitions and terms:
- “Suez Canal vessel transits”: The monthly count of vessels completing a transit of the Suez Canal as reported by the SCA (“NO (Vessel)”) in its official statistics. When using the HDX AIS dataset as a fallback, “transits” refer to AIS-derived counts of vessels crossing the canal’s defined geometry, aggregated to calendar-month totals per the dataset’s methodology.
- “Month” and time zone: Months are calendar months measured from 00:00:00 UTC on the first day to 23:59:59 UTC on the last day of the month.
- “At least 15% higher”: November 2025 total transits must be greater than or equal to 1.15 times the July 2025 total transits. This is equivalent to November ≥ 115% of July.

Why this question:
- It is narrowly defined and resolves on a single comparison of two well-defined monthly totals published by authoritative sources (SCA) with robust AIS-based datasets as fallback.
- The outcome is uncertain and research-dependent: forecasters must weigh evolving security risks, carrier routing decisions, and discounting policies versus capacity and demand trends, with recent daily averages and monthly baselines providing context.
resolution_criteria:
What is being measured:
- Let July_2025_NO be the total number of vessels (“NO (Vessel)”) that transited the Suez Canal in July 2025.
- Let Nov_2025_NO be the total number of vessels (“NO (Vessel)”) that transited the Suez Canal in November 2025.

Resolution rule:
- Resolve YES if Nov_2025_NO ≥ 1.15 × July_2025_NO.
- Resolve NO otherwise.

Date bounds and time zone:
- July 2025 is defined as 2025-07-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-07-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- November 2025 is defined as 2025-11-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC.

Primary source of truth (preferred order):
1) Suez Canal Authority official publications. Use the SCA’s published monthly “NO (Vessel)” figures from its Annual Navigation Reports or official monthly/bulletin releases. Example format and definition of “NO (Vessel)” and monthly tables are shown in SCA annual reports. If multiple SCA publications exist, use the latest official figure published by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Fallback sources if the SCA’s November 2025 and/or July 2025 monthly “NO (Vessel)” figures are not publicly accessible by the resolution deadline:
2) AIS-based HDX dataset “Maritime passageway transits during disruptions”: use the Suez Canal monthly series (“Suez Canal Monthly Transits – AIS”), or if needed, sum the Suez Canal daily transits to compute calendar-month totals. Apply the dataset’s Suez Canal geometry and methodology as documented.
3) Credible reporting that explicitly quotes the SCA’s monthly ship count for the relevant months (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, Bloomberg, or Informare). As a reference for July 2025, 1,055 ships transited according to a sector report; this figure may be used for July_2025_NO only if an official SCA figure is not accessible and the HDX AIS series is unavailable. If multiple credible reports disagree, prefer the one that explicitly attributes the figure to the SCA.

Tie-breakers and data revisions:
- If SCA publishes a revision by the deadline, use the latest revision.
- If SCA data are unavailable and HDX AIS data provide a different total than a credible report, use HDX AIS totals due to methodological transparency.

Verification notes:
- The SCA’s Annual Navigation Reports include monthly tables labeled “Monthly NO & Net Ton,” where “NO (Vessel)” is the count used for this question.
- AIS dataset documentation confirms the presence of Suez Canal daily and monthly series and defines AIS-derived transit counts.
- Sector reporting provides the July 2025 baseline of 1,055 ships transited , and daily recovery context (36–37 ships/day versus ~20/day at the Aug 2024 low).

question: By 31 December 2025 (UTC), will the EU newly list at least 20 persons or entities under its Iran restrictive measures pursuant to Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 and Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP?
background:
Summary and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- On 29 September 2025, the Council of the EU announced it had reimposed restrictive measures against Iran and adopted multiple legal acts amending and implementing the Iran regimes, thereby re-establishing a framework that can be updated with further listings through additional Official Journal publications.
- The EU’s Iran restrictive measures relevant to nuclear proliferation are set out in two core instruments: Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012. Listings of designated persons and entities are maintained in annexes to these instruments. For Regulation 267/2012, relevant lists of designated persons, entities, and bodies are in Annexes VIII, IX, XIII, and XIV. For Decision 2010/413/CFSP, relevant lists are in Annexes I–IV. In practice, additions to these annexes are made via Council Implementing Decisions (for the Decision) and Council Implementing Regulations (for the Regulation), published in the Official Journal; several such acts were adopted and published on 29 September 2025 as part of the reimposition package.
- Forecasters should note that subsequent additions (designations) and other list changes, if any, will be published in the Official Journal of the European Union and accessible via EUR-Lex. See definitions and sources below.

Key definitions and sources a forecaster should know:
- Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU): the EU’s official gazette where legal acts are published; it is published online and daily in the L (Legislation) and C (Information and Notices) series. Access: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/oj/direct-access.html; overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Journal_of_the_European_Union
- EUR-Lex: the EU’s official database of EU law and the Official Journal, where acts and annexes can be searched and downloaded. Overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EUR-Lex; portal: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/
- Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012: consolidated texts and annexes (designated persons/entities) including Annexes VIII, IX, XIII, XIV.
- Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP: consolidated text and annexes (designated persons/entities) including Annexes I–IV.

Context for uncertainty/forecastability:
- A major reimposition of measures occurred on 29 September 2025, with multiple amending and implementing acts published the same day. It is plausible that the Council may further update the annexes via additional implementing acts before year-end; however, the volume and timing of any such additions are uncertain, creating a meaningful forecasting problem anchored to a clear documentary source (the OJEU).
resolution_criteria:
Outcome to predict:
- Resolve Yes if at least 20 distinct persons or entities are newly added to any of the designation annexes of Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (Annexes VIII, IX, XIII, XIV) and/or Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP (Annexes I–IV), by legal acts published in the Official Journal of the European Union between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). Resolve No otherwise.

Scope and time window:
- Eligible publications: Only acts published in the OJEU (L series) whose publication date shown on EUR-Lex falls within the window above. If an act is published on the same calendar day but at an unspecified time, treat the OJ publication date as the reference (date-only) timestamp.
- Eligible regimes: Only listings under Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 and Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP count. Additions under other Iran-related EU regimes (e.g., EU human rights regime or other autonomous regimes) do not count unless they simultaneously add the person/entity to the specified annexes of 267/2012 or 2010/413/CFSP.

What counts as a “newly listed” person/entity:
- Counting unit: One (1) per distinct natural person ("individual") or legal person/entity/body ("entity"). For this question: “individual” means a natural person; “entity” means any legal person, entity, or body, consistent with the terminology used in Regulation 267/2012 and Decision 2010/413/CFSP.
- Newly listed means the person/entity appears for the first time as a listed entry in an annex of the specified instruments, by virtue of a legal act published within the time window. If the same person/entity is added to both the Decision and the Regulation (often done via a pair of implementing acts), count them once.
- Exclusions: Do not count (i) relistings of persons/entities already listed before 2025-10-15 UTC under these annexes, (ii) substitutions where an act states the entry for an already-listed person/entity is “replaced” or “amended” (e.g., updated identifying information or grounds), (iii) purely technical corrections or corrigenda, (iv) additions of aliases/transliterations/AKAs for an already-listed person/entity without adding a new person/entity, and (v) transfers between annexes that do not introduce a new person/entity not previously listed.
- Edge cases: If a person/entity is newly added within the window and later delisted within the same window, it still counts as one addition. If identity is unclear due to spelling/transliteration, use the identifying data (e.g., date/place of birth, registration numbers, addresses) in the OJ annex to determine whether an entry is the same person/entity; if doubt remains, do not count it as a new addition to avoid overcounting.

How to resolve (step-by-step):
1) On EUR-Lex, list all OJEU L-series acts published between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (inclusive) that either (a) implement Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP (typically “Council Implementing Decision (CFSP) … implementing Decision 2010/413/CFSP”) or (b) implement Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (typically “Council Implementing Regulation (EU) … implementing Regulation (EU) No 267/2012”). The 29 September 2025 package provides examples of the types of amending/implementing acts used to update these lists.
2) For each such act, open the Annex section and identify entries that constitute additions of persons/entities to the relevant annexes (ignore replacements/amendments/corrections for existing entries).
3) Tally the number of distinct persons/entities added across all eligible acts, deduplicating where the same person/entity is added to both instruments.
4) If the total is >= 20, resolve Yes; otherwise, resolve No.

Definitions and authoritative sources:
- Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (designations in Annexes VIII, IX, XIII, XIV).
- Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP (designations in Annexes I–IV).
- Summary of the EU Iran restrictive measures framework (Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Regulation 267/2012).
- Confirmation that on 29 September 2025 the Council reimposed restrictive measures and adopted multiple amending/implementing acts (illustrating the mechanism by which listings are updated).

Ambiguities and tie-breakers:
- If an act’s annex mixes additions with replacements, count only the clearly indicated additions; if not explicitly labeled, compare the entry to the immediately prior consolidated version of the annex on EUR-Lex to determine whether the person/entity was previously present.
- If two entries appear to refer to the same person/entity with different transliterations or spellings within the window, treat them as one if identifying data indicate the same subject; otherwise, treat them as separate.
- If multiple acts on the same OJ date add the same person/entity to both instruments, count once.

Resolution source of truth:
- The Official Journal of the European Union (via EUR-Lex) for the relevant acts and their annexes. Access: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/oj/direct-access.html. The consolidated texts for the underlying instruments and their annexes are available here for cross-checking.

question: Will the FOMC change the federal funds rate target range at its October 28–29, 2025 meeting?
background:
Status quo and context as of 2025-09-30:
- Meeting schedule and timing: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) has a regularly scheduled two‑day meeting on October 28–29, 2025, with a policy statement customarily released at 2:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the second day and a press conference thereafter. The Federal Reserve’s October 2025 calendar lists “FOMC Meeting – Two-day meeting, October 28–October 29” and notes a press conference on the 29th.
- Current target range: At its September 16–17, 2025 meeting, the FOMC decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 4 to 4‑1/4 percent, as stated in the post‑meeting statement. The accompanying Implementation Note directs operations to maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 4 to 4‑1/4 percent, effective September 18, 2025.

Key definitions and notes for forecasters:
- Federal funds rate target range: For the purposes of this question, this is the numeric lower and upper bounds (in percent) for the federal funds rate targeted by the FOMC, as stated in the FOMC post‑meeting statement and/or accompanying Implementation Note published on FederalReserve.gov. Examples of this phrasing and format are shown in the September 17, 2025 statement and Implementation Note.
- FOMC post‑meeting statement: The Federal Reserve press release titled “Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement,” posted on FederalReserve.gov for each meeting (see, e.g., the September 17, 2025 statement).
- Meeting identification: The meeting at issue is the regularly scheduled FOMC meeting that begins on October 28, 2025, as listed on the Federal Reserve’s calendar.

Why this is forecastable: The October 28–29 meeting falls within the resolution window and follows a recent policy move (September 2025), making a further change plausible but uncertain. The Fed publishes authoritative statements on its website that allow for unambiguous verification.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: Resolve “Yes” if the FOMC post‑meeting statement on FederalReserve.gov for the October 28–29, 2025 meeting announces a federal funds rate target range whose lower or upper bound differs from the target range announced in the post‑meeting statement for the immediately preceding regularly scheduled meeting (September 16–17, 2025). Otherwise, resolve “No”.

What to compare:
- Prior reference value: The target range announced in the September 17, 2025 post‑meeting statement (and, if needed to confirm numeric bounds, its Implementation Note) serves as the baseline for comparison; as of that meeting, the range was 4 to 4‑1/4 percent.
- Target meeting value: The target range as stated in the October 28–29, 2025 meeting’s post‑meeting statement (and/or its Implementation Note, if needed for numeric precision). The statement is customarily released on day two of the meeting; the Federal Reserve’s tentative schedule notes a 2:00 p.m. Eastern Time release for these statements.

Definitions for resolution:
- “Different” means any change in either the lower or upper bound of the stated target range (numeric inequality at either bound suffices).
- “FOMC post‑meeting statement” refers to the Federal Reserve press release titled “Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement” for the relevant meeting, as posted on FederalReserve.gov (see the September 17, 2025 example).
- “Federal funds rate target range” refers to the numeric bounds for the target range specified by the FOMC, as published in the statement and/or the Implementation Note (see examples from September 17–18, 2025).

Scope and edge cases:
- Intermeeting actions: Any intermeeting change prior to October 28, 2025 does not, by itself, determine resolution. Only the range announced in the October 28–29, 2025 post‑meeting statement is compared to the September 16–17, 2025 statement for the purpose of this question.
- Schedule changes: If no FOMC post‑meeting statement is published for a meeting that begins on October 28, 2025 (e.g., due to cancellation), resolve “No.” The identification of the meeting date comes from the Federal Reserve’s published calendar.

Source(s) of truth to check on resolution date:
- FederalReserve.gov page for the October 28–29, 2025 “Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement.” If needed to verify the numeric bounds, use the accompanying Implementation Note. The prior‑meeting baseline is the September 17, 2025 statement and Implementation Note.
- For meeting timing context, consult the FOMC’s tentative schedule announcement and the October 2025 calendar on FederalReserve.gov.

question: Will the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season end with at least 15 named storms?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01 (UTC):
- NOAA’s seasonal outlook (May 22, 2025) forecast 13–19 total named storms (maximum sustained winds ≥39 mph), with a 60% chance of an above-normal season, 30% near-normal, and 10% below-normal. The season runs June 1–November 30.
- NOAA’s August 7 update revised the expected range to 13–18 named storms and noted the ranges are inclusive of storms that had already formed by that date.
- Through the morning of Sept. 29, 2025, nine named storms and three hurricanes had formed; this was one named storm and two hurricanes below the average pace through the end of September, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC) as reported by Weather.com. The New York Times also reported Imelda as the ninth named storm by Oct. 1, 2025. The NHC 2025 advisory archive lists the named Atlantic systems to date (Andrea, Barry, Chantal, Dexter, Erin, Fernand, Gabrielle, Humberto, Imelda). The NHC’s season summary page likewise showed nine named storms and three hurricanes through Sept. 30, 2025.

Key definitions and scope:
- Named storm (Atlantic): A tropical or subtropical cyclone in the Atlantic basin that the NHC officially assigns a name from World Meteorological Organization (WMO) lists. Tropical storms (34–63 kt; 39–73 mph) and hurricanes (≥64 kt; ≥74 mph) are named; subtropical storms (≥34 kt) are also named. NHC uses 1-minute average sustained winds for intensity. See: NHC Glossary definitions for Tropical Storm and Hurricane , Subtropical Cyclone/Storm , and NHC explanation of WMO-maintained name lists.
- Atlantic hurricane season: Officially runs from June 1 to November 30, though named storms can occur outside these dates; the NHC’s final season total for 2025 is the authoritative count for this question.

Why this is forecast-relevant now: With nine named storms recorded by Sept. 29 and NOAA’s updated range at 13–18, whether the final 2025 total reaches ≥15 remains plausibly above or below the threshold given variability in late-season activity.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve “Yes” if the National Hurricane Center’s final 2025 North Atlantic season total lists 15 or more named storms; otherwise resolve “No.”

Primary source of truth:
- NHC “North Atlantic Tropical Weather Summary (2025)” on the NHC Tropical Cyclone Reports index (nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/). The final “Named Storms” total reported for the 2025 Atlantic season on this page will be used for resolution.

Fallback if the primary source is not finalized by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025:
- Use the NHC 2025 Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive (nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2025/) to count the number of named Atlantic systems listed for 2025. Count each system that the archive lists under the Atlantic basin with an assigned name (e.g., Andrea, Barry, …), regardless of whether it was tropical or subtropical, and regardless of subsequent transitions (post-tropical, extratropical), consistent with NHC naming practice and intensity thresholds (Tropical Storm: 34–63 kt; Hurricane: ≥64 kt; Subtropical Storm: ≥34 kt). If the count is ≥15, resolve “Yes”; otherwise, “No.”

Additional rules:
- In the event of discrepancy between sources, the NHC season summary page  supersedes the archive count.
- All dates/times are in UTC.
- This question concerns the Atlantic basin totals as defined and reported by the NHC; no other basin’s activity is relevant.

question: Will Mexico’s imports from China in September 2025 be at least 12% lower year-over-year versus September 2024?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: Mexico–China trade is under policy pressure. In late 2024, Mexico’s tax authority (SAT) announced new tariffs and heightened surveillance affecting goods from Asia starting January 1, 2025, including duties on low-value e-commerce shipments, which could reduce import volumes from China. In September 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) launched a trade and investment barrier investigation into Mexico’s tariff measures, noting Mexico plans duties up to 50% on more than 1,400 products from Asia and that Mexico imported approximately US$130 billion worth of products from China in 2024. These developments create uncertainty about monthly import flows from China.

Official statistical source: INEGI’s Balanza Comercial de Mercancías de México (BCMM) is the authoritative program reporting Mexico’s merchandise trade data. BCMM press releases present figures in US dollars and include both original (non-seasonally adjusted) and seasonally adjusted series; data are compiled primarily from customs declarations, with SAT (tax authority), SE (Economy Ministry), Banco de México, and INEGI as sources. For imports, the attribution of country follows the criterion of country of origin (país de origen), meaning imports are classified to the country where the goods were produced, not where they were shipped from. BCMM is published on a monthly schedule (press releases with “información oportuna”), and the September 26, 2025 release specifies the next publication date was October 27, 2025, illustrating the end-of-month cadence.

Why this forecast is interesting: Monthly imports from China reflect both structural supply chain dynamics and short-run responses to policy changes (e.g., front-running before tariffs, diversion via third countries, or demand shifts). A −12% year-over-year threshold for September balances plausibility and uncertainty—forecasters must weigh policy impacts against macro conditions and trade rerouting. Definitions and resolution are precise and rely on a single public source (INEGI) for rapid verification.

Key definitions and clarifications:
- Imports (of merchandise): As used by INEGI’s BCMM, the value of foreign goods entering Mexico’s national territory, recorded in customs declarations; figures reported in US dollars and available as original (non-seasonally adjusted) values. See general concept of import in trade: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Import.
- Country of origin (país de origen): For Mexico’s imports, the country attribution criterion is country of origin—i.e., where the goods were produced. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rules_of_origin.
- China: The People’s Republic of China (PRC). For resolution, “China” refers to the row labeled “China” in INEGI’s BCMM country-of-origin breakdown for imports. Hong Kong and Macao, if shown separately, are not counted under “China” unless explicitly aggregated by INEGI’s table.
- Currency and series choice: Use the original (cifras originales, non-seasonally adjusted) monthly import value by country of origin, expressed in US dollars (millones de dólares) as published in INEGI’s BCMM press release or associated tables.

Status quo of publication: INEGI’s BCMM timely releases are monthly and list forthcoming publication dates; the September 26, 2025 release shows a next publication date of October 27, 2025, consistent with end-of-month publication for the prior reference month.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and time zone: This question will resolve as soon as INEGI publishes the BCMM “información oportuna” press release covering September 2025 (reference month), provided this occurs by December 31, 2025 at 23:59 UTC. If published earlier, resolution may occur earlier; verification should be possible within ~10 minutes from the INEGI press release.

Data source to use: INEGI’s Balanza Comercial de Mercancías de México (BCMM) press release for the September 2025 reference month (información oportuna). Acceptable sources are:
- The INEGI BCMM press release PDF for the relevant month (as exemplified by BCMM monthly bulletins).
- If the press release does not include a by–country-of-origin table, use the INEGI BCMM dataset or annexed tables accompanying the release that provide the monthly import value by country of origin; ensure values are original (non-seasonally adjusted) and in US dollars.

Exact test and definitions:
- Let V_{Sep2025, China} be Mexico’s September 2025 import value from China, as classified by country of origin and reported by INEGI’s BCMM, using cifras originales (non-seasonally adjusted) in US dollars.
- Let V_{Sep2024, China} be Mexico’s September 2024 import value from China under the same classification and series.
- Compute the year-over-year percentage change: YoY% = (V_{Sep2025, China} − V_{Sep2024, China}) / V_{Sep2024, China} × 100.

Resolution:
- Resolve Yes if YoY% ≤ −12.000% (i.e., a decline of at least 12.000%).
- Resolve No otherwise.

Scope clarifications:
- Use the original (cifras originales) monthly values in US dollars (millones de dólares) reported by INEGI; do not use seasonally adjusted series.
- “China” refers to the PRC as labeled in INEGI’s country-of-origin table; do not include Hong Kong or Macao unless INEGI’s table explicitly aggregates them into “China”.
- If INEGI reports multiple versions (e.g., later revisions), use the first published “información oportuna” figure available by December 31, 2025 at 23:59 UTC.

Verification steps for resolvers:
1) Navigate to INEGI’s Sala de Prensa BCMM release for September 2025 (monthly “información oportuna”). Confirm the document presents import values by country of origin (or access the accompanying country table). Note the values for “China” for September 2024 and September 2025.
2) Ensure the values are cifras originales in US dollars (millones de dólares) as per BCMM methodology.
3) Compute YoY% per the formula above and apply the threshold.

Rationale for source reliability: BCMM is an INEGI program that compiles Mexico’s merchandise trade statistics from customs declarations with contributions from SAT, SE, Banco de México, and INEGI; press releases specify figure types and currency, and country attribution follows country of origin.

Notes:
- This question does not resolve based on unofficial aggregations or third-party dashboards; only INEGI’s BCMM publications or tables are valid.
- If, unexpectedly, the September 2025 BCMM release is not published by December 31, 2025 at 23:59 UTC, the question will be declared non-resolvable under this criterion and should be voided by the platform (however, BCMM’s monthly schedule and listed next publication dates indicate timely availability).

question: By 31 December 2025, will Lotteritilsynet publish a vedtak imposing an overtredelsesgebyr of at least NOK 20 million on Norsk Tipping for the 19 April 2025 Lotto “Supertrekning” error?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
- What “Supertrekning” is: Supertrekning is an extra draw within Lotto that is included when you buy Lotto; you cannot buy participation in Supertrekning on its own. Winners are drawn from all Lotto lines played since the previous Supertrekning, and typically 1 million NOK is awarded to each of 25–50 winners drawn from the pot.
- The incident on 19 April 2025: Lotteritilsynet issued a formal warning (varsel) on 2025-09-29 concerning a technical error in the Lotto Supertrekning on 19 April 2025. Due to an automatic deletion rule affecting “andelsbank” (syndicate) entries, 16,698 players and 682,900 rows (about 0.2% of all rows) were excluded from the draw, and 52 incorrect million-prize winners were drawn. Lotteritilsynet characterized the conduct as grossly negligent and stated the drawing was not carried out correctly under the gambling law. The varsel sets a potential overtredelsesgebyr of up to NOK 25 million and gives Norsk Tipping three weeks to respond before Lotteritilsynet may make a decision (vedtak).
- Legal basis and precedent: The varsel cites the Gambling Act (pengespilloven) § 36 in conjunction with § 8 and the Gambling Regulation (pengespillforskriften) § 6(1)(c) as the legal basis for an overtredelsesgebyr. As precedent and context, Lotteritilsynet published a vedtak on 2025-08-26 imposing an overtredelsesgebyr of NOK 46,000,000 on Norsk Tipping for longstanding drawing-basis errors in Eurojackpot’s national additional prize (since 2016) and Lotto Supertrekning (since 2015). The amount corresponded to 0.45% of Norsk Tipping’s 2024 turnover (after prizes). The decision document (vedtak) was published on Lotteritilsynet’s website and explains the legal basis and considerations for setting the fee and the right to appeal to Lotterinemnda.

Key definitions and scope:
- Lotteritilsynet: Norway’s Lottery and Foundation Authority (Lotteri- og stiftelsestilsynet).
- Supertrekning: As defined by Norsk Tipping, an extra draw included with Lotto purchases; participation is automatic when buying Lotto and each Lotto line equals one entry in Supertrekning.
- “19 April 2025 Lotto Supertrekning error”: The specific incident described in Lotteritilsynet’s 2025‑09‑29 varsel, in which 16,698 players and 682,900 rows (about 0.2%) were wrongly excluded due to deletion of older andelsbank data, leading to 52 incorrect million-prize winners being drawn.
- Overtredelsesgebyr: An administrative fine that Lotteritilsynet can impose for violations of the Gambling Act; the 2025‑09‑29 varsel and the 2025‑08‑26 vedtak both reference pengespilloven § 36 (in conjunction with § 8 and pengespillforskriften § 6(1)(c)) as the legal basis.
- Vedtak: A formal administrative decision by Lotteritilsynet imposing an overtredelsesgebyr, published as a signed decision document (e.g., titled “Vedtak om ilegging av overtredelsesgebyr – Norsk Tipping AS”) on lottstift.no; such vedtak may be appealable to Lotterinemnda, but the appeal does not negate that a vedtak has been published.

Why this is forecastable now: A varsel specific to the 19 April 2025 Supertrekning error was published on 2025‑09‑29 with a three‑week response window, implying a potential vedtak could follow in October–November 2025. The regulator explicitly signaled an amount up to NOK 25 million, creating uncertainty around whether the eventual amount will be at least NOK 20 million. The regulator has recently set large overtredelsesgebyr in similar contexts (e.g., NOK 46 million on 2025‑08‑26).
resolution_criteria:
Question: By 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, will Lotteritilsynet have published a vedtak imposing an overtredelsesgebyr of at least NOK 20,000,000 (twenty million Norwegian kroner) on Norsk Tipping for the “19 April 2025 Lotto Supertrekning error”?

Event window for eligible publications: 2025‑09‑29 00:00:00 UTC through 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC.

Definitions for resolution:
- “Published”: Publicly accessible on Lotteritilsynet’s official website (domain lottstift.no), either as a webpage or PDF decision document. Example format: a PDF decision titled “Vedtak om ilegging av overtredelsesgebyr – Norsk Tipping AS” hosted on lottstift.no.
- “Vedtak”: A formal administrative decision by Lotteritilsynet imposing an overtredelsesgebyr (administrative fine), signed and dated, and stating the amount and legal basis (typically citing pengespilloven § 36 in conjunction with § 8 and pengespillforskriften § 6(1)(c)).
- “Overtredelsesgebyr of at least NOK 20,000,000”: The amount stated in the vedtak is greater than or equal to NOK 20,000,000. If the amount is stated in NOK with thousands separators (e.g., 20 000 000), normal numeric interpretation applies.
- “For the 19 April 2025 Lotto Supertrekning error”: The vedtak must clearly identify that it pertains to the error in the Lotto Supertrekning held on 2025‑04‑19, as described in Lotteritilsynet’s varsel of 2025‑09‑29 (e.g., referencing 52 incorrect million‑prize winners and the exclusion of andelsbank entries).

Resolution rules:
- Resolve YES if, within the event window, Lotteritilsynet publishes on lottstift.no a vedtak that (a) clearly pertains to the 19 April 2025 Lotto Supertrekning error and (b) imposes an overtredelsesgebyr on Norsk Tipping of at least NOK 20,000,000.
- Resolve NO if by 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC no such vedtak has been published on lottstift.no, or if a vedtak is published pertaining to this incident but the imposed overtredelsesgebyr is less than NOK 20,000,000.
- Combined decisions: If Lotteritilsynet issues a combined vedtak covering multiple incidents and states a single aggregate amount without an explicit, unambiguous amount attributed to the 19 April 2025 Supertrekning error, resolve NO. Only count a combined vedtak if it explicitly and unambiguously states an amount of at least NOK 20,000,000 attributable to the 19 April 2025 Supertrekning error (e.g., via a separate section or clearly apportioned amounts).
- Appeals or later modifications: Any appeal or subsequent modification does not affect resolution, provided that the qualifying vedtak was published within the event window.

Primary resolution sources:
- Lotteritilsynet’s official website (lottstift.no), where the varsel for this specific incident was published on 2025‑09‑29 and where vedtak are published (see example prior vedtak).

Notes and references for forecasters:
- Details about the incident (52 incorrect winners; 16,698 players and 682,900 rows excluded; ~0.2% of rows; deletion rule for andelsbank entries; three‑week response window; maximum signaled fee up to NOK 25m) are drawn from Lotteritilsynet’s varsel and accompanying notice.
- Context about how Lotteritilsynet has recently sized overtredelsesgebyr (e.g., NOK 46m, 0.45% of turnover; legal basis cited) is from the 2025‑08‑26 vedtak published on lottstift.no.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC), will the EU and Thailand officially announce the conclusion of negotiations (including “substantive conclusion” or initialling) on their bilateral free trade agreement?
background: Status quo as of Oct 1, 2025: The EU and Thailand relaunched FTA negotiations in March 2023, aiming for an ambitious, modern, and balanced agreement with strong Trade and Sustainable Development provisions. The 6th round of negotiations took place June 23–27, 2025 in Bangkok, with several items closed in principle: Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT), Trade and Sustainable Development (TSD), Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs), and a section on Telecommunication Services within the Trade and Investment chapter. A 7th round was planned for the week of September 29, 2025 in Brussels. On June 5, 2025, Thailand’s Minister of Commerce and the European Commissioner reaffirmed a shared goal of concluding the agreement by the end of 2025. On September 25, 2025, Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the EU had advanced well in FTA talks with Thailand and expected finalisation and signing by next year (2026). Official documents and round reports for the EU–Thailand FTA are published on the European Commission’s Directorate‑General for Trade website, including the EU–Thailand documents page  and the agreement overview page. Definitions: • Free trade agreement (FTA): an agreement under international law forming a free‑trade area between cooperating states, aiming to reduce or eliminate tariffs and other trade barriers; modern FTAs often include services and investment. • European Commission: the EU’s primary executive branch, which represents the EU in trade negotiations and publishes official information and press releases. • European External Action Service (EEAS): the EU’s diplomatic service, supporting the High Representative and publishing official statements on external relations. • Royal Thai Government: the central executive authority of the Kingdom of Thailand, including ministries relevant to trade such as the Ministry of Commerce. • Initialling (of a treaty text): confirms both parties agree on the wording of the initialled document; initialling does not imply consent to signature or ratification. Notes for forecasters: • Announcements of “substantive conclusion” have been used by governments to signal the end of negotiations ahead of legal scrubbing and signature in comparable trade contexts. For this question, such phrasing by the EU or Thailand will count if issued via official channels defined below. • Partial or chapter‑level closures do not count; the announcement must pertain to the overall FTA negotiations. Key sources to monitor: • EU: DG Trade’s EU–Thailand pages ; the European Commission’s official press and news channels. • Thailand: Public Relations Department (PRD) English news ; official statements from the Ministry of Commerce or Department of Trade Negotiations.
resolution_criteria: Time window and scope: • Eligible announcements must be published between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. • The announcement must pertain to the bilateral EU–Thailand Free Trade Agreement negotiations. What resolves “Yes”: • A Yes outcome occurs if, within the time window, an official statement is published on an official EU or Thai government channel that explicitly announces the conclusion of negotiations on the EU–Thailand FTA. Acceptable formulations include: “negotiations have concluded,” “substantive conclusion of negotiations,” “finalisation of negotiations,” or confirmation that the full agreement text has been “initialled” by authorised negotiators. • Accepted official channels: – EU: European Commission websites under the policy.trade.ec.europa.eu domain (e.g., DG Trade’s EU–Thailand agreement pages) , the European Commission’s official press/news portals, or the EEAS official website. – Thailand: Royal Thai Government websites, such as the PRD English site , the Ministry of Commerce, or the Department of Trade Negotiations. • Accepted formats: press releases, official news items, or joint statements published on these official websites. What resolves “No”: • If no such official announcement is published on the specified official channels within the time window, resolve No. Exclusions and clarifications: • Third‑party media reporting alone does not count unless it directly hosts or reproduces an official joint statement issued by the EU or Thailand; the source must be traceable to an official government publication. • Announcements limited to closing individual chapters, launching additional rounds, or expressing intentions/goals (e.g., targeting conclusion by a certain date) do not count. • Statements forecasting signature in 2026 without announcing conclusion of negotiations do not count. Verification: • At resolution, provide the direct URL to the official EU or Thai government webpage hosting the announcement, and verify date/time (UTC) of publication or the timestamp on the page. • Primary reference locations include: – EU DG Trade EU–Thailand documents page  and agreement overview. – EEAS official news site. – Thailand PRD English news portal  and relevant Ministry of Commerce/Department of Trade Negotiations pages. Edge cases: • If an official government joint statement announcing substantive conclusion is posted on only one party’s official site, this still counts as Yes, provided it clearly states the conclusion of negotiations for the EU–Thailand FTA. • If initialling is announced without the phrase “conclusion,” resolve Yes, as initialling of the full agreement text indicates the negotiated text has been agreed by the parties.

question: Will any candidate be elected on the first count in Ireland’s 2025 presidential election?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- Polling day and times: The 2025 Irish presidential election will be held on Friday, 24 October 2025, with polling from 7:00 to 22:00 local time, as set by the Presidential Election Order made by the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage on 3 September 2025. RTÉ likewise notes polling on Friday 24 October, with counting beginning at 09:00 the following day (Saturday, 25 October).
- Official results publication: The Presidential Returning Officer’s official site states that results will be available on Saturday, 25 October 2025 at https://www.presidentialelection.ie/election-results/index.html. That results section includes fields for the national “Quota,” “Valid Poll,” first count “1st preference votes,” and first count status, indicating it will publish the first-count totals and the quota used to determine a first-count election.
- Voting system and what the first count means: The election uses preferential voting (PR–STV) for a single office; voters rank candidates 1, 2, 3…. After polling, ballot papers are sorted by first preferences and the number of first-preference votes for each candidate is reported to the Presidential Returning Officer; this is the “first count”. The Presidential Returning Officer calculates the “quota,” and in a single-seat presidential contest a candidate who receives a number of votes equal to or greater than fifty percent of valid votes plus one is declared elected; if no one reaches the quota on the first count, the lowest candidate is excluded and votes are transferred until a candidate reaches the quota.
- Field of candidates (as of close of nominations): The official Notice of Poll lists three candidates on the ballot: CATHERINE MARTINA ANN CONNOLLY (Independent TD), JIM GAVIN, and HEATHER HUMPHREYS. With three candidates, a first-count win is plausible but not assured.
Key definitions and where to find them on official sources:
- Presidential Returning Officer (PRO): The official who ascertains and declares the result based on reports from local returning officers and publishes results on the official site.
- First count: The initial national aggregation of first-preference votes (the ‘1’ rankings) reported to the PRO after ballots are sorted by first preferences.
- Valid votes / Valid Poll: Ballots deemed valid under Irish electoral rules and counted toward the result; the official results page displays “Valid Poll” and “Invalid Ballot Papers,” which the PRO uses to compute the quota.
