- Consolidation: If the Court consolidates No. 25-364 with another case and issues a certiorari grant under a different lead docket number, this resolves to Yes only if the No. 25-364 docket or the orders list explicitly reflects that certiorari has been GRANTED as to No. 25-364 (e.g., “certiorari granted; case consolidated with No. 25-XXX”).
- Certiorari before judgment: Although the Washington petition seeks standard certiorari (28 U.S.C. § 1254(1)), a grant of certiorari before judgment recorded for No. 25-364 would also count as Yes.

Verification steps for resolvers:
- First, check the Supreme Court docket for No. 25-364 for any entry indicating certiorari GRANTED; note the date and the exact phrasing.
- Second, check the Supreme Court orders list published on or before December 31, 2025 for an entry explicitly granting certiorari in No. 25-364.
- If needed, corroborate via SCOTUSblog’s case page or reporting that cites the grant order.

question: England Q3 2025 new‑build completions: higher than Q3 2024?
background:
What is being forecast: Whether the total number of new‑build dwelling completions in England in July–September 2025 (Q3 2025) will be strictly higher than in July–September 2024 (Q3 2024), using the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities (DLUHC) quarterly “Housing supply: indicators of new supply, England” statistical release as the source.

Context/status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- The Indicators of New Supply series is a recurring quarterly publication on GOV.UK; DLUHC states these national statistics are released every three months and the collection lists each quarter’s England release.
- The April–June 2025 (Q2 2025) release reports that seasonally adjusted new‑build dwelling completions were 34,990, a 2% decrease vs the prior quarter and a 19% decrease vs the same quarter a year earlier. The document also pre‑announces that the July–September 2025 (Q3 2025) statistics are expected to be published in December 2025 (provisional). It further notes that quarterly comparisons should use seasonally adjusted figures.
- Definitions and data sources: In this series, a new‑build dwelling completion is regarded as occurring when a dwelling becomes ready for occupation or when a completion certificate is issued, whether or not it is occupied. These figures are compiled from building control inspection data submitted by local authorities, the National House‑Building Council (NHBC), other approved inspectors, and the Building Safety Regulator (BSR), with coverage applying to England only. Technical notes caution that, for the July–September 2024 period, BSR data had not yet been incorporated, so figures may undercount some higher‑risk buildings; DLUHC also explains that reporting can be revised in subsequent releases to incorporate late returns.

How quarters are defined and what will be compared:
- Calendar quarter mapping used by DLUHC in this series: Q1 = January–March, Q2 = April–June, Q3 = July–September, Q4 = October–December. The April–June 2025 release explicitly maps these months and is the basis for interpreting Q3 as July–September.

Why this should be reasonably uncertain: Completions lag starts and are sensitive to financing conditions, costs, and pipeline dynamics. With Q1 and Q2 2025 showing weakness relative to 2024 on a YoY basis, but with potential stabilization and project pipelines feeding through, both an increase or decrease in Q3 2025 relative to Q3 2024 appear plausible.

Key definitions for clarity:
- England: As used by DLUHC, coverage applies to England only in these statistics.
- New‑build dwelling: A self‑contained residential unit meeting DLUHC’s dwelling definition (self‑containment behind a single door), counted when complete as described above. Communal establishments are excluded unless providing self‑contained units; see the series’ technical notes for details.
- Completion (for this series): The dwelling is ready for occupation or has a completion certificate issued, regardless of actual occupation.
- Quarterly figures to use: For quarterly comparisons, DLUHC indicates the seasonally adjusted series should be used; therefore, this question will resolve using seasonally adjusted totals for completions across all tenures at the England level as presented in the Q3 2025 England release.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: YES if the seasonally adjusted total number of new‑build dwelling completions in England for July–September 2025 (Q3 2025) is strictly greater than the seasonally adjusted total for July–September 2024 (Q3 2024); NO otherwise (including if equal).

Primary resolution source:
- DLUHC’s “Housing supply: indicators of new supply, England: July to September 2025” release page, expected December 2025 (provisional). question: Will Cyprus be designated to the U.S. Visa Waiver Program (VWP) by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Overview and definitions:
- Visa Waiver Program (VWP): A U.S. government program administered by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in consultation with the Department of State that permits nationals of designated countries to travel to the United States for business or tourism for up to 90 days without a visa; travelers must obtain Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) approval and meet all other requirements. Official DHS page: https://www.dhs.gov/visa-waiver-program. Official State Department page: https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/us-visas/tourism-visit/visa-waiver-program.html.
- Designated country: DHS updated its procedures in December 2024 to stop listing VWP countries in the Code of Federal Regulations and instead maintain a public, authoritative list on the DHS VWP webpage. Under this rule, a “designated country” is any country the Secretary of Homeland Security (in consultation with the Secretary of State) has designated for participation, and DHS maintains the current list at https://www.dhs.gov/visa-waiver-program.
- Cyprus: This question refers to the sovereign state commonly called the Republic of Cyprus. For clarity on the entity, see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus.

Status quo as of October 1, 2025:
- The DHS VWP page lists 41 “Current Program Countries” and does not list “Cyprus” anywhere on the page. The State Department’s VWP page likewise lists participating countries and does not include Cyprus.

Recent context relevant to forecasting:
- DHS designated Israel to the VWP in 2023 (effective implementation for travel began on November 30, 2023).
- Policy background and eligibility criteria: Under INA §217, countries must meet conditions including a nonimmigrant visitor (B) visa refusal rate under 3% (or averaged across two fiscal years), robust security information-sharing, e-passport issuance, and other border and document security requirements. As of late 2024, Cyprus, Bulgaria, and Romania were noted as EU members aspiring to join the VWP.
- In 2025, DHS announced Romania’s designation on January 10, 2025, with ESTA updates anticipated on or around March 31, 2025.

Why this is a balanced forecasting question:
- Designations are discretionary and depend on meeting statutory security and travel criteria and interagency judgments. The program has seen recent changes (Israel 2023; Qatar referenced in 2024; Romania announcement in 2025), but Cyprus is not yet on the list, and media and policy signals about timing have been mixed. Forecasters can weigh technical readiness (e.g., refusal rates and information-sharing agreements), U.S.–Cyprus bilateral developments, and political timing.

Notes on sources and resolution:
- The DHS VWP page is the authoritative list for designated countries following the December 27, 2024 rule update. The State Department VWP page is a corroborating source and provides traveler-facing details.
resolution_criteria:
- Question: Will “Cyprus” be listed as a current program country on DHS’s Visa Waiver Program webpage by the resolution time?
- Resolution time: 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
- Primary source of truth: The DHS Visa Waiver Program page at https://www.dhs.gov/visa-waiver-program. Resolve Yes if that page lists “Cyprus” under “Current Program Countries” at the resolution time; otherwise resolve No.
- Start date and window for eligible changes: This market’s observation window begins at 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and runs through 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. However, resolution is determined solely by whether Cyprus appears on the DHS VWP list at the resolution time, regardless of the exact date of designation, consistent with DHS’s practice of maintaining the authoritative list on its website.
- Tie-breakers/backup sources: If the DHS VWP page is inaccessible or clearly inconsistent across versions at the resolution time, use credible, contemporaneous DHS publications (e.g., DHS press releases) and the State Department’s VWP page for corroboration. Examples: DHS news releases announcing designations (e.g., Israel 2023 and Romania 2025 announcements) and State’s VWP country list. In cases of conflict, the DHS VWP page governs per the December 2024 rule update.
- Term definitions and scope clarifications:
  - “Cyprus” refers to the Republic of Cyprus (the internationally recognized sovereign state). Any listing of “Cyprus” on the DHS VWP page counts as inclusion; partial or regional programs (e.g., the Guam-CNMI Visa Waiver Program) do not count toward this question unless Cyprus appears on the main DHS VWP list for INA §217.
  - “Visa Waiver Program” refers to the INA §217 program administered by DHS in consultation with State, as described on DHS and State websites.

question: Will Bangladesh’s “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” be ≥ $32.0 billion as of end‑November 2025?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025‑09‑30:
- Bangladesh Bank (BB) publishes a monthly “Foreign Exchange Reserve (Monthly)” table that lists two series, “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” and “Foreign Exchange Reserves (as per BPM6),” with values shown in million US dollars. As of the latest months available on that page, the “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” series shows: June 2025 = 31,772.0; July 2025 = 29,799.8; August 2025 = 31,166.2 (all in million US$). These imply that the gross measure has fluctuated around the low‑to‑mid $30 billions during mid‑2025.
- BB’s monthly “Exchange Rate & Foreign Exchange Market Dynamics” PDF reports end‑of‑month “Gross international reserve (BPM6)” levels (a narrower, internationally standardized concept). It noted USD 26.74 billion at 30 June 2025 and USD 24.78 billion at end‑July 2025, attributing the July dip partly to Asian Clearing Union settlements.
- BB’s “Balance of payments [Monthly Data]” page also reports “Gross official reserves” and “Gross official reserves (as per BPM6)” in million US dollars; for July, it shows 29,800 and 24,779, respectively, consistent with the other BB sources at similar dates.

Key definitions/clarifications for forecasters:
- Target series: “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” exactly as labeled on Bangladesh Bank’s Foreign Exchange Reserve (Monthly) page; units are million US dollars (“In million US $”). This question does not use the BPM6 series for resolution, but it is noted for context; BPM6 refers to the IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, Sixth Edition, which defines official reserve assets (components include monetary gold, SDRs, reserve position in the IMF, and other reserve assets).
- Threshold interpretation: “$32.0 billion” means 32,000.0 million US$. The comparison is made against the November 2025 value as displayed in the “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” column on the BB page.

Why this is forecastable with uncertainty:
- The gross reserves series has been near but below $32 billion in recent months (31,166.2 million in August; 31,772.0 million in June), making a November reading ≥ 32,000.0 million plausible but not assured. Month‑to‑month swings reflect flows (e.g., remittances, exports/imports), external financing, and outflows such as ACU settlements—drivers that can move the series several hundred million dollars within a few weeks.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if Bangladesh Bank’s “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” for November 2025 is greater than or equal to 32,000.0 million US dollars; otherwise resolve “No”.

Primary source and exact check:
- Use the Bangladesh Bank “Foreign Exchange Reserve (Monthly)” page. Read the value in the “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” column for the row corresponding to November 2025 (which, per BB’s presentation, will appear within the fiscal year 2025–2026 section). Units are million US dollars; compare the displayed figure directly to 32,000.0 million (i.e., ≥ 32.0 billion).

Timing and snapshot:
- Determine the outcome based on the value displayed on the BB page as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. If BB later revises figures after that cutoff, revisions are ignored for this question’s resolution.

Fallbacks if the primary page is unavailable or missing November 2025 by the cutoff:
1) Use BB’s “Balance of payments [Monthly Data]” page and take the November 2025 value listed under “Gross official reserves” (in million US$). Treat that figure as equivalent to the “Foreign Exchange Reserves (Gross)” concept for the purpose of this resolution, and compare it to 32,000.0 million. If both sources are available but disagree, prefer the dedicated “Foreign Exchange Reserve (Monthly)” page.
2) If neither page is accessible at the cutoff due to temporary technical issues, use a publicly accessible archived snapshot (e.g., from the Internet Archive) of either page captured on or before 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, applying the same preference order.

Notes:
- This question is binary (Yes/No). It concerns the November 2025 monthly figure as reported by Bangladesh Bank. It does not use the BPM6 series for resolution, though BPM6 context is provided for background and definitional clarity.

question: Will New York City’s Central Business District Tolling Program (congestion pricing) be active and collecting tolls at 11:59 pm ET on December 31, 2025?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Definition and geography. The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP) charges a toll for vehicles entering Manhattan’s Congestion Relief Zone (CRZ). The CRZ is defined by the MTA as the area of Manhattan south of and including 60th Street, excluding the FDR Drive, West Side Highway/Route 9A, and the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel connections to West Street. Entering the CRZ means moving from outside the CRZ onto local streets and avenues within the CRZ. Travel exclusively along excluded roadways (e.g., FDR Drive or West Street/West Side Highway) without exiting to local streets does not incur a toll; the MTA provides concrete examples of tolled and untolled movements, including specific connections among FDR Drive, the Brooklyn and Manhattan bridges, the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel, Queens Midtown Tunnel, Queensboro Bridge, Lincoln Tunnel, and Holland Tunnel.
- Launch and ongoing operation. The MTA’s press release states the program launched on Sunday, January 5, 2025 at 12:00:01 a.m. ET, charging a toll for motorists to enter Manhattan below 60th Street (the CBD/CRZ). The MTA’s CBDTP project page describes the program as active, stating: “Since January 5, 2025, vehicles entering the Congestion Relief Zone in Manhattan … are being charged a toll”.
- Hours/rates context (for what “collecting tolls” entails). The official toll schedule shows tolling is continuous, with differentiated rates by time: peak periods are 5 a.m.–9 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m.–9 p.m. on weekends; overnight rates (off-peak) are 75% lower, confirming toll collection continues overnight at reduced rates.
- Recent developments and risk context. On February 19, 2025, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Federal Highway Administration announced termination of federal approval for New York City’s cordon pricing plan under the Value Pricing Pilot Program, citing program scope and revenue-setting concerns. Despite this, MTA communications indicated ongoing operation later in 2025; a September 2025 MTA press release stated, “Congestion pricing is working, it is legal, and the cameras are staying on,” and presented 2025 operational metrics (e.g., reductions in zone entries and travel time improvements). These dynamics create policy/legal risk relevant to the forecast while establishing that, as of early fall 2025, tolling remained in effect.

Key references for forecasters:
- MTA CBDTP project page: https://www.mta.info/project/CBDTP 
- MTA CRZ FAQs and tolling information (definitions, examples): https://congestionreliefzone.mta.info/faqs; https://congestionreliefzone.mta.info/tolling 
- MTA press releases: Launch (Jan 5, 2025) and subsequent updates: https://www.mta.info/press-release/new-york-joins-world-cities-launch-of-first-nation-program-deliver-cleaner-air-less; September 2025 status update: https://www.mta.info/press-release/icymi-less-traffic-safer-streets-summer-comes-end-governor-hochul-highlights 
- USDOT/FHWA announcement (Feb 19, 2025) terminating federal approval: https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/us-department-transportation-terminates-tolling-approval-new-york-citys-cordon
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the program’s status at precisely 2025-12-31 11:59:59 pm Eastern Time (ET).

Definitions (for this market):
- Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP): The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) program that charges tolls to vehicles entering the CRZ in Manhattan.
- Congestion Relief Zone (CRZ): The area of Manhattan south of and including 60th Street, excluding the FDR Drive, West Side Highway/Route 9A, and the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel connections to West Street. Travel solely on excluded roadways without exiting to local streets does not incur a toll; the MTA’s FAQs provide concrete examples of tolled/untolled routes and how detection points determine whether a vehicle remained on excluded roadways.
- Active and collecting tolls: For this resolution, “active” means that the MTA is charging tolls for vehicles entering the CRZ at the time of resolution (i.e., toll collection is in effect, whether at peak or overnight rates). The CBDTP toll schedule indicates tolling is continuous with peak and overnight time windows; thus, tolling is considered “active” so long as entries to the CRZ are tolled according to the schedule in effect.
- Suspension/termination: “Suspended” means the MTA has officially announced a halt to toll collection for entries into the CRZ. “Terminated” means the MTA (or its TBTA subsidiary) has officially ended the program.

Resolution sources and hierarchy:
- Resolve YES if, as of the resolution timestamp, the MTA indicates that the CBDTP is in effect—i.e., that vehicles entering the CRZ are being charged a toll—on any of the following official sources: the CBDTP project page, the MTA’s Congestion Relief Zone/tolling site, an MTA press release, or an MTA service/customer notice.
- Resolve NO if the MTA has officially suspended or terminated toll collection for CRZ entries on or before the resolution timestamp (evidenced by an MTA press release, service/customer notice, or an explicit announcement on the CBDTP project page or CRZ site).
- In the event of conflicting information across MTA sources, prioritize a dated MTA press release or service/customer notice over undated website copy. If official MTA web properties are unavailable at resolution, use credible media reports (e.g., AP, Reuters, NYT) that directly cite an official MTA announcement.

Date range and timezone:
- This question concerns the program’s status at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 ET. All times are Eastern Time. Historical information prior to that timestamp is provided only for context and does not by itself determine resolution.

question: By 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, will the Government of the Russian Federation or Rosatom publicly announce a formal financial commitment (loan, line of credit, or direct funding) specifically for constructing a second nuclear power plant in Belarus at a site distinct from Astravets (Ostrovets)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Belarus currently operates the Astravets (also called Ostrovets) Nuclear Power Plant in the Astravyets District, Grodno Region, consisting of two VVER-1200 units supplied by Atomstroyexport (Rosatom). It is Belarus’s only nuclear power station and is located roughly 40 km east of Vilnius. The first plant was predominantly financed by Russia: in November 2011 Russia agreed to lend up to $10 billion over 25 years to finance 90% of the construction contract for the two-unit Astravets plant.
- On 2025-09-26, President Alexander Lukashenko proposed either expanding Belarus’s nuclear capacity with a new plant in eastern Belarus or adding capacity, with the aim of supplying electricity to Russian-controlled areas in Ukraine. Reporting noted that President Vladimir Putin appeared supportive, but did not specify whether Russia would provide financial backing at that meeting. The official Kremlin readout the same day shows Putin expressing support and saying “Financing should not be an issue. If you have a consumer ready to buy the electricity at your price, it should not be a problem at all,” but this did not constitute a formal financing commitment.
- On 2025-09-29, Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev described the prospective Belarus project as a “unique” nuclear power plant in terms of quality, economic parameters, cooperation, and localization, but no specific financing commitments were announced in that context.
- Lukashenko has also stated that savings from the first plant’s loan are sufficient to build another unit, and that Belarus is considering either a third unit at the existing site or a new plant in the east; however, this statement did not specify any new Russian financing for the proposed second plant.
- A feasibility study for new nuclear capacity (either a new unit at Astravets or a new station) was planned in 2025, with no financing details specified in that reporting.

Key definitions and entities:
- Second nuclear power plant (in this question) refers to a new nuclear power station at a site other than the existing Astravets/Ostrovets NPP (i.e., a distinct greenfield nuclear power plant separate from the Astravets site).
- Rosatom is the Russian State Atomic Energy Corporation, a state-owned entity that oversees nuclear energy activities and international NPP exports (see Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosatom).
- Government of the Russian Federation denotes Russia’s highest federal executive body (see Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Russia).
- Loan: an agreement where a lender provides money to a borrower with the obligation to repay, typically with interest (see Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loan).
- Line of credit: a flexible credit facility up to a specified limit, where interest is generally paid only on drawn amounts (see Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_credit).

Why this is uncertain but plausible: Belarus has precedent for Russian-backed financing of nuclear construction (the $10bn, 25-year loan for Astravets) , Russian political leadership has voiced openness in principle to further nuclear cooperation (though without committing funds) , and Rosatom has publicly signaled interest in the prospective project , but as of 2025-09-30 no formal financing has been announced.
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Announcements must be made between 00:00:00 UTC on 2024-10-01 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31. The question resolves as soon as qualifying evidence is available.

Resolution: Resolve “Yes” if, within the time window, there is a public announcement by either (a) the Government of the Russian Federation or (b) Rosatom, that constitutes a formal financial commitment specifically for the construction of a second nuclear power plant in Belarus at a site distinct from Astravets (Ostrovets). Otherwise resolve “No.”

What counts as a qualifying announcement:
1) Issuer and channels (primary sources):
   - Government of Russia: official publications or statements on en.kremlin.ru (including official readouts), government.ru, or publication of a decree/resolution on publication.pravo.gov.ru (or Rossiyskaya Gazeta’s official publication of such acts). Government of Russia is as defined in Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Russia).
   - Rosatom: official press releases or statements on Rosatom’s official sites (e.g., rosatom.ru press center or atommedia/AtomMedia official press pages). Rosatom is as defined in Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosatom).

2) Content requirements: The announcement must:
   - Specify the financial instrument as one of the following: a state loan, an intergovernmental line of credit, or direct funding/budgetary allocation/committed equity from the Russian federal budget or Rosatom. Loan and line of credit are used in their standard meanings (see Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_credit).
   - Include a specific nominal amount or maximum cap (in any currency, e.g., RUB, USD, EUR).
   - Explicitly earmark the funding for the construction of a new nuclear power plant in Belarus at a site other than Astravets (Ostrovets). For the avoidance of doubt, this MUST be a new station (a greenfield NPP) and NOT an additional generating unit at the existing Astravets site.

3) What does NOT count:
   - Memoranda of understanding, framework agreements, or statements of intent without a specific funding amount.
   - Feasibility studies, site evaluations, or pre-FID work without a formal financing facility amount.
   - Financing for grid infrastructure, substations, or non-NPP facilities in Belarus.
   - Financing for additional units at the existing Astravets/Ostrovets NPP (e.g., a third unit at the same site).
   - Media reports citing anonymous sources if no on-the-record official statement with the required details is available.

4) Secondary-source fallback (if primary sources are unavailable or inaccessible):
   - Accept secondary reporting ONLY if it provides an on-the-record quote or clearly attributes the announcement to a named Russian government official or Rosatom official and includes the financial instrument and amount; and at least two independent reputable outlets report the same announcement (e.g., TASS, AP, Reuters, BelTA). Note: as of 2025-09-30, reporting indicated Putin’s support in principle without specifying financing, and Rosatom’s CEO lauded the project’s uniqueness—neither of which constitute formal commitments.

Disambiguations and definitions for this market:
- “Second nuclear power plant in Belarus” means a new nuclear power station at a different site than the existing Astravets/Ostrovets NPP (Belarus currently has only that one station).
- “Publicly announce” means publication on an official channel listed above, or an on-the-record statement by a named official recorded on those channels; or, per the secondary fallback, two independent reputable outlets attributing the announcement to a named official with the required specifics.

Verification and ease of resolution:
- A resolver will check the official sites listed above for any press releases, decrees, or announcements meeting the criteria. If none are found, they will check reputable wires (e.g., TASS, AP, Reuters) for qualifying secondary reporting.

Status quo reference points (for forecasters):
- Existing plant and site: Astravets/Ostrovets in Grodno Region; two VVER-1200 units.
- Prior financing precedent: Russia agreed to a $10bn, 25-year loan financing 90% of the Astravets project.
- Recent signals: Belarus proposed a new plant to supply Russian-held areas in Ukraine; Putin expressed support but did not specify financing; Rosatom’s CEO called the prospective project “unique”; no formal financing has been announced as of 2025-09-30.

Timezone: All times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

question: Will the EU adopt a “19th package of sanctions against Russia” between 00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59 UTC on 31 December 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30: In 2025, the European Union (EU) has already adopted three Russia sanctions packages: the 16th package on 24 February 2025 (Council press release) , the 17th package on 20 May 2025 (European Commission news item) , and the 18th package on 18 July 2025 (Council press release). The Council of the EU maintains an official timeline page listing these packages and their dates, demonstrating that the packages are sequentially numbered (“16th,” “17th,” “18th”). EU sanctions against Russia are implemented via legal acts, notably amendments to Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 and related CFSP decisions, prepared after political agreement and adopted by the Council; the Council/Commission then announce adoption via official press releases, and the legal acts are published in the Official Journal (OJ) L series.

Key definitions and references a forecaster may need:
- European Union (EU): Supranational political and economic union of European states. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union
- Council of the European Union (the Council): The institution where government ministers from EU countries adopt laws and coordinate policies. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union
- Restrictive measures (sanctions): In EU usage, legally binding measures such as asset freezes, travel bans, and sectoral economic restrictions, often adopted under Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 for Russia. See the Council’s overview of EU sanctions against Russia.
- Official Journal of the European Union (OJ): The EU’s official gazette where adopted legal acts are published. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Journal_of_the_European_Union
- “Sanctions package against Russia”: A set of EU restrictive measures that the EU’s official communications explicitly label as the Nth package of sanctions against Russia (e.g., “16th package,” “17th package,” “18th package”). For example, the Council press release on 18 July 2025 states “EU adopts 18th package of economic and individual measures” and links to the corresponding legal acts in the OJ.

Status quo sources (examples):
- 16th package adoption (24 Feb 2025): Council press release 
- 17th package adoption (20 May 2025): European Commission press release 
- 18th package adoption (18 July 2025): Council press release 
- Council timeline enumerating packages and dates: Consilium timeline page 
- General explanation of EU sanctions process and legal basis: Council overview 

Why this question has balanced uncertainty: In 2025 the EU has adopted three packages (Feb, May, July), indicating active and ongoing sanctions policy, but further packages often depend on political consensus among Member States and negotiation over scope and measures. While another package in Q4 2025 is plausible, it is not guaranteed. The clear labeling convention and official publication practice enable unambiguous resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and time zone:
- Eligible events must occur between 00:00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025.

Operational definitions:
- “Sanctions package against Russia”: A package is counted only if an official EU source explicitly labels it as the “19th package of sanctions against Russia” (or equivalent phrasing such as “EU adopts 19th package of economic and individual restrictive measures against Russia”). Acceptable official sources are:
  1) A Council of the EU press release (Consilium website) using “adopts” (or “adopted today”) and “19th package” for Russia ;
  2) The Council’s official timeline page listing “19th package of sanctions against Russia” with a date in the event window ;
  3) A European Commission press release that explicitly states the Council “adopted” the “19th Russia sanctions package” with a date in the event window.

- “Adopted”: For the purpose of this question, adoption is satisfied by official EU communication stating that the Council has adopted the 19th package (per sources above). Publication of the corresponding legal acts in the Official Journal (OJ) is not required for resolution, but if OJ publication is used as corroboration, it must consist of legal acts that amend Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 and/or the related CFSP decision and are clearly described as part of the 19th Russia sanctions package.

Inclusions:
- Packages that the EU officially labels as the “19th package of sanctions against Russia” during the event window, regardless of scope (economic and/or individual measures), count.

Exclusions:
- Measures or packages that are not explicitly labeled as the “19th package of sanctions against Russia” (e.g., Belarus alignment packages, hybrid-threat measures, or other sanctions regimes) do not count.
- Announcements of intent, proposals, negotiations, or “expected” measures without an official statement of adoption do not count.
- Packages labeled for other countries or regimes (Belarus, Iran, etc.) do not count unless the same announcement explicitly identifies them as the EU’s “19th package of sanctions against Russia.”

Resolution:
- Resolve “Yes” if any acceptable official EU source (as defined above) publishes, within the event window, an announcement that the EU has adopted the “19th package of sanctions against Russia.”
- Resolve “No” otherwise.

Primary sources to check on or after 31 December 2025:
- Council/Consilium press releases (e.g., for prior packages: 16th and 18th) 
- Council’s timeline page enumerating sanctions packages and dates 
- European Commission press releases (e.g., for the 17th package) 

Tie-breaking and conflicts:
- If sources appear to conflict, prefer the Council’s Consilium press releases and timeline for final determination.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the Council of the European Union adopt and have published in the Official Journal at least one legal act that amends or implements EU restrictive measures against Iran?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On 2025-09-29, the Council of the European Union reimposed restrictive measures related to Iran, adopting multiple legal acts that amend or implement the EU’s Iran sanctions framework, including Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1975 amending Regulation (EU) No 267/2012, Council Implementing Regulations 2025/1980 and 2025/1982, Council Decisions (CFSP) 2025/1972 and 2025/1978, and a Council Implementing Decision (CFSP) 2025/1971. As an example, Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1975 is recorded as adopted on 2025-09-29 and published in the Official Journal, amending Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 concerning restrictive measures against Iran. 

Definitions and frameworks:
- EU “restrictive measures (sanctions)” are non-punitive measures imposed by the Council against non-EU countries, entities, or individuals, intended to bring about a change in policy or activity inconsistent with international law, human rights, rule of law, or democratic principles.
- The EU currently applies sanctions frameworks “against Iran” spanning: human-rights-related measures (Regulation (EU) No 359/2011; Decision 2011/235/CFSP), nuclear-proliferation-related measures (Regulation (EU) No 267/2012; Decision 2010/413/CFSP), and drones/missiles/military-support-related measures (Regulation (EU) 2023/1529; Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532). These regimes include travel bans, asset freezes, prohibitions on making funds available, and sectoral trade/transport/financial restrictions.
- The Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU) is the EU’s official gazette of record; only legal acts published in the OJEU are binding, and since 2013, its electronic form via EUR-Lex has legal value. 

Why this question is non-trivial: The Council’s comprehensive package on 2025-09-29 demonstrates active policy movement, and subsequent listings or technical implementing acts are plausible but not ensured. Forecasters must weigh geopolitical developments, EU decision-making cadence, and publication timing in the OJEU.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: 
- Yes if at least one eligible Council act both (a) is adopted between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, and (b) is published in the Official Journal by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. 
- No otherwise. 

Eligible acts (only Council acts): Any of the following where the subject matter explicitly concerns EU restrictive measures (sanctions) against Iran:
- A Council Regulation amending Regulation (EU) No 267/2012; Regulation (EU) No 359/2011; Regulation (EU) 2023/1529; or their successor/consolidated texts within the Iran sanctions regimes.
- A Council Implementing Regulation implementing any of the above Regulations (e.g., listings of persons/entities, technical adjustments).
- A Council Decision (CFSP) amending Decision 2010/413/CFSP; Decision 2011/235/CFSP; or Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532.
- A Council Implementing Decision (CFSP) implementing any of the above Decisions.

Definitions and scope:
- “Restrictive measures (sanctions)” are as defined in the EUR-Lex glossary: non-punitive measures intended to induce a change in policy or activity by targeted parties. 
- “Against Iran” means the act’s subject concerns the Islamic Republic of Iran under the EU’s Iran-specific sanctions frameworks described on the Council’s Iran sanctions policy page, including human rights, nuclear proliferation activities, and drones/missiles/military support frameworks. Acts whose principal subject is another jurisdiction or theme (e.g., Russia-only sanctions where Iran is mentioned tangentially) do not count unless the act explicitly amends or implements an Iran-designated framework. 
- “Adopted” means the date shown in the heading/title block of the act (e.g., “of [date]”), which is the Council’s formal adoption date. 
- “Published” means the act appears in the Official Journal (OJEU); only OJEU-published acts are binding and the electronic OJEU via EUR-Lex is the source of record. 

Exclusions:
- Non-binding Council conclusions, statements, or press releases; Commission delegated or implementing acts; EEAS guidance; national implementing measures; and acts not specifically amending or implementing the Iran sanctions frameworks. 

Verification sources:
- Primary: Official Journal entries via EUR-Lex (electronic OJEU). Eligible acts will have OJEU pages similar in structure to Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1975. 
- Secondary: Council press releases listing adopted acts (e.g., the 2025-09-29 package press release enumerating specific Iran-related Regulations/Decisions). 

Resolution timing:
- The question resolves as soon as an eligible act satisfying both adoption and publication conditions is identified within the time window (Yes). If none is identified by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve No at that time.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the European Commission announce a Digital Markets Act (DMA) fine against any designated gatekeeper?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- What the DMA is and how fines work: The EU’s Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925) empowers the European Commission to fine designated “gatekeepers” for non-compliance. The Commission can impose fines up to 10% of a company’s total worldwide annual turnover, rising to 20% for repeated infringements, and can impose periodic penalty payments up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover.
- First DMA non-compliance fines (April 2025): On 23 April 2025, the European Commission announced non-compliance decisions under the DMA against Apple and Meta, imposing fines of €500 million and €200 million, respectively. These announcements were made via an official press release and the Commission’s Digital Strategy website. An Official Journal summary notes the legal basis for Apple’s fine as Article 30(1) DMA, explicitly referencing articles 29(1)(a), 30(1)(a), and 31(1)(h) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
- Gatekeepers (who can be fined under the DMA): As of the latest official gatekeepers page, the Commission lists Alphabet, Amazon, Apple (including for iPadOS), ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft, and Booking (for Booking.com) as designated gatekeepers.
- Enforcement pipeline (illustrative of ongoing scrutiny): On 25 March 2024, the Commission opened DMA non-compliance investigations into Alphabet, Apple, and Meta, noting that infringements can lead to fines up to 10% of worldwide turnover (20% for repeat cases).

Why this should be uncertain (and interesting): The Commission has demonstrated willingness to fine under the DMA but the timing and targets of any additional fines remain contingent on evolving investigations and compliance measures. The Q4 2025 window follows the first wave of decisions and leaves open the possibility of further enforcement actions, without certainty they will occur precisely in that period.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive), will the European Commission publicly announce that it has imposed a monetary fine under the Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925) on any designated gatekeeper?

Definitions
- Digital Markets Act (DMA): Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 governing “gatekeepers” and their “core platform services,” including enforcement via fines and periodic penalty payments.
- Gatekeeper: An undertaking designated by the European Commission as a gatekeeper under the DMA. For practical purposes, any entity listed on the Commission’s official “DMA Gatekeepers” page at the time of the announcement qualifies (e.g., Alphabet, Amazon, Apple (incl. iPadOS), ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft, Booking).
- DMA fine (what counts): A monetary penalty that the Commission states it has imposed for non-compliance with the DMA (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925). This includes fines adopted pursuant to Article 30 of the DMA; EU documentation for earlier decisions explicitly references Article 30(1) for such fines. Fines under other legal bases (e.g., TFEU Articles 101/102 or the Digital Services Act) do NOT count.
- Periodic penalty payments: Recurring penalties intended to compel compliance; these are distinct from fines and do NOT count toward resolving this question.
- Publicly announce / announcement: Publication by the European Commission of an official press release or news item stating that the Commission “has fined” (or equivalent wording indicating an imposed fine) a gatekeeper for breaching the DMA. Acceptable outlets are: (a) the Commission’s Press Corner (official press releases), or (b) the Commission’s Digital Strategy/DMA news pages. Examples of past acceptable announcement venues include the April 23, 2025 press release and Digital Strategy news page for the Apple and Meta fines. Media reports, leaks, interviews, social media posts, or company statements do not count as announcements for the purposes of this market.

Time window and time zone
- Eligible announcements must be published between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.
- If the Commission source displays only a publication date (no time), the date shown is considered authoritative; if a time is displayed, compare it using UTC.

Inclusions
- Any single qualifying announcement during the window resolves YES, regardless of the fine amount or which gatekeeper is fined.
- Multiple fines announced in the window still resolve the question as a single YES.

Exclusions and edge cases
- Announcements of investigations, statements of objections, commitments, warning letters, or intents to fine do not count.
- Imposition of periodic penalty payments (Article 31) alone does not count.
- Fines not explicitly tied to the DMA (e.g., antitrust or DSA fines) do not count.

Source(s) of truth for resolution
- Primary: European Commission Press Corner press releases and/or Commission Digital Strategy/DMA news pages for the relevant announcement(s).
- Where needed for legal basis confirmation, an Official Journal summary citing Article 30(1) DMA may be used, though the press release/news item within the window is sufficient for timing of the announcement.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the IAEA publicly report Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched up to 60% U-235 at or below 396.8 kg (U mass)?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported that as of 13 June 2025, Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched up to 60% U‑235 totaled 440.9 kg of uranium (U mass) in the form of UF6, an increase of 32.3 kg from the previous report. The same IAEA Director General report (GOV/2025/50, published 3 September 2025) describes major verification challenges since 13 June 2025, including the Agency’s loss of continuity of knowledge regarding inventories of nuclear material, withdrawal of inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran’s subsequent suspension of cooperation, leaving the IAEA unable to conduct in-field verification and unable to quantify changes to the stockpile with prior confidence. Contemporary news coverage also cited the 440.9 kg figure and contextualized it as a slight increase before the mid-June attacks on nuclear facilities, noting the IAEA as source. Definitions and terms: 
- Uranium enrichment: The process of increasing the concentration of uranium‑235 (U‑235) in uranium through isotope separation; enrichment percentage (e.g., 60%) refers to the fraction of U‑235 by mass in the uranium.
- Uranium‑235 (U‑235): A fissile isotope of uranium with natural abundance ~0.72% in unprocessed uranium; enrichment increases its proportion.
- Uranium hexafluoride (UF6): A volatile compound used in gaseous diffusion and gas centrifuge enrichment; IAEA reporting commonly distinguishes “kg of uranium (U mass)” contained in UF6 from total UF6 mass.
- “U mass”: For this question, “U mass” means kilograms of uranium content, not kilograms of UF6. The baseline 440.9 kg is explicitly reported by the IAEA as kg of uranium (in the form of UF6) enriched up to 60% U‑235.
- “Enriched up to 60% U‑235”: For this question, this category follows IAEA usage and refers to uranium material whose U‑235 assay is within the IAEA’s “up to 60%” inventory category, i.e., material at or near 60% U‑235 assay as reported by the IAEA.
Source documents and cadence: The principal source is IAEA Director General reports to the Board of Governors (e.g., GOV/2025/50, derestricted and posted on iaea.org) and any IAEA Director General public statements on iaea.org that include quantitative stockpile figures. The September 3, 2025 GOV/2025/50 report is the latest public, authoritative stockpile figure as of this writing. Reuters and AP articles corroborate the same figure and provide context but are secondary sources.
resolution_criteria:
Baseline and threshold: Baseline is 440.9 kg of uranium (U mass) enriched up to 60% U‑235, as of 13 June 2025, per IAEA GOV/2025/50. The threshold for resolution is 396.8 kg (i.e., a decrease of at least 10% relative to the baseline).
Event window and time zone: Eligible publications are those publicly posted between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC (UTC) on iaea.org.
What counts as “IAEA publicly report”: Any of the following, provided they are publicly accessible on iaea.org:
- A derestricted IAEA Director General report to the Board of Governors that includes a numerical figure for Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched up to 60% U‑235, expressed as kilograms of uranium (U mass), as of a stated date.
- An official IAEA “Statement” or “News Center” item by the Director General that includes a numerical figure for Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched up to 60% U‑235, expressed as kilograms of uranium (U mass), as of a stated date.
Primary metric and units: The primary metric for resolution is the IAEA‑reported kilograms of uranium (U mass) in the “enriched up to 60% U‑235” category. If both U mass and UF6 mass are provided, U mass governs. Figures reported only in UF6 mass will not be converted and will not count toward resolution unless the document itself states the corresponding U mass for the 60% category.
Yes/No rules:
- Resolve Yes if any eligible IAEA public document (as defined above) published within the event window explicitly reports the 60% stockpile at or below 396.8 kg (U mass) as of its stated measurement date.
- Resolve No if, by the end of the event window, no eligible IAEA public document reports a numerical U mass figure at or below 396.8 kg for the 60% category, including the case where no quantitative update is published.
Document precedence and conflicts: If multiple eligible IAEA documents are published within the window, use the most recent publication time (UTC). If figures conflict, the most recently published eligible IAEA document supersedes earlier ones for resolution.
Exclusions: Media reports not posted on iaea.org (e.g., wire services citing confidential reports) do not count as “publicly reported” for resolution, though they informed the background.
Verification steps: A resolver will visit iaea.org’s Document Library and News Center to locate any derestricted Director General reports or statements published in the event window and verify whether a numerical U mass figure for uranium enriched up to 60% U‑235 is at or below 396.8 kg.

question: Will a binding, definitive agreement transferring control of TikTok’s U.S. operations be publicly announced between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of September 30, 2025:
- The Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (Public Law 118-50; often referred to as H.R. 7521) prohibits distribution, maintenance, or updates of certain foreign adversary–controlled apps in the U.S., with relief if a “qualified divestiture” is executed. The Act defines both “foreign adversary controlled application” and “qualified divestiture,” including requirements that U.S. operations no longer be controlled by a foreign adversary and that operational relationships (e.g., algorithm cooperation, data sharing) with formerly affiliated foreign adversary–controlled entities be precluded.
- On September 16, 2025, the White House issued “Further Extending the TikTok Enforcement Delay,” extending the enforcement delay under prior executive actions to December 16, 2025, and instructing the Attorney General to defend exclusive federal authority to enforce the Act.
- On September 25, 2025, the White House published “Saving TikTok While Protecting National Security,” stating the President has determined a proposed TikTok U.S. divestiture plan would constitute a qualified divestiture under the Act and directing the Attorney General not to enforce the Act for 120 days from that date to permit completion of the divestiture.
- DOJ/AG guidance applied the Act’s prohibitions to TikTok as effective January 19, 2025, and described temporary non-enforcement periods to allow assessment and potential resolution strategies.

Why this matters for forecasting: The combination of statutory prohibitions, executive delays, and an identified proposed divestiture framework creates real uncertainty about whether a binding, definitive agreement will be publicly announced before year-end 2025. A definitive agreement is often evidenced by SEC Form 8-K Item 1.01 filings (for public registrants) or formal press releases; Item 1.01 defines “material definitive agreement” as one that provides for obligations material to and enforceable against the registrant (or rights enforceable by the registrant), whether or not subject to conditions.

Key definitions and references forecasters may consult:
- TikTok: A short-form video platform operated by TikTok (ByteDance) offering services globally, including in the U.S. (general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok).
- ByteDance: Parent company of TikTok (general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ByteDance).
- “Material definitive agreement”: As defined by SEC Form 8-K Item 1.01(b), an agreement with obligations or rights that are material and enforceable (commonly used to delineate binding definitive deals and distinguish them from non-binding term sheets, LOIs, or MOUs).
- “Qualified divestiture”: As defined in Section 2(g)(6) of the Act; the President’s determination is through an interagency process and must result in U.S. operations not being controlled by a foreign adversary and preclude operational relationships with such entities.

Status quo suggests multiple pathways to a publicly verifiable announcement before year-end (company press releases, SEC filings, or formal U.S. Government statements). However, completion (closing) is different from announcement/entry into a definitive agreement; this question concerns the latter.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, there is a public announcement evidencing that ByteDance/TikTok and a buyer (or consortium) have entered into a binding, definitive agreement that transfers control of TikTok’s U.S. operations, or an equivalent corporate arrangement that clearly meets the Act’s “qualified divestiture” criteria.

To count, the announcement must meet all of the following:
1) Announcement type: At least one of the following publicly accessible sources must clearly evidence entry into a binding, definitive agreement:
   - An SEC Form 8-K filing by a U.S.-listed party to the agreement disclosing “Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement” under Item 1.01 ;
   - An official press release posted on the corporate website or official newsroom of ByteDance Ltd., TikTok, or a buyer/consortium member party to the agreement;
   - A formal public statement or Presidential action posted on whitehouse.gov or an official U.S. Government website indicating the agreement has been executed and constitutes a qualified divestiture under the Act.

2) Definitive agreement requirement: The agreement must be legally binding and definitive (not a letter of intent, memorandum of understanding, term sheet, or other non-binding framework). For public registrants, the SEC’s Item 1.01 definition of “material definitive agreement” is the standard: an agreement providing obligations material to and enforceable against the registrant or rights enforceable by the registrant. For private companies, the press release or official statement must clearly indicate a signed, binding purchase, merger, asset transfer, joint venture formation, or similar definitive agreement, not a preliminary or non-binding arrangement.

3) Scope: The agreement must explicitly cover TikTok’s U.S. operations such that control of U.S. operations is transferred to an entity not controlled by ByteDance or TikTok, or must be formally recognized by the U.S. Government as a “qualified divestiture” under Section 2(g)(6) of the Act. Evidence that the arrangement satisfies a qualified divestiture (via a formal White House or DOJ/AG statement) is sufficient to meet the scope requirement. Closing of the transaction is not required; entry into the agreement is sufficient.

4) Timing: The public announcement must occur within the inclusive window from 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 to 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Exclusions:
- Non-binding documents (LOIs, MOUs, term sheets) do not count.
- Internal or leaked documents without official public release do not count.
- Agreements signed before October 15, 2025 or announced after December 31, 2025 do not count.

Resolution procedure:
- A human resolver will verify the announcement via the specified sources. If multiple announcements exist, the earliest qualifying public announcement within the window will be used for resolution.
- If no qualifying public announcement is found, resolve No.

Primary authoritative references for verification include: the relevant White House executive actions (Sept 16 extension to Dec 16, 2025; Sept 25 order identifying a proposed qualified divestiture and directing 120 days of non-enforcement) , the Act’s definitions and divestiture criteria , and SEC Form 8-K Item 1.01 for the definition of “material definitive agreement”. DOJ/AG published application of the Act to TikTok provides background on effective dates and non-enforcement periods.

question: Will the December 2025 WASDE project U.S. 2025/26 corn exports at ≥ 3,000 million bushels?
background: Overview and context as of October 1, 2025: The World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) is a monthly USDA report prepared by the World Agricultural Outlook Board (WAOB) that provides forecasts of supply and use for major commodities, including U.S. and global coarse grains such as corn. The USDA has scheduled the December 2025 WASDE for release on December 9, 2025 at 12:00 PM ET. In recent months, USDA’s projection for U.S. 2025/26 corn exports has moved higher: the August 2025 WASDE showed U.S. corn exports at 2,875 million bushels for 2025/26 , and the September 2025 WASDE increased that projection to 2,975 million bushels. In the WASDE, this projection appears in the table titled “U.S. Feed Grain and Corn Supply and Use,” under the “CORN” section, row “Exports,” with units expressed in “Million Bushels”. The WASDE also footnotes the corn marketing year timing: “Marketing year beginning September 1 for corn…” ; ERS documentation likewise defines the corn marketing year as running from September 1 to August 31 (e.g., 1998/99 refers to the period beginning September 1, 1998 and ending August 31, 1999). For unit clarity, a bushel is a U.S. customary unit historically based on dry volume; in U.S. agriculture, the bushel is often standardized as a commodity-specific weight, and for shelled maize (corn) at 15.5% moisture, one bushel is conventionally 56 pounds (25.4 kg). Forecasters should focus on the WASDE table value itself, which is published in million bushels.
resolution_criteria: What will be checked: The question resolves based on the value shown for “Exports” under “CORN” in the “U.S. Feed Grain and Corn Supply and Use” table in the December 2025 WASDE. Specifically, we will read the “Exports” entry for marketing year 2025/26 (“2025/26 Proj.” column) in that table. If the value is ≥ 3,000 million bushels, resolve Yes; otherwise, resolve No. Units and definitions: • “Million bushels” means the numeric value printed in the WASDE table, where 3,000 million bushels equals 3.00 billion bushels. • “Corn marketing year 2025/26” refers to the period September 1, 2025–August 31, 2026, per USDA/ERS marketing year definition and the WASDE table footnote. Source to use: Use the December 2025 WASDE as posted by USDA (World Agricultural Outlook Board) on the USDA OCE WASDE page. The USDA’s public WASDE page lists the official 2025 release schedule, with the December 2025 release set for December 9, 2025 at 12:00 PM ET. Use the December 2025 report that is publicly available on that page. Timing and version: Resolve using the version of the December 2025 WASDE available on USDA’s website as of 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. Rounding and interpretation: Use the integer value shown in “Million Bushels.” If the table shows 3,000, that counts as ≥ 3,000; if it shows 2,999 or 2,995, that does not. Do not infer from narrative text; rely strictly on the table value. Fallback if the USDA site is temporarily inaccessible: If the USDA site is down at resolution time, use credible re-publications or official USDA communications that directly reproduce the December 2025 WASDE table (e.g., the PDF mirrored by USDA’s OCE or ERS properties). If no official mirror exists, delay resolution until the USDA site or official mirror is accessible. No other third-party estimates will be used. Supporting context (not used for resolution): August 2025 WASDE “Exports” for corn in 2025/26 = 2,875 million bushels; September 2025 WASDE = 2,975 million bushels.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will any company that is a DAX40 or MDAX constituent as of 2025-10-15 publish an ad‑hoc announcement explicitly stating that a cybersecurity incident disrupted its operations?
background:
Context and definitions a forecaster should know:

- What is an ad‑hoc announcement in Germany: Under the EU Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) Article 17, issuers must promptly publish insider information via an ad‑hoc announcement (Ad‑hoc‑Mitteilung). BaFin explains the purpose, obligations, and dissemination requirements (e.g., Europe‑wide electronic distribution, storage, publication on issuer website) for such disclosures.

- Relevant index universes:
  - DAX: Tracks the performance of the 40 largest companies listed on the Regulated Market of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, administered by STOXX Ltd.; constituent selection is based on free‑float market cap and minimum quality/profitability rules.
  - MDAX: Tracks 50 German midcap stocks that follow DAX companies in size (or are otherwise ineligible for DAX but meet minimum standards), administered by STOXX Ltd..

- Cyber threat environment in Germany: The Federal Cyber Security Authority (BSI) assesses that the IT security situation in Germany “has been and remains worrying” in its 2024 report. As an example of a cyberattack type that can disrupt availability, BSI describes Distributed Denial‑of‑Service (DDoS) attacks as deliberate overloading of services, leading to denial of service for legitimate users.

- Example of the type of disclosure this question targets: On 13 Feb 2024, VARTA AG published an ad‑hoc announcement under Article 17 MAR stating it had been the target of a cyberattack and that IT systems and production were proactively shut down, affecting operations. This is provided purely as an illustrative precedent of wording that clearly indicates operational disruption due to a cyber incident.

- Resolution sources: EQS News is a widely used dissemination platform for regulatory disclosures and explicitly categorizes “Ad‑hoc” announcements with dedicated item pages (including timestamp and issuer), which can be used to verify eligible publications; issuers also publish ad‑hoc items on their investor relations websites. DAX/MDAX definitions and index administration are documented by Qontigo/STOXX (for constituent verification as of 2025‑10‑15, see Resolution Criteria).

Why this is forecastable: Germany’s cyber threat posture suggests non‑trivial odds of material incidents leading to ad‑hoc disclosures, but it is far from certain that such an incident will both occur and be disclosed as ad‑hoc in the specified window. The outcome plausibly lies between low and moderate probabilities, creating room for meaningful disagreement and research‑driven forecasting.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the publication of at least one qualifying ad‑hoc announcement within the specified window.

- Time window (inclusive, UTC): From 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. An announcement’s publication time will be determined by the timestamp on the ad‑hoc item page or issuer’s ad‑hoc posting; if given in CET/CEST only, it will be converted to UTC for eligibility.

- Universe of companies: All companies that are constituents of either DAX40 or MDAX at 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC. “DAX40” and “MDAX” refer to the indices administered by STOXX Ltd. (a Qontigo company) per their official definitions. For any candidate announcement, constituent status as of the timestamp above must be verifiable from STOXX/Qontigo’s official constituent lists or press releases archived around that date (e.g., the most recent review effective before 2025‑10‑15). If needed, alternative corroboration may include the index factsheet/constituent list captured by an authoritative archive on/near that date.

- What counts as an eligible publication (“ad‑hoc announcement”):
  - It must be a regulatory ad‑hoc disclosure under Article 17 MAR (Ad‑hoc‑Mitteilung/Insiderinformation) by the issuer, as evidenced by: (a) the issuer’s item labeled “Ad‑hoc” on a recognized dissemination platform such as EQS News, or (b) the issuer’s investor relations page with explicit labeling as an Article 17 MAR ad‑hoc disclosure (e.g., containing phrasing like “Veröffentlichung einer Insiderinformation gemäß Artikel 17 der Verordnung (EU) Nr. 596/2014”); screenshots/archives acceptable. Corporate news/press releases that are not ad‑hoc do not count.

- Content requirements (both required in a single ad‑hoc):
  1) It must explicitly disclose a cybersecurity incident, meaning it uses clear terminology indicating a malicious or unauthorized cyber event (e.g., “Cyberangriff,” “Cyberattack,” “Ransomware,” “Hackerangriff,” “IT‑Sicherheitsvorfall,” “DDoS‑Angriff”). As an example of a defined cyber incident type, BSI describes DDoS as a deliberate overloading that leads to service unavailability.
  2) It must explicitly state that the incident disrupted operations. Acceptable phrasings include, but are not limited to: production/fulfilment halted or reduced; business operations/services unavailable; systems taken offline causing interruption; facility shutdowns due to the incident. Wording similar to the VARTA ad‑hoc (e.g., “IT‑Systeme und damit auch die Produktion wurden … vorübergehend … heruntergefahren”) clearly qualifies. Mere disclosure of data exposure/privacy breach without explicit operational disruption does NOT qualify.

- Language: German or English publications are acceptable, provided the criteria above are met.

- Duplicates/corrections: If an ad‑hoc is corrected or replaced, the final version published within the window will be used for eligibility. If multiple ad‑hoc items relate to the same incident, one qualifying item is sufficient for a YES resolution.

- Resolution: YES if at least one qualifying ad‑hoc announcement is published within the time window by any issuer in the defined universe. NO otherwise. 

- Primary resolution sources to verify: 
  - EQS News ad‑hoc item page(s) for the issuer(s) within the window.
  - Issuer investor relations “Ad‑hoc/Insiderinformation” page(s) containing the MAR Article 17 ad‑hoc text.
  - For index membership verification at 2025‑10‑15: Qontigo/STOXX official index materials describing DAX/MDAX and their administration; use constituent lists/press releases effective around that date to confirm membership.

question: Will the Bank of England’s MPC reduce Bank Rate at its December 2025 meeting?
background:
Definitions and scope:
- Bank Rate: the UK’s core policy interest rate, i.e., the rate the Bank of England pays on reserves held by banks/building societies and the rate it charges on certain lending to them.
- MPC refers to the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee (see Bank of England website for MPC information). This question concerns the MPC’s December 2025 policy decision, as formally announced in the Bank of England’s “Monetary Policy Summary and minutes” for December 2025.
- Time window: This question resolves based on outcomes announced between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. The December 2025 MPC announcement is scheduled for 18 December 2025; the Bank of England’s December Monetary Policy Summary page indicates it will be published at 12:00 (UK local time).

Status quo as of late September 2025 (context for forecasters):
- At the MPC meeting ending 17 September 2025, Bank Rate was maintained at 4.0%. The vote was 7–2 to hold, with two members preferring a 25 bp cut to 3.75%. The MPC reiterated that monetary policy is “not on a pre-set path” and that it would remain responsive to data. The Committee also expected CPI inflation to rise slightly around September before falling back towards target thereafter.
- UK CPI inflation (ONS headline CPI, 12-month rate) was 3.8% in August 2025, unchanged from July 2025, according to the latest ONS bulletin at the time.

Primary resolution source:
- Bank of England “Monetary Policy Summary and minutes – December 2025” page (official source-of-truth; to be published by the Bank at the stated time).

Why this is forecastable: There is plausible uncertainty between a cut vs. hold/increase given recent inflation dynamics, prior vote splits, and MPC guidance emphasizing data dependence rather than a preset path.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will the Bank of England’s MPC reduce Bank Rate at its December 2025 meeting?

Resolution event and timing:
- This question resolves upon publication of the Bank of England’s “Monetary Policy Summary and minutes – December 2025,” expected on 18 December 2025 at 12:00 UK local time, and in any case no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. All times in this question are UTC unless otherwise specified.

Operational definitions for adjudication:
- “Bank Rate” means the UK’s official policy rate as defined by the Bank of England.
- “Reduce” / “cut” means the MPC sets Bank Rate to a level strictly lower than the level in effect immediately prior to the December 2025 decision. Evidence of a cut will typically be clear in the official communication (e.g., headline language such as “Bank Rate reduced to X%”) and/or by comparing the newly announced Bank Rate to the previously effective rate.

How to resolve:
- Use the Bank of England’s December 2025 Monetary Policy Summary and minutes page as the sole source-of-truth to determine the decision.
- Resolve “Yes” if the December 2025 Monetary Policy Summary/minutes states that Bank Rate was reduced relative to its level immediately prior to the meeting (i.e., the decision is a cut). Resolve “No” if Bank Rate was maintained or increased.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- If the Bank of England does not publish the December 2025 Monetary Policy Summary/minutes by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve “No.”
- If the December 2025 meeting is rescheduled but the Monetary Policy Summary/minutes for that meeting are still published by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve based on that publication.
- If multiple versions or updates are posted on the publication date, resolve based on the latest official version available on the Bank of England website as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Media reports, third-party data providers, and press conferences do not override the official Monetary Policy Summary/minutes page for resolution.

Start date for eligible outcomes: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC. End date: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

question: Will ACMA impose a monetary enforcement action on Optus related to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage by December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Incident: On 18 September 2025, Optus experienced an outage that prevented some customers from connecting to Australia’s Triple Zero (000) emergency number. Government and media reporting indicate about 600 failed Triple Zero calls and multiple deaths linked to the outage. The incident has been described as stemming from a network firewall upgrade in which established processes were not followed. Less than two weeks later, a fresh outage affecting emergency call services occurred, intensifying scrutiny.
- Regulator action: The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) announced on 22 September 2025 that it had commenced an investigation into Optus’s compliance with emergency call service regulations and related obligations, and stated it will make its findings public once concluded.
- Enforcement toolkit and precedent: ACMA’s compliance and enforcement policy includes monetary instruments such as infringement notices (specified penalties payable if accepted) and civil penalties (pecuniary penalty orders via the Federal Court). As precedent, ACMA reported Optus paid three infringement notices totalling $12,000,420 for breaches related to the November 2023 Triple Zero outage.

Key definitions and links for forecasters:
- ACMA: Australia’s communications regulator; investigation page and media releases are published at acma.gov.au.
- Optus: For this question, “Optus” means Singtel Optus Pty Limited or any Australian subsidiary (e.g., Optus Mobile Pty Ltd, Optus Networks Pty Ltd) that ACMA treats as part of the Optus group for enforcement in relation to the specified incident.
- Triple Zero (000): Australia’s primary emergency number; general background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_zero (link provided for definition/reference only).

Why this is forecastable: ACMA has an open investigation with stated intent to publish findings , monetary penalties are within its enforcement toolkit , and Optus has previously received (and paid) significant ACMA penalties for emergency call service breaches. Whether ACMA will impose a monetary enforcement action tied specifically to the 18 September 2025 outage by year-end is plausible yet uncertain, and will be publicly verifiable.

Notes on data sources for resolution: ACMA typically announces enforcement outcomes via articles/media releases on acma.gov.au and periodic compliance reports. Major wire services and national outlets (e.g., Reuters, ABC) also cover significant ACMA enforcement actions and can serve as secondary confirmation.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will ACMA impose a monetary enforcement action on Optus related to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive)?

Operational definitions:
- Monetary enforcement action (for this question) means either of the following, provided it explicitly relates to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage:
  1) ACMA issues an infringement notice to Optus that specifies a monetary penalty amount (payment to the Commonwealth) for contraventions under relevant legislation or instruments (e.g., the Telecommunications Act), as described in ACMA’s compliance and enforcement policy ; or
  2) An Australian court makes a civil penalty (pecuniary penalty) order against Optus in proceedings brought by (or on the application of) ACMA for contraventions relating to the outage.

- Explicit relation to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage means the ACMA publication (or the court order) directly references “Triple Zero”/“000” and the date or factual description that uniquely identifies the 18 September 2025 incident (e.g., “18 September 2025”, “September 2025 outage causing ~600 failed Triple Zero calls”).
- Optus means Singtel Optus Pty Limited or any Australian subsidiary within the Optus group that ACMA names in relation to this incident.

Start and end of eligibility window:
- Start: 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC
- End: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC

Resolution rules:
- Resolve YES if, within the eligibility window, ACMA publishes on acma.gov.au that it has issued an infringement notice to Optus that explicitly ties the notice to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage; or if an Australian court publishes an order within the window imposing a pecuniary penalty on Optus in ACMA-initiated proceedings explicitly tied to that outage. Payment of an infringement notice is not required for YES; issuance by ACMA suffices, provided the issuance is publicly announced on acma.gov.au within the window. If both occur, resolve YES.
- Resolve NO if, by the end of the window, neither of the above has occurred; or if ACMA only announces non-monetary actions (e.g., remedial directions, warnings, code directions, or acceptance of an enforceable undertaking without any specified monetary penalty), or actions/penalties that do not explicitly relate to the 18 September 2025 outage.

Primary resolution sources (in order of preference):
1) ACMA website publications (articles/media releases, enforcement pages) on acma.gov.au that announce issuance of infringement notices or other enforcement outcomes, or periodic reports summarizing such outcomes.
2) If applicable, an Australian court order imposing a pecuniary penalty (e.g., the Federal Court of Australia online registry/judgments). If a court order is used, it must explicitly reference the 18 September 2025 outage.
3) Secondary confirmation only if needed for clarity: major credible outlets (e.g., Reuters, ABC) reporting and linking to the ACMA notice or court order.

Tiebreakers and edge cases:
- If ACMA announces that it has commenced civil penalty proceedings but no court order imposing a penalty is made within the window, do NOT count this as monetary enforcement (resolve NO absent other eligible actions).
- If ACMA issues multiple enforcement instruments, at least one must be a monetary one (as defined above) explicitly tied to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage for YES.
- If an ACMA publication or court document references the September 2025 outage but is ambiguous as to the date, use explicit mention of “18 September 2025” or the contemporaneous description (e.g., ~600 failed Triple Zero calls) to confirm eligibility.
- The date for timeliness is the publication date shown on the ACMA page or the date of the court order. If only a date (not time) is shown, treat it as occurring on that date; ensure it is on or before 2025-12-31 when interpreted against the UTC cutoff.

Supporting context for forecasters:
- ACMA has publicly stated it commenced an investigation into the 18 September 2025 outage and will publish findings.
- Media and official timelines report around 600 failed Triple Zero calls and multiple deaths linked to the 18 September 2025 outage.
- ACMA has previously imposed a large monetary penalty on Optus for Triple Zero-related breaches tied to the November 2023 outage (three infringement notices totalling $12,000,420).

question: Will OFAC add at least five Venezuela‑related persons or entities to the SDN List under E.O. 13224 and/or E.O. 14059 between 2025‑10‑15 and 2025‑12‑31 (UTC)?
background:
Context as of 2025‑09‑30:
- On July 25, 2025, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated Cartel de los Soles as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT), citing material support to Tren de Aragua and the Sinaloa Cartel, and stated Treasury would continue to crack down on these organizations and their facilitators.
- The Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List is OFAC’s authoritative list of individuals and entities whose property is blocked and with whom U.S. persons are generally prohibited from dealing. SDNs include terrorists and narcotics traffickers designated under various sanctions authorities; the list is frequently updated and changes are recorded by OFAC.
- Executive Order (E.O.) 14059 (Imposing Sanctions on Foreign Persons Involved in the Global Illicit Drug Trade) authorizes sanctions on foreign persons involved in the proliferation of illicit drugs; it was issued on December 15, 2021, and is implemented by OFAC. E.O. 13224 (as amended) is the main counterterrorism authority used to designate SDGTs (referenced in OFAC’s July 25, 2025 action).
- OFAC posts sanctions actions and designations on its Recent Actions and Press Releases pages, which serve as public, authoritative logs of actions and their cited legal authorities. OFAC also maintains an Archive of Changes to the SDN List that shows when names were added, modified, or removed, enabling verification of “add” events by date. For programmatic, file‑level verification, OFAC’s Sanctions List Service (SLS) provides the SDN List in machine‑readable formats (CSV, XML, fixed‑field) and a delta file archive; the publicly available data specification guide documents record structure and fields used for entries (e.g., name records, types, addresses).
