- Numeric comparison: Compare the published number as-is (do not round). Treat different formatting (e.g., thousands separators, varying decimal precision) as equivalent to the underlying numeric value.
- If the CBN publishes multiple pages with similar tables and there is a discrepancy, the page titled “DAILY NIGERIAN FOREIGN EXCHANGE MARKET (NFEM) RATES (₦/US$)” under the CBN Exchange Rates section prevails. 

Verification time: The question resolves when the applicable figure for 31 December 2025 is published per the hierarchy above. FMDQ indicates Closing Rates are published at 17:00 WAT for the observation window of 9:00–16:00, which supports timely availability if the fallback is needed.

question: Will all four of India’s national Labour Codes be fully in force (all provisions commenced) by December 31, 2025?
background:
Summary of what’s being forecast: India has enacted four national Labour Codes intended to consolidate and modernize labour regulation: the Code on Wages, 2019; the Industrial Relations Code, 2020; the Code on Social Security, 2020; and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Code, 2020. Under each Code’s commencement clause, provisions come into force on dates appointed by the Central Government via notification in the Official Gazette, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions. The Gazette of India is the Government of India’s public journal and an authorized legal instrument for publishing such notifications.

Status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- By statute, each Code requires Central Government commencement by Gazette notification; partial, staged commencement is legally permitted because different dates may be appointed for different provisions. As an illustration, certain provisions of the Code on Wages, 2019 related to the Central Advisory Board were brought into force on December 18, 2020, vide S.O. 4604(E).
- Implementation has been closely linked to state/UT rulemaking and coordination with the Centre. At a two-day national conference on January 29–30, 2025, chaired by the Union Labour Minister, the government highlighted that over 32 States/UTs had pre-published draft rules under the labour codes and stated that all 36 States/UTs were expected to complete pre-publication of harmonized draft rules by March 31, 2025. This reflects ongoing steps toward full implementation, but final legal commencement for central Codes depends on Central Government notifications in the Gazette.

Why this is forecastable now: Historically, the government has signaled an intent to implement the Codes in a coordinated manner, but timelines have slipped. Because commencement can be partial and staged by provision, forecasters must assess political prioritization, inter-governmental coordination, and administrative readiness between now and end-2025. Verification will hinge on whether each Code’s remaining provisions have been appointed a commencement date by the deadline (see Resolution Criteria below), which can be checked quickly in the Gazette/India Code portals.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and time zone:
- Eligible commencement notifications are those published at any time from 2019-01-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). The question resolves at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What must happen for “Yes”:
- Resolve Yes if, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, all four of the following central Acts are wholly commenced (i.e., all provisions of the Act have been brought into force by Central Government notification(s) in the Gazette of India with appointed effective dates on or before the deadline):
  1) Code on Wages, 2019
  2) Industrial Relations Code, 2020
  3) Code on Social Security, 2020
  4) Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020

Definitions and counting rules:
- Wholly commenced (all provisions commenced): Under Section 1(3) of each Code, “It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint; and different dates may be appointed for different provisions…” Thus, a Code is “wholly commenced” once every provision of that Code has an appointed commencement date by Central Government notification(s) in the Gazette of India.
- Notification means a notification published in the Gazette of India (or a State’s Official Gazette for state notifications); for purposes of this market, only Central Government notifications relevant to commencing provisions of the central Codes in the Gazette of India qualify.
- Effective date: If a notification specifies that a provision “shall come into force on” a stated date, that date is the commencement date for that provision. If a notification appoints a future date, that provision counts only if the appointed date is on or before 2025-12-31 (UTC). If a time is not specified, treat the provision as commencing at 00:00 local time on the stated date; for this question we compare dates (not times) to the UTC deadline.
- Partial commencement does not suffice for Yes. All provisions of each Code must be commenced by the deadline. If any provision of any Code remains uncommenced as of the deadline, resolve No.
- State/UT draft or final rules, or administrative circulars, do not by themselves constitute commencement of a central Code; only Central Government Gazette notifications commencing provisions count.

Acceptable sources for resolution (primary sources preferred; in case of discrepancy, the Gazette of India prevails):
- The Gazette of India (eGazette portal): https://egazette.gov.in/ (authoritative publication of Central Government notifications).
- India Code pages for each Code (often list “Commencement Notifications” and text of Gazette notifications):
  • Code on Wages, 2019: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/15793 (contains commencement notifications incl. S.O. 4604(E), 18 Dec 2020).
  • Code on Social Security, 2020 (official text; check for commencement notifications): https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/16823.
  • Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (official text; check for commencement notifications): official MoLE text https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/ir_gazette_of_india.pdf.
  • OSH Code, 2020 (official text): https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/186_2019_ls_eng_0.pdf.
- Secondary confirmation (non-controlling): Ministry of Labour & Employment or PIB press releases for context; e.g., PIB note on the 29–30 Jan 2025 conference about state readiness and harmonized draft rules: https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleseDetailm.aspx?PRID=2097446.

Edge cases:
- If a Code is repealed and re-enacted in substantially similar form under a different short title before the deadline, only the four Codes listed above count; commencement of a replacement Act would not satisfy this question unless it bears exactly the same short title as listed.
- If a court stays operation of a commenced provision after its appointed date, the provision still counts as commenced for this question (the legal act of commencement occurred).
- If notifications are issued but appoint commencement dates after 2025-12-31, they do not count toward full commencement.

Rationale for difficulty: Although the Centre can commence provisions via Gazette notification, practical implementation has depended on state rulemaking and coordination, and staged commencement is legally possible. Recent government communications emphasize harmonizing state draft rules (as of Jan 2025), leaving uncertainty about whether the Centre will complete full commencement by end-2025.

question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will Iran and at least one of the E3 (France, Germany, United Kingdom) or the United States publicly announce the initiation of formal talks on Iran’s nuclear program?
background:
Status quo as of September 30, 2025: On August 28, 2025, the E3 (France, Germany, and the United Kingdom) notified the UN Security Council that Iran was in significant non-performance of its commitments under the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), thereby initiating the snapback process under UNSC Resolution 2231. A draft resolution led by China and Russia to delay the snapback failed at the Security Council on September 26, 2025. The United States confirmed that UN sanctions were reimposed the evening of September 27, 2025 (8:00 p.m. EDT), concluding the snapback process initiated by the E3 on August 28 , and the EU Council detailed the restrictive measures reimposed on September 29, 2025. Reuters contemporaneous reporting also describes the snapback taking effect at 0000 GMT on Sunday, September 28, 2025, and notes Western intentions to return to a mixture of pressure and dialogue going forward.

In July–September 2025, the E3 publicly offered Iran a limited, one-time extension to delay snapback conditioned on concrete steps, including resuming direct and unconditional negotiations with the United States, restoring IAEA access, and accounting for Iran’s high-enriched uranium stockpile; the E3 emphasized that reimposed UN sanctions are not the end of diplomacy. As of mid–September 2025, statements at the IAEA Board and by European officials indicated Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile was far above JCPOA limits (overall stockpile at 48× the JCPOA cap; >440 kg enriched up to 60%), and that the IAEA lacked continuity of knowledge and access to comprehensively verify stocks and activities. On September 23, 2025, Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei publicly ruled out negotiations with the United States on the nuclear program, calling US demands a “diktat,” while Iranian and European officials held discussions on the margins of UNGA. Statements from US and European representatives at the UN underscored that snapback does not preclude a diplomatic resolution in the future.

Why this question: Despite heightened pressure, both Western actors and Iran’s interlocutors have signaled that diplomacy remains possible, creating plausible room for movement in Q4 2025. The event—publicly announced initiation of formal nuclear talks—would be a clear, binary signal with non-trivial uncertainty.

Key concepts and references forecasters may find useful:
- JCPOA (2015 Iran nuclear deal): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action
- UNSC Resolution 2231: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_2231
- IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency
- Iran’s nuclear program overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran
- Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (official English name and role): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(Iran) 

Typical official sources for announcements/readouts:
- Iran MFA: https://www.mfa.gov.ir (English portal commonly available at https://en.mfa.ir)
- US Department of State: https://www.state.gov (Press releases/readouts: https://www.state.gov/press-releases/)
- UK FCDO: https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/foreign-commonwealth-development-office (News: https://www.gov.uk/government/announcements)
- French MFA (MEAE): https://www.diplomatie.gouv.fr/en/ (Country file/news pages host Iran-related statements)
- German Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt): https://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/en/newsroom
- Credible wire services (fallback if primary sources are temporarily inaccessible): Reuters (https://www.reuters.com), Associated Press (https://apnews.com), AFP (https://www.afp.com)
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves to Yes if, between October 15, 2025, 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025, 23:59:59 UTC, BOTH of the following occur:

1) Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) issues a public, official announcement stating that formal talks/negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program have begun, or are scheduled to begin on a specified date on or before December 31, 2025 (UTC). The announcement must be published either on an official Iranian government web domain (e.g., mfa.gov.ir) or on an official, verified social media account of the Iran MFA or the Foreign Minister.

2) At least one of the following counterparts issues a public, official announcement, either jointly or reciprocally, describing the same initiation of formal talks/negotiations (as in 1) on Iran’s nuclear program: the US Department of State, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs (MEAE), or the German Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt). The announcement must be published on the counterpart’s official web domain or an official, verified social media account.

Definitions and clarifications:
- Formal talks/negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program: A structured, official negotiation process between state representatives concerning Iran’s nuclear activities, safeguards, enrichment, the JCPOA, UNSCR 2231, and/or related nuclear terms. The announcement must use terms such as “formal talks,” “negotiations,” “a negotiating round,” or “talks will begin,” and explicitly reference the nuclear program (or widely used synonyms such as “nuclear issue,” “nuclear file,” “JCPOA,” “IAEA safeguards,” or “Resolution 2231”). Track II/backchannel or purely unofficial meetings do not count.
- Joint announcement: A single statement co-issued by Iran’s MFA and at least one counterpart ministry/department listed above, posted on at least one of their official domains or official verified accounts.
- Reciprocal announcement: Separate statements from Iran’s MFA and the counterpart ministry/department listed above, referencing the same initiation of talks/negotiations, issued within 168 hours (7 days) of each other.
- Publicly announce: Publication on an official government website or an official, verified account on major platforms (e.g., X/Twitter, Facebook, YouTube), where the issuing entity is clearly identified as Iran’s MFA or the specified counterpart ministry/department. Media reports alone do not count unless used as a fallback per Evidence below.
- Eligible counterparts: US Department of State, UK FCDO, French MEAE, German Auswärtiges Amt. Iran’s MFA official English name and role: “Ministry of Foreign Affairs” of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
- Date/time: All timing is in UTC. Only announcements within the window October 15, 2025, 00:00:00 UTC through December 31, 2025, 23:59:59 UTC are considered.
- Scheduling versus occurrence: Announcements that “will begin” count if the specified first session date is on or before December 31, 2025 (UTC). If, by December 31, 2025 (UTC), an official cancellation of the scheduled first session is announced by either party, the initiation does not count.
- Exclusions: Announcements solely about humanitarian exchanges, regional security talks unrelated to the nuclear file, technical IAEA meetings without negotiation between Iran and the E3/US, or generalized statements of willingness to talk absent a concrete initiation or scheduled negotiating round.

Evidence required to resolve Yes:
- URLs to the qualifying announcements on the official website(s) and/or posts on official, verified social media accounts of Iran’s MFA and the relevant counterpart. If official sites are temporarily inaccessible at resolution time, credible wire service reporting (e.g., Reuters, AP, AFP) that directly quotes or captures the official announcements may be accepted, provided it clearly identifies the issuing entity and the content of the announcement.

Resolution sources and verification approach:
- Primary: Official government press releases/statements/readouts on the sites listed in Background and in the Definitions above. The resolver will verify language explicitly initiating formal nuclear talks and the timing (UTC) of publication.
- Secondary (fallback, if needed): Credible wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, AFP) that reproduce or quote the official announcement text.

Outcome determination:
- Yes if both 1) and 2) occur as defined within the stated window.
- No if the criteria are not met by December 31, 2025, 23:59:59 UTC.

Context sources for the status quo and diplomatic posture: E3 snapback initiation and conditions for delay ; UNSC vote failure to extend sanctions relief and member statements on diplomacy ; US confirmation of snapback completion and statement that diplomacy remains an option ; EU Council description of reimposed measures ; Reuters analysis on timing and the mix of pressure and dialogue ; IAEA-related stockpile and access context ; Khamenei statement ruling out US talks.

question: By 2025-12-31, will Tata Capital’s official NSE Close Price be at least 10% above its IPO cap price of ₹326 (i.e., ≥ ₹358.60)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30: Reuters reports that Tata Capital has set an IPO price band of ₹310–₹326 per share and will open the offer for bids on 2025-10-06. Coverage characterizes it as India’s largest IPO/listing so far in 2025, with up to 210 million new shares and up to 265.8 million shares offered by existing shareholders, and a targeted valuation around $15 billion. The IPO will list the company’s equity shares on Indian exchanges, and the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) will publish end‑of‑day data including a Close Price for the security. NSE’s Market Feed specification for the Capital Market segment states that during the trading day the previous day’s close is disseminated, and after market close the current day’s Close Price is calculated; end‑of‑day data includes a "Security close price for the day" field. The NSE maintains daily archives for Capital Market (Equities) reports (commonly referred to as the EOD “bhavcopy”) that contain official end‑of‑day data needed for resolution.

Why this is forecastable: The threshold compares the official NSE Close Price on the 2025-12-31 trading day against 110% of the IPO cap price (₹326), i.e., ₹358.60. Given the scale of the offering and uncertainties about listing dynamics, sector conditions, and broader market performance into year‑end 2025, the outcome is non‑trivial.

Definitions for corporate action adjustments: This market question compares per‑share prices across time. To preserve comparability, the threshold will be adjusted for stock splits/reverse splits and for bonus share issues, which mechanically change the per‑share price without changing proportional ownership. A stock split increases the number of shares outstanding and proportionally reduces the per‑share price (e.g., 2‑for‑1 halves the per‑share price). A bonus issue (bonus shares) distributes additional shares to existing shareholders for free, typically reducing the per‑share price proportionally while keeping ownership proportions unchanged. A rights issue offers existing holders the right to buy additional shares, often affecting market price via the theoretical ex‑rights price, but it does not deterministically set a mechanical price ratio in the same way; no adjustment will be made for rights issues under this question.
resolution_criteria:
Primary proposition: Resolve “Yes” if the official NSE Close Price for Tata Capital Limited’s equity shares on the NSE trading day dated 2025-12-31 (India Standard Time, UTC+5:30) is greater than or equal to ₹358.60; otherwise resolve “No”.

- Close Price definition and source: "Close Price" means the security’s official close price as calculated by the NSE after market close and disseminated in its end‑of‑day data for the Capital Market (Equities) segment (the "Security close price for the day" field). The primary resolution source will be the NSE’s official Capital Market (Equities) daily archives (“Archives of Daily / Monthly Reports (EQ)” – commonly known as the EOD bhavcopy) for the trading date 2025-12-31. If needed for verification, the value may be cross‑checked against the security’s Close Price shown on the NSE website’s quote page for the same trade date.
- Currency and threshold: Values are in Indian rupees (₹). The threshold is 110% of the IPO cap price ₹326 = ₹358.60. Compare the NSE-reported Close Price (which is typically reported to two decimal places) to the threshold rounded to two decimal places (₹358.60). If they are equal (≥), resolve “Yes”.
- Observation date: Use the NSE trading session bearing the trade date 2025-12-31 (IST). If there is no NSE trading session with that trade date (e.g., exchange holiday), use the immediately preceding NSE trading day’s Close Price for the security.
- Listing/suspension contingencies: If Tata Capital has not commenced trading on the NSE by 2025-12-31, resolve “No”. If the security is listed but trading is halted or suspended for the entirety of the 2025-12-31 session, use the most recent prior NSE trading day’s official Close Price.
- Corporate action adjustments (before comparison): Adjust the ₹358.60 threshold only for stock splits/reverse splits and bonus share issues that become effective on or before the relevant observation date. For a split or bonus with announced ratio y‑for‑x (post‑split shares per pre‑split share), multiply the threshold by x/y. For a consolidation/reverse split where y < x, this increases the threshold accordingly. Examples: 2‑for‑1 split or 1:1 bonus → divide threshold by 2; 3‑for‑2 split → multiply threshold by 2/3. Do not adjust the threshold for cash dividends (ordinary or special), rights issues, buybacks, demergers/spin‑offs, or any other events.
- Security identification: "Tata Capital Limited" refers to the company whose IPO referenced by Reuters set a price band of ₹310–₹326 and opens 2025-10-06, identified in Indian media as India’s largest IPO/listing so far in 2025. The forecast concerns its equity shares listed on the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE), Capital Market segment.
- Evidence requirement: The resolver must capture the NSE source file or webpage showing the Close Price for the specified trade date from the NSE daily archives (primary). If the NSE site is temporarily inaccessible, resolution may rely on cached mirrors of the same NSE file or multiple independent reputable financial news/data services reproducing the NSE Close Price for that date; however, the NSE archive is the intended source of truth.

This question will be resolved after the publication of the NSE’s official end‑of‑day data for the 2025-12-31 trade date and no later than 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC.

question: Trade impact: Will Brazil’s exports to the United States in Aug–Nov 2025 be at least 15% lower than in Aug–Nov 2024 (FOB, USD; Comex Stat)?
background:
Context and policy shock
- On July 30, 2025, a U.S. Executive Order imposed an additional ad valorem duty of 40% on certain products of Brazilian origin, effective at 12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time on August 6, 2025; this duty stacks on top of other applicable duties (bringing many covered lines to an effective 50% cumulative tariff), and includes detailed exclusions listed in Annex I. Goods loaded and in transit before the effective date are exempt if entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption before 12:01 a.m. EDT on October 5, 2025.
- Coverage is not universal: several key sectors and products were excluded (e.g., civil aircraft, energy/petroleum, wood pulp, fertilizers, pig iron, precious metals, some mining exports). Analysts noted that the breadth of exemptions reduces the effective average tariff rate relative to headline levels, with Goldman Sachs estimating ~30.8% on Brazilian shipments; some major exports (e.g., beef, coffee) were not shielded.

Data source and measure
- This question resolves using Brazil’s official foreign trade statistics portal, Comex Stat, which is the government platform for foreign trade data and supports monthly exports by partner queries. Users can access detailed exports and imports data and conduct specific searches; it is Brazil’s platform for foreign trade data.
- Exports will be measured on an FOB basis in U.S. dollars as reported by Comex Stat. Free on Board (FOB) refers to the value of goods at the point of shipment, excluding ocean freight, insurance, and subsequent transport costs; risk transfers to the buyer once goods are loaded on board.

Why this is forecastable now
- The tariff shock begins partway through August 2025 with a transition window for in-transit cargo through October 5, 2025, and many exclusions. These features create uncertainty about the magnitude and timing of effects on Brazil→U.S. goods exports during Aug–Nov 2025, relative to the same months in 2024.
- For context (not used for resolution), U.S. Census reports that U.S. goods imports from Brazil were $3.94B in August 2024, $3.33B in September 2024, $3.33B in October 2024, and $3.98B in November 2024 (customs value, not seasonally adjusted). Note that the resolution uses Brazilian export data (FOB, USD) from Comex Stat, not U.S. import data.
resolution_criteria:
What will be measured
- Outcome: Whether the total FOB value (USD) of Brazil’s exports of goods to the United States during Aug–Nov 2025 is at least 15% lower than the corresponding total for Aug–Nov 2024.

Definitions
- Exports: Goods exports as reported by Comex Stat (Brazil’s official foreign trade statistics portal).
- Valuation: FOB (Free on Board) value in U.S. dollars, as reported by Comex Stat. FOB excludes ocean freight, insurance, and onward costs; see definition of FOB in international trade.
- United States: The partner labeled “United States” in the Comex Stat partner/country filter.
- Periods: Aug–Nov 2024 and Aug–Nov 2025 refer to the calendar months August, September, October, and November of the respective years.

Exact calculation steps (replicable)
1) Navigate to Comex Stat (https://comexstat.mdic.gov.br/).
2) Use the module that allows monthly exports by partner (e.g., “General Data/Dados Gerais”). Set filters as follows:
   - Measure: Export value – FOB (US$).
   - Period: August 2024 through November 2024 (inclusive). Partner/country: United States. Sum the monthly export values (FOB, USD) across Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov 2024 to obtain Baseline_2024.
   - Period: August 2025 through November 2025 (inclusive). Partner/country: United States. Sum the monthly export values (FOB, USD) across Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov 2025 to obtain Total_2025.
3) Compute the percentage change = (Baseline_2024 − Total_2025) / Baseline_2024.
4) Resolution:
   - YES if percentage change ≥ 0.15 (i.e., Total_2025 ≤ 0.85 × Baseline_2024).
   - NO otherwise.

Scope and notes
- Goods only: Comex Stat covers trade in goods; services are out of scope.
- Data vintage: Use the values visible on Comex Stat at the time of resolution (latest available/revised as of the resolution timestamp).
- Rounding: Perform the sums using the most granular figures Comex Stat displays/exports (do not round monthly values before summing). Compare using full precision; only the final comparison threshold of 15% governs the outcome.

Resolution timing and source
- Primary resolution source: Comex Stat (Brazil’s official foreign trade data portal).
- Resolution window: Resolve once Comex Stat has posted monthly export values for all of Aug, Sep, Oct, and Nov 2025, no later than 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. If data are posted earlier, the question can be resolved earlier within the Oct 15–Dec 31, 2025 window.

Relevant policy details for context only (not used directly in the calculation)
- Additional 40% ad valorem duty effective August 6, 2025 at 12:01 a.m. EDT (stacking with prior duties), with exemptions including goods in transit loaded before that date if entered before October 5, 2025; several sectors/products are excluded per Annex I.
- Reporting indicated numerous exclusions (e.g., civil aircraft, energy, orange juice, wood pulp, pig iron, precious metals; large share of mining exports) and an expected lower effective rate on average shipments; some categories like beef and coffee were not exempted.

question: Will U.S. coal-fired generator retirements dated between 2025-01-01 and 2025-11-30 exceed 10.0 GW (net summer capacity)?
background:
Why this matters: Coal-by-rail volumes and utility fuel mixes depend on the pace of coal power retirements. This question tracks actual retirements recorded in official generator inventory data and sets the window to allow resolution by year-end 2025.

Status quo and how to track it: Actual generator retirements are recorded in the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s (EIA) Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory (Form EIA-860M). Each monthly release includes a generator-level inventory with fields for primary energy source, operational status (including “retired”), and the retirement date. Forecasters can monitor year-to-date retirements across 2025 using successive EIA-860M releases and compute the cumulative net summer capacity of coal-fired units retired during the calendar months January–November 2025.

Key definitions and scope:
- Coal-fired generator: A generator whose primary energy source is coal, identified in EIA data by primary energy source codes for coal, including but not limited to bituminous (BIT), subbituminous (SUB), lignite (LIG), waste coal (WC), and refined coal (RC) as coded in EIA generator inventories.
- Retirement: A generator whose operational status is listed as “retired” with a retirement effective date in 2025. Temporary mothballing or “out of service (temporary)” does not count.
- Capacity basis: Net summer capacity (MW), i.e., the maximum output of a generator during peak summer conditions, summed across qualifying retired generators; see EIA’s definition of net summer capacity for context (https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/).
- Geography: United States means the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia.

Uncertainty: Although EIA also publishes articles on planned retirements, actual retirements can differ due to market conditions, policy, reliability needs, and fuel price dynamics—creating genuine uncertainty about whether the cumulative 2025 (Jan–Nov) retirements exceed 10.0 GW.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory (Form EIA-860M) November 2025 release (the dataset reflecting retirements dated through November 2025), accessible at https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia860m/.

Event window and time zone:
- Count retirements with effective retirement dates between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. If only a month/year is provided in the data, treat the effective date as the last calendar day of that month for inclusion.

Units counted (inclusion rules):
- Include generator-level records where:
  1) Primary energy source is coal (EIA codes BIT, SUB, LIG, WC, RC), and
  2) Operational status is “retired” (or EIA-860M equivalent retired status code) with an effective retirement date in the window, and
  3) The plant is located in the United States (50 states or DC).
- Capacity metric to sum: the generator’s Net Summer Capacity (MW) as reported in EIA-860M (use the capacity applicable at the time of retirement, if a specific “retired capacity” field is shown; otherwise use the last reported net summer capacity for the generator). Convert MW to GW by dividing by 1,000. Compare the total precisely to 10,000 MW.

Exclusions and edge cases:
- Exclude units listed as cancelled (never operated), temporarily out of service, long-term standby, test mode, or similar non-retired statuses.
- Conversions/fuel-switches: Count only if the coal-fired generator itself is marked “retired.” If a coal unit converts to another fuel without an intervening “retired” status, it shall not be counted.
- Reactivations: If a generator appears with a retirement effective date in the window but is not listed as “retired” in the November 2025 EIA-860M (e.g., subsequently reactivated), it is not counted.
- Multi-fuel plants: Count only the generator records whose primary energy source is coded as coal.
- Partial retirements: Count generator retirements only at the generator level; partial derates that do not change status to “retired” do not count.

Threshold and outcomes:
- Resolve YES if the summed net summer capacity of qualifying retirements strictly exceeds 10.0 GW (>10,000 MW).
- Resolve NO if the sum is less than or equal to 10.0 GW (≤10,000 MW).

Fallback if the November 2025 EIA-860M is not posted by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC:
- Use the most recent EIA-860M release available by that time and apply the same inclusion rules to retirements with effective dates through 2025-11-30. If multiple EIA files exist (e.g., CSV and XLSX), any consistent one may be used. If a tie-break is needed (e.g., conflicting versions), prefer the latest timestamped release available on the EIA-860M page as of the resolution time.

question: Will the EU open Cluster 1 (“Fundamentals”) of accession negotiations with Ukraine by 31 December 2025?
background: Context as of 2025-09-30: • Formal opening of accession talks: The EU held the first Intergovernmental/Accession Conference with Ukraine on 25 June 2024 to open accession negotiations. • Clusters approach and order: Under the revised enlargement methodology, negotiating chapters are grouped into clusters; the negotiating framework indicates the “fundamentals” cluster (also referred to as “Cluster 1: Fundamentals”) is opened first. The 2024 Enlargement Package reiterates that, subject to conditions, the Commission looks forward to opening negotiations on clusters starting with the fundamentals as soon as possible in 2025. • What “Fundamentals” covers: In the revised methodology, the Fundamentals cluster encompasses the rule of law, fundamental rights, the functioning of democratic institutions, public administration reform, and the economic criteria. • Status signal in mid-2025: The European Council on 26 June 2025 “took good note of the assessment of the Commission that the fundamentals cluster is ready to be opened,” and invited the Council to take next steps on a merit-based approach, with clusters opened when conditions are met. • How an opening is officially announced: Council of the EU (Consilium) press releases following Accession/Intergovernmental Conferences use explicit formulations such as “opened negotiations with [country] on Cluster 1: Fundamentals.” For example, for Albania on 15 October 2024: “The second meeting of the Accession Conference with Albania at ministerial level opened negotiations with Albania on Cluster 1: Fundamentals …” and it notes that Fundamentals are “the first to be opened and the last to be closed”. • Commission communications: The European Commission’s DG NEAR also publishes official news/press material on such steps (e.g., announcing the opening of accession negotiations with Ukraine on 25 June 2024). Definitions and clarifications: • “Cluster 1: Fundamentals” (or “the fundamentals cluster”) refers to the first cluster in the revised enlargement methodology, covering rule of law, fundamental rights, democratic institutions, public administration reform, and economic criteria. • “Open (opening) negotiations on the Fundamentals cluster” means an EU Accession/Intergovernmental Conference decision explicitly noting that negotiations with Ukraine on Cluster 1: Fundamentals are opened, communicated in an official EU press release (see example phrasing for Albania above). • “EU Accession/Intergovernmental Conference” refers to the formal intergovernmental meeting between the EU and an acceding country at which negotiating steps are taken and announced in Consilium press releases (see the 25 June 2024 Ukraine press release as an example of this format). • Time zone: All dates/times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Additional resources for concept definitions: • EU enlargement: acquis communautaire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquis_communautaire) • EU enlargement methodology and clusters (overview page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_European_Union) Note: These general references are provided for concept clarity; resolution will rely on official EU sources cited below.
resolution_criteria: Question: Will the EU open Cluster 1 (“Fundamentals”) of accession negotiations with Ukraine between 2025-01-01 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC? Resolution: • YES if, within the stated time window, an official press release on consilium.europa.eu (Council/Consilium) about an Accession/Intergovernmental Conference explicitly states that negotiations with Ukraine on Cluster 1 (the “Fundamentals” cluster) are opened. Acceptable formulations include, but are not limited to: “opened negotiations with Ukraine on Cluster 1: Fundamentals,” “opened the Fundamentals cluster with Ukraine,” or “opening of negotiations on the Fundamentals cluster with Ukraine,” provided the context clearly indicates that Cluster 1 negotiations are opened, not merely planned or deemed ready. • As a fallback, if and only if no relevant Consilium press release is available, a European Commission official news/press page explicitly stating that negotiations on Cluster 1: Fundamentals with Ukraine were opened during the time window will suffice. • The following do NOT count as opening: statements about readiness, intent, timelines, or preparatory/screening progress (e.g., “ready to be opened”) without an explicit statement that the cluster has been opened. • Publication timing: The qualifying press release (or Commission news/press page in the fallback case) must be published by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC. • Primary source to check: Consilium press releases for Accession/Intergovernmental Conferences with Ukraine (press/press-releases or meeting pages). Background support: – Accession negotiations were formally opened with Ukraine on 25 June 2024. – The fundamentals cluster is opened first under the negotiating framework; the Commission looked forward to opening clusters, starting with fundamentals, as soon as possible in 2025. – On 26 June 2025, the European Council noted the Commission’s assessment that the fundamentals cluster is ready to be opened and invited next steps on a merit-based basis. Adjudication notes: • If multiple official sources exist and are consistent, prefer the Consilium press release. If sources conflict, the Consilium press release takes precedence. • If no qualifying official EU source exists by the deadline, resolve NO. • Examples of qualifying phrasing can be taken by analogy from Albania’s 15 October 2024 press release documenting a Fundamentals cluster opening.

question: EU: Will the European Commission publish an official legal act between Oct 1 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC) imposing a 25%–50% ad valorem duty on imports of Chinese‑origin steel (CN Chapter 72) or articles of iron or steel (CN Chapter 73)?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Media reporting indicates the European Commission is preparing China‑specific steel tariffs. On Sept 25–26, 2025, Reuters (citing Handelsblatt) reported the Commission plans to impose tariffs of 25% to 50% on Chinese steel and related products “in the next few weeks”.
- In her Sept 10, 2025 State of the Union address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Commission “will propose a new, long-term trade instrument to succeed the expiring steel safeguards,” signalling forthcoming structural changes to EU steel trade policy.
- On July 18, 2025, the Commission launched a consultation on future measures to safeguard the EU steel sector and reiterated a commitment in its Steel and Metals Action Plan to present a legislative proposal by Q3 2025 to replace the current safeguard regime, which legally expires on 30 June 2026.
- Separately, on Oct 1, 2025, Reuters reported the Commission plans to propose cutting steel import quotas and hiking duties on over‑quota volumes to 50%, with a package expected to be unveiled around Oct 7; these are sector‑wide safeguard proposals, not necessarily China‑specific.
- Earlier in 2025, the Commission tightened the existing safeguard measure (TRQs) with changes announced on March 25, 2025, including reducing liberalisation and restricting use of unused quotas, with staged entry into force from April 1 and July 1, 2025.
- The Commission routinely imposes trade defence duties via Commission Implementing Regulations published in the Official Journal (OJ). For example, Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1508 imposed a definitive anti‑dumping duty on certain organic coated steel products originating in the People’s Republic of China.
- The Official Journal’s electronic edition on EUR‑Lex is the authentic source for EU legal acts; the OJ is published in two series, with the L (Legislation) series containing legal acts. As of July 2013, only the electronic edition is authentic.

Definitions relevant to this question:
- “Ad valorem duty”: A duty whose amount is a percentage of the value of the imported good (i.e., based on customs value), as per the general definition of an ad valorem tax/duty.
- “Chinese‑origin”: Origin determined under the EU’s non‑preferential rules of origin in Article 60 of the Union Customs Code and its Delegated Act: goods are of Chinese origin if they are wholly obtained in China or, when multiple countries are involved, if they underwent their last substantial transformation in China.
- “Steel (CN Chapter 72) or articles of iron or steel (CN Chapter 73)”: Operationalized here using the Harmonized System/Combined Nomenclature chapters—Chapter 72 covers iron and steel; Chapter 73 covers articles of iron or steel. The Combined Nomenclature (CN) is the EU’s tariff and statistical nomenclature used to classify goods for customs and trade measures.

Why this is a high‑entropy, plausibly resolvable question by year‑end:
- Credible reporting points to imminent 25%–50% China‑specific steel tariffs, but as of Oct 1 they have not yet been officially adopted; at the same time, a separate safeguard package (including a 50% over‑quota duty) is being proposed, complicating the policy landscape and leaving room for either outcome by Dec 31, 2025.
- EU trade defence actions are regularly announced and published in the OJ, making verification straightforward.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve YES if, between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-01 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31, the European Commission publishes in the Official Journal (OJ) L series an authentic legal act (e.g., a Commission Implementing Regulation) that imposes an ad valorem duty rate within the inclusive range 25.0% to 50.0% on imports of products classified under CN Chapter 72 (iron and steel) or CN Chapter 73 (articles of iron or steel) that are specified as “originating in the People’s Republic of China.” Resolve NO otherwise.

Eligibility and clarifications:
- Acceptable legal acts: Commission Implementing Regulations imposing provisional or definitive anti‑dumping or countervailing duties, or other Commission legal acts that expressly impose an ad valorem duty on imports “originating in the People’s Republic of China.” Acts must be published in the OJ L series’ authentic electronic edition on EUR‑Lex. Example of format/reference only: Commission Implementing Regulations imposing anti‑dumping duties on Chinese steel products (e.g., 2025/1508).
- Product scope: The act must cover goods with CN headings within Chapter 72 or Chapter 73. For operationalization, “steel and steel‑related products” in this question strictly means CN Chapter 72 (iron and steel) and CN Chapter 73 (articles of iron or steel).
- Country of origin: “Chinese‑origin” is determined by EU non‑preferential rules of origin (wholly obtained or last substantial transformation in China). The legal act must explicitly state the origin as the People’s Republic of China.
- Duty type and level: The duty must be expressed as an ad valorem percentage rate within 25.0%–50.0% inclusive. If an act lists multiple company‑specific or product‑specific ad valorem rates, the criterion is met if any listed rate applicable to Chinese‑origin goods within CN 72 or 73 falls within this inclusive range. Acts that set only specific (amount-per‑ton) duties, minimum import prices, or formulas without an explicit ad valorem percentage do not count.
- Exclusions: Origin‑neutral safeguard measures (e.g., over‑quota safeguard duties or tariff‑rate quota changes applying to all origins) do not count, even if they result in a 50% rate, unless the act explicitly imposes a country‑specific ad valorem duty on China. VAT, excise taxes, carbon border measures (e.g., CBAM), or other non‑customs duties are excluded.
- Timing: Only acts published between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-01 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31 are eligible.

Resolution procedure:
1) Primary source: Check the Official Journal L series on EUR‑Lex (daily view) for the relevant period to identify Commission Implementing Regulations or other Commission legal acts imposing ad valorem duties on Chinese‑origin steel (CN 72) or articles of iron or steel (CN 73).
2) Verify that the act explicitly states origin as the People’s Republic of China and provides an ad valorem percentage rate within 25.0%–50.0%. If multiple rates are listed, confirm that at least one qualifying rate applies to products in CN 72 or 73.
3) If such an act is found, resolve YES; if none is found for the period, resolve NO.

Notes and definitions sources for resolvability and terms: Official Journal authenticity and L/C series ; example of Commission Implementing Regulation imposing duties on Chinese steel ; ad valorem definition ; non‑preferential origin rules ; Combined Nomenclature role and chapters 72 and 73 scope.

Rationale for forecasters:
- Reported plans for 25%–50% China‑specific steel tariffs “within weeks,” an announced steel policy package, and an ongoing shift from expiring safeguards create a plausible window for new Commission legal acts before year‑end.

question: Will Meta or Adam Mosseri publicly state that Threads has at least 500 million monthly active users between October 15 and December 31, 2025?
background:
Overview and current status as of 2025-09-30:
- Product in question: Threads is Meta’s text-based social network. For term clarity, see the Threads (social network) page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(social_network).
- Recent official user numbers: On 2025-08-12, Adam Mosseri (Head of Instagram) publicly stated that Threads has “more than 400 million monthly active users (MAUs).” TechCrunch reported the announcement and linked Mosseri’s post; the article also notes Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had said in late April that Threads topped 350M MAUs.
- Usage momentum: Third-party analytics (Similarweb) cited by TechCrunch show Threads recorded 115.1M daily active users (DAUs) on mobile (iOS/Android) in June 2025, up 127.8% YoY. In late September 2025, Forbes (citing Similarweb) reported Threads briefly surpassed X (formerly Twitter) in global mobile DAUs for the first time and included multiple daily comparisons from mid-to-late September. Forbes also reported a Zuckerberg remark that Instagram now has 3 billion monthly active users.
- Why this is non-trivial: The event requires both reaching the threshold and a qualifying public disclosure by a specific set of official speakers/channels within the stated window. Meta does not routinely publish MAUs for Threads on a fixed schedule, so whether they will state ≥500M MAUs before year-end is uncertain despite strong growth indicators.

Key terms and definitions for this question:
- “Threads”: Meta’s social networking product branded “Threads.” It must be unambiguously the Threads service (not Instagram, Facebook, or WhatsApp). Reference link for context: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(social_network).
- “Monthly active users” (“MAUs”): For resolution purposes here, this means the metric explicitly named “monthly active users,” “MAUs,” or “monthly active people” by Meta or the speaker in the qualifying statement. Statements about “daily active users” (DAUs), “weekly active users,” “registered users/accounts,” “downloads,” “web visits,” or similar do not count.
- “Publicly state”: A statement that is published to the general public (not a private communication) via one of the qualifying official channels listed below.
- “Qualifying official channels”: Any of the following:
  1) Meta or Instagram official websites/blogs/newsrooms (e.g., https://about.fb.com/news/),
  2) Meta SEC filings (e.g., on EDGAR: https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/#/category/company),
  3) Direct public posts by Mark Zuckerberg or Adam Mosseri on their official social profiles on Threads, Instagram, or Facebook.
- “Qualifying phrasing”: The statement must explicitly assert that Threads has at least 500,000,000 monthly active users. Acceptable phrasings include “≥500 million MAUs,” “at least 500 million monthly active users,” “over 500 million monthly active users,” etc., provided it clearly refers to Threads.
- Language: Statements in any language are acceptable if they meet the criteria above; translations are acceptable if the original post is accessible and the numeric threshold is unambiguous.

Status quo data points (for context, not for resolution):
- 400M MAUs announcement by Mosseri on 2025-08-12.
- 115.1M mobile DAUs in June 2025 per Similarweb (as cited by TechCrunch).
- Threads surpassing X in mobile DAUs at several points in mid-to-late September 2025 (as cited by Forbes/Similarweb).

Notes on what will NOT count:
- Any third-party estimate without an official Meta/Zuckerberg/Mosseri statement does not count.
- Statements that do not mention “monthly” (e.g., only “users,” “DAUs,” “web visits”) do not count.
- Combined or aggregated metrics that include services other than Threads (e.g., “Instagram+Threads”) do not count.
- Statements published outside the specified window do not count, even if reported during the window.
resolution_criteria:
This resolves to Yes if and only if all of the following are true:
- Time window: A qualifying statement is published between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2026-01-01 07:59:59 UTC (the latter is equivalent to 2025-12-31 23:59:59 Pacific Time).
- Speaker/channel: The statement appears on a qualifying official channel, defined above (Meta/Instagram official site/blog/newsroom; Meta SEC filing; direct public posts by Mark Zuckerberg or Adam Mosseri on their official Threads/Instagram/Facebook profiles).
- Content: The statement explicitly says that Threads has at least 500,000,000 monthly active users (MAUs), using unambiguous phrasing that clearly refers to Threads.

Acceptable resolution sources:
- A URL to the qualifying statement itself (e.g., a Meta/Instagram Newsroom post; a post on Zuckerberg’s or Mosseri’s official profile; an SEC filing on EDGAR).
- Reputable media coverage (e.g., TechCrunch, The Verge, Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) only if it directly quotes or embeds the qualifying statement and the original statement is publicly accessible via a link. Coverage may be used to aid verification but the original qualifying statement must exist and be publicly accessible.

Resolution process:
- YES: Verifier confirms a qualifying statement was published within the window that meets all criteria above.
- NO: If no qualifying statement meeting the criteria is found by 2026-01-01 07:59:59 UTC, resolve No.

Context references informing the background (not used for resolution unless they themselves contain a qualifying statement within the window): TechCrunch’s report of Mosseri’s 400M MAUs announcement and Similarweb’s June 2025 DAUs ; Forbes’ report of Threads briefly surpassing X in mobile DAUs and Zuckerberg’s Instagram 3B MAUs remark.

question: Will Nigeria’s crude oil production (OPEC MOMR secondary sources) be ≥ 1.60 mb/d for the latest month shown in the December 2025 MOMR?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is published on a fixed 2025 schedule, with the December 2025 issue scheduled for Thursday, 11 December 2025. This ensures the question will resolve within the October 15–December 31, 2025 window.
- The MOMR contains a standard table reporting “crude oil production based on secondary sources” for countries participating in the Declaration of Cooperation (DoC), including Nigeria, expressed in thousand barrels per day (tb/d). Recent reports list Nigeria’s values as follows:
  • July 2025 MOMR (latest month shown: June 2025): Nigeria 1,547 tb/d; prior months: May 2025 1,528 tb/d; April 2025 1,522 tb/d.
  • August 2025 MOMR (latest month shown: July 2025): Nigeria 1,559 tb/d; prior months: June 2025 1,543 tb/d; May 2025 1,513 tb/d.
- Units and conversions: tb/d means thousand barrels per day; mb/d means million barrels per day. 1 mb/d = 1,000 tb/d. Therefore, 1.60 mb/d equals 1,600 tb/d. Definitions: “barrel” is a unit of volume for crude oil, and “barrels per day” (b/d) is a production flow unit; see reference definitions (e.g., Wikipedia: “Crude oil” and “Barrels per day”).

Key term definitions for this question:
- Nigeria: The country officially known as the Federal Republic of Nigeria (see country definition, e.g., Wikipedia: “Nigeria”).
- Crude oil: Use OPEC’s category labeled “crude oil” as presented in the MOMR “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” table. This is the value used for resolution, without adding or subtracting any other categories.
- Secondary sources: As labeled in the MOMR table (“based on secondary sources”). For the purposes of resolution, only the figure in the relevant table for Nigeria will be used as the measure.
- Latest month shown: The most recent calendar month presented as a column in the December 2025 MOMR table titled “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d.” In typical MOMR tables, the latest month is the rightmost column among the month columns.

Why this threshold is plausible:
- Nigeria’s reported production on a secondary-source basis rose from 1,522–1,528 tb/d in April–May 2025, to 1,547 tb/d in June and 1,559 tb/d in July 2025. A threshold of 1.60 mb/d (1,600 tb/d) is close to recent values, making either outcome plausible by year-end.

Where to find the resolution source:
- The December 2025 MOMR will be available via OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report page (opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html), which lists the 2025 release calendar including 11 December 2025.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the December 2025 OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) as published on the OPEC website.

Resolution rule:
- Identify the December 2025 MOMR and open the report’s table titled “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d.”
- Locate the Nigeria row and the value for the latest month shown (the most recent calendar month presented as a column in that table).
- If that Nigeria value is ≥ 1,600 tb/d (equivalently ≥ 1.60 mb/d), resolve Yes. Otherwise, resolve No.

Source of truth and timing:
- Use the December 2025 MOMR hosted on OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report page, which lists the 2025 release dates including Thursday, 11 December 2025. The table format and data series (Nigeria crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d) are evidenced in recent 2025 MOMRs.
- Resolution will be based on the version of the December 2025 MOMR available on OPEC’s website as of 23:59 UTC on 2025-12-31. If multiple versions exist, use the latest version available on the OPEC site by that cutoff.

Operational notes:
- Measurement units: tb/d = thousand barrels per day; mb/d = million barrels per day. Conversion: 1 mb/d = 1,000 tb/d.
- No other data sources (e.g., direct communications, national agencies, other OPEC tables such as NGLs) will be considered—only the specified table in the December 2025 MOMR.
- If, contrary to schedule, the December 2025 MOMR is not published by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, resolve based on the most recent MOMR published in 2025 by that cutoff, applying the same table and rules. The schedule indicates publication on 11 December 2025, so this contingency is unlikely.

question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, will the Council of the European Union adopt at least one Iran-related sanctions listing that adds 15 or more new persons or entities to EU restrictive measures?
background: Status quo as of 2025-09-30: On 2025-09-29, the Council of the European Union announced that it reimposed nuclear-related restrictive measures on Iran (“snapback”), covering travel bans, asset freezes, and sectoral economic/financial sanctions, following the reimposition of UN sanctions [4961a]. The EU’s Iran-related sanctions frameworks currently include: (a) the nuclear proliferation framework based on Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 ; (b) the human-rights framework based on Council Decision 2011/235/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 359/2011, under which the Council has continued to list individuals and entities (e.g., 2025-04-14: seven individuals and two entities) ; and (c) the framework addressing Iran’s military support to Russia’s war of aggression and to armed groups in the Middle East and Red Sea region, based on Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532 and Council Regulation (EU) 2023/1529, the scope of which was broadened on 2024-11-18 by Council Decision (CFSP) 2024/2894 to explicitly cover support to armed groups and entities in the Middle East and the Red Sea region. Recent listing sizes in Iran-related actions demonstrate variability and plausibility around the 15-target threshold. For example, on 2024-10-14, the Council sanctioned seven individuals and seven entities (14 total) in response to Iran’s missile and drone transfers to Russia , while on 2025-04-14 under the human-rights framework, the Council listed seven individuals and two entities (nine total). The Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU) is the authentic daily publication of EU legal acts and is the primary source to verify adopted listings; since 2013, electronic editions on EUR-Lex are legally authentic.
resolution_criteria:
Definitions and scope:
- Time window: Events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.
- Council of the European Union: The EU institution in which ministers of member states adopt EU acts.
- Official Journal of the European Union (OJEU): The legally authentic electronic gazette of EU acts, published daily by the Publications Office; electronic editions are legally authentic.
- Iran-related restrictive measures frameworks (eligible regimes): Any EU sanctions framework whose legal acts expressly target Iran, namely:
  (a) Nuclear proliferation-related restrictive measures against Iran (e.g., acts under Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012) ;
  (b) Serious human-rights violations in Iran (e.g., acts under Council Decision 2011/235/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 359/2011) ;
  (c) Iran’s military support to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and to armed groups and entities in the Middle East and Red Sea region (e.g., acts under Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532 and Council Regulation (EU) 2023/1529, as amended, including by Council Decision (CFSP) 2024/2894).
- Listing (for this question): The adoption of a Council Implementing Decision and/or Council Implementing Regulation (collectively, “implementing acts”) that adds named natural persons (“individuals”) or legal persons, entities or bodies (“entities”) to an annex of one of the eligible Iran-related sanctions frameworks above. Implementing acts typically specify additions to annexes by name and identifying details in the OJEU; Council press releases often summarize and state counts.
- “Adds 15 or more new persons or entities”: In a single implementing act, the number of newly added entries (individuals and/or entities) listed in the act’s annex(es) is greater than or equal to 15. Only additions count toward the threshold; delistings, modifications, or re-listings/updates do not reduce the count. Multiple distinct acts published or announced on the same day are each evaluated separately; cumulative totals across multiple acts do not count unless at least one individual act meets the threshold.

Resolution:
- Resolve YES if, within the time window, at least one eligible implementing act either: (i) is published in the OJEU (EUR-Lex) with annex(es) that newly add 15 or more individuals and/or entities to an eligible Iran-related framework, or (ii) is announced via a Council of the EU press release dated within the window and clearly states that 15 or more individuals and/or entities are being added under an eligible Iran-related framework. If both an OJEU publication and a Council press release exist and provide differing counts for the same act, the OJEU publication governs.
- Otherwise resolve NO.

Primary sources for resolution:
- Official Journal publications (EUR-Lex) for implementing acts under the frameworks listed above.
- Council of the EU press releases on consilium.europa.eu for announcements and counts when OJEU publication is not yet available by the end of the window [4961a, fc2e61, 3b581d].

Notes for verifiers:
- The 2025-09-29 snapback press release provides current context but falls outside the window; it is included here to frame the status quo [4961a].
- Examples of press releases that state explicit counts include 2024-10-14 (seven individuals and seven entities) and 2025-04-14 (seven individuals and two entities).

question: Will full-year FY2026 U.S. appropriations be enacted into law by December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo and context as of 2025-10-01: The U.S. federal fiscal year 2026 (FY2026) runs from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026. On October 1, 2025, much of the U.S. government began a shutdown after Congress failed to reach a funding agreement; the Senate had rejected a short-term funding bill that would have extended operations through November 21, 2025. Congress.gov’s Appropriations Status Table for FY2026 tracks progress of the twelve regular appropriations measures and notes relevant continuing resolution activity (e.g., H.R. 5371; S. 2882). Uncertainty remains over whether lawmakers will enact full-year FY2026 appropriations by year-end, potentially via an omnibus or a set of minibuses.

Key definitions for forecasters:
- Fiscal Year 2026 (FY2026): The U.S. federal fiscal year that runs from 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30.
- Appropriations bill (United States): Legislation that appropriates federal funds to government departments, agencies, and programs; Congress typically passes twelve regular appropriations bills each fiscal year.
- Continuing resolution (CR): Temporary appropriations legislation used when regular appropriations are not enacted; generally continues prior funding levels for a defined period to avoid a shutdown.
- Omnibus spending bill: A single consolidated appropriations bill that packages multiple regular appropriations into one larger measure; a “minibus” packages more than one but fewer than all appropriations bills.

Canonical list of the twelve regular FY2026 appropriations measures (subcommittee jurisdictions), per Congress.gov’s FY2026 Appropriations Status Table :
1) Agriculture
2) Commerce–Justice–Science
3) Defense
4) Energy–Water
5) Financial Services
6) Homeland Security
7) Interior–Environment
8) Labor–HHS–Education
9) Legislative Branch
10) Military Construction–Veterans Affairs
11) State–Foreign Operations (House) / National Security–Dept of State (Senate)
12) Transportation–HUD

Primary source to monitor and resolve this question:
- Congress.gov Appropriations Status Table: FY2026 (tracks each bill’s status through “Presidential Approval” and references continuing resolutions and consolidated measures).

Why this is uncertain and non-trivial:
- Current conditions include an active shutdown and competing strategies (CRs vs. full-year appropriations; omnibus/minibus tactics). Negotiations across chambers and the White House, plus potential policy riders, create genuine uncertainty over enactment of full-year FY2026 funding before year-end.
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Definitions and scope:
- “Full-year FY2026 appropriations” means statutes enacted (i.e., reaching “Presidential Approval” status on Congress.gov) that provide regular appropriations through 2026-09-30 for all federal programs and activities covered by the twelve subcommittee jurisdictions listed in the FY2026 Appropriations Status Table.
- This can occur via: (a) enactment of all twelve regular appropriations bills individually, or (b) enactment of one or more consolidated measures (an omnibus or multiple minibuses) that collectively provide full-year FY2026 appropriations coverage for all twelve jurisdictions.
- Funding via continuing resolutions (CRs) does not count as “full-year FY2026 appropriations” for any jurisdiction that remains under a CR on the resolution date.

Eligible enactment window:
- For purposes of this market, enactments counted toward “Yes” may occur at any time between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, provided they meet the definition above.

Resolution:
- Yes: By 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, Congress.gov shows that (i) each of the twelve FY2026 regular appropriations jurisdictions has reached “Presidential Approval,” or (ii) one or more consolidated appropriations statutes enacted by that time collectively provide full-year FY2026 appropriations across all twelve jurisdictions.
- No: Otherwise, including if any jurisdiction remains funded via a CR (i.e., lacks full-year FY2026 appropriations) as of the resolution timestamp.

Primary source of truth:
- Congress.gov Appropriations Status Table: FY2026, including the “Presidential Approval” column and any notes indicating coverage via consolidated appropriations (omnibus/minibus) and the presence of continuing resolutions.

Verification steps for resolvers:
1) At or immediately after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, open the Congress.gov FY2026 Appropriations Status Table and check each of the twelve jurisdictions for “Presidential Approval.” If all twelve show “Presidential Approval,” resolve Yes.
2) If fewer than twelve show “Presidential Approval,” check whether an enacted consolidated appropriations statute (omnibus/minibus) covers the remaining jurisdictions with full-year FY2026 appropriations. Congress.gov’s table and accompanying bill entries typically indicate divisions/coverage; if such coverage exists across all jurisdictions, resolve Yes.
3) If any jurisdiction lacks full-year appropriations coverage by the resolution timestamp (e.g., remains under a CR), resolve No.

question: Will the December 2025 WASDE project the U.S. 2025/26 corn yield at ≤ 186.0 bushels per harvested acre?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- USDA’s World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) is a monthly report released by USDA’s Office of the Chief Economist at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time (ET). The published 2025 release schedule includes December 9, 2025.
- In the August 2025 WASDE, USDA reported: “The season’s first survey-based corn yield forecast, at a record 188.8 bushels per acre, is 7.8 bushels higher than last month’s projection.” This is the first survey-based estimate for the 2025/26 marketing year.
- In the September 2025 WASDE, USDA lowered the projected national average U.S. corn yield for 2025/26 to 186.7 bushels per harvested acre.
- The yield metric used in the WASDE U.S. corn supply-and-use table is labeled “Yield per Harvested Acre Bushels” (unit: bushels per acre).
- Definitions of key terms used in this question:
  • WASDE: A monthly USDA report providing forecasts for U.S. and global agricultural commodities. It is prepared by Interagency Commodity Estimates Committees chaired by USDA’s World Agricultural Outlook Board, and is released at 12:00 noon ET.
  • Corn (maize): In U.S. usage, “corn” refers to Zea mays (maize), the cereal grain widely cultivated and used for food, feed, and industrial purposes.
  • Bushel (bu.): In U.S. grain markets, a bushel for corn is standardized at 56 pounds at a reference moisture (commonly 15.5%).
  • Acre: A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet (approximately 4,047 square meters).
  • 2025/26 marketing year (for corn): The U.S. corn marketing year runs from September 1 to August 31; thus, 2025/26 refers to September 1, 2025–August 31, 2026.

Why this is high-entropy and interesting: The August survey-based estimate (188.8 bu/acre) was reduced in September (186.7 bu/acre), showing meaningful in-season uncertainty. A threshold of 186.0 bu/acre lies close to the latest projection, making both “Yes” and “No” plausible outcomes as additional harvest data and revisions feed into the October/November/December WASDEs.
resolution_criteria:
- Resolution date and source: This question will resolve using the figure reported in the USDA December 2025 WASDE released at 12:00 p.m. ET on December 9, 2025. The resolution source is the report as posted on USDA’s official WASDE page (USDA Office of the Chief Economist: WASDE Report) on the release date.
- Precisely which number will be read: The U.S. 2025/26 corn “Yield per Harvested Acre” as printed in the U.S. corn supply-and-use table, labeled “Yield per Harvested Acre Bushels” (unit: bushels per acre).
- Threshold and decision rule: If the printed value for the U.S. 2025/26 corn “Yield per Harvested Acre” in the December 2025 WASDE is ≤ 186.0, resolve Yes; otherwise resolve No. The comparison is made to the value as printed in the December report; if the number is printed without a decimal (e.g., “186”), it is treated as 186.0 for threshold purposes.
- Timing detail: The value used for resolution will be the one published on the USDA WASDE page as of 23:59 UTC on December 9, 2025. Any subsequent revisions or errata posted after that cutoff will not affect resolution. All times are provided in ET for release (as per USDA) and a UTC cutoff for clarity.
- Scope clarifications:
  • “U.S. 2025/26 corn” refers to the U.S. national average for the corn marketing year September 1, 2025–August 31, 2026.
  • “Yield per Harvested Acre” refers specifically to the national yield metric (bushels per harvested acre) in the WASDE U.S. corn table.
  • Units: “bushels” and “acres” as defined in U.S. customary usage; for corn, a bushel is standardized at 56 pounds; an acre is 43,560 square feet.
- Fallback: If, contrary to the published schedule, USDA does not release a December 2025 WASDE by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, the question will be resolved using the most recently released WASDE in December 2025 (if any). If no WASDE is released in December 2025, the market will consider the question non-resolvable; however, USDA’s official schedule lists a December 9, 2025 release at 12:00 p.m. ET.

Primary references for verification on resolution day:
- USDA Office of the Chief Economist: WASDE Report page with the December 2025 release (12:00 p.m. ET).
- For contextual benchmarks prior to resolution: August 2025 WASDE (188.8 bu/acre, first survey-based estimate) ; September 2025 WASDE (186.7 bu/acre).

question: By 23:59 on 31 December 2025 (NZDT), will New Zealand’s Official Cash Rate be 2.50% or lower?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Definition: The Official Cash Rate (OCR) is the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s (RBNZ) key policy interest rate used to influence short‑term interest rates and support its price stability mandate. The OCR affects the interest rates on deposits and loans that registered banks have with the RBNZ, which in turn influences banks’ retail lending and deposit rates (see RBNZ overview page: https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/monetary-policy/about-monetary-policy/the-official-cash-rate). A general description of the OCR as the bank rate set by the central bank in New Zealand (and Australia) is also available on Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_cash_rate.
- Review cadence and publication: The RBNZ’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) reviews the OCR seven times a year and publishes decisions and statements on its website, including a prominent display of the current OCR and the next scheduled update time. As of the latest page snapshot, the OCR was shown as 3.0%, last updated at 2:00 pm on 20 Aug 2025, with the next update scheduled for 2:00 pm on 8 Oct 2025 (all local New Zealand time) (https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/monetary-policy/about-monetary-policy/the-official-cash-rate).
- Recent status: On 20 Aug 2025, the MPC voted to decrease the OCR by 25 basis points to 3.0% (official RBNZ news release: https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/hub/news/2025/08/ocr-lowered-to-3-percent). The RBNZ maintains a consolidated list and timeline of past OCR decisions and associated documents dating back to 1999 (https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/monetary-policy/monetary-policy-decisions).
- Timezone for resolution: New Zealand observes New Zealand Daylight Time (NZDT, UTC+13) during the summer period that includes 31 December. The IANA timezone for most of New Zealand is Pacific/Auckland (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_New_Zealand).

Why this question and threshold: With the OCR currently at 3.0% and at least two scheduled decision opportunities remaining before year‑end, a threshold of 2.50% (two 25 bp cuts below today’s level) creates meaningful uncertainty while remaining realistic, encouraging research into New Zealand macro conditions, inflation, growth, and RBNZ communications.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve “Yes” if the Official Cash Rate (OCR) of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) in effect at 23:59 on 31 December 2025, New Zealand Daylight Time (NZDT; IANA timezone Pacific/Auckland, UTC+13 during December) is less than or equal to 2.50%. Resolve “No” otherwise.

Key definitions and clarifications:
- “Official Cash Rate (OCR)”: The policy rate set by the RBNZ that influences overnight interest rates for banks, as defined on the RBNZ’s OCR explainer page (https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/monetary-policy/about-monetary-policy/the-official-cash-rate) and consistent with general definitions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_cash_rate). This question refers to the headline OCR level, not projections or forecasts.
- “In effect at 23:59 on 31 December 2025 (NZDT)”: The rate level that is operative at that exact local time in New Zealand. Note that New Zealand is on NZDT (UTC+13) on 31 December; comparisons are made in local time, not UTC.
- Numerical interpretation: “≤ 2.50%” includes exactly 2.50%.

Primary resolution source(s):
1) RBNZ’s past decisions page, which lists each OCR decision and rate level with dates: https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/monetary-policy/monetary-policy-decisions.
2) RBNZ’s OCR explainer/current OCR page, which displays the current OCR and update timestamps: https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/monetary-policy/about-monetary-policy/the-official-cash-rate.

Procedure:
- On or after 1 January 2026 NZDT, check the RBNZ pages above. Determine the OCR that was in effect at 23:59 NZDT on 31 December 2025 using the most recent decision prior to that time (from the “Past monetary policy decisions” page) and/or the displayed current OCR with its last updated time. If both sources are available but differ due to latency or page display issues, the specific RBNZ decision media release linked on the “Past monetary policy decisions” page for the last decision before the cutoff time is the tiebreaker.
- If the RBNZ website is temporarily unavailable, use widely recognized reputable reporting of the latest OCR decision (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, Bloomberg, or major New Zealand outlets) until the official site becomes available again. Once accessible, defer to the official RBNZ materials as above. 

Current baseline (for forecasters’ convenience): As of 20 Aug 2025, the OCR is 3.0% per the RBNZ’s pages; the next scheduled update was listed for 8 Oct 2025 at 2:00 pm local time. The 3.0% rate stems from the 20 Aug 2025 MPC decision to cut by 25 bp.

question: Will the House or Senate Judiciary Committee formally announce an investigation into the late-September 2025 FBI agent firings between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On September 26–27, 2025, major outlets reported that the FBI fired more than a dozen agents; CNN reported 15 agents, while AP said roughly 20, and Reuters described sources placing the number between 15 and 22. Several of the terminated agents were among those photographed kneeling during 2020 racial justice protests, an action some described as a de‑escalation tactic. The FBI Agents Association (FBIAA) condemned the firings and, per AP, called on Congress to investigate; an earlier FBIAA statement on 2025-08-07 warned that summary firings without due process would undermine safety and urged FBI leadership to follow established legal processes. Congressional oversight activity around the FBI was already salient in mid-September: the Senate Judiciary Committee held its annual FBI oversight hearing on 2025-09-16, with Chairman Grassley publishing opening remarks and materials on the committee’s official press page. On 2025-09-17, House Judiciary Committee Democrats issued a press release criticizing Director Patel for “sacking” experienced agents and endangering public safety, though that document focused on broader concerns and did not itself announce a formal committee investigation specifically into the late-September firings.

Key definitions and links a forecaster may need:
- “United States House Committee on the Judiciary” (House Judiciary Committee) is a standing committee overseeing the administration of justice within federal courts, agencies, and law enforcement. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_the_Judiciary. Official committee site and press pages (House majority): https://judiciary.house.gov/.
- “United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary” (Senate Judiciary Committee) is a standing committee overseeing DOJ and related matters, including the FBI. Background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary. Official committee site and press pages: https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/.
- “Late-September 2025 FBI agent firings” refers to the firings reported on 2025-09-26 and 2025-09-27 involving “more than a dozen” FBI agents, including some who were photographed kneeling during 2020 protests.

Why this could plausibly resolve either way before year-end: There is live controversy and pressure (including a public call for congressional investigation per AP) but formal committee investigations require explicit committee action. The committees are active in FBI oversight (e.g., the Senate’s annual oversight hearing), yet it remains uncertain whether they will formally open an investigation focused specifically on these firings.
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive).

Resolve Yes if, during the time window, either the House Judiciary Committee or the Senate Judiciary Committee formally announces an investigation specifically into the “late-September 2025 FBI agent firings,” as defined above. A qualifying announcement must meet at least one of the following conditions:
1) An official press release, webpage, or post published on the committee’s official domain explicitly states that the committee (or one of its subcommittees) is “opening,” “launching,” or “conducting” an “investigation,” “inquiry,” or “probe” focused on the late-September 2025 firings (e.g., judiciary.house.gov for the House Committee; judiciary.senate.gov for the Senate Committee).
