These figures are reported by Agencia EFE and explicitly attributed to the Ministerio del Interior’s latest biweekly balance. As of 31 July 2025, the Canary Islands maritime cumulative was 11,575 people in 191 boats, down 46.1% year over year, per Canarias public broadcaster RTVC citing the Ministry’s 31 July biweekly report.
- Why this threshold: Flows on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands are volatile intra-year; after a slower first half of 2025 relative to 2024, late-year surges remain possible. A 20,000-person cutoff for the Canary maritime subtotal appears plausibly on either side given year-to-date levels as of late July and mid-August 2025.

Key definitions and sources:
- “Irregular arrivals” and “arrivals by sea/maritime arrivals” are taken exactly as counted and presented by the Spanish Ministry of the Interior in its biweekly Informe quincenal series; no external reclassification or adjustment will be made for this question.
- “Canary Islands” refers to the Spanish autonomous community of the Canary Islands; see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands. For resolution we rely solely on the Ministry’s Canary Islands maritime subtotal as presented in the relevant report.
- Official publication page for the series (location where the PDF is expected to be posted): Ministerio del Interior – Balances e Informes: https://www.interior.gob.es/opencms/es/prensa/balances-e-informes/.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution target and timeframe:
- This question refers to the cumulative number of people arriving by sea to the Canary Islands during the period from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 to 2025-12-15 23:59:59 (local time in Spain). The authoritative value will be the cumulative Canary Islands maritime arrivals as presented in the Ministry of the Interior’s biweekly report covering “Datos acumulados desde el 1 de enero al 15 de diciembre de 2025.”

Exact rule:
- Resolve “Yes” if the Ministerio del Interior’s “Informe quincenal sobre inmigración irregular – Datos acumulados desde el 1 de enero al 15 de diciembre de 2025” PDF shows fewer than 20,000 cumulative arrivals for the Canary Islands by sea (the Canary Islands maritime subtotal) as of 15 December 2025. Resolve “No” otherwise.

Primary source of truth and where to find it:

This page lists and links the biweekly “Informe quincenal sobre inmigración irregular” PDFs for 2025, including editions with cutoffs such as 31 July, 15 August, 31 August, and 15 September 2025; by consistent biweekly pattern, a 15 December 2025 report is expected to be posted before year-end.

Versioning and tie-breakers:
- If multiple PDF versions for the 15 December 2025 cutoff exist, use the latest version published on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC as hosted on interior.gob.es. Do not adjust numbers based on later revisions; use the value in that latest-on-or-before-Dec-31 version.

This mirrors how EFE and RTVC have accurately relayed Ministry figures for 31 July and 15 August 2025, including the Canary maritime subtotal.

What exactly to read in the PDF:

The count must be taken verbatim from the Ministry’s report; no external estimates or alternative datasets are permitted.

question: Will a publicly announced pharma/biotech merger or acquisition with a headline transaction value strictly greater than $50,000,000,000 occur between 2025-09-22 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context and motivation: Forecasters are evaluating the chance of a very large (“megadeal”) transaction in the pharmaceutical/biotechnology sector before year-end 2025. Megadeals of this size have happened historically in pharma/biotech and are typically motivated by patent cliffs, pipeline strategy, and growth ambitions. Such transactions are widely reported by companies (press releases and regulatory filings) and major newswires.

Scope and sector: This question covers transactions where at least one party (acquirer or target) is a pharmaceutical company (engaged in discovering, developing, producing, and marketing medicinal drugs; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_industry) or a biotechnology company (uses biological processes/organisms to develop products, including therapeutics; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology). The deal can be global (any jurisdiction).

Status quo (as of 2025-09-22): Large pharma/biotech deals have been announced in 2025, but this question focuses specifically on whether any single transaction announced in the remaining period will exceed $50 billion. Forecasters should consider typical drivers (e.g., patent expirations, financing costs, antitrust climate, late-stage pipeline assets) and monitor company IR pages, SEC filings, and credible newswires.

Suggested sources to track announcements and values: Company press releases/IR pages; U.S.-listed companies’ SEC Form 8-K filings (Item 1.01); major newswires (e.g., Reuters, Bloomberg, AP); respected industry trackers (e.g., deal databases). For non-USD announced values, use the Federal Reserve H.10 daily noon buying rates for currency conversion at the announcement date: https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h10/current/.
resolution_criteria:
What must happen for YES:
- Between 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, a single merger or acquisition (see definitions below) is publicly announced by either party (company press release on an official investor relations site; or, for U.S.-listed parties, an SEC Form 8-K disclosure of a “material definitive agreement”; or credible reporting by a major newswire) in which the headline transaction value is strictly greater than $50,000,000,000 USD.

Eligible transaction types:
- Merger of equals, statutory merger, or acquisition of control (≥50% voting interest) of one company by another.
- Reverse merger that results in the acquirer obtaining control of the target.

Excluded transaction types:
- Asset purchases, licensing/collaboration agreements, joint ventures, minority-stake investments (<50%), recapitalizations, internal reorganizations, SPAC business combinations, and sovereign divestments without change of corporate control.

Sector eligibility:
- At least one party (acquirer or target) must be a pharmaceutical company (per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_industry) or a biotechnology company (per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology).

Announcement evidence hierarchy (any one is sufficient):
1) Company press release posted on an official investor relations website.
2) SEC Form 8-K Item 1.01 filing (for U.S.-listed parties) disclosing entry into a material definitive agreement.
3) Credible reporting by a major newswire (e.g., Reuters, Bloomberg, AP) that clearly states a definitive agreement has been signed along with a headline transaction value.

Defining the “headline transaction value”:
- Use the largest single figure the announcing party characterizes as the transaction’s headline value at announcement (e.g., “transaction value,” “enterprise value,” “equity value,” “consideration of up to $X”), inclusive of cash, stock, assumed debt if explicitly included, and quantified contingent value rights/earn-outs if they are explicitly included in the headline or total consideration figure.
- If multiple figures are presented (e.g., equity vs enterprise value), use the figure that the announcement frames as the transaction’s headline value. If a range is given, use the maximum stated value. The value must be strictly greater than $50,000,000,000.
- Mixed cash/stock deals: Use the headline value stated in the announcement (often based on exchange ratio and a stated reference stock price). If both press release and regulatory filing present values, use the press release’s headline value unless the SEC filing clearly supersedes it.

Currency conversion:
- If the headline value is not in USD, convert using the Federal Reserve H.10 daily noon buying rate for the relevant currency on the calendar date of the announcement (UTC date basis). If the announcement date falls on a non-business day, use the most recent prior business day’s rate.

Multiple related agreements:
- Only a single, discrete transaction counts. Do not aggregate separate deals. Amendments after announcement do not change resolution; the initial announcement headline value controls.

Ambiguities and tie-breakers:
- If sector classification is unclear, use the company’s self-description on its IR site and widely recognized industry categorizations.
- If credibility of a report is in question, prefer company press releases and/or SEC filings over third-party reporting.

Outcome determination:
- YES if at least one eligible announced transaction meets the criteria above within the time window.
- NO otherwise.

Resolution date and time zone:
- Resolve based on announcements made between 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, using UTC for all time cutoffs.

question: EU Iran sanctions: Will the Council adopt at least one additional act modifying Decision 2010/413/CFSP or Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On 2025-09-29, the Council of the EU reimposed and updated nuclear-related restrictive measures on Iran, adopting multiple legal acts that amend or implement the EU’s Iran sanctions framework based on Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP and Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012. Specifically, the Official Journal/EUR‑Lex shows:
- Council Decision (CFSP) 2025/1972 of 29 September 2025 amending Decision 2010/413/CFSP.
- Council Decision (CFSP) 2025/1978 of 29 September 2025 amending Decision 2010/413/CFSP.
- Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1975 of 29 September 2025 amending Regulation (EU) No 267/2012.
- Council Implementing Decision (CFSP) 2025/1971 of 29 September 2025 implementing Decision 2010/413/CFSP (i.e., updating annexed listings).
- Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1980 of 29 September 2025 implementing Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (i.e., updating annexed listings).
- Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1982 of 29 September 2025 implementing Regulation (EU) No 267/2012.
The Council’s press release confirms the snapback context (E3 notification under the JCPOA leading to the reimposition of UN and EU measures) and that the EU measures include listings and autonomous EU provisions. Decision 2010/413/CFSP is the core CFSP act establishing nuclear-related restrictive measures against Iran, amended multiple times since 2010. Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 operationalizes these sanctions in EU law and has been repeatedly amended and implemented via annex changes. Implementing acts (Implementing Decisions/Regulations) typically add, remove, or modify designated persons/entities and annex text; the 2025/1980 entry clearly illustrates such additions across Iranian state-owned banks, energy entities, IRGC-linked organizations, and other actors.
Why this forecast is non-trivial: After a major package adopted on 2025-09-29, further Council activity before year-end is plausible (e.g., additional listings or technical amendments), but not guaranteed—creating uncertainty suitable for forecasting. The resolution depends on clear, document-verifiable criteria within a short fixed window.
Key terms and definitions used in this question (for clarity; authoritative references provided where helpful):
- Council of the European Union: The EU institution where national ministers adopt EU laws and policies. See encyclopedia overview (e.g., Wikipedia’s “Council of the European Union”).
- Legal act (for this question): A Council Decision (CFSP), Council Regulation, Council Implementing Decision (CFSP), or Council Implementing Regulation published in the EU Official Journal and indexed on EUR‑Lex.
- Adoption date: The date stated in the title of the act on its Official Journal/EUR‑Lex page (e.g., “of 29 September 2025” on the OJ entry). For examples, see the OJ/EUR‑Lex entries cited above [203ea1; e94eaa; 405162; d68500; 22e3d0; 9ef952].
- Iran-related restrictive measures: Acts that amend or implement Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP and/or Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 concerning restrictive measures against Iran [837e7d; c3626d].
- Amending vs. Implementing (operationalization for this question): “Amending” acts explicitly say “amending Decision 2010/413/CFSP” or “amending Regulation (EU) No 267/2012” in their titles; “Implementing” acts explicitly say “implementing Decision 2010/413/CFSP” or “implementing Regulation (EU) No 267/2012” and modify annexes (e.g., designations) [203ea1; 405162; d68500; 22e3d0].
Baseline for this question: The acts adopted on 2025-09-29 cited above are considered the baseline and do not count toward resolution.
Useful sources to consult at resolution time:
- EUR‑Lex Official Journal entries for EU acts (e.g., the specific OJ pages for acts cited above).
- Council of the EU press releases for context (e.g., “Iran sanctions snapback: Council reimposes restrictive measures” of 2025‑09‑29).
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves to Yes if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive), there exists at least one EU Council legal act published on EUR‑Lex/Official Journal that meets ALL of the following:
1) Type: It is a Council Decision (CFSP), Council Regulation, Council Implementing Decision (CFSP), or Council Implementing Regulation.
2) Subject: It concerns restrictive measures against Iran by explicitly amending or implementing Council Decision 2010/413/CFSP and/or Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (as indicated in the act’s title and/or operative provisions) [837e7d; c3626d].
3) Function: It either:
   a) explicitly “amends” Decision 2010/413/CFSP or Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (the title includes “amending …”), or
   b) explicitly “implements” Decision 2010/413/CFSP or Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (the title includes “implementing …”) and modifies annexes/listings under those instruments (e.g., adds, removes, or alters designated entries) [d68500; 22e3d0].
4) Adoption date window: The act’s adoption date (the date stated in the title on the OJ/EUR‑Lex page) is between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC) inclusive. The 2025‑09‑29 baseline acts do not count [203ea1; e94eaa; 405162; d68500; 22e3d0; 9ef952].
Resolution procedure for a human resolver (single-source verification preferred):
- Step 1: On EUR‑Lex (Official Journal), search for Council acts adopted in the window that include “Iran” and reference Decision 2010/413/CFSP or Regulation (EU) No 267/2012. Confirm they are of the specified types.
- Step 2: Open the act’s EUR‑Lex/OJ page and verify:
   • The title and type (Decision/Regulation; Implementing/Amending).
   • The adoption date shown in the title lies within the specified window (UTC).
   • The act amends or implements Decision 2010/413/CFSP or Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 (as per title/operative text).
- Step 3: If at least one qualifying act is found, resolve Yes; otherwise, resolve No.
Notes:
- Only acts adopted by the Council of the EU count (Commission acts do not count).
- Publication must be visible on EUR‑Lex/Official Journal at resolution time; private drafts or press reports alone are insufficient.
- If multiple qualifying acts exist, a single one suffices for Yes.
- Acts adopted on 2025‑09‑29 are explicitly excluded (baseline) [203ea1; e94eaa; 405162; d68500; 22e3d0; 9ef952].

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 (ET), will the U.S. federal government announce a binding agreement or completed purchase to acquire a direct equity stake in at least one U.S.-listed critical minerals extraction or processing company other than MP Materials (NYSE: MP) or Lithium Americas (NYSE: LAC)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- On Aug 22, 2025, the U.S. government secured a 10% equity stake in Intel via conversion of previously issued government funds into non-voting stock.
- On July 2025, the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) agreed to purchase $400 million of convertible preferred stock in MP Materials and received a warrant, both initially priced at $30.03 per share; on an as-converted and as-exercised basis, this positioned DoD to become MP Materials’ largest shareholder with an effective 15% stake.
- On Sept 23, 2025, Reuters reported the administration was seeking an equity stake of up to 10% in Lithium Americas amid renegotiations of a large Energy Department loan, underscoring an active policy of taking equity in critical materials companies.
- For definitional clarity, the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2022 List of Critical Minerals contains 50 mineral commodities (e.g., lithium, rare earth elements, cobalt, graphite, manganese, nickel) and describes “critical minerals” as non-fuel minerals essential to the economy/national security with vulnerable supply chains. “U.S.-listed” refers to listing on a U.S. national securities exchange (e.g., NYSE, Nasdaq), as defined by the SEC. The SEC definition of “equity security” includes common stock, preferred stock, any security convertible into such stock, and warrants/rights to purchase such stock.
Why this is forecastable now: The federal government has already taken equity in MP Materials and Intel, and is reportedly pursuing equity in Lithium Americas; whether it will announce at least one additional equity purchase in another U.S.-listed critical minerals miner/processor by year-end is uncertain and consequential for U.S. industrial policy and related markets.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and counting rule:
- The question resolves based on announcements made between 00:00:00 Eastern Time on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 Eastern Time on December 31, 2025 (inclusive).
- It resolves Yes if at least one qualifying announcement occurs in that window; otherwise No.

What qualifies (all must be met):
1) U.S. federal government actor: The announcing/acquiring party must be the U.S. federal government acting through the Executive Office of the President or an executive branch department/agency or wholly owned federal government corporation (e.g., Department of Defense, Department of Energy, Department of the Treasury, Department of Commerce, U.S. International Development Finance Corporation). State/local governments or pension funds do not qualify.
2) Direct equity stake: The federal actor must execute a binding agreement to acquire, or complete the purchase of, an equity security issued by the company itself (or a consolidated subsidiary), for cash or as consideration in a transaction. “Equity security” follows the SEC definition and includes common stock, preferred stock, any security convertible into such stock, and warrants/rights to purchase such stock; pure debt without conversion features and grants/tax credits/loans without warrants or convertibility do not qualify.
3) Qualifying company: The issuer must (a) have equity listed on a U.S. national securities exchange as defined by the SEC (e.g., NYSE, Nasdaq) at the time of the announcement , and (b) be primarily engaged in the extraction (mining) or processing/refining of one or more minerals on the USGS 2022 List of Critical Minerals. For pre-revenue developers, “primarily engaged” may be established by the company’s latest annual report (Form 10-K/20-F) describing its principal business as exploration/development of one or more USGS-listed critical minerals.
4) Exclusions: Any announcement regarding MP Materials Corp. (NYSE: MP) or Lithium Americas Corp. (NYSE: LAC) does not count toward resolution, including increases to existing government stakes in either company.

Definition of “announce” and acceptable sources:
- “Announce” means any of the following becomes publicly available within the time window: (i) an official U.S. government press release or statement on a.gov/.mil domain stating that a binding agreement has been executed or a purchase has closed; (ii) a company-issued press release on its investor relations site disclosing the government as purchaser or counterparty to a definitive agreement; or (iii) a filing on the SEC’s EDGAR system (e.g., Form 8‑K Items 1.01 or 3.02, prospectus supplement) naming the U.S. government entity as a purchaser or party to a definitive agreement. If primary documentation is unavailable, contemporaneous reporting by major wire services (AP, Reuters, Bloomberg) may be used to establish the announcement provided the report clearly states that a definitive equity purchase agreement has been executed or that a purchase has closed.

Timestamping and ties:
- If a source includes a timestamp, Eastern Time is used; if only a date is provided, the announcement is deemed to have occurred on that date in Eastern Time. If sources disagree on timing, primary filings on EDGAR take precedence, followed by official.gov releases, then company press releases, then wire-service reports.

Non-qualifying examples (for clarity):
- Loans, grants, tax credits, guarantees, or offtake contracts without any equity security component do not qualify.
- Purchases of exchange-traded funds or index funds, or indirect holdings through third-party funds, do not qualify.

Status quo references for forecasters:
- Intel 10% government stake, structure, and timing.
- DoD’s MP Materials investment via convertible preferred and warrant, at $30.03 per share, positioning DoD as largest shareholder on an as-converted/as-exercised basis (~15%).
- Reported pursuit of up to a 10% equity stake in Lithium Americas amid DOE loan renegotiation.
- USGS 2022 List of Critical Minerals (50 minerals) and definition context.
- SEC materials on national securities exchanges and equity security definition (for what counts as U.S.-listed and equity).

question: By December 31, 2025 (23:59:59 UTC), will the FOMC target range for the federal funds rate be 3.75%–4.00% or lower?
background:
Definitions and context
- Federal funds rate: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight on an uncollateralized basis. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for this rate, typically expressed with lower and upper bounds (e.g., 0.00%–0.25%).
- FOMC: The committee within the Federal Reserve System responsible for U.S. monetary policy, including decisions about interest rates and the growth of the money supply; it sets the short‑term objective for open market operations, usually a target level/range for the federal funds rate.

Status quo (as of late September 2025)
- On September 17, 2025, the FOMC voted to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 4%–4¼%. The accompanying Implementation Note directs the Desk to undertake open market operations as necessary to maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 4% to 4¼%, and it set the interest on reserve balances (IORB) rate at 4.15%, effective September 18, 2025.
- In the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) released with the September 16–17, 2025 meeting, the median projection for the year‑end 2025 federal funds rate (defined as the midpoint of the projected appropriate target range) is 3.6%. The SEP explicitly notes that these projections refer to the midpoint of the target range at the end of the specified year.
- The next regularly scheduled year‑end policy meeting is on December 16–17, 2025, and is associated with a SEP, per the Federal Reserve’s posted FOMC calendar.

Why this question is non‑trivial
- The current target range is 4%–4¼% following the September decision , while the September SEP median implies a level around 3.6% (midpoint) by end‑2025. Reaching 3.75%–4.00% or lower by December 31, 2025 would require at least one additional policy action relative to the current setting, which is plausible but uncertain given incoming data and the FOMC’s dual mandate.
resolution_criteria:
Timing and scope
- Start date: October 1, 2025, 00:00:00 UTC.
- End date: December 31, 2025, 23:59:59 UTC.
- This question resolves based on the target range for the federal funds rate that is in effect at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. Earlier changes are relevant only insofar as they determine the range in effect at the cutoff.

What counts as the “target range”
- Use the range explicitly stated by the Federal Reserve (e.g., “in a target range of X to Y percent”). This phrasing appears in official FOMC communications such as press releases and Implementation Notes (e.g., “target range of 4 to 4‑1/4 percent”).

Resolution rule
- Resolve Yes if, as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, the FOMC’s stated target range is exactly 3.75%–4.00% or any lower range (e.g., 3.50%–3.75%, 3.25%–3.50%, etc.).
- Resolve No if the target range is 4.00%–4.25% or any higher range (e.g., 4.25%–4.50%, 4.50%–4.75%, etc.).

Source of truth and how to verify
- Primary source: the Federal Reserve Board’s official monetary policy press release/statement and/or Implementation Note for the most recent FOMC action governing the target range in December 2025, as published on federalreserve.gov. For reference, the September 17, 2025 FOMC press release states the range change and the Implementation Note specifies the operational directive and IORB, illustrating the exact language used to define the range.
- If multiple FOMC actions occur in December 2025, use the last action whose effective range is in force as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. If no action occurs in December, use the latest prior action still in force as of the cutoff. The December 16–17, 2025 meeting is scheduled and is associated with a SEP, which is when a year‑end decision is typically made.

Notes
- Do not use market rates (e.g., the effective federal funds rate) to resolve this question; only the officially stated target range in FOMC communications is relevant.
- For definitional clarity on the federal funds rate and the FOMC’s role, see.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will GAO publish at least two new Impoundment Control Act violation decisions (excluding B-337202, B-337203, B-337208, B-337204.1, and B-337204.2)?
background:
Context and current status (as of 2025-09-30):
- The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) issues legal decisions and opinions under the Impoundment Control Act of 1974 (ICA) and maintains a resource page describing the ICA, GAO’s responsibilities, and links to recent decisions. The GAO page explains what constitutes deferrals and rescissions, GAO’s review role, and states that the ICA does not permit “pocket rescissions” (withholding funds proposed for rescission through their expiration).
- In 2025 to date, GAO has issued multiple decisions concluding that executive branch actions violated the ICA, including:
  - B-337202 (Department of Health and Human Services—Head Start funds): Published 2025-07-23; GAO concluded HHS violated the ICA by withholding Head Start program funds.
  - B-337203 (HHS/NIH—National Institutes of Health grants): Published 2025-08-05; GAO concluded NIH violated the ICA by withholding budget authority from obligation or expenditure.
  - B-337208 (Department of Energy—Renew America’s Schools Program): Published 2025-07-31; GAO concluded DOE violated the ICA by delaying obligation of FY 2025 Schools Program funds for policy reasons.
  - B-337204.1 (Department of Homeland Security/FEMA—FY 2025 Federal Assistance): Published 2025-09-15; GAO found FEMA violated the ICA with respect to the Emergency Food and Shelter Program (EFSP) and the Shelter and Services Program (SSP), while finding no ICA violation for several other FEMA grant programs at that time.
  - B-337204.2 (DHS/FEMA—supplemental decision): Published 2025-09-29; GAO again concluded FEMA violated the ICA, including with respect to EFSP, SSP, and the Next Generation Warning System Grants Program (NGWS).
- These decisions and GAO’s ICA resource page provide clear examples of what counts as an ICA violation finding and where new decisions are posted for verification.

Key definitions and links for forecasters:
- Impoundment Control Act (ICA): Federal law governing when and how the executive branch may withhold or cancel budget authority after appropriation. GAO explains ICA mechanisms (deferral, rescission), GAO’s review responsibilities, and notes that “pocket rescissions” are not permitted.
- GAO ICA decisions: For this market, a “decision” means a GAO Office of General Counsel legal decision/opinion posted on gao.gov with a GAO product page showing a “Published” date and a B‑number (e.g., B‑337202). Examples are linked above and on GAO’s ICA page.
- “Violation decision”: A GAO ICA decision that explicitly concludes that an agency or entity violated the ICA (e.g., containing language such as “we conclude that  violated the ICA”).

Why this is forecastable now: Through late September 2025, GAO has already published multiple violation findings across several agencies (HHS, NIH, DOE, DHS/FEMA), suggesting continued investigative activity into year-end; however, it is uncertain how many additional violation decisions, if any, will be published between mid‑October and December, making the outcome nontrivial.

Primary sources to monitor:
- GAO Impoundment Control Act page (overview and links to recent decisions): https://www.gao.gov/legal/appropriations-law/impoundment-control-act.
- Individual GAO product pages for ICA decisions (each shows a “Published” date and the decision text), such as B‑337202, B‑337203, B‑337208, B‑337204.1, and B‑337204.2.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on GAO Office of General Counsel ICA decisions published on gao.gov between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

Operational definitions:
- Eligible “decision”: A GAO legal decision/opinion addressing the Impoundment Control Act that (a) has a unique GAO B‑number and a product page on gao.gov with a visible “Published” date, and (b) contains an explicit conclusion that an agency/entity violated the ICA (e.g., “we conclude/find that  violated the ICA”). Examples of such explicit language appear in B‑337202, B‑337208, B‑337204.1, and B‑337204.2.
- Publication timestamp used for eligibility: the “Published” date displayed on the GAO product page. For inclusion, the page’s Published date must fall on or after 2025-10-15 and on or before 2025-12-31 (no time-of-day is required since GAO displays dates; treat dates as calendar dates in UTC).
- Counting rule: Each unique B‑number counts at most once. If a single decision finds multiple program violations within one agency, it still counts as one decision. Errata or corrections that do not create a new B‑number do not count separately.

Exclusions (do not count toward the threshold):
- The following 2025 GAO ICA violation decisions, all published before 2025-10-15, are explicitly excluded from counting toward this question’s threshold:
  - B‑337202 (HHS—Head Start; published 2025‑07‑23).
  - B‑337203 (HHS/NIH; published 2025‑08‑05).
  - B‑337208 (DOE—Renew America’s Schools; published 2025‑07‑31).
  - B‑337204.1 (DHS/FEMA; published 2025‑09‑15).
  - B‑337204.2 (DHS/FEMA; published 2025‑09‑29).

Resolution rule:
- Resolve Yes if two (2) or more eligible GAO ICA violation decisions are published within the eligibility window defined above.

question: By 2025-12-31, will the U.S. enact at least $800 million in new appropriations for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI)?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Senate Appropriations Committee action: On 2025-07-31, the Senate Appropriations Committee approved a FY2026 Defense appropriations bill that includes $800 million for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI), and $225 million for the Baltic Security Initiative. The measure advanced by a 26–3 vote; overall defense funding in the bill is roughly $852–853 billion. Reuters reported the administration did not request Ukraine aid and the House bill earlier in the year did not include Ukraine aid, underscoring cross-chamber and executive–legislative divergence. The Hill likewise described the Ukraine-related total as approximately $1 billion when including the Baltic allocation, while specifying $800 million directly for USAI.
- FY2026 NDAA (authorization) context: The Senate Armed Services Committee’s FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) executive summary indicates USAI is extended through 2028 and increases authorized funding to $500 million; authorizations set policy and recommended levels but do not themselves provide budget authority (appropriations do).

Key definitions and sources a forecaster should know:
- Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI): A Department of Defense program to build Ukraine’s capacity to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity by providing equipment, training, and related support. Authoritative description: Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA) program page: https://samm.dsca.mil/program/USAI.
- Appropriations vs. authorizations in U.S. law: Appropriations bills provide budget authority (funding) for agencies and programs, typically for one fiscal year; an authorization bill establishes/continues programs and may set recommended funding levels but does not itself provide budget authority. See Wikipedia overviews: Appropriation bill (United States): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appropriation_bill_(United_States) ; Authorization bill: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authorization_bill.
- U.S. “public law” and enactment: A bill becomes public law when enacted (signed by the President, allowed to become law without signature, or enacted over a veto). Public laws are cited as Pub. L. X–Y and are published on Congress.gov and in the Statutes at Large. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_law_(United_States).
- U.S. federal fiscal year (FY): The federal FY runs from October 1 to September 30 and is named for the calendar year in which it ends (e.g., FY2026 runs 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial:
- The Senate Appropriations Committee has explicitly endorsed an $800 million USAI appropriation for FY2026, but House posture and the administration’s prior request increased uncertainty about whether any 2025-enacted law will contain that level of USAI funding by year-end.

Notes on scope and threshold choice:
- This question narrows to a specific, well-defined Ukraine-only line item—USAI—rather than broader, regional security lines (e.g., the Baltic Security Initiative), to ensure unambiguous counting. The $800 million threshold reflects the Senate Appropriations Committee’s proposed USAI level, which creates live uncertainty given cross-chamber differences.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and timezone:
- Eligible laws: Any U.S. public law enacted between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Question and outcome:
- Resolve Yes if, within the event window, the sum of all new budget authority specifically appropriated to the “Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative” (USAI) equals or exceeds $800,000,000 as stated in the enacted statutory text of one or more public laws.
- Resolve No otherwise.

What counts as “appropriated to USAI”:
- Count only explicit appropriations that name “Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative” or “USAI” in the enacted statutory text and assign a dollar amount. Typical language appears in Defense Appropriations or supplemental appropriations acts (e.g., “For the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, $___, to remain available until …”). Appropriations provide budget authority (as defined in U.S. practice for appropriation bills).

What does NOT count:
- Authorization language alone (including NDAA provisions) does not count toward this total; authorizations are distinct from appropriations.
- Appropriations not specific to USAI (e.g., European Deterrence Initiative, Baltic Security Initiative, general transfer/replenishment authorities, or broad accounts without USAI designation) do not count.
- Reprogramming actions, transfers, drawdown authority usage, or obligations from previously enacted, unobligated balances do not count (the question concerns new budget authority enacted in 2025).

Aggregation and netting:
- If multiple public laws enacted in 2025 appropriate funds to USAI, sum all such amounts to determine whether the $800,000,000 threshold is met. If a 2025-enacted public law rescinds any 2025 USAI appropriations, subtract rescissions enacted within the event window to compute a net total as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Verification sources and procedure:
- Primary source: The text of enacted public laws on Congress.gov (e.g., the public law pages for relevant 2025 appropriations/supplementals). Public laws are official “Acts of Congress” enacted via signature, lapse, or veto override and published/cited as Pub. L. X–Y.
- USAI program definition for identification: DSCA USAI program page: https://samm.dsca.mil/program/USAI.
- Background for context on appropriations vs. authorizations: Appropriation bill (United States) ; Authorization bill.

Ties and edge cases:
- If the enacted text references USAI funding indirectly (e.g., “amounts under section … (USAI)”), the resolver will confirm the cited section is the USAI account and that a dollar amount is appropriated in the law’s text to that account.
- If all USAI appropriations enacted in 2025 total less than $800,000,000 net of any same-year rescissions by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve No.

Cited facts underpinning the threshold and status quo:
- Senate Appropriations Committee advanced a defense bill with $800 million for USAI; plus $225 million for the Baltic Security Initiative; 26–3 committee vote; total DoD funding about $852–853 billion.
- The FY2026 NDAA executive summary extends USAI through 2028 and sets authorization at $500 million (authorization, not appropriation).
- Appropriations vs. authorizations, public law enactment, and fiscal-year definitions as above.

question: Will the number of trucks collected through the UN2720 Mechanism at Gaza’s perimeter crossings during December 1–31, 2025 (UTC) be at least 900?
background:
Context and mechanism definitions:
- The UN2720 Mechanism is a UN-operated system to facilitate, coordinate, monitor, and verify humanitarian relief consignments to Gaza; UNOPS supports its operationalization and the mechanism provides tracking and verification via monitors and partner cross-verification.
- The UN2720 Monitoring & Tracking Dashboard is the authoritative, live source that reports movements of UN-manifested humanitarian aid, including status categories: Offloaded, Collected, Arrived, and Intercepted. It tracks metrics including Trucks, Pallets, and Weight (t). The “Collected” status refers to aid consignments collected from any of the crossings along Gaza’s perimeter. Data presented are only humanitarian relief consignments processed through the UN2720 Mechanism and are subject to change based on on-the-ground monitors and partner verification.
- Important caveat: truck sizes on the Gaza side are typically smaller than trucks arriving from the Israeli side, so the number of trucks reaching crossings on the Israeli side does not directly correspond to the number collected on the Gaza side.
- OCHA’s crossings data notes a “collected humanitarian truckloads” series monitored by UN agencies; it excludes fuel and some cargo collected by NGOs and third parties, and after May 7 commercial trucks are not captured in totals (due to limited direct observation of private-sector cargo). Some collected truckloads have not reached destinations due to security incidents and looting.

Status quo and recent reporting (as of 2025-09-30):
- OCHA reported that between 20 July and 3 August 2025 at least 12,000 metric tons (MT) of food items procured through the UN-coordinated aid mechanism were brought into Gaza; and at least 14,000 MT of food aid were collected from crossings in July 2025. OCHA also noted that only eight organizations have been able to manifest cargo under the UN2720 mechanism, and that a large share of aid was offloaded or looted before reaching warehouses during that period.
- The UN/UNOPS publish recurring “UN 2720 Mechanism for Gaza” monthly overview infographics (e.g., October 2024–August 2025), which summarize mechanism activity and metrics; these serve as a secondary consolidated source for monthly totals and methodology notes.

Key definitions and scope for this question:
- Truck: The unit labeled “Trucks” on the UN2720 Monitoring & Tracking Dashboard. No conversion to tonnage or other units will be performed; counts rely on the dashboard’s “Trucks” metric.
- Collected: As defined on the UN2720 Monitoring & Tracking Dashboard, consignments “Collected From any of the crossings along Gaza’s perimeter”.
- Crossings along Gaza’s perimeter: The border entry points into Gaza; examples referenced include Kerem Shalom/Karem Abu Salem and Erez West/Zikim crossings within dashboard notes.
- UN-manifested humanitarian relief consignments: Aid movements processed through and recorded by the UN2720 Mechanism; the dashboard includes only these consignments.
- Timezone: All times are Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial:
- The volume of aid movements under UN2720 is volatile due to operational access, approvals, security, and logistics constraints. The specific December truck count is unknown as of 2025-09-30; both outcomes (≥900 vs. <900) are plausible given recent variability in approvals, looting/interceptions, and corridor operations.
- The threshold is set to create meaningful uncertainty for forecasters without requiring conversion assumptions between trucks and tonnage.

Primary sources for forecasters and adjudication:
- UN2720 Monitoring & Tracking Dashboard (Collected): https://app.un2720.org/tracking/collected.
- UN2720 Mechanism overview and data pipeline description: https://info.un2720.org/#about.
- UN/UNOPS monthly overview series on ReliefWeb: https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/un-2720-mechanism-gaza-infographics-monthly-overviews-october-2024-august-2025.
- OCHA situational and crossings data context: https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/gaza-humanitarian-response-update-20-july-2-august-2025 ; https://www.ochaopt.org/data/crossings.
resolution_criteria:
Adjudication window and outcome:
- The adjudication timepoint is 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Resolve Yes if the count of Trucks under the “Collected” status for consignments with collection timestamps between 2025-12-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive) is ≥900; otherwise resolve No.

Primary resolution method:
1) At or immediately after the adjudication timepoint, access the UN2720 Monitoring & Tracking Dashboard’s Collected page: https://app.un2720.org/tracking/collected.
2) Identify the “Trucks” metric and obtain the December 2025 total for Collected consignments. If the dashboard provides a date-range control, set it to the inclusive December window defined above. If the dashboard shows a single cumulative total, use any built-in monthly/period view or official December total indicated on the dashboard at that time.

Secondary resolution method (only if the dashboard does not provide an unambiguous December total at adjudication time):
3) Use the official UN/UNOPS “UN 2720 Mechanism for Gaza: Monthly Overview (December 2025)” infographic on ReliefWeb as the authoritative monthly total for Collected trucks (or Trucks Collected) for December 2025. Note: the series of monthly overview infographics is a recurring publication by UN and UNOPS and has covered months up to August 2025; December 2025 is expected to be similarly reported.

Scope and exclusions:
- Only UN-manifested humanitarian relief consignments processed through the UN2720 Mechanism count toward the total. Commercial (private sector) trucks after May 7 are excluded from totals due to lack of UN direct observation; fuel and some NGO/third-party cargo are also excluded per OCHA’s crossings data notes.
- The unit of account is “Trucks” as displayed on the UN2720 dashboard; no tonnage-based conversions or external truck counts (e.g., from non-UN sources) are permitted.

Tiebreakers and conflict resolution:
- If there is a discrepancy between the UN2720 dashboard and the monthly overview infographic, prefer the dashboard’s December total displayed at or immediately after the adjudication timepoint (as the live, primary source of record).
- If the dashboard lacks an explicit December total and the monthly infographic is unavailable by the adjudication timepoint, the question will be adjudicated once the monthly infographic is published, using its December Trucks Collected total. This fallback is used solely if the dashboard cannot unambiguously provide the December total.

Verification notes:
- The adjudicator should retain a screenshot or export of the dashboard view showing the December 2025 Trucks Collected total, or the December 2025 monthly infographic, to support the resolved outcome.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (inclusive), will the United States cast a veto in the UN Security Council on any draft resolution that explicitly calls for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On 2025-09-18, during the Security Council’s 10,000th meeting, a draft resolution that demanded an immediate, unconditional, and permanent ceasefire in Gaza received 14 votes in favour and 1 against (the United States) but was not adopted due to the negative vote by a permanent member (i.e., a veto). UN News likewise reported that the United States “once again vetoed a UN resolution demanding an immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire in the Gaza Strip,” and noted this was the sixth such US veto related to Gaza ceasefire texts, with the prior veto in June. These sources are indicative of the official documentation and media coverage used to verify Security Council voting outcomes and the language of the draft resolutions.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- United Nations Security Council veto: On non-procedural (substantive) decisions, any of the five permanent members (P5) can block adoption by casting a negative vote; procedural matters are not subject to veto; adoption otherwise requires at least nine affirmative votes. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power.
- Ceasefire: A temporary stoppage of fighting; synonymous terms include “truce” and “cessation of hostilities”. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceasefire.
- Gaza Strip: A Palestinian territory commonly referred to as “Gaza”. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip.

Primary sources for resolution: Security Council official meeting coverage and press releases (press.un.org) and UN News (news.un.org) typically report vote tallies and whether a draft “was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent Council member,” as well as the operative language (e.g., “immediate ceasefire”). Major wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP) usually corroborate such votes; however, the official UN meeting coverage is the intended primary source for resolution verification.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone: The eligible period runs from 2025-10-15 00:00:00 to 2025-12-31 23:59:59, inclusive, in Eastern Time (America/New_York).

Question restated precisely: Resolve “Yes” if, during the above window, the United States (i.e., the permanent member of the UN Security Council representing the United States of America) casts a veto on any UN Security Council draft resolution that explicitly calls for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip. Resolve “No” otherwise.

What counts as a “veto”: For the purposes of this question, a veto means a negative vote by the United States on a non-procedural draft resolution that results in the draft not being adopted, as recognized in official UN Security Council meeting coverage (e.g., language that the draft “was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent Council member”) or as shown by a voting record with at least nine votes in favour and the United States voting against. Abstentions or absences do not constitute a veto. Procedural matters are excluded.

What counts as “explicitly calls for an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip”:
- The draft resolution’s operative text must include the word “immediate” modifying one of the following terms referring to the stoppage of fighting: “ceasefire,” “cessation of hostilities,” or “truce,” and must specify that this applies to Gaza/the Gaza Strip. Example qualifying language (non-exhaustive): “demands an immediate ceasefire in the Gaza Strip,” “calls for an immediate cessation of hostilities in Gaza,” “demands an immediate truce in the Gaza Strip.” The geographic reference may be phrased as “Gaza,” “the Gaza Strip,” or equivalent formulations that unambiguously refer to the Gaza Strip.
- Drafts lacking the word “immediate” in connection with the ceasefire/cessation/truce (e.g., “durable ceasefire,” “lasting ceasefire,” or “toward a ceasefire” without “immediate”) do not qualify.

Inclusions and exclusions:
- Include any such draft regardless of who sponsors it, provided it is voted on by the Security Council as a non-procedural matter within the time window.
- Exclude procedural votes, amendments voted separately from the main draft, presidential statements (PRSTs), press statements, General Assembly resolutions, and any texts whose ceasefire language is limited to areas outside Gaza or does not include “immediate.”
- If multiple qualifying drafts are vetoed by the United States in the window, any single instance suffices for “Yes.” If the United States votes against but there are fewer than nine votes in favour (so the draft fails without a veto), that does not count.

How it will be resolved (sources and method):
- Primary source: the official UN Security Council meeting coverage/press release for the relevant meeting(s) on press.un.org. The resolver will verify (a) that the United States cast a negative vote, (b) that the draft was not adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent member, and (c) that the draft’s operative text explicitly called for an immediate ceasefire (or immediate cessation of hostilities/truce) in Gaza, as reflected in the UN’s description of the draft.
- Secondary confirmation (if needed): UN News coverage summarizing the vote and language (news.un.org). If discrepancies arise, the UN’s official meeting coverage/record takes precedence.
- In edge cases where the exact operative phrasing is not quoted in press coverage, the resolver will rely on the UN’s meeting coverage characterization (e.g., “demanding an immediate ceasefire in Gaza”) and, if available, the circulated draft text number referenced in the UN materials.

Decision rule: Resolve “Yes” if all three conditions are met within the time window: (1) the US cast a negative vote; (2) the draft failed due to the US veto; (3) the draft explicitly called for an immediate ceasefire (or immediate cessation of hostilities/truce) in Gaza as defined above. Otherwise resolve “No.”

question: Will the U.S. federal funds rate target range upper bound be at or below 3.75% at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Why this matters: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for the U.S. federal funds rate, a key short-term policy rate that influences borrowing costs across the economy, including commercial and residential real estate financing. Lower policy rates generally reduce interest expenses and can support transaction volumes and valuations, which is directly relevant for real estate market activity.

Definitions and context:
- Federal funds rate: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances to each other overnight; see overview (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate).
- FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee): The Fed body that sets the target range; overview (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Open_Market_Committee).
- Target range upper bound: The “high” endpoint of the FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate; the Fed publishes a historical table with “Low” and “High” values and effective dates (https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/fedexplained/accessible-version.htm).
- DFEDTARU: The Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit series on FRED, expressed in percent per annum, typically shown at a daily frequency and sourced from the Board of Governors (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU).
- UTC: Coordinated Universal Time for timestamps (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time).

Status quo (for forecasting baseline): Assumption for this prompt only—verify independently. As of 2025-09-22, the most recent FOMC decision in mid-September 2025 set the target range to 4.00%–4.25%, implying DFEDTARU = 4.25%. Forecasters should confirm the latest value on FRED and the Fed’s table before making forecasts.

Why the 3.75% threshold: This cut-off aims to center probabilities for late-2025 outcomes, making the question non-trivial and sensitive to the number and timing of any further FOMC changes in Q4 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end of measurement window:
- Start date/time: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC (events before this are out of scope for interpretation, but only the end-date level determines resolution).
- End timestamp for evaluation: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What is being measured:
- The FOMC target range upper bound (“High” endpoint) of the U.S. federal funds rate at the evaluation timestamp defined above. This is the policy rate’s upper bound, not the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) published by the New York Fed.

Primary resolution source (use this first):
- FRED series “Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit” (DFEDTARU): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU. Retrieve the observation with date 2025-12-31. If that observation is present, use its value (percent per annum) to resolve:
  • YES if DFEDTARU ≤ 3.75
  • NO if DFEDTARU > 3.75

Fallbacks if the primary source is unavailable, lacks a 2025-12-31 observation, or shows a clear data error:
1) Board of Governors “FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate” table: https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/fedexplained/accessible-version.htm. Identify the row whose effective date/time makes the published “High” value in force at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Resolve based on that “High” value (YES if ≤ 3.75, else NO).
2) If further confirmation is needed, use the most recent FOMC statement/press release setting the target range that is effective at the evaluation time, available at: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm (navigate to the relevant FOMC press release). Use the high end of the announced target range.

Time-zone and intra-day changes:
- If the FOMC implements a change on 2025-12-31 with a specific effective time, interpret that effective time in U.S. Eastern Time and convert to UTC to determine whether it is in force at 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31.
- If multiple changes occur on 2025-12-31 (rare), use the level in force at 23:59:59 UTC.

Revisions and data discrepancies:
- If DFEDTARU or Fed table values are revised after 2025-12-31, use the value as displayed when resolving on or immediately after the close of 2025-12-31 UTC (within 7 calendar days). If primary and fallback sources conflict, prefer the Board of Governors table; if unavailable, use the latest applicable FOMC press release.

Clarifications:
- Do not use the Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) for resolution; only the target range upper bound applies.
- Units are percent per annum, unrounded. If the source displays with two decimals, use the displayed precision.
- This question resolves definitively to YES or NO based on the value determined above.

question: Will Aena rescind or formally suspend Madrid–Barajas’s overnight-stay ban between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of Oct 1, 2025: Aena (Aeropuertos Españoles y Navegación Aérea) manages Spain’s airport network and is majority state-owned via ENAIRE. Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas Airport (IATA: MAD) is Madrid’s main international airport. Starting July 24, 2025, Aena prohibited overnight stays (“pernoctar”) at Madrid–Barajas, stating that airports are transit infrastructures not suited for habitation, and coordinating with municipal social services after the City of Madrid opened a specific shelter; multiple reputable outlets reported the ban and Aena’s stated rationale. Earlier, in May 2025, Aena strengthened nighttime access controls (typically 21:00–05:00) to address a rise in people seeking shelter in terminals, limiting entry to passengers, companions, and staff during those hours. NGOs had estimated hundreds of people were previously staying overnight in the terminal areas.

Definitions and scope used in this question:
- Aena: Spain’s airport operator as defined by its Wikipedia entry.
- Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas Airport: The airport complex serving Madrid as defined by its Wikipedia entry.
- Overnight stay (“pernoctar”): For resolution purposes, a policy permitting or forbidding persons to remain in public terminal areas of Madrid–Barajas for the primary purpose of sleeping or lodging during night hours. As a practical proxy, references to “pernoctar” or “no podrán permanecer en las instalaciones por la noche” in official communications will be used to identify whether overnight stays are allowed or prohibited.
- The “ban” referred to here: The airport-wide prohibition on overnight stays at Madrid–Barajas announced and effective July 24, 2025, as reported by RTVE and Euronews.
- Rescind/Reverse: A formal announcement that the July 24, 2025 overnight-stay prohibition is annulled, lifted, or otherwise no longer in effect (airport-wide).
- Formal suspension: A formal announcement halting enforcement of the July 24, 2025 prohibition (airport-wide) for at least 48 consecutive hours, explicitly allowing overnight stays again during the suspension period.
- Competent governmental authority: An organ of the Government of Spain or the Community of Madrid with legal remit over airport operations or public order (e.g., Ministry of Transport or Delegación del Gobierno) issuing a directive applicable to Madrid–Barajas. This question relies on the existence of official communications customarily published by these bodies.

Why this is forecastable: Policy reversals or suspensions can occur due to legal challenges, political pressure, or operational considerations, but are uncertain. The event has clear, checkable sources if it happens (Aena’s press portal or government directives), and it is plausibly neither extremely likely nor extremely unlikely given the recent controversy.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and timezone:
- Eligible announcements must be published between Oct 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC and Dec 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC.

Resolution rule:
- Yes if, within the event window, either (a) Aena publishes an official press release or website update, or (b) a competent governmental authority publishes an official directive or press note, that explicitly rescinds, reverses, or formally suspends the July 24, 2025 airport-wide prohibition on overnight stays (“pernoctar”) at Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas, thereby allowing overnight stays again (even temporarily). A “formal suspension” counts only if it applies airport-wide and lasts at least 48 consecutive hours.
- No otherwise.

What qualifies as an official communication:
- Aena: A press release or formal announcement on aena.es under the Corporativa/Prensa section (press releases and photonews), or an official PDF press note hosted on aena.es. While the July 24, 2025 ban was widely reported by major outlets , the authoritative reversal/suspension must appear in an Aena or government official channel.
- Government: An official directive, resolution, or press note hosted on a gov.es domain (e.g., Ministerio de Transportes), the Boletín Oficial del Estado (boe.es), or the Delegación del Gobierno en la Comunidad de Madrid (madrid.gob.es or equivalent official site).

Exclusions and clarifications:
- Changes limited to access controls (e.g., who may enter during night hours) do not count unless the communication explicitly lifts the “pernoctar” prohibition (airport-wide). Prior access-control tightening, such as limiting entry 21:00–05:00 to passengers/companions/staff, does not by itself constitute a ban reversal.
- Terminal-specific or gate-specific exceptions do not count; the reversal/suspension must apply to the airport as a whole.
- Ultra-short exceptions (less than 48 consecutive hours) do not count as a formal suspension.
- Statements by non-official third parties without an accompanying official document or press note do not count.

Primary resolution sources to check on Dec 31, 2025:
- Aena’s press releases portal (Corporativa/Prensa). If a reversal/suspension occurred, it would be announced there.
- Government official portals or BOE if the directive comes from a public authority.
- If needed for corroboration: major reputable outlets (e.g., RTVE, El País, Reuters/AP) reporting the official reversal/suspension with direct citation of the underlying document.

question: Between Oct 1, 2024 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC), will OFAC issue a general or specific license that authorizes Ecopetrol to purchase Venezuelan natural gas?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Ecopetrol S.A. is Colombia’s largest and primary petroleum company. Ecopetrol has explored importing natural gas from Venezuela to mitigate domestic supply risks, including via the Trans-Caribbean (Antonio Ricaurte) gas pipeline that connects Venezuela and Colombia.
- The U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers and enforces U.S. economic and trade sanctions. Venezuela-related U.S. sanctions are administered under OFAC’s Venezuela sanctions program (31 CFR Part 591).
- OFAC issues two types of authorizations: general licenses (GLs), which are self-executing authorizations that allow a class of transactions without applying, and specific licenses (SLs), which are written authorizations issued to a particular person/entity in response to an application.
- As of early September 2025, Reuters reported that Ecopetrol could not buy Venezuelan natural gas due to U.S. sanctions; Ecopetrol’s chair stated the company was blocked from buying Venezuelan gas (and from acquiring Monómeros), absent U.S. authorization. Earlier in 2024, Ecopetrol publicly indicated it had applied to OFAC for a specific license to import Venezuelan gas.
- OFAC maintains public pages where it posts program materials and selected general licenses, including for Venezuela.
- Natural gas is a fossil fuel gas primarily composed of methane; it is distinct from liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), which primarily consists of propane and butane. OFAC has, for example, issued GLs related to LPG in Venezuela, which is a different commodity from natural gas.

Why this is forecastable: U.S. sanctions policy toward Venezuela has been dynamic. An explicit OFAC authorization (general or specific) that permits Ecopetrol to purchase Venezuelan natural gas is a discrete legal event that could plausibly occur or not occur before year-end 2025, and does not require physical gas flows to begin to resolve the question.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Count qualifying events that occur between 2024-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. The question will be resolved on or immediately after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (UTC).

Question restatement:
- Resolve YES if, within the window, OFAC issues an authorization (as defined below) that permits Ecopetrol S.A. to purchase Venezuelan natural gas. Resolve NO otherwise.

What qualifies as an authorization:
- General license (GL): A publicly posted OFAC general license whose text explicitly authorizes transactions involving the purchase or import of “natural gas” (or “liquefied natural gas”/“LNG”) from Venezuela. Because GLs are not addressed to a single entity, for a GL to count here it must be accompanied (by the end of the window) by either:
  • An official Ecopetrol announcement stating that the GL enables Ecopetrol to purchase Venezuelan natural gas; or
  • Coverage by at least one major international news organization stating that the GL enables Ecopetrol to purchase Venezuelan natural gas (examples: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg). This requirement ensures the GL’s applicability to Ecopetrol is clear and not a matter of interpretation.
- Specific license (SL): An OFAC specific license issued to Ecopetrol S.A. that authorizes the company to purchase “natural gas” (or “liquefied natural gas”/“LNG”) from Venezuelan counterparties (e.g., PdVSA or affiliates). Because SLs are typically not public, this path requires Ecopetrol to officially announce receipt of the SL and its scope, with corroboration by at least one major international news organization (examples: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg).

Definitions (for use in resolving the question):
- OFAC: The Office of Foreign Assets Control of the U.S. Department of the Treasury, which administers and enforces sanctions.
- Venezuela-related sanctions program: The OFAC program codified at 31 CFR Part 591 and associated executive orders and guidance, as described on OFAC’s Venezuela program page.
- General license (GL): An OFAC authorization that is self-executing and allows a class of transactions without applying for a license, subject to stated terms and conditions.
- Specific license (SL): A written authorization issued by OFAC to a particular person or entity in response to a license application, permitting a specified transaction(s).
- Ecopetrol S.A.: Colombia’s largest and primary petroleum company.
- Natural gas: A fossil fuel gas primarily composed of methane; includes its liquefied form (LNG). For avoidance of doubt, this excludes liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), which primarily consists of propane and butane.
- Venezuelan natural gas: Natural gas produced in, originating from, or exported by entities located in Venezuela (including PdVSA or its affiliates).
- Official Ecopetrol announcement: A press release or statement on Ecopetrol’s official website or an official securities/regulatory filing by Ecopetrol (e.g., a Form 6-K), explicitly stating that Ecopetrol has received an OFAC specific license to purchase Venezuelan natural gas, or that a newly issued OFAC general license enables Ecopetrol to purchase Venezuelan natural gas.
- Major international news organization: A widely recognized wire service or newspaper with fact-checking standards and global reach (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, Bloomberg). Reuters coverage is cited here as an example of the type of reporting used in the background on this topic.

What does NOT count:
- Authorizations that only cover LPG (liquefied petroleum gas), refined products, maintenance/wind-down activities, or other activities that do not explicitly authorize purchasing “natural gas” or “liquefied natural gas” do not count.
- Informal statements, guidance, FAQs, policy speeches, or letters that are not an OFAC license do not count.
- Announcements or reporting without explicit mention of authorization to purchase “natural gas” (or “LNG”) do not count.

Primary resolution sources (checked in this order):
1) OFAC’s Selected General Licenses page for newly issued Venezuela-related GLs that explicitly reference natural gas.
2) OFAC’s Venezuela-related sanctions program page and linked “Recent Actions” entries for posted GLs or program updates.
3) If a specific license is claimed: Ecopetrol’s official press releases or regulatory filings announcing receipt of an OFAC SL authorizing the purchase of Venezuelan natural gas, corroborated by at least one major outlet (e.g., Reuters).

Edge cases and tie-breakers:
- If an authorization is issued within the window and later revoked before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the market will still resolve YES (issuance within the window is sufficient).
- If wording in a GL is ambiguous (e.g., authorizes “hydrocarbons” without mentioning natural gas), the market will resolve NO unless Ecopetrol’s official announcement or major-outlet reporting explicitly states the GL enables Ecopetrol to purchase Venezuelan natural gas by the end of the window.
- If multiple authorizations are issued, the earliest qualifying authorization within the window determines a YES outcome.

Status quo references for forecasters:
- Reuters report that Ecopetrol remained blocked by U.S. sanctions as of early September 2025.
- Reporting that Ecopetrol applied for an OFAC specific license in 2024.
- OFAC’s Venezuela sanctions program overview and examples of Venezuela-related GLs.

question: Pueblo Question 2A: Will voters approve increasing the City of Pueblo’s sales and use tax rate from 3.7% to 4.7% at the November 4, 2025 Coordinated Election?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Measure placement and wording: The City of Pueblo has six measures on the November 4, 2025 ballot, including Question 2A, which proposes increasing the City’s sales and use tax rate from 3.7% to 4.7%. The official ballot language cites adoption of Ordinance No. 11000 and specifies that the additional 1% revenue will be collected, retained, and spent as a voter-approved revenue change notwithstanding Article X, Section 20 of the Colorado Constitution (TABOR). The same wording appears on the Pueblo County sample ballot.
- Election date and certification timeline: Colorado’s 2025 Coordinated Election is scheduled for November 4, 2025. County canvass and official abstracts must be completed by November 26, 2025, with final canvass uploaded to ENR by the next business day, indicating certified results should be available in late November. Pueblo County Elections is coordinating the City’s election and provides key dates and contact information on its official page.
- Expected revenue impact: The City’s estimate embedded in the ballot language is $26,142,985.56 in the first fiscal year beginning January 1, 2026; local reporting has characterized the proposal as an approximate $26 million annual increase [16ac8a, c1f7f].
- Definitions context: Colorado imposes sales tax on retail sales of tangible personal property, prepared food and drink, certain services, and accommodations; use tax is a complement to sales tax, imposed for the privilege of storing, using, or consuming tangible personal property in Colorado when sales tax was not collected at purchase. TABOR (Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights) in Colorado’s constitution (Article X, Section 20) requires voter approval for tax rate increases and governs revenue/spending limits; a voter-approved revenue change allows governments to retain/spend revenue beyond those limits when approved by voters.
- Official results source: Pueblo County’s Elections/Clerk & Recorder site publishes official election results (example: May 6, 2025 official results) and serves as the authoritative repository for certified results; it will host the November 2025 Coordinated Election results upon certification.

What a forecaster should know:
- The question resolves based on the certified outcome of a single, local ballot measure with clear, official sources and statutory certification deadlines.
- Ballots were anticipated to be mailed around October 10, 2025 as part of the coordination agreement noted by the City; this provides context on voter engagement timelines.
- Campaign dynamics and fiscal context have featured in local coverage, which may inform priors but are not required for resolution [c1f7f].
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and scope:
- Start date: 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC.
- End date: 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC.
- Event: Certification of results for City of Pueblo Question 2A at the November 4, 2025 Coordinated Election.

Operational resolution rule:
- Resolve "Yes" if the certified official results published by the Pueblo County Clerk & Recorder/Elections Office show that, for City of Pueblo Question 2A, the count of "Yes" votes exceeds the count of "No" votes. Resolve "No" otherwise (including a tie). The determination is made solely based on the certified totals for that ballot question as reported by the County.

Primary resolution source:
- Pueblo County Elections official results page and/or the Clerk & Recorder Elections portal hosting certified results for the November 2025 Coordinated Election (example results index and Elections portal demonstrate where official/certified results are posted).

Certification timing assurance:
- Colorado’s statutory deadline requires completion of the canvass and submission of the official abstract of votes by November 26, 2025, with final canvass uploaded to ENR by the next business day, ensuring certified results exist before the resolution end date.

Definitions (with references/links for clarity):
- "City of Pueblo sales and use tax rate": The municipal sales and use tax rates applicable within the City of Pueblo as set by ordinance; Question 2A proposes changing these rates from 3.7% to 4.7% via Ordinance No. 11000. City Sales Tax Division overview: https://www.pueblo.us/180/Sales-Tax-Division.
- "Sales tax": In Colorado, sales tax applies to retail sales of tangible personal property, prepared food and drink, certain services, and accommodations (authoritative guidance) https://tax.colorado.gov/sales-tax-guide.
- "Use tax": In Colorado, consumer use tax complements sales tax and is imposed for the privilege of storing, using, or consuming tangible personal property in Colorado when sales tax was not collected at purchase (authoritative guidance) https://tax.colorado.gov/sites/tax/files/documents/Consumer_Use_Tax_Guide_Apr_2024.pdf.
- "TABOR" and "voter-approved revenue change": TABOR is Article X, Section 20 of the Colorado Constitution; a voter-approved revenue change allows retention/spending of revenue beyond TABOR limits when approved by voters. Background/reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxpayer_Bill_of_Rights.
- "Certified official results": The final, canvassed and certified totals for ballot measures as published by the Pueblo County Clerk & Recorder/Elections Office; the County’s results index demonstrates publication of official results for prior elections and will host the November 2025 certified results.

Disambiguation notes:
- Only votes cast on City of Pueblo Question 2A count. Undervotes/overvotes are handled per election administration and do not factor into the approval determination beyond what is included in certified "Yes" and "No" totals.
- If multiple reports exist, use the latest certified report issued by the Pueblo County Clerk & Recorder for the November 4, 2025 Coordinated Election.
- If, contrary to statutory deadlines, certified results are not posted by the County by the end date, resolution will be delayed until the County posts certified results; however, this contingency is not expected given state deadlines.

question: Will FERC approve SPP’s High Impact Large Loads (HILL) tariff revisions between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01
- Southwest Power Pool (SPP) is a U.S. regional transmission organization (RTO) that manages grid reliability and wholesale power markets across portions of 14 states. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) is the independent U.S. agency that regulates interstate transmission and wholesale electricity markets and issues binding orders on matters such as tariff revisions.
- In mid-September 2025, SPP’s board approved a High Impact Large Load (HILL) policy to accelerate interconnection of very large loads such as AI data centers and advanced manufacturing, citing urgency and the need to balance reliability and affordability. The policy establishes a 90‑day study-and-approval process to interconnect qualifying large loads when paired with on‑site or nearby generation, or with current/planned generation, integrating transmission service, generation and load interconnection studies in one coordinated framework. Utility Dive reports that the board action was adopted as Revision Request 696 (RR696), that the associated tariff revisions will require FERC approval, and that SPP peak load is projected to rise from about 56 GW to roughly 105 GW over the next decade.
- Definitions and thresholds. SPP materials define a HILL as a commercial or industrial load (or increase) at a single site connected via one or more shared points of interconnection or delivery, with thresholds at: (a) 10 MW or more when connected at voltage levels at or below 69 kV; or (b) 50 MW or more when connected at greater than 69 kV. Electric storage resources are excluded. HILLs are deemed non‑conforming loads and must register per Attachment AE and follow processes in a new Attachment BA [ee82cf; 3ddcfe]. The broader HILL framework includes a High‑Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) designed to study a HILL and its supporting generation in parallel on a 90‑day timeline, aimed at customers that cannot tolerate interruptions.
- Conditional service option. In parallel with HILLGA, SPP has described a Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (CHILLS) concept that offers the same 90‑day study but provides up to five years of interruptible transmission service in exchange for agreed curtailment rights, allowing large loads to connect months faster while preserving system reliability; this can be paired with colocated or feeder‑connected generation or storage during curtailments. SPP’s HILL information page similarly describes CHILL service as providing conditional access with potential curtailment to protect regional reliability, and HILLGA as enabling parallel studies of loads and their supporting generation on a 90‑day path to agreements.
- Filing/approval pathway. Implementing the HILL framework requires revisions to SPP’s Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT). SPP stakeholder materials indicate creation of a new Attachment BA for HILL processes and related adjustments to Attachments AE and BB, while noting that certain elements (e.g., CHILLS) may proceed in separate filings; they also note that a related provisional load process in Attachment AX was pending at FERC in 2025 (Docket No. ER25‑2430) with a requested effective date of August 4, 2025. Utility Dive’s reporting notes that the HILL policy’s tariff revisions require FERC approval.
Why this is forecastable now
- As of early October 2025, SPP’s board has approved the HILL policy and SPP has described the intended 90‑day study framework and associated tariff architecture, but FERC approval is still required and the timing is uncertain. Given potential multiple filings and the scope/novelty (e.g., non‑firm CHILLS service, parallel HILLGA studies), approval by year‑end is plausible but far from assured, creating forecasting uncertainty [441c88; 60fc77; 1226e6; ee82cf].
resolution_criteria:
Question statement
- Resolve YES if, between 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025 (inclusive), FERC issues one or more orders that approve and make effective tariff sheets revising SPP’s Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) to implement the core HILL framework as defined below. Otherwise resolve NO.

Definitions (for this market)
- FERC order: A directive or ruling issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. For this question, both Commission orders and delegated letter orders qualify.
- SPP: Southwest Power Pool, the regional transmission organization described in the background.
