- HILL core framework (what must be approved to count as “implementing HILL”): Tariff language that (a) formally establishes the “High Impact Large Load” category with thresholds at 10 MW or more when connected at or below 69 kV, or 50 MW or more when connected above 69 kV, with HILLs treated as non‑conforming loads; and (b) establishes a 90‑day study-and-approval pathway for interconnecting qualifying HILLs and/or conducting a High‑Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) that studies a HILL and its supporting generation in parallel [ee82cf; 3ddcfe; 441c88; 1226e6]. Note: The 90‑day pathway may be codified via a new Attachment BA and/or other OATT sections identified in SPP materials.

What counts as approval
- Qualifying orders include those that: “accept for filing,” “approve,” or otherwise make effective the relevant tariff sheets implementing the HILL core framework described above, even if subject to subsequent compliance filings or clarifications, so long as the operative tariff language creating the HILL definition/thresholds and the 90‑day study framework is accepted and assigned an effective date. Orders that set aspects for hearing or require compliance may still qualify provided they make the operative language effective [2846ac; ee82cf; 441c88; 1226e6; 3ddcfe].

What does NOT count
- Orders limited to unrelated SPP tariff changes, deficiency letters, orders setting the matter for hearing without making the operative HILL language effective, or orders that reject/deny the HILL core framework.
- Orders approving only legacy delivery‑point (Attachment AQ) or provisional load (Attachment AX) processes without establishing the HILL category (with thresholds as above) and a 90‑day HILL/HILLGA study path.

Evidence required to resolve
- Primary: A FERC eLibrary order(s) in the relevant SPP ER docket(s) showing acceptance/approval and effective date of tariff sheets implementing the HILL core framework within the stated time window (the market admin will verify order issuance time in UTC).
- Secondary (if needed): An SPP web page or press release explicitly stating that FERC approved the HILL tariff revisions, citing the FERC docket number and order date within the window; or credible trade press citing the order and docket (e.g., Utility Dive), which the market admin will cross‑check against FERC eLibrary [441c88; 60fc77].

Time window and timezone
- Eligible orders must be issued between 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025 (inclusive). All times are in UTC.

Edge cases and tie‑breakers
- Partial approvals: If multiple orders are issued across separate filings, resolve YES if, taken together within the time window, they make effective tariff language that (a) establishes the HILL definition with the thresholds above; and (b) establishes a 90‑day HILL/HILLGA study framework. If either (a) or (b) is not approved/effective by the deadline, resolve NO [ee82cf; 3ddcfe; 441c88; 1226e6].
- Subsequent rehearing/appeal: If FERC issues a qualifying order within the time window and no order staying or vacating that approval is issued within the same time window, count it as approval for resolution purposes. If a stay/vacatur is issued within the window, the market resolves based on the status as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

question: Will Congress enact a law by December 31, 2025 that extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits (ARPA/IRA enhancements to IRC §36B) to any tax year beyond 2025?
background:
Summary of the status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
• What the enhanced ACA premium tax credits (ePTCs) are: ePTCs are the temporary American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA; P.L. 117-2) changes to the Affordable Care Act’s Premium Tax Credit (PTC) under Internal Revenue Code §36B, later extended by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA; P.L. 117-169) through the end of tax year 2025. ARPA: (1) eliminated the 400% Federal Poverty Level (FPL) income cap for PTC eligibility, and (2) replaced the applicable percentage schedule to lower required premium contributions, which for households at or above 400% FPL effectively caps the benchmark contribution at 8.5% of income. The IRA extended these ARPA provisions for tax years 2023–2025.
• What the underlying Premium Tax Credit (PTC) is: The PTC is a refundable, advanceable tax credit under IRC §36B designed to help eligible individuals and families afford insurance purchased on the ACA marketplaces (exchanges). Key terms used in PTC calculations include Federal Poverty Level (FPL), the benchmark plan (second-lowest-cost silver plan in the rating area), and the applicable percentage schedule that caps the required premium contribution as a share of income.
• Expiration timing: Under current law, the ARPA/IRA ePTC enhancements sunset after December 31, 2025 (i.e., they apply through tax year 2025). Independent health-policy analysis confirms the IRA extension through 2025 and discusses impacts if ePTCs expire after 2025.
• Legislative and fiscal context heading into Q4 2025: On September 19, 2025, the U.S. Senate rejected a House-passed stopgap funding bill (continuing resolution) that would have funded federal agencies through November 21, 2025, by a 44–48 vote, highlighting uncertainty over near-term legislative vehicles. As of September 26, 2025, the Congress.gov FY2026 Appropriations Status Table shows no FY2026 appropriations bills enacted (no Presidential Approval dates listed), underscoring that year-end negotiations could include health policy riders. One current legislative effort specifically aimed at extending the ePTCs is H.R. 5145 (119th Congress), titled the “Bipartisan Premium Tax Credit Extension Act”.

Definitions and links for forecasters:
• Affordable Care Act (ACA): Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act.
• Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §36B: The statutory section establishing the PTC; general overview in CRS report.
• Federal Poverty Level (FPL): HHS poverty guidelines used in PTC calculations; defined in CRS  and at https://aspe.hhs.gov/topics/poverty-economic-mobility/poverty-guidelines.
• Benchmark plan (second-lowest-cost silver plan): The premium used in the PTC formula; defined in CRS.
• Enhanced ACA premium tax credits (ePTCs): The ARPA/IRA temporary modifications to IRC §36B that (i) eliminate the 400% FPL eligibility cap and (ii) implement a revised applicable percentage schedule that lowers required premium contributions (including the 8.5% cap at ≥400% FPL for benchmark premiums), in effect for tax years 2021–2025.

Why this question has non-trivial uncertainty: Whether Congress uses a late-2025 legislative vehicle (e.g., omnibus appropriations or a negotiated health package) to extend the ARPA/IRA PTC enhancements beyond 2025 is actively contested, with meaningful partisan and fiscal trade-offs and multiple plausible pathways (or failure) before year-end.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
• Eligible enactments must occur between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025. Resolution will be determined at or shortly after 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

What counts as “extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits beyond 2025” (for this question):
• The law must explicitly continue the ARPA/IRA enhanced PTC regime under IRC §36B for any tax year after 2025 (e.g., 2026 or later). For this question, “enhanced PTC regime” means BOTH of the following ARPA/IRA features remain in effect under IRC §36B beyond tax year 2025: (i) elimination of the 400% FPL income cap for PTC eligibility; and (ii) retention of the ARPA applicable percentage schedule that lowers required premium contributions (including the 8.5% of income cap for households at or above 400% FPL for benchmark plan premiums).
• Partial extensions that do not include both elements above (e.g., an extension that removes the subsidy cliff but does not retain the ARPA applicable percentage schedule, or vice versa) resolve as No.
• Administrative or regulatory actions (e.g., agency guidance) do not count; only enactment of a federal statute that amends or extends the relevant provisions of IRC §36B counts.

Operational resolution rule:
• Resolve Yes if, by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, a federal statute has been enacted (signed by the President and assigned a Public Law number) and the statutory text shows the ARPA/IRA enhanced PTC features defined above continue to apply to any tax year beyond 2025 (i.e., the sunset is moved or removed for those features). Primary source: Congress.gov bill status page showing “Became Public Law” and the Public Law text (on Congress.gov or GovInfo) reflecting the extension. Secondary cross-checks (not determinative) may include reputable health policy trackers such as KFF.
• Resolve No if no such Public Law is enacted by the deadline, or if any enacted law extends only a subset of the enhancements such that both features defined above are not retained beyond 2025.

Clarifications:
• “Public Law” means a law enacted by Congress and signed by the President or enacted over a veto; the presence of a Public Law number and “Became Public Law” status on Congress.gov will be used to confirm enactment by the deadline. If the President signs the bill but Congress.gov has not yet updated the status by the deadline, the GovInfo publication of the Public Law or authoritative White House release can be used to confirm enactment.
• The extension must apply nationally to the IRC §36B PTC and is not satisfied by pilot programs or temporary administrative actions.
• The ACA, PTC under IRC §36B, FPL, benchmark plan definitions are as in CRS sources cited above.

Sources for resolution and background claims:
• CRS on ePTC expiration and ARPA/IRA features.
• KFF analysis confirming extension through 2025 and impacts of expiration.
• Reuters reporting on the Sept. 19, 2025 Senate rejection of a CR.
• Congress.gov FY2026 Appropriations Status Table indicating no FY2026 appropriations enacted as of Sept. 26, 2025.
• Congress.gov page for H.R. 5145 (119th Congress) titling the “Bipartisan Premium Tax Credit Extension Act”.

question: Will the Bank of Canada lower its target for the overnight rate at its December 10, 2025 09:45 ET announcement?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- The Bank of Canada (BoC) implements monetary policy by setting a target for the overnight rate, also referred to as the policy interest rate. It adjusts this target on eight fixed announcement dates each year. The policy interest rate is defined by the BoC as the target for the overnight rate, which is the primary tool used to control inflation. The BoC further defines the “target for the overnight rate” as the average rate the Bank aims to see in the market for overnight money market financing. Authoritative BoC references on these terms:
  • Policy interest rate overview: https://www.bankofcanada.ca/core-functions/monetary-policy/key-interest-rate/ 
  • Understanding our policy interest rate: https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/06/understanding-policy-interest-rate/ 
  • Policy instrument definitions (Target for the overnight rate, Bank Rate, deposit rate): https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/indicators/key-variables/policy-instrument/ 
- Scheduled late‑2025 dates and times: The BoC’s 2025 schedule lists an interest rate announcement on October 29, 2025 (with a Monetary Policy Report) and another on December 10, 2025, with announcements occurring at 09:45 Eastern Time (ET). The BoC’s Upcoming Events page likewise shows an Interest Rate Announcement on December 10, 2025 at 09:45 ET, and provides a direct link to the announcement page. The specific December 10, 2025 announcement page exists and is the intended location for the press release.
- Current policy rate: On September 17, 2025, the BoC reduced its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50%, and noted the next scheduled announcement date as October 29, 2025.

Why this question is interesting: The December decision follows the October 29 announcement and late‑year data. Given evolving inflation and growth dynamics, forecasters may reasonably disagree on whether further easing continues by December versus a hold or reversal.

Key term definitions (with authoritative links):
- Target for the overnight rate (policy interest rate): As defined by the BoC, the target for the overnight rate is the average rate the Bank aims to see in the overnight market; it is the BoC’s primary policy tool.
- Overnight rate / overnight money market financing rate: The rate at which major participants lend/borrow one‑day funds; the BoC targets this via its policy instrument.
- “Lower” in this question means strictly less than the immediately prior target for the overnight rate (a positive decrease). For general reference, a basis point is 0.01%: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point.
- Time zone: ET refers to North American Eastern Time. In December, this is Eastern Standard Time (EST; UTC−5). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone.

Relevant official pages for forecasters:
- BoC 2025 schedule news release: https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/bank-canada-publishes-2025-schedule-policy-interest-rate-announcements-other-major-publications/ 
- Upcoming Events (December 10, 2025 announcement at 09:45 ET): https://www.bankofcanada.ca/press/upcoming-events/ 
- September 17, 2025 rate decision (sets current 2.50%): https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/09/fad-press-release-2025-09-17/ 
- December 10, 2025 Interest Rate Announcement page (resolution source): https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/12/interest-rate-announcement-december-10-2025/
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based solely on the Bank of Canada’s official Interest Rate Announcement press release published at 09:45 ET on December 10, 2025.

Primary resolution source:
- The BoC’s “Interest Rate Announcement — December 10, 2025” page: https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2025/12/interest-rate-announcement-december-10-2025/. The BoC’s Upcoming Events page confirms the announcement time (09:45 ET) and links to this page. The 2025 schedule also lists this date and time.

Operational resolution rule:
- Resolve “Yes” if the target for the overnight rate announced at 09:45 ET on December 10, 2025 is strictly lower (numerically less) than the immediately prior target for the overnight rate in effect before the announcement; otherwise resolve “No.”

Definitions and scope:
- “Target for the overnight rate” and “policy interest rate” are terms used by the BoC to refer to the same policy instrument; use the BoC’s definitions and language as authoritative.
- “Immediately prior target for the overnight rate” means the most recently established target in effect prior to the December 10, 2025 announcement (regardless of whether it was set on October 29, 2025 or via any subsequent decision).
- Only the decision announced at the scheduled December 10, 2025 09:45 ET press release is considered. Any intraday or later changes (if any) do not affect resolution.

Procedure for resolvers:
1) Open the primary source page for the December 10, 2025 announcement. Identify the stated target for the overnight rate (policy interest rate) in the press release.
2) Determine the immediately prior target by consulting the most recent preceding BoC rate decision press release (e.g., September 17, 2025 set 2.50% and noted the next scheduled date as October 29, 2025 ; use the appropriate most recent preceding decision at the time of resolution).
3) Compare the announced December 10 target to the immediately prior target. If the December 10 target is strictly lower, resolve “Yes”; else resolve “No.”

Timing and timezone:
- The relevant decision is the press release published at 09:45 ET (Eastern Time) on December 10, 2025. ET in December corresponds to EST (UTC−5). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone.

This question is designed to resolve promptly on December 10, 2025 and, in any case, before December 31, 2025, using a single authoritative source from the Bank of Canada.

question: Will S&P Dow Jones Indices announce the addition of StandardAero (NYSE: SARO) to the S&P MidCap 400 by December 31, 2025?
background:
Overview of the index and process:
- The S&P MidCap 400 is designed to measure the performance of 400 mid‑sized U.S. companies and serves as a benchmark for the mid-cap segment of the U.S. equity market. Changes to index composition are made on an as‑needed basis and are announced publicly by S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P DJI). S&P DJI posts index composition changes to its website and releases them to major news services; for the S&P U.S. Indices, additions/deletions are typically announced at 05:15 PM Eastern Time with at least three business days’ advance notice (the committee may deviate at its discretion). S&P DJI’s “Index Announcements” articles display section labeling and datelines/timestamps on the spglobal.com/spdji site (example article showing this formatting: “Index Announcements” with a dated New York dateline).

Key eligibility criteria relevant to potential inclusion (as of July 1, 2025):
- For the S&P MidCap 400, eligibility is determined by the S&P U.S. Indices Methodology, including: U.S. domicile; listing on an eligible U.S. exchange; financial viability (positive GAAP earnings in the most recent quarter and in aggregate over the last four quarters); liquidity thresholds; and market‑cap guidelines. As of July 1, 2025, the total company market capitalization range for the S&P MidCap 400 is US$8.0 billion to US$22.7 billion, with a minimum float‑adjusted market cap threshold at the security level equal to at least 50% of the index’s minimum company threshold. IPOs are generally required to have traded on an eligible exchange for at least 12 months before consideration; there is no fast track entry for S&P Composite 1500 candidates (which includes the S&P MidCap 400).

Company context (StandardAero):
- StandardAero, Inc. priced its upsized initial public offering at $24.00 per share, and its common stock was expected to begin trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker “SARO” on October 2, 2024. On its first trading day, Reuters reported an equity valuation of approximately $10.38 billion and confirmed trading on the NYSE under ticker SARO.N.
- StandardAero reported strong Q2 2025 results: revenue of $1,528.9 million (+13.5% YoY), net income of $67.7 million, and adjusted EBITDA of $204.6 million (+20.1% YoY), with segment details provided in its August 13, 2025 investor relations press release.

Why this is plausibly uncertain:
- By mid‑October 2025, StandardAero has surpassed the 12‑month post‑IPO trading window for S&P Composite 1500 eligibility. Its size at IPO suggests it could fit within the S&P MidCap 400 market‑cap guidelines as of July 1, 2025 (ranges are reviewed periodically), but actual inclusion is discretionary and depends on committee decisions, sector balance, and ongoing eligibility metrics.

Definitions used in this question:
- “S&P MidCap 400” refers to the S&P 400 index maintained by S&P DJI, as described on S&P’s official index page.
- “S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P DJI) official announcement” refers to an index composition change communication published on spglobal.com/spdji in the Index Announcements section or a press release on the S&P DJI site, consistent with the methodology’s description that changes are posted to S&P’s website and distributed to major news services; S&P U.S. Indices changes are typically posted at 05:15 PM Eastern Time.
- “StandardAero (NYSE: SARO)” refers to StandardAero, Inc., the issuer whose common stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SARO, as indicated in the company’s IPO pricing press release and contemporaneous Reuters coverage.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes, between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 Eastern Time (ET, America/New_York) and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 ET inclusive, an official announcement stating that StandardAero will be added to the S&P MidCap 400.

Resolve “Yes” if all of the following are true:
1) S&P DJI publishes an item on spglobal.com/spdji that clearly states that StandardAero (or its successor name, if renamed) will be added to the S&P MidCap 400. Acceptable sources include:
   - An article in S&P DJI’s Index Announcements section, or
   - An S&P DJI press release on spglobal.com/spdji.
   The S&P U.S. Indices Methodology specifies that such changes are publicly posted on S&P’s website and released to major news services, with typical posting time at 05:15 PM ET. The Index Announcements articles display section labeling and datelines/timestamps on the S&P DJI site (see example of format/timestamp presentation).
2) The publication timestamp shown on the S&P DJI page falls within the window above (ET). If the page shows only a date without time, the date must be within the window.
3) The item unambiguously identifies the issuer (e.g., “StandardAero” and ideally ticker SARO) and the target index (“S&P MidCap 400” or “S&P 400”). If S&P DJI uses a new legal name or ticker for the same issuer due to a name/ticker change, that still counts as long as it clearly refers to StandardAero, Inc. (e.g., via name continuity or context in the announcement).

Notes and edge cases:
- Effective date: The announcement may specify an effective date after December 31, 2025 (e.g., early 2026); this still counts as “Yes” as long as the qualifying announcement is published within the window.
- Corrections/reversals: If S&P DJI publishes such an addition announcement within the window and later (on or before the cutoff) publishes a formal correction/reversal stating the addition will not occur, the resolution follows the latest S&P DJI communication on or before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 ET (i.e., “No” if reversed before the deadline).
- Migrations: If the announcement describes a migration of StandardAero into the S&P MidCap 400 from another S&P index, it counts as an addition for the purposes of this question.
- Non‑qualifying sources: Third‑party summaries, blogs, or exchange listing pages do not by themselves qualify. However, if the S&P DJI site is inaccessible at resolution time, the forecaster may use a major newswire article (e.g., Reuters, AP) that directly quotes and links to the S&P DJI announcement as secondary confirmation, but the primary resolution source is the S&P DJI site.

Start date and time zone:
- Eligible announcements must be published on or after 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 ET and on or before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 ET. ET refers to U.S. Eastern Time (America/New_York). The methodology indicates S&P U.S. Indices changes are typically published at 05:15 PM ET.

Primary resolution sources (public, authoritative):
- S&P U.S. Indices Methodology (for the definition of official communications/announcement practices).
- S&P DJI Index Announcements pages on spglobal.com/spdji, which display section labeling and datelines/timestamps (example of presentation).

Context sources (for forecasters’ background only):
- S&P MidCap 400 index page (definition and purpose).
- StandardAero IPO pricing and NYSE ticker information.
- Reuters first‑day trading valuation and ticker confirmation.
- StandardAero Q2 2025 financial results.

question: Will the ECB announce a reduction in the deposit facility rate at either its 30 Oct or 18 Dec 2025 monetary policy decision?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: The European Central Bank (ECB) currently sets the deposit facility rate (DFR) at 2.00%, effective from 11 June 2025. At its latest monetary policy meeting on 11 September 2025, the Governing Council kept the three key ECB interest rates unchanged, with the DFR remaining at 2.00%. Earlier in 2025, the ECB lowered the three key rates by 25 basis points at its 30 January, 6 March, 17 April, and 5 June meetings, bringing the DFR from 2.75% to 2.00% over that period.

Upcoming decisions: The ECB Governing Council has scheduled monetary policy meetings on 29–30 October 2025 (hosted by Banca d’Italia in Florence) and 17–18 December 2025 (in Frankfurt). ECB monetary policy decisions are published via an official press release at 14:15 CET on the day of the Governing Council monetary policy meeting.

Key definition: The “deposit facility” is a standing facility of the Eurosystem that counterparties may use to make overnight deposits at a national central bank; such deposits are remunerated at a pre-specified interest rate (the deposit facility rate).

Why this is forecastable: As inflation projections are around target and growth has shown only modest momentum through 2025, further rate cuts in late 2025 are plausible but not assured; the September 2025 hold underscores uncertainty about additional easing. Forecasters can analyze inflation dynamics, labor market data, credit conditions, ECB communication, and market pricing to estimate the likelihood of a further reduction in the DFR at either the October or December decision.

Time standard and scope: Publication times are CET (as used by the ECB). The question concerns only the monetary policy decisions announced via the ECB’s official “Monetary policy decisions” press releases on 30 October 2025 and 18 December 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve Yes if the ECB’s official “Monetary policy decisions” press release published on either 30 October 2025 or 18 December 2025 states that the interest rate on the deposit facility will be decreased (by any positive amount) relative to its level prior to that decision; otherwise resolve No. 

Definitions and sources: 
- Deposit facility rate (DFR): As defined by the ECB glossary (the interest rate paid on overnight deposits at a national central bank within the Eurosystem). 
- Eligible press releases: The ECB “Monetary policy decisions” press releases published at 14:15 CET on the day of the Governing Council monetary policy meeting. The relevant meetings are scheduled for 29–30 October 2025 (Florence) and 17–18 December 2025 (Frankfurt). 

Operationalization: 
- “States that the interest rate on the deposit facility will be decreased” includes clear ECB wording such as “The Governing Council decided to lower the interest rate on the deposit facility …” or listing a new DFR level that is lower than the pre-decision level (e.g., from 2.00% to a lower figure) within the press release. 
- Effective dates: ECB decisions typically specify an effective date (e.g., “with effect from …”). A decrease counts for resolution if the press release announces a lower DFR, regardless of whether the effective date is after the decision date. 
- Pre-decision level reference: The DFR level prior to the decision may be verified via the ECB’s “Key ECB interest rates” page (e.g., 2.00% with effect from 11 June 2025 as of 2025-10-01). 

Timing window: Eligible announcements must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00 CET and 2025-12-31 23:59 CET, but only the two specified decision dates are evaluated. If either meeting is rescheduled within 2025, evaluate the monetary policy decision press release published on the second day of that meeting in 2025; if no decision press release is published on the relevant date(s), resolve No.

question: At the daily close on December 31, 2025, will Spain’s 10-year government bond yield be lower than France’s?
background:
Status quo as of October 1, 2025: Public market data sources show Spain’s 10-year government bond yield around 3.26% and France’s around 3.53%. In late 2024, French borrowing costs briefly rose above Spain’s for the first time since 2008, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters, reflecting a notable shift in investor perceptions. Reuters further reported a broader narrative in October 2024 in which investors began demanding more compensation to lend to France than to Spain, with explanations tied to France’s weaker fiscal outlook and slower growth versus Spain’s improving debt metrics and stronger growth; the article also noted Spain’s multiple post-crisis ratings upgrades versus France’s downgrades.

Why this matters: The Spain–France relative position has recently flipped compared to historical norms, and whether Spain’s 10-year yield remains below France’s at year-end depends on evolving fiscal policy, macro data, and ECB policy. As of today, the gap favors Spain, but it has been narrow and subject to reversal, making the outcome uncertain and forecastable.

Definitions and key terms:
- Government bond: A debt security issued by a national government. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_bond
- Yield (yield to maturity in context of these series): The quoted yield for a given maturity series (10 years) as reported by the chosen data source for each country. Trading Economics describes these as over-the-counter interbank yield quotes for this maturity. See conceptual overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yield_(finance)
- 10-year government bond yield (Spain/France): The country-specific 10-year maturity yield series as displayed on the designated resolution source pages (primary: Investing.com historical data pages for “Spain 10-Year Bond Yield” and “France 10-Year Bond Yield”; backup: Trading Economics country pages for “Government Bond 10y”).
- Daily close (for resolution): The value in the “Close” column for the calendar date December 31, 2025 on the Investing.com Historical Data pages specified below. If the “Close” value for that date is not available on Investing.com for either country by January 7, 2026, use the Trading Economics page value labeled for December 31, 2025.
- Strictly lower: Numerical comparison of Spain’s value versus France’s value; Spain must be less than France. Equality does not count as lower.

Current context sources:
- Spain 10-year yield page: https://tradingeconomics.com/spain/government-bond-yield (latest value and description of series) 
- France 10-year yield page: https://tradingeconomics.com/france/government-bond-yield (latest value and description of series) 
- Reuters background on inversion: https://www.reuters.com/markets/europe/french-borrowing-costs-rise-above-spains-first-time-since-2008-2024-09-24/ 
- Reuters analysis of Spain vs France investor preferences: https://www.reuters.com/markets/rates-bonds/why-bond-investors-favour-spain-over-france-2024-10-01/ 

Resolution Criteria:
- Observation date: December 31, 2025. The question resolves after the daily close values for that date are published.
- Primary source (one source of truth):
  • Spain: Investing.com “Spain 10-Year Bond Yield – Historical Data” at https://www.investing.com/rates-bonds/spain-10-year-bond-yield-historical-data
  • France: Investing.com “France 10-Year Bond Yield – Historical Data” at https://www.investing.com/rates-bonds/france-10-year-bond-yield-historical-data
  Use the “Close” column values for the row labeled December 31, 2025 on each page. Investing.com confirms these pages provide “closing yield” in the Historical Data table.
- Comparison rule: Parse each “Close” value as a numeric value (percent). If Spain’s value is strictly less than France’s, resolve YES; otherwise resolve NO.
- Precision: Use the numeric values as displayed in the “Close” column (no additional rounding beyond what is shown on the page). If both values display with different decimal precision, compare the parsed numeric values directly.
- Backup source (only if primary is unavailable for either country by January 7, 2026): Trading Economics country pages for “Government Bond 10y”:
  • Spain: https://tradingeconomics.com/spain/government-bond-yield 
  • France: https://tradingeconomics.com/france/government-bond-yield 
  Use the page’s daily value for December 31, 2025 for each country. If both primary and backup are available but conflict, prefer the primary (Investing.com) values.
- Edge cases:
  • If the Investing.com page lists the date but the “Close” is non-numeric (e.g., “N/A”) for a country, treat that country as unavailable and use the backup source for that country.
  • Equality: If Spain’s value equals France’s (as numeric values), resolve NO.
- Timezone: The date used for resolution is the calendar date labeled “Dec 31, 2025” on the resolution source pages. No conversion is required; the displayed date row governs.

This question resolves on December 31, 2025, once the relevant data is published on the specified pages. It can logically resolve to either YES or NO, and relies on widely available public data sources that regularly publish daily 10-year yield series for Spain and France.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve YES if the Spain “Close” value for December 31, 2025 is strictly less than the France “Close” value for December 31, 2025, as displayed on the Investing.com Historical Data pages listed below. Otherwise resolve NO.

Primary (Investing.com Historical Data pages):
- Spain: https://www.investing.com/rates-bonds/spain-10-year-bond-yield-historical-data
- France: https://www.investing.com/rates-bonds/france-10-year-bond-yield-historical-data
These pages state they provide the “closing yield” in the Historical Data table.

Procedure:
1) After December 31, 2025, open the two Investing.com Historical Data pages above.
2) Ensure the frequency is Daily and the date range includes the year 2025.
3) For each country, locate the row labeled “Dec 31, 2025” and record the numeric value shown in the “Close” column.
4) Compare Spain’s Close value to France’s Close value:
   • If Spain’s value < France’s value, resolve YES.
   • If Spain’s value ≥ France’s value, resolve NO.

Precision and parsing:
- Use the numeric values as displayed in the “Close” column. Compare the parsed numeric values directly; do not apply additional rounding.
- Equality counts as NO.

Backup (only if primary is unavailable for either country by January 7, 2026):
- Spain: Trading Economics “Spain 10-Year Government Bond Yield” https://tradingeconomics.com/spain/government-bond-yield 
- France: Trading Economics “France 10-Year Government Bond Yield” https://tradingeconomics.com/france/government-bond-yield 
For any country lacking a usable Investing.com Close value for Dec 31, 2025 (missing row, “N/A”, or page unavailable), use the TE page’s daily value labeled for Dec 31, 2025 for that country. If both Investing.com and TE provide values but they conflict on the outcome, prefer the Investing.com values.

Notes:
- The series definitions: Trading Economics describes these 10-year yields as over-the-counter interbank yield quotes for this maturity.
- Time/date handling: The date used is the calendar date as labeled on the relevant source page. No timezone conversion is applied.
- Resolution timing: The question resolves once the Dec 31, 2025 values are available on the specified pages (no later than January 7, 2026).

This criterion ensures a clear, unambiguous, and quick (≤10 minutes) resolution path using widely accessible public data sources.

question: Will the European Commission open an EMFA-related infringement case against Italy over public service media governance/funding between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- European Media Freedom Act (EMFA): Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 establishes a common framework for media services in the EU. The core provisions of EMFA entered into application on 8 August 2025, per the European Board for Media Services announcement (“core provisions … officially enter into application”). The EMFA includes Article 5 on “Safeguards for the independent functioning of public service media providers.” A reliable reproduction of the final text sets out governance and funding safeguards, including appointment/dismissal criteria and adequate, sustainable, and predictable funding that safeguards editorial independence. Analytical commentary by the Centre for Media Pluralism and Media Freedom (CMPF) summarises Article 5’s intent and requirements regarding governance (appointment and dismissal procedures) and funding guarantees.
- Infringement procedure basics: Under Article 258 TFEU, the Commission initiates an infringement procedure by sending a “letter of formal notice” to the Member State, which typically allows two months for reply; if issues persist, the Commission may issue a reasoned opinion and ultimately refer the matter to the Court of Justice. In its public “infringements package” communications, the Commission uses the formulation “decided to open an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to [Member State] (INFR(YYYY)####) for failing to …”.
- Italy/RAI context: Civil society analysis (Italian NGO CILD) argues that governance and funding arrangements at Italy’s public broadcaster RAI conflict with EMFA Article 5, citing politically driven executive appointments and unstable funding (e.g., licence fee changes), and notes that EMFA opens paths for oversight, appeals, and potential Commission infringements based on citizen/association reports.
Definitions and links:
- European Media Freedom Act (EMFA): Regulation (EU) 2024/1083. See authentic text via EUR-Lex ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1083/oj
- Public service media providers: Entities entrusted with a public service remit and receiving public funding for that purpose; EMFA Article 5 governs their independence and funding safeguards.
- Public service media governance (for this question): The frameworks and procedures for appointment and dismissal of the head of management and/or members of the management board (or equivalent highest decision-making authority) of public service media providers, as covered by EMFA Article 5(2).
- Public service media funding (for this question): Funding procedures and financial resources for public service media providers that must be based on transparent, objective criteria, guaranteeing adequate, sustainable, and predictable resources that safeguard editorial independence, as covered by EMFA Article 5(3).
- Infringement procedure initiation: The European Commission “opens an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice” under Article 258 TFEU.
Why this is an uncertain, non-trivial forecast: EMFA’s key obligations have only recently become applicable (Aug 2025) , and whether the Commission will act specifically against Italy over Article 5 governance/funding by year-end depends on legal assessment, monitoring, and political prioritisation. Commission infringement packages are announced periodically, but the timing and scope of EMFA enforcement actions are uncertain. Italy’s RAI governance/funding controversies raise plausible triggers , yet Commission action is not guaranteed.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will the European Commission initiate a formal infringement procedure against Italy related to EMFA compliance for public service media governance and/or funding between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC?

Resolve Yes if, within the specified window, the European Commission publicly announces that it has opened an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to Italy (under Article 258 TFEU), and that announcement explicitly cites Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 (the European Media Freedom Act) non-compliance concerning (a) public service media governance (appointment/dismissal frameworks for the head of management or members of the management board) and/or (b) public service media funding (funding procedures/resources) as described in EMFA Article 5(2)-(3).

Operational definitions for resolution:
- “Initiate a formal infringement procedure” means the Commission’s decision to open an infringement procedure via a letter of formal notice, as per Commission terminology and process.
- “Publicly announces” means publication on an official European Commission channel, such as:
  - Press Corner press release or “Infringements package: key decisions” communication (e.g., PDF or web page) where the language “decided to open an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to Italy (INFR(YYYY)####)” appears and EMFA/Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 non-compliance related to public service media governance/funding is explicitly cited.
  - Alternatively, listing on the Commission’s “Infringement decisions” portal (https://ec.europa.eu/atwork/applying-eu-law/infringements-proceedings/infringement_decisions/) showing a decision to send a letter of formal notice to Italy referencing EMFA non-compliance related to public service media governance/funding.
- “Explicitly cites EMFA” means the announcement names Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 and references non-compliance elements aligning with Article 5 governance/funding safeguards (appointment/dismissal procedures; adequate, sustainable, predictable funding with editorial independence).
- “Italy” refers to the Member State of Italy (Republic of Italy).

Resolve No if no such announcement is published during the specified window.

Timing and scope notes:
- Only letters of formal notice published within the window count as initiation; reasoned opinions or Court referrals without a preceding letter of formal notice in the window do not count.
- The alleged infringement must concern EMFA compliance related to public service media governance and/or funding (Article 5(2)-(3)); EMFA issues unrelated to Article 5, or non-EMFA media matters, do not count.

Primary resolution sources to check within 10 minutes:
- European Commission Press Corner “Infringements package: key decisions” postings (language exemplar provided).
- Commission memo on infringement procedure stages for terminology.
- EMFA Article 5 text reproduction for governance/funding definitions ; CMPF analysis for context on Article 5 provisions.

Additional background confirmation (not required for resolution but informative):
- EMFA core provisions entered into application on 8 August 2025.
- Civil society claims of Italy/RAI non-compliance and potential pathways to oversight and infringements.

question: Will the EPA’s final 2027 total renewable fuel volume be at least 24.0 billion RINs by December 31, 2025?
background:
The U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) requires the EPA to set annual volume requirements for four categories of renewable fuel, including “total renewable fuel,” via notice-and-comment rulemaking. In the last finalized “Set 1” rule, EPA set the 2025 total renewable fuel requirement at 22.33 billion RINs (one RIN equals one ethanol‑equivalent gallon).

As of 2025-09-22, EPA has proposed “Set 2” standards for 2026–2027 with total renewable fuel volumes of 24.02 billion RINs (2026) and 24.46 billion RINs (2027), docket EPA‑HQ‑OAR‑2024‑0505. On 2025-09-16, EPA issued a supplemental proposed rule addressing small refinery exemptions and related reallocations; these remain proposals pending a final rule.

Final RFS rules are published in the Federal Register; the 2026–2027 action’s proposed rule was published there on 2025-06-17. This question asks whether the final rule, if published by 2025‑12‑31, will set the 2027 “total renewable fuel” applicable volume at ≥24.0 billion RINs.
resolution_criteria:
Start date/time: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC. End date/time: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

YES if, on or before the end date, the EPA publishes in the Federal Register a FINAL rule for the Renewable Fuel Standard that specifies the 2027 “total renewable fuel” applicable volume at 24.0 billion RINs or higher. “Total renewable fuel” refers to the RFS program category encompassing all qualifying renewable fuel; “RIN” means Renewable Identification Number, the compliance credit used in RFS; 1 RIN equals one ethanol-equivalent gallon.

Primary resolution source: the Federal Register publication of the final rule setting 2026–2027 RFS standards (Docket EPA‑HQ‑OAR‑2024‑0505), as displayed on federalregister.gov (use the “Publication Date” field to determine timeliness). If the final rule expresses the 2027 total renewable fuel volume in gallons rather than RINs, convert using 1 RIN = 1 ethanol‑equivalent gallon. Compare the published 2027 total renewable fuel applicable volume to the 24.0 billion RIN threshold without rounding (i.e., 24.00 billion = 24,000,000,000 RINs).

NO if no such final rule is published by the end date/time, or if a final rule is published by the deadline but sets the 2027 total renewable fuel applicable volume below 24.0 billion RINs. If multiple final-rule documents affecting the 2027 total renewable fuel volume are published within the window (e.g., corrections), use the most recent final publication within the window. Subsequent litigation or stays after publication do not affect resolution.

question: Will plug-in electric vehicles reach at least 25.0% of global light-vehicle sales in November 2025?
background:
Context for forecasters as of 2025-09-22 (UTC):
- Scope in this question is plug-in electric vehicles (PEVs), defined as the union of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). BEVs are vehicles powered exclusively by electricity stored in on-board batteries and propelled solely by electric motors (see general definition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicle). PHEVs are hybrid vehicles equipped with a rechargeable traction battery that can be charged from an external source, in addition to an internal combustion engine (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plug-in_hybrid).
- “Global light-vehicle sales” refers to worldwide sales/registrations of new light vehicles, which for industry data providers typically include passenger cars and light trucks/light commercial vehicles up to about 3.5 tonnes gross vehicle weight. This scope mirrors how leading trackers report overall auto market totals; forecasters should be aware that different regions bundle SUVs/crossovers into passenger/light-vehicle categories. Background on the light-vehicle concept: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_truck and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_commercial_vehicle.
- “Market share” means the percentage of total global light-vehicle sales represented by PEVs in the specified calendar month: share = 100% × (BEV+PHEV new registrations in that month) / (total new light-vehicle registrations in that month). General notion of market share: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_share.
- Practical data notes: Monthly global PEV sales and share are commonly tracked and published by EV-Volumes and Rho Motion; secondary summaries often appear in trade press (e.g., Autovista24, CleanTechnica) that cite the primary datasets. Regional dynamics matter (China currently leads global adoption; Europe is strong; the U.S. lags), and monthly shares can fluctuate due to incentives, model launches, and seasonality. Forecasters should monitor November 2025 data releases from these sources.
- This question deliberately uses a single month (November 2025) so that a definitive source should be available by year-end 2025, allowing timely resolution.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether the reported global plug-in electric vehicle (BEV+PHEV) share of light-vehicle sales in November 2025 is at least 25.0%.

Event window and timing:
- Measurement period: 2025-11-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC (i.e., the calendar month of November 2025).
- Resolution deadline: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Definitions and calculation:
- Plug-in electric vehicles (PEVs) = BEVs + PHEVs. BEV definition reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_electric_vehicle. PHEV definition reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plug-in_hybrid.
- Global light-vehicle sales = worldwide new light-vehicle (passenger + light commercial up to ~3.5 t GVW) registrations/sales as generally used by industry trackers.
- Market share threshold = 25.0% (greater than or equal to 25.0% qualifies as meeting the threshold). Use the share value as directly reported by the resolution source; do not recompute unless explicitly required by the fallback step below.

Primary resolution source (priority order):
1) EV-Volumes monthly reporting of “global plug-in share” (BEV+PHEV) for November 2025 on ev-volumes.com (news or dashboard pages). If EV-Volumes publishes a November 2025 global plug-in share figure by the deadline, that figure will determine resolution (Yes if ≥25.0%; No if <25.0%).
2) If (1) is not available by the deadline, use Rho Motion’s November 2025 global PEV share as published on rhomotion.com or in a publicly accessible November/December 2025 news post/brief.
3) If neither (1) nor (2) provides an explicit November 2025 global PEV share by the deadline, but one provides November 2025 global PEV unit sales and the same source provides November 2025 total global light-vehicle unit sales, compute share as 100% × (PEV units / total light-vehicle units) using those two numbers from the same source.
4) If none of the above is available by the deadline, resolve using two independent secondary outlets that explicitly cite EV-Volumes or Rho Motion and report the November 2025 global PEV share (e.g., Autovista24, CleanTechnica). If both secondary sources agree on a single value crossing the threshold, use that; if they disagree across the threshold, prefer the value that can be traced most directly (verbatim) to EV-Volumes over other sources.

Ties, rounding, and revisions:
- Threshold comparison uses the value as reported to one decimal place (or greater precision if provided). A reported 25.0% or higher is a Yes; 24.9% or lower is a No.
- If the source later revises November 2025 figures after the resolution deadline, the initial value available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC is binding for this market’s resolution.

Exclusions:
- Non-plug-in hybrids (HEVs) and fuel-cell vehicles (FCEVs) are excluded from the numerator.
- Used vehicle sales are excluded.

Start date for question validity:
- This question covers the specific month (November 2025) and will resolve between 2025-12-01 and 2025-12-31, based on publications available by the resolution deadline.

All dates/times are UTC.

question: By the close of COP30 (Nov 21, 2025), will the COP or CMA adopt an operative decision that requests Parties to submit updated NDCs or long-term strategies by a deadline in 2026?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:

- Conference timing and venue: The 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30) is scheduled to be held in Belém, Brazil, from November 10 to 21, 2025. The UNFCCC Secretariat has formally messaged Parties that CMA7 (the session of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement held alongside COP30) will convene from Monday, 10 November, to Friday, 21 November 2025 (per decision 17/CP.28, para. 4).

- What the COP and CMA are: COP is the supreme decision-making body of the UNFCCC, composed of Parties to the Convention. CMA is the body of Parties to the Paris Agreement; it oversees implementation of the Agreement and takes decisions to promote its effective implementation.

- Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs): Under the Paris Agreement, NDCs are national climate action plans or pledges communicated by Parties, primarily focused on mitigation but often including adaptation elements. Parties prepare, communicate, and maintain NDCs, updating them every five years with progression over time.

- Long-term strategies (LT-LEDS/LTS): Paris Agreement Article 4.19 calls on Parties to formulate and communicate long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies.

- Recent process mandates relevant to NDC cycles:
  - Glasgow Climate Pact, Decision 1/CMA.3 (COP26) requested Parties to revisit and strengthen the 2030 targets in their NDCs by the end of 2022, aligning with the Paris Agreement temperature goal.
  - Outcome of the first Global Stocktake (adopted at COP28/CMA5, Decision 1/CMA.5) informs the next round of NDCs. Parties have been guided to submit their next NDCs with certain features (e.g., economy-wide coverage aligned to 1.5°C; encouraged to use an end date of 2035), and to communicate their NDCs in 2025 ahead of COP30/CMA7.
  - UNFCCC Secretariat’s message to Parties (citing Decision 1/CP.21, para. 25, and Decision 1/CMA.5, para. 166) reminds Parties to communicate their NDCs at least 9 to 12 months in advance of CMA7, i.e., no later than 10 February 2025.

Why this question is uncertain and interesting: Mandates already set deadlines around early 2025 for communicating the next NDCs; and Article 4.19 “invites/should strive” language has historically lacked fixed deadlines. The question tests whether COP30 will tighten process by adopting an operative request that sets a specific submission deadline falling in calendar year 2026 for either updated NDCs or long-term strategies. Precedent exists for operative requests with explicit timing (e.g., Glasgow’s 2022 revisit request for NDCs) , but Parties may resist new deadline obligations tied to 2026, especially for LTS/LT-LEDS, which to date have flexible timing.

Key definitions and scope used in this forecast:
- COP30: The 2025 UN climate conference held 2025-11-10 to 2025-11-21 in Belém, Brazil.
- COP/CMA “decision”: A formal decision text adopted in plenary by either COP or CMA (e.g., decisions numbered 1/CP.30 or 1/CMA.7). Prior to adoption, such texts are considered “draft decisions”; decisions are only adopted in plenary.
- “Parties”: States that are Parties to the UNFCCC (for COP decisions) or Parties to the Paris Agreement (for CMA decisions).
- “Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)”: National climate action pledges communicated under the Paris Agreement framework; updated on a five-year cycle with progression.
- “Long-term strategies” (LT-LEDS/LTS): Long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies communicated under Article 4.19 of the Paris Agreement.
- “Operative paragraph”: A numbered clause of an adopted decision containing operative language (e.g., “Decides,” “Requests,” “Calls upon,” “Urges,” “Invites”). For the purpose of this question, only paragraphs that use the verb “Requests” addressed to “Parties” and that direct them to “submit,” “communicate,” or “update” an NDC or LTS count toward a Yes resolution (see Resolution Criteria for exact matching).
- “Deadline in 2026”: A deadline explicitly stated within calendar year 2026 (e.g., “by 30 June 2026,” “by 2026,” “no later than 31 December 2026”). Deadlines stated only relative to an event (e.g., “as soon as possible” or “before the next CMA”) without an explicit “2026” are out of scope.

Date window for eligible events: Only decisions adopted between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-11-21 23:59 UTC at COP30/CMA7 are considered. The question resolves using publicly available decision texts posted thereafter (see Resolution Criteria).

Primary sources for verification:
- UNFCCC official decisions page and COP30/CMA7 decisions section (publicly posted adopted decisions; authoritative for final texts). As backup or corroboration, IISD Earth Negotiations Bulletin’s summary and closing coverage confirms adopted outcomes.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve Yes if, by 2025-11-21 23:59 UTC, at least one formally adopted decision of COP or CMA at COP30 contains an operative paragraph that meets ALL of the following:

1) Actor and verb: The paragraph uses the verb “Requests” and is addressed to “Parties.” Paragraphs that use “Invites,” “Encourages,” “Calls upon,” or “Urges” do not qualify for Yes.

2) Action: It directs Parties to “submit,” “communicate,” or “update” either:
   - Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) , or
   - Long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies (LT-LEDS/LTS).

3) Timing: It specifies a deadline explicitly falling in calendar year 2026 (e.g., “by 30 June 2026,” “by 2026,” “no later than 31 December 2026”). Relative or unspecified timing (e.g., “as soon as possible,” “ahead of the next CMA”) does not qualify unless the paragraph explicitly includes the year “2026.”

4) Adoption: The decision is adopted in plenary at COP30/CMA7 (not merely a draft). Adoption is determined by presence of the final decision posted on the UNFCCC website with an official decision code (e.g., 1/CP.30, 2/CMA.7). Decisions are only adopted in plenary.

If multiple decisions are adopted, only one meeting these criteria is sufficient for Yes. If no adopted decision meets all criteria, resolve No.

Inclusions and examples that would count (illustrative):
- “Requests Parties to submit updated NDCs no later than 31 December 2026.” (Yes)
- “Requests Parties to communicate long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies by 2026.” (Yes)

Exclusions and examples that would not count:
- “Invites Parties to consider updating their NDCs by 2026.” (No; verb is “Invites”)
- “Encourages Parties to communicate LTS as soon as possible.” (No; lacks explicit 2026)
- “Requests Parties to submit their next NDCs by February 2025.” (No; deadline not in 2026)
- “Requests Parties to submit their NDCs ahead of CMA8.” (No; lacks explicit 2026)

Eligible decisions must be adopted between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-11-21 23:59 UTC at COP30/CMA7.

Resolution source and method:
- Primary: UNFCCC official decisions page for COP30/CMA7 (final adopted decisions). Verify whether any adopted decision contains a qualifying operative paragraph. As necessary for corroboration of adoption and content, refer to IISD Earth Negotiations Bulletin’s COP30 coverage and decision summaries.

Context references for forecasters:
- COP30 dates/location: Belém, Brazil, Nov 10–21, 2025.
- CMA7 convening and NDC timing reminder: Parties to communicate NDCs at least 9–12 months before CMA7, i.e., no later than 10 Feb 2025.
- NDCs overview/definition:.
- Long-term strategies definition (Article 4.19):.
- Glasgow Decision 1/CMA.3 requesting 2022 revisit of 2030 NDC targets:.
- Global Stocktake outcome context informing NDC 3.0 (e.g., encouragement of 2035 end dates; guidance on ambition):.

question: U.S. 30-year mortgage rate: Will Freddie Mac’s PMMS show ≥ 6.50% for the last weekly 30‑year FRM average published in December 2025?
background:
Overview and definitions
- Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS): Freddie Mac’s long‑running weekly survey that reports national average mortgage rates. Since November 2022, PMMS averages are computed from loan application data submitted to Freddie Mac’s Loan Product Advisor and are limited to first‑lien, conventional, conforming, fully amortizing purchase mortgages for borrowers with 20% down (LTV ~80%) and excellent credit (e.g., ≥740 FICO), for owner‑occupied single‑family properties in the contiguous U.S..
- Publication cadence and dating: PMMS is published weekly, typically on Thursdays at 12:00 p.m. ET. If a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, PMMS publishes on the Wednesday of that week. The PMMS “week” covers applications from 12:00 a.m. ET Thursday through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Entries are dated by the publication date (e.g., “September 25, 2025”). 
- Where to find the data: Freddie Mac maintains public archives listing weekly 30‑Year Fixed‑Rate Mortgage (30‑Yr FRM) averages by date. These pages display the rate to two decimal places and clearly show the weekly dates (e.g., Sep 11, 18, 25, 2025). The current‑week snapshot is also shown on the Mortgage Rates landing page.

Status quo as of late September 2025
- As of the PMMS publication dated September 25, 2025, the 30‑year FRM averaged 6.30%.
- Recent weekly readings in September 2025 have been in the mid‑6% range, including 6.26% (Sep 18) and 6.35% (Sep 11) per the archive. Some weeks have touched 6.50% (e.g., Sep 4, 2025).

Why this matters for forecasting
- The late‑year outcome depends on macroeconomic data, Federal Reserve policy guidance, and mortgage‑Treasury spread dynamics. With recent PMMS readings around the mid‑6% range and occasional prints at 6.50%, whether the final December 2025 weekly publication lands at or above 6.50% remains uncertain enough to support non‑trivial forecasting.

Key terms (for clarity)
- “30‑Year FRM average” refers to the national average interest rate (not APR) for the 30‑year fixed‑rate mortgage series reported by PMMS, as defined by Freddie Mac’s methodology in effect at the time of publication.
- “Publication date” is the date shown on the PMMS archive entry for that weekly release (e.g., “December 24, 2025” or “December 31, 2025”), which follows the cadence described above.
resolution_criteria:
How this question resolves
- Scope: Consider all PMMS weekly publications with a publication date between 2025‑12‑01 00:00 ET and 2025‑12‑31 23:59 ET, inclusive. Identify the weekly publication with the latest publication date within that window (“the last weekly PMMS publication dated in December 2025”). Note: PMMS is typically published Thursdays at 12:00 p.m. ET, and if that Thursday is a U.S. holiday, publication occurs on Wednesday of that week.
- Metric used: For that last December 2025 publication, take the “30‑Yr FRM” Average Rate value as displayed on the Freddie Mac PMMS archive page (no additional rounding by the resolver; use the value as shown to two decimal places).
- Resolution rule: Resolve “Yes” if that displayed 30‑Yr FRM Average Rate is greater than or equal to 6.50%. Resolve “No” if it is below 6.50%.
- Source of truth: The Freddie Mac PMMS archive pages that list the weekly 30‑Yr FRM averages and publication dates. Acceptable sources include: https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/archive and/or https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/pmms_archives. If multiple official Freddie Mac pages present the weekly rate for the same date, the PMMS archive(s) take precedence over press releases or third‑party sites.
- Edge cases: If, contrary to normal practice, no PMMS weekly publication is dated in December 2025, resolve this question as “No.” This preserves a definite binary outcome while relying on the PMMS publication cadence as documented.

question: Mexico PEF 2026: Will the Secretaría de Salud (Ramo 12) be allocated at least 68,000 mdp in the approved budget?
background:
Summary of the status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- What is being forecast: whether, in Mexico’s approved Presupuesto de Egresos de la Federación (PEF) for the fiscal year 2026, the federal Secretariat of Health (Secretaría de Salud, SSa) within budgetary Ramo 12 (Salud) is allocated at least 68,000 millones de pesos mexicanos (mdp).
- Process and timing: The Mexican Constitution assigns to the Chamber of Deputies the exclusive power to approve the PEF and sets deadlines: the Executive must submit the Initiative of the Ley de Ingresos and the PPEF by September 8, and the Chamber must approve the PEF by November 15. This means the final approved budget amount for SSa should be known by mid-November 2025, enabling resolution before year-end.
- Proposed amount for 2026 (context): Media and fact-check reports on the Proyecto de Presupuesto de Egresos de la Federación (PPEF) 2026 indicate that the proposed allocation for the Secretaría de Salud is around 66,825–66,826 mdp, with some outlets describing this as a decrease versus 2025 in real terms or relative to other components of the health sector.
- Sectoral context: The 2026 Paquete Económico projects total health spending of about 996,528 mdp (a 5.9% increase vs. 2025), equivalent to roughly 2.6% of GDP, amid ongoing fiscal constraints and demographic/epidemiological pressures. This context suggests legislative reallocations within the health sector are plausible.
- Where the figures live: The official budget portals publish “Ramo 12 – Salud” documentation, with a “Presupuesto Ramo” section that provides the tables by dependency (dependencia), and separate materials for “Entidades de Control Indirecto” (e.g., OPDs such as National Institutes and specialty hospitals). This is where forecasters and resolvers will read the approved figure.

Key definitions and units (for clarity and to avoid ambiguity):
- Secretaría de Salud (SSa): Mexico’s federal executive department in charge of public health policy and services; the entity of interest for this question (not to be conflated with OPDs under Ramo 12).
- Ramo (budgetary branch/classification): An administrative classification that identifies a ramo/sector and the responsible units in the federal budget; Ramo 12 corresponds to Salud. Budget assignments are captured in pesos (nominal) in the PEF/PPEF documentation.
- PEF (Presupuesto de Egresos de la Federación): The annual budget decree that the Chamber of Deputies must approve by November 15; our resolution relies on the approved PEF 2026.
- mdp: millones de pesos mexicanos. “Peso mexicano” has ISO code MXN; 1 mdp = 1,000,000 MXN.

Why the 68,000 mdp threshold: The PPEF 2026 context figure (~66.8k mdp) places 68,000 mdp within plausible reach of legislative adjustments, creating meaningful uncertainty and forecastable entropy without being trivial.

Date window for eligibility: This question pertains to the approved PEF 2026 and resolves based on actions occurring between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. The constitutional deadline implies resolution by mid-November 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve Yes if, in Mexico’s approved PEF 2026, the Secretaría de Salud (within Ramo 12 – Salud) has a total allocation of at least 68,000 mdp; resolve No otherwise.

Operational details for resolution:
- What to read: Use the approved PEF 2026 “Presupuesto Ramo” tables for Ramo 12 – Salud. Locate the dependency row labeled “Secretaría de Salud” (the central ministry, not OPDs) and read the figure in the column labeled “Gasto neto total.” This is the “total allocation” for this question. Do not add budgets of “Entidades de Control Indirecto” (OPDs) or any other entities; only the dependency-level Secretaría de Salud amount counts.
- Units: If the table reports pesos (MXN) rather than mdp, convert by dividing by 1,000,000. Compare the resulting amount to the threshold 68,000 mdp (i.e., 68,000,000,000 MXN). “mdp” is defined as millones de pesos mexicanos (MXN).
- Primary source of truth: The approved PEF 2026 decree as published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación (DOF). Secondary/confirmatory source: the official PEF portal hosting Ramo 12 – Salud “Presupuesto Ramo” tables after approval (pef.hacienda.gob.mx). If there is any discrepancy between portal tables and the DOF decree, the DOF decree prevails. The Chamber of Deputies’ constitutional approval deadline is November 15.
- Timeframe: Resolution is based on the PEF 2026 approved between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. In the unlikely event approval/publication occurs after November 15 but before December 31, use the final approved amount available by December 31. If multiple official publications exist (e.g., errata), use the latest version published by December 31, 2025.
- Examples (non-exhaustive):
  - If the approved table shows Secretaría de Salud Gasto neto total = 67,950 mdp, resolve No.
  - If it shows 68,000 mdp or 68,000,000,000 MXN, resolve Yes.

Citations for claims in this question:
- Constitutional process and Nov 8/Nov 15 deadlines; Chamber’s authority over PEF.
- PPEF 2026 context level for SSa (~66,825–66,826 mdp) and media characterization of decrease.
- Health sector context (total health 996,528 mdp; +5.9% vs 2025; ~2.6% of GDP).
- Where to find Ramo 12 materials and separation of dependency vs OPDs (“Entidades de Control Indirecto”) on official budget portals.
- Definitions: Secretaría de Salud ; Ramo classification and that figures are captured in pesos (nominal) ; Mexican peso and ISO code (MXN) underlying mdp.

question: Between 00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59 UTC on 2025-12-31, will Ofcom announce that it has opened an investigation into Instagram or TikTok over alleged non‑compliance with the Online Safety Act’s children’s protections related to suicide, self‑harm, or eating‑disorder content?
background:
Summary of the regime and current status (as of 2025-10-01):
- Online Safety Act children’s protections and scope. Ofcom’s Protection of Children Codes were issued on 2025-07-04 and come into force on 2025-07-25, requiring services likely to be accessed by children to implement measures to protect them, including to prevent children from encountering certain content categories. The Codes define “primary priority content [that is harmful to children]” to include eating‑disorder content, regulated pornographic content, self‑harm content, and suicide content. The children’s safety regime emphasizes proportionate measures including safer feeds, highly effective age assurance on the riskiest services, fast action on harmful content, stronger governance, and easy reporting and complaints for children.
- Illegal content and other duties timeline. The illegal harms regime is already enforceable; providers had to complete illegal content risk assessments by March 16, 2025, and Ofcom can enforce from March 17, 2025. The Act and government explainer highlight duties around tackling suicide and self‑harm related content, including rapid removal of illegal content (e.g., under the Suicide Act 1961) and protections for children from content encouraging or instructing suicide or self‑harm.
- Ofcom enforcement activity in 2025. Ofcom has been actively opening investigations under the Online Safety Act. For example, “Ofcom has today launched investigations into whether seven file‑sharing services, 4chan and porn provider First Time Videos have failed to comply with their duties under the UK’s Online Safety Act”. In its September 2025 industry bulletin, Ofcom reports that “to date, this has included opening investigations covering 35 porn services, as well as 11 investigations relating to other areas of online safety,” and notes an extensive monitoring and impact programme “primarily focused on the biggest platforms where children spend most time – including Facebook, Instagram, Roblox, Snap, TikTok and YouTube”.
- Where Ofcom publishes investigation announcements. Ofcom’s Enforcement Guidance states that shortly after sending a case opening letter, “we will therefore generally also announce that we have opened an investigation on the Ofcom website, and/or in a media release”. Ofcom’s Online safety hub provides central access to online safety news, updates, and enforcement pages.

Key definitions for this question:
- Children: A person under the age of 18 (“Child user: A United Kingdom user who is under the age of 18.”).
- Primary priority content harmful to children: In the Codes, this “comprises eating disorder content, regulated pornographic content, self‑harm content, and suicide content”. For precision, the Codes refer to the statutory definitions: “suicide content” (content described in section 61(3) of the Act), “self‑harm content” (section 61(4)), and “eating disorder content” (section 61(5)).
- Investigation announcement: Per Ofcom’s Enforcement Guidance, an “opened investigation” is one Ofcom has decided to open after initial assessment, and Ofcom will generally “announce that we have opened an investigation on the Ofcom website, and/or in a media release”.

Why this is forecast‑worthy now: The children’s Codes entered into force on 2025‑07‑25, imposing concrete duties tied to keeping children from encountering suicide, self‑harm, and eating‑disorder content. Ofcom’s 2025 enforcement posture includes multiple investigations and a monitoring programme explicitly focused on major platforms such as Instagram and TikTok , making an investigation into one of these services by year‑end plausible but uncertain. Resolution will be discrete and verifiable on Ofcom’s site.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and event timing:
- Eligible announcements are those published between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025‑10‑15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025‑12‑31 (inclusive). Announcements published outside this window do not count.

What resolves YES:
- Resolve YES if, within the window, Ofcom publishes on ofcom.org.uk a page and/or media release that states it has opened (or launched) an investigation into Instagram or TikTok, and the announcement explicitly references alleged non‑compliance with the UK Online Safety Act’s children’s protections in relation to suicide, self‑harm, or eating‑disorder content. Acceptable phrasings include Ofcom’s standard language that it has “opened an investigation” or “launched an investigation” under the Act.
- The announcement must:
  1) Name Instagram and/or TikTok as a subject of the investigation (e.g., by service name; naming a corporate entity is acceptable if the text clearly identifies the Instagram or TikTok service as the subject), and
  2) Explicitly link the suspected non‑compliance to the Act’s children’s protection duties concerning preventing children from encountering “primary priority content [harmful to children]” in at least one of these categories: suicide content, self‑harm content, or eating‑disorder content (as used in Ofcom’s Codes and the Act: sections 61(3)–(5)).

What resolves NO:
- Resolve NO if no such announcement meeting the above criteria is published on ofcom.org.uk within the window.

Clarifications and definitions (apply strictly):
- Children means persons under 18.
- Primary priority content categories are as defined in Ofcom’s Codes (eating‑disorder, self‑harm, suicide; pornographic content is listed in the Codes but is not relevant to this question unless the announcement also explicitly references suicide, self‑harm, or eating‑disorder content).
- Investigation announcement means Ofcom’s public statement indicating it has “opened an investigation” (or “launched an investigation”), as per its Enforcement Guidance; an unannounced internal action, a request for information, a monitoring programme update, or a consultation does not count.
- Where to check: Ofcom typically publishes such announcements on its website (e.g., Online safety hub, enforcement pages, press releases). The June 2025 “opens nine new investigations” page is an example of the announcement format (“Ofcom has today launched investigations…”).

Exclusions (do not count as YES):
- Announcements that concern other Online Safety Act duties without explicit linkage to children’s protections regarding suicide, self‑harm, or eating‑disorder content.
- Announcements naming only corporate groups without clearly identifying the Instagram or TikTok service as the subject.
- Announcements about fines, provisional notices of contravention, or confirmation decisions not accompanied by or explicitly tied to the opening of an investigation within the window.
- Announcements from non‑UK regulators or third‑party media without an Ofcom publication on ofcom.org.uk.

Adjudication notes for the resolver:
- Use Ofcom’s Online safety hub and news/enforcement pages as the primary resolution sources. If multiple relevant pages exist, the earliest qualifying Ofcom page within the window is sufficient. If the Ofcom page uses the phrasing “opened an investigation”/“launched an investigation” and satisfies the content criteria above, count it.
- If Ofcom opens an investigation but delays public announcement beyond the window, do not count it; this market resolves on publication timing, not internal action.
- Timezone is UTC, and the endpoints are inclusive.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the Council of the EU adopt at least one autonomous Iran-related sanctions package beyond UN snapback transposition?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- On 2025-09-29, following activation of the JCPOA’s UN “snapback” mechanism, the Council of the European Union reimposed a set of restrictive measures against Iran. The Council’s press release states that the reimposed measures include both those adopted by the UN Security Council and automatically transposed into EU law, and EU autonomous measures. Under the JCPOA/UNSCR 2231 framework, “snapback” enables automatic reimposition of previously lifted UN sanctions upon notification of significant non-performance; the mechanism is veto-proof and operates on a fixed timeline under UNSCR 2231 (2015).
- The EU maintains several autonomous Iran-related sanctions regimes in parallel to UN measures, and regularly updates them. These include: (a) the regime targeting serious human rights violations in Iran (Decision 2011/235/CFSP and its implementing Regulation 359/2011), which imposes asset freezes/prohibitions and is reviewed and amended via Council acts [edff86; a9dc27]; and (b) the regime targeting Iran’s military support to Russia’s war (notably UAVs/drones and missiles), established by Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532 and implemented via a Council regulation, under which travel bans, asset freezes, and trade restrictions can be applied/autonomously expanded [edff86; 8cc2e9].
- Example of recent autonomous action (for context): On 2025-04-14, the Council imposed restrictive measures on seven individuals and two entities over serious human rights violations in Iran, via amendments under the 2011/235 CFSP/359/2011 framework, as announced in a Council press release.
- EU sanctions (restrictive measures) are adopted by the Council by unanimity. Where measures include economic/financial provisions, a CFSP Decision is accompanied by a Council Regulation. These legal acts enter into force upon publication in the Official Journal of the EU (OJ). The OJ is the EU’s authentic gazette for legal acts and the definitive record for verification.

Key definitions and references for forecasters:
- “Restrictive measures” (EU sanctions): targeted measures such as travel bans, asset freezes, prohibitions on making funds/economic resources available to listed parties, and sectoral trade/financial/transport restrictions, as described by the Council in its Iran sanctions materials [917fa8; edff86].
- “EU autonomous” (in this context): measures that the EU adopts independently under its Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP), separate from and potentially in addition to UN Security Council sanctions; the EU both implements UN sanctions and adopts autonomous ones, with both types published in the OJ [7b96c9; edff86].
- “Listing”: adding a person/entity to an Annex of a Council act (e.g., Regulation 359/2011 Annex I), which triggers asset freezes and related prohibitions; listings/amendments are made by Council acts and published in the OJ.
- Relevant autonomous Iran-related regimes (non-exhaustive but sufficient for resolution): (i) human rights regime (Council Decision 2011/235/CFSP and Council Regulation 359/2011) [a9dc27; edff86]; (ii) Iran’s military support to Russia regime (Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532; implemented via a Council regulation) [8cc2e9; edff86].
- “UN snapback transposition” (for exclusion): EU legal steps that solely implement the UN reimposition of Iran sanctions under UNSCR 2231’s snapback, as reflected in the Council’s 2025-09-29 package [917fa8; 788bc2].

Primary sources to verify outcomes:
- Council of the EU press releases (for announcements of Iran-related restrictive measures) [917fa8; 12197e].
- Official Journal (OJ) on EUR-Lex (authoritative publication of Council Decisions/Regulations).
- Overviews of EU sanctions against Iran (to understand regimes and scope).
- Foundational legal texts for definitions (Decision 2011/235/CFSP; Regulation 359/2011; Decision 2023/1532) [a9dc27; 8cc2e9].
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible acts must be ADOPTED between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. For avoidance of doubt, “adopted” refers to the date stated in the title line of the legal act as published in the Official Journal (e.g., “Council Decision (CFSP) … of [date]”) [0f79b2; a9dc27].

What counts toward a “Yes” resolution:
