- A “sanctions package” is defined as a Council action on a single calendar day that is: (A) announced via a Council press release concerning Iran; and (B) evidenced in the OJ by one or more Council legal acts that do any of the following within an EU autonomous Iran-related regime:
  1) Add at least one new person or entity to a sanctions Annex (i.e., a new “listing” as defined in Regulation 359/2011) under the human rights regime (Decision 2011/235/CFSP/Regulation 359/2011) [a9dc27; edff86]; or
  2) Add at least one new person or entity or expand sectoral prohibitions/trade restrictions under the regime established by Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/1532 (Iran’s military support to Russia’s war) [8cc2e9; edff86]; or
  3) Establish or amend another clearly EU-autonomous Iran-related restrictive measures framework (i.e., a CFSP Decision and, where applicable, a Council Regulation) that applies to Iran and is not solely implementing a UN Security Council resolution [7b96c9; b51553].
- If multiple legal acts are adopted and announced in one press release on the same day for Iran, they are considered one “package” for counting purposes. For this question, we only need at least one such package in the time window.

Exclusions (do NOT count):
- Legal acts whose stated purpose is solely to implement or transpose UN sanctions reimposed via the JCPOA “snapback” mechanism (i.e., acts like those forming the 2025-09-29 snapback transposition) [917fa8; 788bc2].
- Purely technical corrections that do not add new listings and do not expand prohibitions.

Resolution sources and tie-breakers:
- Primary verification will be via: (i) the relevant Council press release on consilium.europa.eu; and (ii) the corresponding legal act(s) in the Official Journal on EUR-Lex [917fa8; 12197e; 0f79b2]. If there is any discrepancy between a press release and the legal acts, the Official Journal prevails as the authoritative record.
- If at least one qualifying package (as defined above) is adopted within the time window, resolve “Yes.” Otherwise, resolve “No.”

Operational notes:
- The resolver should search the Council press releases for Iran-related restrictive measures during the window (examples of typical format provided in [917fa8; 12197e]), then confirm the corresponding Council Decision/Implementing Decision and any Regulation/Implementing Regulation in the OJ. The Official Journal is accessible via the EUR-Lex OJ portal.
- EU adoption procedure and instruments (for context on what to look for) are outlined in the Council’s procedural page; relevant acts are CFSP Decisions and, where economic/financial measures are involved, Council Regulations.

question: Will any official COP30 decision adopted in Belém include the exact phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels” by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo (as of 2025-09-30): COP30, the 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference, is scheduled to take place in Belém, Brazil, from 10 to 21 November 2025. At COP28 (2023), Parties agreed language in the first global stocktake that called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” stopping short of a full phase-out, which makes future wording at COP30 uncertain and contested.

Where COP decisions are published: UNFCCC publishes adopted decisions on its Decisions portal and session-specific pages (e.g., COP, CMP, CMA). See: https://unfccc.int/decisions and the COP30 overview page: https://unfccc.int/cop30.

Why this matters for forecasting: The exact wording of negotiated decision texts is a focal point of international climate diplomacy. Moving from “transitioning away” (COP28) to an explicit “phase-out of fossil fuels” at COP30 would be a significant rhetorical and policy shift, but is uncertain given divergent positions among Parties.

Key context for forecasters:
- Conference logistics: COP30 dates and location are fixed as above.
- Precedent language: The COP28 UAE Consensus referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, and further efforts toward the phase-down of unabated coal power.
- Resolution sources: UNFCCC’s official sites are expected to host the adopted decisions from COP30 (COP, CMA, CMP), typically as PDFs or HTML.

Note: This question is designed to resolve on a single verifiable proposition (presence/absence of the exact phrase) with an unambiguous source of truth by 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and time zone:
- Eligible documents: Decisions adopted at COP30 (Belém, Brazil), including decisions of the COP (Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC), CMA (Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement), and CMP (Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Kyoto Protocol) during 10–21 November 2025.
- Resolution time: The question will be resolved based on documents publicly available by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Definitions:
- “COP30”: The 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference, held in Belém, Brazil, from 10–21 November 2025.
- “Decision document” / “adopted decision”: An official UNFCCC-published document (PDF or HTML) that records a decision adopted by COP30 sessions (COP, CMA, or CMP), usually denoted by a decision number and session identifier (e.g., 1/CMA.7). Drafts or proposals that are not adopted do not count. Documents must be hosted on unfccc.int.
- “Contains the exact phrase”: The English-language text of the adopted decision document includes the contiguous phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels”, case-insensitive, with the words in that order, and using a standard hyphen or dash between “phase” and “out” (acceptable connectors: U+002D hyphen-minus or U+2013 en dash). Variants such as “phase out of fossil fuels” (no hyphen), “phaseout of fossil fuels” (compound word), “phase-out of fossil fuel” (singular), or “transitioning away from fossil fuels” do not count. The phrase may appear anywhere in the body text of the decision (including preambular/operative paragraphs and annexes). Occurrences solely in non-content areas (navigation headers/footers autogenerated by the website) do not count.
- Language scope: Only the English version counts for resolution. Translations in other languages are not considered.

What counts as a Yes:
- Resolve Yes if at least one adopted COP30 decision (COP, CMA, or CMP) published on unfccc.int contains the exact phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels” per the definition above by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

What counts as a No:
- Resolve No if no adopted COP30 decision published on unfccc.int by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025 contains the exact phrase as defined.

Primary resolution sources and method:
- Sources: UNFCCC Decisions portal (https://unfccc.int/decisions) and the COP30 session pages (https://unfccc.int/cop30). These are the authoritative locations where adopted decisions are published.
- Method: A resolver will visit the COP30 decisions pages (covering COP, CMA, and CMP sessions) and open each adopted decision document available by the resolution deadline. Using document search in the English version, the resolver will check for the exact phrase “phase-out of fossil fuels” (case-insensitive). If present in any single adopted decision’s body text or annex, resolve Yes; otherwise, resolve No.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- If a decision is clearly adopted at COP30 but not yet posted on unfccc.int by 23:59 UTC Dec 31, 2025, it will not be considered; only documents published on unfccc.int by the deadline count.
- If the phrase appears only within quoted text inside the decision’s body/annex, it still counts.
- If the phrase appears with different punctuation around it (e.g., commas, semicolons) but the internal sequence “phase-out of fossil fuels” remains contiguous, it counts.
- If the phrase appears across a line break with a hyphen at the end of a line (i.e., “phase-
out of fossil fuels”), it counts.
- If multiple documents are updated after initial publication, the version available on unfccc.int at 23:59 UTC Dec 31, 2025 is the one that counts.

Citations for factual background:
- COP30 dates and location: 10–21 November 2025 in Belém, Brazil.
- COP28 background language (“transitioning away from fossil fuels”; “phase-down of unabated coal power”): summary reporting of the global stocktake outcome.

question: By 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, will the most recent eligible public IAEA publication between October 15 and December 31, 2025 report Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235 as at least 460.0 kilograms (U mass)?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01
- Latest known level: A confidential IAEA report seen by Reuters on September 3, 2025 stated that Iran’s stock of uranium enriched to up to 60% U‑235 was 440.9 kg as of June 13, 2025. An independent analysis of the same IAEA report specifies the figure as 440.9 kg (U mass) as of June 13, 2025 and lists other enrichment-category stockpiles, consistent with IAEA reporting conventions. Reuters also characterized 60% enrichment as close to “weapons grade”.
- IAEA access/inspection status: In his September 8, 2025 introductory statement to the Board of Governors, the IAEA Director General said the Agency halted verification activities during June attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and withdrew inspectors by the end of June due to safety concerns; as of early September, the Agency had not had access to verify Iran’s high-enriched uranium for almost three months and was negotiating modalities to resume inspections. The IAEA chronology confirms public statements and briefings on Iran in September 2025.
- UN “snapback” context: The reimposition (“snapback”) of UN sanctions on Iran was completed on September 27, 2025 at 8:00 p.m. EDT, reactivating prior Security Council resolutions; the process had been initiated on August 28, 2025, and involved France, Germany, and the United Kingdom.
- IAEA publication channels and cadence: The IAEA publicly posts the Director General’s Iran-related Board reports (GOV documents) and related verification/monitoring documents on its “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” page, which serves as a central repository for these reports and indicates a roughly quarterly reporting rhythm; the page links directly to PDFs of current-year reports. The IAEA also posts Director General statements and news releases on iaea.org.

Key definitions (for clarity in this forecast)
- Uranium-235 (U‑235): A fissile isotope of uranium that constitutes about 0.72% of natural uranium and is the target of enrichment.
- Enriched uranium: Uranium with a higher mass percentage of U‑235 than natural uranium (0.72%); low-enriched uranium (LEU) is <20% U‑235; highly enriched uranium (HEU) is ≥20% U‑235 (percentages by mass).
- “U mass”: In IAEA reporting and technical analyses, stockpiles are often expressed as kilograms of uranium (element-only), excluding other elements in chemical compounds (e.g., fluorine in UF6). The September 2025 analysis of the IAEA report denotes the 60% stockpile as “kg (U mass),” reflecting this convention; IAEA enrichment percentages are specified by mass.
- “Uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235” (the “60% category”): The phrasing used by IAEA and media summaries refers to uranium whose U‑235 assay is reported at or near 60% (commonly stated as “up to 60% U‑235”). For this question, references to “60%,” “up to 60%,” or “60 percent U‑235” are treated as referring to this category as presented by IAEA publications.

Why this is forecastable now
- As of June 13, 2025, Iran’s 60% stockpile stood at 440.9 kg (U mass). Subsequent access interruptions, evolving cooperation, and the September 27, 2025 UN snapback reimposition create uncertainty about stockpile trajectory through Q4 2025. IAEA typically produces at least one public report/statement in Q4, enabling an up-to-date figure to be available before year-end. The 460.0 kg threshold is close enough to the last known level to make both outcomes plausible.

Where to find the resolution source
- IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports (for GOV documents on safeguards and verification/monitoring): https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/focus/iran/iaea-and-iran-iaea-board-reports 
- IAEA Director General statements and IAEA News Center (for public statements/news releases that may include quantified figures): https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/statements/ and https://www.iaea.org/news.
resolution_criteria:
Question
- Resolve Yes if, by 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, the most recent eligible IAEA publication in the defined window reports Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235 as ≥460.0 kilograms (U mass). Otherwise resolve No.

Eligible publications (all must be met)
- Source: An official, publicly accessible IAEA item on iaea.org in one of these categories: (a) IAEA Director General report (GOV document) linked on the “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” page; or (b) an official IAEA news release or Director General statement posted on iaea.org that includes a quantified figure for Iran’s 60% stockpile.
- Publication window: Published on iaea.org (visible publication date on the item’s page) between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31, inclusive.
- Content: Explicitly contains a single quantified figure for the total stockpile of uranium enriched to (up to) 60% U‑235, expressed in kilograms. If both “kg” and “(U mass)” are provided, use the “kg (U mass)” value. If only “kg” is provided and context indicates stockpiles are reported as uranium mass, treat it as kg (U mass). If only non-metric units are given, convert to kilograms using 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg and use that numeric value for comparison.

“Most recent” rule
- If multiple eligible items exist, use the one with the latest publication date-time shown on iaea.org. If two eligible items share the same publication date-time, use the one with the latest last-updated timestamp if shown; if still tied, use the item with the higher document number (e.g., later GOV/2025/XX). If timestamps are not shown, treat the date as the determinant.

Counting the 60% figure
- Qualifying text includes “uranium enriched to 60%,” “enriched up to 60% U‑235,” or equivalent IAEA phrasing for the 60% category. Use the explicitly stated total for that category. Do not sum subcomponents unless the IAEA item explicitly provides a total or unambiguously indicates that the listed components are additive and exhaustive; if only partial components are listed and no total is given, the item is not eligible and should be skipped.

Numeric comparison
- Compare the stated (or converted) number to the threshold: Yes if ≥460.0 kg; No if <460.0 kg. Use the numeric value printed in the IAEA item without attempting to adjust for measurement uncertainty or implied rounding. If a range is given, use the midpoint. If only qualitative language is used (e.g., “around 460 kg”) but a numeric value appears, use the numeric value as printed.

Edge cases and fallbacks
- If no eligible IAEA item (as defined above) is published in the window that contains a quantified 60% stockpile figure, resolve No (verifiable by absence on the IAEA Board Reports page and IAEA statements/news pages).
- If an eligible item is published but is later corrected/updated before the resolution deadline, use the latest version as of 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Definitions and references (for clarity)
- Uranium-235 (U‑235): fissile isotope; ~0.72% of natural uranium.
- Enriched uranium and HEU/LEU thresholds are defined by mass percent U‑235.
- “U mass” denotes uranium element mass; IAEA enrichment percentages and stockpile figures are given by mass; September 2025 reporting/analysis explicitly uses “kg (U mass)” for the 60% stockpile.

Status-quo citations for forecasters
- 60% stockpile at 440.9 kg (U mass) as of June 13, 2025.
- IAEA inspector withdrawal and paused access in June; verification of high-enriched uranium overdue as of early September.
- UN sanctions snapback completed September 27, 2025 at 8:00 p.m. EDT.
- IAEA publicly posts Iran Board reports and DG statements/news on iaea.org (central repository and September 2025 examples).

question: EU’s 19th Russia sanctions package: Will it include a legal ban on imports of Russian‑origin LNG?
background: Status quo as of Oct 1, 2025: Reuters reported on Sept 18–19, 2025 that the European Commission was preparing the EU’s 19th Russia sanctions package and discussing a proposal to bring forward a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports, with a phase‑out to be complete by Jan 1, 2027; such measures require unanimous approval by EU governments. Russia’s share in EU LNG imports fell to 14% in Q2 2025 (from 22% in Q1 2021), and Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands and France import Russian LNG; about 19% of Europe’s gas still came from Russia in 2025 via TurkStream and LNG shipments. The EU’s 14th sanctions package (adopted June 24, 2024) introduced the first LNG‑related measures: Article 3r of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 (as amended by Council Regulation (EU) 2024/1745) prohibited providing reloading services in the EU for transshipment operations of LNG of Russian origin (CN code 2711 11 00), with ship‑to‑ship and ship‑to‑shore transfers covered and a transition period for pre‑existing contracts; Article 3u prohibited importing Russian LNG via EU terminals not connected to the interconnected gas system, with specified exceptions. The base legal act for EU Russia sanctions is Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, which is amended by subsequent packages and published in the Official Journal (EUR‑Lex). Key definitions: Liquefied natural gas (LNG) is natural gas cooled to a liquid state for storage or transport, typically ~−162 °C. "Origin" of goods (used to determine "Russian‑origin LNG") follows non‑preferential origin rules in Article 60 of the Union Customs Code: goods wholly obtained in a country have that origin; if production involves multiple countries, origin is where the last substantial, economically‑justified processing resulting in a new product or important stage occurred. Forecasters should note the distinction between: (a) bans on reloading/transshipment and terminal‑type‑specific import restrictions already in force , versus (b) a general, legal prohibition on purchasing, importing, or transferring Russian‑origin LNG into the Union, which is what this question targets. Negotiation dynamics (member state unanimity, energy security concerns, and external political pressure) make both outcomes plausible by late 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Eligible events must occur between Oct 15, 2025 at 00:00:00 UTC and Dec 31, 2025 at 23:59:59 UTC.

Resolution: Resolve Yes if, within the time window, the Council of the EU formally adopts what is publicly described by EU institutions as the "19th package" of sanctions against Russia, and the legal text adopted and published in the Official Journal (EUR‑Lex) explicitly includes a general prohibition on purchasing, importing or transferring, directly or indirectly, liquefied natural gas (LNG) falling under CN code 2711 11 00 that is "originating in Russia" or "exported from Russia" into the Union. The prohibition may include transitional provisions and a future effective date (e.g., Jan 1, 2027), but must be codified as binding law in the 19th package (not merely a political objective or guidance). Definitions:
- LNG: Liquefied natural gas as commonly defined, i.e., natural gas cooled to liquid form; see Wikipedia for a general definition.
- Russian‑origin LNG: Determined under non‑preferential origin rules in Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 (Union Customs Code).
- 19th package and formal adoption: The set of amending EU legal acts publicly labeled by the Council/Commission as the 19th package and adopted by the Council (and published in the Official Journal); prior packages (e.g., the 14th) were announced via Council press releases and published in the Official Journal.

Important exclusions: Measures limited to (i) reloading/transshipment bans (e.g., Article 3r language such as "prohibited to provide reloading services"), or (ii) import restrictions only through LNG terminals not connected to the interconnected gas system (e.g., Article 3u), do not satisfy the "general import ban" criterion unless the adopted 19th package also includes the explicit general prohibition described above.

Primary source of truth: Official Journal (EUR‑Lex) entries publishing the legal acts of the 19th package (amendments to Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 and/or related acts). The 14th package’s LNG provisions were published as Council Regulation (EU) 2024/1745; the 19th package should have analogous Official Journal publication.

Secondary corroboration (if needed): Council of the EU press release announcing adoption and summarizing the package’s energy measures, plus credible reporting (e.g., Reuters) that the adopted 19th package includes an LNG import ban.

Scoring: Resolve No if no 19th package is formally adopted in the window, or if it is adopted without the explicit, general prohibition on importing Russian‑origin LNG into the Union as defined above. If the package sets only a terminal‑specific import restriction or only a transshipment/reloading ban, resolve No.

question: By 23:59:59 UTC on 31 Dec 2025, will at least 60 companies on the 2025 Fortune 500 list have publicly announced production deployments of post-quantum cryptography?
background:
Context for forecasters as of 2025-09-22:
- What counts as post-quantum cryptography (PQC): Cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against attacks by quantum computers (also called quantum-resistant/quantum-safe). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-quantum_cryptography.
- Standards and ecosystem: NIST’s PQC standardization effort provides the primary reference set of algorithms and terminology (e.g., ML‑KEM derived from Kyber for key establishment; ML‑DSA derived from Dilithium and SLH‑DSA derived from SPHINCS+ for digital signatures). See: https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/post-quantum-cryptography.
- Example deployments (illustrative): Some large Internet platforms have rolled out hybrid PQC in TLS or other production uses (e.g., Google Chrome enabling a Kyber hybrid TLS key agreement; Cloudflare supporting post-quantum key agreement to browsers and to origins). See: https://blog.chromium.org/2023/08/protecting-chrome-traffic-with-hybrid.html and https://blog.cloudflare.com/pq-2024/.
- Policy momentum: U.S. federal guidance (OMB M‑23‑02) directs agencies to inventory cryptography and prepare for PQC migration, signaling broader enterprise movement. See: https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/M-23-02-M-Memo-on-Migrating-to-Post-Quantum-Cryptography.pdf.
- Reference set of companies: This question uses the Fortune 500 (2025) list of the largest U.S. companies by revenue, published by Fortune here: https://fortune.com/ranking/fortune500/2025/.
- There is no central registry of PQC production deployments; evidence will come from company publications and regulatory filings. The threshold (≥60 companies) is set to make the outcome uncertain and research-intensive.
resolution_criteria:
This market resolves YES if, between 2023-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive), at least 60 distinct companies that appear on the Fortune 500 (2025) list at https://fortune.com/ranking/fortune500/2025/ have each published a qualifying announcement of a production deployment of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) per the definitions below. Otherwise, it resolves NO.

Key definitions and scope:
- Fortune 500 (2025) company: Any company listed on Fortune’s 2025 Fortune 500 page (URL above) as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Each such company can be counted at most once.
- Post-quantum cryptography (PQC): Cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers (aka quantum-resistant/quantum-safe), including but not limited to algorithms standardized or named in the NIST PQC effort (e.g., ML‑KEM/CRYSTALS‑Kyber for key establishment; ML‑DSA/CRYSTALS‑Dilithium and SLH‑DSA/SPHINCS+ for digital signatures). Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-quantum_cryptography and NIST PQC project page: https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/post-quantum-cryptography.
- Production deployment / production system: A deployment in a live production environment serving real users or live business operations (not test, dev, staging, PoC, or limited pilot). Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deployment_environment. “Generally available (GA)” offerings are considered production; reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_release_life_cycle.
- Publicly announced: A statement published by the company on any of the following official channels: (a) press release/newsroom on the company’s domain; (b) investor relations site or transcript of an earnings call posted there; (c) SEC filing (e.g., 8‑K, 10‑K, 10‑Q) on EDGAR (https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search-and-access); (d) official corporate blog or official product documentation/release notes on the company’s domain. Third‑party/vendor announcements do not qualify unless the Fortune 500 company republishes them on its official channel.

What qualifies as a “production deployment” of PQC (examples, any one is sufficient if unambiguously stated):
- Transport-layer or application security using a PQC key establishment in production (e.g., TLS using ML‑KEM/CRYSTALS‑Kyber, including hybrid modes, for any portion of customer or internal production traffic).
- Software/firmware code signing or document signing using ML‑DSA/CRYSTALS‑Dilithium or SLH‑DSA/SPHINCS+ in production workflows.
- Key establishment, key wrapping, or key exchange in production systems using ML‑KEM/CRYSTALS‑Kyber (or successor as defined by NIST PQC) for protecting data at rest or in motion.
- A generally available (GA) product/service feature enabling customers to use PQC (as above) in production.

What does NOT qualify:
- Research, pilots, proofs of concept, beta/preview programs, or limited internal tests not serving production traffic.
- Quantum key distribution (QKD) or “quantum” hardware absent PQC; PQC must be explicitly referenced.
- Vague statements of intent/roadmaps without an explicit claim that PQC is in production or GA.
- Third‑party claims not published or endorsed on the company’s official channels.

Counting rules and edge cases:
- Each qualifying company is counted once regardless of multiple announcements.
- Subsidiaries/brands: Announcements by a wholly owned subsidiary count for the parent if the announcement is on an official channel of the parent or explicitly states deployment across the parent’s products/services or enterprise. If only a vendor/partner announces, it does not count unless cross‑posted by the Fortune 500 company on an official channel.
- Mergers/acquisitions/spinoffs during the window: Count the entity if (i) the entity appears on the Fortune 500 (2025) list and (ii) a qualifying announcement was published by that entity or its legal successor on an official channel during the window.
- Language: The announcement must clearly indicate PQC (or synonymous terms “post‑quantum,” “quantum‑resistant,” “quantum‑safe”) and that it is in production/GA. Algorithm names (e.g., ML‑KEM/Kyber, ML‑DSA/Dilithium, SLH‑DSA/SPHINCS+) may be used to establish PQC.

Adjudication and evidence:
- The resolver will compile a list of qualifying companies by reviewing the official sources above. Screenshots and archival links (e.g., the Internet Archive) may be used to verify time of publication if needed.
- In case of ambiguity, the announcement will not count unless it explicitly claims production/GA use of PQC as defined here.
- Final tally is the number of distinct Fortune 500 (2025) companies with at least one qualifying announcement within the window. If the tally is ≥60, resolve YES; otherwise, NO.

question: Will Germany’s adopted 2026 federal budget appropriate at least €82.70 billion to Einzelplan 14 (Defense) by December 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of October 1, 2025:
- The German federal cabinet approved the Regierungsentwurf (government draft) for the 2026 federal budget on July 30, 2025. In this draft, projected expenditures for defense are described as approximately €82.7 billion.
- The official Gesamtplan and budget overviews for the Regierungsentwurf 2026 list the “veranschlagte Ausgaben” (appropriations/expenditure estimates) for Einzelplan 14 (Bundesministerium der Verteidigung) at 82,687,437 thousand euros, i.e., €82,687,437,000.
- Parliamentary reporting further breaks out defense-related funding for 2026 into the core budget and the Bundeswehr special fund (Sondervermögen Bundeswehr): €82.69 billion in Einzelplan 14 and €25.51 billion from the special fund, totaling about €108.2 billion in defense-related outlays.
- Public reporting on the 2026 budget proposal outlines the planned parliamentary schedule for passage in the fall, including first and second readings and Budget Committee deliberations in November, with Bundesrat consideration in December.

Why this matters for forecasting:
- The adopted (promulgated) Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2026 can differ from the Regierungsentwurf following Bundestag/Bundesrat negotiations. Given the draft figure of €82.687 billion for Einzelplan 14, a threshold at €82.70 billion introduces real uncertainty: small upward changes would clear the threshold, while unchanged or downward adjustments would not.

Key terms and definitions (with links):
- Bundeshaushalt (German federal budget): The annual budget of the Federal Republic of Germany, passed as a law (Haushaltsgesetz). See: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundeshaushalt
- Haushaltsgesetz (budget law): The law adopting the federal budget; promulgated in the Bundesgesetzblatt. See: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haushaltsgesetz_(Deutschland)
- Einzelplan: An individual budget plan within the federal budget. “Einzelplan 14” refers to the budget plan of the Federal Ministry of Defence (Bundesministerium der Verteidigung). An example of a prior Einzelplan 14 document is available here (2025): https://www.bundeshaushalt.de/static/daten/2025/soll/draft/epl14.pdf
- Veranschlagte Ausgaben: Appropriations (planned expenditures) recorded as “Summe der Ausgaben” for each Einzelplan in the budget tables. For 2026, the Regierungsentwurf lists Einzelplan 14 at 82,687,437 thousand euros.
- Sondervermögen des Bundes (special funds of the federal government): Funds outside the core budget established for specific purposes; the Bundeswehr Sondervermögen is separate from Einzelplan 14 and should not be counted toward Einzelplan 14’s total appropriations. See: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonderverm%C3%B6gen_des_Bundes. The 2026 breakdown shows €25.51 billion from the Bundeswehr special fund in addition to the core budget.

Current status quo numbers to inform an initial forecast:
- Einzelplan 14 (Regierungsentwurf 2026): €82,687,437,000.
- Press release language: “etwa 82,7 Milliarden Euro” for defense expenditures in 2026.
- Additional defense-related funds via Sondervermögen Bundeswehr (not part of Einzelplan 14): €25.51 billion; total defense-related outlays cited at ~€108.2 billion.
- Legislative timetable for budget passage is concentrated in November and December 2025.

Notes on measurement:
- Budget tables commonly present amounts in thousands of euros. For resolution, amounts will be evaluated in euros (i.e., thousand-euro figures multiplied by 1,000).
- Only the core budget’s Einzelplan 14 (“Summe der Ausgaben”) counts toward the threshold; allocations to special funds (Sondervermögen), even if defense-related, are excluded.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves at 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

Resolution standard:
- Yes if, by the resolution time, the Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2026 (federal budget law 2026) has been promulgated in the Bundesgesetzblatt (BGBl), and the “Summe der veranschlagten Ausgaben” (total appropriations/planned expenditures) for Einzelplan 14 (Bundesministerium der Verteidigung) in the adopted law is greater than or equal to €82,700,000,000.
- No if either (a) the promulgated Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2026 shows Einzelplan 14 with a “Summe der Ausgaben” below €82,700,000,000, or (b) no Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2026 has been promulgated by the resolution time.

What exactly is measured:
- The figure to be checked is the total “Summe der Ausgaben” for Einzelplan 14 as recorded in the adopted budget law’s official tables (usually presented in thousands of euros). For avoidance of doubt, the threshold corresponds to 82,700,000 thousand euros.
- Exclusions: Any allocations to the Bundeswehr Sondervermögen (special fund) or other Sondervermögen are explicitly excluded, as they do not form part of Einzelplan 14 in the core budget.

Acceptable resolution sources:
- Bundesgesetzblatt (BGBl) online publication of the Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2026 (official promulgation). This is the primary source.
- If BGBl is inaccessible, the official Bundeshaushalt website (bundeshaushalt.de) showing the adopted budget’s tables for 2026 (not the Regierungsentwurf) is acceptable.

Operational details and edge cases:
- Units and rounding: Use the exact figures in euros as published; do not round for threshold comparison. If the published tables are in thousands of euros, multiply by 1,000 to convert to euros.
- If multiple official publications differ, the BGBl promulgated text/tables take precedence over other sources.
- Supplementary budgets (Nachtragshaushalt) are only considered if they have been promulgated by the resolution time and explicitly amend the 2026 Einzelplan 14 “Summe der Ausgaben.” If a supplementary budget meeting these criteria exists, use the latest promulgated law in force by the resolution time.

Start date for eligible events:
- The observation window for adoption/amendment runs from 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 through the resolution time on December 31, 2025.

Relevant context references:
- Cabinet approval and draft framing of ~€82.7bn for defense (July 30, 2025).
- Regierungsentwurf 2026 tables showing Einzelplan 14 at 82,687,437 thousand euros.
- Parliamentary breakdown separating core budget (EP14) and Bundeswehr special fund, totaling ~€108.2bn defense-related outlays.
- Public schedule and process milestones for passage in fall 2025.

question: By 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, will the NHC’s 2025 North Atlantic Summary report “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” of at least 100?
background:
Context and definitions
- Accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) is a metric of tropical cyclone activity that sums the square of a storm’s maximum sustained wind speed (in knots) every six hours, counting only periods when the storm is at least tropical storm strength (≥34 kt). The sum is scaled by 10^-4 so that one ACE unit equals 10^-4 kn^2.
- The U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) maintains a running “North Atlantic Summary (2025)” page that includes a table with “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” for the Atlantic basin and notes that the ACE total shown is only for the basin being summarized. The table also displays an “as of” timestamp in UTC and columns comparing activity to the 1991–2020 normal.

Status quo as of today (for forecasters)
- On the NHC’s 2025 North Atlantic Summary page, the table shows: Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2): 84.2, with an “as of” timestamp of 09 UTC 30 September 2025, and indicates the ACE is 11% below the 1991–2020 normal at that time.

Primary sources
- NHC 2025 North Atlantic Summary (Atlantic basin): https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2025&basin=atl 
- NHC Tropical Cyclone Reports index (navigation fallback if the direct link structure changes): https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/ 
- ACE definition and units: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: Yes if the NHC’s 2025 North Atlantic Summary table shows a “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” value greater than or equal to 100.0 at the time of resolution; No otherwise.

Resolution timing and timezone
- Resolution check time: exactly 23:59 UTC on 2025-12-31.

Primary source of truth
- The value used for resolution will be the “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” as displayed on the NHC’s 2025 North Atlantic Summary page for the Atlantic basin at: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2025&basin=atl.

Definitions and measurement details
- “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” refers to the single numeric value shown in the NHC summary table for the Atlantic basin. This is the NHC-published ACE total for the Atlantic basin only, as noted on the page (“Note the ACE total in this table is only for the basin being summarized”).
- No rounding will be applied beyond what is displayed on the page. For example, 99.9 is treated as <100 (No); 100.0 (or any number ≥100.0) is treated as ≥100 (Yes).
- Ignore any “vs 1991–2020 Normal” comparisons or percentage differences; only the “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” value itself determines the outcome.

Contingencies
- If the direct basin page above is unreachable or its URL structure changes, navigate via the NHC Tropical Cyclone Reports index at https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/ to the “2025 North Atlantic Summary” and use the “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” value shown there.
- If NHC pages are temporarily inaccessible at the exact resolution time, use the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine snapshot closest to 23:59 UTC on 2025-12-31 for the page listed above. If multiple snapshots are within ±1 hour, use the later one within that window.
- If neither live pages nor archived snapshots are available, resolve based on credible secondary citations of the NHC 2025 North Atlantic Summary “Total ACE” published on or immediately after 2025-12-31 by reputable outlets (e.g., NOAA/NHC communications or widely recognized media). This contingency should be used only if primary/archived sources are unavailable.

Notes
- This question resolves solely by reference to the NHC’s “Total ACE (x10^4 kt^2)” for the Atlantic basin as published on the designated page at the specified time. The formal definition of ACE and its units are provided for clarity only and are not independently recalculated for resolution.

question: Will the year-over-year change in BEA’s Core PCE price index for November 2025 be at least 2.8%?
background:
Definition and series: The "Core PCE price index" refers to the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index excluding food and energy, published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). BEA describes this series and displays its "Change From Month One Year Ago" (i.e., the 12‑month percent change) on its data page for the PCE price index excluding food and energy. This series is part of BEA’s monthly Personal Income and Outlays release.

Release timing and availability: BEA’s public release schedule lists "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" as a news release on December 23, 2025 at 8:30 AM (U.S. ET), ensuring the November 2025 figure is available before year‑end. As a reference for typical wording and timing, the August 2025 news release shows how BEA states the 12‑month percent changes for headline PCE and for PCE excluding food and energy and notes the next release timing (e.g., "October 31, 2025, at 8:30 a.m. EDT").

Status quo: Recent core PCE 12‑month percent changes shown by BEA include June 2025: +2.8%, July 2025: +2.9%, and August 2025: +2.9%. The August 2025 news release states: "Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 2.9 percent from one year ago". These recent values provide context for the November 2025 forecast.

Why this question: Core PCE is the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge. Setting the threshold at 2.8% targets a range where informed forecasters can reasonably disagree based on trends, energy pass‑throughs, shelter components, and goods disinflation, while still resolving cleanly via a single authoritative source.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end of eligibility window: This question concerns the November 2025 reference month and will resolve based on data published between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC.

Primary metric: The "year-over-year change" is the 12‑month percent change that BEA labels "Change From Month One Year Ago" for the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index excluding food and energy. "At least 2.8%" means greater than or equal to 2.8%.

Resolution source and priority: Use the BEA as the sole source of truth. Resolve using the value for November 2025 reported in the "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" news release and/or its associated data tables hosted on bea.gov, which are scheduled for publication on December 23, 2025. If the news release text and tables differ, use the numeric value in the BEA release tables for November 2025.

Exact resolution rule: Resolve YES if BEA’s reported 12‑month percent change for the PCE price index excluding food and energy (core PCE) for November 2025 is greater than or equal to 2.8%. Resolve NO if it is strictly less than 2.8%.

Precision and rounding: Use the figure exactly as displayed by BEA on the release page/tables at the time of publication within the eligibility window. Do not apply any additional rounding beyond what BEA displays.

Revisions: If BEA revises the November 2025 figure after initial publication but before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, use the latest figure displayed by BEA within that window. Any revisions posted after that cutoff are ignored.

Links and examples: BEA’s release schedule page where the "Personal Income and Outlays, November 2025" entry appears is at bea.gov/news/schedule. BEA’s data page defining and displaying the PCE price index excluding food and energy and its "Change From Month One Year Ago" is at bea.gov/data/personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index-excluding-food-and-energy. The August 2025 Personal Income and Outlays news release illustrates BEA’s standard phrasing for the 12‑month percent change measures.

question: Will the European Commission adopt at least one fining non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act against a designated VLOP/VLOSE between Oct 15, 2024 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Enforcement powers under the Digital Services Act (DSA): Since 17 February 2024, the European Commission ("the Commission") can adopt non-compliance decisions imposing administrative fines of up to 6% of a provider’s worldwide annual turnover for breaches of DSA obligations. It can also impose periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover for delays in complying with remedies, interim measures, or commitments. Separate procedural fines (up to 1%) exist for failures such as providing incorrect or misleading information or refusing inspections.
- Who is supervised directly by the Commission: Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs) are defined as services with average monthly active recipients reaching or exceeding 10% of the EU population (i.e., at least 45 million users). The Commission directly supervises and enforces DSA obligations for designated VLOPs/VLOSEs. The Commission maintains a live overview of designated services and its enforcement activities on its “Supervision of the designated VLOPs and VLOSEs” page (updated periodically; page notes include updates through September 2025).
- Investigations and preliminary steps to date: The Commission has opened proceedings and issued preliminary findings in several cases concerning designated services. For example, on 15 May 2025 the Commission informed TikTok of its preliminary view that TikTok’s ad repository breached DSA obligations. Such preliminary findings are without prejudice to the outcome and can, after further procedure, lead to non‑compliance decisions that may impose fines.

Why this question is forecastable now: As of the date above, the Commission has active investigations and preliminary findings against multiple designated services, the sanctioning framework is in force, and it is plausible that at least one case could culminate in a fining non‑compliance decision by year‑end 2025. At the same time, procedural timelines, rights of defense, and possible commitments can delay or avert fines, creating non‑trivial uncertainty.

Key definitions and links for forecasters:
- Digital Services Act (DSA): EU Regulation establishing obligations for intermediary services and enhanced supervision/enforcement for the largest platforms and search engines. See Commission overview of enforcement powers and timelines.
- Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) / Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE): Services with average monthly active recipients in the EU ≥ 45 million (≈10% of EU population). Designation triggers additional obligations and Commission supervision. The current list of designated services is maintained here: “Supervision of the designated VLOPs and VLOSEs”.
- Non-compliance decision imposing a fine ("fining non-compliance decision"): A formal Commission decision that definitively establishes a breach of DSA obligations and imposes an administrative fine (up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover) and may order corrective measures and enhanced supervision. This is distinct from procedural fines (e.g., for incomplete replies) and from periodic penalty payments.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve "Yes" if, between 2024-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC inclusive, the European Commission publicly adopts at least one non-compliance decision under the DSA that (a) definitively establishes a breach of the DSA by a provider of a designated VLOP or VLOSE, and (b) imposes an administrative fine (“fining non-compliance decision”). Resolve "No" otherwise.

Definitions and inclusions/exclusions:
- "Designated VLOP/VLOSE": A service that appears as designated on the Commission’s live supervision page at the time of the decision. The provider can be any legal entity responsible for that designated service.
- "Fining non-compliance decision": A Commission decision establishing a breach of DSA obligations and imposing an administrative fine (up to 6% of the provider’s worldwide annual turnover). Decisions solely imposing periodic penalty payments, interim measures, commitments without fines, or procedural fines (e.g., for incorrect/misleading information or refusal to cooperate) do not count.
- "Publicly adopts": The decision is announced via a Commission press release/news item (e.g., Commission Press Corner or the Digital Strategy enforcement news) and/or the decision text is published on an official Commission website. The decision’s adoption date reported by the Commission determines whether it falls inside the time window.

Sources of truth for resolution (any one is sufficient):
- Commission press releases/news or enforcement pages announcing the adoption of a non‑compliance decision imposing a fine under the DSA against a designated VLOP/VLOSE.
- If needed for verification, the published decision text on an official Commission website.

Edge cases:
- If multiple decisions are adopted the same day, only one is needed for "Yes".
- If a decision is adopted in the window but published later, use the Commission-reported adoption date. If the adoption date cannot be verified from official Commission sources by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve based on the publication/announcement date instead.
- Appeals or subsequent judicial developments do not affect resolution once adoption is established.

Notes for forecasters:
- The Commission’s enforcement framework explains relevant procedures, timelines, and sanction types. The list of designated services and enforcement activity timeline are available on the supervision page. Recent preliminary findings (e.g., TikTok ad repository, May 2025) illustrate active cases that could progress to fining decisions within the forecast window.

question: Will the EU hold an Intergovernmental (Accession) Conference with Ukraine between 00:00 UTC on 15 Oct 2025 and 23:59 UTC on 31 Dec 2025?
background:
Definition and process: In the EU enlargement context, “accession negotiations take place at intergovernmental conferences (often called an ‘accession conference’) between ministers and ambassadors of the EU member states and a candidate … [and] can be held at either ministerial or deputy level.” This is the label the Council of the EU (Consilium) uses for the formal sessions of negotiations with candidates such as Ukraine.

Status quo (as of 2025-10-01): The EU and Ukraine held their first Intergovernmental Conference (IGC)/Accession Conference at ministerial level on 25 June 2024, which formally opened accession negotiations. Consilium’s official press release (“EU opens accession negotiations with Ukraine”) and the corresponding meetings page (“First Accession Conference with Ukraine”) document this event and illustrate the standard way such conferences are recorded on the Consilium website. The Consilium Ukraine policy page also notes that “On 25 June 2024, the EU held its first intergovernmental conference with Ukraine, formally opening the membership negotiations”.

Cadence and purpose: According to the EU’s negotiating framework for Ukraine (adopted June 2024), the Intergovernmental Conference “will provide political steer and a forum for political dialogue,” “take stock of the overall accession process,” indicate what clusters/chapters could be opened/closed, and “will take place at least once a year … with at least one meeting per twelve-month period at ministerial level,” with the possibility of additional deputy-level meetings.

Near-term agenda signals: EU leaders met for an informal European Council in Copenhagen on 1 October 2025, with the agenda explicitly including support for Ukraine and “Ukraine’s EU path,” including reform efforts and steps toward accession. This creates plausible political windows for an additional IGC/Accession Conference before year-end, but it is not guaranteed.

Where resolution information will appear: Consilium typically documents IGCs via (a) press releases under /press/press-releases/ (e.g., “EU opens accession negotiations with Ukraine,” 25 June 2024) and/or (b) meetings pages under /meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/ (e.g., “First Accession Conference with Ukraine,” 25 June 2024). These provide the official meeting title, date, and summary needed to verify occurrence and timing.

Helpful references (non-exhaustive):
- Consilium policy explainer for Ukraine (definition of accession/IGC and the 25 June 2024 milestone): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/ukraine/ 
- Press release (25 June 2024): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/06/25/eu-opens-accession-negotiations-with-ukraine/ 
- Meetings page (25 June 2024): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2024/06/25/ukraine/ 
- Negotiating framework (June 2024): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/hzmfw1ji/public-ad00009en24.pdf 
- Informal European Council agenda (Copenhagen, 1 Oct 2025): https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/european-council/2025/10/01/ 

Note: “Intergovernmental Conference” and “Accession Conference” are treated as synonyms in this context; both ministerial- and deputy-level conferences are eligible for this question.
resolution_criteria:
Yes-resolution: Resolve YES if an official Consilium page documents that an EU–Ukraine Intergovernmental Conference (also called an Accession Conference) occurred with a meeting date between 00:00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, inclusive. Eligible official documentation includes any of the following on the consilium.europa.eu domain:
- A Consilium press release page explicitly stating that an intergovernmental (accession) conference with Ukraine was held, with the meeting date within the window (for reference format, see “EU opens accession negotiations with Ukraine,” 25 June 2024 ).
- A Consilium “Meetings” page categorized under International ministerial meetings (or equivalent), explicitly titled or described as an intergovernmental (accession) conference with Ukraine, with the meeting date within the window (for reference format, see “First Accession Conference with Ukraine,” 25 June 2024 ).

Definitions and scope clarifications:
- “Intergovernmental (Accession) Conference” is the formal session of accession negotiations as defined by Consilium for EU enlargement; in Consilium’s own words, “Accession negotiations take place at intergovernmental conferences (often called an ‘accession conference’) … [and] can be held at either ministerial or deputy level.” Both ministerial- and deputy-level conferences count for this question.
- The event must be specifically the EU–Ukraine intergovernmental/accession conference. If an IGC is held in a multi-country format (e.g., back-to-back sessions for multiple candidates), it counts if a session explicitly for Ukraine is held and documented by Consilium within the time window.
- What does not count: Association Council meetings, European Council or Council (GAC) meetings, working party meetings, or other events not explicitly labeled by Consilium as an “intergovernmental conference” or “accession conference” with Ukraine.

Date/time treatment:
- Use the meeting date displayed on the Consilium page to determine whether the conference occurred within the window. Only meetings dated between 00:00:00 UTC on 15 October 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025 are eligible. Timezone for the window is UTC.

Fallback evidence (only if needed): If, by 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, no relevant Consilium page is available but there is clear, contemporaneous reporting from at least one major international wire service (e.g., Reuters, AP, AFP) or Politico Europe that an EU–Ukraine intergovernmental/accession conference occurred on a specific date within the window, the question will resolve YES on that basis. Otherwise, resolve NO.

No-resolution: Resolve NO if no qualifying Consilium documentation (or the fallback credible reporting described above) exists by 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025 indicating that an EU–Ukraine intergovernmental/accession conference occurred within the specified window.

Adjudication notes and examples (non-exhaustive):
- Example of acceptable press release format: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/06/25/eu-opens-accession-negotiations-with-ukraine/.
- Example of acceptable meetings page format: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2024/06/25/ukraine/.
- Purpose/cadence context (non-binding for resolution but informative): The negotiating framework indicates IGCs provide political steer, take stock, and are expected at least annually, potentially increasing the plausibility of a Q4 2025 conference.

question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00 PET and 2025-12-31 23:59 PET, will at least one Lima urban public transport company other than “La 50” suspend all operations for ≥7 consecutive days due to extortion?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30: Multiple urban transport companies in Lima have recently faced extortion and violent attacks. Empresa de Transportes San Sebastián, known as “La 50,” suspended services indefinitely starting September 29 due to a wave of extortions and murders; other companies including Huáscar, Roma, and Santa Catalina also announced suspensions citing lack of safety guarantees. Broader sector impacts include a sharp reduction in active drivers and fleets: enabled public transport drivers fell from about 56,000 (July 2024) to roughly 22,000 (August 2025), with ~30% of the fleet stopped due to lack of drivers. From January to July 2025, 65 drivers were murdered. Companies like Santa Catalina, Evipusa, 41 S.A., Huáscar (line C), and Las Flores (line 57) reported attacks and withdrawals from circulation following shootings and extortion notes. An investigative report details the DESA II extortion network’s methods (threats, shootings, grenades) and systematic “cupo” collection targeting bus companies in Lima Norte, reinforcing the climate of terror affecting operators. Separately, over 70 formal transport companies plan a sector-wide “paro” (strike) on October 2, 2025 to protest extortion and contract killings; this collective action is distinct from company-specific suspensions of service.

Definitions and scope for this question:
- Lima urban public transport company: A concessionary operator providing regular public urban transport in Lima Metropolitana or Callao using buses, microbuses, and/or combis on fixed routes, administered and regulated by the Autoridad de Transporte Urbano para Lima y Callao (ATU). This excludes taxis, mototaxis, and interprovincial operators. See: Transporte público regular de Lima y Callao (Wikipedia) and ATU (Wikipedia).
- “La 50”: Empresa de Transportes San Sebastián, colloquially known as “La 50,” which has already suspended service due to extortion.
- Extortion: Pressure with threats to compel action and obtain money or other benefit, per the Real Academia Española definition (extorsión). Extortion-related violence (e.g., shootings, grenade attacks) qualifies if extortion is explicitly cited as the reason for suspension in the announcement or reporting.
- Time zone: Peru Time (PET) is UTC−05:00; Peru has one time zone and does not observe daylight saving time. All dates/times in this question use PET.

Why this is a non-trivial, plausibly uncertain forecast: The environment shows ongoing, severe extortion pressures and recent multi-company suspensions , suggesting a real possibility of additional prolonged suspensions. However, operators may adapt (security measures, police actions, collective protests), making it uncertain whether any further company will halt all operations for at least seven consecutive days specifically citing extortion within the specified window.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves to Yes if, between 2025-10-15 00:00 PET and 2025-12-31 23:59 PET inclusive, at least one Lima urban public transport company other than “La 50” (Empresa de Transportes San Sebastián) suspends all operations for seven or more consecutive calendar days, with extortion explicitly cited as the reason.

Key terms and measurement details:
- Eligible company: A concessionary operator of regular public urban transport in Lima Metropolitana or Callao regulated by ATU, operating buses/microbuses/combis on fixed routes (not taxis, mototaxis, interprovincial). Verification relies on ATU’s regulatory scope and the “transporte público regular” description.
- “Suspend all operations”: The company halts its regular public transport service across all its authorized routes (i.e., no revenue service trips on any of its routes) for the duration. Partial suspensions (e.g., shortened routes, reduced frequencies, suspending a single route while continuing others) do not count.
- Duration: At least seven consecutive calendar days in PET (UTC−05:00). For adjudication, duration can be established by: (a) a credible report or official announcement of the resumption date following an earlier suspension announcement; (b) two credible reports/official statements at least seven days apart both confirming the company remained fully suspended; or (c) a credible report explicitly stating the suspension lasted ≥7 days.
- “Extortion explicitly cited”: The company’s official announcement or credible reporting must state extortion (extorsión) as the reason for the suspension (extortion may be accompanied by threats/violence); definition per RAE.

Inclusions:
- Suspensions announced by the company via official channels (e.g., verified website/social media) or confirmed by credible national/regional media (e.g., El Comercio, RPP, América TV, Infobae Perú), or by municipal/ATU communications.

Exclusions:
- Sector-wide “paro” (strike/protest) actions, even if related to extortion, do not count as a company suspension unless the company separately announces a full suspension of its service for ≥7 days due to extortion.
- Suspensions primarily citing other reasons (e.g., maintenance, regulatory sanctions, labor disputes unrelated to extortion).
- Partial service reductions or temporary interruptions shorter than seven consecutive calendar days.

Resolution sources: The adjudicator will resolve using publicly available official company announcements (websites/verified social accounts), ATU or municipal notices, and/or credible media reports (e.g., El Comercio, RPP, América TV, Infobae Perú) that document both the suspension (with extortion as the reason) and the duration criteria. If at least one qualifying suspension is verified, resolve Yes; if none are verified, resolve No.

question: Will the Federal Register publish a U.S. proposal or rule that bases tariffs on imported electronic devices’ chip content between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Summary of current status (as of 2025-10-01):
- Reuters reported on 2025-09-26 that the administration is considering imposing tariffs on foreign electronic devices where the tariff amount would depend on the device’s “chip content,” either by the number of chips in the device or the estimated value of the chips within it. A 25% rate was discussed, with a 15% rate considered for devices from the EU and Japan. The plan was described as under consideration and could change, and the reporting did not indicate that formal rulemaking had begun.
- The Federal Register (FR) is the official journal of the U.S. federal government; it publishes proposed and final rules, notices, and presidential documents (such as executive orders and proclamations), and publication in the FR constitutes constructive legal notice to the public (https://www.federalregister.gov/). See overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Register.
- A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) is the public notice by which a U.S. federal agency proposes to add, amend, or repeal a regulation and invites public comment; NPRMs are published in the Federal Register (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notice_of_proposed_rulemaking). In addition to NPRMs (Proposed Rules), the FR also publishes Final Rules and agencies may, under specified circumstances, use interim final or direct final rules (see the Federal Register’s guide “A Guide to the Rulemaking Process”: https://uploads.federalregister.gov/uploads/2013/09/The-Rulemaking-Process.pdf).
- Definitions relevant to this question:
  • Tariff: a duty imposed by a government on imports (or, rarely, exports), typically paid by the importer. Tariffs may be specific (per-unit) or ad valorem (percentage of value). See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff.
  • Integrated circuit (IC), also known as a microchip or “chip”: a compact assembly of electronic circuits fabricated on a semiconductor substrate, commonly silicon. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_circuit.

Why this is forecastable: The policy is under active consideration but not yet in rulemaking as of late September 2025, and it faces economic, legal, and diplomatic trade-offs, creating genuine uncertainty about whether a formal proposal or rule that uses a chip-content-based tariff methodology for imported electronic devices will be published in the Federal Register before year-end [4ab095; b6853f].
resolution_criteria:
Time window and time zone:
- The question resolves based on Federal Register publications dated between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. The controlling reference is the publication date shown on the document’s Federal Register entry.

Resolution source:
- Federal Register documents at https://www.federalregister.gov/ are the sole source for resolution. The resolver will search the Federal Register for relevant publications in the specified window.

What counts as “Yes” (any one of the following qualifies):
- A Federal Register document in any of these categories: Proposed Rule (e.g., Notice of Proposed Rulemaking), Rule (Final Rule, Interim Final Rule, or Direct Final Rule), or Presidential Document (Executive Order or Proclamation), that meets both Conditions A and B below [b6853f; 68b2b7; 41836b].
  Condition A (Scope): The document applies to imported electronic devices (finished goods) as defined below, with the precise product scope taken from the document itself (e.g., by HTS headings/subheadings, or explicit terms like “electronic devices,” “consumer electronics,” “finished electronic products,” etc.).
  Condition B (Chip-content-based tariff methodology): The document proposes or implements a tariff calculation in which the tariff owed for a covered device depends on at least one of the following:
    • the number of integrated circuits (“chips”) contained in the device; or
    • the appraised value, or proportion of value, attributable to the integrated circuits contained in the device.

Definitions (for this market’s purposes):
- Federal Register (FR): The official journal of the U.S. federal government that publishes agency rules (proposed and final), notices, and presidential documents; publication constitutes constructive legal notice.
- Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM): A public notice issued by a federal agency to propose a regulatory change and solicit comment; NPRMs are published in the FR.
- Tariff: A duty/tax on imports, generally paid by the importer; may be specific or ad valorem.
- Integrated circuit (IC) / “chip”: A compact assembly of electronic circuits fabricated on a semiconductor substrate (e.g., silicon). Synonyms: microchip, chip.
- Imported electronic device (finished good): For this question, a finished product imported into the U.S. that contains at least one integrated circuit. The exact set of products covered is determined by the scope defined in the qualifying Federal Register document (e.g., by reference to HTS classifications or explicit product descriptions).

What does NOT count:
- Documents that solely set or adjust tariffs on semiconductors or discrete chips themselves (i.e., not on finished electronic devices).
- Documents that set a uniform tariff on electronic devices without conditioning the tariff on chip count or chip-value share (i.e., not chip-content-based).
- Agency press releases, speeches, blog posts, or web pages that are not published in the Federal Register.
- Items posted on the Federal Register’s Public Inspection page that are not published in the Federal Register within the window.

Examples to clarify (illustrative, not exhaustive):
- Counts: An NPRM titled “Tariffs on Imported Electronic Devices Based on Semiconductor Content” that proposes a formula such as “25% of estimated chip-content value” (Counts as Yes if published within the window) [41836b; b6853f].
- Does not count: A rule or proclamation that imposes a flat 25% tariff on all imported smartphones regardless of chip content (No), or a rule adjusting tariffs on imported integrated circuits themselves but not on finished devices (No).

Resolution:
- Resolve Yes if at least one qualifying Federal Register document (as defined above) is published within the window; otherwise resolve No. The resolver can verify by locating the document(s) on federalregister.gov and confirming the publication date, document category, scope, and that the tariff methodology meets Condition B [b6853f; 68b2b7; 41836b].

question: Between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Nov 30, 2025, will at least three new named storms be first officially named by the National Hurricane Center in the Atlantic basin?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Official season window and typical late-season activity: The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 to November 30, with most activity between mid-August and mid-October. Typical formation dates for later-season storms still extend into October–November (e.g., the 13th named storm typically forms by Oct 25 and the 14th by Nov 19).
- 2025 seasonal outlook (updated Aug 7, 2025): NOAA’s update kept the season tilted above normal, calling for 13–18 named storms, 5–9 hurricanes, and 2–5 major hurricanes, and characterizing the overall odds as 50% above-normal, 35% near-normal, 15% below-normal.
- 2025 season-to-date: As of 03 UTC on Sep 30, 2025, the North Atlantic summary listed 9 named storms, 3 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes; ACE ~83.2 (x10^4 kt^2). The NHC 2025 advisory archive lists named storms to date including Andrea, Barry, Chantal, Dexter, Erin, Fernand, Gabrielle, Humberto, and Imelda.
- Definitions and conventions used for this question: NHC defines a Tropical Storm as a tropical cyclone with maximum sustained 1-minute winds of 34–63 kt, and a Subtropical Storm as a subtropical cyclone with maximum sustained winds of 34 kt or more. NHC advisories are issued in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and include the official advisory time in the header (e.g., 0300Z, 0900Z, 1500Z, 2100Z). For geographic scope, the Atlantic basin consists of the North Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico.
Primary resolution source: NHC’s 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive (Atlantic) will be used to identify each named system and the UTC time of the first advisory where the system is first named as a Tropical Storm or Subtropical Storm , applying the UTC conventions documented by NHC.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-11-30 (inclusive), will at least three (3) new named storms be first officially named by the National Hurricane Center (NHC) in the Atlantic basin?

Operational definition of terms:
- Atlantic basin: The North Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico.
- Named storm (for counting): A tropical or subtropical cyclone that receives an official name from NHC when it first attains Tropical Storm or Subtropical Storm intensity (i.e., maximum sustained 1-minute surface winds of at least 34 kt), as reflected in NHC advisory products. We rely on NHC’s definitions of Tropical Storm and Subtropical Storm.
- First officially named time: The UTC timestamp of the earliest NHC advisory in the 2025 archive for that cyclone in which the cyclone is first referred to as “Tropical Storm [Name]” or “Subtropical Storm [Name]”. Use the advisory header time shown in the archived product (UTC). If the first naming occurs in a “Special Advisory” or “Intermediate Advisory,” that product’s UTC header time is used.

Counting rules:
- Include a cyclone if and only if its first officially named time (as defined above) falls between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.
- Systems that formed earlier as disturbances or depressions but are first named within the window count; systems first named before the window do not count even if they strengthen within the window.
- Count each unique cyclone at most once. Renaming of the same cyclone does not occur in the Atlantic basin under normal NHC practice; if an exceptional renaming occurred, only the first naming time is considered.
- “Potential Tropical Cyclone” advisories, tropical depressions, post-tropical cyclones, and extratropical cyclones that never receive a tropical or subtropical storm name do not count.

Resolution procedure (to be executed on or after 2025-12-01 UTC and no later than 2025-12-31 UTC):
1) From the NHC 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive, open the Atlantic section and list all named cyclones for 2025.
2) For each candidate cyclone, open Advisory Number 1 and any earlier “Special” or “Intermediate” advisories if present, and identify the earliest advisory where the system is first referenced as “Tropical Storm [Name]” or “Subtropical Storm [Name]”. Record that advisory’s UTC header time.
3) Count how many cyclones have a first officially named time within the inclusive window 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC to 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC.
4) Resolve “Yes” if the count is ≥ 3; otherwise resolve “No”.

Primary sources:
- NHC 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive (Atlantic) for names and advisory times.
- NHC advisory time conventions and UTC usage.

Notes:
- This market resolves based on the operational advisory archive as posted on nhc.noaa.gov. Any subsequent post-season reanalysis that modifies best-track genesis/naming times does not affect resolution, which is tied to the archived advisory header times.
- All dates/times are in UTC.

Status quo context (non-binding for resolution):
- Official Atlantic season dates and typical late-season formation timing.
- NOAA’s Aug 7, 2025 update maintained above-normal probabilities and 13–18 named storms.
- Through 03 UTC Sep 30, 2025, there were 9 named storms listed in the North Atlantic summary; the 2025 advisory archive lists nine named storms to date.

question: Will ACMA publicly find that Optus breached at least one emergency-call-related rule for the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage by 31 December 2025?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- Triple Zero (000) is Australia’s primary national emergency telephone number for police, fire, or ambulance, and the emergency call service is regulated at the federal level. The Department of Infrastructure notes that the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) regulates and monitors the provision of the emergency call service under the Emergency Call Service Determination and related law. ACMA’s public guidance describes how Triple Zero works and when to use it.
- On 18 September 2025, Optus experienced an outage affecting Triple Zero access. On 22 September 2025, ACMA announced it had commenced an investigation into Optus’s compliance with emergency call service regulations and other related rules for that incident, and said it will make its findings public once the investigation concludes. In that statement, ACMA cited three specific instruments and described the obligations in scope: (1) Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination 2019 (e.g., ensure emergency calls are successfully carried; undertake welfare checks on callers who made unsuccessful emergency calls during a significant network outage; notify the Emergency Call Person (Telstra) as soon as possible of a significant network outage), (2) Telecommunications (Customer Communications for Outages) Industry Standard 2024 (e.g., put up-to-date outage information on websites and communicate with customers via channels such as apps, email, SMS, media or call centres; notify specified stakeholders including the relevant ministerial department, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, the National Emergency Management Agency and the ACMA), and (3) Communications Alliance Industry Code C536: Emergency Call Service Requirements.
- ACMA’s summary of the Emergency Call Services Determination 2019 highlights key obligations, including maintaining emergency call networks and facilities, notifying Emergency Call Persons (ECPs) and other providers of significant outages, and conducting welfare checks on individuals who tried to call during a large network outage.
- Precedent: Following the nationwide Optus outage on 8 November 2023, ACMA determined that Optus breached emergency call rules by failing to provide access to Triple Zero for 2,145 people and failing to conduct 369 welfare checks; ACMA announced penalties totaling more than A$12 million on 8 November 2024.

Definitions used in this question:
- ACMA: The Australian Communications and Media Authority.
- Optus: Singtel Optus Pty Limited and/or its subsidiaries, as referenced by ACMA in its enforcement actions (e.g., ACMA’s 2024 announcement concerning “subsidiaries of Singtel Optus Pty Limited (Optus)” ). Any ACMA finding that any such Optus group entity contravened/breached the specified instruments counts for this question.
- Triple Zero (000): Australia’s primary national emergency number and emergency call service as described by the Department of Infrastructure and ACMA public materials.
- Emergency-call-related rules/obligations (for the purposes of this market): The obligations set out in any of the following instruments, to the extent they relate to emergency call carriage or to mandated actions during/after outages affecting emergency call access: (a) Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination 2019; (b) Telecommunications (Customer Communications for Outages) Industry Standard 2024; (c) Communications Alliance Industry Code C536: Emergency Call Service Requirements. These are the instruments ACMA explicitly cited as being in scope for the 18 September 2025 outage investigation. For accessible descriptions of ECSD 2019 obligations, see ACMA’s public explainer.
- Emergency Call Person (ECP): For Australia’s 000/112 service, the ECP is Telstra; ACMA’s statement refers to notifying “the emergency call person (Telstra)” about significant outages.

Why this is forecastable now: ACMA has opened an investigation and stated it will publish findings when concluded, but as of 2025-09-30 the outcome is not yet known. Prior precedent shows ACMA has made breach findings and issued penalties in a similar context (the 2023 outage), yet timelines and facts could differ, making a year-end publication uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
YES if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC inclusive, ACMA publishes on the acma.gov.au domain an official item (e.g., media release, article/news post, investigation outcome/report, decision/notice) that explicitly states that Optus (Singtel Optus Pty Limited and/or its subsidiaries) breached, contravened, or failed to comply with at least one of the following, in relation to the 18 September 2025 Triple Zero outage: (a) Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination 2019; (b) Telecommunications (Customer Communications for Outages) Industry Standard 2024; or (c) Communications Alliance Industry Code C536: Emergency Call Service Requirements. The ACMA’s 22 Sep 2025 statement confirms these instruments are in scope for the investigation.

- The publication must clearly link the breach/contravention/failure to comply to the 18 September 2025 outage (e.g., “in relation to the Triple Zero outage on 18 September 2025”).
- Acceptable wording includes ACMA stating that Optus “breached,” “contravened,” or “failed to comply with” any of the listed instruments; examples of such language are used by ACMA in prior enforcement (e.g., “failed to provide access to the emergency call service,” “failed to conduct welfare checks”).
- The publication date/time used for eligibility is the date/time shown on the ACMA page (acma.gov.au) in UTC-equivalent; if only a local timestamp is shown, convert to UTC for assessment.

NO if no such ACMA publication exists by the end of the eligibility window, or if ACMA publishes only interim updates, statements of ongoing investigation, or materials that do not clearly state a breach/contravention/failure to comply tied to the 18 September 2025 outage and one of the listed instruments. Publications about different incidents or dates, or about entities other than Optus (as defined above), do not count.

Primary resolution sources to check (non-exhaustive examples):
- ACMA’s dedicated statement on the Optus Triple Zero investigation (for context on the instruments and scope; final outcome will be published by ACMA when concluded).
- ACMA’s news/articles and media releases sections at acma.gov.au.
- Any ACMA investigation outcome, enforcement decision, or infringement notice page on acma.gov.au that explicitly states an Optus breach/contravention for the 18 Sep 2025 outage and cites one of the listed instruments.

Notes:
- If ACMA simultaneously publishes across multiple ACMA pages, any one qualifying page is sufficient.
