- Third-party media reports alone do not qualify; the decisive evidence must be on acma.gov.au. If the ACMA site is temporarily unavailable but the same page is accessible via an official government web archive (e.g., National Library of Australia/Internet Archive snapshot of the acma.gov.au page), the archived ACMA page may be used for resolution as long as its content and timestamp clearly meet the above criteria.
- This market does not require ACMA to issue penalties; a clear ACMA finding of a breach/contravention/failure to comply is sufficient, as per the language ACMA used in the 2023 outage penalties announcement.

question: Will the United States impose a triple‑digit (≥100%) ad valorem tariff on PRC‑origin imports between 05:01 UTC on November 10, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: In spring 2025, the U.S. briefly imposed triple-digit tariffs on many Chinese-origin goods (about 145%), which sharply reduced seaport imports, before a truce lowered rates. Following negotiations announced May 12, 2025, the U.S. reduced extra tariffs on China to 30% from 145%, while China cut to 10% from 125% for a 90-day period. On August 12, 2025, the U.S. extended this tariff truce by an additional 90 days, preventing the immediate reversion to triple-digit duties; the extension runs until 12:01 a.m. EST on November 10, 2025 (05:01 UTC). The continuation of the suspension and its timing were implemented via executive order and reflected in Federal Register notices, specifying effective times for entries “for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption”. As of late September 2025, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer characterized about 55% U.S. tariffs on Chinese imports as a “good status quo,” while warning that, absent another extension, rates could snap back to around 145% on the U.S. side and 125% on China’s side on November 10, potentially halting trade.

Definitions used for clarity:
- Tariff/ad valorem duty: A tariff is an import tax paid by the importer; ad valorem duties are calculated as a percentage of the customs value of the goods.
- Chinese imports (PRC-origin): For this question, “Chinese imports” means goods whose country of origin is determined to be the People’s Republic of China under U.S. rules. “Country of origin” means the country of manufacture, production, or growth of an article of foreign origin entering the United States, with substantial transformation rules applicable; marking rules and origin determinations are codified in 19 CFR Part 134. For avoidance of doubt, executive orders in 2025 applying reciprocal country-specific ad valorem duties referenced PRC-origin imports and have included Hong Kong and Macau within their scope when specified.

Context on instruments and publication:
- The 90-day truce and its extension were announced in press reporting and implemented via executive orders that modified/suspended country-specific ad valorem duties, with details published on the White House Presidential Actions page and in the Federal Register (including effective times).
- Press coverage by Reuters has consistently documented the truce parameters (U.S. at 30%, China at 10%), prior triple-digit rates (U.S. 145%, China 125%), and the November 10 snapback risk absent extension.

Why this should be non-trivial to forecast: As of October 2025, negotiators could extend the truce again, partially adjust reciprocal duty rates, or allow a snapback to triple-digit rates. Outcomes depend on evolving U.S.–China talks, domestic economic conditions, and executive actions, all of which are uncertain but resolvable by year-end.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window: Events eligible for resolution must occur between 05:01 UTC on November 10, 2025 (the moment the current 90-day suspension is scheduled to end at 12:01 a.m. EST) and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.

What counts as “triple-digit tariff rate”: For the purposes of this question, this refers to a country-specific ad valorem duty rate of at least 100% applicable broadly to PRC-origin imports under the 2025 reciprocal tariff regime established and modified via executive orders (i.e., not limited to a narrow set of HTS subheadings but applied as a blanket country-specific rate). The relevant rates are those stated in executive orders and corresponding amendments to the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) and published in the Federal Register/White House Presidential Actions pages.

Operationalization of “implemented”: A rate is considered implemented if an official U.S. instrument (executive order or Federal Register notice) sets an ad valorem duty of ≥100% for PRC-origin imports and that rate is in effect for goods “entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption” during the resolution window. Effective times are as stated in the applicable instrument (typically 12:01 a.m. local U.S. time converted to UTC for this question).

Resolution:
- Resolve Yes if, at any point within the resolution window, the country-specific ad valorem duty rate applicable to PRC-origin imports is ≥100%, as evidenced by an official executive order or Federal Register notice that is effective during the window. A brief period (even a single calendar day) counts, provided the rate is in effect for entries.
- Resolve No if no such ≥100% rate is in effect at any time during the resolution window. This includes cases where the truce is extended further, rate adjustments keep the country-specific ad valorem duty below 100%, or other measures maintain rates below the threshold.

Verification sources:
- Primary: FederalRegister.gov notices implementing or modifying reciprocal tariff rates and HTSUS notes/headings; the White House Presidential Actions page publishing executive orders that set, suspend, or modify the rates, including effective dates/times.
- Secondary (if needed for corroboration only): Reuters reporting that clearly states the official rate in effect and timing (e.g., prior reporting of 145% U.S. rate and 30% truce rate), used only to confirm interpretations of official actions.

Key term references for adjudication:
- Tariff/ad valorem duty definition: Wikipedia entry for “Tariff” (for general understanding of ad valorem percentage).
- Country of origin determination: 19 CFR Part 134, §134.1 (to determine PRC-origin articles).

question: Will INDEC’s headline unemployment rate for Q3 2025 be below 7.5%?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: INDEC (Argentina’s national statistics institute) disseminates quarterly labor market indicators from the Encuesta Permanente de Hogares (EPH) via the series titled “Mercado de trabajo. Tasas e indicadores socioeconómicos.” The headline unemployment rate shown in these press releases is the tasa de desocupación for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos,” presented prominently on the first page and in the main table (Cuadro 1.1), and rounded to one decimal (Spanish formatting uses a comma). INDEC defines the tasa de desocupación as the percentage between the unemployed population and the economically active population; the unemployed are persons who, having no occupation, are actively seeking work and are available to work (open unemployment). Latest published figures: Q1 2025 unemployment (Total 31 aglomerados) was 7.9% ; Q2 2025 was 7.6%. The “Mercado de trabajo. Tasas e indicadores socioeconómicos. Tercer trimestre de 2025” release is scheduled on INDEC’s official calendar for December 18, 2025. These are the values and schedule that will determine the resolution of this question.

Definitions used in this question:
- “Tasa de desocupación” (unemployment rate): percentage of the unemployed population over the economically active population (PEA), as defined and reported by INDEC in its labor market press releases.
- “Unemployed population”: persons with no occupation who are actively seeking work and available to work; corresponds to open unemployment, per INDEC.
- “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos”: the EPH coverage used by INDEC for the headline labor market indicators, including the unemployment rate; the figure appears as “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos” in the press release and is rounded to one decimal.
- “Headline unemployment rate” in this question refers specifically to the tasa de desocupación for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos” in INDEC’s Q3 2025 “Mercado de trabajo. Tasas e indicadores socioeconómicos” press release.
- Decimal formatting: INDEC uses Spanish formatting (e.g., 7,6%) and rounds to one decimal; for comparison we interpret 7,4% as 7.4%, 7,5% as 7.5%, etc. The comparison is made directly to the published one-decimal figure.

Publication timing: INDEC’s calendar lists the Q3 2025 labor market press release on December 18, 2025; the calendar does not specify a timezone. For resolution cutoffs in this market question, all times are measured in UTC.
resolution_criteria:
Time window for eligible events: October 15, 2025 00:00:00 UTC through December 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC.

Source of truth: INDEC’s official Q3 2025 labor market press release (“Mercado de trabajo. Tasas e indicadores socioeconómicos. Tercer trimestre de 2025”) published on indec.gob.ar. This series is the same format used for Q1 and Q2 2025 (e.g., PDFs posted under INDEC’s press releases), where the headline rate appears on the first page and in Cuadro 1.1 for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos”. The scheduled publication date per INDEC’s calendar is December 18, 2025.

Metric to compare: the tasa de desocupación for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos” as printed in the Q3 2025 press release (one decimal, Spanish formatting).

Decision rule:
- Resolve Yes if the published tasa de desocupación for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos” in the Q3 2025 press release is strictly below 7.5% (i.e., 7,4% or less; equivalently ≤7.4% when interpreted with a dot as the decimal separator).
- Resolve No if the published figure is 7,5% (7.5%) or higher.

Clarifications:
- Only the headline tasa de desocupación for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos” is considered. Subgroup rates (by sex, age, region), seasonally adjusted values, alternative definitions, or separate indicators are excluded.
- Use the first Q3 2025 “Mercado de trabajo” press release posted by INDEC during the time window. If INDEC issues an erratum or formal correction during the time window, use the latest corrected figure posted within the window.
- If INDEC has not published the Q3 2025 “Mercado de trabajo. Tasas e indicadores socioeconómicos” press release by December 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC, resolve No.

Verification procedure (expected to take under 10 minutes):
1) Navigate to indec.gob.ar and locate the Q3 2025 “Mercado de trabajo. Tasas e indicadores socioeconómicos” press release (look for the PDF). The Q2 press release demonstrates the format and where the headline rate appears (first-page key figure box and Cuadro 1.1).
2) Read the tasa de desocupación for “Total 31 aglomerados urbanos” as printed (one decimal). Compare to 7.5% using the strict rule above.
3) Confirm that the press release publication date is within the time window. The scheduled date is December 18, 2025 per INDEC’s calendar.

question: Portugal: Will a Chega deputy be elected Secretary of the Mesa of the Assembly of the Republic between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (Lisbon time)?
background:
Status quo and context as of 2025-10-01:
- What is the Mesa and the Secretary role: The Mesa da Assembleia da República (the Assembly’s Bureau) is an organ composed of 1 President, 4 Vice-Presidents, 4 Secretaries, and 4 Vice-Secretaries. During plenary meetings, the Mesa is constituted by the President and the Secretaries. The roles are described on the Assembly’s official “Sobre a Mesa” page.
- How Mesa members are elected: Under the Regimento da Assembleia da República, Vice-Presidents, Secretaries, and Vice-Secretaries are elected by list, and candidates are considered elected if they obtain an absolute majority of votes of Deputies “em efetividade de funções” (in active office). Elections are conducted by secret ballot. See Article 23 (election and majority) and Article 97 (secret ballot) of the Regimento.
- Composition and June 2025 election: Following the XVII Legislature’s start, the Assembly announced on 2025-06-03 the election of Mesa members, listing the Secretaries elected: Francisco Figueira (PSD), Gabriel Mithá Ribeiro (CH), Joana Lima (PS), and Germana Rocha (PSD). The current official “Mesa” composition page on parlamento.pt provides the up-to-date list of members and their party affiliations and serves as the authoritative roster.
- Recent failed attempt to elect a Chega Secretary: On 2025-09-26, Chega’s nominee Francisco Gomes failed to be elected Secretary of the Mesa, receiving 98 votes in favor, 18 against, and 61 blank ballots (177 deputies present). The election required 116 votes in favor (an absolute majority) according to the Assembly’s rules, per reporting by RTP Madeira.
- Party definition (Chega): Chega (CHEGA!) is a Portuguese political party founded in 2019, characterized as national conservative and right‑wing populist.

Why this matters for forecasting: After the failed September vote, it is uncertain whether cross‑party bargaining will allow a Chega deputy to obtain the absolute majority required to be elected as a Secretary of the Mesa before the end of 2025. The outcome depends on parliamentary dynamics, attendance, and party strategies under the rules above.
resolution_criteria:
Binary (Yes/No). Time window and timezone: The question pertains to elections held between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 and 2025-12-31 23:59:59, Lisbon local time (Europe/Lisbon).

Operational definitions:
- “Deputy”: A member of Portugal’s Assembly of the Republic (Deputado), as referenced throughout the Regimento da Assembleia da República.
- “Deputy from Chega”: A Deputy who, at the time of the relevant election, is officially listed on the Assembly’s website as belonging to the Chega parliamentary group (CH). This can be verified via the Deputy’s official profile page and/or listings of parliamentary groups on parlamento.pt.
- “Secretary of the Mesa”: One of the four “Secretários” that make up the Mesa, distinct from Vice‑Secretaries, as defined on the Assembly’s official Mesa information pages.
- “Elected”: As per the Regimento, a candidate is considered elected when they obtain an absolute majority of votes of Deputies in active office in a secret‑ballot plenary vote (Regimento Article 23 and Article 97).

Resolution source and procedure (primary):
- Primary source: the official “Mesa” composition page on the Assembly’s website (parlamento.pt) as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 Lisbon time, which lists the Secretaries and their party affiliations.

What counts as Yes:
- Yes if a person who is a Deputy from Chega is elected to the office of “Secretário da Mesa” in a plenary vote held within the time window, and the Assembly’s official Mesa composition page lists that person as a Secretary by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 Lisbon time. The election must be for the role “Secretário” (not Vice‑Secretário) and must have been conducted by secret ballot with the candidate obtaining an absolute majority of Deputies in active office, per the Regimento.
- The election date is the date of the plenary vote (as reflected in official Assembly communications such as press releases or records). If multiple such elections occur within the window, any one successful election meeting the above suffices for “Yes.” If the elected Secretary later resigns or is replaced before 2025-12-31, the outcome remains “Yes” provided the election occurred within the window and the official site listed them as Secretary at any time before the resolution timestamp.

What counts as No:
- No if no Deputy from Chega is elected Secretary of the Mesa in the time window, or if any Chega Deputy is only elected outside the time window, or is elected to a different office (e.g., Vice‑Secretary or Vice‑President), or is designated in an acting capacity without a formal election as defined in the Regimento.

Secondary/backup sources:
- If the primary page is temporarily inaccessible or not yet updated at the resolution timestamp, rely on official Assembly communications on parlamento.pt that announce Mesa elections (e.g., the 2025-06-03 announcement format) , and/or official plenary records posted on the Assembly’s site. In case of rare ambiguity, contemporaneous reporting by major Portuguese outlets (e.g., RTP) may be used to corroborate the occurrence and result of the vote.

Notes:
- The September 2025 failed vote for Chega’s Francisco Gomes (98 in favor; 116 required) illustrates the absolute‑majority threshold in practice but does not itself resolve this question, as it precedes the start of the counting window.
- All references to election mechanics (absolute majority; secret ballot; roles) derive from the Regimento and official Mesa pages.

question: Will NYC’s Congestion Relief Zone tolling be active at 2025-12-31 23:59 ET?
background:
Summary of the policy as of 2025-09-30:
- Official program/name and scope: New York City’s Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), commonly referred to as congestion pricing, charges vehicles that enter the Congestion Relief Zone (CRZ) in Manhattan. The CRZ is defined by the MTA as “local streets and avenues at or below 60 Street” in Manhattan, and tolling began on January 5, 2025. The MTA’s CRZ tolling portal confirms that vehicles are tolled upon entry to the CRZ and outlines the current toll structure. NYC311 also states that tolling is in effect 24/7 and directs users to the MTA for toll details and updates.
- Current toll structure (context for forecasters): As of 2025, the MTA indicates an initial $9 peak toll (with E‑ZPass) for passenger vehicles, with lower overnight rates; vehicles of different classes (motorcycles, trucks, buses, taxis/FHVs) have different rates and rules. Tolls apply when entering the CRZ and some vehicles are charged only once per day. Details and definitions (e.g., peak periods, crossing credits, E‑ZPass vs. Tolls by Mail) are provided on the MTA tolling page.
- Litigation/status quo factors: Multiple legal challenges have been filed in federal and state courts. Notably, on May 27, 2025, U.S. District Judge Lewis J. Liman issued a preliminary injunction blocking the Trump administration’s attempt to end the program, allowing congestion pricing to continue during litigation. Reporting the next day indicated the program was likely to remain in place through late 2025 while the judge considered the case timeline, signaling a decision could take until year-end. Several other lawsuits challenging the program were dismissed in July 2025, while some matters (e.g., trucking litigation) remained pending; a litigation tracker summarizes case statuses and key dates useful for assessing risk of suspension.

Why this is forecastable now: As of late May–July 2025, court actions favored continued operation for months but did not guarantee uninterrupted operation through December 31, 2025. Political, legal, or operational developments could still lead to suspension or modification before year-end, creating meaningful uncertainty that forecasters can evaluate using legal timelines, political signals, and MTA communications.

Key references and where to monitor status:
- MTA CBDTP project page (official program overview, boundaries, start date).
- MTA Congestion Relief Zone tolling portal (operational status, tolling details).
- NYC311 Congestion Pricing page (states tolling is in effect 24/7 and links to MTA for details/updates).
- Press and court reporting on litigation dynamics (for context): NYT (injunction) and Bloomberg (timeline likely through year-end) ; RPA litigation tracker for consolidated case status summaries.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome space: Yes/No.

Definition of terms:
- Congestion Relief Zone (CRZ): The area of Manhattan where the CBDTP toll applies, defined by the MTA as “local streets and avenues at or below 60 Street”.
- Active (for this question): At the resolution timestamp, the program is “in effect” and vehicles entering the CRZ are being tolled (i.e., the MTA indicates tolling is in effect and not suspended at that time). Evidence that tolls are being collected for CRZ entry satisfies “active”.
- Resolution timestamp: 2025-12-31 23:59 Eastern Time (ET; America/New_York).

Start date for eligibility and window: This question resolves based on the status at the single instant of 2025-12-31 23:59 ET. Events before or after that instant do not affect resolution; only the status at that moment counts.

How to resolve:
- Resolve Yes if, as of 2025-12-31 23:59 ET, any official MTA source clearly indicates that tolling is in effect for entering the CRZ. Primary sources, in order of precedence:
  1) MTA CBDTP project page , and/or
  2) MTA Congestion Relief Zone tolling portal.
  Secondary corroboration (if needed): NYC311 Congestion Pricing page stating tolling is in effect.
- Resolve No if, as of the resolution timestamp, the above sources indicate that tolling is suspended, halted, or otherwise not being collected for CRZ entries.

Ambiguity and tie-breakers:
- If sources conflict, prefer official MTA sources over NYC311; within MTA sources, prefer the page with the most specific operational status language at that time (e.g., the tolling portal over a general project page).
- If none of the above webpages are accessible at the time of resolution, use contemporaneous reporting from at least two of the following reputable outlets published on or immediately after the resolution date, explicitly describing the program’s operational status at that time: Associated Press, Reuters, The New York Times, Bloomberg.
- If there is a temporary outage of the websites but no evidence of a suspension (e.g., standard maintenance), do not count that as “inactive.” Only explicit suspension/cessation per sources above counts as No.

Edge cases:
- Partial suspensions that still charge tolls for CRZ entries at the resolution timestamp count as Active (Yes).
- If tolls are set to $0 (waived) for all CRZ entries at the resolution timestamp, that counts as Not Active (No), as vehicles would not be tolled for entry.

question: Between October 1 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will Apple add dedicated App Store Review Guidelines language explicitly governing AI chatbots or AI companion/romance bots?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Apple’s App Store Review Guidelines page includes Section 4.7 (“Mini apps, mini games, streaming games, chatbots, plug-ins, and game emulators”), which already mentions “chatbots” and lays out general requirements (privacy, objectionable content filtering, age ratings, etc.), but does not contain language explicitly about “AI chatbots” or AI companion/romance bots. The page shows “Last Updated: June 9, 2025.” 
- Relevant general guidelines include 1.1.4 (overtly sexual or pornographic material) and 1.2 (User-Generated Content), which set broad content rules but are not explicitly targeted at AI chatbots or AI romantic/companion bots. 
- Apple has precedent for announcing guideline updates on the Apple Developer News site; for example, a January 25, 2024 post stated that 4.7 was edited to set forth new requirements for mini apps, mini games, streaming games, chatbots, and plug-ins. 

Why this question may be uncertain and interesting:
- Generative AI is proliferating in consumer apps, and “AI companions”/romance bots are drawing scrutiny from platforms and regulators. Apple could add explicit, dedicated rules for these categories in Q4 2025, but it is not assured.

Baseline text (for forecasters’ reference):
- 4.7 headline and overview mention “chatbots,” and 4.7.1–4.7.5 detail general rules (privacy compliance, objectionable content filtering/reporting/blocking, data-sharing consent, index of software, age rating propagation). The current text does not include explicit phrasing like “AI chatbot” or “AI companion” or “romance bot.” 
- 1.1.4 defines disallowed overtly sexual content; 1.2 sets UGC moderation and removal expectations; both are general. 

Primary source to check for resolution: App Store Review Guidelines page (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/). As of 2025-06-09, it contains the above baseline references. 
Secondary corroboration source (for dating updates, if needed): Apple Developer News (https://developer.apple.com/news/), which historically posts guideline update notices. Example precedent from 2024: “Updated App Store Review Guidelines now available.”
resolution_criteria:
Timeframe and timezone:
- Eligible updates must be published between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Definitions (with external references for clarity):
- “App Store Review Guidelines” means Apple’s official App Review Guidelines page for iOS/iPadOS/tvOS/watchOS/macOS apps, currently located at https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/.
- “Chatbot” means a software agent that interacts via text or voice to simulate conversation; in modern usage often powered by machine learning/LLMs (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatbot and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model).
- “AI chatbot” means a chatbot explicitly described by Apple in the App Store Review Guidelines as using artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, or large language models; or a chatbot that Apple explicitly refers to with “AI” in conjunction with “chatbot(s)” in the guidelines text.
- “AI companion/romance bot” means a chatbot marketed or designed to simulate companionship, romance, intimacy, or “girlfriend/boyfriend” relationships, including phrases such as “AI companion(s),” “romance bot(s),” “romantic companion(s),” “girlfriend/boyfriend bot(s),” or equivalent phrasings that explicitly denote AI-based romantic/companion interactions.
- “Dedicated language explicitly governing” means newly added rule text (after 2025-10-01) that (a) contains at least one explicit phrase from the trigger list below, and (b) imposes requirements or restrictions specifically on that class of apps (i.e., includes normative language such as “must,” “may not,” “should,” “are prohibited,” “require,” etc.).

Trigger phrase list (any one is sufficient if used in a normative rule sentence):
- “AI chatbot” or “artificial intelligence chatbot”
- “AI companion(s)” or “artificial intelligence companion(s)”
- “romance bot(s)” or “romantic companion(s)”
- “girlfriend bot” or “boyfriend bot”
- Phrases pairing “AI” and “chatbot(s)” within the same sentence that imposes a rule (e.g., “AI chatbots must …”).
- Phrases pairing “AI” and “companion(s)” within the same sentence that imposes a rule (e.g., “AI companions are prohibited from …”).

Resolution logic:
- Resolve Yes if, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the App Store Review Guidelines page contains newly added dedicated language (as defined above) governing AI chatbots or AI companion/romance bots and at least one of the following is true:
  1) The page’s “Last Updated” metadata shows a date within the eligibility window (2025-10-01 to 2025-12-31), and the dedicated language is present on the page. 
  2) Apple Developer News carries a post within the eligibility window announcing guideline updates, and the dedicated language is present on the guidelines page by the end time. 
- Resolve No if neither condition is met. Specifically, do not count:
  - General mentions of “chatbots” without “AI” qualifiers (e.g., the existing mention in 4.7 and its general requirements) unless Apple adds explicit AI-targeted rule language per the trigger list. 
  - General content and UGC rules (e.g., 1.1.4 and 1.2) unless Apple revises them to explicitly and normatively govern AI chatbots or AI companions using a trigger phrase. 

What the resolver should do on or after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC:
1) Open the App Store Review Guidelines page and check the “Last Updated” date and the text for any new rule sentences containing one of the trigger phrases. 
2) If needed to establish timing, check Apple Developer News posts dated in the eligibility window that announce guideline updates; confirm the guideline page reflects the dedicated language by the end time. 
3) Apply the decision rules above to resolve Yes/No.

Notes:
- The baseline as of 2025-06-09 includes “chatbots” in 4.7 and general content/privacy rules, but no explicit “AI chatbot” or “AI companion/romance bot” dedicated rules. This baseline is provided to clarify what does not count. 
- The Apple Developer News precedent shows Apple publicly announces guideline updates, supporting the expectation that any late-2025 change will have a clear public source.

question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will DOL, HHS, or Treasury publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) proposing to rescind or modify regulatory text adopted in the 2024 MHPAEA Final Rule?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- The tri-agencies (Department of Labor/EBSA, Department of Health and Human Services/CMS, and Department of the Treasury/IRS) published the 2024 Final Rule titled “Requirements Related to the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act” in the Federal Register on September 23, 2024 (Federal Register citation 89 FR 77586; FR Doc. 2024-20612). The rule’s effective date is November 22, 2024, and it amends and adds MHPAEA-related regulations at 26 CFR 54.9812-1 and 54.9812-2; 29 CFR 2590.712 and 2590.712-1; and 45 CFR 146.136 and 146.137 (with HHS-only amendments to 45 CFR 147.160 and 45 CFR 146.180).
- On May 15, 2025, the Departments issued a joint non-enforcement statement. They requested that ERIC’s litigation challenging portions of the 2024 Final Rule be held in abeyance and stated they are reconsidering the 2024 Final Rule, including whether to issue a notice of proposed rulemaking rescinding or modifying the regulation through notice-and-comment rulemaking. The statement says the Departments will not enforce the 2024 Final Rule (to the extent it is new relative to the 2013 final rule) prior to a final decision in the litigation, plus an additional 18 months; it also confirms staggered applicability dates beginning with plan years on or after January 1, 2025, and for individual market policy years on or after January 1, 2026.
- A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) is a proposed rules document published in the “Proposed Rules” section of the Federal Register, typically labeled with preamble fields including AGENCY, ACTION (e.g., “proposed rule”), SUMMARY, and DATES, and it is the mechanism for agencies to propose amending CFR text via notice-and-comment rulemaking.
Key definitions and references:
- MHPAEA: The Paul Wellstone and Pete Domenici Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act of 2008 (overview: https://www.cms.gov/marketplace/private-health-insurance/mental-health-parity-addiction-equity; general background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Law_110-343).
- 2024 MHPAEA Final Rule: The final rule published at 89 FR 77586 (FR Doc. 2024-20612), titled “Requirements Related to the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act,” issued jointly by IRS/Treasury, EBSA/DOL, and CMS/HHS, and amending/adding the MHPAEA regulations as listed above.
- NPRM: A document published in the “Proposed Rules” section of the Federal Register that proposes changes to CFR text and solicits public comment. For resolution, an NPRM must be labeled as a proposed rule and be publicly available on federalregister.gov.
Why this question is meaningful and uncertain:
- The Departments have explicitly stated they are reconsidering the 2024 Final Rule and are weighing issuing an NPRM to rescind or modify it, but timing and scope depend on litigation posture, internal policy decisions, and interagency coordination, creating real uncertainty as to whether an NPRM will be published within the specified window.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and time zone:
- Eligible events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
What resolves “Yes”:
- Resolve Yes if, within the event window, the Federal Register (federalregister.gov) contains at least one document in the “Proposed Rules” section that:
  1) Lists as AGENCY any of: Department of Labor (Employee Benefits Security Administration), Department of Health and Human Services (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services), or Department of the Treasury (Internal Revenue Service), and
  2) Is labeled ACTION: “proposed rule” (i.e., an NPRM), and
  3) Proposes to rescind or modify (delete, revise, or replace) regulatory text that was adopted by the 2024 MHPAEA Final Rule published at 89 FR 77586 (FR Doc. 2024-20612).
- The NPRM may be joint (issued by multiple Departments) or issued by any single Department among DOL, HHS, or Treasury. It qualifies if the preamble explicitly references the 2024 Final Rule (e.g., cites “Requirements Related to the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act,” 89 FR 77586, or FR Doc. 2024-20612) or clearly proposes amendments to any of the MHPAEA regulatory provisions amended/added by that Final Rule (26 CFR 54.9812-1/-2; 29 CFR 2590.712/-1; 45 CFR 146.136/146.137; and HHS-only amendments at 45 CFR 147.160 and 45 CFR 146.180).
What does not count:
- Documents outside the “Proposed Rules” section (e.g., Notices, Guidance).
- Advanced Notices of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRMs) or Requests for Information, unless they are explicitly labeled as a “proposed rule.”
- Press releases, agency web posts, or Regulations.gov entries without corresponding Federal Register publication.
- NPRMs that discuss MHPAEA but only address enforcement policy or guidance without proposing changes to CFR text adopted by the 2024 Final Rule.
What resolves “No”:
- If no qualifying NPRM, as defined above, is published on federalregister.gov within the event window, resolve No.
Primary source of truth:
- Federal Register website (federalregister.gov). NPRMs are published in the Proposed Rules section and labeled accordingly.
Supporting references confirming the 2024 Final Rule scope and identifiers (for verification when assessing any NPRM’s linkage to the 2024 rule):
- 2024 MHPAEA Final Rule metadata and CFR parts amended/added (89 FR 77586; FR Doc. 2024-20612).
Additional context (non-essential for resolution but relevant for forecasters):
- The Departments’ non-enforcement statement, litigation context, and explicit contemplation of issuing an NPRM to rescind/modify the 2024 Final Rule.

question: Will total pledges to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage reach at least USD 1.2 billion by December 31, 2025?
background:
Overview: This question asks whether cumulative pledges to the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) will meet or exceed USD 1.2 billion by the end of 2025. The FRLD is an entity under the UNFCCC/Paris Agreement framework, operationalized following COP28 to assist particularly vulnerable developing countries in responding to loss and damage from climate change. As of late June 2025, official reporting indicated pledges of approximately USD 788.8 million (USD equivalent), with USD 361.0 million received in the Fund. COP30 (November 2025) and associated high-level events are focal points for potential additional pledges before year-end.

Key definitions and context for forecasters:
- Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD): An international climate finance fund established under the UNFCCC/Paris Agreement process. See the UNFCCC FRLD landing page for official context: https://unfccc.int/fund-for-responding-to-loss-and-damage.
- Pledge: An announced commitment to provide funds to the FRLD, typically requiring conversion into a fully executed contribution agreement or arrangement before funds are "received in the Fund." In official reporting, the interim Trustee (World Bank) distinguishes between "total amount of pledges" and "amount received in the Fund"; the FRLD Board report to COP30/CMA7 notes USD 788.8 million in pledges and USD 361.0 million received as at June 27, 2025.
- USD equivalent: Official FRLD reporting expresses cumulative pledges in USD equivalent, implying conversion from other currencies to USD for standardization.

Status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
- Latest official tallies: Total pledges to the FRLD stood at USD 788.8 million, and the amount received in the Fund was USD 361.0 million, with "as at" date June 27, 2025. This sets the baseline from which additional pledges might be announced and recognized before December 31, 2025.

What forecasters should monitor:
- Official FRLD/UNFCCC publications (e.g., FRLD Board reports and interim Trustee status-of-resources reports) that update the pledges total.
- The FRLD official website pledge/contributions page (linked via https://www.frld.org/) for near-real-time updates on pledges.
- Announcements and communiqués during COP30 and year-end climate finance events that are subsequently reflected in official FRLD tallies.

Date range and timezone:
- Eligible pledges include any FRLD pledges announced at any time, provided they are reflected in an official FRLD/UNFCCC source with an "as of" date on or before December 31, 2025.
- The resolution cut-off is December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC.

Why this is non-trivial: With official pledges around USD 789 million in mid-2025, it is plausible but uncertain whether cumulative pledges will surpass USD 1.2 billion by year-end. Outcomes depend on diplomatic dynamics, donor fiscal space, and whether announcements are formalized and recorded in official tallies.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome: Binary.
- Resolve "Yes" if the total amount of pledges to the FRLD, expressed in USD equivalent, is at least USD 1,200,000,000 as of the resolution cut-off (December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC), per official FRLD/UNFCCC sources. Otherwise, resolve "No."

Primary resolution source hierarchy:
1) The most recent official FRLD Board or interim Trustee document posted on the UNFCCC website (unfccc.int) that explicitly reports the "total amount of pledges" (USD equivalent) and includes an "as of" date on or before December 31, 2025. Examples include: "Report of the FRLD Board to COP30/CMA7" and "Status of resources report of the Trustee" (document series FRLD/B.x/5/Rev.y). Use the latest available document by publication date and/or the latest "as of" date if multiple documents exist.
2) If no such UNFCCC document reporting the pledges total is available by the cut-off, use the FRLD official website pledge/contributions dashboard (linked via https://www.frld.org/), provided it shows a cumulative pledges figure with an "as of" date on or before the cut-off.

Tie-breakers and ambiguity resolution:
- If multiple official sources differ, prefer the UNFCCC document over the FRLD website, and within UNFCCC documents, prefer the one with the latest "as of" date on or before December 31, 2025.
- Use the exact USD figure reported by the source. If a source provides only qualitative phrasing (e.g., "just under $1.2 billion"), and no precise number is given, defer to the latest UNFCCC document with a precise figure.

Term definitions to govern inclusion:
- "Pledges" are counted exactly as the official source counts them, i.e., the cumulative total of announced commitments to the FRLD regardless of whether they have been converted into contribution agreements or received in the Fund. "Amount received in the Fund" is not used for resolution unless explicitly stated; only the "total amount of pledges" in USD equivalent determines the outcome.

Temporal scope:
- Pledges announced at any time count as long as they are reflected in the official tally used for resolution with an "as of" date on or before December 31, 2025, 23:59 UTC.

Verification steps (for resolvers):
- Locate the latest relevant UNFCCC FRLD document by Dec 31, 2025 (e.g., the FRLD Board report to COP30/CMA7) and record the "total amount of pledges" figure and its "as of" date.
- If unavailable, check the FRLD website pledge/contributions page for the cumulative pledges figure and "as of" date.
- Compare the figure to the USD 1.2 billion threshold to determine "Yes" or "No."

question: Will at least three named storms with UK impact dates be recorded between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), per the Met Office UK Storm Centre?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:

- Storm naming in the UK and nearby countries is coordinated by the Western Storm Naming Group (the UK Met Office, Ireland’s Met Éireann, and the Netherlands’ KNMI). A storm is named when it is expected to cause disruption or damage significant enough to warrant an amber or red warning, considering both the potential impact and the likelihood of those impacts. Wind is the primary consideration, but heavy rain (e.g., flooding risk) or snow can also lead to naming.
- The Met Office UK Storm Centre serves as the official, contemporaneously updated source for named storms and includes a season table with columns such as “Date named” and “Date of impact on UK and/or Ireland and/or Netherlands.” The UK Storm Centre states it provides the latest updates and information as storms are named and impact the UK.
- Recent base rates:
  - The 2023/24 UK storm season had 12 named storms, the highest since naming began in 2015.
  - In the 2024/25 season, six named storms are listed overall, with at least two storms showing UK impact dates in October (e.g., Ashley) and one in December (e.g., Darragh), illustrating that late-year activity can include multiple named events. As of January 21, 2025, five storms had been named (with further storms named later in the season).
- Ongoing programme: The Met Office and partners publish a new list of storm names each September and maintain the UK Storm Centre page throughout the season.

Why this threshold/time window:
- Late autumn and early winter often see multiple named storms in the UK, but counts vary by year. Setting the threshold at three for the period October 15 through December 31 (UTC) targets a range with genuine uncertainty that should reward careful forecasting.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC inclusive, there are at least three distinct named storms for which the Met Office UK Storm Centre lists a UK impact date within that window. Otherwise, it resolves No.

Definitions and counting rules:
- Named storm: Any storm entry appearing on the Met Office’s UK Storm Centre season page for 2025/26 (UK Storm Centre index: https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/warnings-and-advice/uk-storm-centre/index) with an official name under the Name Our Storms programme. Storms are named by the Western Group (Met Office, Met Éireann, KNMI) when impacts are expected to warrant amber or red warnings; while wind is the primary driver, heavy rain or snow can also lead to naming.
- UK impact date: The date shown in the UK Storm Centre table’s “Date of impact on UK and/or Ireland and/or Netherlands” field specifically corresponding to the United Kingdom. If the table displays a date range for the UK (e.g., “26–27 November”), any portion of that range intersecting the window counts. If the table’s combined column does not explicitly distinguish the UK for a given storm, use that storm’s dedicated page within the UK Storm Centre to confirm whether the UK had an impact date and what date(s) that impact occurred; the UK Storm Centre indicates that these pages provide the latest updates as storms are named and impact the UK.
- Timezone: All date comparisons are in UTC.
- Start and end of the window: Start at 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC; end at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Counting: Count unique named storms once each. If a single storm has multiple UK impact dates within the window, it still counts as one. Only storms with a UK impact date within the window are eligible.

Primary resolution source:
- Met Office UK Storm Centre 2025/26 season page (and the linked per-storm pages from within the UK Storm Centre), which includes “Date named” and “Date of impact on UK and/or Ireland and/or Netherlands” and is updated contemporaneously as storms are named and impact the UK.

Verification steps for the resolver:
1) Navigate to the UK Storm Centre index and open the 2025/26 season table; identify storms listed with UK impact dates.
2) For each storm, confirm the UK impact date(s) and determine whether at least one date falls within the window. If needed, open the storm’s dedicated UK Storm Centre page for clarity.
3) Tally the number of distinct storms with UK impact date(s) in the window; resolve Yes if the count is ≥3; otherwise resolve No.

Notes:
- Background metrics: The 2023/24 season having 12 named storms and the 2024/25 season listing six named storms (including examples with late-year UK impacts) are provided solely as context to inform forecasting and do not affect resolution.
- Western Group and impact-based naming criteria references are provided to define ‘named storm’ clearly.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31, will the Santa Barbara County Board of Supervisors adopt an ordinance amending the Land Use & Development Code to set a 40-foot maximum building height for apartment buildings with 20 or more units in unincorporated areas?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01: Local reporting indicates Santa Barbara County staff have proposed zoning amendments that include allowing apartment buildings with 20 or more units to be built up to 40 feet tall (an increase from 35 feet), with associated setback adjustments, and that these amendments were headed to the Planning Commission for a vote on October 29. The Santa Barbara County Land Use & Development Code (LUDC) governs zoning and development standards in the County’s unincorporated areas; the County explains that properties in unincorporated Santa Barbara County are assigned zones that set permissible uses and standards. Official, executed Board-adopted ordinances are published in the County Ordinances Archive, which contains scanned copies of ordinances as adopted by the Board of Supervisors and is the authoritative place to verify adoption and text.

Definitions and scope used in this question:
- Unincorporated area: Land not governed by a municipal (city/town) government; in the U.S. context, these are areas of a county outside any incorporated city, typically governed directly by the county. This question concerns unincorporated areas of Santa Barbara County governed by the County’s LUDC.
- Apartment building: A multi-unit residential building containing multiple self-contained housing units (apartments) within a single structure.
- Unit (for the phrase “20 or more units”): For clarity, a “unit” is a self-contained housing unit (dwelling) intended for independent living, consistent with the U.S. Census Bureau’s definition of a housing unit. If the adopted ordinance uses a defined term (e.g., “dwelling unit”), that term as used in the ordinance controls for resolution.

Why this is forecastable now: As of late September 2025, the change was still in the proposal/review phase with Planning Commission action pending, and it is uncertain whether the Board will adopt an ordinance before year-end that specifically sets the maximum height to 40 feet for buildings with 20+ units in unincorporated areas. The County maintains authoritative, timely publication of adopted ordinances for verification.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible adoption events are those occurring between 2025-10-15 00:00 and 2025-12-31 23:59, Pacific Time (PT). The adoption date/time is determined by the date recorded on the executed ordinance’s “PASSED, APPROVED AND ADOPTED” line, as published by the County. If only a date (no time) is provided, that calendar date in PT is used.

What resolves Yes:
- Resolve Yes if, during the window above, the Santa Barbara County Board of Supervisors adopts an ordinance that amends the Santa Barbara County Land Use & Development Code (LUDC) to establish a maximum building height of 40 feet specifically for apartment buildings containing 20 or more units in unincorporated areas governed by the LUDC. The ordinance text must explicitly (a) set the maximum height to 40 feet, and (b) apply the 40-foot standard based on a threshold of 20 or more units. The standard may apply countywide within LUDC-covered unincorporated zones that allow multi-unit residential, or to one or more such LUDC zones; a countywide change is not required so long as at least one LUDC zone in unincorporated areas is amended accordingly. Verification will be done by reading the text of the executed, adopted ordinance.

What resolves No:
- Resolve No if no such ordinance is adopted within the window, or if any ordinance adopted in the window sets a different height (e.g., 35 feet or 45 feet), uses a different unit threshold, or applies only outside unincorporated areas governed by the LUDC (e.g., applies solely to incorporated cities or to codes other than the County’s LUDC).

Clarifications and edge cases:
- Adoption event definition: “Adopt” means the Board of Supervisors takes final action to pass the ordinance (typically second reading and adoption), resulting in an executed ordinance bearing the adoption date and signatures; staff proposals, Planning Commission recommendations, or first readings do not qualify.
- Effective dates: If the ordinance’s effective date falls after 2025-12-31, this still resolves Yes so long as the adoption date is within the window.
- Terminology: If the ordinance uses “dwelling units,” “multi-family,” or similar defined terms, those terms control for determining whether the threshold of “20 or more units” is met. For the purpose of interpretation, “apartment building” refers to multi-unit residential buildings as commonly understood; however, resolution hinges on the ordinance text itself.
- Coastal/other codes: This question only concerns amendments to the County’s LUDC for unincorporated areas. Ordinances that amend only other codes (e.g., Fire Code) or apply only to incorporated municipalities do not count.

Primary resolution source:
- County of Santa Barbara – County Ordinances Archive (scanned copies of executed, adopted ordinances). The presence of an executed ordinance meeting the criteria above, with an adoption date in the window, resolves the market. If multiple ordinances are adopted, any one meeting the criteria is sufficient for Yes.

Background/source notes for forecasters:
- Proposal context (reported height increase to 40 feet for 20+ unit buildings and PC scheduling) is from local reporting to help understand baseline status as of late September 2025.
- LUDC governs unincorporated areas of the County.
- Definitions for unincorporated area and apartment building/unit are provided for clarity; if ordinance-defined terms differ, the ordinance text governs for resolution.

question: According to EIA’s December 2025 Short-Term Energy Outlook, will U.S. retail electricity sales to the commercial sector in 2025 be at least 3.0% higher than in 2024?
background:
Why this question and proxy: U.S. data center electricity use has risen rapidly and is a growing share of national demand. DOE/LBNL reported that data centers consumed about 176 TWh in 2023 (~4.4% of total U.S. electricity) and projected substantial further increases toward 2028, driven in part by AI and cloud growth. Direct, official national totals for “data center electricity consumption” are not published on a monthly cadence, so this question uses a close, timely proxy that EIA publishes every month: retail electricity sales to the commercial sector, which includes most data center loads per standard utility classification. This proxy should reflect near-term growth attributable to data centers while ensuring unambiguous resolution before year-end 2025.

Key definitions and references:
- Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO): EIA’s monthly forecast and estimates of U.S. energy supply, demand, and prices, including tables for annual retail electricity sales by sector (United States total). The December 2025 edition is the primary resolution source. Reference page: https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/
- Retail electricity sales to the commercial sector: As defined by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (commercial sector generally comprises non-manufacturing business establishments, including services). EIA glossary: https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/ (commercial sector).
- United States: The 50 states and the District of Columbia (as used in EIA national totals).

Status quo context (as of 2025-09-22):
- Data centers: 176 TWh consumption in 2023 and ~4.4% of U.S. electricity, with projections of continued rapid growth.
- EIA routinely notes data centers as a driver of commercial electricity demand in its analyses; the STEO provides annual-by-sector retail sales that can be compared year over year in the December 2025 edition.

Interpretation: This market resolves based on what the December 2025 STEO estimates for 2024 and 2025 commercial-sector retail sales, not on later revisions or actuals published in 2026+.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end dates: Events eligible for resolution must occur between 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. This market resolves upon publication of the December 2025 edition of the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), or at the deadline if already published.

What is measured: U.S. retail electricity sales to the commercial sector for calendar years 2024 and 2025, as reported in the December 2025 STEO (United States totals). Use the table in the STEO that reports annual retail electricity sales by sector and year (units typically in billion kilowatthours, i.e., billion kWh).

Computation: Compute percentage change as (Sales_2025 − Sales_2024) / Sales_2024. Interpret “at least 3.0% higher” as the inequality (Sales_2025 − Sales_2024) / Sales_2024 ≥ 0.030. Use the numeric values as listed in the December 2025 STEO with their published precision; do not round inputs beyond what is published. The percent change comparison is evaluated on the resulting quotient without additional rounding (i.e., compare the computed value directly to 0.030).

Resolution source hierarchy:
1) Primary: December 2025 STEO (https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/). Use the national United States totals for retail electricity sales to the commercial sector for years 2024 and 2025 from the relevant table.
2) If the December 2025 STEO edition is not available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, use the most recent STEO edition published on or before that time (typically November 2025). The same table and fields apply.

Outcome:
- YES if the computed percentage change is ≥ 3.0%.
- NO otherwise.

Clarifications:
- This resolves on the figures and edition specified (STEO as of the resolution date). Any later revisions or re-publications do not affect the outcome.
- Scope is national U.S. totals (50 states + D.C.). U.S. territories are excluded unless explicitly included by EIA in the national totals table.
- If the STEO table presents multiple cases or scenarios, use the “baseline” or central case that EIA presents as the main U.S. outlook in the December (or fallback) edition. If multiple tables list the same metric, use the canonical table for retail electricity sales by sector.
- Links are provided for navigation; exact table numbering may vary over time, but the metric is unambiguous (annual U.S. retail electricity sales to the commercial sector for 2024 and 2025).

Examples do not apply; the resolution will use the actual figures in the specified STEO edition.

question: Between October 1 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will the European Union adopt a Ukraine loan facility of at least €120 billion that is explicitly backed by immobilized Russian central bank assets?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30: In late September 2025, the European Commission circulated a proposal for a large, interest-free "reparations loan" to Ukraine, leveraging immobilized Russian central bank assets (primarily cash at Euroclear in Belgium) without outright confiscation. Reporting describes the proposed facility as around €140 billion, zero-interest, and backed by these immobilized assets; EU ambassadors were set to discuss the plan on Friday, followed by EU leaders at an informal summit in Copenhagen the next week, with advocates aiming for agreement by end-October. The scheme interacts with an existing G7 arrangement that uses windfall profits (interest) from frozen Russian assets to back a loan; under the new approach, cash would be transferred/used, and those windfall profits would cease, with part of the facility allocated to replace backing for the existing G7 credit. Key legal/political hurdles include the EU’s current inability to confiscate sovereign assets (only use interest), unanimity constraints in renewing sanctions that immobilize assets, and concerns about sovereign immunity and financial stability; proponents contemplate legal workarounds (e.g., qualified majority for sanctions prolongation) and robust guarantees by member states. Support has been voiced by figures including the German chancellor, while some leaders emphasize avoiding outright confiscation and respecting international law.

Definitions and clarifications to ensure resolvability:
- "European Union" refers to the political and economic union of 27 European countries; see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union
- "Loan facility" (or "loan package") means a legally established EU lending instrument that authorizes a total principal amount for loans to Ukraine; the "amount" refers to the maximum authorized principal across all tranches under the act.
- "Immobilized (frozen) Russian central bank assets" refers to assets of the Central Bank of Russia immobilized in the EU under restrictive measures; see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bank_of_Russia and Euroclear: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euroclear. In current proposals, these assets are used as collateral/guarantee funding or via transfer of cash, and/or via use of windfall profits/interest they generate.
- "Explicitly backed" means the adopted EU legal act or an official EU document (e.g., Council press release about the act’s adoption) clearly states that immobilized Russian central bank assets (including cash held at Euroclear) or the windfall profits/interest from such assets are being used to fund, guarantee, collateralize, or otherwise back the facility.
- "Adopt" means formal adoption of a legally binding EU act (e.g., Council Decision, Regulation, Implementing Decision) establishing the facility, as indicated by publication in the Official Journal (OJ) or an official Council adoption communication; see: Official Journal portal https://eur-lex.europa.eu/oj/direct-access.html and Council press releases https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/.

Why this is non-trivial: The proposed size (~€140bn), the novel legal mechanism leveraging immobilized sovereign assets, unanimity vs qualified-majority issues, and national guarantees create substantial uncertainty about whether a sufficiently large, explicitly asset-backed facility will be adopted by year-end. Setting the threshold at €120bn balances plausibility: the public proposal centers on €140bn, but downsizing or delay is possible, making both Yes and No plausible.

Additional context: Most Russian central bank assets in the EU are held at Euroclear, estimated around €176bn; the Commission’s proposal contemplated allocating €45bn to back an existing G7 credit and up to €140bn for the new facility, with cash disbursed in tranches and subject to conditions; sanctions on Russia need semiannual renewals, and legal design aims to avoid outright confiscation while addressing sovereign immunity concerns.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on events occurring between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Resolve Yes if, by the deadline, the European Union formally adopts a legally binding act establishing a loan facility to Ukraine with a total authorized principal amount of at least €120,000,000,000, and the act or an official EU adoption communication explicitly states that immobilized Russian central bank assets (including cash at Euroclear) and/or the windfall profits/interest they generate are used to fund, guarantee, collateralize, or otherwise back the facility.

Acceptable evidence of adoption and explicit backing includes any of the following:
- Publication of the adopted act in the Official Journal (OJ L series) stating the amount and explicit backing (as defined above). OJ portal: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/oj/direct-access.html.
- An official Council of the European Union press release or register entry confirming adoption of the act and describing the amount and explicit backing. Council press releases: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/; Council register: https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/documents-publications/public-register/.
- If, exceptionally, publication lags but the Council or the European Commission issues an official communication clearly confirming adoption and the specified features, this is acceptable provided it unambiguously references the adopted act and its parameters. Commission press corner: https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/home.

Definitions applied in resolution:
- "Loan facility" means the specific instrument established by the adopted act; the "amount" is the maximum authorized principal for loans under that instrument.
- "Explicitly backed" requires textual reference in the act/official communication to immobilized/frozen assets of the Central Bank of Russia (e.g., assets at Euroclear) and/or their windfall profits/interest being used to fund, guarantee, collateralize, or otherwise back the facility. General references to "sanctions" without specifying the use of immobilized Russian central bank assets do not suffice.
- Multi-instrument packages: If several acts adopted together comprise a single facility documented as one package, sum the authorized principal amounts. However, amounts authorized in separate, unrelated acts are not combined.
- Interest terms: The facility may be interest-free or interest-bearing; interest terms do not affect resolution.

Resolve No if no such adoption satisfying all of the above occurs by the deadline.

Edge cases:
- Political agreements (e.g., European Council conclusions) without formal adoption do not count.
- Instruments using only general EU budget guarantees or other collateral, without explicit reference to immobilized Russian central bank assets or their windfall profits/interest, do not count.
- If the act is adopted but states an amount below €120bn, resolve No.

Rationale for the window and sources: As of late September 2025, the Commission’s paper was circulated to ambassadors and EU leaders planned to discuss the proposal at an early-October summit in Copenhagen, with proponents aiming for agreement by end-October, making the Oct–Dec window appropriate. Official EU publications (OJ, Council press) provide unambiguous resolution sources accessible by Dec 31, 2025.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025, will at least one U.S.-listed spot Solana (SOL) ETF/ETP begin trading?
background: Status quo as of Oct 1, 2025: On Sept 17–18, 2025, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved rule changes permitting three national securities exchanges to adopt generic listing standards for exchange-traded products (ETPs) that hold spot commodities, including digital assets. Under these generic standards, an exchange may list and trade eligible Commodity-Based Trust Shares that meet the requirements without first submitting a separate proposed rule change (a 19b‑4) to the SEC, thereby streamlining listings and reducing barriers to bringing spot digital-asset products to market. Commissioner Hester Peirce’s statement explains key eligibility paths: the commodity may trade on a market that is an Intermarket Surveillance Group (ISG) member, or underlie a futures contract trading at least six months on a CFTC‑regulated designated contract market, or already have an ETF that provides ≥40% NAV exposure listed on a national securities exchange; exchanges must also post specific information about eligible ETPs within five business days of trading commencement. Reuters reported that, following this decision, the first products expected to launch under the new rules include ETFs tied to Solana and XRP, potentially debuting as early as October 2025; the process reduces the maximum time from filing to launch to roughly 75 days (down from 240+ days under the prior regime). Definitions: An exchange‑traded fund (ETF) is an investment fund that trades on a stock exchange and is a type of exchange‑traded product. An exchange‑traded product (ETP) is a security that trades intraday on a national stock exchange; ETFs are one category of ETPs, alongside ETNs and exchange‑traded commodities/commodities trusts. The SEC’s press release and Commissioner statement clarify that "Commodity‑Based Trust Shares" under the approved generic standards include spot digital asset products (i.e., crypto asset commodities). Solana is a public blockchain platform; SOL is the native cryptocurrency of Solana, and "spot SOL" refers to the immediate (non‑derivative) market for the SOL token. Authoritative resolution sources will exist at decision time because exchanges are required to post information on listed ETPs within five business days of trading commencement , and exchanges like Cboe BZX publish Daily Listed Securities Reports enumerating issues listed on the exchange. Reuters has also been covering these developments and would report trading commencements when they occur. This setup yields a high‑entropy question: procedural hurdles have been reduced, but whether a specific SOL product lists and commences trading within the window remains uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Eligible events are those occurring between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. Outcome: Resolve Yes if at least one U.S.‑listed spot Solana ETF/ETP commences trading on a U.S. national securities exchange within the window. Otherwise resolve No.

Definitions and scope:
- U.S.‑listed: Listed and trading on one of the U.S. national securities exchanges covered by the SEC’s generic listing approvals—Nasdaq, NYSE Arca, or Cboe BZX.
- Spot Solana ETF/ETP: An exchange‑traded product (including but not limited to ETFs structured as commodity‑based trust shares) that seeks to provide exposure to the spot market price of SOL (the native token of the Solana blockchain) by holding SOL directly or via a commodity trust referencing spot SOL; products that derive exposure solely from futures, swaps, or other derivatives are excluded. For avoidance of doubt, "ETF/ETP" includes Commodity‑Based Trust Shares listed under an exchange’s generic listing standards for spot commodities/digital assets.
- Commences trading: The first on‑exchange execution of a trade in the security on its primary listing exchange (an opening auction execution qualifies). Evidence must include an official exchange source or issuer announcement, as specified below.

Qualifying evidence (any one suffices):
1) Official exchange listing/new‑issue/commencement notice naming the product and symbol with an effective/first‑trade date within the window (e.g., Nasdaq/NYSE Arca/Cboe BZX website notices; exchanges are required to post information within five business days of trading commencement).
2) Inclusion of the product in the exchange’s official listed‑securities or daily list report showing the product listed and trading (e.g., Cboe BZX Daily Listed Securities Report).
3) The exchange’s official quote/market activity page or time‑and‑sales showing an executed trade in the product within the window (exchange website).
4) Issuer’s press release or website announcement stating that trading commenced on Nasdaq, NYSE Arca, or Cboe BZX on a date/time within the window (issuer website), corroborated by at least one of 1–3 above.

Exclusions and edge cases:
- Products trading OTC, on alternative trading systems, or on non‑U.S. venues do not qualify.
- Derivatives on an ETF/ETP (e.g., options) do not qualify unless the underlying ETF/ETP itself has commenced trading within the window.
- If trading begins and is subsequently halted or suspended, the question resolves Yes as long as at least one on‑exchange execution occurred within the window.

Resolution procedure: On or after 2026‑01‑01 00:00 UTC, the resolver will check the exchanges’ official postings (per 1–3) and/or issuer announcements to determine whether a qualifying product commenced trading within the window. Primary sources include: SEC‑mandated exchange postings within five business days of trading commencement  and the Cboe BZX Daily Listed Securities Report for confirmation of listings. Context about the regulatory change enabling such listings is documented by the SEC press release and Reuters reporting.

question: Will the EU formally switch the renewal of Russia-related CFSP sanctions from unanimity to qualified majority voting (QMV) between 00:00 UTC on Oct 1, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context and current procedure as of Oct 1, 2025:
- What EU sanctions are: EU “restrictive measures” (sanctions) are adopted via a Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) Council decision, often paired with a Council regulation to implement economic/financial measures; the CFSP decision is adopted by the Council, and legal acts enter into force upon publication in the Official Journal.
- Voting rules in CFSP: By default, CFSP decisions are taken unanimously; constructive abstention is permitted. There are exceptions where the Council may act by QMV (e.g., implementing decisions), and the European Council may, by unanimity, decide to expand QMV use via the passerelle in Article 31(3) TEU.
- What QMV means in the Council: A qualified majority requires at least 55% of member states (currently 15 of 27) representing at least 65% of the EU population; a blocking minority requires at least four Council members.
- The Russia-related CFSP sanctions regimes most relevant to “renewal/prolongation”: The EU maintains (i) listings targeting persons/entities undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity (Council Decision 2014/145/CFSP), regularly prolonged by amending its expiry date (e.g., Decision (CFSP) 2025/528 set it to 15 Sep 2025) ; and (ii) sectoral/economic measures (Council Decision 2014/512/CFSP).
- Status quo renewals in 2025: The Council prolonged the individual listings to 15 March 2026 on 12 Sep 2025 ; in 2025 the Council also renewed other Russia-related measures on multiple dates (e.g., 14 Mar, 30 Jun).
- Reported proposed change: In late Sep 2025, multiple reports (citing an internal Commission note) stated the Commission suggested changing the sanctions renewal rule from unanimity to QMV to reduce the risk of vetoes when extending Russia packages. Earlier, on 13 Sep 2024, the Commission presented options to EU ambassadors to secure longer renewals tied to frozen Russian assets, including configurations involving QMV for unfreezing and longer renewal periods, reflecting institutional exploration of alternatives to frequent unanimous rollovers.

Why this is forecastable and non-trivial: Moving renewal/prolongation votes for Russia-related CFSP decisions from unanimity to QMV would require a formal and explicit legal change (e.g., a European Council decision under Article 31(3) TEU or a Council act that clearly places prolongations within a QMV-eligible category). Political signals suggest interest in such changes, but legal, political, and diplomatic hurdles make adoption before end-2025 uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
Definitions:
- “EU” refers to the institutions competent for CFSP decisions: the Council of the European Union and the European Council.
- “Russia-related CFSP sanctions” refers specifically to: (a) Council Decision 2014/145/CFSP concerning restrictive measures targeting persons/entities undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity ; and (b) Council Decision 2014/512/CFSP concerning sectoral restrictive measures related to Russia.
- “Renewal” or “prolongation” means the formal extension of the application period of an existing CFSP sanctions decision by amending its expiry clause (e.g., amending a provision to “apply until [date]”), as routinely done for 2014/145/CFSP and 2014/512/CFSP.
- “Unanimity” means all Member States voting in favour are required for adoption in the Council when unanimity applies.
- “Qualified majority voting (QMV)” means the Council’s double-majority rule: at least 55% of Member States representing at least 65% of the EU population; a blocking minority requires at least four Member States.
- “Passerelle” refers to the mechanism allowing the European Council, acting unanimously, to authorize the Council to act by QMV in CFSP cases beyond the default, per Article 31(3) TEU.

Question timeframe:
- Eligible actions must be adopted and published between 00:00 UTC on Oct 1, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025.

Resolution:
- YES if, within the timeframe, there is an EU legal act published in the Official Journal (OJ) that explicitly establishes that renewal/prolongation decisions for at least one of the two specified Russia-related CFSP decisions (2014/145/CFSP or 2014/512/CFSP) will henceforth be adopted by QMV rather than unanimity. Acceptable forms include:
  - A European Council decision under Article 31(3) TEU stating the Council shall act by QMV for renewal/prolongation of these CFSP sanctions ; or
  - A Council decision/legal act that explicitly defines the voting rule for prolongations of these CFSP decisions as QMV (e.g., by citing Article 31(2) TEU where applicable and clearly stating that the Council “shall act by qualified majority” for such prolongations).
- For YES, the act must be adopted and published in OJ during the timeframe and must clearly reference the voting rule change (e.g., the legal basis or explicit wording). Press releases may be used for guidance, but the final determination relies on the text published in the OJ.
- NO otherwise (including if: no such act is adopted; the act is adopted but not published in OJ by the deadline; or the act concerns only non-renewal matters and does not explicitly change the voting rule for prolongations of the specified CFSP decisions).

Verification notes for resolvers:
- Check EUR-Lex for OJ publications of: (i) any European Council decision invoking Article 31(3) TEU to authorize QMV for CFSP renewal decisions ; (ii) amendments to Council Decision 2014/145/CFSP or 2014/512/CFSP whose recitals/articles explicitly define QMV for their prolongations ; and (iii) Consilium policy pages and press releases for cross-reference on renewals.

question: By December 31, 2025 (UTC), will the United States enact a continuing appropriations law whose stated expiration date extends any covered federal appropriations beyond January 31, 2026 (UTC)?
background: Context as of 2025-09-30: When the 12 regular annual appropriations acts are not enacted by the start of the fiscal year (October 1), Congress often enacts a continuing appropriations act (commonly called a continuing resolution or CR) to temporarily fund covered programs and activities until action on the regular appropriations is completed. CRs have explicit duration language: budget authority provided by a CR ends on the specific expiration date stated in the law, or upon enactment of the applicable regular appropriations act, whichever occurs first. CRs can be interim (days/weeks/months) or full-year (through September 30). As of September 19, 2025, the U.S. Senate rejected a House-passed CR that would have funded the government through November 21, 2025, by a 44–48 vote, leaving funding unresolved ahead of the October 1 deadline. Definitions and process: A continuing appropriations act (continuing resolution, CR) is typically a joint resolution (though continuing appropriations can also be provided via a bill) enacted to provide temporary funding to continue certain programs and activities when regular appropriations are not yet in place. The regular appropriations process comprises 12 annual measures developed by corresponding House and Senate Appropriations subcommittees; these bills provide most federal funding for the fiscal year. For purposes of determining the duration of a CR, the relevant “expiration date” is specified in the text of the CR itself (often in a section akin to Sec. 106), and marks when the continuing funding authority lapses absent enactment of the applicable regular appropriations for the covered activities. Why this matters: End-of-year funding dynamics often involve short extensions that may or may not cross into February; a full-year CR (covering the remainder of FY2026 through September 30, 2026) is possible but uncertain. This question targets a threshold (post–January 31, 2026) designed to create genuine forecasting uncertainty around whether any enacted CR by year-end 2025 will extend temporary funding into February 2026 or later. Useful references and definitions for forecasters: - Continuing resolution (CR): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuing_resolution - Appropriations bill (regular appropriations): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appropriations_bill_(United_States) - Congress.gov index for enacted public laws: https://www.congress.gov/public-laws (we will use the public law text pages to verify CR enactments and expiration language).
resolution_criteria: Event window: Only laws enacted between October 1, 2025 at 00:00:00 UTC and December 31, 2025 at 23:59:59 UTC are eligible. Definitions (authorities in brackets): - Continuing appropriations act / continuing resolution (CR): A law enacted to provide temporary funding to continue certain programs and activities when regular appropriations acts are not yet enacted. CRs commonly take the form of joint resolutions but can also be bills. - Regular appropriations acts: The 12 annual appropriations measures that fund most federal agencies for the fiscal year, developed by the House and Senate Appropriations Committees and their 12 subcommittees. - Funding expiration date of a CR: The date specified in the CR text when budget authority provided by the CR lapses, unless earlier terminated upon enactment of applicable regular appropriations for the covered activities. Resolution question: By the end of the event window, has a CR been enacted whose own stated expiration date is later than January 31, 2026 (UTC) for at least one covered project or activity? Operationalization: - The forecaster (or resolver) will identify all public laws enacted during the event window that include continuing appropriations provisions (i.e., are continuing appropriations acts/CRs). - For each such law, examine the statutory text (as posted on Congress.gov) to find the section that sets the availability of appropriations under the act (e.g., a section similar to Sec. 106 in past CRs) and read the explicit expiration date or dates. - Resolves Yes if at least one CR enacted during the event window states an expiration date after January 31, 2026 (UTC) for any covered project or activity (including if the CR is full-year through September 30, 2026). - Resolves No if no CR enacted during the event window states any expiration date after January 31, 2026 (UTC).
