Notes and edge cases: - Regular appropriations acts enacted during the window do not count toward resolution unless the law also contains continuing appropriations provisions; only the continuing appropriations provisions’ expiration date(s) are relevant. - If a CR contains different expiration dates for specific agencies or programs, any one date later than January 31, 2026 (UTC) triggers a Yes. - If a CR’s availability terminates upon enactment of a regular appropriations act before its stated expiration date, that does not affect this question’s resolution; the criterion is whether the CR’s stated expiration date is after January 31, 2026 (UTC), regardless of earlier termination conditions. Source of truth on enactments and expiration dates: Congress.gov public law text pages for any continuing appropriations acts enacted during the event window (see https://www.congress.gov/public-laws for indexing). We rely on CRS definitions of CRs, regular appropriations, and duration/expiration to operationalize terms. Status quo examples for context (not part of resolution): The Senate rejected a House-passed CR through November 21, 2025 on September 19, 2025 (44–48), illustrating current funding uncertainty.

question: Will the National Assembly of Armenia include an item on expressing non-confidence in Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan on the agenda of a sitting between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of September 30, 2025:
- On September 26, 2025, the National Assembly’s With Honor (Pativ Unem) faction convened parliamentary hearings on a draft statement titled “National Crisis and Governance Failure,” discussing practical steps toward an “impeachment process,” a term used colloquially by participants for the constitutional procedure of expressing non-confidence in the Prime Minister. The faction stated they would bring the process to parliament once 54 signatures are secured, and the Armenia (Hayastan) faction indicated support at committee and plenary stages.
- Around those hearings, reporting indicated that 34 lawmakers from the opposition Hayastan (28) and With Honor (6) factions had backed the initiative to seek non-confidence, with at least 36 deputies required to propose such a decision and 54 votes needed for it to pass.
- Under Armenia’s Constitution (Article 115), the National Assembly may express non-confidence in the Prime Minister via a draft decision presented by at least one-third of the total number of deputies, concurrently proposing a new Prime Minister candidate; the decision is adopted by the majority of the total number of deputies, with timing and restriction clauses (e.g., debate 48–72 hours after submission; not during martial law/state of emergency; six-month interval if a previous attempt fails). The National Assembly’s Rules of Procedure designate the issue of expressing non-confidence in the Prime Minister as an item subject to mandatory consideration that is included in the draft agenda of regular sessions/sittings.

Why this formulation:
- In Armenia’s parliamentary system, the legally precise mechanism is a motion to express non-confidence in the Prime Minister, not “impeachment.” Using agenda inclusion of this specific item on the National Assembly’s official website as the pars pro toto indicator makes the event unambiguous and verifiable.
- As of September 30, 2025, opposition coordination and signature counts suggest genuine uncertainty about reaching the procedural threshold to trigger formal consideration, making the question non-trivial.

Definitions and references:
- Prime Minister of Armenia: see Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Armenia) for role definition.
- National Assembly of Armenia: see Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(Armenia)).
- “Expressing non-confidence in the Prime Minister”: the constitutional procedure defined in Article 115 of the Constitution of the Republic of Armenia; key elements include submission by at least one-third of deputies, concurrent nomination of a new PM candidate, and adoption by a majority of the total number of deputies.
- “Included on the agenda of a sitting”: the issue “Expressing non-confidence in the Prime Minister” appears in the published draft agenda (regular or special sitting) on the National Assembly’s official website (http://www.parliament.am). The Rules of Procedure identify this as an issue subject to mandatory consideration and inclusion in the draft agenda.
resolution_criteria:
- Time window: Eligible events must occur between 00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2025.
- What counts as a Yes:
  1) The National Assembly of the Republic of Armenia (NA) publishes, on its official website (http://www.parliament.am), a draft agenda of a sitting (regular or special) that includes an item explicitly titled or described as “Expressing non-confidence in the Prime Minister,” consistent with the constitutional procedure in Article 115.
  2) The agenda inclusion must be for a sitting scheduled within the time window or published within it; either suffices for “included on the agenda.”
- Evidence standard: The primary resolution source will be the NA’s official website. Acceptable evidence includes:
  • A published draft agenda page listing the item.
  • An official NA news post stating that the item has been included in the agenda of a sitting (for example, the NA’s news category pages like those used to announce hearings and agenda items).
- What does NOT count:
  • Media reports without corroboration on the NA’s official website.
  • Committee-level discussions, hearings, or press conferences that do not result in agenda inclusion.
  • A draft decision submitted but not yet included in the NA sitting agenda.
- Resolve Yes if such agenda inclusion is present within the time window; resolve No otherwise.
- If the NA website is temporarily inaccessible at resolution time, the arbiter may use a cached official page (e.g., web.archive.org copy of a parliament.am page) or an NA-posted PDF of the agenda hosted on the same domain. Secondary sources (e.g., Reuters, AP) should be used only to find the relevant official NA page and not as sole evidence.

Notes on thresholds and process (for forecasters’ reference):
- Submission threshold: at least one-third of deputies must present the draft decision and concurrently nominate a PM candidate.
- Agenda inclusion: the issue is subject to mandatory consideration and is included in the draft agenda for regular sessions/sittings.
- Reported status quo as of late September 2025: opposition hearings were convened; 34 lawmakers were said to back the initiative; thresholds cited were 36 signatures to propose and 54 votes to pass.

question: By 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, will ByteDance’s ownership in the U.S.-based TikTok joint venture be publicly confirmed as strictly below 20.0%?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30: On September 25, 2025, the White House announced a framework for a “qualified divestiture” of TikTok’s U.S. application into a new U.S.-based joint venture that would be majority-owned and controlled by U.S. persons, with ByteDance Ltd. and affiliates to own less than 20% and to have limited governance rights. The announcement directed the Attorney General not to enforce the Act for 120 days to allow completion of the divestiture. The Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (the “Act”) was enacted in April 2024 and defines the contours of a “qualified divestiture,” including eliminating foreign adversary control and precluding operational relationships such as algorithm cooperation or data-sharing with foreign-adversary controlled entities. The statutory scheme also uses a 20% ownership threshold as part of how “control by a foreign adversary” can be assessed in certain contexts. Major media reports following the September 25, 2025 announcement echoed that ByteDance’s ownership in the new entity would be below 20%.

Why this is forecastable now: As of today, public statements describe intended ownership and governance, but they do not necessarily constitute post-close confirmation of the actual equity cap table. Whether a clear, public confirmation of ByteDance’s resulting equity percentage in the U.S. TikTok joint venture will be published by year-end remains uncertain, and it may depend on deal timing and the specificity of company or investor disclosures.

Pointers to key documents and concepts: The White House Fact Sheet and Presidential Action provide the authoritative description of the qualified divestiture plan as announced on September 25, 2025. The Act’s text defines “qualified divestiture” and the broader criteria for removing foreign adversary control. The Act was signed in April 2024.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and time zone: The question considers eligible public confirmations made between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Question to resolve: Resolve “Yes” if, within the resolution window, there is a public disclosure that explicitly confirms that ByteDance Ltd. (including relevant affiliates, as defined below) owns strictly less than 20.0% of the equity of the U.S.-based TikTok joint venture described in the September 25, 2025 Presidential Action; otherwise resolve “No.” “Strictly less than 20.0%” means <20.000% (e.g., 19.999% qualifies; 20.000% does not).

What counts as the “U.S.-based TikTok joint venture” (JV): The U.S.-incorporated entity formed to operate TikTok’s U.S. application pursuant to the “qualified divestiture” framework described by the White House on September 25, 2025 (Fact Sheet and Presidential Action). If the entity is renamed or restructured but clearly identified as the vehicle that operates the U.S. TikTok application under that framework, it qualifies.

What counts as “ByteDance’s ownership”: The aggregate equity ownership percentage held, directly or indirectly, by ByteDance Ltd. and its affiliates, where “affiliate” means any entity controlling, controlled by, or under common control with ByteDance Ltd. (consistent with standard corporate usage). If a qualifying disclosure explicitly states the percentage “owned by ByteDance and its affiliates,” that figure will be used. If a disclosure provides separate subtotals for ByteDance and its affiliates, the sum will be used. If only ByteDance Ltd.’s stake is reported without affiliates, and no affiliate stakes are disclosed, the reported figure will be used.

What counts as a qualifying public disclosure (in order of precedence if multiple conflict):
1) A U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing on EDGAR (e.g., Form 8-K, 10-K, S-1, proxy statement, or an exhibit thereto) by the JV or by any publicly traded U.S. investor/parent that directly discloses the JV ownership table or ByteDance’s exact or bounded percentage in the JV as of or after the closing of the divestiture.
2) An official company communication posted on an official website or press wire (press release, investor presentation, FAQs, or blog post) by any of: the JV; TikTok (U.S. entity); ByteDance; or a publicly traded U.S. investor named as an owner in the JV, that explicitly states ByteDance’s percentage (either a specific number <20.0% or wording such as “less than 20%”) as of or after closing.
3) A U.S. Government document or statement (e.g., a White House Fact Sheet, Presidential Action, or DOJ/CFTC/CFIUS-related public notice) that explicitly states ByteDance’s percentage ownership as of or after closing. Statements describing intended future ownership (e.g., “will be less than 20%”) do NOT qualify; the disclosure must describe current or closing ownership.
4) Coverage by a major, reputable outlet (e.g., AP, Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, NYT, FT, CNBC, NBC) that directly quotes or links to one of the qualifying disclosures above. Media reports based solely on anonymous sources or without direct linkage do NOT qualify.

Key wording requirement: The disclosure must use unambiguous language confirming that ByteDance’s stake is strictly less than 20.0% (e.g., “ByteDance owns 18%,” or “ByteDance and its affiliates hold less than 20%”). If a disclosure reports an exact number, that number must be <20.0%. If it uses an inequality, it must explicitly say “less than 20%,” “below 20%,” or equivalent clear phrasing. Terms like “minority,” “small,” or “limited” ownership without a numeric or explicit “<20%” do not qualify.

Closing vs. intent: To count, the disclosure must pertain to ownership at closing or currently, not merely an agreement in principle or proposed terms. Statements in the September 25, 2025 White House documents that describe intended ownership (e.g., “will hold less than 20%”) are not sufficient for resolution.

Handling multiple or conflicting disclosures: If multiple qualifying disclosures differ, use the most recent disclosure within the window from the highest-precedence source category above. If, after applying precedence and recency, ambiguity remains (e.g., differing basis of calculation), resolve “No.”

Definitions and helpful references:
- ByteDance Ltd.: the China-based parent of TikTok (see corporate background pages such as Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ByteDance).
- Equity ownership: percentage interest in the JV’s equity securities. If a disclosure specifies the basis (e.g., “fully diluted, as-converted”), use that basis; otherwise, interpret the percentage as stated in the disclosure (general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_(finance)).
- Qualified divestiture: as defined in the Act and described in the statute.

Automatic “No” conditions:

- The divestiture has not closed by the end of the window, or only prospective (“will be”) statements are available.

Primary context sources for forecasters:

question: Will BIS add at least one NORINCO‑affiliated entity to the Entity List between October 15 and December 31, 2025?
background:
Context and definitions a forecaster needs to know, with sources:
- What is the Entity List? The U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) maintains the Entity List in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations as Supplement No. 4 to 15 CFR Part 744. Additions, removals, and modifications are effected via rules published in the Federal Register. BIS describes the Entity List as identifying persons for whom there is reasonable cause to believe they are, or pose a significant risk of becoming, involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests; listed parties face license requirements and a general presumption of denial for items subject to the EAR.
- Recent cadence/context: On September 16, 2025 (effective September 12, 2025), BIS published “Additions and Revisions to the Entity List,” adding 32 entities across multiple countries for reasons including support to China’s military modernization, advanced computing/IC supply chains, and diversion to Russia/Iran, among others.
- Affiliates policy change (contextual): On September 29, 2025, BIS issued an interim final rule expanding end‑user controls to cover affiliates (a 50 percent ownership rule) of certain listed entities, with immediate effect and a comment period, aiming to close diversion/circumvention loopholes; BIS also highlighted this expansion in a same‑day announcement. This change automatically subjects qualifying affiliates to the same restrictions, separate from whether those affiliates are individually named on the Entity List. Note: This question resolves only on whether BIS adds at least one qualifying entity by name via a Federal Register rule in the specified window (see Resolution criteria), not whether entities become covered automatically under the affiliates rule.
- Who/what is NORINCO? “NORINCO” refers to the Chinese state‑owned defense conglomerate China North Industries Group Corporation Limited (also known as Norinco Group; within China also referred to as China Ordnance Industries Group Corporation Limited) and its marketing arm China North Industries Corporation, commonly branded as “NORINCO”.

Why this is non‑trivial now: BIS’s active 2025 enforcement cadence (e.g., the 32 additions on Sept 16, 2025) and the late‑September affiliates IFR underscore heightened focus on China‑related defense/dual‑use supply chains and diversion risks, making a targeted end‑of‑year addition of a NORINCO‑related entity plausible but uncertain.

Primary source(s) to check at resolution time:
- Federal Register: BIS rules amending Supplement No. 4 to Part 744 (Entity List).
- BIS Federal Register notices landing page for convenience (links through to Federal Register content).
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution (Yes/No), based on Federal Register publication dates.

Question: Will BIS add at least one NORINCO‑affiliated entity to the Entity List between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (inclusive), as evidenced by a Federal Register rule published in that date window?

Operational definitions and rules:
1) Time window and source of truth
- The only source of truth for additions is the Federal Register publication of a BIS rule that amends Supplement No. 4 to Part 744 (the Entity List). The window is defined by the Federal Register “Publication Date,” which must be between 2025‑10‑15 and 2025‑12‑31 inclusive. Public Inspection postings do not count unless and until the rule is published in the Federal Register within the window.

2) What counts as “added to the Entity List”
- The rule must add at least one new entry (i.e., a distinct entity line) to Supplement No. 4 to Part 744. Revisions that solely modify license text, addresses, or license review policies for already‑listed entries do not count. De‑listings are irrelevant to resolution.

3) What counts as “NORINCO‑affiliated entity” for this market question
A new entry qualifies if at least one of the following is true based solely on the text of the Federal Register rule:
   a) The entity’s English‑language name, as listed in the heading of the new entry or in its “a.k.a.”/aliases, includes the case‑insensitive substring “NORINCO”. Examples that would qualify if added: “NORINCO International Cooperation Ltd.” or “China North Industries Corporation (NORINCO)”.
   b) The rule explicitly identifies the added entity as a subsidiary, alias, or “a.k.a.” of any of the following: “China North Industries Group Corporation Limited,” “China North Industries Corporation,” “Norinco Group,” or otherwise explicitly ties it to NORINCO by name in the entry text (e.g., in the heading or alias lines).
Notes: For the purpose of this question, determinations based on external corporate records or general knowledge do not count; the affiliation must be explicit in the Federal Register text. Automatic coverage via the September 29, 2025 affiliates interim final rule (i.e., 50%‑owned entities becoming restricted without being individually named) does not count unless the affiliate is itself newly added by name to the Entity List via a rule published within the window.

4) Lists that do not count
- Actions concerning the Unverified List, the Military End‑User List, or other lists are out of scope; only additions to the Entity List (Supplement No. 4 to Part 744) are considered.

5) How to verify
- Search FederalRegister.gov for BIS rules amending “Supplement No. 4 to part 744—Entity List” with Publication Dates between 2025‑10‑15 and 2025‑12‑31. Open each rule and check the entries added to confirm whether any new entity meets 3(a) or 3(b). The eCFR is not the timeliest source, so use the Federal Register as the primary reference.

Resolution:
- YES if at least one qualifying entity is added within the window per 1) and 2) and meets 3).
- NO otherwise.

Citations: Entity List structure and update mechanism ; BIS’s description/purpose of the Entity List ; Sept 16, 2025 additions context ; Sept 29, 2025 affiliates IFR and announcement context ; NORINCO naming/definitions.

question: Will UK Export Finance announce at least one specific financing commitment for an Australian critical minerals project between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- UK Export Finance (UKEF) has launched a Critical Minerals Supply Finance offering that provides a guarantee to a bank making a loan to an overseas project which has an offtake agreement in place with a UK exporter, covering projects including mining, processing, manufacturing and recycling of critical minerals products.
- The UK Government announced that UKEF can provide financial support for overseas projects that source critical minerals for use in major UK industries. The announcement explicitly referenced suppliers in countries with vast mineral deposits, including Australia.
- In the Australia–UK Ministerial Consultations (AUKMIN) joint statement of July 2025, ministers highlighted cooperation on resilient critical minerals supply chains and stated: “UKEF has up to £5bn in finance support available for projects in Australia and will work closely with Export Finance Australia”.
- Export Finance Australia (EFA) and UKEF signed an MoU to deepen cooperation, citing shared interests such as critical minerals and the potential for joint financings; EFA’s newsroom is the publication venue for such MoUs on the Australian side.
- UKEF’s product set commonly operates via guarantees to lenders (e.g., Buyer Credit facilities), and UKEF maintains a glossary where “Commitment” is defined as a case where UKEF has agreed the terms of its support and provided its commitment to the bank/exporter, even if a guarantee has not yet been issued.
- Official UKEF announcements (news and press releases) are published on GOV.UK under the UK Export Finance organisation page, which aggregates “News and communications” for UKEF.

Key definitions and lists relevant to this market:
- Critical minerals (Australia): The Australian Government maintains Australia’s Critical Minerals List and Strategic Materials List, which identify minerals important to modern technologies, economies, and national security. These lists are published and updated by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources.
- UKEF Critical Minerals Supply Finance: A UKEF product that provides a guarantee to a bank lending to an overseas project with a qualifying offtake agreement with a UK exporter for critical minerals products.
- UKEF “Commitment”: Per UKEF’s glossary, a case not yet the subject of an issued guarantee, but for which UKEF has agreed the terms of its support and provided its commitment to the bank/exporter (i.e., UKEF has agreed to accept the risk).

Why this is interesting/uncertain: The AUKMIN statement and subsequent policy communications create a clear pipeline and political impetus (including up to £5bn of finance support available for projects in Australia and collaboration with EFA), yet the timing and specifics of first Australian project-level commitments are uncertain. Forecasters must assess feasibility of eligible Australian project pipelines, offtake linkages with UK exporters, due diligence timelines, and deal execution/announcement practices at UKEF.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will UKEF announce at least one specific financing commitment for an Australian critical minerals project between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31?

Definitions (must be used for resolution):
- Announcement: A publication on the GOV.UK domain attributed to UK Export Finance (UKEF) in its “News and communications” feed (press release, news story, or ministerial statement) that is publicly accessible and dated. The authoritative location is the UKEF organisation page on GOV.UK aggregating UKEF “News and communications”. For timing, the item’s “Published” date is used. If only a date (no time) is shown, it is treated as 00:00 UTC on that date for the purpose of this market.
- Australian critical minerals project: A named project physically located in Australia (within the sovereign territory of the Commonwealth of Australia) that involves extraction, processing, refining, manufacturing, or recycling of a mineral included on Australia’s Critical Minerals List or Strategic Materials List as maintained by the Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources at the time of the announcement. Examples include projects focused on lithium, nickel, cobalt, rare earths, etc., where applicable per the list.
- Financing commitment (UKEF): Either of the following qualifies:
  (a) Issuance of a UKEF guarantee or insurance covering finance for the project (e.g., buyer credit, loan guarantee), as explicitly stated in the announcement ; or
  (b) A UKEF “Commitment” as defined in UKEF’s glossary—i.e., UKEF has agreed the terms of its support and provided its commitment to the bank/exporter, even if a guarantee has not yet been issued—explicitly stated in the announcement.
- Specific: The announcement must identify the project by name and/or sponsor and state that UKEF is supporting that project, not merely referencing a general policy, MoU, or sector-wide initiative.

Inclusion criteria (all must be met):
1) The announcement is published between 00:00:00 UTC on 2025-10-15 and 23:59:59 UTC on 2025-12-31 (based on the “Published” date shown on the GOV.UK item). Updates to items first published before the window do not qualify.
2) It names a specific project located in Australia that is in the critical minerals domain as defined above.
3) It explicitly states that UKEF has either issued a guarantee/insurance or has provided a “Commitment” (as per UKEF’s definition) to support financing for that project.
4) It provides at least one of the following additional specificity indicators: (i) a financing amount or UKEF maximum liability; or (ii) the UKEF product used (e.g., Critical Minerals Supply Finance).

Exclusions:
- General policy statements, product launches, MoUs, roadmaps, or cooperation announcements without a named project and explicit UKEF guarantee/commitment do not count.
- Announcements concerning projects outside Australia do not count.
- Media coverage not published on GOV.UK does not count for resolution (though it may be used by forecasters for research). Only the GOV.UK UKEF “News and communications” publication qualifies as the resolution source.

Primary resolution source and where to look:
- GOV.UK “News and communications” for UK Export Finance: https://www.gov.uk/search/news-and-communications?organisations[]=uk-export-finance&parent=uk-export-finance.

Relevant policy and product context (for forecasters; not required for resolution):
- UKEF can support overseas critical minerals projects supplying UK industry, including potential suppliers in Australia.
- AUKMIN 2025 noted UKEF’s up to £5bn in finance support available for projects in Australia and cooperation with Export Finance Australia.
- UKEF’s Critical Minerals Supply Finance describes the targeted guarantee offer for overseas critical minerals projects with UK offtake; announcements may cite this product when relevant.

question: Will OPEC crude oil production in November 2025 be at least 1.0 million barrels per day higher than its January–March 2025 average?
background:
Context: In 2023–2025, OPEC and partners (“OPEC+”) implemented and began unwinding voluntary production cuts. Cohesion, compliance, and spare capacity have driven uncertainty about how much output will actually rise in 2025. To ensure clear, timely resolution by December 31, 2025, this question focuses on OPEC (member countries only) crude oil production, using OPEC’s own Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) “secondary sources” table, which is a widely referenced benchmark and typically publishes November data in the December report.
Scope and definitions:
- OPEC: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries; member list and publications at https://www.opec.org/.
- Crude oil production: As reported in the OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) “OPEC crude oil production (secondary sources)” tables. For this metric, OPEC’s crude oil production excludes condensates and natural gas liquids (NGLs).
- Barrel (bbl): Standard oil barrel of 42 US gallons; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrel_(oil).
- Million barrels per day (mb/d): 1.0 mb/d = 1,000,000 barrels per day.
- Month and averaging: Monthly averages as shown in MOMR. Baseline is the simple arithmetic average of the total OPEC crude production for January 2025, February 2025, and March 2025, using values reported together in the December 2025 MOMR for consistency.
- Timeframe: Baseline months are January–March 2025 (inclusive). Measurement month is November 2025 (November 1–30, 2025, UTC). The question considers developments between 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, but only the specified production months are used for resolution.
Status quo: OPEC+ had begun unwinding parts of earlier cuts during 2025, with uneven member-level execution and varying capacity. This creates genuine uncertainty over whether OPEC’s aggregate crude production increase by late 2025 will exceed 1.0 mb/d versus early-2025 levels.
Data availability: The OPEC MOMR is published monthly; the December 2025 edition is expected to include November 2025 production. See https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html and the OPEC digital publications portal (https://publications.opec.org/momr).
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves using the OPEC December 2025 Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) “OPEC crude oil production (secondary sources)” totals.
- Compute the baseline: Take the total OPEC crude oil production values for January 2025, February 2025, and March 2025 as presented (together) in the December 2025 MOMR and calculate their simple average.
- Compute the measured value: Take the total OPEC crude oil production for November 2025 from the same December 2025 MOMR.
- Resolution: If (November 2025 total) − (Jan–Mar 2025 average) ≥ 1.000 mb/d, resolve YES; otherwise resolve NO.
- Precision and rounding: Use the values as published in the December 2025 MOMR. Do the arithmetic with the unrounded numerical values if available; if only rounded values are available (e.g., to two or three decimal places in mb/d), use those as given. No seasonal adjustments.
- Source and fallback: Primary source is the OPEC December 2025 MOMR accessible via https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html or https://publications.opec.org/momr. If, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the December 2025 MOMR is not publicly available, resolve using credible reporting that reproduces the same MOMR figures (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) and clearly cites the OPEC December 2025 MOMR. If multiple credible reports disagree, prefer OPEC’s publication if it becomes available by the deadline; otherwise, prefer reports that quote exact table figures from the MOMR and provide verifiable excerpts.

question: Will NPCI report at least 21.5 billion UPI transactions in November 2025?
background:
Context and data source:
- Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is India’s instant interbank payment system developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), enabling peer‑to‑peer (P2P) and person‑to‑merchant (P2M) transfers via mobile devices. NPCI is the umbrella organization for retail payments systems in India and operates UPI.
- NPCI publishes official monthly UPI data on its Unified Payments Interface (UPI) Product Statistics page. In that table, the number of transactions is labeled “Volume (in Mn)” and the total transacted amount is labeled “Value (in Cr.)”. The page notes that, from August 2018 onward, transactions having debit/credit to the same account are excluded from UPI counts.
- As of the latest data visible on that page (accessed for this question’s setup), the table shows July 2025 Volume = 19,467.95 million and August 2025 Volume = 20,008.31 million; corresponding Value figures are 25,08,498.09 crore and 24,85,472.91 crore respectively. These imply an increase of roughly 540.36 million transactions (about 2.8%) from July to August 2025, based on the figures cited.
- Units and terms used by NPCI: “Mn” denotes millions (10^6). “Cr.” denotes crores, where one crore equals ten million (10,000,000) Indian rupees. In this question, “billion” refers to the short‑scale billion, i.e., 1,000,000,000 (10^9).
- NPCI also provides an official UPI Daily Statistics page with columns “Approved Count (In million)” and “Amount (Rs. In Crores),” which can be used to aggregate daily values if needed.

Why this is forecastable now:
- The November 2025 UPI monthly total will only be known after the month ends and NPCI publishes the figure. As of today, the November 2025 value has not yet been published, and recent monthly volumes around 20 billion make a threshold of 21.5 billion plausible yet uncertain, creating a balanced forecasting task.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome definition (Yes/No):
- Resolve YES if, by 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, the NPCI UPI Product Statistics page displays “Volume (in Mn)” for Nov‑25 that is greater than or equal to 21,500.00. Otherwise resolve NO.

Primary resolution source (authoritative):
- NPCI Unified Payments Interface (UPI) Product Statistics page: https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/product-statistics. Use the figure exactly as displayed in the “Volume (in Mn)” column for the row labeled Nov‑25. Note: Per NPCI’s own notes on that page, UPI counts exclude transactions where debit and credit are to the same account from August 2018 onward; no adjustments should be made beyond using the figure as shown.

Fallback if the primary source is inaccessible or Nov‑25 is not yet displayed by the deadline:
- Use NPCI’s official UPI Daily Statistics page: https://www.npci.org.in/what-we-do/upi/upi-daily-statistics. Sum the “Approved Count (In million)” for all calendar dates from 2025‑11‑01 00:00:00 to 2025‑11‑30 23:59:59 in Indian Standard Time (IST; UTC+05:30). Round the final sum to two decimals using round‑half‑up and compare to 21,500.00. If the rounded sum is ≥ 21,500.00, resolve YES; otherwise NO.

Precedence and discrepancies:
- If both sources are available and disagree, the UPI Product Statistics page (monthly table) takes precedence.

Evidence capture and timing:
- The resolver will capture a timestamped snapshot (screenshot or PDF) of the relevant NPCI page(s) on or before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC. Only information published on NPCI’s official website(s) as cited above will be used to resolve this question.

Definitions and links for clarity:
- UPI: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Payments_Interface 
- NPCI: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Payments_Corporation_of_India 
- Crore: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crore 
- Billion (short scale): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billion 
- IST (UTC+05:30): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Standard_Time

question: Will CMS’s CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule set an aggregate Medicare payment increase of at least 2.0% for dialysis facilities?
background:
What is being forecast: Whether the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) will finalize an aggregate increase in total Medicare payments to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) dialysis facilities of at least 2.0% for Calendar Year (CY) 2026, relative to CY 2025, as measured by CMS’s own “overall impact” (aggregate percent change in total payments) for all ESRD facilities in the CY 2026 ESRD Prospective Payment System (PPS) final rule.

Context: CMS annually updates payment policies and rates for outpatient dialysis services under the ESRD PPS via notice-and-comment rulemaking (a mid-year proposed rule followed by a late-year final rule). Dialysis providers’ revenues are materially influenced by Medicare reimbursement policy. The final rule typically includes an “impact analysis” estimating the percentage change in total Medicare payments to ESRD facilities under finalized policies compared with the prior year baseline. This figure incorporates market basket updates, statutory adjustments, budget-neutrality factors, and policy changes, and it can differ from the change in the ESRD PPS base rate.

Definitions and references for forecasters:
- CMS: the US federal agency administering Medicare and Medicaid. https://www.cms.gov/
- ESRD (End-Stage Renal Disease): the final stage of chronic kidney disease; patients often require dialysis. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End-stage_kidney_disease
- Dialysis facility / ESRD facility: a Medicare-certified provider/supplier furnishing outpatient maintenance dialysis services under the ESRD PPS. See CMS ESRD PPS overview: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/prospective-payment-systems/end-stage-renal-disease-esrd
- ESRD PPS: the Medicare prospective payment system that bundles payment for renal dialysis services furnished to ESRD beneficiaries. CMS overview page above.

Status as of today (2025-09-22): CMS customarily issues the ESRD PPS final rule in Q4 for the upcoming calendar year, and it includes an explicit estimate of the aggregate “overall impact” on total payments to ESRD facilities versus the prior year. Forecasters should monitor the Federal Register publication of the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule and the accompanying CMS fact sheet for the precise aggregate percentage.

Where the resolving data will appear: The CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule will be published in the Federal Register (and summarized on CMS’s site). CMS also typically posts a Newsroom fact sheet summarizing the finalized percentage change in total payments and the finalized base rate. The CMS ESRD Payment Regulations and Notices page lists proposed and final rules: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/prospective-payment-systems/end-stage-renal-disease-esrd/esrd-payment-regulations-and-notices
resolution_criteria:
Time window: From 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Yes-resolution: Resolve Yes if, by the deadline, an official CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule (including any official corrections or correcting amendments published before the deadline) states that the aggregate percent change in total Medicare payments to ESRD facilities (the “overall impact” or equivalent descriptor, covering all ESRD facilities in aggregate, both freestanding and hospital-based) for CY 2026 relative to CY 2025 is greater than or equal to 2.00%.

No-resolution: Resolve No if, by the deadline, (a) the finalized aggregate percent change is below 2.00%, or (b) no CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule (or official display copy/correction) establishing such an aggregate percentage has been issued by CMS or published in the Federal Register.

Primary resolution source and hierarchy:
1) Federal Register publication of the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule (controls in case of conflict with other sources). https://www.federalregister.gov/
2) CMS Newsroom fact sheet for the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule (used if it explicitly states the aggregate percent change and the Federal Register final rule is not yet available by the deadline). https://www.cms.gov/newsroom
3) CMS ESRD Payment Regulations and Notices page listing the CY 2026 ESRD PPS final rule (used for confirmation and document access). https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/prospective-payment-systems/end-stage-renal-disease-esrd/esrd-payment-regulations-and-notices

Measurement details and tie-breakers:
- Metric: Use the single aggregate percentage change CMS provides for “total (aggregate) payments to all ESRD facilities” under finalized CY 2026 policies versus CY 2025 baseline, as presented in the final rule’s impact analysis or the official CMS fact sheet. Do not use the base rate change or facility-specific subgroup impacts.
- Precision: Compare the exact numeric value as printed by CMS. If presented to one decimal place, compare that figure as printed. If presented to two or more decimals, compare the printed figure without re-rounding. “At least 2.0%” means ≥ 2.00%.
- Multiple values: If both a narrative and a table present values, use the table titled “Impact on total payments” (or closest equivalent) covering all ESRD facilities. If CMS provides only separate facility-type impacts without an “all facilities” line, calculate a weighted aggregate only if CMS provides an explicit all-facilities aggregate elsewhere; otherwise, defer to the single aggregate figure CMS labels for all ESRD facilities.
- Corrections: If CMS issues an official correction or correcting amendment before the deadline that revises the aggregate percentage, use the latest such document available before the deadline.
- Timezone: All timing references are in UTC.
- Exclusions: Any third-party analyses, media summaries, or stakeholder estimates do not count for resolution unless they are quoting the official CMS documents above.

question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, will crude oil flows via the Druzhba pipeline to Hungary or Slovakia be halted for 48 consecutive hours or more?
background:
Context and definitions
- Druzhba pipeline: The Druzhba (Friendship) pipeline is one of the world’s longest crude oil pipeline systems, transporting oil from Russia to several European countries. It splits into northern and southern branches at Mazyr (Belarus); the southern branch runs via Ukraine and supplies Slovakia and Hungary (among others). The Russian section is operated by Transneft; national segments are operated by entities including Transpetrol (Slovakia) and MOL/Hungarian operators in Hungary.
- Crude oil: Naturally occurring liquid hydrocarbons used as refinery feedstock; this question concerns crude oil (not refined products) moving through Druzhba.
- Alternative route context (Adria/JANAF): The Adria (JANAF) pipeline connects with the Druzhba network near Šahy, Slovakia, offering an alternative route relevant to Hungary and Slovakia. As of late September 2025, Hungarian oil group MOL and Croatian operator JANAF disputed whether the Adriatic/Adria pipeline could reliably supply MOL’s Hungarian and Slovak refineries at sufficient capacity; MOL cited test limitations, while JANAF said it could cover their needs and rejected MOL’s claims. Reuters and other reports characterize Hungary and Slovakia as largely dependent on Russian oil delivered via Druzhba, with the Adria line viewed as the key alternative.

Recent status quo (as of 2025-10-01)
- 2025 saw multiple disruptions to the southern Druzhba flows:
  - On Aug 18, 2025, Russian crude oil flows to Hungary and Slovakia via Druzhba were halted following what Hungary described as a Ukrainian attack on a transformer station. MOL (Hungary) and Transpetrol (Slovakia) confirmed that supplies had stopped; the timing of resumption was initially unclear. Flows then resumed to Hungary and Slovakia late on Tue Aug 19, per officials’ statements, including Hungary’s foreign minister and Slovakia’s economy minister, with MOL noting production was not disrupted during the temporary shutdown.
  - Subsequently, officials said supplies could be suspended for at least five days after another Ukrainian strike, and Slovakia’s Transpetrol confirmed an interruption; a Russian industry source also said supplies could be halted for a few days. Russian crude supplies to Hungary and Slovakia via Druzhba restarted on Thu Aug 28, 2025, according to MOL and Slovakia’s economy minister.
  - Reuters also noted a brief suspension in March 2025 after a Ukrainian drone attack on a metering station, with shipments resuming the same day.
- These August events and late-September JANAF/MOL capacity disputes frame ongoing risk to Q4 2025 continuity of Druzhba deliveries to Hungary and Slovakia.

Why this question is interesting
- The southern Druzhba leg runs through a conflict zone and has recently suffered attacks and multi-day outages, while the main alternative (Adria/JANAF) remains contested in terms of sustained capacity, creating nontrivial uncertainty about whether another prolonged halt (>=48 hours) will occur in Q4 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Binary outcome
- Resolve Yes if, at any time between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive), there exists a continuous period lasting at least 48 hours during which crude oil flows via the Druzhba pipeline to either Hungary or Slovakia are halted (i.e., no deliveries). Resolve No otherwise.

Key definitions and scope
- "Via the Druzhba pipeline" means deliveries along the southern branch of the Druzhba network that supply Hungary and Slovakia (not seaborne, rail, truck, or other pipeline routes). For a general description of the pipeline and its southern branch, see the Druzhba pipeline overview.
- "Crude oil" refers to unrefined petroleum, as commonly defined.
- "To Hungary or Slovakia" means deliveries into either country’s territory through Druzhba; an eligible halt may affect one or both countries. A halt in one country counts as a qualifying event even if the other country continues to receive Druzhba deliveries.
- "Halted" means that the relevant operator(s) or government authority(ies) state that flows/shipments/deliveries through Druzhba are halted/suspended/stopped to the affected country, or a major wire service reports such a halt, quoting those authorities. Reductions or slowdowns that do not amount to a halt do not count. Planned maintenance, attacks, technical failures, sanctions, or any other cause all count if they result in a halt.
- Consecutiveness: The 48 hours must be uninterrupted; any resumption during the interval breaks consecutiveness. The event qualifies if there exists a 48-hour sub-interval entirely contained within the question window during which a halt is in effect.

Timing and timezone
- All timing is assessed in UTC. If a source provides local times, they will be converted to UTC. If a source provides dates without times for start and/or end, the following conservative rule applies: treat a date-only start as beginning at 00:00:00 UTC of that date, and a date-only end/resumption as beginning at 00:00:00 UTC of the stated resumption date (i.e., end is exclusive). If multiple sources report different times, prefer statements from the relevant pipeline operators (e.g., Transpetrol, MOL) or national energy/competent ministries; if still conflicting, use the earlier start and later end times that are supported by the most authoritative sources to compute a minimum guaranteed duration.

Eligible sources for resolution
- The question will be resolved based on at least one of the following:
  1) Direct official statements (press releases, website posts, or official social media) by relevant operators or government authorities for the affected country (e.g., Transpetrol in Slovakia; MOL/Hungarian operators; Slovakia’s Ministry of Economy; Hungary’s Ministry of Energy/Foreign Affairs), or the upstream operator Transneft; or
  2) Reports by reputable international wire services (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, Bloomberg, AFP) that explicitly state that Druzhba flows were halted/suspended/stopped to Hungary and/or Slovakia, and which attribute this information to the relevant authorities.
- The August 2025 disruptions were publicly reported/confirmed by these types of sources (e.g., MOL, Transpetrol, and Reuters) and illustrate the kind of evidence that will be used for resolution.

Inclusions and exclusions
- Inclusions: Any cause of halt (attack, technical fault, maintenance, legal action). Halts that affect only one of the two countries count. If a halt begins before the window, it only counts if there exists a continuous 48-hour sub-interval entirely within the window. If a halt begins within the window and continues beyond Dec 31, 2025, only the portion within the window is considered; it counts only if a continuous 48-hour sub-interval lies entirely within the window.
- Exclusions: Partial flow reductions that do not constitute a halt; interruptions to non-Druzhba routes (e.g., Adria/JANAF) do not count for this question. Alternative deliveries via Adria/JANAF or other modes do not negate a Druzhba halt.

Adjudication notes
- If sources disagree on whether a halt occurred, preference will be given to official operator or competent ministry statements. If ambiguity remains and there is insufficient evidence to establish a continuous >=48-hour halt within the window, resolve No.
- Examples of precedent reporting that would qualify (purely illustrative): Reuters articles in Aug 2025 detailing halts and resumptions confirmed by MOL and Transpetrol.

question: Minnesota: Will the November 2025 Budget & Economic Forecast project a nonnegative FY 2026–27 General Fund budgetary balance?
background:
Summary of context as of 2025-10-01
- Minnesota Management & Budget (MMB) produces the state’s Budget & Economic Forecast twice each year, typically near the end of November and February. The forecast reflects current law and incorporates national and state economic outlooks, and caseload/enrollment and formula-driven spending assumptions. The forecast materials are published on MMB’s Forecast portal (mn.gov/mmb/forecast/forecast/).
- In the February/March 2025 forecast release, MMB reported that the projected General Fund budgetary balance for the FY 2026–27 biennium was $456 million, which was $160 million lower than the November 2024 estimate. This figure appears in the February 2025 Budget & Economic Forecast PDF and is also summarized on MMB’s website dated March 6, 2025.
- In the November 2024 forecast, MMB projected a $616 million General Fund budgetary balance for FY 2026–27, down from end-of-session estimates earlier in 2024.
- Terminology and definitions used by MMB:
  - General Fund: Minnesota’s main operating fund; major revenue streams include individual income, corporate, and sales taxes; revenues are non‑dedicated and appropriated by the legislature.
  - Fiscal year (FY): Runs July 1 to June 30. The FY 2026–27 biennium spans July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2027 (i.e., FY 2026 and FY 2027) because Minnesota biennia run from July 1 of an odd‑numbered year through June 30 of the next odd‑numbered year.
  - Budgetary balance (projected): The forecasted end‑of‑biennium balance derived under current law before the legislature enacts the next biennial budget; MMB notes this projected balance is a starting point for the Governor’s and legislature’s budget process and is not considered a surplus until appropriations are enacted. Forecast documents present both “Budgetary Balance” and, for comparison, “Budgetary Balance without discretionary spending inflation”.
  - Units/format: Forecast tables present amounts in nominal U.S. dollars, typically “($ in millions)”.
Why this question has uncertainty
- The FY 2026–27 projection moved from $616 million (November 2024) to $456 million (February/March 2025), reflecting changing economic assumptions and forecast updates under current law. Given MMB’s semiannual updates and sensitivity to macroeconomic conditions, policy baselines, and caseloads, the November 2025 forecast could plausibly show either a small positive or a negative balance.
resolution_criteria:
Question
- Resolve whether, between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, the Minnesota Management & Budget (MMB) November 2025 Budget & Economic Forecast projects a nonnegative General Fund budgetary balance for the FY 2026–27 biennium.
Operational resolution steps
1) Source document:
   - Use the official November 2025 Budget & Economic Forecast materials published on MMB’s Forecast portal: https://mn.gov/mmb/forecast/forecast/. If multiple files are posted (e.g., summary and full report), use the full Budget & Economic Forecast PDF for November 2025; if there is an official erratum or update posted by MMB by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, use the most recent official version in that window.
2) Metric to read:
   - Identify the FY 2026–27 General Fund “Budgetary Balance” as presented in the November 2025 report’s “Next Biennium: FY 2026–27” general fund budget tables or equivalent summary table. Specifically use the line labeled “Budgetary Balance” (which includes discretionary spending inflation, when MMB presents both variants). Do not use the alternative line “Budgetary Balance without discretionary spending inflation.” Prior MMB forecasts show both measures distinctly, so this instruction removes ambiguity.
3) Units and sign:
   - Use the figure as displayed in the report (typically in millions of U.S. dollars). Treat “nonnegative” as greater than or equal to $0. If the figure is exactly $0 (or $0 million), that counts as nonnegative.
4) Binary outcome:
   - YES if the November 2025 report’s FY 2026–27 General Fund Budgetary Balance (as defined above) is ≥ $0.
   - NO if it is < $0.
5) Timing and versioning:
   - Resolve upon publication of the November 2025 forecast, using the latest official November 2025 report posted by MMB between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC. If no November 2025 forecast is posted by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, the market should be voided (not applicable) due to lack of required resolution source (historically, MMB publishes in November/February).
Definitions (for clarity)
- Minnesota General Fund: As defined by MMB; the state’s main operating fund supported by major tax revenues and appropriated by the legislature.
- Biennium and fiscal years: Minnesota FY runs July 1–June 30; the FY 2026–27 biennium consists of FY 2026 (2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30) and FY 2027 (2026-07-01 to 2027-06-30).
- Budgetary balance (projected): The end-of-biennium balance under current law before enactment of the next biennial budget; used as a starting point for budget development. Do not conflate with “Budgetary Balance without discretionary spending inflation” which MMB may also show for comparison.
Notes for resolvers and forecasters
- The February/March 2025 forecast showed $456 million for FY 2026–27 (with the main “Budgetary Balance” measure), $160 million lower than November 2024’s $616 million, illustrating recent movement in the outlook.
- The Budget & Economic Forecast reflects current law and macroeconomic assumptions reviewed with the Council of Economic Advisers; consult the report’s methodology section if needed.
Citations:  Budget and Economic Forecast – MN.gov;  Forecast Overview / Minnesota Management and Budget (MMB);  February 2025 Budget & Economic Forecast (PDF);  November 2024 Budget & Economic Forecast (PDF);  Key Budget Terms / Minnesota Management and Budget (MMB).

question: On 2025-12-31, will AGSI report EU27 underground gas storage “fullness” at or above 74.0%?
background:
What this question measures
- Metric: “Storage fullness” (field full on AGSI) is defined as Storage / Working Gas Volume (WGV) expressed in percent. WGV is “the maximum amount that can be stored at the facility (technical capacity).” AGSI publishes these as part of its daily dataset; examples in the documentation show full to two decimal places and WGV and gasInStorage in TWh with four-decimal precision.
- Scope: EU27 aggregate as published on the AGSI transparency platform (agsi.gie.eu). AGSI is operated by Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) and provides daily inventory reporting for underground gas storages; GIE states the AGSI platform covers 100% of the underground gas storage market in the EU27. The EU aggregate is retrievable via the AGSI API at https://agsi.gie.eu/api?type=eu (dataset entry name “EU”, code “eu”).
- Timing and updates: AGSI data represent inventories at the end of the previous gas day. Updates occur daily at 19:30 CET and again at 23:00 CET to include late submissions; datasets include fields gas_day (current Gas Day Start date) and gasDayStart (the start date of the reported gas day).

Definitions and references
- EU27: The 27 current member states of the European Union as of 2025: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden.
- Underground gas storage (UGS): Storage of natural gas in subsurface facilities, typically in depleted gas reservoirs, aquifers, or salt caverns.
- AGSI transparency platform: GIE’s Aggregated Gas Storage Inventory platform providing daily inventory reporting and EU-wide coverage for UGS; accessible at agsi.gie.eu.

Status quo (as of late Q3 2025)
- Europe-wide: As of August 25, 2025, European storage stood at 76% of capacity (≈85 bcm), below 92% a year prior and below the 10-year average (80.5%). Reuters reported Europe was still expected to reach 90% by the start of the October heating season, helped by ample LNG availability as Asian demand eased.
- Policy context: EU storage policy targeted a 90% fill level to be reached at any point between October 1 and December 1, 2025.
- Country examples: Germany was at 75% in mid-September 2025. Poland reported 100% fullness on September 24, 2025.

Why this may be uncertain
- The end-December fullness will depend on realized winter temperatures and demand, LNG and pipeline supply conditions, and intra-winter withdrawals. While the EU aimed to reach ~90% by early Q4, historical early-winter draws can reduce stocks substantially by year-end; weather and supply shocks can materially move the EU aggregate. The 74.0% threshold is chosen to balance plausibility of both Yes and No outcomes given the above context and the late-summer starting point.
resolution_criteria:
Question: On 2025-12-31 (CET), will the AGSI EU aggregate underground gas storage “fullness” (full) be at least 74.0%?

Primary source of truth
- AGSI API EU aggregate endpoint: https://agsi.gie.eu/api?type=eu. Use the entry with code "eu" (name "EU"). The relevant date field is gasDayStart, and the relevant metric is full (percentage). The AGSI API and field definitions, including full, gasDayStart, and update schedule, are documented by GIE. Platform coverage and purpose are documented by GIE.

Resolution steps (all times CET/UTC+1 on 2025-12-31)
1) At or after the second daily AGSI publication (scheduled for 23:00 CET) on 2025-12-31, retrieve the EU aggregate dataset from the API. Identify the record where gasDayStart = 2025-12-31. Extract full (the EU aggregate storage fullness in %). AGSI documentation specifies two daily updates at 19:30 CET and 23:00 CET and that data represent inventories at the end of the previous gas day.
2) Compare the extracted value full (as a real number with the precision provided by AGSI) to the threshold 74.0.
- If full ≥ 74.0, resolve YES.
- If full < 74.0, resolve NO.

Tiebreakers and contingencies
- If the 23:00 CET update is not yet available, use the latest available AGSI publication on 2025-12-31 (e.g., the 19:30 CET update) and the same record with gasDayStart = 2025-12-31.
- If the API is unavailable, use the AGSI web UI EU aggregate page displaying the same fields and date labels; the UI and API convey the same dataset/fields as per GIE documentation.
- Ignore any retroactive corrections published after 23:59 CET on 2025-12-31; resolve using the latest available value published on 2025-12-31 CET publications, per the schedule documented by GIE.
- The AGSI status flag (E/C/N) does not affect resolution; use the published value of full for the specified gasDayStart.

Key term precisions
- EU27: as listed above.
- Underground gas storage: as defined above.
- full: Storage / Working Gas Volume (WGV) in percent; WGV is the maximum amount that can be stored (technical capacity).
- Date label: Use the record whose gasDayStart equals 2025-12-31, as labeled by AGSI.

question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will the IMF Executive Board complete the Fifth Review under Sri Lanka’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Sri Lanka is implementing an IMF-supported program under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) approved by the IMF Executive Board on March 20, 2023, in the amount of SDR 2.286 billion (about US$3 billion).
- The IMF Executive Board completed Sri Lanka’s Fourth Review on July 1, 2025, providing immediate access to SDR 254 million (about US$350 million).
- IMF staff concluded a visit to Colombo on July 21–25, 2025, noting continued reform momentum and that the timing of the Fifth Review would be discussed with the government.

Definitions and scope for this question:
- IMF Executive Board: The governing body that conducts the IMF’s daily business and takes formal decisions on member country programs. See: https://www.imf.org/en/About/executive-board
- Extended Fund Facility (EFF): An IMF lending arrangement designed to assist countries with structural balance-of-payments problems. See: https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/IMF-Lending and https://www.imf.org/en/Topics/imf-lending
- Sri Lanka’s EFF arrangement: The specific 48‑month program for Sri Lanka approved on March 20, 2023, under which reviews are conducted (e.g., first, second, third, fourth, etc.).
- Review “completion” (for this market): A review is considered completed only when the IMF Executive Board has formally completed that numbered review (here: the Fifth Review) under Sri Lanka’s EFF arrangement. Evidence will typically be a press release titled along the lines of “IMF Executive Board Completes the [Nth] Review Under the Extended Fund Facility with Sri Lanka,” as exemplified for the Fourth Review.
- Fifth Review: The next sequential review following the Fourth Review under Sri Lanka’s current EFF arrangement. If the Board completes combined reviews (e.g., “Fifth and Sixth Review”), this question resolves “Yes” provided the Board’s action explicitly states that the Fifth Review was completed (even if combined with another review).
- Staff-Level Agreement (SLA): An agreement between IMF staff and the authorities that precedes any Board decision; an SLA does not constitute completion of a review and does not satisfy this question’s criteria (see examples of SLA announcements and distinction from Board completion on imf.org press releases; the Board decision language is distinct and was used for the Fourth Review ).

Why this is non-trivial: Public indications suggest the Fifth Review is expected for fall 2025 but the exact timing depends on reform implementation and Board scheduling, introducing genuine uncertainty about whether completion occurs within the specified window.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether the IMF Executive Board completes Sri Lanka’s Fifth Review under the current EFF arrangement between 00:00:00 UTC on October 15, 2025 and 23:59:59 UTC on December 31, 2025, inclusive.

Resolve “Yes” if all of the following are true:
1) There is official IMF evidence that the Executive Board completed the Fifth Review under Sri Lanka’s EFF arrangement, and
2) The Executive Board decision date for that completion falls within the window above.

Adjudication details:
- Primary source: IMF press release(s) on imf.org (News > Press Releases) and/or the Sri Lanka country page (https://www.imf.org/en/Countries/LKA) containing explicit language that the “IMF Executive Board completed the Fifth Review under the Extended Fund Facility with Sri Lanka” (or substantively identical phrasing). For reference on phrasing and structure, see the Fourth Review completion press release.
- Decision date: Use the Executive Board decision date as stated in the IMF communication (e.g., “On [date], the IMF Executive Board completed…”). If the press release is published on a different day than the Board decision, the Board decision date governs. Example precedent: the Fourth Review press release states the Board completed the review on July 1, 2025.
- Combined reviews: If the IMF completes combined reviews (e.g., Fifth and Sixth together), this counts as “Yes” provided the IMF’s official communication explicitly says the Fifth Review was completed.
- What does not count: Staff-Level Agreements (SLAs), staff visits, statements of intent, or staff recommendations without an Executive Board decision do not satisfy completion. IMF staff indicated that the timing of the Fifth Review would be discussed with the authorities after the July 2025 staff visit, but that does not constitute Board completion.
- Backup sources: If imf.org is unavailable, resolution may use credible reporting from major international newswires (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) that clearly states the IMF Executive Board completed the Fifth Review under Sri Lanka’s EFF and specifies the Board decision date. If such reports conflict, prefer the IMF source when it becomes available; otherwise, resolve based on the preponderance of credible reports.

Resolution:
- YES if the Board decision date for completing the Fifth Review is on or after 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.
- NO otherwise (including if the Fifth Review is completed before 2025-10-15 UTC or after 2025-12-31 UTC, or is not completed at all by the end of the period).

question: Canada: Will the federal government introduce a bill establishing essential (minimum) service requirements specific to Canada Post between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Context and status quo as of Oct 1, 2025
- On September 25, 2025, the Government of Canada announced a transformation plan for Canada Post to stabilize finances and modernize operations, including authorizing the end of remaining door-to-door delivery (conversion to community mailboxes), adjusting delivery standards (e.g., shifting non-urgent mail to ground transport), lifting the moratorium on rural post office closures, and reviewing the stamp-rate process. On the same day, the Canadian Union of Postal Workers (CUPW) launched a national strike in response to the reforms; Canada Post stated that, during the strike, mail and parcels would not be processed or delivered, with service guarantees suspended.
- Business groups have called for essential-services legislation to ensure continuity of postal service during reforms and labour disruptions; for example, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) urged Ottawa to adopt temporary or permanent essential-services legislation so that service continues while reforms take effect.
- In the broader federal labour framework, the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) uses the concept of “maintenance of activities” to describe services that must be maintained during a legal work stoppage to prevent an immediate and serious danger to public safety or health; these are commonly referred to as essential services. Treasury Board guidance similarly defines an essential service in the federal public sector context as one necessary for the safety or security of the public, identified where there are reasonable grounds to believe safety or security would be at risk if a work stoppage interrupted the work. Recent federal labour law changes have also been summarized as introducing a ban on replacement workers and requiring employers and unions to negotiate a “Maintenance of Activities Agreement” (essential services agreement), with the CIRB empowered to decide essential activities if no agreement is reached.
- Canada Post’s core statutory functions and terminology are set out in the Canada Post Corporation Act, which grants the Corporation the sole and exclusive privilege of collecting, transmitting, and delivering letters within Canada and defines key terms such as mail, post, post office, and “transmit by post”.

Data sources relevant for resolution
- LEGISinfo (Parliament of Canada) tracks the stages of federal bills, including the “Introduction and First Reading” stage in each chamber; First Reading is an official milestone used to mark a bill’s introduction. The House of Commons’ procedure page describes the “Introduction and First Reading” stage as the formal introduction of a bill without debate.

Why this matters and why the outcome is uncertain
- Given the strike and the scope of reforms, there is active debate about maintaining postal service continuity during labour disruptions. The federal government may choose to introduce legislation specifically imposing minimum or essential service obligations on Canada Post; alternatively, it may rely on existing or general labour law mechanisms or pursue non-legislative approaches, making the timing and specificity of any government bill uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
Yes/No question
- Resolve YES if, between 00:00 ET on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 ET on December 31, 2025, a Government of Canada bill is introduced in either chamber of Parliament (House of Commons or Senate) and receives First Reading, where the bill explicitly establishes essential (minimum/maintenance-of-activities) service requirements specific to Canada Post (i.e., postal services continuity during a strike or lockout), whether by (a) amending the Canada Post Corporation Act to impose such requirements on Canada Post, or (b) otherwise creating or amending statutory provisions that expressly apply to Canada Post or “postal services” and that mandate the maintenance of specified postal operations during a work stoppage. Otherwise resolve NO.

Definitions and inclusions/exclusions (with authoritative references)
- Government bill: a written legislative initiative submitted to Parliament by the government (i.e., introduced by a Minister) for approval and possible amendment before becoming law; private Members’ bills (introduced by MPs who are not Ministers) do not qualify for this question. Government bills can be introduced in either the House of Commons or the Senate.
- Introduction and First Reading: the formal introduction of a bill in a chamber; First Reading is an official milestone tracked by LEGISinfo and, in the House of Commons, occurs without debate.
- Pro forma bills: Bills C‑1 and S‑1, introduced at the opening of each session for procedural purposes, are not substantive and do not qualify.
- Essential services / maintenance of activities: activities that must be maintained during a legal work stoppage to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public; commonly referred to as essential services. Treasury Board guidance similarly defines essential services in the federal public sector as necessary for the safety or security of the public. For the purposes of this question, “essential (minimum) service requirements” or “maintenance-of-activities obligations” refers to statutory requirements to maintain specified operations during a strike or lockout.
- Postal services / Canada Post: Canada Post’s core functions and scope are defined in the Canada Post Corporation Act, including its exclusive privilege to collect, transmit, and deliver letters, and definitions of “mail,” “post,” “post office,” and “transmit by post.” References in a bill that explicitly apply to the Corporation or to “postal services” as defined or used in that Act will be treated as postal-service-specific.
- What counts: The bill must, on its face (short title, long title, summary/legislative intent text on LEGISinfo, or bill text), explicitly (i) reference Canada Post (the Corporation) or postal services and (ii) establish, mandate, or amend essential/minimum/maintenance-of-activities service obligations specific to Canada Post operations during a strike or lockout. Omnibus or budget bills qualify if they contain such explicit postal-service-specific provisions.
- What does not count: (i) private Members’ bills; (ii) non-legislative instruments (e.g., regulations, orders-in-council, administrative directives); (iii) bills that address essential services generally without any explicit postal-service-specific provision; (iv) pro forma Bills C‑1/S‑1.

Date range and time zone
- Eligible introductions are those that receive First Reading between 00:00 Eastern Time (ET) on October 15, 2025 and 23:59 ET on December 31, 2025, inclusive.

Primary resolution sources
- LEGISinfo (Parliament of Canada) entry for any qualifying bill, showing the chamber, sponsor (Minister), and “Introduction and First Reading” date/time/status.
- If needed for disambiguation (e.g., to confirm sponsorship or the bill’s subject matter), official Government of Canada releases or the full bill text posted on LEGISinfo will be consulted.

Edge cases and tie‑breakers
- If multiple bills are introduced, only one needs to meet the criteria to resolve YES.
- If a bill is introduced but the qualifying postal-service-specific essential-service provisions are removed before First Reading (i.e., they are not in the version introduced), it does not count. Conversely, amendments after First Reading are irrelevant to eligibility; resolution is based on the content of the bill as introduced and recorded at First Reading.
- If LEGISinfo and a chamber journal record conflict on the First Reading date, LEGISinfo will be treated as the source of truth for this question.

Background sources cited above
- Government of Canada announcement on Canada Post transformation and media coverage: ; Canada Post strike notices and reporting: ; business groups’ calls for essential services legislation: ; definitions and process references: ; labour-law context summary:.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will Oracle file an SEC Form 8‑K (Item 1.01) or a periodic report disclosing entry into a material definitive agreement to acquire or commit to acquire an equity stake in the new U.S. TikTok entity established for a qualified divestiture under the 2024 law?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
- U.S. law and litigation: In April 2024, Congress enacted the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (PAFACAA), which restricts distribution/hosting of specified “foreign adversary controlled applications” (including TikTok) in the U.S. unless a “qualified divestiture” occurs within statutory timelines. On 2025-01-17, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the law’s divest‑or‑ban framework in TikTok Inc. v. Garland, with the opinion discussing the enforcement timeline and the statute’s focus on severing foreign control (divestiture) while allowing a one-time presidential extension for progress toward divestiture.
- Executive actions and timeline extensions in 2025: The White House subsequently issued executive actions delaying enforcement as negotiations proceeded, and on 2025-09-25 published a statement and order describing a proposed qualified divestiture plan for TikTok’s U.S. operations: creation of a new U.S.-based joint venture, majority owned and controlled by U.S. persons, with ByteDance and affiliates below 20% and governance safeguards; the order also directed an additional 120-day enforcement delay to allow consummation of the divestiture and outlined earlier delay orders (to April 5, June 19, September 17, and December 16, 2025).
- Reported deal structure and investors (late September 2025): Reuters reporting on 2025-09-25–26 indicates that Oracle, Silver Lake, and Abu Dhabi-based MGX are expected to be main investors in the new U.S. TikTok entity with a combined stake reported around 45–50%, with ByteDance holding less than 20% and U.S. persons holding a majority, consistent with the divestiture plan; governance details include a seven-member board with six American-appointed seats.
- SEC disclosure trigger: When a U.S.-listed company like Oracle enters into a “material definitive agreement” not made in the ordinary course, it generally must file a Form 8‑K under Item 1.01 within four business days, describing the date, parties, relationships, and material terms of the agreement; the term “material definitive agreement” is defined in Item 1.01(b). If the triggering event occurs within four business days before filing a periodic report, the company may disclose it in that periodic report (e.g., 10‑Q/10‑K) instead of a separate 8‑K (with exceptions not relevant here).
- Oracle’s EDGAR identifier: Oracle Corporation files with the SEC under CIK 0001341439; this is the EDGAR entity to monitor for any Form 8‑K, 10‑Q, or 10‑K filings in the relevant period.

Key definitions (used for resolution):
- Oracle: Oracle Corporation, SEC CIK 0001341439; disclosures may describe agreements entered by Oracle or its consolidated subsidiaries but must be disclosed by Oracle Corporation in its EDGAR filing.
- Form 8‑K Item 1.01 “Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement”: An agreement providing for obligations or rights that are material to and enforceable by/against the registrant, including those subject to conditions; triggers an 8‑K within four business days when not made in the ordinary course of business, with specified content requirements. The SEC allows disclosure in a periodic report if the event occurs within four business days before filing, except for specified items (Items 4.01, 4.02) not applicable here.
- Qualified divestiture and “foreign adversary controlled application”: As set forth in PAFACAA, TikTok and ByteDance are explicitly covered; the law prohibits distribution/hosting in the U.S. absent a qualified divestiture and provides timing and designation mechanisms.
- New U.S. TikTok entity (the “U.S. TikTok JV”): For this question, this means the U.S.-incorporated company (corporation or LLC) established to operate the U.S. TikTok application pursuant to a qualified divestiture plan under PAFACAA, as described in the 2025-09-25 White House materials and consistent with subsequent official determinations (e.g., majority U.S. ownership/control, ByteDance and affiliates below 20%). This definition is functional: if the divestiture plan results in a specific named entity (e.g., a joint venture company) that operates TikTok in the U.S. and meets the plan’s ownership/control criteria, that entity is the “U.S. TikTok JV.”
- “Acquire or commit to acquire an equity stake”: For this question, means Oracle becoming party to a binding agreement (e.g., stock purchase agreement, subscription agreement, shareholders’/investors’ rights agreement, merger agreement) that creates or will create an ownership interest for Oracle (directly or via a wholly‑owned consolidated subsidiary) in the U.S. TikTok JV. Non‑binding LOIs, MOUs, or term sheets do not satisfy this; Item 1.01 can cover agreements subject to conditions if the agreement itself is binding. Indirect exposure solely via an unaffiliated investment fund (e.g., as a limited partner) does not count unless Oracle itself is a named party to the binding agreement acquiring equity in the U.S. TikTok JV.

Why this is forecastable: As of late September 2025, a plan identifying Oracle among the principal investors has been publicly reported and described by the White House, but consummation timelines and definitive documentation remain uncertain before year‑end, creating non‑trivial uncertainty over whether Oracle will disclose a binding investment agreement within the specified window.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, will Oracle Corporation (CIK 0001341439) file on EDGAR either (a) a Form 8‑K that discloses, under Item 1.01, entry into a material definitive agreement for Oracle (or a consolidated subsidiary) to acquire or commit to acquire an equity stake in the U.S. TikTok JV, or (b) a Form 10‑Q or Form 10‑K that, in lieu of a separate 8‑K pursuant to SEC guidance, discloses that such an Item 1.01‑type agreement was entered and describes its material terms?

Definitions and inclusions:
- “File” means the EDGAR system shows the filing as accepted with a filing date/time stamp within the above UTC window for Oracle’s CIK 0001341439.
