- Qualifying disclosures include: (i) a Form 8‑K with Item 1.01 describing Oracle’s entry into a binding agreement to invest in or own equity of the U.S. TikTok JV; (ii) a Form 10‑Q/10‑K filed within the window that, consistent with SEC staff guidance, discloses within four business days of the triggering event the entry into such a binding agreement (e.g., within “Subsequent Events,” “Other Information,” or equivalent), in which case the periodic report filing itself suffices.
- The agreement may be subject to conditions (e.g., regulatory approvals, closing conditions) and still qualifies if it is a “material definitive agreement” per Item 1.01(b) and is binding on the parties.
- The U.S. TikTok JV is defined functionally as the U.S.-incorporated entity operating TikTok’s U.S. application pursuant to a qualified divestiture under PAFACAA and as described in the White House’s 2025-09-25 materials (majority U.S. ownership/control; ByteDance under 20%). Disclosures must clearly identify that the agreement pertains to acquiring equity in that entity (by name or by unambiguous description).

Exclusions (will NOT count toward a Yes resolution):
- Press releases, investor presentations, or media reports that are not EDGAR filings by Oracle.
- Disclosures about non‑equity commercial arrangements (e.g., cloud hosting, security, MSA) unless they are part of a binding agreement that also includes Oracle’s commitment to acquire equity in the U.S. TikTok JV; pure commercial contracts without an equity component do not qualify.
- Non‑binding documents (LOIs, MOUs, term sheets) not constituting a binding agreement, even if disclosed.
- Filings by entities other than Oracle Corporation (CIK 0001341439) unless incorporated by reference into Oracle’s filing within the window.

Resolution source and procedure:
- Primary source: Oracle’s EDGAR filings page (CIK 0001341439). The resolver will search for Form 8‑K, 10‑Q, and 10‑K filings within the specified window and read Item 1.01 (or analogous periodic report sections) and any attached exhibits (e.g., stock purchase/subscription agreements) to determine whether they disclose entry into a qualifying binding agreement.
- If a qualifying disclosure is found within the window, resolve Yes. If none is found, resolve No at 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

Notes:
- Legal and policy context informing plausibility includes the Supreme Court’s January 2025 decision upholding PAFACAA and the White House’s September 2025 statement/order outlining the qualified divestiture plan and enforcement delay, and Reuters reporting naming Oracle among the main investors; these do not themselves affect resolution except insofar as they inform whether such an agreement is likely to be executed and disclosed within the window.

question: Will the FOMC change the target range for the federal funds rate at its December 9–10, 2025 meeting?
background:
Definitions and institutions:
- Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC): The committee within the U.S. Federal Reserve System that sets U.S. monetary policy, including decisions affecting the federal funds rate; it meets regularly, votes on policy, and oversees open market operations.
- Federal funds rate and target range: The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to each other overnight on an uncollateralized basis. Since December 2008, the Federal Reserve has set a target range (lower and upper bounds) for the federal funds rate rather than a single point target.

Event timing and sources:
- The Federal Reserve’s December 2025 schedule lists an FOMC two‑day meeting on December 9–10, a press conference on December 10, and release of minutes on December 30. This page serves as the official schedule reference for December 2025 events.
- The Fed’s press release page for 2025 serves as the canonical location where monetary policy press releases (including the post‑meeting FOMC statement) are posted and organized by date and category.
- The FOMC calendars page provides meeting calendars, statements, and minutes, and notes that the FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year. It also links to policy statements and minutes for each meeting, providing a secondary path to the December 2025 statement and minutes.
- The FOMC announced its tentative schedule for 2025, including that for regularly scheduled meetings the policy statement is released at 2:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the second day and the Chair’s press conference is at 2:30 p.m. Eastern Time. This applies to the December 9–10, 2025 meeting.

Status quo as of today:
- At the September 17, 2025 meeting, the FOMC lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4 to 4‑1/4 percent, as stated in the FOMC statement and the accompanying Implementation Note (effective September 18, 2025).

Why this is a good forecasting question:
- The December meeting is scheduled and the decision is publicly announced the same day, ensuring resolvability by year‑end via an authoritative source.
- As of early fall 2025, the FOMC recently changed the target range and forecasters debate further moves, making the December outcome meaningfully uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
What is being forecast:
- Whether the FOMC’s post‑meeting policy statement released on December 10, 2025 (U.S. Eastern Time) announces a target range for the federal funds rate that differs from the target range announced in the policy statement of the immediately preceding FOMC meeting.

Key definitions for resolution:
- “Target range for the federal funds rate” means the specific lower and upper bounds stated by the Federal Reserve for the federal funds rate. If the post‑meeting statement uses descriptive language, the accompanying Implementation Note’s numeric range will be used as the definitive values for comparison.
- “Immediately preceding FOMC meeting” means the last FOMC meeting prior to December 10, 2025 for which a monetary policy press release (“Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement”) was posted. The reference statement will be identified on the 2025 press releases page.
- “Change” means any difference in either the lower bound or the upper bound of the target range relative to the bounds in the prior meeting’s statement. If both bounds are identical to the prior statement, resolve No; otherwise resolve Yes.

Inclusions and exclusions:
- Only the target range change announced in the December 10, 2025 post‑meeting statement counts for resolution. Intermeeting actions or other announcements outside the December 10 statement do not by themselves resolve this question.
- Changes to other policy rates or tools (e.g., the discount rate, Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB), Overnight Reverse Repurchase (ON RRP) rate), forward guidance language, or balance sheet policies do not count unless they are accompanied by a change in the target range.

Timeframe and timezone:
- The relevant event window is the FOMC meeting held December 9–10, 2025, with resolution based on the post‑meeting statement released December 10, 2025, in U.S. Eastern Time.

Source of truth for resolution:
- Primary: The Federal Reserve Board’s monetary policy press release (the FOMC post‑meeting statement) posted on December 10, 2025 on the 2025 press releases page.
- Secondary/backup: The FOMC calendars page providing links to statements and minutes , and the dedicated December 2025 schedule page showing the meeting and press conference timing.
- For exact numeric bounds if needed: The Implementation Note accompanying the December 10, 2025 statement.

question: By December 31, 2025, will the Council of the EU adopt and publish in the Official Journal a decision suspending preferential tariff treatment under the EU–Israel Association Agreement?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Agreement: The EU–Israel Association Agreement (Euro‑Mediterranean Agreement; CELEX: 22000A0621(01); OJ L 147, 21.6.2000) establishes the framework for EU–Israel relations, including trade preferences. Title II (Free movement of goods) prohibits customs duties on industrial products and sets arrangements for agricultural goods; Protocol 4 defines “originating products” and administrative cooperation necessary to claim preferential tariff treatment. Article 2 designates respect for human rights and democratic principles as an “essential element” of the Agreement.
- Commission proposal: On 2025-09-17, the European Commission proposed that the Council of the EU suspend certain trade‑related provisions of the Agreement (i.e., Israel’s preferential market access), stating the Council must adopt the decision by qualified majority; the decision enters into force on adoption, notification follows, and the suspension takes effect 30 days after notification to the Association Council. Reuters reporting the same day indicated the proposed suspension would affect about €5.8bn of Israeli exports and yield ~€227m/year in duties; it also noted that the trade suspension requires a qualified majority in the Council.
- Legal basis and voting: Article 218(9) TFEU empowers the Council, on a Commission or HR/VP proposal, to adopt a decision suspending application of an agreement; Article 218(8) sets default voting by qualified majority, with unanimity exceptions for concluding certain agreements (distinct from decisions under paragraph 9). Qualified majority voting (QMV) in the Council is defined as at least 55% of member states (15 of 27) representing at least 65% of the EU population voting in favour.
- Publication/resolution source: Since July 2013, only the electronic edition of the Official Journal (OJ) on EUR‑Lex is authentic; since 2023‑10‑01, acts are published individually (“act‑by‑act”). The OJ (notably its L series for legislation) is the authoritative source to verify Council Decisions and their publication dates.

Definitions and terms:
- Council of the EU (“the Council”): The EU institution composed of national ministers, distinct from the European Council; together with Parliament it is the main decision‑making body and concludes international agreements and adopts decisions under Article 218 TFEU.
- EU–Israel Association Agreement: The Euro‑Mediterranean Agreement (CELEX: 22000A0621(01)), including Title II on Free movement of goods and Protocol 4 on rules of origin for preferential tariff treatment.
- Preferential tariff treatment (under the Agreement): The elimination/reduction of customs duties and other trade concessions granted to goods “originating” in Israel or the EU under Title II and related protocols; eligibility requires compliance with Protocol 4 rules of origin and submission of proofs of origin (e.g., EUR.1 or invoice declaration).
- Qualified Majority Voting (QMV): Adoption in the Council when at least 55% of member states (minimum 15 of 27) representing at least 65% of the EU population vote in favour.
- Official Journal (OJ) publication: The act’s authentic publication on EUR‑Lex’s OJ pages, with an OJ citation/date; this is the authoritative record for EU legal acts.

Why this is uncertain and researchable:
- The proposal is politically salient and requires Council agreement by QMV; member‑state positions (e.g., Germany) and coalition dynamics create genuine uncertainty before year‑end.
- Forecasters can track Council agendas, member‑state statements, and legal drafting, then verify resolution via the OJ.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible acts must be both adopted and published between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC.

Resolution (YES):
- Resolve YES if, within the time window, a legal act titled “Council Decision” (or equivalent Council act) is published in the authentic electronic Official Journal on EUR‑Lex, whose operative provisions explicitly suspend the application of preferential tariff treatment for goods originating in Israel under the EU–Israel Association Agreement. Acceptable formulations include any of the following, provided they are clearly stated in the operative articles:
  1) “suspending the application of certain trade‑related provisions of the Euro‑Mediterranean Agreement establishing an association between the European Communities and their Member States, of the one part, and the State of Israel, of the other part (CELEX: 22000A0621(01))”, or
  2) “goods originating in Israel shall not benefit from preferential tariff treatment under the Association Agreement for the duration of this Decision”, or
  3) “suspending the application of Title II (Free movement of goods) provisions on elimination of customs duties for products originating in Israel under the Association Agreement”.
- The act must be adopted by the Council of the European Union pursuant to Article 218(9) TFEU (or otherwise clearly as a Council act suspending application of the Agreement) and published in the Official Journal (authentic electronic edition) by the deadline.
- The act must identify the Agreement by its official name or CELEX citation (e.g., “Euro‑Mediterranean Agreement… (CELEX: 22000A0621(01); OJ L 147, 21.6.2000)”).

Resolution (NO):
- Resolve NO if no such Council Decision is published in the OJ within the time window, or if any act is adopted but not published in the OJ by the deadline.

Verification steps (for the resolver):
- Navigate to EUR‑Lex Official Journal pages (Direct access to OJ; daily L‑series view) and search for Council Decisions published during the window. Confirm:
  a) the issuing institution is the Council of the European Union,
  b) the act’s operative provisions suspend preferential tariff treatment under the EU–Israel Association Agreement as per acceptable formulations,
  c) the OJ publication date and citation fall within the specified UTC window. The OJ electronic edition on EUR‑Lex is the authentic source.

Notes and exclusions:
- Acts of the European Council, Commission communications, draft proposals, or press releases do not count.
- Sanctions listings or measures not explicitly suspending preferential tariff treatment under the Agreement do not count.
- References to bodies set up by the Agreement (e.g., Association Council) only count if the Council Decision itself suspends application under Article 218(9) and is published in the OJ during the window.

Key sources:
- Commission proposal and stated QMV/adoption/effect timeline.
- TFEU Article 218(8)–(9) text.
- QMV thresholds definition.
- OJ authenticity and act‑by‑act publication.
- Agreement’s Article 2 and Title II trade provisions ; Protocol 4 rules of origin underpinning preferential treatment.
- Agreement’s CELEX and OJ citation.
- Reuters overview of scope and QMV requirement.

question: UK: Will the UK add at least 30 new targets to the Consolidated List under the Iran (Nuclear) sanctions regime between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- The UK’s Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) maintains the Consolidated List of financial sanctions targets, which is the official record of individuals and entities subject to UK financial sanctions and is updated on GOV.UK. Entries include fields such as the regime name, “Listed on” (the date the target was added to a regime on the Consolidated List), “UK Sanctions List Date Designated,” “Last Updated,” and a unique “Group ID” that groups all aliases/records for a single target.
- The E3 (UK, France, Germany) announced on 28 August 2025 that they had triggered the UN “snapback” under UNSCR 2231, ending sanctions relief for Iran.
- Following this, the UK issued a Financial Sanctions Notice on 29 September 2025 stating that 71 entries were added to the Consolidated List and are now subject to an asset freeze under the Iran (Nuclear) regime. The regime-specific Consolidated List for Iran (Nuclear) is published by OFSI and organizes entries for individuals and entities; it showed a last updated date around 01/10/2025, reflecting recent changes. The UK Sanctions List page also recorded regime updates indicating substantial Iran (Nuclear) changes around late September 2025.
- The regime-specific page for Iran (Nuclear) on GOV.UK explains that it lists asset-freeze targets designated due to proliferation-related activity in Iran and provides links to regulations and notices.

Why this question may be uncertain/high-entropy:
- A major tranche of Iran (Nuclear) designations was made on 29 September 2025 , but the extent of further UK additions through year-end is uncertain and depends on policy decisions, intelligence, coordination with allies, and implementation of snapback-related measures.

Definitions used in this question:
- “Consolidated List” refers to OFSI’s official database and documents listing all UK financial sanctions targets.
- “Regime: Iran (Nuclear)” refers to the specific UK sanctions regime label as used on the Consolidated List and regime-specific publications.
- “Target” means a distinct individual or entity subject to an asset freeze listed under the Iran (Nuclear) regime on the Consolidated List, counted by unique Group ID to avoid double-counting aliases.
- “New target” in the context of the resolution means a target whose “Listed on” date under the Iran (Nuclear) regime falls within the resolution window (see criteria below).
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on official UK government publications as of 2025-12-31.

Event window and timezone:
- Count targets added between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive).

What counts as a “new target”:
- A “new target” is any distinct person or entity with Regime Name “Iran (Nuclear)” on the Consolidated List whose “Listed on” date is within the window above.
- Count distinct Group IDs only; multiple records/aliases for the same Group ID should be counted once.
- Exclude entries whose only change within the window is an amendment (reflected by “Last Updated”) rather than initial inclusion; the relevant field for inclusion is “Listed on”.

Threshold and resolution:
- Resolve Yes if 30 or more distinct Group IDs meet the “new target” definition within the window. Resolve No otherwise.

Primary source of truth and how to verify:
- Use the regime-specific Consolidated List for Iran (Nuclear) published by OFSI (the PDF that lists individuals and entities under the Iran (Nuclear) regime and includes “Listed on,” “UK Sanctions List Date Designated,” “Last Updated,” and “Group ID” fields). Access the latest version available at year-end via GOV.UK’s regime page and its linked document; as of early October 2025, this exists and shows up-to-date entries.
- If needed for cross-checking or if the regime PDF is temporarily unavailable, use the OFSI Consolidated List search page on GOV.UK, which is updated alongside the Consolidated List and supports grouping by Group ID and filtering by regime.

Background evidence of recent activity (for forecasters’ context; not directly used to resolve):
- E3 snapback initiation on 28 August 2025.
- 71 additions announced on 29 September 2025 via an official Financial Sanctions Notice.
- UK Sanctions List page records recent Iran (Nuclear) regime updates consistent with these actions.

Resolution steps:
1) On or shortly after 2025-12-31 (UTC), open the regime-specific Iran (Nuclear) Consolidated List PDF and identify all entries whose “Listed on” date falls between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 inclusive; tally distinct Group IDs.
2) If necessary, corroborate counts using the Consolidated List search tool (group by Group ID, filter by Regime Name “Iran (Nuclear)”).
3) Compare the count to the threshold (30) and resolve Yes/No accordingly.

All terms and sources referenced above are defined and hosted on GOV.UK, the authoritative publisher for UK sanctions information.

question: Between 2025-12-01 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will at least five distinct Russian federal subjects have mainstream reports of shortages or rationing of AI-92 or AI-95 gasoline?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- Reuters reported that shortages began in Russia’s Far East and Crimea in August 2025 and later appeared in the Volga, southern, and central regions; popular grades AI-92 and AI-95 were “frequently absent,” with particular strain at independent stations. Another Reuters piece noted that shortages and supply disruptions had been reported for more than a month in “more than 10 regions,” specifically mentioning Sevastopol (Crimea) and Nizhny Novgorod.
- In response to persistent shortages, Russia-controlled Crimea imposed a 30‑day price freeze and rationing, limiting motorists to 30 liters per transaction (announced Sept. 29, 2025). Additional reporting summarized caps and per‑transaction limits in Crimea (Ai‑92 capped at 70 RUB/l; Ai‑95 at 76 RUB/l; diesel at 75 RUB/l; sales limited to 30 liters) and estimated a nationwide gasoline shortfall of roughly 400,000 tons versus a typical ~2 million tons per month by late September.
- The Moscow Times reported refining capacity reductions of about 17% (≈1.1 million barrels/day) on some days, widespread rationing from Kaliningrad to the Far East, and about half of Crimea’s gas stations running dry, attributing the crisis to Ukrainian strikes and knock-on effects. ISW assessed that gasoline shortages continued across Russia and occupied Ukraine, with limits of 10–20 liters per customer in several oblasts and reports of stations selling only diesel in some areas.
- Definitions of grades: AI‑92 and AI‑95 refer to gasoline with Research Octane Numbers (RON) of 92 and 95, respectively; the letter “I” indicates the research method of octane measurement (RON).
- Federal subjects: Russia has 89 federal subjects classified into republics, krais, oblasts, federal cities, an autonomous oblast, and autonomous okrugs. Russia claims to have annexed several Ukrainian regions since 2014/2022; however, Crimea and Sevastopol are internationally disputed, and the 2022 claims (Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson) are not internationally recognized and are only partially occupied.

Why this question: As of late September 2025, shortages and rationing appear geographically widespread but policy responses (e.g., export restrictions, emergency imports, price controls) may alleviate shortages by December. Whether at least five distinct federal subjects are reported to have shortages or rationing of AI‑92/AI‑95 during December remains uncertain and decision‑relevant for forecasters.
resolution_criteria:
Overview
- This question resolves based on whether, during the period 2025-12-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (the “Observation Window”), there are qualifying reports for at least five distinct Russian federal subjects indicating shortages or rationing of AI‑92 or AI‑95 gasoline.

Key definitions (with sources for clarity where applicable)
- Russian federal subject: A top‑level constituent entity of the Russian Federation (e.g., oblasts, krais, republics, federal cities, autonomous oblast, autonomous okrugs). For this question, the following apply:
  - The Republic of Crimea and the federal city of Sevastopol count as federal subjects for the purpose of counting reports, notwithstanding their disputed status.
  - The four Ukrainian regions claimed by Russia in 2022 (Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson) do NOT count for this question, to avoid ambiguity given their partial occupation and non‑recognition.
- AI‑92 and AI‑95 gasoline: Motor gasoline grades with Research Octane Numbers (RON) of 92 and 95, respectively; “I” indicates the research method (RON). Any reference to these grades using common transliterations or Cyrillic (e.g., “Ai‑92,” “A‑92,” “АИ‑92”; “Ai‑95,” “A‑95,” “АИ‑95”) qualifies.
- Shortage (operationalized for resolution): Evidence that AI‑92 or AI‑95 is unavailable (out of stock) at retail filling stations in the subject; OR that purchase limits (“rationing”) are imposed on AI‑92 or AI‑95 due to supply constraints during the Observation Window. Rationing includes per‑transaction or per‑day caps (e.g., liters per customer) or bans on sales in portable containers that are explicitly framed as measures to address supply shortages, as documented in analogous prior reporting.
- Retail filling station: A consumer‑facing fuel station selling motor gasoline to the public.
- Distinct subjects: Multiple reports within the same federal subject count once; reports in different federal subjects count separately.

Qualifying sources
- Reports must be published during the Observation Window by at least one of the following: Reuters, Associated Press (AP), Agence France‑Presse (AFP), Bloomberg, Interfax, TASS, RBC (RBK), Kommersant, RIA Novosti, The Moscow Times, Meduza, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), or an official regional government website or press service. English or Russian language reporting both qualify. Examples of prior relevant reporting include Reuters on AI‑92/AI‑95 being frequently absent and on rationing/price freezes in Crimea, The Moscow Times on nationwide rationing and refinery outages, Meduza on tonnage shortages and price caps, and ISW on continued shortages and purchase limits.

What counts as a qualifying report for a subject
- A qualifying report must explicitly mention AI‑92 or AI‑95 in the context of unavailability (out of stock) or rationing within the federal subject during December 2025. Mentions limited to other grades (e.g., diesel) do not qualify. Reports referencing a city, district, or locality are attributed to the encompassing federal subject.
- The report must indicate current conditions in December 2025 (e.g., present‑tense descriptions or explicit dating to December 2025). Articles that only recount shortages from earlier months without indicating December conditions do not qualify.

Resolution mechanics
- YES: If five (5) or more distinct Russian federal subjects have at least one qualifying report during the Observation Window.
- NO: Otherwise.
- Timekeeping: Publication time is assessed in UTC. If multiple outlets publish the same event, it counts once for that federal subject. If both AI‑92 and AI‑95 are affected in a single subject, it counts as a single subject.
- Evidence to resolve: The resolver will compile links to qualifying reports and note the federal subject named in each. The body text should clearly state out‑of‑stock conditions or rationing limits for AI‑92 or AI‑95 during December 2025, consistent with the types of conditions reported earlier in 2025.
- If credible, widely‑covered official statements are issued (e.g., regional government orders imposing rationing limits) during the Observation Window, they qualify when they explicitly apply to AI‑92 or AI‑95; price‑cap decrees alone do not qualify unless linked to rationing or out‑of‑stock conditions for these grades.

Start and end dates (UTC)
- Start: 2025‑12‑01 00:00:00 UTC
- End: 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC

Intended ease of resolution
- The list of qualifying outlets and explicit requirement to name AI‑92/AI‑95 are designed to allow a human resolver to verify the outcome in about 10 minutes by collecting 0–5 articles, depending on whether the threshold is met early in the month. Prior months’ coverage demonstrates that such reporting is common and attributable to specific federal subjects.

question: Will the Federal Reserve lower the federal funds target range midpoint by at least 75 basis points between 2025-09-22 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Why this matters: Changes in the federal funds rate influence borrowing costs across the economy and are especially salient for capital-intensive sectors such as REITs (e.g., cost of debt, acquisition economics, and dividend competitiveness versus bonds).

Definitions and context a forecaster needs:
- Federal funds rate: The overnight interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to each other; in recent years, the FOMC sets a target range for this rate. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate and the Federal Reserve Board overview: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm
- Target range: The lower and upper bounds for the federal funds rate set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and announced in Implementation Notes with effective dates. See Implementation Notes via: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases.htm (Monetary Policy section) and the FOMC page: https://www.federalreserve.gov/fomc/
- Basis point (bp): One hundredth of one percentage point (0.01 percentage points). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point
- Midpoint of the target range: The arithmetic mean of the lower and upper bounds of the target range (e.g., a 4.00%–4.25% range has a 4.125% midpoint).

Status quo and data access as of the start date (2025-09-22):
- The baseline (start) target-range midpoint is the midpoint of the FOMC’s target range in effect at 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC, as published by the Federal Reserve. Forecasters can verify this via the Federal Reserve Board’s Open Market Operations page (historical table of target range changes and effective dates): https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm; the relevant Implementation Note for the most recent FOMC action (find under Monetary Policy press releases): https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases.htm; and the Board’s Economy at a Glance – Policy Rate panel for current display: https://www.federalreserve.gov/economy-at-a-glance-policy-rate.htm

Uncertainty drivers (non-exhaustive): Inflation and labor-market data, FOMC projections and communications, financial stability concerns, and macro surprises can shift the path of policy. Multiple scheduled/unscheduled policy actions could occur within the window, but only the net change between the defined timestamps matters for this question.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end window:
- Start: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC
- End: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC

Measurement object and unit:
- Object: The FOMC’s federal funds rate target range (the policy target for the federal funds rate). If at any time within the window the FOMC specifies a single target rate instead of a range, treat that single rate as the midpoint by definition.
- Midpoint: Arithmetic mean of the lower and upper bounds of the target range, expressed in percentage points (ppt). Example: 4.00%–4.25% → midpoint 4.125%.
- Basis point (bp): 0.01 percentage points.

What must happen for “YES”:
- Let M_start be the midpoint of the federal funds target range in effect at 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC.
- Let M_end be the midpoint of the federal funds target range in effect at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Resolve YES if M_end ≤ M_start − 0.75 percentage points (i.e., a decrease of at least 75 bps). Otherwise resolve NO.

Notes and edge cases:
- Net change only: Intermediate hikes/cuts within the period do not directly affect resolution; only the net difference between M_start and M_end matters.
- Effective timing: Use the range “in effect” at the exact timestamps above in UTC. If an FOMC action is announced on a date but has an effective time after the end timestamp, it does not count at end. Similarly, if a change became effective just before the start timestamp, it counts for start.
- Ranges that include quarter fractions (e.g., “4 to 4-1/4 percent”): Convert to decimals (e.g., 4.25%) before averaging the bounds.
- Policy framework change: If the FOMC changes how it communicates the federal funds target (e.g., switches between a range and a point), use the Board of Governors’ own description on the Open Market Operations page and Implementation Notes to determine the policy target, treating a single point as the midpoint.

Primary resolution source (for both start and end values):
- Federal Reserve Board, Open Market Operations page (historical table showing the FOMC’s target federal funds rate or range, basis-point changes, levels, and effective dates): https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm

Secondary/backup sources (if needed to confirm the range in effect at the exact timestamps):
- Federal Reserve Board, Implementation Note(s) for the most recent FOMC action before each timestamp (Monetary Policy press releases): https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases.htm
- Federal Reserve Board, Economy at a Glance – Policy Rate (current display of target range): https://www.federalreserve.gov/economy-at-a-glance-policy-rate.htm
- FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) series for Federal Funds Target Range – Upper Limit (DFEDTARU) and – Lower Limit (DFEDTARL) to compute midpoints historically if necessary: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU and https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARL

Tiebreaker and conflicts:
- If sources conflict, prefer (1) Open Market Operations page; then (2) Implementation Note(s); then (3) Economy at a Glance; then (4) FRED series. All times are interpreted in UTC for inclusion/exclusion at the boundary timestamps.

question: Italy power prices: Will the November 2025 PUN Index GME monthly average be ≥ 110.00 €/MWh?
background:
What is being forecast: This question asks whether the November 2025 monthly average of the PUN Index GME (Italy’s electricity Day-Ahead Market reference index) will be at least 110.00 €/MWh.

Key definitions and sources:
- PUN Index GME: The reference price of electricity traded in the Day-Ahead Market (MGP) that GME calculates under Article 13 of Legislative Decree 210/21 and according to the Ministerial Decree (MASE) of 18 April 2024. Formally: “PUN Index GME shall mean the reference price of electricity traded in the MGP that GME calculates under Article 13 of Legislative Decree 210/21 … in accordance with the procedures indicated in Article 1, para. 2 of the Ministerial Decree of MASE of 18 April 2024 ….”. The GME glossary summarizes it as the average of zonal prices in the Day-Ahead Market, weighted for purchases pertaining to withdrawal portfolios.
- Legal and methodological update in 2025: Per GME’s notice, effective 1 January 2025, in continuity with the prior PUN, GME calculates this reference price as the weighted average of zonal prices and it retains the name “PUN Index GME,” as provided by the MASE Decree of 18 April 2024. GME’s publications page describes PUN Index GME as the reference index of electricity traded in the MGP and links to the results page where values are published.
- Units: Electricity prices in GME’s electricity market are expressed in Euro per MWh. The Integrated Electricity Market Rules specify the unit of measurement for unit prices is Euro/MWh.
- Day-Ahead Market (MGP): The MGP is the main auction market within GME’s spot market where blocks of energy for the following day’s market time intervals (MTUs) are traded; accepted bids/offers clear at zonal marginal prices. GME also computes a compensatory component versus the PUN Index GME for accepted withdrawal bids.
- Calculation granularity: GME calculates the PUN Index GME with respect to the minimum market time interval (MTU) available in the MGP, as an average of zonal prices weighted by purchased quantities; examples in GME’s technical rules cover hourly and quarter-hourly MTUs [52370c; c3dbde].
- Arithmetic mean: The arithmetic mean is the sum of values divided by their count.

Status quo and recent context (for forecasters): In 2024, the PUN Index GME averaged 108.52 €/MWh, its lowest in four years, with monthly prices rising above 100 €/MWh from June and peaking around 128 €/MWh in August and 131–135 €/MWh in November–December 2024, largely tracking natural gas dynamics. The 2025 methodological continuity and publication by GME remain in force [b53a5e; 2aabd3]. Daily/MTU-level PUN Index GME values are published on GME’s MGP results pages linked from the PUN Index GME publications page.

Why this threshold may be uncertain: Italian wholesale electricity prices exhibit significant sensitivity to natural gas prices, hydro/wind output, seasonal demand, imports/exports, and outages. With 2024’s average at ~108.5 €/MWh and late-2024 months well above 110 €/MWh , setting the November 2025 threshold at 110.00 €/MWh targets a range where both higher and lower outcomes are plausible given typical volatility and fundamentals.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution: YES if the November 2025 monthly average of the PUN Index GME is greater than or equal to 110.00 €/MWh; NO otherwise.

How to compute the monthly average precisely:
1) Data to use: Use the PUN Index GME values as published by GME for each minimum market time interval (MTU) in the Day-Ahead Market (MGP) covering the delivery dates from 2025-11-01 through 2025-11-30 inclusive, as displayed on the GME “MGP – Results – PUN” page linked from the PUN Index GME publications page. The PUN Index GME is defined and calculated by GME for each MTU as a weighted average of zonal prices (see formal definition and methodology references) [c3dbde; 52370c; b5291e].
2) Eligible time window: Include all MTUs for delivery on calendar dates 2025-11-01 to 2025-11-30 inclusive. For the avoidance of doubt, November refers to the calendar month in Italy; the MGP MTUs are labeled by GME using local market dates, and November 2025 in Italy is entirely in Central European Time (CET, UTC+1). If in November 2025 the MGP uses hourly or quarter-hourly MTUs, include all such MTUs falling on those calendar dates [52370c; 158e83].
3) Monthly average formula: Compute the unweighted arithmetic mean across all included MTU-level PUN Index GME values in November 2025. Formally, if there are n MTUs in November 2025 with PUN Index GME values x1 … xn (in €/MWh), compute (x1 + x2 + … + xn) / n. This is equivalent to a time-weighted average because each MTU has equal duration within the month.
4) Comparison and rounding: Perform the calculation using the values as published by GME (which may have more than two decimals per the rules) [52370c; c3dbde]. Compute the monthly average to at least three decimal places before comparison. Resolve YES if the computed monthly average ≥ 110.000 €/MWh; otherwise resolve NO.
5) Primary source of truth: GME’s official PUN Index GME publications page and the linked “MGP – Results – PUN” results page will serve as the authoritative source for the MTU-level values. The legal basis, definitions, and units are governed by GME’s Integrated Electricity Market Rules and associated Technical Rules [c3dbde; 52370c; b5291e].
6) Timing of resolution: Resolve once all November 2025 MTUs have been published by GME and are available online, no earlier than 2025-12-10 00:00 UTC and no later than 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC. If GME issues revisions after initial publication, use the values available as of 2025-12-15 23:59 UTC for the computation.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- If GME changes the MTU granularity (e.g., from hourly to quarter-hourly) during November 2025, include all MTUs that GME labels as occurring on the relevant calendar dates; the arithmetic mean across MTUs still applies.
- If one or more MTUs are missing or unavailable online, first check the same-day entries for the PUN Index GME on the GME results page; if still missing as of 2025-12-15 23:59 UTC, exclude only the unavailable MTUs from both the numerator and denominator when computing the mean and document which entries are missing.
- Currency and units are €/MWh as per GME’s rules.

Definitions (with sources):
- PUN Index GME: Reference price of electricity traded in the MGP, calculated by GME under the cited legislation and MASE decree. Also described in GME’s glossary as the average of zonal prices in the MGP weighted for purchases.
- MGP (Day-Ahead Market): GME’s main auction market for next-day delivery where bids/offers for MTUs are submitted and clear at zonal marginal prices; GME computes a compensatory component versus the PUN Index GME for accepted withdrawal bids.
- MTU (Minimum Market Time Interval): The smallest time interval for which the MGP is settled and for which GME calculates the PUN Index GME (e.g., hourly or quarter-hourly), per GME’s rules/technical documentation [52370c; c3dbde].
- Arithmetic mean: Sum of values divided by the number of values.

Context data for forecasters: In 2024, the PUN Index GME averaged 108.52 €/MWh and increased above 100 €/MWh from June, with the highest monthly values in late 2024 (August ~128 €/MWh, November–December ~131/135 €/MWh), broadly tracking gas price movements. The 2025 methodology retains continuity with the prior PUN and remains published by GME [b53a5e; 2aabd3].

Where to find the data:
- PUN Index GME publications page (which defines the index and links to the MGP results “PUN” page).
- Integrated Electricity Market Rules and Technical Rule references governing definitions, units, and calculation method [c3dbde; 52370c; b5291e].

question: Will an executed amendment to Lithium Americas’ DOE ATVM loan grant the U.S. government an equity stake by Dec 31, 2025?
background:
Summary of status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- DOE loan and project structure: Lithium Americas Corp. (LAC) closed a $2.26B loan with the U.S. Department of Energy under the Advanced Technology Vehicles Manufacturing (ATVM) program on 2024-10-28 to finance the Thacker Pass lithium project; the loan carries a 24-year maturity, with repayments starting 2029-01-20 and final maturity on 2048-10-20. Following its JV transaction with General Motors, LAC holds a 62% interest in Thacker Pass and is project manager.
- Construction/financing progress: LAC and GM announced Final Investment Decision (FID) for Phase 1 on 2025-04-01, targeting Phase 1 completion in late 2027; Orion Resource Partners closed a $250M strategic investment. Company updates in Q2 2025 note major construction progress and anticipated first draw on the DOE loan in 2H 2025.
- Negotiations on loan terms in September 2025: On 2025-09-24, LAC stated it is in discussions with DOE and GM regarding first draw conditions, potential amendments to the DOE loan and associated documents, and corresponding consideration, noting incremental DOE requests and that talks are ongoing (no deal concluded as of that date).
- Federal equity stake being pursued: On 2025-09-26, the Associated Press reported the White House is moving forward with a deal that would allow the U.S. government to take a “very small” (<10%) equity stake in LAC as part of changes to the ~$2.3B DOE loan; LAC confirmed ongoing discussions with DOE and GM on loan conditions. On 2025-09-30, Reuters reported that DOE will take a 5% equity stake in LAC and a separate 5% stake in the Thacker Pass JV via no‑cost warrants, tied to renegotiation of the $2.26B loan; Energy Secretary statements indicated Washington would take a stake, with terms being finalized around 2025-09-29. Earlier, on 2025-09-23, Reuters reported the administration sought up to a 10% stake in LAC amid renegotiation of the loan’s amortization, and that LAC had offered no‑cost warrants equating to 5–10% of common shares.

Why this is forecastable now: The public record indicates active negotiations and reported terms for a federal equity stake linked to a loan amendment, but formal execution and disclosure of an amended loan agreement have not yet occurred. Execution before year‑end is plausible yet uncertain given commercial, legal, and political factors.

Key definitions for this question (with references):
- “Equity stake”: any equity security or equity‑linked right that confers a present or future ownership interest in an entity (e.g., common shares, membership interests, or warrants/rights/options to acquire such interests). See general definitions of equity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_(finance)) and stock warrants (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrant_(finance)).
- “Amended loan agreement”: any executed amendment(s) or modification(s) to the definitive DOE ATVM loan agreement (initially closed 2024-10-28 for Thacker Pass) or its associated material transaction documents that are publicly disclosed by LAC or DOE as having been executed, and that explicitly include the U.S. federal equity stake as consideration or a condition related to the loan.
- “Executed”: signed by all required parties such that the amendment is effective per the document or official announcement (evidenced by a dated press release or SEC filing by LAC, or an official DOE/White House announcement).
- “U.S. federal government”: a U.S. executive department or agency (e.g., DOE) or a federal instrumentality acting on its behalf (not state/local governments nor government‑sponsored enterprises).
- Entities: “Lithium Americas Corp.” refers to the publicly listed parent company; “Thacker Pass JV” refers to the joint venture that owns the project (Lithium Nevada Ventures LLC, owned 62% by LAC and 38% by GM).

Current baselines and sources you can check quickly on resolution date:
- LAC’s Newsroom and SEC EDGAR page for Form 8‑K or other filings (LAC has used 8‑Ks to disclose material definitive agreements in 2025) [1ed6c0, 8f4d2].
- DOE or White House press releases, and major wire services (AP, Reuters) that cite on‑the‑record officials or publish copies of documents.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will an executed amendment to Lithium Americas’ DOE ATVM loan grant the U.S. federal government an equity stake between 12:00:00 am Eastern Time on 2025-10-15 and 11:59:59 pm Eastern Time on 2025-12-31?

Resolves Yes if, within the above time window, there is public confirmation from at least one official source that both of the following are true:
1) An amendment (or set of amendments) to the definitive DOE ATVM loan agreement or its associated material transaction documents for the Thacker Pass project has been executed (i.e., signed and effective), and
2) As part of that amendment, the U.S. federal government receives (or is granted rights to receive) an equity stake in either (a) Lithium Americas Corp. or (b) the Thacker Pass JV (Lithium Nevada Ventures LLC). The equity stake may be conveyed via equity securities or equity‑linked instruments (e.g., no‑cost warrants) as long as they provide a right to present or future ownership.

Acceptable official sources (primary sources preferred):
- Lithium Americas press release or SEC filing (e.g., Form 8‑K, 10‑Q, 10‑K) that explicitly states both execution of a loan amendment and the U.S. federal equity stake [8f4d2, 1ed6c0].
- A U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) or White House press release that explicitly states both elements.
- If primary sources are not yet posted, a major wire service report (Associated Press or Reuters) that quotes named officials or includes/documented evidence explicitly stating both elements will suffice. In case of conflict, SEC filings by LAC take precedence.

Additional clarifications:
- Size of the stake: No minimum percentage is required; any non‑zero equity stake qualifies if explicitly tied to the loan amendment. Public reporting in late September 2025 described contemplated stakes of about 5% in LAC and 5% in the JV via no‑cost warrants, tied to renegotiation of the $2.26B loan , and earlier reports discussed less‑than‑10% stakes , but these figures are background only and not thresholds for resolution.
- What does not count: (a) A standalone equity transaction by the U.S. government that is not explicitly linked to an executed amendment of the DOE loan (e.g., an investment absent any loan modification); (b) a non‑binding term sheet or LOI without execution; (c) press speculation or anonymous sourcing without corroboration by the official sources above.
- Timezone: All times are Eastern Time (U.S.).

Resolves No if the above conditions are not met by 11:59:59 pm Eastern Time on 2025-12-31.

Context citations: Loan program, maturity and JV ownership ; construction/FID timeline and expected DOE loan draw ; company disclosure of ongoing amendment talks and consideration ; reporting on U.S. pursuit of equity stake and contemplated 5%+5% warrants tied to loan renegotiation.

question: On December 31, 2025 (UTC), will Ukraine’s underground gas storage “working gas” be at least 11.2 bcm?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- System overview: Ukraine has 13 underground gas storage (UGS) facilities with a total working capacity of about 30.9 bcm per year; Ukrtransgaz operates 12 of these facilities.
- Seasonal lows in early 2025: Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data cited by S&P Global Commodity Insights reported Ukrainian working gas stocks at 34.4 TWh, equivalent to 3.2 bcm, as of February 3, 2025. This underscores how low inventories can fall after winter withdrawals.
- Autumn 2024 benchmark: Ahead of the 2024–25 heating season, Ukraine’s storage stood at 12.5 bcm on October 28, 2024 per S&P Global Commodity Insights.
- Autumn 2025 status and plans: As of September 17, 2025, Ukraine had approximately 11–12 bcm in storage (11 bcm per a Ukrainian grid official; 12 bcm per energy consultancy ExPro). The government’s target for winter storage is 13.2 bcm. Analysts and former officials estimated Ukraine needed an additional 1–2 bcm costing roughly $0.5–$1.0 billion, with imports mainly via Hungary and increasing via Poland; import capacity over existing interconnectors exceeds 60 mcm/day. Last winter’s 12.8 bcm proved insufficient amid Russian attacks cutting domestic output by about 0.5 bcm.

Why 11.2 bcm? Inventories typically peak in late October/early November and then decline with heating demand. Given mid-September levels near 11–12 bcm and plans to inject more gas before withdrawals begin, an end-of-December threshold of 11.2 bcm aims to maximize uncertainty and discriminability for forecasters.

Key definitions and links for clarity:
- “Underground gas storage (UGS)” refers to subsurface reservoirs used to store natural gas, such as depleted fields, aquifers, or salt caverns; see Underground gas storage (Wikipedia): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_gas_storage.
- “Working gas” (also called “working gas volume”) is the portion of gas in storage that can be withdrawn under normal operations; it excludes “buffer” or “cushion” gas that remains in the reservoir to maintain pressure. See U.S. EIA glossary entries for Working Gas and Base (Cushion) Gas: https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php.
- “bcm” means billion cubic metres; “cubic metre” unit overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_metre.
- “Ukrtransgaz (UTG)” is Ukraine’s storage system operator: https://utg.ua/en/.

Status quo summary (cited): 13 UGS, ~30.9 bcm working capacity ; 3.2 bcm in early Feb 2025 ; 12.5 bcm late Oct 2024 ; 11–12 bcm mid-Sept 2025 with a 13.2 bcm winter target and planned purchases/imports.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the amount of “working gas” in Ukraine’s underground gas storage at end-of-day December 31, 2025, measured in bcm.

Event time and timezone:
- The measurement time is 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- If the primary source reports the figure in local time (Kyiv time), we will convert to UTC for equivalence and accept values explicitly labeled “as of end-of-day December 31, 2025.”

Primary metric and unit:
- The metric is total “working gas” in all Ukrainian UGS facilities, in bcm. “Working gas” excludes buffer/cushion gas (see EIA glossary link in Background).

Resolution rule:
- Resolve Yes if the reported working gas volume in Ukrainian UGS is ≥ 11.2 bcm at the specified time.
- Resolve No if it is < 11.2 bcm at that time.

Primary source of truth (preferred):
- An official Ukrtransgaz (UTG) publication stating the end-of-day December 31, 2025 working gas volume in bcm. Acceptable channels include: UTG’s website (https://utg.ua/en/), official press releases, or official UTG social media posts (e.g., X/Twitter) that clearly state the figure and date.

Secondary sources (if the primary source is unavailable for that exact timestamp):
- Credible wire services or industry publications that cite UTG’s figure for end-of-day December 31, 2025, e.g. Reuters, Interfax-Ukraine, S&P Global Commodity Insights. Use the first such report published no later than January 5, 2026 and ensure it attributes the number to UTG and clearly references the date.

Important exclusions and tie-breaking:
- Use “working gas” figures only; statements that include buffer/cushion gas are not eligible. If multiple credible sources disagree, prefer the source directly from UTG. If two UTG statements conflict, prefer the later statement that explicitly specifies end-of-day December 31, 2025.
- Do not use data reported solely in energy units (e.g., TWh/GWh) unless the source also provides the corresponding bcm value or an explicit conversion specific to Ukraine for that reporting period. This avoids ambiguity from varying calorific values.

Verifiability: A resolver should be able to find a single UTG statement or a wire-service report citing UTG within ~10 minutes. Context on the system and prior data comes from IEA , S&P Global on February 2025 levels , S&P Global on October 2024 levels , and Reuters on September 2025 status, targets, and import plans.

Start date: Not applicable (the question assesses a single measurement at a specific time rather than events over a range).

Ambiguity handling:
- If the only available figure is reported for “end of December 2025” without a precise timestamp, use that value provided it is explicitly attributed to UTG and clearly excludes buffer gas.
- If Ukraine’s UGS are partially offline due to damage, still measure the total working gas in the operational facilities at the specified time; the threshold applies to the aggregate “working gas” across all UGS in Ukraine as defined above.

question: Will at least one Atlantic tropical cyclone first reach Category 3 (major hurricane) intensity between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-11-30 23:59 UTC?
background: Context and status quo (as of 2025-10-01): NOAA’s updated 2025 Atlantic hurricane season outlook (issued Aug 7, 2025) projected 13–18 named storms, 5–9 hurricanes, and 2–5 major hurricanes, and stated the season remained on track for above-normal activity. The Saffir–Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale (SSHWS) defines Category 3 hurricanes as 111–129 mph sustained winds, and Categories 3–5 are termed “major hurricanes”. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) and National Weather Service define “maximum sustained wind” as the highest 1-minute average wind at 10 meters over unobstructed exposure at a given time , and NHC defines a hurricane as a tropical cyclone with maximum sustained winds of at least 64 kt (74 mph) using the U.S. 1-minute average. The NHC issues operational advisories in UTC at regular 6-hour cycles (0300, 0900, 1500, 2100 UTC), with Special Advisories and Tropical Cyclone Updates (TCUs) issued at any time for significant changes, and these products include the current maximum sustained wind (intensity). For verification, NHC maintains a 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive that hosts the operational advisory packages for each storm. The “Atlantic basin” refers to the North Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico. The forecasting window in this question focuses on the late-season period from October 15 through November 30, 2025 (UTC), which lies within the official Atlantic hurricane season (June 1–November 30) as defined by NHC.
resolution_criteria: Yes resolution: Resolve “Yes” if any Atlantic tropical cyclone’s first attainment of Category 3 (major hurricane) intensity occurs between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-11-30 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. “First attainment” is defined operationally as the earliest NHC product issuance in which the cyclone’s maximum sustained winds are stated as at least 111 mph (i.e., Category 3 or higher on the SSHWS), using the U.S. 1-minute average at 10 m exposure. Eligible NHC operational products are: Tropical Cyclone Public Advisory (TCP), Tropical Cyclone Forecast/Advisory (TCM), Special Advisory, and Tropical Cyclone Update (TCU); we will use the product’s UTC issuance time printed in the header to determine whether it falls within the window. The cyclone must be within the NHC Atlantic basin area of responsibility (North Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico). No resolution: Resolve “No” if no such first attainment occurs within the stated window. Scope and clarifications: • Only operational NHC advisory products are used for resolution; any post-storm reanalysis or later database revisions do not affect the outcome. • If a TCU or Special Advisory first announces the upgrade to major hurricane intensity before the next scheduled advisory, that TCU/Special Advisory’s UTC issuance time governs. • If a cyclone reached Category 3 intensity for the first time before 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC (even if it remains Cat 3+ during the window), it does not count. If it first reaches Category 3 intensity at or after 2025-12-01 00:00 UTC, it does not count. Verification sources: • NHC 2025 Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive (storm-specific pages for the Atlantic) to retrieve the earliest operational product showing maximum sustained winds ≥111 mph and its UTC issuance time. • NHC product documentation to confirm intensity fields and UTC issuance conventions, and eligible product types (TCP/TCM/TCU/Special Advisory). Definitions and references for forecasters: • Major hurricane and Category 3 threshold (SSHWS). • Maximum sustained wind (1-minute, 10 m). • Hurricane (NHC definition) and Atlantic season dates. • Atlantic basin geography. • 2025 seasonal context (NOAA August update).

question: Will INPE’s PRODES estimated annual deforestation rate for Brazil’s Legal Amazon (Aug 1, 2024–Jul 31, 2025) exceed 6,500 km²?
background:
What is being measured and by whom:
- PRODES is Brazil’s official satellite-based program that measures annual clear‑cut deforestation (“corte raso”) in the Brazilian Legal Amazon and reports it in square kilometers. PRODES defines deforestation as the complete removal of primary forest cover by clear‑cutting or the final stage of progressive forest degradation where there is complete loss of canopy, regardless of subsequent land use; PRODES quantifies deforested areas larger than 6.25 hectares. PRODES typically reports an annual “estimated” rate (“estimativa da taxa”) for the period August 1 to July 31, followed later by a consolidated rate. For 2024, the estimate was published with methodology and timing details, noting that results are typically presented in November.

Geographic scope:
- “Legal Amazon” (Amazônia Legal) is a socio‑geographic region established by Brazilian federal law that includes the states of Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Pará, Rondônia, Roraima, Tocantins, the northern part of Mato Grosso, and part of Maranhão. It is a planning region and is distinct from the Amazon biome; PRODES Amazonia monitors this Legal Amazon region.

Recent baseline and cadence:
- For the 2022–2023 cycle (Aug 2022–Jul 2023), INPE reported a consolidated PRODES rate of 9,064 km² (a decrease from the prior period).
- For the 2023–2024 cycle (Aug 2023–Jul 2024), the official PRODES rate announced on Nov 6, 2024 was 6,288 km², the lowest result in 9 years according to the government’s presentation. INPE’s technical note with the 2024 estimate (covering Aug 1, 2023–Jul 31, 2024) also reports 6,288 km² and explains the estimation timeline (estimate in Nov; consolidation later).

Context for 2025 (informative only; not used for resolution):
- In February 2025, early-warning deforestation alerts (from DETER, a separate INPE system) reached a historical low for that month in the Legal Amazon at 80.95 km², down 64.26% versus February 2024. DETER alerts are not the same as PRODES annual rates but are sometimes used as leading indicators.

Why this is forecastable now:
- The PRODES estimate for the Aug 1, 2024–Jul 31, 2025 period is typically published in November and should be available well before Dec 31, 2025, while the final consolidated figure usually follows in the subsequent year. The 6,500 km² threshold is close to the most recently published year (6,288 km² for 2023–2024), aiming for a non‑trivial forecast.
resolution_criteria:
Question:
- Resolve “Yes” if, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (INPE) publishes an official PRODES estimated annual deforestation rate (“estimativa da taxa de desmatamento”) for the Brazilian Legal Amazon for the period Aug 1, 2024 through Jul 31, 2025 that is strictly greater than 6,500.0 km². Otherwise resolve “No”.

Event window and units:
- Measurement period: Aug 1, 2024 00:00:00 UTC to Jul 31, 2025 23:59:59 UTC (the PRODES “year” for Amazonia Legal).
- Measurement: square kilometers (km²) of deforestation as defined by PRODES.
- Threshold interpretation: “exceed” means strictly greater than 6,500.0 km².

Definitions (binding):
- “PRODES estimated annual deforestation rate” (for Amazônia Legal): The single km² value labeled as the PRODES estimate for the relevant cycle (Aug–Jul) published by INPE for the Legal Amazon region (Amazônia Legal). PRODES monitors clear‑cut deforestation in primary forests and tallies areas larger than 6.25 hectares; it defines deforestation as complete removal of primary forest cover by clear‑cutting or the final stage of progressive degradation with total canopy loss.
- “Legal Amazon” (Amazônia Legal): The region established by Brazilian federal law for planning purposes, encompassing Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Pará, Rondônia, Roraima, Tocantins, the northern part of Mato Grosso, and part of Maranhão; distinct from the Amazon biome.

Primary resolution source (in order of preference; all official):
1) An INPE technical note or news release on a gov.br domain that states the PRODES Amazônia Legal estimated rate for the Aug 2024–Jul 2025 cycle (e.g., analogous to the 2024 technical note and the Nov 6, 2024 announcement presenting 6,288 km²).
2) An official Brazilian federal government announcement (e.g., MCTI or Planalto/SECOM) that reports the PRODES Amazônia Legal estimated rate for the Aug 2024–Jul 2025 cycle (analogous to the Nov 6, 2024 release).

Disambiguation and conflicts:
- If multiple official INPE publications present different PRODES estimate values for the same Aug 2024–Jul 2025 cycle on or before the deadline, use the most recent INPE publication timestamped on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- If no INPE publication of the PRODES estimated rate for the Aug 2024–Jul 2025 cycle can be found by the deadline, resolve “No” (i.e., not exceeding 6,500 km² as officially known by that date). This mirrors the typical cadence where estimates are published in November, while consolidated figures often appear in the following year.

Notes:
- This question intentionally uses the estimated rate (not the later consolidated rate), because consolidated values for the Aug 2024–Jul 2025 period are typically released in the following year (2026), after the market close date for this forecast.
- Examples of prior official publications include: the consolidated 2022–2023 PRODES rate of 9,064 km² , and the 2023–2024 PRODES rate of 6,288 km² announced on Nov 6, 2024 , consistent with the 2024 technical note.

question: By 2025‑12‑31 (23:59:59 UTC), will the EU publish in the Official Journal a binding legal act that imposes a prohibition on “new investments” by EU persons in one or more special economic zones located in the Russian Federation?
background:
Status quo as of 2025‑10‑01: On 2025‑09‑19, the European Commission proposed a 19th package of sanctions against Russia that, among other measures, explicitly included “a ban on investments in Russian Special Economic Zones linked to the war”. Independent reporting on the proposal likewise stated that the package envisaged bans on investment in certain Russian special economic zones relevant for the war effort. In a related statement on 2025‑09‑20, President von der Leyen said the Commission was “restricting transactions with entities in special economic zones,” indicating the SEZ concept is a specific focus area within the package. The most recently adopted package prior to the proposal was the 18th package on 2025‑07‑18.

What counts as adoption/publication of EU sanctions: EU restrictive measures are adopted by the Council, apply to any person or entity under EU jurisdiction (anyone in EU territory, any EU national worldwide, and companies incorporated under the law of an EU member state), and are made legally binding upon publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (OJ). The OJ is the EU’s official gazette for legal acts and is accessible on EUR‑Lex.

Definitions and legal context relevant to this question:
- Special Economic Zone (SEZ): An area within a country whose business and trade laws differ from the rest of the country, typically to encourage investment via incentives such as customs, tax, and regulatory facilitation. An illustrative example in Russia is the Alabuga SEZ (an industrial/production SEZ in Tatarstan), which open‑source reporting links to drone production for Russia’s military, highlighting why SEZs may be considered “linked to the war” in EU discussions. This example is provided for context; the resolution relies solely on the text of EU legal acts as described below.
- New investments (EU sanctions usage): Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 uses a well‑established formulation when it prohibits “new investments,” e.g., in the Russian energy or mining sectors. Prohibited forms include: (a) acquiring new or extending existing participation in a legal person operating in the relevant sector in Russia; (b) granting new loans or credit or otherwise providing financing (including equity capital) to such a person; (c) creating new joint ventures with such a person; and (d) providing investment services directly related to (a)–(c). This common formulation will be used to interpret whether a published act imposes “a prohibition on new investments.”

Why this is forecast‑worthy now: The Commission’s proposal signals intent but Member State negotiations could alter scope, timing, and drafting. Measures could emerge as an explicit “investment ban in SEZs,” a narrower listing‑based prohibition covering only some SEZs, or be softened (e.g., to “transactions” rather than “investments”). Whether the final, published legal text will contain a binding prohibition on new investments in SEZs by EU persons before year‑end remains uncertain.

Source to check for resolution: The Official Journal on EUR‑Lex, where Council Regulations/Decisions on Russia sanctions are published.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and time zone: Eligible acts are those first published in the Official Journal of the European Union between 2025‑10‑01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

Question will resolve Yes if and only if at least one binding EU legal act published in the OJ within the window contains an operative prohibition (in its enacting terms or annexes; recitals alone do not count) that does any of the following with respect to one or more special economic zones located in the Russian Federation:
1) Expressly states a “prohibition on investments” (or “new investments”) by persons under EU jurisdiction in such SEZs; or
2) Uses the established “new investments” construction from Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 to prohibit, in relation to such SEZs, one or more of the following activities: (a) acquiring new or extending existing participation; (b) granting new loans or credit or otherwise providing financing, including equity capital; (c) creating new joint ventures; (d) providing investment services directly related to (a)–(c).

For the purposes of this question:
- “EU persons”/scope of application means any person or entity within EU territory, any EU national wherever located, and any company or organisation incorporated under the law of an EU member state.
- “Special economic zone” refers to a zone within the Russian Federation that is recognised as an SEZ in the text of the EU act itself (e.g., by explicitly using the term “special economic zone(s)” and/or listing specific zones by name). General characteristics of SEZs are as described by standard references , but resolution hinges on the act’s own wording.
- “Binding EU legal act” means a Council Regulation and/or Council Decision (or equivalent binding legal instrument) that imposes restrictive measures; adoption is evidenced by publication in the OJ.

Exclusions and clarifications:
- A measure that only restricts or prohibits “transactions with entities in special economic zones” without imposing an investment/new‑investment prohibition as defined above will not satisfy the criterion and resolves No.
- References confined to recitals, press releases, Q&As, or non‑binding guidance do not count; only the binding legal text published in the OJ counts.
- It is sufficient if the prohibition applies to specific named SEZ(s) in Russia; it need not cover all Russian SEZs.
- If multiple qualifying acts are published, a single qualifying act is sufficient for a Yes.
- If a qualifying act is published within the window and subsequently amended, suspended, or repealed within the window, the question still resolves Yes (the event of publication of the prohibition occurred within the window).

Operational resolution steps for the arbiter:
1) Search the OJ on EUR‑Lex for Russia sanctions acts published in the window.
2) Read the enacting terms and annexes to identify whether they contain either an explicit “prohibition on investments (new investments)” in Russian SEZs or the 833/2014‑style prohibition covering (a)–(d) above targeted at Russian SEZs.
3) If found, resolve Yes; otherwise resolve No.

Context sources for forecasters:
- Commission statement on the 19th package proposing a ban on investments in Russian SEZs (2025‑09‑19) ; contemporaneous reporting.
- Statement noting restrictions on transactions with entities in SEZs (2025‑09‑20).
- Applicability/adoption mechanics (Council; OJ publication).
- OJ/EUR‑Lex as source of truth.
- Example of an SEZ implicated in war‑related production (Alabuga).

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will Gazprom or CNPC publicly announce that the Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline project has reached Final Investment Decision (FID)?
background:
Summary of the status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
• On 2025-09-02, reporting indicated that Gazprom announced a “legally binding memorandum” to build the Power of Siberia 2 (PoS‑2) gas pipeline, envisioned to deliver about 50 billion cubic metres (bcm) per year to China via Mongolia; however, pricing, construction details, and timeframes were not announced. The lack of pricing and schedule disclosures suggests that a project‑sanctioning decision had not yet been made as of that date.
• On 2025-09-03, President Vladimir Putin said that pricing for PoS‑2 gas would be “market‑based,” reiterated the 50 bcm/year design for PoS‑2 via Mongolia, and noted separate plans to raise Power of Siberia 1 supplies to 44 bcm/year from 38 bcm/year, with Far Eastern route deliveries targeted to rise from 10 to 12 bcm/year; commercial terms for PoS‑2 were to be finalized later.
• The Power of Siberia 2 project is a proposed Russia‑to‑China natural gas pipeline. Earlier iterations were known as the “Altai gas pipeline”; the currently preferred concept routes via Mongolia (the Mongolian section is often referred to as “Soyuz Vostok”). The design capacity commonly cited for the Mongolian route is around 50 bcm/year. The Altai/PoS‑2 label has historically referred to a Russia‑to‑China pipeline concept, with the Mongolian route later gaining preference.
• Definition for use in this question: A Final Investment Decision (FID) is the last step of determining whether to move forward with the sanctioning and construction of an infrastructure project—that is, the formal decision to proceed to full‑scale execution.

Why this is forecastable now: The September 2025 memorandum raised expectations but left key commercial elements unresolved (e.g., pricing and timing), making an explicit FID announcement by year‑end plausible but uncertain. Forecasters must weigh negotiation dynamics between Gazprom and CNPC, macro conditions, and political signals.

Key references for context and definitions:
• Reuters coverage of the September 2025 memorandum and outstanding terms.
• S&P Global Commodity Insights coverage of Putin’s “market‑based” pricing comments, PoS‑2 capacity, and PoS‑1 expansion figures.
• Global Energy Monitor overview of PoS‑2/Soyuz Vostok (project description, route via Mongolia, 50 bcm/y capacity).
• Wikipedia article on the Altai gas pipeline (context for the PoS‑2 alias and project history).
• Natural Gas Intelligence glossary definition of FID.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and time zone:
• Eligible announcements are those first made public between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. The question resolves as soon as sufficient evidence is available, and no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Entities and project covered:
• “Power of Siberia 2” (PoS‑2) refers to Russia’s proposed pipeline project to deliver natural gas to China via Mongolia, with a commonly cited design capacity around 50 bcm/year. Earlier iterations were known as the Altai gas pipeline; the Mongolian section is often referred to as Soyuz Vostok. The announcement must unambiguously pertain to this project.

Definition of “Final Investment Decision (FID)” for resolution purposes:
• FID means the final decision to proceed with project sanctioning and full‑scale execution (also commonly described as “taking FID” or “project sanction”).

What counts as a qualifying “publicly announced” FID:
Resolve Yes if, within the time window, any one of the following occurs and explicitly states that FID has been taken for PoS‑2:
1) An official press release or statement posted on the official corporate website or verified newsroom of Gazprom PJSC (or Gazprom Group) or China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) that includes the exact term “Final Investment Decision” or “FID,” or an unambiguous synonym such as “project sanctioned,” clearly referring to PoS‑2 as defined above; or
2) An official regulatory disclosure by Gazprom or CNPC to a recognized exchange/regulator (e.g., disclosures compliant with applicable Russian or Chinese securities/ministerial requirements) that explicitly states that FID has been taken for PoS‑2; or
3) A report by a major wire service (e.g., Reuters, Interfax) that directly quotes a named Gazprom or CNPC official stating that FID has been taken for PoS‑2. The quote must unambiguously indicate that the final decision to proceed with the project has been made.

Exclusions and clarifications:
• NOT sufficient: Memoranda of understanding, memoranda (including “legally binding memoranda”), framework agreements, heads of terms, feasibility studies, pre‑FID engineering (FEED), EPC contract awards, route or environmental approvals, government‑to‑government communiqués, or pricing framework statements, unless the communication explicitly states that FID has been taken for PoS‑2. The September 2025 memorandum reported by Reuters, for example, did not include pricing/schedule and therefore did not constitute an FID.
• Partial segment FIDs: An FID taken only for a sub‑segment (e.g., the Mongolian “Soyuz Vostok” section) will count ONLY if the announcement explicitly states that this constitutes the FID for the overall Power of Siberia 2 project. Otherwise, partial or enabling‑works decisions do not count.
• Language: Announcements in Russian or Chinese are acceptable. Reliable translations (including those provided by the issuer or quoted verbatim by major wire services) may be used to determine whether the FID criterion is satisfied.

Source hierarchy and tie‑breaking:
• If sources conflict, prioritize (1) the issuer’s official press release or regulatory filing; failing that, (2) a major wire service report with a direct quote from a named company official; failing that, (3) multiple independent major outlets corroborating the same explicit FID claim. If ambiguity remains after applying these rules, resolve No.

Resolution:
• YES if any qualifying source above appears within the time window and explicitly states that FID has been taken for PoS‑2.
• NO otherwise, including if no such explicit announcement is found by the deadline.

Notes for resolvers:
• For context on the September 2025 memorandum and outstanding commercial terms, see Reuters. For pricing comments and capacity figures, see S&P Global Commodity Insights. For definitions of PoS‑2/Soyuz Vostok and design capacity, see Global Energy Monitor  and the Altai gas pipeline article. For the FID definition applied here, see Natural Gas Intelligence.

question: Will the VIX close’s 30‑trading‑day rolling average exceed 20.0 at any point between 2025-09-22 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Summary and definitions:
- The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) is a benchmark measuring the market’s expectation of 30‑day forward-looking volatility of the S&P 500, calculated from SPX option prices. The VIX is disseminated intraday; this question uses the official daily closing value (“close”).
- Official daily VIX closing values are published by Cboe on its VIX Historical Data page, which serves as the primary resolution source. The St. Louis Fed’s FRED series VIXCLS mirrors the Cboe daily close and can serve as a secondary source if the primary is unavailable.
- Status quo: The latest FRED observation (VIXCLS) available as of 2025-09-12 shows a VIX close of 14.76, indicating mid‑teens volatility in the recent period.
Rationale for threshold/window: A sustained 30‑trading‑day average above 20.0 indicates an extended period of elevated equity‑market volatility, which historically corresponds with heightened hedging/risk aversion and often higher derivatives activity. The 30‑trading‑day window avoids brief spikes while remaining short enough to plausibly occur within the resolution window.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and timing:
- Eligible period: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. Only VIX trading days whose Cboe‑published date falls within this range are eligible for inclusion in windows.
What resolves “Yes”:
- Define a “trading day” as any U.S. market day for which Cboe publishes an official VIX daily closing value on its VIX Historical Data page.
- For every set of 30 consecutive trading days entirely within the eligible period, compute the arithmetic mean of the 30 official VIX closing values (no rounding before averaging; use the numeric values as published). If any such 30‑trading‑day mean is strictly greater than 20.0, resolve “Yes”. Otherwise, resolve “No”.
Calculation specifics:
- “30‑trading‑day rolling average” means the arithmetic mean over windows of 30 consecutive trading days (excluding weekends/market holidays because no official close is published). “Above 20.0” means strictly greater than 20.0.
- Use Cboe’s published daily closing values as the authoritative dataset. In the unlikely event the Cboe page is inaccessible at resolution time, use the FRED VIXCLS daily close as the fallback. If both are inaccessible, defer resolution until data are accessible.
- If Cboe later revises specific closes during the eligible period, use the values as they appear on the Cboe Historical Data page at the time of resolution. In case of discrepancy between Cboe and FRED, Cboe prevails.
Definitions and references:
- “VIX”/“Cboe Volatility Index” refers to the index defined by Cboe as a measure of 30‑day expected volatility implied by S&P 500 options ; see also the encyclopedic overview.
Resolution timing:
- The market will be considered resolved once the official VIX closing value for 2025-12-31 (if it is a trading day) is published by Cboe, or earlier if a qualifying 30‑trading‑day average is observed and verified using the above method.
