question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the IAEA publicly report conducting any in-field verification at an Iranian safeguarded nuclear facility other than Bushehr?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01
- Following attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in mid-June 2025, the IAEA Director General stated that the Agency “stopped conducting verification activities in Iran” and, by the end of June, withdrew all inspectors due to safety concerns. He also noted that, since June 13, the Agency had no access to safeguarded nuclear facilities in Iran except for the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP), which was inspected “a few days” prior to his Sept 8 statement.
- The IAEA’s Sept 3, 2025 report (GOV/2025/50) documents that the Agency stopped all in‑field verification and monitoring activities in Iran on June 13, 2025, withdrew inspectors by end‑June for safety reasons, and has had no access to any safeguarded nuclear facilities since June 13, with the exception of BNPP. It further notes a loss of continuity of knowledge of nuclear material inventories and that, since June 13, monitoring has relied on analysis of commercially available satellite imagery and open sources.
- On July 2, 2025, Iran enacted a law suspending cooperation with the IAEA; this is noted in the Sept 3 report. On June 13, 2025, the IAEA also publicly highlighted the security situation and referenced a Board of Governors resolution adopted June 12, 2025 on Iran’s safeguards obligations.

Key terms and definitions (with authoritative sources)
- International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA): the UN nuclear watchdog; official site hosts reports, statements, and news.
- Safeguards and verification: a set of technical measures through which the IAEA verifies States’ compliance with peaceful-use obligations.
- Inspection: a set of verification activities carried out by IAEA inspectors at a facility or location outside facilities to verify that declared nuclear material remains in peaceful use; includes ad hoc, routine, and special inspections.
- Inspection activities (in-field verification): verification activities performed by IAEA inspectors during and in connection with inspections at facilities, including nuclear material accountancy, application of containment/surveillance, environmental sampling; design information verification (DIV) is normally performed during facility visits and may occur during inspections. For the purpose of this question, “in-field verification” refers to any such on-site safeguards verification activity by IAEA inspectors at a nuclear facility in Iran.
- Examples of in-field safeguards activities that DO count: design information verification (DIV), physical inventory verification (PIV), routine/ad hoc/special inspections at a safeguarded nuclear facility.
- Activities that do NOT count as in-field verification: remote monitoring (data transmitted off-site for evaluation) and analysis of open-source information such as commercial satellite imagery.
- Iranian safeguarded nuclear facility (for this question): any nuclear facility in Iran that the IAEA identifies and treats as a facility under Iran’s NPT Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement in its official reports. Examples listed in recent IAEA reporting include: Fordow Fuel Enrichment Plant (FFEP), Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant (FEP) and Pilot FEP (PFEP), Uranium Conversion Facility (UCF), Fuel Manufacturing Plant (FMP), Fuel Plate Fabrication Plant (FPFP), Enriched UO2 Powder Plant (EUPP), Khondab/Arak Heavy Water Research Reactor (KHRR), Heavy Water Production Plant (HWPP), Tehran Research Reactor (TRR), Jaber Ibn Hayan Multipurpose Laboratory (JHL), and the Molybdenum, Iodine and Xenon Radioisotope Production facility (MIX), among others; BNPP (Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant) is explicitly excluded by the question wording.

Resolution sources context
- The IAEA’s “Monitoring and Verification in Iran” topic page aggregates relevant Iran safeguards reports, statements, and news and can serve as a discovery hub. The IAEA’s “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” page aggregates Board/DG reports on Iran by year. Director General statements are published on iaea.org (e.g., the Sept 8, 2025 Board statement). These official iaea.org sources will be used for resolution.

Why this is forecastable
- As of early September 2025, only limited activity at BNPP had occurred, while broader in-field verification remained halted; subsequent developments could plausibly lead either to partial resumption at another facility or continued suspension through year-end, leaving meaningful uncertainty for forecasters.
resolution_criteria:
Question
- Resolve whether, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, the IAEA publicly reports that its inspectors conducted any in-field verification at an Iranian safeguarded nuclear facility other than the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP).

Start and end dates (UTC)
- Eligible publication window: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What counts as a qualifying report
- A qualifying “public report” must be an official IAEA publication on iaea.org published within the window, specifically one of the following:
  1) An IAEA Board of Governors report (GOV/… document) or Director General report posted on the IAEA’s “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” page ; or
  2) A Director General statement posted on iaea.org (News Center > Statements) ; or
  3) An IAEA News/Press release or article posted under the IAEA’s Iran “Monitoring and Verification in Iran” topic page.

Event that must be reported
- The qualifying IAEA publication must explicitly state that IAEA inspectors conducted in-field verification (see definitions below) at at least one Iranian safeguarded nuclear facility other than BNPP. The publication must either:
  a) Name at least one such non-BNPP facility (e.g., FFEP, Natanz FEP/PFEP, UCF, FMP, FPFP, EUPP, KHRR/Arak, HWPP, TRR, JHL, MIX, etc.) ; or
  b) State unambiguously that inspections/in-field verification occurred at a safeguarded nuclear facility other than BNPP (e.g., wording that clearly excludes BNPP).

Definitions to apply
- “In-field verification” (counts): on-site safeguards verification activities by IAEA inspectors at a facility, including inspections (ad hoc, routine, special), design information verification (DIV), physical inventory verification (PIV), nuclear material accountancy checks, application of containment/surveillance, and environmental sampling performed at the facility.
- “Not in-field verification” (does not count): remote monitoring with data transmitted off-site, analysis of commercial satellite imagery, or other open-source assessments without inspector presence at the facility.
- “Iranian safeguarded nuclear facility”: a nuclear facility in Iran that the IAEA treats as a facility under Iran’s NPT Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement in its official reports (examples listed above). BNPP is excluded by the question wording.

What does NOT qualify
- Any activity solely at BNPP (Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant) does not qualify.
- References to “inspections” or “monitoring” that do not clearly indicate inspector presence on-site at a safeguarded nuclear facility (e.g., remote monitoring, satellite analysis) do not qualify.
- Third-party media reports or statements by non-IAEA officials do not qualify unless they are IAEA publications on iaea.org as specified above.

Resolution
- YES if at least one qualifying IAEA publication (as defined) is posted on iaea.org within the publication window and explicitly indicates that in-field verification by IAEA inspectors occurred at any Iranian safeguarded nuclear facility other than BNPP on or after 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC.
- NO if no such qualifying IAEA publication is posted within the window.

Tie-breaking and conflicts
- If multiple IAEA publications within the window conflict, prefer (in order): Board of Governors GOV reports > Director General reports/statements > IAEA News/Press releases. If conflicts remain, prefer the most recent publication within the window.

Documentation for resolvers
- Use the following IAEA pages to search for qualifying publications: “Monitoring and Verification in Iran” topic page ; “IAEA and Iran – IAEA Board Reports” aggregation page ; and the IAEA News Center Statements section (example of format and hosting shown in the DG’s Sept 8, 2025 statement). Context on the June 2025 halt in in‑field verification, withdrawal of inspectors, Bushehr-only access, and loss of continuity of knowledge is documented in GOV/2025/50 and DG statements.

question: Will the Canada Post segment report a Q3 2025 loss before tax of at least $300 million?
background: Context as of 2025-09-30: Canada Post’s financial results have been deteriorating. In Q2 2025, the corporation reported its largest-ever quarterly loss before tax of $407 million for the Canada Post segment, attributing the decline primarily to sharp weakness in Parcels due to labour uncertainty; the Group of Companies loss before tax for the same quarter was $325 million. In Q3 2024, Canada Post (segment) recorded a loss before tax of $315 million, with Parcels revenue down 5.8% year-over-year and parcel volumes down 9.6%. For full-year 2024, Canada Post reported a loss before tax of $841 million (segment) – its seventh consecutive annual loss – and indicated that ongoing customer shifts and structural challenges would affect results into 2025, with management communicating expectations of larger, unsustainable losses ahead absent major changes. Canada Post publishes quarterly financial results both as corporate news releases and as formal quarterly financial reports; the corporate news release list serves as the public index for such announcements. The Quarterly financial reports page states that federal Crown corporations must publicly release Q1–Q3 reports within 60 days of each quarter’s end, and it hosts the PDFs for these reports (e.g., the Q3 2024 report), implying Q3 2025 should be posted by late November 2025. These data points together suggest elevated uncertainty for Q3 2025, with plausible outcomes above or below the $300 million threshold.
resolution_criteria:
Eligible period and time zone: This question resolves based on publications available up to 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Definitions and scope:
- Canada Post segment: The core postal operations reported separately from the Canada Post Group of Companies (which includes subsidiaries such as Purolator). Where both are reported, use the ‘Canada Post’ segment figure, not the Group of Companies figure.
- Q3 2025: The third fiscal quarter of 2025 as defined in Canada Post’s official financial reporting (i.e., the quarter referred to in the Q3 2025 quarterly financial report and corresponding corporate news release).
- Loss before tax (LBT): The figure explicitly labelled “loss before tax” for the Canada Post segment for Q3 2025, as stated in the sources below. Use the value as presented (typically rounded to the nearest million). If Canada Post reports a profit before tax for Q3 2025 instead of a loss, treat this as LBT < $300,000,000 for the purposes of resolution.
- Currency: All dollar figures are interpreted as Canadian dollars (CAD), consistent with Canada Post’s reporting.

Question: Resolve Yes if the Canada Post segment’s Q3 2025 loss before tax is greater than or equal to $300,000,000 CAD. Resolve No if it is less than $300,000,000 CAD, or if no qualifying source (see below) has published a Q3 2025 figure by the deadline.

Primary resolution source (precedence order):
1) The Q3 2025 Quarterly Financial Report PDF posted on Canada Post’s “Quarterly financial reports” page. If posted, use the “loss before tax” figure for the Canada Post segment for Q3 2025 from this report. This page is the authoritative host for these reports and indicates Crown corporations must publish Q1–Q3 reports within 60 days of quarter-end.
2) If the Q3 2025 Quarterly Financial Report is not yet available by the deadline, use the Q3 2025 corporate news release on Canada Post’s “Corporate news releases” list, taking the “loss before tax” figure for the Canada Post segment for Q3 2025 as stated there.

Conflict handling: If both sources exist and the figures conflict, the Quarterly Financial Report PDF (source 1) takes precedence over the corporate news release.

Non-publication contingency: If neither source has published a Q3 2025 figure by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, resolve No (the proposition was not met by the deadline).

Notes for verifiers: Examples of how these figures are presented include the Q2 2025 news release (“loss before tax of $407 million” for the Canada Post segment) and the Q3 2024 news release (“loss before tax of $315 million”). Corporate news releases and quarterly PDFs are listed at the URLs indicated by the cited pages.

question: Between 2025-10-01 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will an EU or G7 government legally constitute a special-purpose vehicle (or equivalent) with the stated purpose of holding and managing immobilised Russian sovereign cash or its extraordinary revenues to service, secure, or repay loans to Ukraine?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- G7 $50B loan architecture: In June 2024, G7 countries agreed to provide around $50 billion in loans to Ukraine, to be serviced and repaid by future flows of interest (“extraordinary revenues”) accruing on frozen Russian sovereign assets; annual flows were often cited in the ~€2.5–€3.5 billion range. 
- EU legal framework for extraordinary revenues: On 12 Feb 2024, the EU adopted a decision and a regulation requiring EU central securities depositories (CSDs) holding >€1 million of Central Bank of Russia (CBR) assets to segregate the extraordinary cash balances and the ensuing net profits, prohibiting disposal; this was a precursor to channeling those net profits to support Ukraine. On 21 May 2024, the Council greenlit using net windfall profits from immobilised Russian assets, with funds paid biannually from CSDs; the regime took effect from 15 Feb 2024. 
- Revenue distribution mechanism: On 25 Oct 2024, G7 finance ministers approved the ERA (Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration) Loan initiative, under which the distribution of extraordinary revenues to repay ERA lenders is managed via the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism (ULCM), agreed by EU co‑legislators. 
- Early 2025 implementation: On 10 Jan 2025, the European Commission disbursed the first €3 billion tranche of its contribution under an exceptional Macro‑Financial Assistance (MFA) loan to Ukraine, specifying that Ukraine is not expected to directly repay; repayment will be ensured by extraordinary profits from immobilised Russian assets collected through the ULCM. 
- Notably, none of the cited EU or G7 documents establishing the current revenue use and distribution arrangements explicitly create or rely on a new special‑purpose holding vehicle for the immobilised cash itself; instead, they focus on directing and distributing extraordinary revenues from EU‑based CSDs (notably where most CBR‑linked assets are immobilised) to service loans.

Key definitions and links for clarity:
- Special purpose vehicle (SPV): A separate legal entity created for a specific, narrow purpose, often with a ring‑fenced balance sheet and defined mandate. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special-purpose_entity (link provided for definitional clarity; not a resolution source).
- G7: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States, plus the European Union as a non‑enumerated member. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 (link provided for definitional clarity; not a resolution source).
- Immobilised Russian sovereign assets and extraordinary revenues: As used in the EU framework, these refer to assets and reserves of the CBR immobilised under EU restrictive measures, and the net windfall profits accruing to EU CSDs due to those measures, respectively.
- Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism (ULCM): The EU mechanism designated to collect and allocate extraordinary revenues to service ERA loans to Ukraine.

Why this question: Creating an SPV (or legally equivalent vehicle) to hold and manage immobilised cash or its extraordinary revenues would mark a distinct governance step beyond the current ULCM distribution framework, with meaningful legal, financial, and political implications. It is plausible within the time window yet uncertain, making for a high‑entropy, research‑sensitive forecast.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible acts must occur between 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- The market question resolves as soon as determinative evidence is available, and no later than 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What resolves “Yes”:
Resolve Yes if, within the time window, there is conclusive public evidence that an SPV or legally equivalent vehicle has been legally constituted by one or more EU institutions/member states or G7 governments, and all of the following conditions are met:
1) Establishment: The vehicle is constituted by a formal legal act that creates a distinct legal personality or an explicitly ring‑fenced fund or facility with its own governing rules (e.g., EU regulation/decision in the Official Journal; an intergovernmental treaty/accord deposited or ratified; a national law or decree; a corporate registry incorporation where the controlling shareholder(s) are EU/G7 government(s) or the EU itself).
2) Purpose: The founding instrument explicitly states the vehicle’s primary purpose is to hold and manage immobilised Russian sovereign cash balances and/or the extraordinary revenues therefrom (as defined in EU acts) in order to service, secure, or repay loans to Ukraine (including loans under the ERA/ULCM framework or a substantively similar arrangement).
3) Source of funds: The instrument authorizes the vehicle to receive transfers of such cash balances or extraordinary revenues from an EU CSD (e.g., Euroclear) or from an EU‑designated collection mechanism (e.g., ULCM).

What resolves “No”:
Resolve No if by the cutoff there is no such constituting legal act, or if announcements/MoUs exist without creating a distinct legally constituted vehicle, or if any created entity lacks the explicit purpose described above. Specifically, the following do NOT by themselves qualify:
- The continued operation of the ERA/ULCM revenue distribution without a newly constituted special‑purpose holding vehicle.
- EU Council/Commission acts that only direct CSD extraordinary revenues to EU budgetary channels or existing facilities, without creating a new vehicle to hold/manage the immobilised cash or those revenues.
- Press releases or statements that do not correspond to a constituting legal act, or vehicles created solely by private actors without EU/G7 governmental establishment.

Acceptable resolution sources (examples):
- EUR‑Lex (Official Journal) for EU regulations/decisions: https://eur-lex.europa.eu (use the specific act page for verification).
- Government gazettes or official registers (e.g., Belgium’s Moniteur Belge for a Belgium‑registered vehicle; national legislation databases for other G7/EU states).
- Depositaries’ treaty records for intergovernmental agreements.
- Corporate registries showing incorporation of a government‑owned vehicle with qualifying purpose in its statutes.
- Major wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg) may be used to corroborate and locate the primary legal document but are not sufficient alone; the constituting legal instrument must be identifiable.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- Funding vs. formation: The vehicle need not have received funds yet; a valid constituting legal act with the enumerated purpose suffices for Yes.
- Naming: Terms such as “facility,” “fund,” “entity,” “trust,” or similar qualify if the other Yes criteria are met.
- Scope of assets: For this question, “immobilised Russian sovereign cash” includes cash balances and net extraordinary revenues generated by immobilised CBR assets at EU CSDs, as used in EU legal acts.
- Non‑qualifying related mechanisms: The ULCM itself, as a distribution mechanism for extraordinary revenues, does not count as an SPV for this question absent a constituting act meeting the Yes criteria.

Examples for guidance (non‑exhaustive, hypothetical):
- Yes example: An EU decision creates the “Ukraine Reparations Asset Management Facility,” a government‑owned entity empowered to receive extraordinary revenues from Euroclear via the ULCM and to manage them to service ERA loans; the decision is published in the Official Journal (Yes).
- No example: A Commission press release announces continued biannual transfers of net windfall profits from CSDs to EU budget instruments under existing law, with no new legal entity created (No).

question: At COP30, will Parties adopt an official decision that commits to scaling climate finance for developing countries to at least USD 1 trillion per year by 2035?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Event and timing: The 30th UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) is scheduled for 10–21 November 2025 in Belém, Brazil.
- Current finance landscape from COP29 (2024): Governments agreed to a New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance of at least USD 300 billion per year by 2035 for developing countries, and additionally agreed to secure efforts of all public and private entities to scale up finance to developing countries to USD 1.3 trillion per year by 2035. Analysis by the World Resources Institute characterizes the USD 300 billion as a commitment and the USD 1.3 trillion as an aspirational mobilization target calling on all actors, rather than a binding commitment by Parties. The “Baku to Belém Roadmap to 1.3T” was launched to scale up public and private finance toward USD 1.3 trillion for developing countries, with the process expected to be a major focus leading up to COP30. The COP29 and COP30 Presidencies have been mandated to explore how to scale finance to USD 1.3 trillion (emphasizing grants, concessional and non-debt-creating instruments) and to report back by COP30.
- Why this is uncertain and interesting: COP29 set a quantified goal well below USD 1 trillion (USD 300 billion), while establishing a roadmap process aimed at USD 1.3 trillion that—so far—does not constitute a binding Party commitment. Whether COP30 elevates that roadmap into an operative, quantified commitment by Parties at or above USD 1 trillion per year by 2035 is a live negotiation question with high policy salience and meaningful uncertainty.

Definitions and term clarity:
- Parties: The countries and regional organizations that are Parties to the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement; at UN climate conferences, Parties meet in multiple formal sessions (e.g., COP, CMP, CMA) to adopt decisions. See overview of UN Climate Change Conferences structure.
- Decision text: An official decision adopted in plenary at COP30 (e.g., under COP 30, CMP 20, or CMA 7) and published by UNFCCC as a session decision.
- International climate finance: Finance for climate mitigation/adaptation directed to developing countries, generally cross-border and from public and private sources. For clarity on “climate finance,” see the UNFCCC/SCF definition: “Finance that aims at reducing emissions, and enhancing sinks of greenhouse gases and aims at reducing vulnerability of, and maintaining and increasing the resilience of, human and ecological systems to negative climate change impacts”. In this question, “international climate finance … to developing countries” requires the decision language to specify developing countries or “developing country Parties.”
- Currency and amount: “USD 1 trillion per year” means at least 1,000,000,000,000 United States dollars annually. Acceptable synonymous phrasings include “one trillion US dollars,” “US$1 trillion,” “USD 1,000 billion,” or “$1 tn.”
- Operative commitment vs non-commitment: For this question, an operative commitment is decision text using verbs such as “decides,” “agrees,” “adopts,” or “commits” applied to Parties and setting the quantified finance level. Non-commitment language (e.g., “notes,” “welcomes,” “recognizes,” “encourages,” “invites,” “calls on/all actors”) does not count.

Primary sources for resolution:
- UNFCCC COP30 page hosting official information and links to decisions and session documents.
- UNFCCC Decisions portal (session filters typically include COP/CMP/CMA for the relevant year). If for any reason final decisions are not yet posted on Dec 31, 2025, rely on official UNFCCC press releases or the COP30 Presidency communications summarizing adopted decisions, and corroborating coverage by credible wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, AFP).
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Eligible decision adoptions occur between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC.

Resolve YES if, by 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, at least one official COP30 outcome decision text (adopted under COP 30, CMP 20, or CMA 7) includes all of the following:
1) A quantified finance level of at least USD 1 trillion per year (see Currency and amount definitions).
2) A specified timeframe “by 2035.”
3) The beneficiary scope explicitly refers to “developing countries” or “developing country Parties.”
4) The operative verb applies to Parties (e.g., “decides,” “agrees,” “adopts,” “commits”) such that Parties are committing to the quantified level. Language directed to “all actors,” “non-State actors,” or generic “efforts to mobilize” without committing Parties does NOT satisfy this criterion.

Resolve NO if no such decision text meeting all four criteria is adopted and publicly available by the resolution deadline, or if references to USD 1 trillion per year by 2035 exist only in non-commitment or non-Party-directed language (e.g., a roadmap, call to action, or encouragement).

Source of truth and verification steps:
- Primary: The official UNFCCC publication of COP30 decisions. Start from the COP30 conference page  and navigate to Decisions for COP 30/CMA 7/CMP 20. Open each finance-related decision and search for language meeting the four criteria. Record the exact decision identifier (e.g., “X/CMA.7”) and the excerpt.
- Fallback (if decisions are not yet posted by the deadline): Use official UNFCCC press releases or COP30 Presidency communications that quote the adopted decision text. Cross-verify with credible wire services (e.g., Reuters, AP, AFP) that reproduce or quote the operative language.

Notes:
- Synonymous phrasings for the amount and timeframe (e.g., “one trillion US dollars annually by 2035”) count if they unambiguously meet the threshold and date.
- If multiple decisions exist, the presence of any single decision meeting all four criteria is sufficient for a YES outcome.
- Language that sets a lower figure (e.g., USD 300 billion per year by 2035) or that merely establishes a “roadmap” or “efforts to mobilize” toward USD 1.3 trillion does not satisfy the commitment requirement.

question: Will UK headline CPI (12‑month rate) for November 2025 be at least 3.5%?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30: The Office for National Statistics (ONS) schedules its statistical bulletin “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025” for publication on 17 December 2025 at 07:00 (UK local time), and notes it is not yet published as of now. The latest published headline Consumer Prices Index (CPI) annual rate is 3.8% for the 12 months to August 2025 (“The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 3.8% in the 12 months to August 2025, unchanged from July.”). The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Summary (September 2025) states: “Twelve-month CPI inflation was 3.8% in August, and is expected to increase slightly in September, before falling towards the 2% target thereafter.”.

Definitions and scope:
- Consumer Prices Index (CPI): The UK measure of consumer price inflation published monthly by the ONS. For background and wording conventions, see the ONS bulletin for August 2025.
- 12‑month rate (year-over-year, YoY): The percentage change in the CPI over the 12 months to the specified month, expressed in percent. ONS bulletins phrase this as “The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by X% in the 12 months to [month year]…”.
- Headline CPI: For this question, “headline CPI” means the CPI 12‑month rate (not CPIH, not “core” CPI, and not any seasonally adjusted, trimmed, or alternative measure).
- At least: Greater than or equal to (≥).
- Units and rounding: Resolution uses the CPI 12‑month rate value as reported in the ONS bulletin text and/or headline figures for November 2025, which ONS typically reports to one decimal place. No independent recalculation or alternative rounding is applied.

Why this is non-trivial: As of August 2025, headline CPI is 3.8% , and the Bank of England indicated a near-term uptick in September followed by a decline towards target. Whether November’s YoY CPI prints at or above 3.5% depends on developments in energy, food, administered prices, and base effects, creating plausible uncertainty around the 3.5% threshold within the time frame. 

Key source to monitor: The ONS bulletin page “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025” (release scheduled 17 December 2025, 07:00).
resolution_criteria:
- Question: Will the UK headline CPI 12‑month rate for November 2025 be at least 3.5%?
- Start and end for eligibility: This question pertains solely to the CPI 12‑month rate for November 2025. Resolution will occur after the scheduled ONS publication on 2025-12-17.
- Primary resolution source: The ONS statistical bulletin page “Consumer price inflation, UK: November 2025”.
- Measured quantity: The CPI 12‑month rate (YoY) for November 2025, as presented by ONS in the bulletin’s headline figures and/or main points (e.g., phrased as “The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by X% in the 12 months to November 2025”). This phrasing is consistent with ONS conventions.
- Decision rule: If the published CPI 12‑month rate for November 2025 is ≥ 3.5%, resolve Yes; otherwise resolve No.
- Time zone and timing: Resolution will use the value as displayed on the bulletin page on and after publication on 2025-12-17. For avoidance of ambiguity, the check will be performed no later than 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC. If ONS issues an official correction to the November 2025 bulletin before 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC, the corrected value will be used; corrections after that time will be disregarded.
- Exclusions: CPIH, “core” CPI, alternative inflation measures, or any values derived from datasets other than the named bulletin are not considered unless the bulletin is temporarily unavailable; in such a case, the same November 2025 CPI 12‑month rate as reported by ONS on the bulletin page once accessible will be used.

Source-of-truth schedule and current status: ONS indicates the November 2025 CPI bulletin is scheduled for 17 December 2025 at 07:00 and is not yet published as of today. The most recent CPI 12‑month rate published is 3.8% for August 2025 , and the Bank of England expects a slight rise in September followed by a move towards 2% thereafter.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC), will there be at least one publicly posted DSCA “Major Arms Sales” notification for Colombia or an official DoD/Colombia MoD announcement of a new U.S. defense contract for Colombia?
background:
Status quo as of Oct 1, 2025: On Sept 16, 2025, the U.S. designated Colombia as having “failed demonstrably” to meet counternarcotics obligations; the determination stated U.S. assistance remained vital, indicating a national interest waiver preserved aid. On Sept 17, 2025, Colombia publicly announced it was halting purchases of U.S. arms in reaction to the decertification.

Relevant institutions and processes:
- Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA): A U.S. Department of Defense agency that manages security cooperation programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS). DSCA posts proposed FMS notifications as press releases on its “Major Arms Sales” page, with standard elements including country, items, and estimated cost.
- Foreign Military Sales (FMS): A U.S. government program through which foreign governments purchase U.S. defense articles and services; the U.S. DoD (through DSCA) procures on their behalf.
- Arms Export Control Act (AECA) Section 36 congressional notification: For certain arms sales meeting defined monetary thresholds, DSCA delivers the required certification notifying Congress; thresholds and review periods vary by country group (e.g., for non-NATO/non-major allies, MDE ≥ $14m, defense articles/services ≥ $50m, design/construction ≥ $200m; 30-day review).
- U.S. Department of Defense contract announcements: The DoD publishes contract awards (≥ $7.5m) daily at 5 p.m. ET on its official site; these announcements can include base awards and modifications.

Why this matters: Colombia’s halt suggests a potential pause in new U.S. defense procurements, but political, operational, and procurement needs may still drive activity via FMS or other channels. DSCA notifications signal proposed sales; DoD contract announcements signal awarded work that can include FMS to partner nations. Forecasters should track DSCA’s “Major Arms Sales” page and DoD contracts pages, as well as official Colombian MoD communications, to detect any resumption.

Links to recurring sources where resolution-relevant information is typically posted:
- DSCA Major Arms Sales page: https://www.dsca.mil/press-media/major-arms-sales 
- DoD Contracts page: https://www.defense.gov/News/Contracts/ 
- Colombia Ministry of Defense site (news): https://www.mindefensa.gov.co/prensa/noticias (site homepage: https://www.mindefensa.gov.co/) (navigation shown via site search results; forecasters should verify any specific announcement appears on these official domains) [No citation for the exact news URL beyond site discovery, but DoD/DSCA sources are primary]

Key definitions used in resolution criteria below are grounded in the above sources.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible events must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

Resolution (YES/NO):
- Resolve YES if at least one of the following is publicly posted during the time window:
  1) A DSCA “Major Arms Sales” press release that lists the Government of Colombia as the purchasing country for a proposed Foreign Military Sale (FMS) (as posted on https://www.dsca.mil/press-media/major-arms-sales).
  2) A U.S. Department of Defense official contract announcement (posted on https://www.defense.gov/News/Contracts/) for a new base contract or new delivery order that explicitly references Foreign Military Sales to Colombia (e.g., includes phrasing such as “Foreign Military Sales (Colombia)” or “to the Government of Colombia”).
  3) An official press/news announcement on the Colombia Ministry of Defense’s official domain (mindefensa.gov.co) or on the official domain of a Colombian armed service (e.g., ejercito.mil.co, fac.mil.co, armada.mil.co) stating that the Ministry or service has signed a new purchase contract with a U.S.-headquartered defense supplier for defense articles or services, and clearly identifying the contract as signed within the time window. The announcement must state that a contract/agreement has been signed (MoUs/LOIs do not count) and must name the U.S. supplier and the military equipment or services being procured.

Definitions and clarifications:
- “DSCA ‘Major Arms Sales’ press release”: A press release on DSCA’s official “Major Arms Sales” page that states “The State Department has made a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale” and that “The Defense Security Cooperation Agency delivered the required certification notifying Congress,” and includes the purchasing country, description of items/services, and estimated cost.
- “Foreign Military Sales (FMS)”: The U.S. government program through which DoD (via DSCA) procures defense articles/services on behalf of foreign governments.
- “AECA Section 36 congressional notification”: The legal requirement for DSCA to notify Congress of certain proposed sales meeting specified thresholds and review periods; thresholds for non-NATO/non-major allies include MDE ≥ $14m and defense articles/services ≥ $50m; for NATO/major allies the thresholds are higher and review periods shorter.
- “U.S. Department of Defense official contract announcement”: An entry on the DoD’s News/Contracts page which the DoD publishes daily for awards of ≥ $7.5m, containing contract details such as contractor, amount, contracting activity, and, when applicable, references to FMS customers. For this market, the announcement must explicitly reference Colombia as the FMS customer.
- “New base contract or new delivery order”: A contract award that is not solely a modification to an existing contract. Announcements that are pure modifications (e.g., “modification to a previously awarded contract”) do not count unless they clearly state they add a new, distinct delivery order or new scope specifically and explicitly for Foreign Military Sales to Colombia within the announcement text. To avoid ambiguity, only base awards and new delivery orders count.
- “Official announcement” (Colombia): A publication on the official website of Colombia’s Ministry of Defense or of a Colombian service branch, clearly labeled as a news release or communiqué, that explicitly states a contract has been signed, identifies the U.S. supplier, and describes the military equipment/services.
- “U.S. defense supplier”: A company headquartered in the United States that manufactures or provides defense articles/services regulated under the AECA/ITAR framework; for the purpose of this question, the supplier’s U.S. headquarters must be evident from the company’s official site or from the announcement itself.
- “Defense articles/services”: As generally used in the FMS/AECA context, items or services for military use, including those appearing on the U.S. Munitions List; in practice, DSCA and DoD announcements unambiguously identify defense articles/services.

Exclusions (do NOT count):
- Announcements involving only non-U.S. suppliers.
- Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs), Letters of Intent (LOIs), framework agreements, or general cooperation agreements without a signed purchase contract.
- Renewals, extensions, or amendments to existing contracts that do not constitute a new base award or new delivery order.
- Deliveries, training milestones, or sustainment activities without an associated new contract signing or DSCA notification in the time window.
- Direct Commercial Sales (DCS) that are not publicly and unambiguously posted via an official government source meeting the above criteria (this question centers on DSCA notifications and DoD/Colombian MoD official postings).

How to verify at resolution:
- Check DSCA’s “Major Arms Sales” page for any notifications listing Colombia during the window.
- Check the DoD News/Contracts page for any entries during the window that explicitly reference Foreign Military Sales to Colombia or awards “to the Government of Colombia,” and confirm they are base awards or new delivery orders.
- Check mindefensa.gov.co (and official Colombian service domains) news/press sections for official announcements of signed contracts with U.S.-headquartered defense suppliers within the window.

Resolve NO if none of the above conditions are met within the defined time window.

Notes:
- DSCA’s thresholds and posting conventions are specified by DSCA resources and the AECA framework.
- The background context of decertification and Colombia’s announced halt is provided for forecasting context only and does not itself determine resolution.

question: Will ANRE approve and publish a decision, effective by December 31, 2025, setting the regulated natural-gas supply price (without VAT) at the exit from low‑pressure distribution networks at least 10% above its September 1, 2025 level?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Supply/billing transition: Moldovagaz and Energocom signed a seven‑month transitional agreement under which Energocom supplies natural gas to end consumers from September 1, 2025, while Moldovagaz continues billing and customer service. The article states that current tariffs remain in effect until ANRE approves new regulated prices.
- Market liberalization steps: The Energy Ministry indicated that by October 1, 2025 ANRE would approve a schedule for gradual market liberalization and launch a consumer price‑comparison tool, with Energocom taking over the public service obligation (PSO) role for gas supply and procuring on the free market.
- ANRE’s regulated price framework and recent decisions: ANRE maintains a page listing regulated prices/tariffs by service, pressure level, unit, and VAT status for natural gas under PSO and last‑resort supply. Prices are expressed in lei per 1000 m³ without VAT, and categories are indexed to network pressure classes (low/medium/high/transport). The page references recent decisions, including HCA nr. 517 of 25.08.2025 for Energocom’s last‑resort supply prices and prior adjustments for Moldovagaz, and details pressure classifications used in Moldova’s gas network.
- Baseline price in effect on 2025-09-01: ANRE Decision HCA nr. 517 (25.08.2025) approves regulated natural‑gas supply prices (without VAT, lei/1000 m³) for Energocom under last‑resort supply, effective September 1, 2025. The price applicable at the exit from low‑pressure distribution networks is 13,886 lei/1000 m³ (without VAT). HCA 517 explicitly states these prices, units, VAT status, and effective date (September 1, 2025).
- Evidence of recent price adjustments: In late 2024, ANRE adjusted regulated supply prices for Moldovagaz effective December 1, 2024, illustrating that regulated prices are actively revised; these were also specified per pressure level and without VAT.

Key definitions and units (for this question):
- Regulated natural‑gas supply price: The ANRE‑approved price per 1000 m³ (without VAT) for supplying natural gas to final consumers under public service obligation/last‑resort supply, published in formal ANRE decisions and summarized on ANRE’s natural gas page.
- Household proxy: For the purposes of this question, “regulated household gas tariff” means the regulated natural‑gas supply price (without VAT, lei/1000 m³) at the exit from low‑pressure distribution networks (“ieșire din rețelele de distribuție a gazelor naturale de joasă presiune”) as defined and published by ANRE. This proxy focuses the forecast on a single, public, consistently reported price point.
- Pressure categories: Moldova’s gas network pressure classes used by ANRE include low (≤0.005 MPa), medium (>0.005–≤0.3 MPa), high (>0.3–≤1.2 MPa), and transport (transmission network), which are referenced in ANRE’s price/tariff tables.
- Units and taxation: Prices are expressed in Moldovan lei (MDL) per 1000 cubic meters and are “fără TVA” (without VAT) in the ANRE price tables.

Baseline value and threshold:
- Baseline: 13,886 lei/1000 m³ (without VAT), the low‑pressure exit regulated supply price effective on September 1, 2025 under HCA 517.
- Threshold: 10% above baseline equals ≥ 15,274.6 lei/1000 m³ (without VAT). Any exact published price at or above 1.10 × 13,886 qualifies.

Why this is forecastable and non‑trivial: ANRE’s timing and magnitude of adjustments depend on procurement costs (Energocom buys on regional hubs), seasonal demand, regulatory methodology, and the transition from Moldovagaz to Energocom. The agency has adjusted prices multiple times historically, but whether a ≥10% increase will be approved and effective by year‑end is uncertain and researchable using public decisions.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and time zone:
- Eligible decisions must be approved/published between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What counts for resolution:
- Define the metric: For this question, the “regulated household gas tariff” is the regulated natural‑gas supply price (without VAT, lei/1000 m³) at the exit from low‑pressure distribution networks, as specified in formal ANRE decisions (e.g., HCA format) and summarized on the ANRE natural gas page.
- Baseline: 13,886 lei/1000 m³ (without VAT), the low‑pressure exit regulated supply price effective on September 1, 2025 per HCA nr. 517 (enters into force on 1 September 2025).
- Threshold: “at least 10% higher” means the published price is ≥ 1.10 × 13,886 = 15,274.6 lei/1000 m³ (without VAT).
- Effective date requirement: The qualifying ANRE decision must specify an effective date on or before 2025-12-31 (local date as stated in the decision text). If multiple decisions are published in the window, a single decision meeting the threshold and effective‑date requirement suffices for “Yes.”

Resolve Yes if:
- ANRE publishes (on anre.md or in the Monitorul Oficial) a formal decision within the event window that sets the regulated natural‑gas supply price (without VAT) at the exit from low‑pressure distribution networks to a value ≥ 15,274.6 lei/1000 m³, and that decision’s effective date is on or before 2025-12-31.

Resolve No if:
- No such ANRE decision is published in the event window, or any published decision’s specified low‑pressure exit price is < 15,274.6 lei/1000 m³, or the decision’s effective date is after 2025-12-31.

Primary source of truth and how to verify:
- Check ANRE’s official natural gas page (which lists regulated prices, units, VAT status, pressure categories, and links/refs to decisions) for updated price tables and decision references. For exact values, consult the relevant ANRE decision PDF(s), structured like HCA nr. 517 which includes a price table and effective date. If the ANRE website is temporarily unavailable, verification via the corresponding decision publication in the Monitorul Oficial (Official Gazette of the Republic of Moldova) also counts.

Out of scope:
- Distribution service tariffs, transmission entry/exit tariffs, auxiliary services, VAT changes, and non‑regulated commercial offers are excluded; only the regulated supply price at the low‑pressure distribution exit point under PSO/last‑resort supply applies.

question: By 31 Dec 2025, will any G7 country show two consecutive quarters of negative q/q real GDP growth with the second quarter being Q3 2025?
background:
Overview: This question operationalizes a “technical recession” signal using official quarterly real GDP data. It asks whether, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, at least one G7 country will have two consecutive quarters of negative quarter-on-quarter (q/q) growth in real GDP, with the second quarter being Q3 2025. This design avoids ambiguity and timing issues inherent in formal “recession” declarations (e.g., by the U.S. NBER) that may occur long after the fact.

Key definitions and context (as of today, 2025-09-22):
- G7: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States. See Group of Seven description for membership and scope: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7.
- Real GDP: Inflation-adjusted gross domestic product; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product#Real_GDP.
- Quarter-on-quarter (q/q) growth: The percent change in seasonally adjusted real GDP from one quarter to the next. “Negative” means strictly < 0.00%.
- Seasonally adjusted (SA): Seasonal adjustment removes predictable calendar effects; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seasonal_adjustment.
- Why target Q2–Q3 2025: Q2 2025 GDP estimates are already available or imminently revised across G7 countries, and Q3 2025 “first” or “second” estimates are typically released by late Oct–Dec. Focusing on whether Q2 and Q3 are both negative enables resolution by year-end even if Q4 data are not yet released.

What to monitor (official resolution sources):
- United States: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) GDP news releases and tables: https://www.bea.gov/data/gdp/gross-domestic-product
- Canada: Statistics Canada “The Daily” and GDP tables (expenditure-based, quarterly): https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/type/data?subject_levels=29
- United Kingdom: Office for National Statistics (ONS) GDP bulletins: https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossdomesticproductgdp
- Germany: Destatis national accounts (BIP) releases: https://www.destatis.de/EN/Themes/Economy/National-Accounts-Domestic-Product/_node.html
- France: INSEE GDP (PIB) releases: https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/2830547
- Italy: ISTAT quarterly national accounts (PIL) releases: https://www.istat.it/en/economy
- Japan: Cabinet Office (ESRI) Quarterly Estimates of GDP: https://www.esri.cao.go.jp/en/sna/sokuhou/sokuhou_top.html

Interpretive notes:
- Agencies use slightly different headline conventions (e.g., U.S. BEA often reports annualized quarter-over-quarter rates (SAAR), while others report non-annualized q/q). The sign (positive/negative) is invariant to annualization. Preliminary/second/third estimates may differ; see resolution rules below.
resolution_criteria:
Start and end of observation window:
- Start: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC. End (resolution deadline): 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Eligible sequence of quarters: Q2 2025 and Q3 2025 only. The second quarter in the sequence must be Q3 2025.

Question restated precisely:
- Resolve YES if, by the resolution deadline, at least one G7 country’s official statistics show that both Q2 2025 and Q3 2025 quarter-on-quarter (q/q) growth rates in seasonally adjusted real GDP are strictly negative (< 0.00%), according to that country’s national statistical authority’s standard quarterly GDP publication.
- Otherwise resolve NO.

Definitions and country-specific measures to use:
- “Real GDP” means the agency’s volume/chain-volume, price-adjusted GDP series.
- “Quarter-on-quarter (q/q) growth” means the agency’s headline quarterly percent change from the preceding quarter on a seasonally adjusted basis. For agencies that headline SAAR (annualized) rates, the SAAR sign determines negativity (a negative SAAR implies negative non-annualized q/q).

Country mappings (acceptable series/measure for each):
- United States: BEA real GDP, quarter-over-quarter annualized growth rate in the quarterly GDP news release (sign determines negativity). Source: BEA GDP page: https://www.bea.gov/data/gdp/gross-domestic-product
- Canada: Statistics Canada expenditure-based real GDP, quarterly percent change (seasonally adjusted; as presented in The Daily). Source: https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/type/data?subject_levels=29
- United Kingdom: ONS GDP (chained volume measure), quarter-on-quarter growth (seasonally adjusted) in “GDP first/quarterly estimate” bulletins. Source: https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossdomesticproductgdp
- Germany: Destatis BIP, price-, seasonally- and calendar-adjusted quarter-on-quarter change. Source: https://www.destatis.de/EN/Themes/Economy/National-Accounts-Domestic-Product/_node.html
- France: INSEE PIB en volume (CVS-CJO), quarter-on-quarter change. Source: https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/2830547
- Italy: ISTAT PIL (valori concatenati, destagionalizzati e corretti per gli effetti di calendario), quarter-on-quarter change. Source: https://www.istat.it/en/economy
- Japan: ESRI (Cabinet Office) real GDP, seasonally adjusted, quarter-to-quarter growth rate (first/second preliminary acceptable). Source: https://www.esri.cao.go.jp/en/sna/sokuhou/sokuhou_top.html

Publication and versioning rules:
- Use the latest official estimate published by the relevant agency on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Preliminary, second, and third estimates all count; later revisions after the deadline do not affect resolution.
- If an agency publishes both SAAR and non-annualized q/q in the same release, either may be used to determine the sign; signs must agree (they will). If conflicting values are published within separate documents on the same date, use the more recent timestamp on the agency’s site.
- If Q3 2025 has not been officially published by the agency by the deadline for a given country, that country cannot satisfy the criterion.

Edge cases and clarifications:
- “Negative” means strictly less than +0.00% (i.e., any value < 0.00%). Rounding: use the value as reported to its published precision; a reported −0.0% counts as negative only if the sign is explicitly negative.
- If an agency temporarily withdraws a release, use the last valid version accessible on the agency’s official site before the deadline.
- Only one country meeting the criterion is sufficient for YES. If none meet it, resolve NO.

Primary resolution sources (not exhaustive, but preferred):
- BEA GDP news releases and interactive tables (US): https://www.bea.gov/data/gdp/gross-domestic-product
- Statistics Canada “The Daily” GDP (Canada): https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/type/data?subject_levels=29
- ONS GDP bulletins (UK): https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossdomesticproductgdp
- Destatis national accounts BIP (Germany): https://www.destatis.de/EN/Themes/Economy/National-Accounts-Domestic-Product/_node.html
- INSEE PIB (France): https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/2830547
- ISTAT quarterly national accounts (Italy): https://www.istat.it/en/economy
- Japan ESRI quarterly GDP (Japan): https://www.esri.cao.go.jp/en/sna/sokuhou/sokuhou_top.html

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31, will OFAC impose correspondent or payable-through account (secondary) sanctions on at least one non-U.S. financial institution for knowingly conducting or facilitating a significant transaction on behalf of Cartel de los Soles or Tren de Aragua?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- On July 25, 2025, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Cartel de los Soles (CdS) pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13224 (as amended) and explicitly warned that foreign financial institutions (FFIs) engaging in certain transactions involving the designated person may risk the imposition of secondary sanctions. The release also states that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on U.S. correspondent or payable‑through accounts for an FFI that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person designated under the relevant authority. Press release: https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0207
- OFAC sanctioned Tren de Aragua (TdA) as a transnational criminal organization on July 11, 2024 under E.O. 13581, as amended. The press release describes TdA’s activities across the Western Hemisphere. Press release: https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2459
- The July 25, 2025 OFAC release notes that, on February 20, 2025, the U.S. Department of State designated both TdA and the Sinaloa Cartel as Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) and Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs), bringing TdA within the scope of E.O. 13224 for sanctions purposes.

Key definitions and mechanics:
- Secondary sanctions (for purposes of this market) are correspondent or payable‑through account sanctions (often reflected by inclusion on OFAC’s CAPTA List), which prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining in the United States a correspondent account or payable‑through account for the targeted FFI. OFAC indicates that FFIs may be exposed to such measures under E.O. 13224, as amended, if they knowingly conduct or facilitate a significant transaction on behalf of an E.O. 13224‑blocked person. Overview of CAPTA List: https://ofac.treasury.gov/other-ofac-sanctions-lists; consolidated non‑SDN lists (including CAPTA data): https://ofac.treasury.gov/consolidated-sanctions-list-non-sdn-lists.
- “Knowingly” means that a person has actual knowledge, or should have known, of the conduct, circumstance, or result (OFAC’s interpretation referencing 31 CFR 561.314).
- “Significant” (as in significant transaction/financial services) is assessed by OFAC under a totality‑of‑the‑circumstances test, considering factors such as size, number, and frequency; nature and commercial purpose; management awareness and pattern of conduct; nexus to blocked persons; impact on program objectives; whether deceptive practices were used; and other relevant factors [5332cb; dd8a8a].
- CAPTA List publication: OFAC publishes the List of Foreign Financial Institutions Subject to Correspondent Account or Payable‑Through Account Sanctions (CAPTA List) and includes it in the Consolidated Sanctions List data files. Entries specify that an FFI is subject to prohibitions or strict conditions on correspondent or payable‑through accounts.

Why this is forecast‑relevant now: OFAC’s July 2025 action against Cartel de los Soles both elevated the profile of Venezuelan‑linked designations and highlighted secondary‑sanctions exposure for FFIs dealing with E.O. 13224‑blocked persons tied to Venezuela (e.g., CdS, and—following February 2025—TdA). Whether OFAC moves from signaling to actual imposition of CAPTA‑style restrictions on an FFI by year‑end is uncertain, creating meaningful forecast entropy [5b9b0b; cbc7f1].
resolution_criteria:
Time window: Eligible actions must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive.

Question resolves “Yes” if, during the time window, OFAC publicly imposes correspondent or payable‑through account sanctions (i.e., prohibitions or strict conditions on opening or maintaining a correspondent or payable‑through account in the United States) on at least one non‑U.S. financial institution, and the announcement states that the basis is the institution knowingly conducting or facilitating one or more significant transaction(s) on behalf of Cartel de los Soles (CdS) or Tren de Aragua (TdA), each designated under E.O. 13224 (as amended). Evidence may come from any of the following official OFAC sources:
- An OFAC press release or Recent Actions notice explicitly imposing correspondent/payable‑through account sanctions (CAPTA‑style restrictions) on the institution pursuant to E.O. 13224 for knowingly conducting or facilitating significant transaction(s) on behalf of CdS or TdA [5b9b0b; cbc7f1].
- The institution’s appearance on OFAC’s CAPTA List with an associated announcement (press release/Recent Actions) tying the determination to knowingly conducting or facilitating significant transaction(s) on behalf of CdS or TdA under E.O. 13224 [ec5329; cbc7f1].

Definitions for resolution purposes:
- Non‑U.S. financial institution: An entity identified by OFAC as a foreign financial institution (FFI) when imposing correspondent or payable‑through account sanctions; CAPTA List entries are limited to FFIs and reflect these sanctions.
- Secondary sanctions: For this market, correspondent or payable‑through account sanctions under E.O. 13224 (as amended)—i.e., prohibiting or imposing strict conditions on the opening or maintaining in the U.S. of a correspondent or payable‑through account of an FFI [cbc7f1; ec5329].
- Knowingly: Actual knowledge, or should have known, of the conduct/circumstance/result.
- Significant transaction/financial services: Determined by OFAC under a totality‑of‑the‑circumstances assessment considering factors including size/number/frequency, nature and commercial purpose, management awareness/pattern of conduct, nexus to blocked persons, impact on program objectives, deceptive practices, and other relevant factors [5332cb; dd8a8a].
- On behalf of: The OFAC announcement must attribute the significant transaction(s) to having been conducted or facilitated for, or to the benefit of, the named blocked person (CdS or TdA) using language to that effect (e.g., “on behalf of”) consistent with OFAC’s usage under E.O. 13224 [cbc7f1; 5b9b0b].

Clarifications and exclusions:
- Actions solely imposing blocking sanctions (e.g., adding an institution to the SDN List without CAPTA‑style correspondent/payable‑through account restrictions) do not count as “secondary sanctions” for this market.
- The basis must be CdS or TdA under E.O. 13224; CAPTA sanctions imposed under other programs/authorities unrelated to CdS/TdA do not count [cbc7f1; 5b9b0b].
- Only public, on‑the‑record OFAC announcements or list publications count; leaks, media reports without OFAC confirmation, or third‑party analyses are insufficient.
- If multiple FFIs are sanctioned in a single action, any one meeting the above conditions suffices for a “Yes.” If no such action occurs in the time window, resolve “No.”

Primary resolution sources:
- OFAC press releases and Recent Actions pages that announce E.O. 13224‑based correspondent/payable‑through account sanctions and state the “knowingly” and “significant transaction” basis with respect to CdS or TdA [5b9b0b; cbc7f1].
- OFAC’s CAPTA List page and data files to verify whether an entity is an FFI subject to correspondent/payable‑through account sanctions.

question: During COP30 (Nov 10–21, 2025), will newly announced pledges to the FRLD total at least USD 1.0 billion?
background:
Context as of Oct 1, 2025
- What the FRLD is: The Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) is an operating entity under the UNFCCC financial mechanism intended to finance responses to loss and damage in climate‑vulnerable developing countries. The FRLD Board formally adopted the acronym “FRLD” in September 2024.
- COP30 dates and venue: COP30 is scheduled for Nov 10–21, 2025 in Belém, Brazil (City Park/Hangar Convention & Exhibition Centre). UNFCCC communications indicate the Daily Programme and announcements run during those dates; registration closes Nov 9, 23:59 CET.
- Status of pledges and funding prior to COP30: Public tallies indicate: (a) total pledges around USD 741 million equivalent as of Feb 2025, with many not yet converted into signed contribution agreements or paid‑in amounts ; and (b) as of June 27, 2025, total pledges reported at USD 788.8 million equivalent, with USD 361.0 million received into the Fund; an initial allocation of USD 250 million through grants was identified for 2025–2026. Climate finance trackers note initial pledges at COP28 (late 2023) and additional pledges through 2024 and COP29, with key contributors including EU member states, the UAE, the UK, and others; the distinction between pledges, signed contribution agreements, and paid‑in contributions is emphasized.
- Near‑term FRLD governance and fundraising signals: The FRLD Board requested a draft long‑term resource mobilization strategy and plan, to be considered at Board meeting B.7, and will report to COP30/CMA7 on implementation and guidance received. Some commentary highlights risks to fundraising momentum (e.g., U.S. withdrawal of Board representation and possible funding retrenchment), increasing uncertainty around COP30 outcomes.

Why this question: COPs are common moments for headline pledges. With COP30 scheduled for Nov 10–21, 2025, a clear, time‑bounded window exists to measure “newly announced” pledges. Current totals and governance steps suggest both upside and downside tail risks for 2025 pledging, making outcomes non‑obvious.
resolution_criteria:
Yes-resolution
- The question resolves Yes if the sum of “newly announced pledges” to the FRLD, first publicly announced between 2025‑11‑10 00:00:00 UTC and 2025‑11‑21 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive, is at least USD 1,000,000,000.

No-resolution
- Otherwise, the question resolves No.

Definitions (must all be met)
- FRLD: The Fund for responding to Loss and Damage established under the UNFCCC; acronym “FRLD” as adopted by its Board.
- COP30 window: The official COP30 dates are Nov 10–21, 2025 in Belém, Brazil; for this question, the qualifying announcement window is defined in UTC: 2025‑11‑10 00:00:00 UTC through 2025‑11‑21 23:59:59 UTC.
- Pledge vs. contribution: A “pledge” is an initial public financial commitment to provide funds to the FRLD, distinct from a “contribution,” which refers to funds under signed contribution agreements and/or paid‑in amounts. Only pledges count for this question; signed/paid status is not required.
- Newly announced pledge: A pledge (or the incremental increase to a previously pledged amount) that is first publicly announced during the COP30 window (as defined above). If a contributor previously pledged X before the window and announces a higher total Y during the window, only the incremental (Y−X) counts. Re‑announcements of previously publicized amounts do not count.
- Eligible contributors: Sovereign states, intergovernmental organizations (e.g., the European Union), and subnational governments are eligible contributors if their pledge is recognized by the FRLD/UNFCCC or the FRLD’s trustee processes. Private or corporate pledges count only if they are explicitly recognized by the FRLD/UNFCCC as pledges to the FRLD.
- Qualifying announcement channels: Official UNFCCC/FRLD communications (e.g., web pages summarizing pledges or official UNFCCC Daily Programme/press materials), official government/IGO announcements (e.g., ministry/department press releases), or Board/Trustee documents that record the pledge. Media reports are acceptable only if they explicitly cite an official announcement and the amount.
- USD handling: If a recognized source states a USD amount for a pledge, use that value. If a pledge is only stated in a non‑USD currency by the recognized source(s), convert to USD using the United Nations Operational Rates of Exchange as of 2025‑11‑21. Round converted values to the nearest USD 1 million for summation. If multiple recognized sources provide different USD equivalents for the same pledge, use the value provided by UNFCCC/FRLD; if absent, use the USD value used by the World Bank FRLD trustee; otherwise, apply the conversion rule above.

Inclusions and exclusions
- Include: Monetary pledges explicitly designated for the FRLD and first announced during the COP30 window, including multi‑year/cumulative pledges provided a clear total amount is specified. Conditional pledges (e.g., subject to parliamentary approval) count if an official amount is stated.
- Exclude: Non‑monetary support (e.g., in‑kind assistance), re‑announcements of amounts already public before 2025‑11‑10 00:00:00 UTC, and pledges to other mechanisms/funds (i.e., not explicitly to the FRLD). If a pledge announced during the window is officially withdrawn before 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC, exclude it.

Primary resolution sources (use in this order)
1) UNFCCC/FRLD official pages that summarize or list pledges, such as the UNFCCC FRLD pledges/tally page and/or FRLD official website pages summarizing pledges (including COP30 wrap‑ups). These sources regularly distinguish pledges from signed contributions/paid‑in amounts and report USD equivalents.
2) World Bank Financial Intermediary Fund (FIF) trustee materials for the FRLD (e.g., status of resources tables) if they explicitly record pledge amounts and timing.
3) Reputable climate finance trackers (e.g., reports from Climate Funds Update) provided they cite official pledge amounts and attribution to FRLD/UNFCCC, and/or wire services (AP/Reuters/AFP) citing official announcements. Use these only if (1)–(2) are unavailable or silent on a specific pledge.

How to determine “newly announced during COP30”
- Establish the pre‑COP30 baseline by using the most recent official UNFCCC/FRLD or trustee tally published prior to 2025‑11‑10 00:00:00 UTC (e.g., the latest Board/trustee status report or UNFCCC pledges page pre‑COP30).
- For each pledge identified in the COP30 window, compare it against the baseline for that contributor and count only the incremental increase.
- If sources disagree on whether a pledge was first announced during the window, use the timestamp of the earliest official announcement. If still ambiguous, prefer UNFCCC/FRLD timestamp; if absent, prefer the official government/IGO press release timestamp in UTC.

Cut‑off and documentation
- Information published up to 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 UTC will be used for resolution. If sources are revised after that time, they will not affect resolution. The outcome should be verifiable by a human within ~10 minutes using the source hierarchy above.

Notes for forecasters (status quo highlights)
- Acronym and institutional status: acronym “FRLD” adopted Sept 2024.
- Pledges to date: approx USD 741m (Feb 2025) ; USD 788.8m (as of June 27, 2025) with USD 361.0m received and a USD 250m initial allocation for 2025–2026.
- Process signals for 2025: Board requested a long‑term resource mobilization strategy; annual report and COP/CMA guidance expected at COP30.
- COP30 logistics window: Nov 10–21, 2025 in Belém; UNFCCC Daily Programme and announcements during those dates.

question: Will Indonesia publicly announce a new government‑to‑government rice import arrangement between 2025‑10‑15 and 2025‑12‑31 (WIB)?
background:
Status quo as of 2025‑09‑30:
- Policy stance: Indonesia’s Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman reaffirmed on 2025‑09‑05 that Indonesia will not import rice until the end of 2025, citing sufficient stocks. The National Food Agency (Badan Pangan Nasional, Bapanas) has also stated that rice import processes were completed in 2024 and that there are no imports in 2025, noting remaining stocks from 2024 imports in Bulog’s reserves.
- Stocks and market conditions: As of 2025‑09‑08, Bulog’s stockpile stood at nearly 4 million metric tons, almost double end‑2024 levels, yet consumers still faced high prices and sporadic retail scarcity; the government ordered Bulog to release 1.3 million tons by year‑end, of which about 210,791 tons had been distributed by 2025‑09‑20.
- Domestic procurement and production: Bulog more than doubled its 2025 domestic rice procurement target to 3.0 million metric tons (up from 1.27 MMT in 2024), with plans to optimize buying during the March–May peak harvest; the government also raised its purchase price for unhusked rice to 6,500 rupiah/kg from 6,000 rupiah effective Jan 15, 2025. Statistics Indonesia expected 2025 rice output to rise to roughly 33–33.5 MMT, exceeding consumption near 31 MMT, supporting the “no imports” policy stance.
Why this is uncertain and interesting: Despite official pledges against imports, Indonesia has historically adjusted rice policy in response to price dynamics, reserve levels, and food security considerations. Late‑year pressures (e.g., inventory quality, price stability, regional supply shifts) could still prompt a government‑to‑government (G2G) import announcement, but credible recent signals and relatively large stocks point the other way.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and time standard:
- Event window: From 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 to 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59, inclusive, according to Western Indonesia Time (WIB, UTC+07:00).

What counts as “rice”:
- For this question, “rice” refers to products classified under Harmonized System heading 1006: rice in the husk (paddy/rough), husked (brown) rice, semi‑milled or wholly milled rice (whether or not polished/glazed, including parboiled), and broken rice. This excludes products outside HS 1006 (e.g., cooked rice preparations, rice flour, or other processed products).

What counts as a “government‑to‑government (G2G) rice import arrangement”:
- A concluded and publicly announced arrangement (e.g., signed memorandum of understanding, contract, inter‑agency procurement assignment, or other binding agreement) to import rice under which:
  1) The Indonesian counterparty is the central government or a central government‑controlled agency (e.g., Perum Bulog), and
  2) The foreign counterparty is a foreign sovereign government or its directly controlled ministry/agency or state‑owned enterprise (SOE), and
  3) The announcement explicitly pertains to rice (as defined above) and either (a) states that an agreement has been signed/concluded, or (b) specifies a firm committed import volume and identifies the foreign counterparty (country and/or named state body/SOE).
- Renewals, extensions, or amendments of prior G2G arrangements count only if they add net new committed volume beyond what was publicly announced before the start of the window.

What does NOT count:
- Non‑G2G transactions (e.g., purchases from private foreign traders without a foreign government/SOE counterparty), sub‑national Indonesian government purchases, tenders or requests for quotation without a concluded arrangement, generic statements of intent to import without a signed/concluded agreement or a firm committed volume and identified G2G counterparty, restatements of previously announced deals that do not add new volume, commodities other than rice as defined above, or purely in‑kind/donated humanitarian shipments without an import arrangement.

What constitutes “publicly announces” and acceptable evidence:
- “Publicly announces” means publication on an official Indonesian government channel (e.g., websites or verified official social media/accounts of Bulog, the National Food Agency/Bapanas, the Ministry of Trade, the Ministry of Agriculture, the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, the Cabinet Secretariat, or the State Secretariat), or credible reporting that directly quotes a named Indonesian central‑government official in their official capacity specifying the new G2G rice import arrangement and the counterparty and/or committed volume. Examples of credible outlets include Reuters, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, Antara, Tempo, and Kompas.

How the question resolves:
- YES if, during the event window (WIB), there is at least one qualifying public announcement of a new G2G rice import arrangement as defined above.
- NO if no such qualifying announcement occurs during the event window.
- If multiple announcements occur, a single qualifying instance suffices for YES.
- In case of conflicting reports, priority is given to official Indonesian government publications; otherwise, convergence among multiple reputable outlets suffices.

Notes for resolvers:
- The policy backdrop as of late September 2025 indicated no imports in 2025 , sizable Bulog stocks , and a domestic procurement push , but these do not constrain the resolution if a qualifying announcement is made within the window.
- Timezone reference: WIB is UTC+07:00 and Indonesia does not observe daylight saving time.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will Stem, Inc. announce an additional exchange, refinancing, or redemption of at least $25 million aggregate principal amount of its outstanding notes?
background:
Company and status quo as of 2025-09-30
- Issuer: Stem, Inc. (NYSE: STEM; CIK: 0001758766). In a liability management transaction disclosed June 30, 2025, Stem exchanged portions of its outstanding convertible notes for new secured notes and warrants. Specifically, Stem exchanged approximately $228.8 million principal of its 0.50% Green Convertible Senior Notes due 2028 and approximately $121.3 million principal of its 4.25% Green Convertible Senior Notes due 2030, along with $10 million cash and accrued interest, for $155.4 million aggregate principal amount of new 12.00%/11.00% Senior Secured PIK Toggle Notes due 2030 and 439,919 warrants, pursuant to a privately negotiated exchange agreement. The company publicly characterized this as exchanging about 77% of the 2028 notes and 51% of the 2030 notes outstanding, raising $10 million cash and issuing $155 million first-lien senior secured notes and 439,919 warrants with a $30.00 exercise price expiring December 1, 2030.
- Resulting balances (as of June 30, 2025): Remaining outstanding principal after the exchange was approximately $68.2 million for the 2028 Convertible Notes, $118.7 million for the 2030 Convertible Notes, and $155.4 million for the new 2030 Senior Secured PIK Toggle Notes; the company recorded a $220.0 million gain on debt extinguishment in connection with the transaction.
- Instrument definitions (for clarity): A convertible bond (or note) is a bond that can be converted into a specified number of shares of the issuer’s common stock (or cash of equal value), combining debt and equity features. A warrant is a security that entitles the holder to buy stock from the issuer at a fixed exercise price until expiration. A callable (redeemable) bond gives the issuer the right to repurchase (redeem) the bond before maturity at specified prices on or after certain dates; issuers often exercise calls to refinance at lower cost. Refinancing means replacing an existing debt obligation with another debt obligation under different terms and/or interest rates.
- Disclosure channels: Public companies disclose major events via Form 8-K “current reports” filed with the SEC; these filings, as well as periodic reports (Forms 10-Q/10-K) and official issuer press releases, are standard venues to announce material financing transactions.
Why this question is interesting now
- Following Stem’s June 30, 2025 exchange and new secured note issuance, material outstanding note balances remain (2028, 2030 convertibles, and 2030 secured notes), creating plausible incentives for further exchanges, redemptions, or refinancing actions in Q4 2025, but not certainty. This makes additional liability management activity a live possibility that depends on financing conditions, liquidity, and counterparty interest.
Primary sources for context (resolver will use these during the resolution window):
- SEC EDGAR filings for Stem, Inc. (CIK: 0001758766) including Forms 8-K, 10-Q, 10-K (and exhibits), which disclose material financing transactions.
- Stem’s investor relations news page for official press releases: https://investors.stem.com/news/.
resolution_criteria:
Question
- Resolve Yes if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (the “Resolution Window”), Stem, Inc. publicly discloses a qualifying transaction that constitutes an additional exchange, refinancing, or redemption of its outstanding notes, with an aggregate principal amount affected of at least $25,000,000. Resolve No otherwise.
Key definitions (all must be interpreted per these definitions for resolution)
- Stem, Inc.: The public company with CIK 0001758766 (NYSE: STEM).
- Notes; Outstanding notes: Any debt securities of Stem described as “notes” in its SEC filings, including but not limited to (i) 0.50% Green Convertible Senior Notes due 2028, (ii) 4.25% Green Convertible Senior Notes due 2030, and (iii) 12.00%/11.00% Senior Secured PIK Toggle Notes due 2030 issued June 30, 2025. “Outstanding” means principal that has not been redeemed, repurchased, exchanged, converted, or cancelled as of the time of the qualifying disclosure.
- Exchange: A transaction where Stem enters into a definitive agreement with noteholders to exchange existing notes for other securities and/or cash (e.g., exchanging convertible notes for new notes and warrants), as evidenced by an executed agreement disclosed by the company.
- Redemption: An issuer-initiated repurchase and cancellation of notes pursuant to redemption/call provisions (in whole or in part) at specified prices/dates under the applicable indenture (i.e., an issuer “call”), which is a form of early repayment typical of callable/redeemable bonds.
- Refinancing: Replacement of existing note obligations with new debt obligations under different terms (e.g., issuing new notes and using proceeds to retire existing notes), or amending existing notes to extend their stated maturity by ≥6 months; in all cases, the disclosure must indicate that the existing notes are being refinanced and the amount affected.
- Additional: Not previously publicly disclosed before 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and distinct from the June 30, 2025 transaction described in Stem’s filings/press releases.
