- Aggregate principal amount affected: The sum of principal of existing notes exchanged, redeemed, repurchased/retired with proceeds of new notes (for refinancing), or subject to a signed amend-and-extend that extends maturity (for refinancing). To qualify, this sum must be ≥$25,000,000.
- Announce; Publicly discloses: Any of the following public channels: (a) SEC Form 8-K “current report,” (b) SEC Form 10-Q or 10-K, or (c) an official Stem press release posted on https://investors.stem.com/news/. For SEC Form 8-K, this aligns with the SEC’s definition of a “current report” used to announce major events.
Timing and timestamp rules
- Resolution Window: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 to 2025-12-31 23:59:59, inclusive, in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
- For SEC filings, use the EDGAR “Accepted” timestamp in the filing header converted to UTC to determine inclusion; for issuer press releases, use the published date/time displayed on the investors.stem.com news item (or embedded newswire timestamp if displayed) interpreted in UTC.
What qualifies (examples)
- Exchange: An 8-K or press release stating Stem entered into a privately negotiated exchange agreement with holders of its 2028, 2030, or 2030 secured notes to exchange ≥$25m principal for new securities and/or cash.
- Redemption: An 8-K or press release announcing Stem’s optional redemption (call) of ≥$25m principal of its notes at the applicable call price.
- Refinancing: An 8-K, 10-Q/10-K, or press release announcing issuance of new notes with proceeds used to retire ≥$25m principal of existing notes (explicitly stated), or a definitive amend-and-extend to existing notes that extends stated maturity by ≥6 months on ≥$25m principal.
What does NOT qualify (exclusions)
- Purely exploratory, non-binding indications (e.g., “considering,” “evaluating”) without a definitive agreement or completed action.
- Equity issuance, warrant adjustments, or credit facility amendments that do not affect notes as defined above.
- Open-market repurchases of notes below $25m aggregate principal unless explicitly characterized by the company as a redemption or refinancing under these definitions.
Sources for resolution
- Primary: SEC EDGAR filings for Stem, Inc. (CIK: 0001758766), including Forms 8-K, 10-Q, 10-K and exhibits covering the Resolution Window.
- Secondary: Official Stem press releases posted on its investor relations site (https://investors.stem.com/news/).
Resolution
- The question resolves to Yes if at least one qualifying disclosure is made within the Resolution Window; otherwise, No. A human resolver should confirm the qualifying disclosure and the ≥$25m principal amount based on the cited sources within ~10 minutes.

question: Will electric two-wheelers be at least 8.20% of India’s two-wheeler retail in November 2025?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-10-01):
- FADA’s latest available monthly press release (August 2025) reports that electric vehicles accounted for 7.60% of two-wheeler (2W) retail in August 2025, unchanged from July 2025, and up from 6.63% in August 2024.
- In the same August release, FADA shows category-wise “Fuel Wise Vehicle Retail Market Share,” with 2W listed as a category and “EV” listed as a fuel type; the 2W EV share value is reported directly as a percentage.
- Methodologically, FADA compiles “Vehicle Retail Data” from India’s Regional Transport Offices (RTOs) in collaboration with the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH) via the Vahan system. The August 2025 press release states data were collated as of 03-09-2025 from 1,391 out of 1,451 RTOs; it also notes that figures do not include Telangana (TS). These coverage/exclusion details are determined by FADA and may vary month to month; for this question, the November 2025 report’s own definitions and coverage will govern resolution.
- Seasonal note: The August 2025 press release mentions that festive-season demand dynamics (e.g., Onam, Ganesh Chaturthi) and policy timing (e.g., GST 2.0 incentive timing) affected purchase conversions around August/September 2025. Forecasters may consider how festive-season dynamics could influence November outcomes.

Definitions and references for clarity:
- Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA): India’s apex national body of automobile retail, which publishes monthly “Vehicle Retail Data” press releases: https://fada.in/ [general reference].
- Two-wheeler (2W) category: The category labeled “2W” in FADA’s monthly Vehicle Retail Data release for November 2025 (the same categorization used in the August 2025 release).
- Electric (EV) fuel type: The “EV” fuel type as labeled in FADA’s “Fuel Wise Vehicle Retail Market Share” section for November 2025 (consistent with August 2025 labeling). For a general definition of electric vehicles, see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle [general reference].
- Retail share for 2W EVs: The percentage of two-wheeler retail attributed to the EV fuel type in FADA’s November 2025 Vehicle Retail Data (i.e., the “EV” percentage within the “2W” row/category in the “Fuel Wise Vehicle Retail Market Share” for that month) [f06513 for format reference].

Why this target/threshold? August 2025’s 2W EV share is 7.60%. A threshold of 8.20% for November 2025 sits close enough to recent levels to be plausibly attainable yet uncertain, especially given India’s festive-season sales patterns and policy cross-currents noted by FADA.
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution: YES if the 2W EV share for November 2025, as published by FADA in its November 2025 Vehicle Retail Data press release, is greater than or equal to 8.20%. NO otherwise.

Primary resolution source:
- The Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) monthly Vehicle Retail Data press release covering November 2025, available via https://fada.in/ (press release section). Use the first FADA-issued press release that covers November 2025 and is published on or before 31 December 2025, 23:59 India Standard Time (IST; UTC+5:30). If multiple versions/corrections of the November 2025 press release are published on or before that time, use the latest version as of that deadline.

What to read from the source and how to compare:
- Use the 2W (Two-Wheeler) category’s EV share percentage shown in the “Fuel Wise Vehicle Retail Market Share” for November 2025, exactly as displayed in the FADA press release (this is the same section used in the August 2025 release to show category-wise EV shares) [f06513 for format reference].
- Compare that reported number against 8.20%:
  - If FADA reports with two or more decimal places, compare the exact reported value to 8.20%.
  - If FADA reports with one decimal place (e.g., 8.2%), interpret it as 8.20%.
  - If FADA reports as an integer (e.g., 8%), interpret it as 8.00%.
- If the press release includes both a chart and a table or explicit numeric statement for the same metric and they conflict, prefer the explicit numeric statement/table. If only a chart is provided (as in the August 2025 example), use the chart value.

Fallback computation (only if the EV share percentage for 2W is not directly shown for November 2025 in the press release):
- If the November 2025 press release provides total two-wheeler retail units and the EV two-wheeler retail units, compute share = (EV 2W units / total 2W units) × 100, and round to two decimal places using standard rounding (half up). Compare the rounded result to 8.20%.

Scope and definitions that govern resolution:
- Use the November 2025 month as defined and reported by FADA in the relevant press release.
- Use FADA’s own categorization and coverage (e.g., included RTOs, excluded states like TS if applicable) exactly as stated in the November 2025 press release; do not adjust or backfill. August 2025 coverage details (1,391 of 1,451 RTOs; TS excluded) are illustrative and were specific to that month.

Timing and timezone:
- The question resolves based on sources published on or before 31 December 2025, 23:59 IST (UTC+5:30). If no FADA November 2025 Vehicle Retail Data press release is publicly available by that deadline, the question should be flagged for admin review.

Verification notes:
- The August 2025 press release demonstrates the presence and layout of the “Fuel Wise Vehicle Retail Market Share” section (including 2W and EV labels) and reports the August 2025 2W EV share as 7.60% , establishing the measurement format expected to be used again for November 2025.

question: Will cumulative pledges to the UNFCCC Fund for responding to Loss and Damage reach at least USD $1.30 billion by 23:59 BRT on November 21, 2025?
background:
Overview and status quo as of today (2025-09-30)
- The Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) is the UNFCCC-linked fund established to assist developing countries particularly vulnerable to climate change in responding to economic and non-economic loss and damage; it was operationalized at COP28 and serves the Paris Agreement. As of April 2025, FRLD had received pledges of USD 786 million from 27 contributors (25 countries, the European Union, and the Belgian region of Wallonia).
- The FRLD’s official pledges page reported a cumulative total of USD 788.80 million as of June 30, 2025, with initial pledges registered from 28 countries and notes on conversion of pledges into signed contribution agreements and releases of initial funding commitments.
- Around COP29 (November 2024), reporting indicated that subsequent announcements increased the FRLD total from USD 674 million to USD 759 million. These figures provide context on pledge growth near COPs.
- COP30 (the 2025 UN Climate Change Conference) will take place in Belém, Brazil, from November 10 to November 21, 2025. Belém observes Brasília Time (BRT; UTC−03:00); Brazil does not presently observe daylight saving time, so November 21, 2025 in Belém is UTC−03:00.
- NRDC maintains a Climate Funds Pledge Tracker covering UN climate funds (including the FRLD), and updates totals as new announcements come in; this can serve as a secondary cross-check source if needed.

Why this threshold?
- As of mid-2025, the FRLD total (~USD 789 million) leaves significant headroom for additional announcements at COP30. A threshold of USD 1.30 billion requires roughly USD 510 million in new or newly confirmed pledges by the close of COP30, which is plausible yet uncertain given typical COP-time dynamics and ongoing discussions about scaling loss and damage finance. This aims to place the forecast in a non-trivial range.

Key definitions (and links)
- Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD): The UNFCCC-linked fund assisting vulnerable developing countries in addressing loss and damage impacts; see authoritative overview.
- Loss and damage (concept): The adverse effects of climate change beyond adaptation, encompassing both irreversible harm (loss) and quantifiable damages; for conceptual background under UNFCCC, see overview.
- Pledge (for this question): A publicly announced financial commitment to the FRLD by an eligible contributor, recognized and listed by FRLD or UNFCCC (e.g., sovereign governments, supranational bodies like the EU, and eligible subnational governments such as Wallonia).
- Cumulative pledges: The USD-denominated sum of all pledges listed by the FRLD (or by UNFCCC in official tables) as of the cutoff time. Where a source displays an explicit total, use that total; otherwise, sum the itemized USD amounts.
- Eligible contributor: Sovereign state, supranational body (e.g., EU), or subnational government if recognized in official FRLD/UNFCCC pledge listings (e.g., Wallonia). Philanthropic/private contributions count only if listed on the official FRLD/UNFCCC pledge pages/tables.
- USD refers to United States dollars.
- COP30 dates/location: November 10–21, 2025, Belém, Brazil.
- Cutoff time and timezone: Close of COP30 defined here as 2025-11-21 at 23:59 BRT (UTC−03:00).

Primary and fallback resolution sources
- Primary: FRLD official pledges page (frld.org/pledges), which publishes a cumulative total and itemized pledges, including USD equivalents and rounding conventions.
- Secondary: UNFCCC FRLD official documents/report tables listing pledges (e.g., board reports and official tables that specify “as at” dates and USD equivalents).
- Tertiary (only if the above are inaccessible or clearly incomplete by December 31, 2025): Credible reporting that states an explicit total for pledges as of COP30 close, e.g., Carbon Brief, Reuters, or AP, with preference for sources that cite official FRLD/UNFCCC figures.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will the cumulative pledges to the FRLD reach at least USD $1.30 billion by the close of COP30 on November 21, 2025?

Eligibility window
- Pledges counted are those recognized and listed by FRLD/UNFCCC at or before the cutoff time (2025-11-21 23:59 BRT; UTC−03:00). Because the metric is cumulative, pledges made prior to this window are included in the total if still recognized at cutoff.

Cutoff and measurement
- Cutoff: 2025-11-21, 23:59 BRT (UTC−03:00).
- Measurement: Resolve using the USD-denominated cumulative pledges total as displayed on the FRLD official pledges page (frld.org/pledges) at or immediately after the cutoff. If an explicit total is displayed, use that. If only itemized USD amounts are listed, sum them. Use the USD equivalents as shown by the official source; do not perform independent currency conversions.

Definitions used for counting
- Pledge: A publicly announced financial commitment by an eligible contributor to the FRLD, recognized/listed by FRLD or UNFCCC in official pledges tables/pages (includes sovereign states, supranational bodies like the EU, and eligible subnational governments such as Wallonia). Philanthropic/private contributions count only if they appear on official FRLD/UNFCCC pledge listings.
- Cumulative pledges: The total USD value of all pledges listed at the cutoff by the official source (FRLD; UNFCCC as fallback). If a pledge is rescinded and removed by the official source before the cutoff, it does not count. Multi-year or instrument-specific pledges (grant vs. concessional loan) are counted at their full USD face value as listed by the official source.

Resolution steps
1) At or after 2025-11-21 23:59 BRT (UTC−03:00), check frld.org/pledges for the cumulative pledges total. Record the total (or sum itemized USD amounts) as of the cutoff. If the displayed total is ≥ USD $1.30 billion, resolve YES; otherwise, resolve NO.
2) If the FRLD pledges page is inaccessible or lacks an explicit total and itemized USD amounts for pledges as of the cutoff, use the latest UNFCCC official FRLD pledge table/report that states figures “as at” a date on or after the cutoff and clearly reflects pledges announced by COP30’s close. Prefer documents with itemized USD amounts or an explicit total; apply the same threshold test.
3) If neither source provides sufficient information by 2025-12-31, resolve using credible reporting (e.g., Carbon Brief, Reuters, AP) that states an explicit FRLD pledges total as of COP30 close; prefer reporting that cites FRLD/UNFCCC figures. Apply the same threshold test.

Tie-breaking and discrepancies
- If FRLD and UNFCCC totals disagree, prefer FRLD’s official pledges page total, as the fund’s own listing is authoritative for this specific metric.

Outcome
- YES: The measured cumulative pledges total is ≥ USD $1.30 billion at cutoff.
- NO: The measured cumulative pledges total is < USD $1.30 billion at cutoff.

Verification scope
- A resolver should be able to verify the result within 10 minutes by checking the FRLD pledges page or, if necessary, the UNFCCC official pledge table/report and/or a credible secondary report.

question: Will TikTok’s U.S. divestiture deal formally close between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- U.S. Executive Order and structure: On September 25, 2025, the White House issued the executive order “Saving TikTok While Protecting National Security,” determining that a proposed plan for a “qualified divestiture” would allow Americans to continue using TikTok while addressing national security concerns. The order describes a U.S.-based joint venture to operate TikTok’s U.S. application, majority-owned and controlled by U.S. persons, with ByteDance and affiliates owning less than 20%. It also directs the Attorney General to delay enforcement of the Act for 120 days to allow time for the divestiture to be completed.
- Deal framing and valuation: Reuters reported the same day that the President signed the order declaring the sale plan ready, with a valuation of about $14 billion and ByteDance to hold less than 20% in the U.S. entity.
- Investor consortium reporting: Prior reporting indicated a U.S. investor consortium led by Oracle and Silver Lake (with other participants reported to include Andreessen Horowitz) controlling roughly 80% of the U.S. TikTok entity. Later Reuters coverage noted expectations that ByteDance would maintain ownership interests but cede control of data, content, and the algorithm to a new U.S. joint venture, raising questions about the extent of divestiture.
- China’s stance: Coverage following the order noted China’s conspicuous public silence about formal approval even as the U.S. President said he had received a green light from China’s President; analysts quoted by CNBC argued China has little incentive to permit a ByteDance divestment. Reuters’ contemporaneous report quoted the U.S. President claiming he told President Xi and “he said go ahead with it,” while also noting Chinese official statements in general terms about market-based negotiations.
- What is “TikTok U.S.” for purposes of this question: TikTok Inc. is an American company incorporated and headquartered in California; its ultimate parent is ByteDance Ltd. (a privately held company with operations in China). TikTok’s proprietary algorithm is owned by ByteDance, and portions of the platform’s source code are developed and maintained in China.

Key definitions and links forecasters may find useful:
- Divestiture: “the partial or full disposal of a company or other entity’s operations or assets through sale, exchange, closure, or bankruptcy.” Investopedia: https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/divestiture.asp.
- Closing (M&A): the final stage of a sale where all conditions are met, documents executed, and consideration is delivered; distinct from signing. Divestopedia: https://www.divestopedia.com/definition/926/closing.
- Qualified divestiture (as used here): as described and determined in the September 25, 2025 executive order “Saving TikTok While Protecting National Security,” which specifies a U.S.-based entity operating TikTok’s U.S. application, majority-owned and controlled by U.S. persons, with ByteDance and affiliates owning less than 20%, and with operational control of algorithms, code, content moderation, and U.S. user data under the U.S. entity’s control and monitored by trusted partners.

Why this question is interesting and plausibly uncertain by year-end:
- The deal sits at the intersection of U.S.–China policy, national security reviews, and complex cross-border corporate carve-outs. While the White House order frames a path and extends a non-enforcement window to enable a closing, valuation, ownership, control, and foreign approvals (or non-objection) introduce material execution risk before December 31, 2025.
resolution_criteria:
Binary resolution as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, for events occurring between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (all times UTC):

Question: Will the TikTok U.S. divestiture deal formally close in this period?

Definitions for this market:
- TikTok U.S. business: the operation of the TikTok application for users in the United States, currently offered by TikTok Inc., an American company incorporated and headquartered in California, whose ultimate parent is ByteDance Ltd..
- Qualified divestiture: the transaction structure determined and described in the September 25, 2025 executive order “Saving TikTok While Protecting National Security,” involving a U.S.-based entity to operate TikTok’s U.S. application, majority-owned and controlled by U.S. persons, with ByteDance and affiliates owning less than 20%, and with control of algorithms/code, content moderation, and U.S. user data under that U.S. entity, as specified in the order.
- Close / Closing: consummation of the transaction (distinct from signing) such that all required approvals and conditions precedent are satisfied, transaction documents are executed, and consideration is delivered, effecting transfer of ownership/control as specified in the definitive agreements.

Resolution:
- YES if, between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, there is credible public evidence that the transaction constituting the qualified divestiture of TikTok’s U.S. business has closed. Evidence must satisfy one of the following:
  (A) An official statement/press release from TikTok and/or ByteDance AND an official statement/press release from the buyer/new U.S. entity (or a public filing by a public buyer, such as a Form 8-K), each explicitly stating that the transaction has “closed” or “been completed,” and clearly identifying that this closing covers TikTok’s U.S. business consistent with the qualified divestiture described in the September 25, 2025 executive order; AND corroboration by at least two independent major news outlets (e.g., Reuters, AP, WSJ, FT, Bloomberg, NYT, CNBC) reporting that the deal has closed; or
  (B) An official U.S. government statement (e.g., from the White House or Department of Justice) that the qualified divestiture contemplated by the September 25, 2025 executive order has been completed/closed, thereby satisfying the Act’s requirements.

- NO if no such evidence exists by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, or if public communications indicate only signing, intent, or conditional approvals without closing (e.g., “framework agreement,” “definitive agreement signed,” or “subject to remaining approvals”).

Additional notes:
- Timezone: All dates/times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
- Start date: Only closings that occur on/after 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC count toward a YES outcome.
- Conflicts: If sources conflict, priority is given to official statements by the transaction parties and U.S. government statements. If ambiguity remains, the market resolves NO.
- Name changes: The new U.S. entity’s name may differ from reporting; what matters is that the closing clearly pertains to the qualified divestiture of the TikTok U.S. business as described in the September 25, 2025 executive order.

question: Will the U.S. implement an across-the-board tariff on all goods of Colombian origin between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- In late January 2025, the White House threatened to impose emergency tariffs of 25% on all Colombian imports, with an increase to 50% after one week, amid a dispute over deportation flights. Following an agreement under which Colombia accepted deportation flights, the White House stated that the fully drafted IEEPA tariffs and sanctions would be held in reserve and not signed unless Colombia failed to honor the agreement. Associated press reporting described the subsequent resumption of deportation flights.
- The United States–Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement (CTPA) has been in force since May 15, 2012; under it, most Colombian goods currently enter the United States duty-free (and without the MPF) as the agreement phases in, with near full duty-free treatment by 2028. As of 2024, USTR reports U.S.–Colombia goods trade of roughly $36.6B, with U.S. goods imports from Colombia at $17.9B and exports at $18.7B; total services trade was about $16.7B, with a $2.5B U.S. services surplus.
- Definitions used below:
  • Tariff: A tax imposed by a government on imported goods, paid by the importer.
  • Country of origin: For U.S. customs purposes, “the country of manufacture, production, or growth of any article of foreign origin entering the United States,” as defined in 19 CFR 134.1(b). CBP applies non-preferential origin rules under 19 CFR Part 134 to determine origin for marking and similar purposes.

Why this is forecastable now: The January 2025 contingency left a Colombia-wide tariff package drafted but on hold, creating genuine uncertainty about whether an across-the-board, Colombia-specific tariff will actually be put into effect before year-end. Forecasters can track official actions (e.g., presidential proclamations, executive orders, Federal Register notices, USTR actions, CBP operational guidance) and political/compliance signals from both governments and trade data releases to update their probabilities.
resolution_criteria:
Question intent: Resolve whether a legally operative, Colombia-specific, across-the-board tariff is actually in effect at any time during the period defined below.

Time window for eligible events: From 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Resolution:
- Resolve “Yes” if, at any moment within the window, there is a legally operative U.S. federal measure that imposes an additional customs duty (ad valorem and/or specific) on all goods of Colombian origin (as defined below), regardless of tariff subheading or product, by virtue of their Colombian origin.
- Resolve “No” otherwise.

Required characteristics of the qualifying measure:
1) Scope (across-the-board): The text of the measure must state that it applies to “all goods of Colombia,” “all merchandise imported from Colombia,” or equivalently worded language that makes it applicable to all products of Colombian origin irrespective of HTS heading/subheading. Narrow measures (e.g., limited to specific sectors/products), quotas/TRQs, licensing regimes, sanctions that block imports without imposing a customs duty, enhanced inspections, and visa/immigration restrictions do not count.
2) Colombia-specific: The measure must explicitly identify Colombia as a covered country. A global tariff applying to all countries does not count. A measure that applies to a list of countries counts if Colombia is explicitly listed and the scope criterion above is met for Colombia.
3) Legal form and effect: The measure must be enacted through a binding federal instrument (e.g., Presidential Proclamation, Executive Order invoking statutory authority such as IEEPA; determinations and implementing notices by USTR/Commerce/CBP; interim/final rules published in the Federal Register) that has entered into legal effect so that entries of goods of Colombian origin are assessed the additional duty during the window. If a measure is signed but its effective date lies outside the window, it does not count. If it is enjoined nationwide before taking effect, it does not count. If it takes effect and is later suspended/terminated, it counts as long as it was in effect at least briefly within the window.

Definitions to be used for resolution:
- “Tariff” means a tax on imported goods collected by customs (e.g., an additional duty rate).
- “Goods of Colombian origin” means goods whose country of origin is Colombia under U.S. non-preferential origin rules: the country of manufacture, production, or growth, as defined in 19 CFR 134.1(b). For avoidance of doubt, origin determinations follow CBP practice under 19 CFR Part 134 (e.g., substantial transformation), not preferential rules of origin under CTPA.
- “Across-the-board” means the measure, by its terms, applies to all goods of Colombian origin regardless of product classification, though it may include enumerated carve-outs inherent to U.S. law (e.g., duty-free return of U.S. goods, temporary importations under bond) or explicit exclusions listed in the instrument. The presence of such exclusions does not disqualify the measure as long as the default rule is that all Colombian-origin goods are subject to the specified additional duty.

What does NOT qualify:
- General/global tariffs applicable to all countries; product- or sector-specific duties (e.g., anti-dumping/countervailing duties, safeguard duties) that do not apply to all goods of Colombian origin; non-tariff measures (quotas, embargoes, licensing only, OFAC blocking sanctions) that do not impose a customs duty; measures announced but not legally in effect during the window.

Primary sources for determination (any one suffices):
- Federal Register entries for Presidential Proclamations, Executive Orders, interim/final rules, or notices establishing country-specific across-the-board tariff measures.
- Official White House/Executive Office postings of signed proclamations or executive orders.
- Harmonized Tariff Schedule (USITC) updates adding entries that impose additional duties on “goods of Colombia” across-the-board.
- CBP Cargo Systems Messaging Service (CSMS) and/or Customs Bulletins that implement such measures for entry processing.

Status quo baseline (for forecasters): As of 2025-09-30, there is no across-the-board, Colombia-specific U.S. tariff in effect; the January 2025 tariff package was drafted but held in reserve after an agreement on deportation flights. The CTPA remains in force and most Colombian-origin goods enter duty-free, which would be reversed or offset if an across-the-board Colombia tariff were implemented. Latest USTR figures indicate U.S. goods imports from Colombia were about $17.9B in 2024, suggesting material trade exposure to any such measure.

Citations supporting background and definitions: White House statement holding IEEPA tariffs in reserve ; Reuters reporting on the 25%–50% threatened tariffs and subsequent hold following an agreement ; AP reporting on the resumption of deportation flights ; CBP page confirming CTPA effective date and duty-free status for most goods ; USTR country/trade summary for 2024 values ; Definition of tariff ; Definition of country of origin.

question: By 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, will any EU sanctions act published in 2025 explicitly restrict Russia’s Mir card payment system and/or the Faster Payments System (SBP)?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-10-01)
- What is Mir? Mir is a Russian card payment system for electronic fund transfers. It is operated by the Russian National Card Payment System (NSPK), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Central Bank of Russia. See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_(payment_system)
- What is SBP? The Faster Payments System (SBP) is a service of the Bank of Russia enabling interbank transfers (24/7/365); the Bank of Russia is the operator and settlement center, while NSPK functions as the operations and payment clearing center. See: https://www.cbr.ru/eng/psystem/sfp/
- EU sanctions landscape in 2025 to date: On 24 February 2025, the EU adopted its 16th sanctions package via Council Regulation (EU) 2025/395, amending Regulation (EU) No 833/2014. That package introduced, among other measures, restrictions related to the use of Russia’s System for Transfer of Financial Messages (SPFS) and to specialized financial messaging services. It did not explicitly mention Mir, NSPK, or SBP by name in the operative text. Subsequent 2025 amendments to Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 include Council Regulation (EU) 2025/932 (20 May 2025) and Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1494 (18 July 2025).
- Why this matters: Explicit EU restrictions directed at Mir and/or SBP would represent a significant expansion of financial-sector sanctions by directly naming Russia’s domestic retail payments infrastructure rather than only imposing broader financial messaging or sectoral constraints.

What will be checked at resolution
- Whether any EU sanctions legal act published in the Official Journal in calendar year 2025 contains operative provisions or annexes that explicitly name and restrict Mir and/or SBP (or their operator, where applicable) as defined below. The Official Journal (OJ) on EUR-Lex is the resolution source; examples of relevant OJ entries in 2025 include Council Regulation (EU) 2025/395 (OJ L, 24 Feb 2025) , Council Regulation (EU) 2025/932 (OJ L, 20 May 2025) , and Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1494 (OJ L, 18 Jul 2025).
resolution_criteria:
Question: By 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025, will any EU sanctions legal act published in calendar year 2025 explicitly restrict Russia’s Mir card payment system and/or the Faster Payments System (SBP)?

Time window for eligible acts
- Start: 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC
- End: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive)
- An act counts if its Official Journal publication date falls within the window.

What counts as an “EU sanctions legal act”
- A Council Regulation or Council Implementing Regulation that imposes or implements restrictive measures related to Russia (e.g., amending Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 or implementing Council Regulation (EU) No 269/2014), and/or a Council Decision (CFSP) establishing or amending restrictive measures regarding Russia, as published in the Official Journal (OJ, series L) on EUR-Lex. The OJ publication is the authoritative source for resolution.

Definitions (with sources)
- “Mir card payment system” (or “Mir”/“MIR”): the Russian card payment system for electronic fund transfers operated by the Russian National Card Payment System (NSPK). See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_(payment_system)
- “NSPK”: the Russian National Card Payment System, operator of Mir; a wholly owned subsidiary of the Central Bank of Russia.
- “Faster Payments System (SBP)”: the Bank of Russia’s service enabling fast interbank transfers; the Bank of Russia is the operator and settlement center, and NSPK is the operations and payment clearing center. See: https://www.cbr.ru/eng/psystem/sfp/

What counts as “explicitly restricts”
- At least one operative provision (e.g., an Article stating “It shall be prohibited…”, “Member States shall…”, etc.) or an annex effecting restrictions (e.g., listings/trade prohibitions/designations) explicitly names any of the following and applies a restriction to it:
  - “Mir” or “MIR” (as a payment system), “Mir payment system”, “National Payment Card System”, “NSPK” (National Payment Card System), or an unambiguous variant referring to the Mir operator; and/or
  - “Faster Payments System” or “SBP” (System for Fast/Faster Payments) in Russia.
- “Restricts” includes, but is not limited to: prohibitions on issuing, acquiring, processing, accepting, or facilitating transactions via Mir or SBP; prohibitions on EU persons/entities connecting to or supporting Mir or SBP; designations/listings that impose asset freezes and related prohibitions on NSPK (for Mir) or impose a specific prohibition on connecting to SBP.
- Mere mention in recitals without an accompanying operative restriction does NOT count. Non-binding guidance, FAQs, press releases, or news reports do NOT count.

What does NOT count
- Restrictions that target only Russia’s SPFS (System for Transfer of Financial Messages) or generic “specialised financial messaging services” without explicitly naming Mir/NSPK or SBP do not count, even though such restrictions exist in prior packages.

Resolution
- YES if at least one eligible EU sanctions legal act, published in the OJ between the start and end timestamps above, contains an operative provision or annex that explicitly restricts Mir/NSPK and/or SBP as defined.
- NO otherwise.

Primary resolution source
- Official Journal of the European Union (EUR-Lex). The resolver will search the OJ (series L) for 2025 EU sanctions acts concerning Russia and verify whether Mir/NSPK and/or SBP are explicitly named in an operative restriction. Example OJ entries to consult include: Council Regulation (EU) 2025/395 (OJ L, 24 Feb 2025) ; Council Regulation (EU) 2025/932 (OJ L, 20 May 2025) ; Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1494 (OJ L, 18 Jul 2025).

Notes
- If multiple acts are published, the presence of any single explicit restriction as defined suffices for YES.
- If an act is adopted in 2025 but published in the OJ after 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, it does not count for this question (publication date governs).
- This question resolves based solely on OJ legal text; press statements or non-binding instruments are out of scope for resolution.

Status quo references (for forecasters)
- The 16th package (Council Regulation (EU) 2025/395) included restrictions related to SPFS and specialized financial messaging services and did not explicitly name Mir/NSPK or SBP in operative provisions. Mir’s operator and role , and SBP’s governance structure , are defined above for clarity. Later 2025 amendments to Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 exist (Council Regulation (EU) 2025/932; Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1494), but their detailed contents should be consulted directly in the OJ at resolution time.

question: By 31 Dec 2025, will IATA’s latest monthly Air Passenger Market Analysis report 2025 year-to-date global passenger traffic growth below 4.0% versus the same period in 2024?
background:
Overview and context as of 2025-09-22 (UTC):
- What is being forecast: Whether industry-wide global passenger traffic growth in 2025—measured year-to-date (YTD) versus the same period in 2024—will be strictly less than 4.0% according to the most recent monthly report that IATA has publicly posted by the end of 2025-12-31 (UTC).
- Why this formulation: Full-year 2025 figures are typically finalized after year-end. Using IATA’s YTD figure from the latest monthly report available by the deadline ensures the market resolves by 2025-12-31 while closely tracking the same underlying metric (RPK-based demand growth) that would be used for full-year comparisons.
- Key terms and data sources:
  - Global passenger traffic: Measured in Revenue Passenger Kilometres (RPKs), a standard industry metric equal to the number of paying passengers multiplied by distance flown; see background reference for definition (e.g., Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenue_passenger_kilometre).
  - Growth (YTD vs prior year): Percentage change in the sum of RPKs for Jan–N 2025 versus Jan–N 2024, where N is the latest month included in the IATA monthly report used for resolution.
  - Source: IATA’s monthly Air Passenger Market Analysis, published on iata.org under the Economics section (e.g., https://www.iata.org/en/publications/economics/). These reports summarize industry-wide global RPK trends and typically include both monthly and year-to-date comparisons.
- Context for forecasters: 2025 demand is influenced by macroeconomic conditions, fuel prices, aircraft supply chains, geopolitics, and regional travel dynamics. The 4.0% threshold is set to create meaningful uncertainty around whether growth decelerates enough, by late-2025, to fall below that level in YTD terms.
- Timeframe: Start date 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC; end date 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Only IATA monthly reports publicly posted by the end date are eligible for resolution.
resolution_criteria:
Binary outcome; resolves on or shortly after 2025-12-31 (UTC) using documents available by the deadline.

Primary metric and definitions:
- Metric: Industry-wide global passenger traffic growth, measured as the percentage change in year-to-date (YTD) global RPKs in 2025 versus the same YTD period in 2024, as reported by IATA’s monthly Air Passenger Market Analysis posted on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- RPKs (Revenue Passenger Kilometres): Paying passengers multiplied by distance flown (see definition link in Background). “Global” refers to the industry-wide aggregate across all regions as presented by IATA in the report.
- YTD period: Jan–N, where N is the latest month included in the specific IATA monthly report used for resolution (e.g., Jan–Oct or Jan–Nov). We use the YTD period exactly as labeled in that IATA report.

Question restated precisely:
- YES if the latest IATA monthly Air Passenger Market Analysis published on or before 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC reports the 2025 YTD global RPK growth figure to be strictly less than 4.0% versus the same YTD period in 2024.
- NO if that reported figure is greater than or equal to 4.0%.

Source selection rules (to avoid ambiguity):
1) Use the most recently published IATA monthly Air Passenger Market Analysis available on iata.org by the deadline. “Published” means an English-language page or PDF hosted under the iata.org domain that is publicly accessible by the deadline.
2) If multiple pages exist for the same month, use the page that IATA’s Economics publications page links to most prominently for that month as of the deadline.
3) If the chosen report presents multiple global figures, use the industry-wide global aggregate. Ignore region-specific or domestic/international-only aggregates.

Figure extraction and rounding:
- Use the explicit 2025 YTD vs 2024 YTD percentage figure as stated in the report (prefer text/tables over charts). If multiple precisions are shown, use the most precise (e.g., one decimal place over whole-number rounding).
- Comparison is strict: “below 4.0%” means < 4.0 percentage points. Exactly 4.0% resolves NO.

Fallbacks (rare):
- If the report does not explicitly state a YTD vs prior-year global growth figure, use the accompanying IATA press release for that month if it states the global YTD figure. If neither contains a global YTD figure, use the next-most-recent IATA monthly Air Passenger Market Analysis (prior month) that does state it.
- If IATA’s site is unavailable at the deadline, use an archived snapshot (e.g., archive.org) captured on or before the deadline.

Start/end window and timezone:
- Eligible publications: 2025-09-22 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (resolution uses the latest eligible report). All times UTC.

Examples and non-examples:
- If the latest report by the deadline states “2025 YTD RPKs up 3.9% vs 2024,” resolve YES.
- If it states “2025 YTD RPKs up 4.0% (or 4.1%) vs 2024,” resolve NO.

Administrative:
- If, despite the fallbacks, no eligible IATA report with a usable global YTD figure is publicly available by the deadline, the question resolves N/A (void).

question: Will NHS England’s elective waiting list (incomplete RTT pathways) at end-October 2025 be at least 7,440,000?
background:
Context and status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- What is being measured: NHS England publishes monthly Referral to Treatment (RTT) waiting times for consultant-led elective care. The “incomplete RTT pathways” series is a snapshot of cases where patients are still waiting to start treatment at the end of the reporting month; this is commonly referred to as the elective waiting list. A patient can be on more than one pathway, so the count is pathways, not unique patients.
- Formal definitions and how the snapshot is taken: Incomplete pathways are “RTT waiting times so far for cases where patients are still waiting to start treatment at the end of the reporting month. This is a ‘snapshot’ on the last day of the reporting period.” The guidance also clarifies what an RTT pathway/period is and that one person may have multiple RTT periods along a pathway, implying the waiting list is not a count of unique people.
- Publication cadence and source: NHS England releases monthly RTT data to a pre-announced timetable, typically about six weeks after month-end and usually on the second Thursday of the month. The 2025–26 releases (including October 2025 when published) are hosted on the RTT waiting times statistics area and the dedicated 2025–26 page.
- Latest figures available: The Statistical Press Notice (SPN) for July 2025 reports approximately 7.4 million incomplete pathways at month-end (with an estimated 6.2 million unique patients), and notes a 2.9% (220,285) decrease in incomplete pathways compared with July 2024. The SPN also reiterates the usual publication cadence. These figures provide a recent baseline ahead of autumn 2025. Earlier in the year, RCS England cited 7.42 million incomplete pathways at end-March 2025.
- Methodology and comparability notes: The SPN outlines methods for handling missing data (estimation for incomplete pathways), and cautions about seasonality when comparing month-on-month figures. From February 2024, community service pathways were removed from RTT datasets (moved to community collections), affecting comparability for some specialties; national totals since then reflect this scope. This question relies on the national total as published by NHS England for October 2025.

Why this threshold and timeframe: As of mid-2025, the waiting list has been around 7.4 million, with modest movements month to month. Setting the threshold at 7,440,000 pathways aims to make the outcome genuinely uncertain while remaining close enough to current levels to avoid triviality. October 2025 data are normally published in mid-December, enabling resolution before year-end.

Key references for forecasters:
- NHS England RTT statistics main page and 2025–26 monthly releases page (source of truth for the October 2025 publication when it appears).
- July 2025 SPN (latest national figures and cadence/method notes).
- RCS England commentary citing the end-March 2025 total (trend context).
resolution_criteria:
- Resolution: Resolve Yes if the NHS England October 2025 RTT monthly publication reports the national total number of incomplete RTT pathways (all specialties, England) at the end of October 2025 to be greater than or equal to 7,440,000; resolve No otherwise.

- Metric to read: Use the unrounded national total for “incomplete RTT pathways” at month-end (the elective waiting list count) as published alongside the October 2025 release. If the Statistical Press Notice (SPN) headlines a rounded figure, the accompanying official data table (national total) will be the source for the exact integer used for resolution. If there is any discrepancy between a rounded figure in the SPN and the integer in the data tables, use the integer from the data tables.

- Source of truth (where to look):
  1) NHS England RTT Waiting Times statistics area, 2025–26 page, entry for October 2025 (SPN PDF and accompanying data tables/CSV).
  2) If the October 2025 SPN is published but the data tables appear separately on the same statistics area, use the first version of the October 2025 national data tables posted there on or before 2025-12-31 UTC.

- Timing: The question concerns the end-of-month snapshot for October 2025 (as defined by NHS England’s RTT guidance: a snapshot on the last day of the reporting period). The question resolves upon the first official publication of October 2025 RTT waiting times on the NHS England statistics site, expected approximately six weeks after month-end (typically the second Thursday of December) and in any case no later than 2025-12-31 UTC.

- Scope and definitions (for avoidance of doubt):
  • “Incomplete RTT pathways” means cases where patients are still waiting to start treatment at the end of the reporting month; this is the elective waiting list. It is a count of pathways, not unique patients.
  • “NHS England” scope refers to England-wide consultant-led RTT data published by NHS England’s Statistics team (this excludes devolved administrations). Use the England total across all specialties published in the official tables.
  • The end-of-month concept and RTT pathway definitions follow NHS England’s RTT rules and guidance.
  • Methodological features such as estimation for missing providers are accepted as part of the official national total as published, and no further adjustments will be made for resolution.

- Versioning and revisions: Resolve based on the first version of the October 2025 RTT publication (SPN and/or tables) that appears on the NHS England statistics site on or before 2025-12-31 UTC. Subsequent revisions published after resolution will not alter the outcome. NHS England’s revisions policy notes that revisions are typically released semi-annually (e.g., January/July).

question: Will the December 2025 OPEC MOMR report IR Iran’s November 2025 crude oil production (secondary sources) at 3,150 tb/d or lower?
background:
Overview and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- OPEC’s Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is a monthly publication, typically released mid-month. OPEC lists the 2025 release dates on its MOMR page, including Thursday, 11 December 2025. The report is accessible through OPEC’s website and its Digital Publications portal.
- The MOMR contains a standardized table titled “Table 5-7: DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d,” which reports country-by-country crude oil production for OPEC and participating Declaration of Cooperation (DoC) countries using “secondary sources,” in units of thousand barrels per day (tb/d). Countries are labeled by name, including “IR Iran.” For example, the August 2025 MOMR includes Table 5-7 and reports IR Iran’s crude oil production for July 2025 as 3,245 tb/d, illustrating the table’s format and a typical one-month lag (August report showing July data). The February 2025 MOMR likewise includes Table 5-7 (“DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d”) with the same structure, labeling, and units.
- In MOMR methodology, “crude oil production” in Table 5-7 is distinct from and excludes NGLs and non-conventional liquids, which are tabulated separately; Table 5-7 figures are compiled by OPEC from independent external providers (“secondary sources”) rather than relying solely on member self-reporting.
- Context: On September 27, 2025 at 0000 GMT, the UN “snapback” reimposition of sanctions on Iran took effect, reinstating measures such as the arms embargo and various targeted restrictions. This development could affect Iran’s production/export dynamics going into November 2025.
- Baseline magnitude: As noted above, IR Iran’s reported crude oil production (secondary sources) was 3,245 tb/d for July 2025 in the August 2025 MOMR. Given the one-month lag pattern, the December 2025 MOMR is expected to include the November 2025 figure in Table 5-7.

Key term clarifications (with authoritative links for definitions):
- OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR): official monthly report and landing page (https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html).
- OPEC Digital Publications portal for MOMR (where monthly editions are posted): https://publications.opec.org/momr.
- “Crude oil” is distinct from NGLs and other liquids; MOMR’s Table 5-7 covers crude oil only, excluding NGLs and non-conventional liquids. General definition of crude oil: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crude_oil (informational link).
- Units: tb/d = thousand barrels per day. Table 5-7 values are presented in tb/d; forecasters should compare directly to the 3,150 tb/d threshold.
- Country labeling: OPEC’s tables label the country as “IR Iran” in Table 5-7.

Why this question has non-trivial uncertainty:
- The re-imposition of UN sanctions (snapback) could tighten compliance/enforcement and affect export channels, but Iran may also take steps to sustain production and off-take. These opposing forces create plausible pathways for November 2025 production to end up on either side of 3,150 tb/d as reported by OPEC’s secondary sources.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on the figure reported for IR Iran in the December 2025 edition of the OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR), specifically in “Table 5-7: DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d.”

- Measurement:
  - Locate the December 2025 MOMR on OPEC’s official channels: the MOMR landing page (https://www.opec.org/monthly-oil-market-report.html) and/or the OPEC Digital Publications portal (https://publications.opec.org/momr). The December 2025 release is scheduled for Thursday, 11 December 2025, and should be available by year-end.
  - In the December 2025 MOMR PDF, find Table 5-7 (“DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d”). Within that table, identify the entry for the country labeled “IR Iran” and read the value corresponding to November 2025. The table presents values in thousand barrels per day (tb/d).

- Resolution rule:
  - Resolve “Yes” if the IR Iran November 2025 value in Table 5-7 is less than or equal to 3,150 tb/d.
  - Resolve “No” if the value is greater than 3,150 tb/d.

- Scope and exclusions:
  - Only the Table 5-7 figure (“crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d”) will be used. Self-reported figures, other tables, narrative text, charts, or external datasets are not used for resolution.
  - “Crude oil production” here excludes NGLs and non-conventional liquids per MOMR’s table taxonomy; do not substitute series that include NGLs/condensates.

- Version control and timing:
  - Use the version of the December 2025 MOMR available on OPEC’s official website/portal as of 23:59:59 UTC on 31 December 2025. If multiple versions exist on OPEC’s site by that cutoff, use the latest one posted by that time.

- Data availability contingency (unlikely):
  - MOMR tables typically exhibit a one-month lag (e.g., the August 2025 MOMR shows July 2025 values), so the December 2025 MOMR is expected to contain November 2025 data in Table 5-7. If, contrary to precedent, the December 2025 MOMR does not include November 2025 values for IR Iran in Table 5-7, then the question will be resolved N/A (void) on 1 January 2026, 00:00:00 UTC.

Primary resolution sources and documentation of facts in this prompt:
- OPEC MOMR landing page with 2025 release dates (shows the December 11, 2025 date).
- OPEC Digital Publications portal for MOMR.
- MOMR Table 5-7 description, units tb/d, labeling, and example value for IR Iran (July 2025 = 3,245 tb/d).
- Clarification that Table 5-7 refers to crude oil production excluding NGLs and non-conventional liquids, compiled from external secondary sources.
- UN snapback sanctions on Iran took effect at 0000 GMT on 27 September 2025.

question: Will the BLS CPI-U report a November 2025 year-over-year increase of at least 12.5% for the “beef and veal” index?
background:
Context and current status (as of 2025-09-30):
- What metric we are forecasting: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) measures the average change over time in prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of goods and services. The CPI routinely reports 1-month and 12-month percent changes; the 12-month change represents the year-over-year (YoY) percent change in the index for a given month (e.g., November 2025 vs. November 2024). BLS publishes both unadjusted and seasonally adjusted figures; for item-level 12-month changes, the news release tables present “Unadjusted percent change,” and BLS recommends unadjusted data for uses requiring stability because seasonally adjusted data may be revised.
- What “beef and veal” means in CPI: The CPI “beef and veal” aggregate covers specific entry-level items (ELIs): Uncooked ground beef (FC011), Uncooked beef roasts (FC021), Uncooked beef steaks (FC031), and Uncooked other beef and veal (FC041, which includes all fresh or frozen veal and beef cuts not in the other beef categories). These descriptions clarify inclusions and exclusions (e.g., veal is included only under FC041; organ meats, beef jerky, and sausages are excluded).
- Latest data point: In the latest available BLS CPI news release (covering August 2025, published September 2025), the 12-month percent change for “Beef and veal” was reported as 13.9% in the “Unadjusted percent change Aug. 2024 – Aug. 2025” column of Table 7 (U.S. city average, by expenditure category).
- External context for 2025 beef price expectations: USDA Economic Research Service (ERS) Food Price Outlook (updated September 2025) projects beef and veal prices to increase 11.6% for calendar year 2025, with a prediction interval of 9.5% to 13.8%, citing tight cattle supplies since 2019 and strong consumer demand. ERS forecasts are expressed as annual average percentage changes (current year’s average vs. prior year’s average), not as a specific month’s 12-month change.
- Timing for resolution: The CPI for November 2025 is scheduled for release on Wednesday, December 10, 2025, at 8:30 AM Eastern Time (ET).

Why this threshold and timing: Choosing a 12.5% YoY threshold focuses on a concrete month-on-month comparison (Nov 2025 vs. Nov 2024) that is regularly published by BLS and will be available before year-end. The threshold is set near recent values and within ERS’s plausible 2025 range, aiming to create meaningful uncertainty around the outcome.

Key definitions (for clarity):
- CPI-U: The CPI for All Urban Consumers, representing over 90% of the U.S. population, based on urban consumer spending patterns.
- 12-month percent change (YoY): The percentage change from the index level for a given CPI category in one month to the same month a year earlier. In the BLS CPI news release tables for item categories, this is reported as “Unadjusted percent change”.
- “Beef and veal” CPI category: The CPI aggregate comprising the entry-level items noted above (FC011, FC021, FC031, FC041).
resolution_criteria:
Primary source and timing:
- Use the BLS “Consumer Price Index Summary” news release that publishes the November 2025 CPI data. As of BLS’s schedule, this release is set for December 10, 2025 at 8:30 AM ET. The question will resolve upon publication of that release.

How to check and decide:
1) In the November 2025 CPI news release, locate the item-level tables that report unadjusted 12-month changes. Acceptable tables are:
   - Table 7: “Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U): U.S. city average, by expenditure category, [reference month], 12-month analysis table,” which displays “Unadjusted percent change [Nov. 2024 – Nov. 2025]” for each category including “Beef and veal”.
   - If Table 7 is unavailable, use Table 2 in the same news release if it reports the “Beef and veal” 12-month percent change (unadjusted) for November 2025 (the CPI news release routinely includes item-level 12-month percent changes).
2) Identify the 12-month percent change for “Beef and veal” (CPI-U, U.S. city average, not seasonally adjusted) for November 2025 as printed in the table.
3) Resolution rule: If that printed 12-month percent change is greater than or equal to 12.5%, resolve Yes; otherwise, resolve No. Use the figure exactly as published by BLS (to the reported precision, typically one decimal place); do not recalculate or apply rounding beyond what BLS reports.

Clarifications and definitions (for unambiguous resolution):
- The “12-month percent change” for November 2025 is the YoY change comparing the CPI-U “Beef and veal” index for November 2025 to November 2024, as defined and routinely presented by BLS; this measure is reported on an unadjusted basis in the news release tables.
- The “Beef and veal” CPI category refers to the CPI aggregate comprising Uncooked ground beef (FC011), Uncooked beef roasts (FC021), Uncooked beef steaks (FC031), and Uncooked other beef and veal (FC041).
- Timezone: The cited BLS release time is Eastern Time per the BLS schedule; if needed for coordination, 8:30 AM ET on December 10, 2025 corresponds to 13:30 UTC (conversion provided for clarity).
- This question pertains strictly to the CPI-U U.S. city average series (not seasonally adjusted) as published in the national BLS CPI news release for November 2025; regional or seasonally adjusted figures do not apply.

question: By December 31, 2025, will at least six of the 12 regular FY2026 appropriations bills be enacted into law?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- What is FY2026? FY2026 is the U.S. federal fiscal year running from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026.
- What are “regular appropriations bills”? In the U.S., there are 12 annual “regular appropriations” bills that fund most discretionary programs for a single fiscal year. They correspond to the jurisdictions of the 12 House and Senate Appropriations subcommittees. Regular appropriations may be enacted as standalone bills or packaged together in a consolidated/omnibus appropriations act with separate divisions for different subcommittee jurisdictions.
- The 12 canonical regular appropriations subcommittee jurisdictions are: (1) Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies; (2) Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies; (3) Defense; (4) Energy and Water Development; (5) Financial Services and General Government; (6) Homeland Security; (7) Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies; (8) Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies; (9) Legislative Branch; (10) Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies; (11) State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs; (12) Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies.
- Status quo: The FY2026 Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov exists and, as of late September 2025, showed no FY2026 regular appropriations enacted (the Presidential Action/Public Law fields were blank). The table is maintained by CRS and tracks Regular Appropriations, Continuing Resolutions, Supplementals, and Budget Resolutions; it also indicates when multiple regular bills are combined into a consolidated act and breaks out divisions by subcommittee jurisdiction.
- Key definitions and sources used for resolution: “Enacted into law” means a bill or joint resolution that has passed both chambers in identical form and has become law via presidential signature, veto override, or becoming law without signature; such laws receive Public Law numbers and are listed on Congress.gov. The FY2026 CRS Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov is the primary tracker for enactment status of each regular bill or of divisions within a consolidated appropriations act.

Why this is forecastable: As of late September 2025, none of the 12 FY2026 regular appropriations were enacted, yet multiple legislative paths (standalones, minibuses/omnibuses, or reliance on continuing resolutions) remain possible over Q4 2025. Whether at least six subcommittee jurisdictions receive full-year regular appropriations by year-end is uncertain and sensitive to congressional negotiations, making it a high-entropy legislative target.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Resolve whether at least six of the 12 regular FY2026 appropriations bills are enacted into law by 11:59:59 pm Eastern Time on December 31, 2025.

Event window: Enactments occurring from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC up to and including 2025-12-31 11:59:59 pm Eastern Time (U.S.).

What counts toward the six:
- Count one for each of the following 12 subcommittee jurisdictions that has its FY2026 regular appropriations enacted into law, whether via a standalone act or as a named division within a consolidated (omnibus/minibus) appropriations act:
  1) Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies; 2) Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies; 3) Defense; 4) Energy and Water Development; 5) Financial Services and General Government; 6) Homeland Security; 7) Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies; 8) Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies; 9) Legislative Branch; 10) Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies; 11) State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs; 12) Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies.
- Consolidated/omnibus acts: If a single consolidated appropriations act includes multiple divisions corresponding to distinct subcommittee jurisdictions (e.g., one division for Defense and another for CJS), each such division counts separately toward the total (i.e., two in this example).

Exclusions:
- Continuing resolutions (CRs) do not count toward the six, even if they provide full-year funding. Only regular appropriations for FY2026 as tracked in the Regular Appropriations section count.
- Supplemental appropriations measures do not count.

Definitions:
- FY2026: U.S. federal fiscal year running from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026.
- Regular appropriations bills: The twelve annual bills aligning with the 12 Appropriations subcommittees that provide discretionary funding for one fiscal year; they may be enacted individually or as divisions within a consolidated appropriations act.
- Enacted into law: A measure that has passed both chambers in identical form and becomes law via presidential signature, veto override, or becoming law without signature; such measures are assigned Public Law numbers and listed on Congress.gov.

Primary resolution source and how to check:
- Use the FY2026 CRS Appropriations Status Table on Congress.gov (Regular Appropriations tab) at https://www.congress.gov/crs-appropriations-status-table/2026. Resolve “Yes” if, as of the deadline, at least six of the 12 jurisdictions show a presidential approval date and Public Law number (or equivalent indication of enactment) for FY2026 regular appropriations; otherwise resolve “No”.

Secondary/back-up sources if needed:
- Relevant Congress.gov bill pages that display “Became Public Law No: …” for FY2026 regular appropriations acts/divisions, and the Congress.gov Public Laws page for the 119th Congress (for PL confirmation). If there is any discrepancy at the deadline, rely on the Appropriations Status Table; if it appears not yet updated but a bill page shows that an FY2026 regular appropriations act/division has become law by the deadline, count it.

Notes:
- This question resolves based on laws enacted into law by the deadline; post-deadline updates do not count.
- The event window and deadline times are inclusive and use UTC for the start and U.S. Eastern Time for the deadline to align with typical congressional reporting cutoffs.

question: Between Oct 15 and Dec 31, 2025 (UTC), will Gazprom publicly announce that it has resumed supplying natural gas to Moldova (including Transnistria) for consumption within Moldova?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On Dec 28–29, 2024, Gazprom stated it would suspend gas exports to Moldova starting at 05:00 GMT on Jan 1, 2025, citing unpaid debts; the claimed arrears were disputed by Moldovan authorities. Moldova’s energy ministry also said on Dec 17, 2024 that Gazprom made no bookings on the Trans‑Balkan pipeline for January, reinforcing expectations of a supply halt with the expiry of the Russia–Ukraine transit agreement at end‑2024. In 2025, Moldova accelerated market reforms: the regulator withdrew Moldovagaz’s gas distribution license in August and designated state‑owned Energocom to take over service to consumers starting Sept 1, amid wider restructuring and an ongoing debt dispute with Gazprom. The Moldovan Energy Ministry reports that, by Sept 2025, Moldova had been procuring gas via Energocom from multiple EU‑based suppliers and routes, with Gazprom deliveries to Transnistria having stopped at the beginning of 2025. Moldovagaz (historically 50% owned by Gazprom, ~35% by Moldova’s government, ~13% by Transnistria) no longer performs wholesale supply but continues distribution functions under ongoing sector unbundling.

Why this matters: A formal resumption announced by Gazprom would signify a shift in the commercial and geopolitical dynamics of Moldova’s gas supply, potentially via the Trans‑Balkan route or other arrangements, and would interact with Moldova’s regulatory changes and debt negotiations. The timing and conditions of any restart are uncertain and analyzable, creating forecasting entropy.

Key references for forecasters:
- Gazprom suspension announcement details (timing, rationale).
- Trans‑Balkan booking status and transit expiry context.
- Moldova’s regulatory changes affecting Moldovagaz and Energocom.
- Moldovagaz ownership and role.
resolution_criteria:
Resolve Yes if, between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025, Gazprom publishes an official communication stating that it has resumed supplying natural gas to the Republic of Moldova (including the Transnistria region) for consumption within Moldova, effective on or before Dec 31, 2025.

Definitions and scope:
- Gazprom: Public Joint Stock Company Gazprom, Russia’s state‑owned energy company. For general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazprom (link provided for identification only).
- Republic of Moldova: The internationally recognized sovereign state; for general reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldova.
- Transnistria: The de facto breakaway region on the left bank of the Dniester River; for reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transnistria.
- Natural gas: A fossil fuel primarily composed of methane; for reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas.
- Publicly announce: An official communication issued on Gazprom’s official channels, specifically either:
  1) Gazprom’s Press Center (https://www.gazprom.com/press/news/), or
  2) Gazprom’s official Telegram channel (https://t.me/gazprom).
  The announcement must be attributable to Gazprom (i.e., published by Gazprom’s official accounts/website) and clearly state that gas supplies to Moldova have resumed (or will resume by Dec 31, 2025).
- Resumed supplying: A restart of physical deliveries to Moldova after the halt that began on Jan 1, 2025 at 05:00 GMT. The announcement must indicate that actual gas flow for consumption within Moldova has started or will start on or before Dec 31, 2025.
- Consumption within Moldova: Gas intended for end‑use within the internationally recognized territory of Moldova, including Transnistria. Transit flows passing through Moldova to third countries do not count.

What counts:
- A Gazprom announcement specifying that Gazprom has resumed (or will resume by Dec 31, 2025) supplies to Moldova/Moldovagaz/Energocom/Transnistria for consumption within Moldova.
- Any route (e.g., via the Trans‑Balkan pipeline or other) and any commercial arrangement (e.g., direct sale to Moldovagaz, Energocom, or another designated Moldovan entity) are eligible, provided the announcement clearly pertains to supplies destined for consumption within Moldova.

What does NOT count:
- Announcements by non‑Gazprom entities unless directly quoting and linking to an official Gazprom announcement.
- Mere capacity bookings, intent statements, or MoUs without a stated effective date on or before Dec 31, 2025.
- Announcements about transit through Moldova to other countries.
- Deliveries of non‑Gazprom gas.

Acceptable secondary sources for verification (if they directly report and reference the official Gazprom announcement): Reuters, Associated Press, Bloomberg, and S&P Global Commodity Insights (example energy desk pages: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/, https://apnews.com/hub/energy, https://www.bloomberg.com/energy, https://www.spglobal.com/commodity-insights/en). Use secondary sources only if the primary Gazprom announcement is clearly cited or quoted.

Timeframe and timezone: Only announcements first published between 00:00 UTC on Oct 15, 2025 and 23:59 UTC on Dec 31, 2025 are eligible. All times are in UTC.

Resolution process:
- YES if an eligible Gazprom announcement, per the above, exists within the timeframe and explicitly states resumption of supplies to Moldova effective on or before Dec 31, 2025 [baseline context: 727ace, 97bcec].
- NO otherwise.

Notes for resolvers:
- Moldova’s sector changes (e.g., Energocom’s role, Moldovagaz license changes) do not affect eligibility; any Gazprom‑announced resumption to any Moldovan entity for consumption within Moldova qualifies.
- Background on the initial halt and transit context is provided for interpreting “resumed supplying”.

question: Will NOAA SWPC report at least one G4 (Severe) or G5 (Extreme) geomagnetic storm between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC?
background:
Context and definitions a forecaster needs:

- NOAA G-scale thresholds and frequencies: NOAA’s Space Weather Scales define G4 (Severe) geomagnetic storms as corresponding to Kp = 8 (including a 9-), and G5 (Extreme) as Kp = 9. The scales also provide average frequency estimates per solar cycle (G4 ≈ 100 events/60 days per cycle; G5 ≈ 4 events/4 days per cycle).
- What is Kp: The planetary K-index (Kp) is a globally averaged indicator of geomagnetic disturbance, derived from magnetometer observations in 3-hour intervals, on an integer scale from 0–9. Kp is used by SWPC to characterize geomagnetic storm magnitude and to decide when to issue alerts and warnings.
- How SWPC “reports” storms operationally: SWPC issues Alerts/Watches/Warnings messages that include “ALERT: Geomagnetic K-index of X” and provide a “Threshold Reached: YYYY Mon DD HHMM UTC” timestamp and the 3-hour “Synoptic Period.” These messages are available in a current JSON feed and archived text files, enabling verification after the fact.
- Archival and corroboration sources: Weekly Highlights and 27-Day Forecast are issued each Monday and include dated summaries of significant space weather events, useful for cross-checks. NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) is the official long-term archive for SWPC products and data.
- Current cycle context: Solar Cycle 25’s updated prediction (released in 2025) indicates the cycle’s progression based on observed data; the earlier 2019 NOAA/NASA/ISES Panel predicted a maximum around July 2025, with uncertainty spanning November 2024–March 2026. Recent activity included a G5 (Extreme) geomagnetic storm in May 2024, underscoring elevated storm potential near maximum.

Key term definitions (all times UTC):
- “Geomagnetic storm” refers to major disturbances of Earth’s magnetosphere caused by solar wind variations, with impacts on satellites, radio signals, GNSS, power grids, and aurora; the Kp index serves as the basis for NOAA’s geomagnetic storm scale (G-scale).
- “G4 (Severe) geomagnetic storm” means Kp reaches 8 (including 9-) during a 3-hour synoptic period, per NOAA’s G-scale.
- “G5 (Extreme) geomagnetic storm” means Kp reaches 9 during a 3-hour synoptic period, per NOAA’s G-scale.
- “Kp index” is the planetary 3-hour range index (integer 0–9) derived from standardized magnetometer stations; SWPC uses it to determine alerts and warnings.
- “Reported by SWPC” means SWPC issued an Alert message stating “Geomagnetic K-index of 8” or “Geomagnetic K-index of 9,” with a “Threshold Reached” timestamp recorded in the message. The authoritative sources to check are SWPC’s Alerts/Watches/Warnings current JSON feed and the archived text files.

Status quo as of 2025-10-01: Solar Cycle 25 is near its predicted maximum window, increasing the plausibility of severe/extreme storms within the question window. SWPC provides continuous operational alerts and maintains accessible archives for verification.
resolution_criteria:
Primary resolution rule:
- Resolve YES if, between 2025-10-15 00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59 UTC inclusive, the SWPC Alerts/Watches/Warnings product contains at least one Alert message that explicitly states either “ALERT: Geomagnetic K-index of 8” or “ALERT: Geomagnetic K-index of 9,” where the message’s “Threshold Reached: YYYY Mon DD HHMM UTC” timestamp falls within the window. Otherwise resolve NO.

Primary sources to use:
- SWPC Alerts/Watches/Warnings current JSON feed: https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/products/alerts.json (contains Alert messages with issue times, synoptic periods, NOAA scale mappings, and “Threshold Reached” timestamps).
- SWPC archived alert text files: ftp://ftp.swpc.noaa.gov/pub/alerts/ (for historical verification if needed).

Definitions and mappings for adjudication:
- G4 corresponds to Kp = 8 (including 9-); G5 corresponds to Kp = 9. These thresholds are defined by NOAA’s Space Weather Scales and are the basis for adjudicating whether the relevant Alert indicates a G4 or G5 storm.
- Kp is a 3-hour planetary index (0–9) used by SWPC to characterize geomagnetic storm magnitude and to determine alert issuance.

Corroboration (if desired but not required):
- SWPC Weekly Highlights and 27-Day Forecast (issued Mondays) may be consulted to cross-check significant events during the window (current weekly text and annual archives are available via SWPC services and FTP).
- NCEI serves as the official long-term archive for SWPC data products; if SWPC’s primary endpoints are temporarily unavailable, consult NCEI’s SWPC Products and Data archive.

Scope, inclusions, and exclusions:
- Inclusion: Any Alert message with “Geomagnetic K-index of 8” or “Geomagnetic K-index of 9” whose “Threshold Reached” timestamp is within the defined window counts as one event; only one such event is required for a YES.
- Exclusions: Watches and Warnings without a corresponding Alert do not count; non-NOAA third-party dashboards or estimated indices (e.g., experimental aurora dashboards) do not count unless reflected as an SWPC Alert in the sources above.
- Timezone: All timestamps are adjudicated in UTC, using the “Threshold Reached” timestamp in the Alert message.

Adjudication notes:
- If multiple alerts occur, any single qualifying alert is sufficient for a YES.
- If the same event is represented in multiple messages (e.g., overlapping synoptic periods), use the “Threshold Reached” timestamp to determine eligibility within the window.
- If the primary SWPC sources are inaccessible at resolution time, the adjudicator should use NCEI’s archive of SWPC products to locate the relevant alert messages.

question: Will Poland promulgate by December 31, 2025 an amendment to the 2009 Polish Citizenship Act that increases the minimum continuous residence for recognition from 3 to 10 years?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: The Act of 2 April 2009 on Polish citizenship (Ustawa z dnia 2 kwietnia 2009 r. o obywatelstwie polskim) governs acquisition and confirmation of Polish citizenship. Article 30 establishes the administrative pathway of “recognition as a Polish citizen” (uznanie za obywatela polskiego). Under Art. 30(1)(1) a foreigner may be recognized as a Polish citizen if they have resided continuously in Poland for at least 3 years on specified residence bases and meet other conditions; the law’s text uses “co najmniej od 3 lat” and “nieprzerwanie” to describe this residency requirement.

Recent development: On 2025-09-29, the President’s Chancellery announced submission to the Sejm of a draft law to amend the Citizenship Act. The proposal explicitly extends the minimum period of uninterrupted residence required for recognition from 3 to 10 years, specifying the relevant bases of stay (permanent residence permit, long-term EU resident permit, or permanent right of residence).

Primary resolution source: Polish laws are promulgated in Dziennik Ustaw (Journal of Laws), which is the official source of law for publication of statutes; since 2012 it is published electronically and serves as the authoritative venue to verify whether an amendment has been promulgated by the cutoff date. Resolver should check the Dziennik Ustaw website for the relevant amending act and its content.

Context for forecasters: This question focuses narrowly on whether the announced change is actually enacted and promulgated by end-2025. It does not require assessing broader migration policy or exceptions within the recognition pathway; the event is the formal promulgation of an amendment that sets the minimum continuous residence at 10 years for recognition. Forecasters may consider legislative timelines, coalition dynamics, committee schedules, and end-of-year promulgation cadence in Dziennik Ustaw.
resolution_criteria:
Date window and time zone: Eligible events must occur between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. All times are UTC.

Definitions and scope:
