- Measurement: For each qualifying decision within the time window, record the magnitude of the reduction (e.g., 25 bps). Sum all such reductions. If any reduction is not a multiple of 25 bps, use the exact amount stated.
- Resolution: YES if the cumulative total is ≥ 75 bps; NO otherwise.
- Primary resolution source: Federal Reserve monetary policy press releases page: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary.htm. If needed for cross-checking, use the FRED series for the upper limit of the target range to verify the step changes: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU.
- Edge cases:
  - If the FOMC announces a change outside a scheduled meeting within the window, it counts if published on the press releases page within the window.
  - Technical adjustments that do not change the target range do not count.
  - If multiple actions occur on the same calendar day, sum all downward changes announced that day.

The question resolves after the last 2025 press release; we will apply the rules above to determine the cumulative cuts.

question: Will at least 30% of the top 50 US P/C insurance groups report production use of AI in underwriting during 2025 (UTC)?
background: Context as of 2025-09-22: This question measures self-reported, production deployment of AI within underwriting by large US property/casualty (P/C) insurance groups, using a fixed, public denominator and strict evidence rules. The denominator is the 50 largest US P/C insurance groups by countrywide direct written premium, taken from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) 2024 Market Share Reports for Property/Casualty Groups and Companies (Top 125 groups by countrywide premium). See the NAIC publications hub for the recurring Market Share Reports series: https://content.naic.org/publications. Forecasters should anticipate verifying numerator events primarily via 2025-dated disclosures on company investor relations sites/newsrooms and SEC filings accessible via EDGAR (https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/). Definitions used here: “Underwriting” follows standard insurance usage (see NAIC glossary: https://content.naic.org/glossary-insurance-terms); “Direct written premium” likewise follows NAIC glossary usage; “AI system” follows the OECD definition (https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles/definition-of-an-ai-system). Industry discussion in 2024–2025 suggests ongoing, uneven adoption of AI across underwriting workflows, with substantial piloting activity and selective production deployments; however, this question resolves solely on documented 2025 statements meeting the criteria below, not on surveys or anecdote.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, at least 30% (i.e., 15 or more) of the denominator groups (defined below) make eligible, on-the-record statements indicating production use of AI in underwriting, as defined below. Otherwise, it resolves No. It may resolve early if the threshold is clearly met before the end date.

Denominator (fixed): The 50 largest US property/casualty insurance groups by countrywide direct written premium listed in the NAIC 2024 Market Share Reports for Property/Casualty Groups and Companies (specifically, the Top 125 groups by countrywide premium; use the top 50 groups from that list). Source location: NAIC publications hub (https://content.naic.org/publications). “Group” and group names are taken exactly as listed by NAIC in that report. If NAIC publishes the Top 125 in multiple files, use the file that shows the countrywide ranking of groups for property/casualty and extract the top 50 groups by countrywide direct written premium.

Key definitions and scope:
- Underwriting: The insurer’s process of evaluating/accepting risk and setting terms/prices for coverage (e.g., risk selection, pricing, binding). See NAIC glossary: https://content.naic.org/glossary-insurance-terms.
- Direct written premium (DWP): Use NAIC glossary meaning for DWP and NAIC’s “countrywide” aggregation as presented in the Market Share report. See NAIC glossary: https://content.naic.org/glossary-insurance-terms.
- AI system: A machine-based system that, for explicit human-defined objectives, makes predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments (e.g., per OECD definition: https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles/definition-of-an-ai-system). For this question, “AI” includes machine learning models and generative AI (e.g., GLMs, tree ensembles, gradient boosting, neural networks/LLMs, or vendor solutions using such techniques). It explicitly excludes purely deterministic rules engines, robotic process automation (RPA) without learning, macros, regex-only parsing, or simple statistical lookups without learned parameters.
- Production use (required): The AI is used in live underwriting workflows affecting real policy decisions or pricing (e.g., risk scoring, price indication, eligibility triage, submission intake/extraction whose outputs feed binding/quotation decisions). Pilots, proofs-of-concept, sandbox testing, or language like “exploring,” “testing,” or “planning” do not qualify unless accompanied by a clear statement that the system is deployed in production for underwriting decisions.
- What counts as “in underwriting”: Qualifying uses include, but are not limited to: risk selection scores used to accept/decline, pricing/indication models, peril-level risk modeling used in rating, and AI-based document/intake systems that populate underwriting/rating inputs used for bindable decisions. Uses confined to claims handling, fraud detection, marketing, customer service, or asset management do not count.

Eligible evidence (must be 2025-dated and publicly accessible by the end date):
- SEC filings (e.g., 10-Q, 8-K, or other forms) accessible via EDGAR (https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/), dated in 2025.
- Company-issued 2025 press releases, investor presentations, earnings call transcripts hosted on the company’s IR site, annual/sustainability/AI reports, product documentation, or official newsroom/engineering blog posts on a corporate domain.
- Statements must be attributable to the group or its subsidiaries (named companies or executives). Third-party vendor claims without the insurer’s on-the-record confirmation do not count.
- The statement must clearly indicate present-tense, production use in underwriting during 2025 (UTC). Prior-year statements only count if they are republished or updated in 2025 and still assert production use.

Counting rules:
- Unit of analysis is the NAIC-listed group. If any US P/C subsidiary within the group meets the criterion and the group or subsidiary makes an eligible statement, count the group as 1; else 0.
- If a statement is ambiguous, it must unambiguously meet all: (a) refers to AI (per above), (b) pertains to underwriting, and (c) indicates production deployment, not merely pilots/plans.
- The market share denominator is fixed from the NAIC 2024 report; changes in 2025 market shares do not affect inclusion.

Resolution procedure:
- The resolver will compile the NAIC 2024 “Top 125 groups” countrywide list and extract the top 50 groups by DWP. Then, for each group, the resolver will search the group’s official site/IR and EDGAR for 2025-dated qualifying statements. Archival copies (e.g., PDFs, screenshots) should be saved.
- The market resolves Yes immediately upon identifying 15 qualifying groups; otherwise, it resolves at 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC based on all qualifying statements published by then.
- If the NAIC 2024 Market Share report becomes temporarily unavailable online, the resolver may use an archived copy of the same report or a library copy clearly referencing the NAIC “Top 125 groups by countrywide premium” list for 2024. If the list cannot be retrieved at all, the question is invalid; however, this is unlikely given the NAIC’s recurring publication and broad availability via regulatory/library channels.

Tie-breakers and exclusions:
- If a statement references “AI” but pertains solely to claims, SIU/fraud, marketing, or customer service chatbots, it does not count.
- If only a vendor asserts the insurer’s underwriting AI deployment and the insurer does not publicly confirm it in 2025, it does not count.
- Deterministic rating rules or traditional actuarial tables without a learned model are excluded; generalized linear models and other learned models are included as AI for this question if used in underwriting decisions.

Outcome: Yes if 15+ groups meet the criteria; No otherwise.

question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, will the U.S. FDA grant at least one De Novo classification or 510(k) clearance for a prescription-only software-based therapeutic intended to treat a mental or behavioral health disorder?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30: In the CY 2025 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule, CMS finalized payment for digital mental health treatment (DMHT) devices furnished as part of behavioral health care. CMS stated that eligible DMHT devices must be FDA 510(k)-cleared or De Novo-authorized and classified under 21 CFR 882.580, and created new HCPCS Level II codes for related services. A CMS summary document lists three new HCPCS codes (G0552, G0553, G0554) for approved DMHT devices used incident to professional behavioral health services under a plan of care. These policies may increase incentives for companies to seek FDA authorizations in late 2025.

What counts as “software-based” and “prescription-only”: FDA recognizes Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) as software intended for one or more medical purposes that performs those purposes without being part of a hardware medical device; SaMD can run on commercial off‑the‑shelf platforms. Prescription devices are defined and labeled under 21 CFR 801.109 (e.g., “Rx only”), and are restricted to sale and use by or on the order of licensed practitioners, with specific labeling requirements.

Relevant FDA device classifications for psychiatric digital therapies: The “computerized behavioral therapy device for psychiatric disorders” is a prescription‑only Class II device under 21 CFR 882.5801, established via an FDA final order; special controls include clinical data validating the behavioral therapy model, software documentation, and labeling requirements. Prior examples of FDA‑authorized prescription digital therapies include reSET (DEN160018), a De Novo‑granted prescription CBT‑based software for substance use disorder , and NightWare (DEN200033), a prescription device using software to reduce sleep disturbance related to nightmares associated with PTSD or nightmare disorder (granted De Novo; Class II under 21 CFR 882.5705).

Primary resolution sources: FDA’s public De Novo database and 510(k) database list decisions with official decision dates and statuses and serve as authoritative sources to verify whether a device was “granted” (De Novo) or cleared (510(k)) within the specified window.

Definition of “mental or behavioral health disorder”: For this question, a mental or behavioral health disorder is one classified in DSM‑5‑TR (e.g., depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, substance‑related and addictive disorders, trauma‑ and stressor‑related disorders). DSM‑5‑TR is the authoritative classification used by U.S. clinicians and researchers.

Why this question is high‑entropy: The combination of a narrow time window (Q4 2025), clear incentive changes (CMS payment and new codes) , and historically limited but real precedents for prescription software therapies  makes the outcome uncertain but plausible within the timeframe.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution window and timezone: Eligible FDA decisions must have a decision date between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, inclusive. For avoidance of doubt, use the “Decision Date” displayed on the FDA database entry (De Novo or 510(k)) as the canonical date; if only a date (without time) is shown, treat it as occurring on that calendar date.

Event to be measured: Resolve YES if at least one device meets all of the following during the resolution window; otherwise resolve NO.

Required criteria:
- Regulatory decision: Either (a) a De Novo classification “Granted” listed in the FDA De Novo database, or (b) a 510(k) clearance listed in the FDA 510(k) database (Substantially Equivalent decision). The decision must be visible on FDA’s official databases: De Novo database: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/denovo.cfm; 510(k) database: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/pmn.cfm.
- Prescription‑only: The device must be prescription‑only. Evidence can be (i) the presence of “Rx only” or equivalent prescription restriction in labeling per 21 CFR 801.109, or (ii) an explicit prescription‑use statement in the FDA decision summary or database entry.
- Software‑based therapeutic: The device’s therapeutic function is performed by software. Devices that meet the FDA‑recognized definition of SaMD (software intended for one or more medical purposes, not part of a hardware medical device) qualify; software that runs on commercial off‑the‑shelf platforms qualifies. Systems that include non‑medical hardware (e.g., consumer devices) are eligible if the therapeutic action is executed by software. Purely hardware‑based therapies without a software therapeutic component do not qualify.
- Intended to treat a mental or behavioral health disorder: The device’s intended use, as described in the FDA decision summary and/or labeling, must include therapeutic treatment, management, or reduction of symptoms for at least one DSM‑5‑TR mental or behavioral health disorder (e.g., substance use disorders, PTSD‑related nightmares, depressive disorders, anxiety disorders). Diagnostic‑only, monitoring‑only, wellness, or general behavioral coaching apps without treatment claims do not qualify.

Clarifications and edge cases:
- Multiple decisions: If multiple eligible devices are authorized in the window, the question still resolves YES; only one is required.
- De Novo vs 510(k): Either pathway counts. For De Novo, look for the status “Granted” and verify the intended use and prescription status in the decision summary PDF when available. For 510(k), verify the “Substantially Equivalent” clearance and intended use/prescription status in the 510(k) summary or database entry.
- Device classifications: Devices classified under 21 CFR 882.5801 (computerized behavioral therapy for psychiatric disorders) are clearly in scope. Devices addressing PTSD‑associated nightmares (e.g., NightWare‑type) can qualify if the decision documents indicate prescription‑only and therapeutic intent for DSM‑5‑TR conditions. Cranial electrotherapy stimulators or other hardware‑based therapies without software as the therapeutic mechanism are out of scope.
- Evidence sufficiency: Primary resolution is from FDA databases. If an FDA decision summary PDF is published (e.g., De Novo summary like DEN160018 for reSET), it may be used to confirm prescription status and intended use.

Start date for eligible events: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC.
End date for eligible events: 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Primary sources of truth: FDA De Novo database and FDA 510(k) database entries showing the decision date and decision status. Supporting definitions and context: SaMD definition ; prescription device labeling requirements ; psychiatric digital therapy device classification and prescription‑only status ; CMS CY2025 PFS DMHT payment and HCPCS codes context.

question: By December 31, 2025 (17:00 UTC), will PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati be absent from the Red List of FDA Import Alert #99-51 (chemical contamination; Cesium-137)?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30:
- Import Alert #99-51 is an FDA enforcement tool titled “Detention Without Physical Examination of Human Food Products That Appear To Have Been Prepared, Packed Or Held Under Insanitary Conditions Resulting in Chemical Contamination.” It authorizes Detention Without Physical Examination (DWPE) of listed firms/products on its Red List. The alert page enumerates firms and products subject to DWPE (the Red List) and specifies the associated “Problems,” including CESIUM-137 when applicable. FDA describes import alerts and DWPE as mechanisms allowing detention of future shipments without physical examination when violations are identified.
- PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati (also referred to by FDA as BMS Foods) is an Indonesian firm that the FDA added to Import Alert #99-51 on 2025-08-14. On the Red List the firm appears as “PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati,” with address “Utama Modern Industri AA 1, Serang, Banten, Indonesia,” product category “16 — Fishery/Seafood Products,” description “All Shrimp Products,” and “Problems: CESIUM-137”. FDA’s safety advisory confirms that FDA detected Cs-137 in a shipment of frozen shrimp from this firm (shipment did not enter U.S. commerce) and that the firm was added to Import Alert #99-51 on 2025-08-14, subjecting its products to DWPE until the violation is resolved. FDA’s page on Cs-137 findings in imported foods in 2025 similarly notes that in early August 2025 FDA detected Cs-137 in shrimp from Indonesia and that PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati was added to Import Alert #99-51; it provides additional context on Cs-137 and FDA’s regulatory approach (e.g., Derived Intervention Level for Cs-137 of 1200 Bq/kg).
- Definitions: “Red List” (entities subject to DWPE) and “Green List” (entities exempt from DWPE) are FDA list types used on import alerts; “DWPE” means Detention Without Physical Examination. FDA’s general import alerts page further explains DWPE and how it applies to firms/products listed on an import alert. FDA also provides guidance on how firms can be removed from DWPE under an import alert (e.g., providing evidence that conditions leading to the violation have been corrected); removal reflects resolution of the underlying issue for the listed firm/product combination.
- Cesium-137 (Cs-137) is a radionuclide cited by FDA on the Import Alert #99-51 page as a chemical contaminant associated with adverse health effects; “CESIUM-137” appears as the stated problem for PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati’s Red List entry on IA 99-51 ; FDA’s broader Cs-137 page provides additional public-health and regulatory context.
Why this is forecastable: Removal from the Red List requires remediation and FDA acceptance of evidence that the conditions leading to Cs-137 contamination have been addressed. As of 2025-09-30, the firm remains listed on IA 99-51 for CESIUM-137, and removal before year-end is plausible but uncertain.
Temporal scope note: This question resolves based on the firm’s status at the specified resolution timestamp, regardless of when any addition/removal may have occurred; earlier changes are captured if reflected on the FDA IA 99-51 page at resolution time.
resolution_criteria:
Resolution timestamp and timezone: 2025-12-31 at 17:00 UTC.
Primary resolution source: FDA Import Alert #99-51 page (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_1187.html), specifically the section “List of firms and their products subject to Detention without Physical Examination (DWPE) under this Import Alert (a.k.a. Red List)”. Supporting FDA references explaining import alerts, the Red List/Green List, and DWPE include FDA’s general Import Alerts page and Industry FAQs/removal guidance.
Operational check at the resolution timestamp:
1) Navigate to the Import Alert #99-51 page and locate the Red List section.
2) Search the Red List for a firm entry matching “PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati.” Use the address published with the firm’s 2025 listing (“Utama Modern Industri AA 1, Serang, Banten, Indonesia”) to confirm identity if needed. If multiple entries exist for the same firm, treat the firm as present if any entry exists.
3) Outcome definitions:
- Resolve YES if “PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati” does NOT appear anywhere on the Red List of Import Alert #99-51 at the resolution timestamp (i.e., the firm has been removed from DWPE under IA 99-51). Presence on any other list type (e.g., Green List) is irrelevant for resolution; only absence from the Red List is required for YES.
- Resolve NO if “PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati” appears on the Red List of Import Alert #99-51 at the resolution timestamp (regardless of the specific “Problems” text or product descriptions).
Scope clarifications:
- This question pertains only to Import Alert #99-51. Listings on other import alerts are not considered for resolution.
- Aliases: FDA’s advisory references the firm doing business as “BMS Foods,” but resolution is based on the firm name as displayed on the IA 99-51 Red List (“PT. Bahari Makmur Sejati”). Use the address above to disambiguate if needed.
- The FDA Import Alert #99-51 page is dynamically updated; the published dates on the alert and individual firm listings reflect changes over time. Resolution relies on the content of the FDA page at the resolution timestamp.
Fallback if the primary source is unavailable at the resolution timestamp: If https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/importalert_1187.html is inaccessible, use the most recent archived snapshot (e.g., Internet Archive) closest to 2025-12-31 17:00 UTC. If FDA permanently relocates the page, use the FDA-hosted successor page for Import Alert #99-51 that includes the Red List.

question: Will Venezuela’s November 2025 crude oil production (OPEC secondary sources) be at least 950 tb/d?
background:
Context and definitions as of 2025-09-30:

- Data source and publication timing: The OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is a recurring publication that “covers major issues affecting the world oil market” and has a published 2025 schedule with the December 2025 edition slated for Thursday, 11 December. This timing ensures the November 2025 production figures are available before year-end.

- What figure we are forecasting: OPEC’s standard table labelled “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” reports monthly crude output for each participating country, including Venezuela. The table title and unit are explicitly given as “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” (tb/d = thousand barrels per day) in the MOMR (e.g., July 2025 edition, Table 5–7). OPEC glossary/notes define b/d as barrels per day and tb/d as thousand barrels per day. A petroleum barrel (bbl) is exactly 42 US gallons, approximately 159 liters.

- Latest status of Venezuela’s crude output (secondary sources): Recent MOMRs report Venezuela at 919 tb/d (June 2025), 924 tb/d (July 2025), and 936 tb/d (August 2025) in the “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” table. The August 2025 MOMR showed 925 tb/d (May 2025), 918 tb/d (June 2025), and 914 tb/d (July 2025) on that same basis. The July 2025 MOMR presented earlier estimates for 2025: 928 tb/d (April), 908 tb/d (May), and 910 tb/d (June). OPEC notes that totals may not add up due to independent rounding, and figures are based on available secondary sources at the time of publication.

- Practical takeaway: As of late Q3 2025, Venezuela’s secondary-sources crude output is in the low-to-mid 900s tb/d range, with August reported at 936 tb/d. Forecasting whether November will be ≥950 tb/d is plausibly uncertain.

Definitions to avoid ambiguity:

- “Crude oil production” and “secondary sources” refer strictly to the Venezuela row in OPEC’s MOMR table titled “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d,” which OPEC presents as monthly average crude output based on secondary sources. Units are tb/d (thousand barrels per day), where 1 barrel (bbl) = 42 US gallons ≈159 liters.

- “November 2025” refers to the calendar month of November 2025 (UTC). The value used is the single monthly figure OPEC reports for that month in the December 2025 MOMR.

- “At least 950 tb/d” means the reported integer tb/d value is ≥950.

Notes on scope:

- This question concerns only the OPEC-reported crude production from secondary sources. It excludes any other measures (e.g., direct communication, NGLs/condensates) and any non-OPEC tables.

- If OPEC revises prior months in later editions, that does not affect resolution; only the November 2025 figure as published in the December 2025 MOMR is considered.
resolution_criteria:
Outcome determination:

- Resolve Yes if the OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) published on Thursday, 11 December 2025 reports Venezuela’s November 2025 crude oil production (based on secondary sources) as ≥950 tb/d in the table titled “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d.” Resolve No otherwise.

- Units and rounding: Use the integer tb/d value as printed in the December 2025 MOMR. OPEC notes that totals may not add due to independent rounding; this does not affect the binary threshold check.

- Source of truth: The December 2025 MOMR (PDF or official digital publication) posted by OPEC. Verification consists of locating the Venezuela row in the table “DoC crude oil production based on secondary sources, tb/d” and reading the November 2025 value.

- Edge cases: If OPEC changes table numbering but retains the standard table title and monthly presentation, use the table matching the exact title and unit. If the title slightly varies but clearly corresponds to the same standard monthly secondary-sources crude production table, use that table. If, contrary to schedule, the December 2025 MOMR is delayed beyond 31 December 2025 (unlikely given the published schedule), the question is resolved using the first official December 2025 MOMR release available before 31 December 2025; if none is available by then, the market should deem the question unresolved. However, per OPEC’s published 2025 schedule, the December 2025 MOMR is set for 11 December 2025.

question: Between October 15 and December 31, 2025 (UTC), will Mexico and South Korea both formally announce the start or resumption of bilateral negotiations toward an FTA or equivalent market-access agreement?
background:
Context as of October 1, 2025:
- Mexico has signaled plans to raise tariffs on imports from countries without a free trade agreement (FTA) with Mexico, which includes South Korea. In mid-September 2025, South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy (MOTIE) convened a meeting with the private sector to assess the impact and develop a response strategy, stating it will work to minimize the possible impact on Korean companies.
- On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in late September 2025, the foreign ministers of South Korea and Mexico discussed the tariff issue, including a plan that could raise tariffs to as high as 50% on certain items from non-FTA countries, and expressed hopes to continue communication and consultations on mutually acceptable outcomes.
- Earlier, Mexico’s Secretariat of Foreign Affairs (SRE) issued a press release stating that Mexico’s foreign secretary and South Korea’s foreign minister agreed to promote a bilateral FTA and support South Korea’s accession to the Pacific Alliance as an Associate State (the latter is plurilateral, not bilateral). This shows political intent to deepen trade ties but is not itself an announcement that negotiations have started or resumed.
- In April 2025, Korean government sources reported plans to accelerate the resumption of FTA negotiations with Mexico, highlighting a desire to reduce tariff burdens; the cited report indicated Korea’s intent, but did not cite an official Mexican announcement of negotiations at that time.
- Definitions and agreement types relevant to resolution:
  - Free Trade Agreement (FTA): South Korea uses the term "free trade agreements" (FTAs) and sometimes comprehensive agreements like Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements (CEPAs). Korea’s FTA overview notes FTAs and mentions CEPA-style agreements with some partners.
  - Mexico’s trade agreement classifications include: FTAs, Economic Complementation Agreements (ECAs), and Partial Scope Agreements (PSAs) under ALADI, plus investment promotion agreements. ECAs and PSAs grant tariff preferences on specific sectors or products and are recognized formal trade agreements in Mexico’s framework.
Rationale for uncertainty: Political and economic pressure from planned tariff changes creates incentives for both governments to initiate or revive negotiations, but domestic politics, regional trade dynamics, and sequencing with other trade priorities can delay or alter timing—making a bilateral and jointly announced negotiation launch plausible yet uncertain within the Oct–Dec 2025 window.
resolution_criteria:
Time window and timezone:
- Eligible announcements must occur between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

What counts for Yes:
- Resolve Yes if BOTH governments (Mexico and South Korea) publicly announce the start or resumption of bilateral negotiations toward any of the following agreement types between the two countries: a Free Trade Agreement (FTA), a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), an Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), or an ALADI Economic Complementation Agreement (ECA) or Partial Scope Agreement (PSA) that grants tariff preferences. Korea’s usage of FTAs and CEPA-type agreements is documented in its FTA overview. Mexico’s recognition of FTAs, ECAs, and PSAs (which confer tariff preferences) is documented by its Secretariat of Economy.

Definitions and clarifications:
- Bilateral: strictly between the Government of Mexico and the Government of the Republic of Korea (South Korea). Plurilateral or regional processes (e.g., CPTPP, RCEP, Pacific Alliance accession) do NOT count.
- Publicly announce: a formal press release, official statement, or joint communique posted on official government websites or press portals (e.g., Mexico’s Secretaría de Economía: economia.gob.mx; Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores: sre.gob.mx; South Korea’s MOTIE: motie.go.kr; or South Korea’s MOFA: mofa.go.kr). A joint communique posted on either side’s official site qualifies. If such a press release is unavailable, credible reporting from major wire services and national outlets (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, Financial Times, Yonhap News Agency, KBS) citing official statements can be used as secondary confirmation.
- Start or resumption of negotiations: the announcement must explicitly state that bilateral negotiations "have begun," "are starting/commencing," "will commence on [date]," "resume," "are resumed," or similar clear language indicating that an official intergovernmental negotiating process toward one of the eligible agreement types is beginning or being restarted.
- Exclusions: Statements of intent to "promote," "explore," or "discuss" an FTA or market access, without explicitly announcing the start or resumption of negotiations, do not count. Announcements related solely to industrial consultations or tariff mitigation strategies (e.g., MOTIE meeting with private sector) do not count. The UNGA-side meeting about tariffs and intent to continue communication does not, by itself, count unless it explicitly announces the start or resumption of negotiations. The SRE press release agreeing to "promote a bilateral FTA" does not count unless it also explicitly states that negotiations have started or are being resumed.

What counts for No:
- Resolve No if by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, both governments have not made qualifying public announcements as defined above within the specified window. Announcements made before 2025-10-15 UTC or after 2025-12-31 UTC do not count toward a Yes.

Primary resolution sources to check at close:
- Mexico: Secretaría de Economía press room (economia.gob.mx) and SRE press room (sre.gob.mx).
- South Korea: MOTIE and MOFA press rooms (motie.go.kr, mofa.go.kr).
- If not found there, corroborating coverage in Reuters/Yonhap/AP/KBS/etc., especially if it quotes or links to official releases. Background sources highlighting recent context include MOTIE’s industry meeting and UNGA foreign-minister discussions on Mexico’s tariff plan , and earlier intent statements by SRE and Korean government sources.

question: Will the FDA approve relacorilant (Corcept Therapeutics) for treating endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing’s syndrome) on or before December 31, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-09-30:
- Relacorilant is Corcept Therapeutics’ investigational, selective cortisol modulator being evaluated to treat patients with endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing’s syndrome). The FDA accepted Corcept’s New Drug Application (NDA) for this indication and set a Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) target action date of December 30, 2025. Relacorilant has U.S. Orphan Drug Designation for treatment of endogenous Cushing syndrome (designated October 15, 2018). The NDA is supported by the pivotal GRACE trial and additional evidence including a long-term extension (GRADIENT) and a Phase 2 study in hypercortisolism.
- Separately, relacorilant is under FDA review for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer with a PDUFA decision date of July 11, 2026; this is a different application and indication and does not pertain to this question.

Key definitions and sources forecasters may consult:
- FDA approval (of an NDA): Formal marketing authorization granted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for a specific indication, evidenced by an FDA approval letter and listing in the FDA’s Drugs@FDA database. See Drugs@FDA database (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/).
- NDA (New Drug Application): The vehicle through which drug sponsors formally propose that the FDA approve a new pharmaceutical for sale and marketing in the U.S. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Drug_Application).
- PDUFA (Prescription Drug User Fee Act) target action date: The FDA’s target date to complete its review and take an action on a drug application (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prescription_Drug_User_Fee_Act).
- Endogenous hypercortisolism / Cushing’s syndrome: A condition of excessive cortisol production by the body (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cushing%27s_syndrome).
- Complete Response Letter (CRL): An FDA letter indicating that the application cannot be approved in its current form (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_response_letter).
- Time zones: UTC (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time) and U.S. Eastern Time (ET) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone).

Why this is a non-trivial, high-entropy question: The PDUFA date falls on December 30, 2025, making approval by year-end plausible, but a CRL or an action that posts after the calendar year is also plausible; forecasters must weigh clinical evidence, labeling/CMC risks, review dynamics, and timing uncertainties.
resolution_criteria:
Event window and time zone:
- Eligible events must occur between 2025-03-03 00:00:00 UTC (the date the FDA acceptance/filing was announced for this NDA) and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 U.S. Eastern Time (ET; UTC−5).

What counts as YES:
- Resolve YES if, by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 ET, the FDA has issued an approval for relacorilant for the treatment of endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing’s syndrome) for the NDA under review referenced above, as evidenced by at least one of the following:
  1) An FDA approval letter posted on FDA.gov for relacorilant for this indication (e.g., accessible via Drugs@FDA),
  2) A relacorilant entry in the FDA Drugs@FDA database showing approval status for this indication,
  3) An FDA press release announcing approval for this indication.
- If primary FDA sources have not yet posted but credible secondary evidence exists (e.g., sponsor press release clearly stating FDA approval of relacorilant for endogenous hypercortisolism with date/time stamps on/before the deadline), the question resolves YES provisionally, subject to later verification via FDA postings.

What counts as NO:
- Resolve NO if, by the deadline, no FDA approval has been issued for relacorilant for endogenous hypercortisolism.
- Resolve NO if the FDA issues a Complete Response Letter (CRL) by the deadline.
- Resolve NO if any FDA action (e.g., approval) occurs after the deadline (i.e., on or after 2026-01-01 00:00:00 ET).

Scope clarifications:
- Only the NDA for relacorilant to treat endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing’s syndrome) is in scope; actions on other indications (e.g., platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, which has a separate PDUFA date of July 11, 2026) do not affect resolution.
- “FDA approval” must be for marketing authorization for the specified indication; accelerated approval, if granted, counts as approval. Advisory committee meetings, internal FDA communications, tentative approvals, approvable letters, or submissions do not count unless accompanied by formal FDA approval.

Primary resolution sources to check on/after the deadline:
- FDA Drugs@FDA database (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/),
- FDA press announcements page (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements),
- Corcept Therapeutics’ investor/press releases (https://ir.corcept.com/news-releases), used only as secondary evidence if primary sources lag.

Context sources for forecasters (claims already cited above):
- FDA filing/acceptance of the NDA and PDUFA date for hypercortisolism ,
- Orphan Drug Designation details ,
- Separate ovarian cancer application timeline.

question: Between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, will crude oil flows via the Druzhba pipeline to either Hungary or Slovakia be halted for ≥48 consecutive hours due to attack-related damage?
background:
Context and status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- What is the Druzhba pipeline: The Druzhba (“Friendship”) pipeline is one of the world’s longest crude oil pipeline networks, transporting crude oil from Russia across Belarus and Ukraine, with branches supplying Poland, Germany, Slovakia, Hungary, and the Czech Republic (see overview and routing). The system carries crude oil (i.e., raw, unrefined petroleum) and includes pumping stations and other above-ground facilities critical for maintaining flow. The southern branch runs through Ukraine and splits near Uzhhorod into lines serving Slovakia and Hungary; the line through Slovakia further branches toward the Czech Republic and southward to Hungary, supplying refineries such as Százhalombatta in Hungary. In-country operators include Transpetrol (Slovakia) and MOL (Hungary); upstream operation on the Russian side is managed by Transneft/Transneft Druzhba.
- Recent disruptions (Aug–Sep 2025): On Aug 18, 2025, flows via Druzhba to Hungary and Slovakia were halted, which Hungarian and Slovak officials attributed to a Ukrainian attack damaging a Druzhba-related facility; Transpetrol confirmed the halt to Slovakia, and Hungary’s foreign minister cited a transformer station hit. Flows then resumed by Aug 19–20, per confirmations from Slovakia’s economy minister, Hungary’s foreign minister, and MOL. On Aug 21–22, supplies were again suspended, with Reuters reporting an expected duration of at least five days after an attack on the Unecha pumping station; Transpetrol confirmed interruption. Hungary later said deliveries could resume in “test mode” (lower volumes) around Aug 28 , and operators/officials confirmed full restart on Aug 28 after the outage caused by the attack. On Sep 7, 2025, Ukraine’s drone forces claimed another strike on Druzhba in Russia’s Bryansk region; however, MOL said deliveries to Hungary were on schedule and Slovakia’s economy minister said supplies were unaffected at that time.
- Why this matters: Hungary and Slovakia are landlocked and have historically relied on Druzhba’s southern branch; attacks on pumping or transformer stations have previously caused multi-day halts, but flows subsequently resumed. The period from mid-October through year-end includes colder months and ongoing wartime dynamics, making another halt plausible but uncertain.

Helpful references for definitions (non-exhaustive):
- Druzhba pipeline (Wikipedia): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druzhba_pipeline 
- Druzhba Oil Pipeline (Global Energy Monitor): https://www.gem.wiki/Druzhba_Oil_Pipeline 
- Pipeline transport (general reference): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipeline_transport (for context on pumping/metering stations; not required for resolution).

Key recent wire reports and official confirmations (examples):
- Halt confirmed and attributed to attack (Aug 18): https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/russian-oil-flows-hungary-slovakia-halted-after-ukrainian-attack-2025-08-18/ 
- Resumption (Aug 19–20): https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/oil-flows-resume-hungary-slovakia-via-druzhba-pipeline-officials-say-2025-08-20/ 
- Suspension with expected ≥5 days after Unecha strike (Aug 22): https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/ukrainian-attack-suspends-russian-oil-flows-hungary-slovakia-2025-08-22/ 
- Test-mode/low-volume restart guidance (Aug 27): https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/hungary-says-oil-deliveries-via-druzhba-could-resume-thursday-test-mode-2025-08-27/ 
- Restart after outage (Aug 28): https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/russian-oil-supplies-through-druzhba-pipeline-restart-after-attack-2025-08-28/ 
- Claimed Sep 7 strike with no HU/SK impact at that time: https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/ukraine-says-it-attacked-druzhba-oil-pipeline-russias-bryansk-2025-09-07/
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether there is a qualifying halt between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC, as defined below.

Definitions (with links and scope):
- Druzhba pipeline: The international crude oil pipeline network described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druzhba_pipeline; for this question, the relevant scope is its southern branch supplying Slovakia and Hungary via Ukraine and associated stations/branches as summarized by Global Energy Monitor.
- Crude oil: Unrefined petroleum transported by Druzhba.
- Flows “to Hungary” or “to Slovakia”: Deliveries of crude oil via Druzhba into the territory of the named country (i.e., across the Slovakia–Ukraine link to Sahy for Slovakia and across the Hungary–Slovakia/Hungary border link to Százhalombatta for Hungary, including the Hungarian branch), irrespective of the origin of the crude; reduced flow does not count as a halt.
- Halted: A period in which reputable sources state that crude oil deliveries via the Druzhba pipeline to the named country are “halted,” “stopped,” “suspended,” or equivalent, implying zero throughput to that country via Druzhba. Reduced or “test mode”/lower-volume operations do not constitute a halt.
- Due to attack-related damage: The halt is causally attributed by reputable sources to damage from a deliberate hostile act (e.g., drone/missile strike or sabotage) targeting Druzhba pipeline infrastructure or directly supporting facilities (such as pumping, transformer, or metering stations) whose function is essential for Druzhba operations; examples in prior reporting include transformer and pumping stations being struck. Causes such as routine maintenance, technical malfunctions not attributed to attack, payment/transit disputes, sanctions/compliance decisions, weather, or voluntary curtailments do not qualify.
- Reputable sources: Any of the following: (a) official statements or press releases by system operators or directly responsible companies/ministries (e.g., Transpetrol, MOL, Transneft/Transneft Druzhba, Slovak Ministry of Economy, relevant Hungarian ministries); (b) major international wire services or outlets with rigorous editorial standards (e.g., Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, Financial Times), especially when attributing cause based on officials/operators.

Event window and measurement:
- Eligible interval: 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC. Only halts whose qualifying ≥48 consecutive hours lie entirely within this interval count toward resolution.
- Duration test (≥48 consecutive hours):
  1) Preferred method: Use explicit duration or start/end times stated by an operator/official or by a reputable outlet (e.g., “halt lasted five days” or timestamps for start and resumption). If any single halt to either country is explicitly reported as lasting at least 48 hours for the qualifying cause, resolve YES.
  2) If explicit duration is not stated, compute the interval from the timestamp of the earliest reputable report that flows to the country are halted (for the qualifying cause) to the timestamp of the earliest reputable report that flows to that country have resumed; if that computed interval is ≥48 hours and there is no intervening reputable report indicating resumption earlier, treat the duration criterion as met. Use UTC when comparing publication timestamps.
- Multiple events: If multiple halts occur in the window, any single halt meeting all criteria triggers a YES.
- Country scope: The condition is satisfied if either Hungary or Slovakia (or both) experiences a qualifying halt.

Resolution:
- Resolve YES if there is at least one period within the event window where flows via Druzhba to either Hungary or Slovakia are halted for ≥48 consecutive hours and reputable sources attribute the halt to attack-related damage as defined above.
- Resolve NO otherwise.

Examples of resolution sources (non-exhaustive):
- Official operator/company/ministry statements (e.g., Transpetrol announcements; MOL newsroom; Slovak Ministry of Economy press releases) and/or wire reports by Reuters/AP/Bloomberg citing those officials. August–September 2025 reportage illustrates the type of confirmations and attributions that would qualify if they occurred within the event window.

question: Before December 31, 2025 (JST), will a yen‑denominated Electronic Payment Instrument (“stablecoin”) be listed for spot trading on an FSA‑registered crypto‑asset exchange in Japan between October 15 and December 31, 2025?
background:
Context as of 2025‑09‑30:
- Japan’s amended Payment Services Act (PSA) took effect on 2023‑06‑01, creating a legal framework for fiat‑redeemable stablecoins by defining them as “Electronic Payment Instruments” (EPIs). Under the amended PSA, only banks, fund transfer service providers, and trust banks/companies licensed or registered in Japan may issue EPIs directly to residents.
- The Japan Virtual and Crypto Assets Exchange Association (JVCEA) is Japan’s certified self‑regulatory organization for crypto‑asset exchanges and related derivatives, recognized under the PSA and FIEA. In October 2024, the JFSA approved JVCEA as a certified association for payment service providers for EPI services, establishing self‑regulatory rules that EPI service providers must follow.
- The Financial Services Agency (FSA) maintains authoritative, up‑to‑date lists of registered firms, including: (a) Crypto‑asset Exchange Service Providers (PDF and XLS), and (b) Electronic Payment Instrument Exchange Service Providers (PDF and XLS). These lists are published on the FSA’s “List of licensed (registered) Financial Institutions” page. The “List of Registered Crypto‑asset Exchange Service Providers in Japan” shows an update “As of 1st September, 2025”. The “List of Registered Electronic Payment Instrument Exchange Service Providers in Japan” document shows “As of 4th March, 2025” and clarifies general consumer cautions and the registration status of EPI intermediaries.
- Recent developments: In August 2025, Reuters reported that JPYC said it would issue the first stablecoin pegged to the yen later in 2025 after receiving a license that week, indicating concrete progress toward a regulated yen‑stablecoin.
- Time zone: Japan Standard Time (JST) is UTC+09:00 and Japan does not observe daylight saving time.

Why this is uncertain and interesting: While the regulatory pathways now exist and at least one issuer has signaled imminent issuance, listing EPIs for spot trading on an FSA‑registered crypto‑asset exchange requires operational readiness, approvals, and market integration across multiple regulated actors. As of late Q3 2025, the first yen‑stablecoin appears close, but whether any will be actively listed for spot trading on a licensed exchange during the specified window remains genuinely uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on public evidence between 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 JST and 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 JST (both inclusive). It asks: Will at least one yen‑denominated Electronic Payment Instrument (EPI) be listed for spot trading on a crypto‑asset exchange that is registered with Japan’s Financial Services Agency (FSA) during this window?

Definitions and scope:
- Japan Standard Time (JST): UTC+09:00; no daylight saving time.
- Crypto‑asset Exchange Service Provider: An entity registered with the FSA under the PSA to provide crypto‑asset exchange services. For the purpose of verifying “licensed exchanges in Japan,” use the official FSA list titled “List of Registered Crypto‑asset Exchange Service Providers in Japan” (PDF/XLS). The exchange must appear on this list as of the listing date.
- Electronic Payment Instrument (EPI): As established by the amended PSA effective 2023‑06‑01, fiat‑redeemable stablecoins are defined as EPIs; only banks, fund transfer service providers, trust banks/companies licensed or registered in Japan may issue EPIs directly to Japan residents. For this question, “yen‑denominated EPI” means an EPI that is fiat‑referenced to the Japanese yen at par (1:1) and redeemable in JPY per its issuer’s terms under Japan’s PSA framework. Algorithmic or non‑redeemable tokens do not qualify.
- Electronic Payment Instrument Exchange Service Provider (for context): A registration category under the PSA for entities that purchase, sell, exchange, manage, or intermediate EPIs. The FSA maintains the official “List of Registered Electronic Payment Instrument Exchange Service Providers in Japan” (PDF/XLS), which may be consulted to understand market infrastructure but is not required for the exchange’s eligibility in this question.
- Listed for spot trading: Publicly accessible, exchange‑hosted spot markets where the yen‑denominated EPI can be traded by customers on the exchange (order‑book or immediate‑trade model) against at least one pairing (e.g., JPY, BTC, ETH, etc.). Evidence must include both (a) an official listing announcement by the exchange and (b) a live market page on the exchange’s website/app showing active order‑book or trade functionality. OTC‑only offerings, internal wallet swaps, custodial transfers without a public market, or closed enterprise networks do not count.

Inclusions/Exclusions:
- Included: Any yen‑denominated EPI stablecoin (fiat‑redeemable) issued under Japan’s PSA that is listed for spot trading on an exchange appearing on the FSA’s registered crypto‑asset exchange list. The exchange may also hold EPI exchange registration; however, the key eligibility criterion for this question is its FSA registration as a crypto‑asset exchange.
- Excluded: Algorithmic stablecoins; non‑redeemable fiat‑referenced tokens; prepaid payment instruments not covered by EPI; “deposit tokens” that are not EPIs or are limited to closed bank systems without public exchange spot markets; OTC‑only desks; listings on platforms not appearing on the FSA crypto‑asset exchange list.

Resolution procedure:
- Resolve Yes if, within 2025‑10‑15 00:00:00 JST to 2025‑12‑31 23:59:59 JST, at least one yen‑denominated EPI meets the “listed for spot trading” definition on a crypto‑asset exchange appearing on the FSA’s registered crypto‑asset exchange list. Verification requires: (1) the exchange’s official listing announcement and (2) the exchange’s live market page(s) showing tradable pairs and order‑book/trade functionality during the window. Optional corroboration may include JVCEA communications or credible media coverage (e.g., Reuters).
- Resolve No if no such listing meeting all criteria is observed within the specified window.

Primary resolution sources:
- FSA “List of licensed (registered) Financial Institutions” page, linking to current lists, including Crypto‑asset Exchange Service Providers and EPI Exchange Service Providers.
- FSA “List of Registered Crypto‑asset Exchange Service Providers in Japan” (PDF/XLS) to confirm the platform’s registration status.
- FSA “List of Registered Electronic Payment Instrument Exchange Service Providers in Japan” (PDF/XLS) for contextual verification of EPI market intermediation.
- JVCEA overview page to confirm SRO status relevant to exchanges and EPI self‑regulation.
- Credible media (e.g., Reuters) if needed to corroborate issuer milestones or timing.

question: Will any lot catalogued as by or attributed to Norval Morrisseau realize at least C$200,000 (including buyer’s premium) at a Canadian live auction between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC?
background:
Context as of 2025-10-01:
- Norval Morrisseau (1932–2007), also known as Copper Thunderbird, was an Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) artist and founder of the Woodlands School of Canadian art.
- Recent auction benchmarks: Waddington’s reported Morrisseau’s “Nature’s Balance” sold for C$183,750 (inclusive of buyer’s premium) in late May 2024, setting a record for a work on paper by the artist. Cowley Abbott’s sale on May 28, 2025 included Morrisseau works with realized prices of C$108,000 (“Conversation with Our White Brother, 1980”) and C$48,000 (“Protection of the Young, 1973”). The current public auction record for Morrisseau is C$312,000 for “Animal Unity” (June 15, 2022).
- Upcoming Canadian fall auction calendar: Heffel lists a Fall 2025 Live Auction on November 19, 2025 (a live, in-room/live-stream event). Waddington’s lists its Major Fall Auction: First Nations Art as an online timed sale beginning to close on November 20, 2025 at 7:00 pm ET (i.e., not a live auction).

Definitions and notes useful for forecasting:
- Buyer’s premium: a charge in addition to the hammer price that the winning bidder pays to the auction house; it is retained by the house.
- Hammer price and price realized: “Hammer price” is the final bid announced by the auctioneer when the gavel falls (exclusive of buyer’s premium); “Price realised” is the sold price including the hammer price plus the buyer’s premium (auction houses may also add applicable taxes/fees to the buyer’s invoice, but the published price realised is typically shown as hammer + buyer’s premium).
- Authorship qualifiers (relevant to what counts as “by or attributed to”): “Artist’s name” denotes a work the auction house opines is by the artist; “Attributed to ” denotes probable authorship but with less certainty; terms such as “Studio of,” “Circle of,” “Follower of,” and “After” indicate works not by the artist’s hand and are excluded for this question.

Why this threshold/timeframe: The C$200,000 threshold is above most recent Morrisseau results yet within historical precedent (C$312,000 in 2022; C$183,750 in 2024 for a work on paper), making both Yes and No plausible outcomes in the Nov–Dec 2025 live-auction window. A major Canadian live sale is scheduled (Heffel, Nov 19), while other houses may also hold live sessions, creating a realistic opportunity set.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether at least one qualifying lot meets the price threshold in the specified period.

Event window:
- Inclusive window: from 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- A “live auction” session qualifies if the auction house schedules and conducts a real-time sale with a human auctioneer calling bids (in-room and/or live-stream). Exclusively online timed sales (e.g., catalogues stating “auction begins to close” at a set time) do not qualify.

Eligible auctions and lots:
- The auction must be held by a Canadian auction house (an auction firm headquartered in Canada) and the qualifying session must be a live auction as defined above. Examples of Canadian houses that run live auctions include Heffel and Cowley Abbott. Waddington’s First Nations Art auction cited here is online timed and thus not eligible.
- The lot must be catalogued by the auction house as either (a) “Norval Morrisseau” (i.e., by the artist) or (b) “Attributed to Norval Morrisseau.” Lots catalogued as “Studio of,” “Workshop of,” “Circle of,” “Follower of,” or “After” are not eligible. For multi-artist lots, the artist must be the sole named creator of the lot.

Price threshold and currency:
- Threshold: C$200,000 inclusive of buyer’s premium.
- For this market, “including buyer’s premium” means the realized price published by the auction house that comprises the hammer price plus buyer’s premium (taxes/ancillary fees, if any, are not required for inclusion in the published realized price).

What counts as a qualifying sale outcome:
- Resolve YES if any eligible live auction session held within the window publishes an official “price realized” (inclusive of buyer’s premium) of at least C$200,000 for an eligible Morrisseau lot, as shown on the auction house’s official sale results page or catalogue for that sale.
- Resolve NO otherwise.

Primary resolution sources:
- The auction house’s official post-sale results pages or catalogues for the relevant sale(s). Examples of authoritative sources include:
  - Heffel auction pages and results (Heffel lists its Fall 2025 Live Auction on Nov 19, 2025).
  - Cowley Abbott’s auction pages and artist sale records (their site publishes realized prices for Morrisseau lots, e.g., May 28, 2025 results).
  - Waddington’s sale pages (noting that some sales are timed online and thus ineligible for this question; still useful for distinguishing sale format).

Adjudication notes and edge cases:
- If a lot is marked “bought-in,” “unsold,” or otherwise fails to meet reserve, it does not count.
- If an auction has multiple live sessions, any session date that falls within the window is eligible. Use the auction house’s listed session date to determine whether it falls within the UTC window (convert if necessary).
- If realized prices differ across sources, the auction house’s own official posted result for that sale takes precedence. If the auction house temporarily withholds or removes realized prices, resolution will rely on contemporaneous reporting by reputable outlets that directly cite the auction house’s realized price (e.g., major wire services or national media). Definitions of buyer’s premium and price realised follow standard auction usage.

Non-qualifying scenarios (for clarity):
- Timed-only online auctions (e.g., “auction begins to close” language) do not qualify.
- Prices quoted without buyer’s premium (hammer only) do not qualify unless the auction house explicitly labels a realized price (hammer + buyer’s premium) meeting the threshold.
- Private treaty sales and post-auction negotiated sales are excluded.

question: Between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC), will the U.S. Navy award at least one Virginia-class submarine-related contract modification with a face value of $500,000,000 or more?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01:
- On 2025-04-30, the Department of the Navy announced contract modifications for construction of two FY2024 Virginia-class submarines (SSN 812 and SSN 813), plus industrial investments and workforce support. The Defense.gov contracts notice lists awarded amounts of $12,418,145,463 to General Dynamics Electric Boat and $1,293,694,000 to Huntington Ingalls (Newport News Shipbuilding), with options that could bring the cumulative value to $18,445,959,971. It specifies relevant contract numbers and obligated funds at award.
- On 2025-03-25, Defense.gov announced a not-to-exceed $1,065,310,000 undefinitized contract action modification to a previously awarded contract for long lead time material associated with Virginia-class Block VI submarines.
- On 2025-09-26, General Dynamics Electric Boat announced it was awarded a $642 million cost-plus-fixed-fee modification to previously awarded contract N00024-20-C-2120 for Virginia-class Lead Yard Support and Development/Design efforts.
- Defense.gov states contracts valued at $7.5 million or more are announced each business day at approximately 5 p.m., providing a reliable, timely resolution source for large awards.
- Virginia-class submarines (SSN-774 class) are U.S. Navy nuclear-powered attack submarines with cruise missile capability; this nomenclature will be used to identify relevant awards.

Why this is uncertain yet plausible for Q4 2025: The Navy has already executed multiple large Virginia-class-related modifications in 2025, including two-ship construction actions and lead yard support. Additional late-year actions are plausible due to ongoing program needs and contracting cadence, but not guaranteed; the specific timing and size of any Q4 actions (≥ $500M) depend on negotiations, program timelines, and funding availability.

Key terms and definitions (with sources):
- "Virginia-class submarine" means the United States Navy SSN-774 class nuclear-powered attack submarines; references to "Virginia-class" or "SSN-774 class" in an award notice identify relevant work.
- "Contract modification" means any written change in the terms of a contract (as defined in FAR 2.101), which covers both bilateral (supplemental agreement) and unilateral changes described in FAR 43.103. For the purposes of this question, only modifications publicly announced on Defense.gov contracts pages will be considered.
- "Face value" of the modification means the dollar value stated in the announcement for the modification being awarded at that time. This includes amounts phrased as "is awarded $X," "not-to-exceed $X," or "ceiling $X" for the modification described. It explicitly excludes any hypothetical future totals stated as "if all options are exercised" or similar language that refers to potential maximums beyond the award being announced. The distinction between award amounts, options, and obligations follows the conventions used in Defense.gov contract notices (e.g., the 2025-04-30 notice clearly separates awarded amounts from cumulative values if options are exercised and from funds obligated at time of award).
- "Award date" means the publication date of the relevant "Contracts for [Date]" entry on Defense.gov (i.e., the date shown at the top of that contract announcements page), which serves as the public record of the award timing.

Primary resolution source:
- Defense.gov Contracts hub: https://www.defense.gov/news/contracts/ — Defense.gov publishes “Contracts for [Date]” notices and is the primary source for DoD contract announcements ≥ $7.5M.

Secondary corroborating sources (if needed for cross-checks, not for primary resolution):
- Navy.mil Press Office releases related to Virginia-class contracting actions.
- Contractor press releases (e.g., General Dynamics Electric Boat; Huntington Ingalls Industries/Newport News Shipbuilding) when they clearly identify Virginia-class contract modifications and values.
resolution_criteria:
This question resolves based on whether at least one qualifying award is publicly announced between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Qualifying event:
- A Defense.gov “Contracts for [Date]” notice that explicitly describes a U.S. Navy (Department of the Navy) contract modification related to the Virginia-class submarine program (identifiable via mention of “Virginia-class,” “SSN-774 class,” or clearly Virginia-class-related scope such as lead yard support, design studies, long-lead materials, or construction), and that states a face value ≥ $500,000,000 for the modification being awarded.

Resolution steps:
1) Search the Defense.gov Contracts hub (https://www.defense.gov/news/contracts/) for all “Contracts for [Date]” pages dated between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC).
2) Identify any entry that mentions Virginia-class (or SSN-774 class) and is clearly a “contract modification” (FAR 2.101 definition; as reflected in the notice’s language such as “contract modification,” “undefinitized contract action modification,” etc.).
3) Determine the face value from the notice’s award description. Accept wording such as “is awarded $X,” “not-to-exceed $X,” or “ceiling $X” for the modification being announced. Exclude any “if all options are exercised … total value … $Y” or other potential future maximums beyond the current award.

Outcome:
- YES if at least one qualifying Defense.gov contracts notice dated within the specified UTC window meets the criteria and the stated face value is ≥ $500,000,000.
- NO otherwise.

Tie-breakers and edge cases:
- If multiple sources report different values for the same modification, use the value and characterization from the Defense.gov “Contracts for [Date]” notice as the authoritative source.
- If the Defense.gov site is inaccessible or missing for a relevant date, and credible official releases (Navy.mil Press Office or contractor press releases) clearly document a Virginia-class contract modification with a face value ≥ $500,000,000 within the time window, resolve based on those releases; however, Defense.gov supersedes in case of conflict.
- Awards that mention Virginia-class only indirectly without explicit identification (e.g., generic submarine-related supply chain work) do not qualify unless the notice explicitly ties the modification to the Virginia-class program.

Time zone and window:
- Eligible announcements must be dated between 2025-10-15 00:00:00 UTC and 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC (inclusive). The “Contracts for [Date]” page’s date stamp is the controlling date for resolution.

question: Will Mexico’s Jan–Oct 2025 goods trade deficit with China be lower than Jan–Oct 2024?
background:
Context as of 2025-09-30 (UTC): Mexico’s bilateral merchandise trade deficit with China has widened in recent years. For full-year 2024, media summarizing INEGI data reported a record deficit of approximately US$119.86 billion (exports ≈ US$9.94b; imports ≈ US$129.80b). For January–June 2025, the deficit reportedly reached about US$57.5 billion (imports ≈ US$62.1b; exports ≈ US$4.6b). In September 2025, Mexico announced plans to raise tariffs on automobiles from China to 50% and to increase levies across >1,400 tariff lines, a policy move with potential implications for bilateral goods flows, though timing suggests effects would mainly show up in late 2025 data.

How the data are measured (INEGI BCMM): INEGI’s Balanza Comercial de Mercancías de México (BCMM) covers international transactions of merchandise (tangible goods) only; services are excluded. Exports are measured on an FOB basis and imports on a CIF basis. Values are published in both Mexican pesos and US dollars, on a monthly frequency. INEGI publishes “cifras oportunas” (timely figures) roughly 25 days after month-end and “cifras revisadas” (revised figures) roughly 40 days after month-end; the revised release includes breakdowns by country. Definitive figures are disseminated about seven months after year-end. INEGI classifies partner countries using ISO ALPHA country codes and provides breakdowns by country and by geographic zone.

Why this question and why Jan–Oct: Country-level monthly data for October 2025 should be included in the “cifras revisadas” (≈40 days after October 31), which are expected to be publicly available before December 31, 2025, enabling unambiguous resolution within the requested window. The Jan–Oct horizon balances timeliness, data availability, and the potential for policy moves and macro trends to affect outcomes.

Key definitions (for clarity):
- Goods/merchandise trade: BCMM’s scope of tangible merchandise only (no services).
- Exports (FOB) and imports (CIF): As defined and used by INEGI’s BCMM.
- Country classification: “China” refers to the entry for the People’s Republic of China as defined in INEGI’s BCMM country catalog (ISO ALPHA codes). Entities such as Hong Kong SAR and Macao SAR are separately classified in that catalog and are not included in “China” for this question.

Recent status and uncertainty: The widening 2024 deficit and record H1 2025 gap suggest upward pressure on the cumulative 2025 deficit, but policy signals in late 2025 could affect import and export behavior, and base effects make the Jan–Oct 2024 vs Jan–Oct 2025 comparison genuinely uncertain.
resolution_criteria:
Question: Will Mexico’s cumulative goods trade deficit with China for January–October 2025 be lower than for January–October 2024?

Operationalization:
- Time windows: “January–October 2024” means the sum over the ten calendar reference months January through October 2024, inclusive. “January–October 2025” means the sum over January through October 2025, inclusive. All timing is in UTC, but monthly aggregates follow INEGI’s calendar-month reference periods.
- Data source: INEGI’s Balanza Comercial de Mercancías de México (BCMM) monthly data, “cifras revisadas” (revised figures) that include breakdowns by country, as publicly available by December 31, 2025. INEGI publishes monthly merchandise trade in US dollars, with exports measured FOB and imports measured CIF.
- Country definition: Use INEGI’s country breakdown for “China” (People’s Republic of China) per its ISO ALPHA country catalog. Do not include flows recorded under Hong Kong, Macao, or Taiwan.
- Measure to compare: For each period (Jan–Oct 2024 and Jan–Oct 2025), compute the cumulative bilateral goods trade deficit with China as D(Y) = Σ(imports from China, CIF, US$) − Σ(exports to China, FOB, US$), summing monthly non-seasonally-adjusted values for the ten months in Y. Values should be taken in current US dollars. Do not use seasonally adjusted series or pesos.

Resolution:
- Resolve Yes if D(2025) < D(2024) (i.e., the Jan–Oct 2025 deficit is strictly smaller than the Jan–Oct 2024 deficit) based on INEGI BCMM revised country-level data available by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.
- Resolve No if D(2025) ≥ D(2024), or if the necessary October 2025 by-country revised data are not published by INEGI by 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Notes:
- Only merchandise (goods) trade counts; services are excluded.
- Use the latest INEGI “cifras revisadas” available as of the resolution timestamp; ignore any subsequent revisions made after 2025-12-31.
- This question is designed to resolve after the release of October 2025 country-level revised data (typically ≈40 days after month-end) and before 2025-12-31, consistent with INEGI’s schedule.

Context sources cited in background for forecasters (not used for resolution): 2024 full-year deficit estimate and trend ; Jan–Jun 2025 deficit ; September 2025 tariff announcement.

question: Will USTR further extend any of the 178 Section 301 China tariff exclusions (extended on Aug 28, 2025) beyond November 29, 2025?
background:
Status quo as of 2025-10-01: On August 28, 2025, the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) announced that certain product-specific exclusions from the Section 301 tariffs on imports from China—previously set to expire on August 31, 2025—were extended through November 29, 2025. A corresponding Federal Register notice stated that the modifications further extended 178 exclusions (164 product exclusions and 14 exclusions for certain solar manufacturing equipment) through November 29, 2025 and identified the controlling HTSUS notes and headings for these exclusions. USTR subsequently opened a public comment period to solicit input on whether any of the 178 effective exclusions warrant further extension beyond November 29, 2025; the comment portal opened September 16, 2025 at 12:01 a.m. EDT and closed October 16, 2025 at 11:59 p.m. EDT.

Definitions and scope:
- USTR: The Office of the United States Trade Representative, part of the Executive Office of the President, responsible for developing and coordinating U.S. trade policy. Official press releases are issued via USTR’s Press Office.
- Federal Register: The official journal of the U.S. federal government where rules, proposed rules, and public notices are published (federalregister.gov).
- Section 301 (of the Trade Act of 1974): Statutory authority enabling the U.S. to take actions (including tariffs) in response to unfair foreign trade practices that burden or restrict U.S. commerce.
- HTSUS (Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States): The primary resource for tariff classification of imported goods into the U.S., assigning ten-digit codes; Section 301 exclusions are typically tied to specific HTSUS subheadings and U.S. notes.
- Exclusions in scope: The 178 exclusions extended via the Federal Register notice published September 2, 2025 (Notice of Product Exclusion Extensions: China’s Acts, Policies, and Practices Related to Technology Transfer, Intellectual Property, and Innovation), covering HTSUS headings 9903.88.69 (U.S. notes 20(vvv)(i), 20(vvv)(ii), 20(vvv)(iii), 20(vvv)(iv)) and 9903.88.70 (U.S. note 20(www)).
- Current expiration: The Federal Register notice specifies these extensions apply to goods entered for consumption (or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption) on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, September 1, 2025, and before 11:59 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time, November 29, 2025.
- “Further extend” / “extension”: For the purposes of this question, an extension means an official action by USTR as reflected in an authoritative U.S. government communication (e.g., a Federal Register notice or USTR press release) that sets a new expiration date/time for any of the 178 exclusions after 2025-11-30 03:59:59 UTC (which corresponds to 11:59 p.m. ET on November 29, 2025 as referenced in the Federal Register notice).

Why this is uncertain: USTR has repeatedly adjusted and extended Section 301 exclusions in response to policy considerations and stakeholder input; the existence of a targeted public comment process on potential further extensions indicates genuine uncertainty about whether, and to what extent, any exclusions will be continued beyond November 29, 2025.

Helpful sources to monitor:
- USTR Press Office (press releases): https://ustr.gov/about-us/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/ 
- Federal Register (USTR notices): https://www.federalregister.gov/
resolution_criteria:
Time window for eligible actions: from 2025-10-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC.

Question: Will USTR further extend any of the 178 exclusions defined above to be effective beyond 2025-11-30 03:59:59 UTC (the UTC equivalent of 11:59 p.m. ET on November 29, 2025 as referenced in the Federal Register notice) ?

Resolve YES if, during the time window, an official U.S. government communication exists (as of 2025-12-31 23:59:59 UTC) that clearly indicates any one or more of the 178 exclusions are extended to a new expiration date/time after 2025-11-30 03:59:59 UTC. Acceptable official communications are:
- A Federal Register notice that modifies the Section 301 action by extending the expiration for any of the exclusions listed under HTSUS headings 9903.88.69 or 9903.88.70 as described in U.S. notes 20(vvv)(i)-(iv) and 20(www) ; or
- An official USTR press release announcing such an extension.

Resolve NO if, by the end of the time window, no such official communication exists and all 178 exclusions lapse at or before 2025-11-30 03:59:59 UTC without further extension.

Counting rule and scope clarifications:
- “Any” means at least one of the 178 exclusions is extended.
- Only the 178 exclusions referenced in the September 2, 2025 Federal Register notice are in scope.
- If USTR extends some exclusions but not others, this resolves YES.
- If USTR revises product descriptions, notes, or HTSUS references without extending the expiration beyond the stated cutoff, this does NOT count as an extension.
- If an extension is made effective retroactively beyond November 29, 2025 but is not announced in an official communication until after 2025-12-31, resolve NO to preserve unambiguous resolvability by the resolution date.

question: Will Russia or China explicitly declare non-implementation of the reimposed UN Security Council sanctions on Iran between 2025-10-15 and 2025-12-31 (UTC)?
background:
Summary of the status quo (as of 2025-09-30):
- On 2025-08-28, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom (the “E3”) notified the UN Security Council that Iran was in significant non-performance of its Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) commitments, thereby triggering the “snapback” mechanism under UN Security Council Resolution 2231 (2015), which restores UN sanctions after a 30-day period absent Council action.
- On 2025-09-26, a China–Russia draft resolution to extend sanctions relief for six months failed in the Security Council by a vote of 4 in favor, 9 against, and 2 abstentions, clearing the way for snapback to take effect.
- UN sanctions that had been lifted under the JCPOA were reimposed at 8 p.m. EDT on 2025-09-27 (0000 GMT on 2025-09-28).
- Russia and China publicly opposed the legality/validity of the E3-triggered snapback. Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on 2025-09-27 that the reimposed sanctions are “unlawful, and [they] cannot be implemented,” and he warned the UN Secretary-General against acknowledging a return of sanctions. In Council debates around the failed 2025-09-26 resolution, both Russia and China argued the E3’s grounds were procedurally and legally untenable and sought a six‑month technical extension to allow diplomacy, which was rejected.
- The EU has aligned its measures with the snapback timeline and described the E3’s Aug. 28 notification and subsequent reimposition in official communications, reinforcing the timeline above.

Key definitions and context for forecasters:
- United Nations Security Council (UNSC): principal UN organ responsible for international peace and security (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council).
- JCPOA and UNSCR 2231 “snapback”: Under UNSCR 2231, if a JCPOA participant notifies the Council of significant non-performance by Iran, UN sanctions previously terminated under 2231 are reimposed after 30 days unless the Council adopts a resolution to continue sanctions relief (often termed “snapback”).
- Reimposed UN sanctions on Iran (the subject of this question): the set of UN Security Council measures that came back into force at 0000 GMT on 2025-09-28 via the snapback described above, including measures revived from earlier UNSC resolutions that had been terminated under UNSCR 2231.
- Government of the Russian Federation: the executive authority of Russia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Russia). Government of the People’s Republic of China: the central government via the State Council and related ministries (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China). For purposes of this question, “Russia” and “China” refer to these sovereign states acting through their national governments and duly authorized officials.

Why this matters and why uncertainty is plausible:
- Russia and China have signaled strong legal/political opposition to the snapback and could choose to formalize a policy of non‑implementation; however, issuing an explicit statement of non‑implementation is politically weighty and may be avoided in favor of more ambiguous language. This makes the prospect of an explicit declaration between mid‑October and year‑end uncertain enough to invite substantive forecasting research.

Notes on sources and verification:
- The timeline and positions above are documented in UN and major international newswire reporting, enabling straightforward verification if an explicit policy statement is later issued.
resolution_criteria:
